title: Why I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | Opinion |  Presented by Kirsty Major : produced by Lauren Hurrell and Bryony Moore executive producer Barbara Speed | The Guardian
description: In advertising, Meta describes their AI glasses as 'iconic style meets Meta AI'. However, online backlash against these glasses has been swift. Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses
Author: Barbara Speed
Headline: In advertising, Meta describes their AI glasses as 'iconic style meets Meta AI'. However, online backlash against these glasses has been swift. Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses
Content: Why I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | OpinionMetaWhy I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | Opinion'Most people don’t want pervert glasses that can film us without our consent,' said a spokesperson from activist group Everyone Hates Elon. The group has launched a series of guerilla adverts deriding non-consensual filming by the glasses as well as an email campaign encouraging people to legally object to being filmed by Meta glasses under general data protection regulations, which over 20,000 people have signed.Rights groups have warned that the glasses threaten the right to privacy, while countries such as Germany are reportedly considering a ban.And while Meta’s safety guidelines say smart glasses should not be used for 'harassment, infringing on privacy rights, or capturing sensitive information', women have taken to social media to share their stories of being filmed by men without their consent.Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses – and read more about the glasses via the link in the bioPresented byKirsty Major: produced byLauren HurrellandBryony Mooreexecutive producerBarbara SpeedWed 5 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergAI (artificial intelligence)

title: Demise of the monoculture: why so many have never heard UK’s record-breaking No 1 single | UK charts | The Guardian
description: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In is longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, and yet it seems to have passed many people by
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In is longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, and yet it seems to have passed many people by
Content: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean collect their Brit award earlier this year.Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/RedfernsView image in fullscreenSam Fender and Olivia Dean collect their Brit award earlier this year.Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/RedfernsUK chartsDemise of the monoculture: why so many have never heard UK’s record-breaking No 1 singleSam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me In is longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, and yet it seems to have passed many people byNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the biggest song in the UK, but have you ever heard it? That was the question many were asking this week, after Sam Fender and Olivia Dean’s Rein Me Inbecame the longest-running No 1 single in UK chart history, spending an unprecedented 19 weeks at the top.The British Phonographic Industry said the song had resonated with listeners “in such a profound way”, while Fender thanked Dean and fans “for making this song the juggernaut that it is”.Yet the record prompted a wave of bafflement online from people who claimed they had never knowingly heard it. “Crazy how monoculture no longer exists because I don’t think I’ve actually ever heard this song,”wrote one useron X.The disconnect has reignited a broader debate about whether Britain’s music charts still reflect a shared national culture. How can a record dominate the charts for nearly five months, and win song of the year at the Brits, while leaving large sections of the public feeling as though it passed them by? Only those living under a rock when the Beatles or Elvis Presley had a No 1 single could have avoided knowing about it.The answer, according to industry experts, is that dominance no longer means ubiquity.“In the era of Top of the Pops, Radio 1 and Smash Hits, the weekly charts were a shared cultural event,” said Chris Anderton, associate professor in cultural economy at Southampton Solent University. Streaming has replaced that with endless choice and algorithmic recommendation, he said, producing what author Eli Pariser called the “filter bubble” – where listeners are “repeatedly served music similar to what they already like”. It’s the same mechanism, Anderton noted, that isolates social media users from opposing viewpoints: taste, like opinion, has been commodified and automated.The record for the longest spell at No 1 was previously held by Frankie Laine, whose I Believe spent 18 weeks at the top in 1953, when the UK singles chart was less than a year old and featured just 12 songs. More recent contenders, including Bryan Adams’ (Everything I Do) I Do It For You, Wet Wet Wet’s Love Is All Around, Drake’s One Dance and Ed Sheeran’s Shape of You, all fell short of breaking the record.Rein Me In was written by Fender for his album People Watching before being re-recorded as a duet and released in June 2025. It took 36 weeks to reach No 1, and has held the top spot on and off since February, seeing off brief challenges from Harry Styles, Olivia Rodrigo, Ariana Grande and Taylor Swift. It also outlasted the “accelerated decline” rules introduced by the Official Charts Company in 2017 to specifically stop streaming hits lingering indefinitely.The mechanics of a No 1 hit single have changed too. Chart position once meant physical sales; today it blends sales with stream-equivalents from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube – so 100 premium streams, or 600 ad-funded ones, equal one sale.But the fragmentation runs deeper than streaming maths, said the music and culture critic Nicolas-Tyrell Scott. Younger listeners now discover music through TikTok, YouTube and personalised algorithms, meaning “it’s not as easy as saying a track is No 1, therefore it’s resonant and dominating in everyone’s sphere of influence”.Gen Z spend just 16% of their average audio day on the radio, Scott noted, against 42% on streaming and 20% on YouTube – and platform algorithms actively reinforce those micro-cultures. “It’s easy to see why a song like this could pass clusters of people by, despite dominating commercially,” he said.Chart analyst James Masterton put it starkly: a single can break records “yet it still struggles with any kind of cultural cut-through”. Unlike past mega-hits, Masterton argued, this one has no film or event attached to it. “It isn’t from a movie soundtrack or connected with any national event. It just … exists.”Weekly chart consumption has grown from around 20m streams at the start of the decade to more than 30m now, Masterton said, but most No 1s this year have clustered around just 60,000 of those streams – proof that while the audience has grown, the biggest hits command a much smaller slice of attention than they once did. Television exposure barely moves the needle either: this year’s Brit awards produced no lasting bump for the acts it celebrated, while radio itself has splintered into narrowly targeted playlists.“This is merely one symptom of what sociologists are noting as the demise of the monoculture,” he said. “With such a vast range of entertainment options available, few creations or productions really need appeal to a large cross section of the public. Which is just as well given how vanishingly few actually do.”Not everyone is convinced the disconnect is genuine. Some online commentators have suggested that claiming never to have heard a massive song says more about performing detachment than actual unfamiliarity.Anderton offered a caveat. Songs such as Padam Padam, or the Brat summer moment, broke through because they escaped streaming and became wider cultural phenomena across television, social media, news coverage and memes. “The ubiquitous hit is not dead,” he said. “It just requires much more than chart success.”Explore more on these topicsUK chartsSam FenderOlivia DeanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thar she blows! Hull Maritime Museum resurfaces with a walk-in whale and a ‘monkey mermaid’ | Architecture | The Guardian
description: The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring city
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring city
Content: She sounds! … the skeleton of a 40ft-long North Atlantic right whale dominates Hull Maritime Museum’s Age of Sail gallery.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowView image in fullscreenShe sounds! … the skeleton of a 40ft-long North Atlantic right whale dominates Hull Maritime Museum’s Age of Sail gallery.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowArchitectureThar she blows! Hull Maritime Museum resurfaces with a walk-in whale and a ‘monkey mermaid’The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring cityCatherine SlessorWed 5 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe star attraction of Hull’s revamped and revitalised Maritime Museum is a colossal 40ft-long skeleton of an North Atlantic right whale, beached more than a century ago. The remains of this leviathan dominate an exhibition space scarcely large enough to contain its stupendous bulk. Children can crawl into its ribcage, like junior Jonahs, popping up in a clear plastic dome as digital images of swimming whales slowly unspool across the ceiling.Docile, leisurely and extremely blubbery – which meant that harpooned carcasses conveniently floated, as well as yielding copious quantities of valuable oil – the North Atlantic right whale was hunted almost to extinction during the whaling era. Today, it’s estimated that there are fewer than 400 left.View image in fullscreenExhibits ahoy … exterior of the revamped Hull Maritime Museum.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowAt the other end of the cetacean scale is a delicately carved whale that can fit into the palm of your hand, studded with miniature harpoons designed for use as toothpicks. It forms part of the museum’s world class collection of scrimshaw, the niche and intensely fiddly folk art of carving and decorating pieces of ivory or bone. Crewmen would while away the long hours “scrimshandering”, inscribing whales’ teeth and walrus tusks with images of ships and patriotic Britannias, or tableaux from their travels and portraits of loved ones. Other bounties on display include the spiralled rapiers of narwhal tusks, surreally fashioned into hatstands and bedposts.Hull’s geography ensured that its history was indisputably maritime. Set at the confluence of the River Hull and Humber estuary, it prospered, successively, through trading, whaling and fishing. Latterly, its historic relationship with the sea has been renewed through the production of wind turbine blades for offshore arrays at the city’s Alexandra Dock. And Hull and the Humber remain one of the UK’s busiest port complexes.View image in fullscreenScrimshandered … sperm whale tooth engraving of the Phoenix of London by Burdett Phoenix, 1820s.Photograph: © Hull Maritime MuseumNonetheless, the sense of city out on a limb, and one that has seen better days, still persists. Hull’s centre is pockmarked with vacant shops, and its docklands, which took a pounding during the second world war, remain apologetically gap-toothed in places, despite the crowded marina and upscale warehouse conversions.The poet Philip Larkin, Hull’s most infamous adopted son, who measured out his life in coffee spoons as head librarian of the city’s university, wrote of “the surprise of a large town … where only salesmen and relations come, within a terminate and fishy-smelling pastoral of ships up streets ...” Larkin had an ambivalent relationship with Hull, but a statue of him, erected in 2010, now greets you at the city’s Paragon station.View image in fullscreenThis Place Called Hull gallery at the refurbished Hull Maritime Museum.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowWhen the dock offices first opened in 1871, Larkin’s “pastoral of ships up streets” would have been an even more emphatic reality. At that time, Hull’s skyline was more ships’ masts than church spires, with vessels crammed into a network of docks. Set on a prominent site overlooking the now infilled Queen’s Dock, the dock offices exude a chest-puffing, Victorian mercantile bombast. Originally designed by Christopher Wray, whose career encompassed a spell in Calcutta’s public works department, the building’s florid and fruity neoclassical style is embellished with Neptunian details such as sea monsters, fishing nets and trident-like railings. An unconventional triangular plan was crowned by chunky pepperpot cupolas at its three corners.Now listed Grade II*, it was converted into the city’s Maritime Museum in 1975. (The museum itself began life in 1912 as the more prosaic Museum of Fisheries and Shipping in the city’s Pickering Park.) Over time, however, the Museum of Hull, as it was known, became tired, shabby and ripe for a reboot. Only two of its four floors were publicly accessible and the main exhibition space was painted shiny grey and lurid Germolene pink.“You also couldn’t read the whole room as a volume because there was this big ramp in the middle going up to a mezzanine level,” says Claire Humphrey, senior architect with conservation specialist Purcell, which oversaw the remodelling. The intrusive ramp has been removed and the colour scheme toned down to a more historically accurate and visually palatable palette: subtle marine blues set against a glacially white ceiling.The £20.4m project follows on from Hull’s successful stint as City of Culture in 2017. Funding came jointly from Hull city council, which contributed £11.8mn, along with the National LotteryHeritageFund, which allocated £7.7m. The remainder was raised through private donations. The rebooting has enabled the museum to double its public space and show 50% more objects from its expansive collection. Around 1,300 artefacts are now on display across the galleries and open storage spaces, many being seen by the public for the first time.View image in fullscreen‘The best room in Hull’ … the museum’s Court Room.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowUnderscored by a reframed approach to curation, new display systems bring Hull’s maritime cornucopia more vividly to life, from dockers’ tools and a stuffed polar bear, to Inuit bootees and a so-called “mermaid” (actually a rather hideous chimera of a monkey fused with a fish). A veritable regatta of model ships, pedantically accurate to the last detail, illustrates the shift from sail to steam, an advance that supercharged the shipping and fishing industries. One of the museum’s most cherished artefacts is a carved wooden figurehead of a bounding dog from the Sirius, the first steamship to complete a transatlantic crossing entirely under steam power in 1838.Other sections explore the rich currents of migration that flowed through Hull, propitiously poised between Old and New Worlds. You can also learn about Lillian Bilocca, the “headscarf revolutionary” who doughtily campaigned to improve safety on fishing fleets in the 1960s. In 150 years of commercial trawling out of Hull, more than 6,000 crewmen were lost, now commemorated in the museum’s simple and dignified memorial space. Yet despite Bilocca’s success, which undoubtedly saved lives, she was ostracised and blacklisted.View image in fullscreenDeep dive … A scrimshaw of a jolly sailor waving the Royal Navy’s flag, from the ship the Cornelia, early 1800s.Photograph: © Hull Maritime MuseumThroughout, the aim has been to carefully restore, repair and and revive, a strategy involving, at times, heroic feats of painstaking toil. The setpiece space of the Court Room, with its heraldic shields of Hanseatic League ports and columns of red and pink scagliola resembling an Italian delicatessen counter, has been renovated to serve as an events venue. Restoring the intricate ceiling decorations of intertwined foliage and starfish required a team of eight conservators working aloft on scaffolding platforms for six weeks, hand-cleaning the plaster with cotton buds to remove decades of accumulated grime. “We were aiming to create the best room in Hull,” says Humphrey, “and I think we achieved it.”The deep dive into Hull’s 800-year-old maritime history does not end with the museum. The remodelled building forms part of a wider circuit that takes in the re-landscaped Queen’s Gardens, originally designed by modernist architect Frederick Gibberd, and a new visitor centre for the Arctic Corsair, a historic trawler (think of it as Hull’s Cutty Sark) that will be permanently berthed in a cavernous dry dock within the North End Shipyard. Associated urban realm improvements literally pave the way for a more structured and civilised experience for both tourists and locals, with a vibe that aims to be more Copenhagen than Humberside.In leveraging Hull’s maritime history in an unsentimental way – after all, the mechanisms of trade and extraction are notoriously unsentimental – these initiatives suggest the possibility of a different kind of civic future. In this context, the museum’s deftly handled and uplifting restoration will surely help to turn the tide.Hull Maritime Museum opens on 8 AugustExplore more on these topicsArchitectureMuseumsHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Football federation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World Cup
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Football federation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World Cup
Content: According to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been ‘holed up’ in Salé, Morocco, this week as he tries to save his presidency.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenAccording to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been ‘holed up’ in Salé, Morocco, this week as he tries to save his presidency.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAFifaInfantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa?Jonathan LiewFederation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World CupWed 5 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn recent decades the city of Salé, just across the river from Rabat on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, has undergone a remarkable transformation. At the start of this century it was a gritty working-class area, whose old town was still weathered enough to serve as a body double for the Somali capital Mogadishu in the film Black Hawk Down. But in recent decades, under the country’s autocratic government, the area has been transformed beyond measure, and largely beyond control.The population has trebled in the space of 40 years. Slums have been cleared, often forcibly, to make way for grand megaprojects: a new tram system, luxury tourist spaces, a sparkling marina, a blue-chip business park called Technopolis, and – since last July – the African headquarters ofFifa. And in a way, this hub of disruption and avarice, unshakeable volition and rampant capitalism, feels like the perfect location from which a besieged warlord might choose to make his desperate last stand.Gianni Infantino scrambling for his future in Morocco with Colombia nextRead moreAccording to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been “holed up” in Salé this week as he tries to save his presidency. Apparently Infantino’s aides have been feverishly calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer Infantino their public support. On Wednesday one of them, Luís Figo,decided to break his silence. “Infantino must go,” he said, condemning his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup to private investors as “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed.” That’ll be a no, then.Meanwhile, the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation are massing forces at the gates. A “governance boycott”, in which members refuse to attend meetings or ratify Fifa decisions, is one idea. A rival World Cup-style competition – which would in effect translate to secession – is the nuclear option. And yes, in the moment this feels good, stirring, cathartic, karmic. We should all take a certain satisfaction in seeing Infantino get his long-deserved kicking. For all this, a pertinent question should also pose itself. Why now? And why like this?It is, after all, almost eight years since Fifa first proposed selling off a slice of its commercial legacy. In 2018 Infantino agreed in principle a deal with the Japanese firm SoftBank – whose main financial backer just so happened to be the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia – for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. The scheme eventually sputtered to a halt, but with virtually none of the screaming and apocalyptic threats seen over the past fortnight.It is four years since the soiled, blood-soaked Qatar World Cup, and the“today I feel gay”speech that turned the sport’s most important administrator into a figure of ridicule. Two years since Saudi Arabia were handed the 2034 tournament in a bidding process no other country appeared to be prepared for. Three years since the Club World Cup was coerced into existence over a chorus of player welfare concerns. Two months sinceOmar Artan was summarily denied entryto a World Cup in which he was supposed to be refereeing. One month sinceFolarin Balogun had his suspension overturnedin a supposedly independent process.View image in fullscreenApparently Gianni Infantino’s aides have been calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer the president their public support.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFor the men and women who – as it turned out – held Infantino’s fate in their hands all along, none of this appeared to be a red line. For years the injustices, the indignities, the reputational and environmental damage, the ruptures to rules and structures, the stitch-ups and dead migrant workers, have been waved through by acclamation. And so it is worth wondering whether anything has materially changed here, beyond the fleeting opportunity for ambitious footballing executives to claim the keys to Infantino’s empire.It is more than a decade since the late Lord Triesman, the former FA chair, described Fifa as a “mafia family”, and nothing about that description feels less true today. This is in many ways a supralegal body operating beyond the boundaries of conventional politics or economics, operating under its own rules and its own moral code, tied together not through popular consent but through a feudal system of tribute and protection, which changes not through legislation or overthrow but by occasional mob-style decapitation.The moral objections to Infantino’s investment plan are manifest, but perhaps more striking still – for a president who has staked everything on his ability to drive revenue – is the economic illiteracy. One hand-picked buyer (Joshua Kushner), one made-up number ($20 billion) and an artificial countdown clock (19 September). Is this really how to fetch the best price for your asset? Or is it how you act when you want to secure a bigger piece of the largesse you have so selflessly created, but are statutorily bound to one more term in your current job?‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayRead moreAnd in hindsight, it seems clear that Infantino’s thirst for bending rules and breaking conventions was a kind of loyalty test, his Yakuza tattoo, a way of demonstrating to the billionaire investor class that he truly was one of them. No wonder his first instinct on finding himself cornered was reportedly to appeal to Donald Trump: his roof, his protection, his kindred spirit.It is often said that Infantino is the symptom and Fifa is the disease. In fact Fifa too is the symptom; the disease is capitalistic fascism, a simple disdain for humanity, a belief that some are born to rule and others are bound to follow. And this is a cancer that will remain embedded in so many of our institutions long after Infantino has taken his last celebrity selfie, long after “45/47” has chowed down his last Oval Office Big Mac, long after the new Fifa regime has swept in through the door wearing the pageant sash of reform.Football, the greatest mass pursuit ever invented, will of course endure. In a way its ingenuity, its ability to adapt and not be crushed by adaptation, is its beauty and its curse. Like the Salé skyline, it warps and shifts and grows and gentrifies and swells beyond recognition. This is still recognisably the same land, the same turf, upon which its ancestors once stood. But the old waterfront is gone for ever.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcom | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: ‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceit
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: ‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceit
Content: Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner in One Night Only.Photograph: Nicole RivelliView image in fullscreenMonica Barbaro and Callum Turner in One Night Only.Photograph: Nicole RivelliComedy filmsReviewOne Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcom‘What if The Purge was for premarital sex?’ is the odd, gimmicky elevator pitch for this slickly made yet ungainly oddity that can’t quite get past the grimness of its conceitBenjamin LeeWed 5 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoing into a romcom, there are always the same questions. Will there be genuine chemistry? Will the rom and the com be equal in parts? And, for the last decade and change, will this be the one that finally resurrects a genre long past its prime? But for Universal’s glossy late summer offeringOne Night Only, notably the first wide-releasing romcomsince April, there are more probing questions than usual. The film is the ungainly result of a four-cocktails-in elevator pitch which imagines a world where single people are only legally allowed to have sex on one night of the year, an idea that has seen it been referred to as “Sex Purge”.On paper, it’s the set-up for a grimHandmaid’s Tale-adjacent horror of a totalitarian state insisting extreme control over the body, but instead it’s used as the backdrop for a sunny meet-cute, screams of protest drowned out by a zippy Top 40 soundtrack. One sits down wondering not just if boy will end up with girl but also how the government would be able to enforce such tyranny and what horrifying punishments lay in store for those willing to pick personal freedom over state-mandated abstinence. If it sounds like far too much for a breezy summer romp to take on, then that’s because it most definitely is, an overstuffed yet undercooked soufflé that can’t quite, ahem, rise to the occasion …Ice Cream Man review – Eli Roth’s junky slasher is one of year’s worst horrorsRead moreIntroductory text informs us, much to the baffled laughter of those at my screening, that “premarital sex has been outlawed in the US” and is now only legal for 12 hours on one night of the year. It’s a “government decreed sexual climate” where it’s now a “badge of honour” to be an incel, the result of what’s described as an “ideological grenade” thrown at Americans by Congress. People have been fitted with biosensors, which detect the chemicals released during sex, and they turn from red to green when one gets married or the sex purge begins, a night of debauchery and chaos as everyone desperately tries to find someone to couple up with (wouldn’t the other 364 days a year be used to plan this a little better?). Protection is mandatory (condom surge pricing goes all the way up to $2,000 apiece) and we’re briefly shown that the price to pay for breaking the law is severe (a poor older man is dragged into a police station for the crime of being horny).New York City is where we spend that time, the natural setting for a film about both singledom and sex, and we follow the routes of Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (recent Oscar nomineeMonica Barbaro) as they hunt for sex against a ticking clock. Owen had a plan with his girlfriend (Maya Hawke) but she chooses the night as an opportunity to hook up with a neighbour, while Allie is urged by her queer roommate, who calls it a night “for the straights”, to put on a revealing dress and get herself out there. Their paths intertwine and for reasons that never quite make sense, decide not to have sex with each other, and instead play wingman from Manhattan to Brooklyn and back again.After the unforgivably unreal use of Glasgow as a junky replacement for New York in last week’sSpider-Man sequel(it often looked like it was setina Broadway musical), one of the film’s biggest aces is its up-close and immersive on-location shooting. Director Will Gluck is a savvy commercial film-maker and there’s a bright and poppy slickness to how his film looks and moves, especially when compared with Netflix’s many murkily flat romcoms. But as with his last film, thesurprise smashAnyone But You, he’s mastered the sleek aesthetic of a 2000s throwback but not much else. His leads here are a merciful improvement (Sydney SweeneyandGlen Powellwere among the most criminally vacant pairings we’ve ever seen in the genre), but again there’s not enough smart or specific writing, from kids’ TV writer Travis Braun, to justify why they wouldn’t just head to bed on first meet (yes, he’s vomited up two omakases near her feet but also, it’s sex purge night, guys!).Eek-cute: the rebirth of the frothy romcom sociopathRead moreIt’s less romcom and more an attempt to be a raunchy (if ultimately rather coy) sex caper as we go from scrape to scrape, involving ineffective and unfunny cameos (Julia Fox! Pete Davidson! Molly Ringwald! Nicholas Braun! Roma Maffia!) and a string of almost-shags. There’s a gimmicky, ADHD quality to the film and its many misfiring pop culture references, as if made to insist a gen Z audience away from their phones, and while I appreciated how this applied detail to the grabby production design (most scenes involve some sort of visual clue as to how the law has affected the day-to-day), it also felt like a distraction, a script made up of moments rather than a fully realised story. There’s no thought-through journey for our characters (he needs to plan less and she needs to sing more or something?) and while the attractively paired Turner and Barbaro are just about sturdy enough to convince us of the motions, theirho-hum banteris mostly too perfunctory to provoke us into caring about how they end up.It might not surprise you where the story takes them but what did surprise me is how progressively sex-negative the film becomes, either ridiculing those who want it or applying a moral superiority to those who don’t.There’s both too much yet not enough world-building here, enough questions answered to encourage us to ask 10 more (why does no one mention masturbation and wouldn’t that also trigger the biosensors?). It’s also just too unavoidably grim of a premise, especially at a dark political moment such as this, for us to ignore the ramifications or root for characters who aren’t trying to actively destroy such a barbaric system (what if Katniss just hadfunduring those Hunger Games?). Instead, One Night Only weirdly plays like lulling government propaganda, a film about sex purge to be released in time for sex purge that says that actually maybe sex purge is a good idea after all.One Night Only is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and the UK on 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsRomance filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be? | Hacking | The Guardian
description: The UK’s AI Security Institute test revealed AI models indulging in unprecedented hacking attempts
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: The UK’s AI Security Institute test revealed AI models indulging in unprecedented hacking attempts
Content: The  AISI said there were 19 examples of rogue behaviour, 17 of them carried out by Anthropic’s Mythos and two by OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe  AISI said there were 19 examples of rogue behaviour, 17 of them carried out by Anthropic’s Mythos and two by OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersHackingExplainerAI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?The UK’s AI Security Institute test revealed AI models indulging in unprecedented hacking attemptsAI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to trick developersDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 5 Aug 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo cutting-edge AI models havetargeted real people and organisationsin the latest safety scare to hit the technology. The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) said the incident was unprecedented but could become more common as the technology becomes increasingly capable.What happened?The AISI, which is owned by the UK government and tests advanced AI models, said in a blog post that two AI agents carried out unprecedented hacking attempts during a cybersecurity evaluation. The agents – tools that carry out computer tasks autonomously – were powered by two models: Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6-Sol. AISI said there were 19 examples of rogue behaviour, 17 of them carried out by Mythos.In the most serious incident, the Mythos agent decided that hacking users on GitHub – a platform used by software developers – would enable it to deploy a piece of software that would allow it to pass the test. It set up accounts with fake online identities and used them to target a software developer on GitHub with the power to approve its malicious code. It also sent emails carrying malware to other individuals.It hoped that getting the malware downloaded would set off a chain of events that would allow it to pass the evaluation. The Sol-powered agent also attempted to access a GitHub account.This novel behaviour was detected on 28 July and took an hour to shut down. At one point AISI shut off all access to the Mythos and Sol models across the entire organisation.Why was AISI alarmed?The institute said the models were showing deceptive behaviour it had not seen before. In one example, the Mythos agent signed off a message on GitHub in Danish to try to convince the Danish-speaking developer it was genuine. In another tactic it used a fake GitHub account to agree with its assertions that the malware it was pushing at developers was not dangerous.The agent used a Tor browser – which anonymises a web user’s identity – to get around sign-up checks on GitHub and create multiple fake accounts.AISI also published the agent’s “reasoning” behind the fake supporting statement ruse. The model, which tackles problems by breaking them down into “steps” that can be viewed by researchers, stated that it would delay posting the fake support message for a few minutes so that it would read as “independent feedback rather than coordinated.”AISI described the behaviour as “sustained”. It kept on trying.How did it all unfold?In a detailed 35-page report into the incident, AISI said that five important factors contributed to the incident:the models were deliberately given open internet access, which enabled them to approach GitHub;AISI deliberately disabled certain cyber guardrails;the institute did not have a separate AI monitoring the tests in real time, which helped the main GitHub incident go undetected for nearly two days;in some cases the models received a “misconfigured” instruction that prevented them from solving the test and thus required them to act outside the boundaries of the evaluation;and the agents were not given explicit instructions prohibiting them from certain behaviour such as sending phishing emails.Did the models know they were targeting real humans?AISI says it is unclear whether the agents “realised” they were targeting real humans. Throughout the attempted hack the Mythos agent reasons about whether it is interacting with real or simulated people and systems. At one point the agent reasons that it is behaving in the real world: “This is happening on real GitHub, so the consequences are genuine.” It also states: “The environment appears to be simulated.”AISI described the agent conducting “OSINT” – or open source intelligence, where a hacker pulls together publicly available information to work out how to breach a target – to study the developer behind the software it wanted to hack. It gained the developer’s email address and looked at their GitHub history to gauge when they would be active.What do experts think?AISI states clearly these models were operating under abnormal conditions of unfettered internet access and lowered cyber guardrails. Calling for the incident to be viewed with “nuance”, it said it had partly enabled the behaviour with its own actions – but it did not anticipate the “extent and severity” of what happened.Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said giving the models access to the open internet and removing some guardrails raised questions about using the rest of the world as “live guinea pigs” for powerful technology.“What we should be alarmed about is not what the models are capable of but the way people are testing them,” he said.AISI said in its report into the GitHub incident that giving a powerful model full internet access was a good way of simulating how far a rogue actor could push an AI. It said such a strategy gives a “more realistic sense of what a model may be capable of once deployed”.Ciaran Martin, the former head of the National Cyber Security Centre – part of the GCHQ intelligence agency – said the circumstances of the incident were unlikely to be replicated in the real world so “it’s not that worrying”. But he said it was the third example in recent weeks, after similar occurrences atOpenAIandAnthropic, that testers have released AI agents and found out about their misbehaviour after the fact.Martin said AISI’s pledge to carry out real-time monitoring of tests in the future “must be the answer”.Explore more on these topicsHackingTechnology sectorInternetAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAIexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarism | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career
Content: Jason Arday is the youngest black person to be appointed a professor at the University of Cambridge.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday is the youngest black person to be appointed a professor at the University of Cambridge.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianUniversity of CambridgeCambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarismSociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and careerPlaybooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: the claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRichard AdamsandLanre BakareWed 5 Aug 2026 16.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Arday, theCambridgeprofessor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career.Arday, who had been dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials, issueda statementon Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.In the statement, published on the Good Law Project website, he wrote: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at theUniversity of Cambridgeand Jesus College.“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreHowever, after days of detailed scrutiny of his previous work and statements, which highlighted apparent discrepancies, Arday said he had “concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.Simon & Schuster had been preparing to publish Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, later this month. His resignation may pause or even halt its publication and planned publicity tours.Cambridge had initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions multiplied over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.The Guardian publishedits own investigationuncovering discrepancies in Arday’s public accounts involving prodigious fundraising feats as well as claims he had been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders.Arday first faced allegations that he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and other academic research late last year, and has rejected the claims. An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded his PhD in 2015, did not uphold the charges of plagiarism but said they were probably caused by “honest and reasonable error”.Arday has denied all accusations of plagarism, telling the Guardian last week: “There have been multiple thorough investigations across several institutions as a result of the allegations, and immense scrutiny, including with an academic misconduct panel who concluded that there was no plagiarism or academic misconduct.”On Wednesday evening, Cambridge announcedit would launch an investigationafter it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.It said in a statement: “The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Prof Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.“Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our misconduct in research policy. This is consistent withour previous statement on the matter.“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.“We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”A spokesperson for Jesus College, Cambridge, said it was launching its own parallel “process”.“Prof Arday’s college fellowship is linked to his university role and we will fully support the university.“Prof Arday remains a fellow during this process. We recognise that this is a very difficult time for him and his family, and ask that they are treated with compassion and respect.”The new investigations may have been triggered by Arday’s claims that he held a string of prestigious visiting fellowships and professorships at other universities, including statements in published biographies dating back to 2018 that he was a visiting fellow or visiting professor at Ohio State University in the US. Ohio State hasdenied that Arday was ever employedin any role.Biographies linked to Arday have also claimed he had visiting professorships at Durham, Glasgow, Coventry and London Metropolitan universities as well as Nelson Mandela University in South Africa.Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology at Cambridge, at the comparatively young age of 37, received wide publicity through Arday’s life story, which includes a diagnosis of autism at the age of three, being unable to speak until he was 11, or read or write until he was 18.Despite those factors, Arday went on to university and swiftly climbed the academic ladder. After receiving his PhD in 2015 he held academic posts at Leeds Beckett, Roehampton and Durham universities, including a brief stint at Warwick University, before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Glasgow University in 2021. By early 2023 he had sought and won appointment to a professorship at Cambridge.Arday also claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days as well as running 600 miles in six days, and raising £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions he revised some of those claims, and instead said he was part of a funding raising group that he cannot name for legal reasons.Arday told the Guardian he had been the target of multiple threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.Jason Arday’s resignation statement in fullDear colleagues,It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming Professor of Sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life. To become the youngest Black professor in the University’s history was something I could scarcely have imagined as a child growing up with a diagnosis of autism, unable to speak until I was eleven years old.The response from so many people across the world was overwhelming. Thousands celebrated not simply my appointment, but what it represented: that talent, perseverance and hope can triumph over even the greatest adversity. It has been the privilege of my life to teach my students, to learn alongside them, and to witness their curiosity, kindness and ambition. They have given me far more than I could ever have given them.Sadly, the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack. While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.I have tried to continue because I believe deeply in the values of higher education, in rigorous scholarship, and in the transformative power of universities. I have tried because of my students, my colleagues and the countless people who have written to tell me that my journey gave them hope.But there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great.I have a family. I want to be present for them. I want to reclaim some peace, some privacy and some semblance of an ordinary life. I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement.For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away.This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge. Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me. It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.To my students: thank you. Teaching you has been the greatest honour of my academic career. Your brilliance, compassion and determination give me enormous hope for the future.To my colleagues and to the many thousands of people, from every corner of the world, who have supported me, defended me, written to me, and believed in me when it mattered most, I offer my deepest gratitude. Your kindness has carried me through some of the darkest moments of my life.This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.I need time to heal. I need time to simply be myself again.And when that time comes, I will return.I will return stronger, wiser and with the same determination that has always defined my journey. There is still so much work to do, and I look forward to doing it alongside so many of you in the years ahead.For now, however, I ask only for understanding, for compassion, and for the space to begin again.With gratitude,Professor Jason ArdayExplore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgePlagiarismHigher educationAcademicsUniversity careersCambridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: Understanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran says | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Joint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Joint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersStrait of HormuzUnderstanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran saysJoint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s securityAndrew Rothin Washington and agenciesWed 5 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran andOmanhave reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is ​being finalised provided certain third parties do not interfere,Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail ⁠Baghaei said on Wednesday.Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran andOmanwould not, by ⁠itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway.The proposed deal between ​Iran and Oman would ‌give Tehran control ‌over ships entering the gulf through the strait of Hormuz, ‌a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, in one of the biggest concessions yet toIran.The deal appears to be a stepping stone toward a broader ceasefire agreement with the US that would reopen the strait of Hormuz for marine traffic and lift a US blockade on Iranian ports that has brought upheaval to global energy markets. It comes as Donald Trump has claimed there could be an announcement as soon as Wednesday on a separate US-Iran peace deal.But the sources pushed backagainst assertions ‌byTrumpthat a deal reopening the strait was imminent, saying important details ​still had to be agreed.If endorsed by the US, the Iran-Oman deal would mark a significant concession by handing partial control over the waterway to Tehran. The strait of Hormuz was a neutral waterway before the US and Israel launched joint strikes in February, prompting Iran to attack shipping in the region.Baghaei described the negotiations between Tehran and Muscat as “professional” and “moving forward”, saying “the two sides had reached a mutual understanding ⁠on the geographical parameters of the route under discussion”.Baghaei ​added ​that, if some third ​parties do not obstruct the process, the joint ​statement between ‌the two ​countries, containing the ​main considerations and key points of understanding, was in the final stages of review and drafting.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzIranOmanMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper | NHS | The Guardian
description: Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand
Content: Yvette Cooper says climate change requires ‘some immediate acute responses’ by health services in the UK.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYvette Cooper says climate change requires ‘some immediate acute responses’ by health services in the UK.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesNHSNHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette CooperHealth secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demandAdapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?Jessica Elgot,Alexandra ToppingandFiona HarveyWed 5 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNHShas been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.The health secretary,Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.Doctors and other medical professionals have warned of the impact that repeated heatwaves are having on the NHS in England, including advice from the Royal College of GPs to cancel surgeries in extreme weather. Radiotherapy machines and MRI scanners have failed in hot weather, wards have overheated and cooling units serving hospitals have broken down.England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, with an estimated 2,877 people dying in the May and June heatwaves.Summers are likely to become increasingly hot in the future, with temperatures topping 40C likely to become more frequent instead of being outliers as the climate crisis takes further hold.chart showing rising UK summer temperatures 1900s-2020sCooper told the Guardian that rising global temperatures were causing challenges for the NHS that it had not encountered before. “This is a new thing for the NHS to have to deal with. There is a remarkable determination of the NHS to respond, but we need much greater resilience.”She said that in her new role as health secretary she had visited her local A&E in Yorkshire where staff described the overcrowding caused by heatwaves. “It would be normal during the winter weeks and months, but not in the summer, to have the very high attendances that they have had,” she said.She said she had discussed a public health awareness campaign with the chief medical officer, Sir Chris Whitty, warning people to look out for elderly relatives and those with young babies to ensure they were coping in the heat.Climate change meant “some immediate acute responses”, Cooper said, adding: “I’ve been clear we now need to prepare for summer pressures in the way that the NHS for a long time has prepared for winter pressures.“We need a much clearer assessment now of what that means, what the pressures are going to be, what management needs to be in place to cope.”The Climate Change Committee, the government’s statutory advisers on net zero, published alandmark report in Maywarning that the UK’s infrastructure was not built for such a climate, and calling for all hospitals and care homes to have air conditioning within the next decade, with all schools to follow by 2050. The CCC advised the government to plan for at least 2C of global heating by 2050, and potentially further rises.Farmers this summer have also warned about how the extreme temperatures caused by the climate crisis were affecting the UK’s food security and ability to cope with drought.No 10 said that improving the UK’s resilience to extreme heat was high on the agenda of the government – including building more reservoirs – saying the focus on tackling climate change must be on “practical resilience alongside cutting emissions”.Cooper said that she and Whitty agreed there needed to be more public information about who was most at risk from extreme heat, because of the “distressing” number of heat deaths.Days each year when temperatures of 30C or more were recorded in Greater London“There is a need for all of us to look out for our elderly neighbours and family members in the heat of summer, exactly as you would if it was freezing cold weather and you would be checking on elderly family members or relatives. We need to do the same thing now, in the summer, in the heatwaves and also for the very young.”She said that cooling hospitals and other facilities would be a key part of the major investment in NHS infrastructure. “That is a new thing we are now having to address and to plan for. That obviously takes time as well to address that. But it is one of the things that’s being looked at now as part of the capital programme,” she said.The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, told a press conference in London on Wednesday that tackling the climate crisis should be higher on the agenda. “I think we need to sit with that reality: 3,000 people have died because of extreme heat,” he said.“The scenes we have seen play out on our television screens are frankly apocalyptic. And yet the response from our government is to pretend none of this is happening. It’s an astonishing dereliction of duty from those whose first responsibility is to keep us safe.”The Royal College of Physicians’ clinical vice-president, Dr Hilary Williams, has said the NHS currently had very little built-in resilience to cope with extreme heat. “The impact of heatwaves on staff cannot be overstated,” she said. “There is a sense of foreboding when we see the weather forecast, because we know what is to come, and there is very little staff can do.”The government has also been urged by MPs to do more to allow people to cool their own homes. More than 50 MPs have written to the UK’s certification agencies to urge them to speed up a process to get air conditioning on to theboiler upgrade scheme, which offers grants for replacing gas boilers with greener alternatives like heat pumps.Despite the governmentexpanding the scheme to air-coolers last year, accreditation agencies have not yet given a stamp of approval.“If people worried about a future of extreme temperatures know they can get a heat pump which will also act as air conditioning they will be more motivated to make the switch – that’s good news for energy bills and the planet,” said Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for Hitchin, who organised the letter. “The agencies accrediting this scheme just really need to get on with it now.”July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England, with no significant rainfall expected in the area for some time.The summer has already seen two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June, fuelling drought and wildfires. About 23 million people across England and Wales areunder a hosepipe ban.The National Farmers’ Union warned earlier this week that Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England. Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult.This year’s El Niño, fuelled by global heating, is also supercharging temperatures:the World Meteorological Organisation confirmedthis week that the weather system developing in the Pacific was likely to be unusually strong.Andy Burnham has been criticised for failing to mention the climate crisis, net zero or the drought and heatwaves in his first weeks in No 10 – though he has promised the government will ramp up efforts to improve the state’s resilience.A spokesperson for the prime minister said: “We recognise that climate change is already affecting communities across the country, through extreme heat, drought and pressure on food production. That’s why we’re focused on practical resilience alongside cutting emissions.”He said the government would put “record investment in water infrastructure, including new reservoirs, while backing farmers to improve water security and strengthen the resilience of British food production.“Planning reforms are also making it easier to deliver on-farm infrastructure, including reservoirs and other productivity improvements.”Explore more on these topicsNHSYvette CooperClimate crisisHealthEnglandHospitalsGPsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakaway | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: A document has shown how Fifa staff were involved in the European breakaway and that the global governing body was prepared to sideline member associations
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: A document has shown how Fifa staff were involved in the European breakaway and that the global governing body was prepared to sideline member associations
Content: The proposed European Super League caused widespread revulsion among fans, including this protest outside Stamford Bridge in 2021.Photograph: Rob Pinney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe proposed European Super League caused widespread revulsion among fans, including this protest outside Stamford Bridge in 2021.Photograph: Rob Pinney/Getty ImagesGianni Infantino‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayDocument shows Fifa staff were involved in projectFifa was prepared to sideline member associationsExclusive byNick AmesWed 5 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino held talks about rebranding the ill-fated European breakaway competition the “Fifa Super League”, with negotiations going as far as the term sheet for an agreement that would have changed the face of European football.The term sheet, whose full contents can be revealed for the first time, is dated October 2020 and proposes renaming any new competition under Fifa’s branding. It outlines the extent to which Infantino’s administration were implicated in a scheme that caused widespread revulsion among fans and excluded clubs in April 2021. It also reveals thatFifawas prepared to sideline its member associations in pushing plans to cut back the number of international windows and outlines how global football’s governing body would have been given special governance and political rights with a “golden share”.Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreIn a week when football is reeling from the fallout after Infantino scrappedhis plan to sell chunks of the World Cupto private investors, the document shows Fifa’s leadership was deeply involved in another attempt to put the sport’s major competitions under corporate control. It sets out a partnership of at least 12 years between Fifa and the Super League and proposes a joint venture that would have run its commercial operations.The document also proposes that an iteration of Fifa’s expanded Club World Cup, referred to as the “global club competition”, would be held annually over an enshrined three-week period and tied directly to the Super League. That tournament would have been a straight knockout competition rather than the group-based version that relaunched in 2025. While the term sheet states that the new tournaments would have to be passed by Fifa’s annual congress and the Fifa council, federations around the world are understood to have been bypassed in the plan’s formation.Infantino was among a number of Fifa staff involved in the project and is understood to have been fully aware of its progression. The term sheet says the founding clubs “want to agree the terms of a partnership” between the Super League and Fifa, leading to the creation of the two competitions. It follows an initial proposal to Fifa by the breakaway clubs, also seen by the Guardian, that sketches the framework for a potential agreement. While non-binding, a term sheet is generally the precursor to a definitive contract and suggests discussions between Fifa and the Super League’s creators were nearing a conclusion at the time.It is unclear whether Infantino and Fifa progressed their role in the project beyond the term-sheet stage. After a version of the scheme was infamously launched without Fifa’s direct involvement in April 2021,ultimately scrappedfollowing large-scale protests, Infantino addressed Uefa’s congress in Montreux saying his organisation could “only strongly disapprove the creation of the Super League”. Multiple sources have stated that an earlier conversation with the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, convened by a third party, hastened Fifa’s president distancing himself from the new venture. Infantino is understood to have told associates afterwards that he had no wish to work against football’s institutions.Yet the evidence of Fifa’s outline agreement with the Super League, coupled with Infantino’s disastrous Football Forward Enterprise scheme, casts doubt on that assertion and suggests multiple attempts to reshape the game without consulting its most important stakeholders. The league would have contained 15 permanent members and five clubs qualifying from existing competitions. It also commits to creating a women’s equivalent, using the same clubs, by an unspecified date. The term sheet refers to Fifa under the name “WO1”, which is also the name used in the British army for a high-ranking officer.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino later changed tack in relation to a European breakaway.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersIn a section outlining the agreement’s key components, it says the Super League “is open to discuss naming the competition WO1 SL”. It also confirms Fifa would be “granted a preferred equity stake in the Super League”, which would give it decision-making capability on format changes, calendar alterations, distribution of solidarity money and the appointment of a chief executive for the competition.Senior figures within European football are understood to have been shocked by the plan to drastically shrink the number of international windows, squeezing them into two fortnight-long spaces each year. Member associations, many of whom are being courted for support by Infantino as he battles to save his tenure this week, may have lost the commercial opportunities available from added visibility for their national teams and found themselves at the behest of a privately run club competition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA separate point in the earlier proposal also notes “reduction of leagues” as a point for discussion. The term sheet states that “a new international match calendar” devised by Fifa, the Super League and “other relevant stakeholders” would be reviewed and implemented with Fifa’s agreement.Clubs participating in the Super League would have been required to join the World Football Club Association (WFCA), which was a short-lived representative body launched by the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez, in 2019. Real were key drivers of the Super League scheme and only closed the door on the project when announcing an agreement with Uefa in February this year.Fifa’s close proximity to the Super League proposal adds to the growing number of privately backed ventures brought to the table by Infantino during his 10-year reign. In 2018 he pressed the case for a $25bn offer from SoftBank, the Japanese institution, to create an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. Close allies within Fifa are understood to have cautioned him against the plan, which failed to gain support after opposition from Europe.Fifa was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoEuropean Super LeagueFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kemi Badenoch gives former neo-Nazi advisory role after he withdraws as Tory candidate | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Joshua Bonehill-Paine says Conservative leader asked him to work with party’s culture and integration commission
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Joshua Bonehill-Paine says Conservative leader asked him to work with party’s culture and integration commission
Content: Joshua Bonehill-Paine said the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, has offered him a role advising the the party’s culture and integration commission on the radicalisation of young men.Composite: Getty Images; Channel 4 News/YoutubeView image in fullscreenJoshua Bonehill-Paine said the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, has offered him a role advising the the party’s culture and integration commission on the radicalisation of young men.Composite: Getty Images; Channel 4 News/YoutubeConservativesKemi Badenoch gives former neo-Nazi advisory role after he withdraws as Tory candidateJoshua Bonehill-Paine says Conservative leader asked him to work with party’s culture and integration commissionBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former neo-Nazi activist who was convicted of harassing a Jewish MP has withdrawn as a Conservative election candidate afterKemi Badenochoffered him a role as an adviser to the party.Joshua Bonehill-Paine said on Wednesday that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections, and that the Conservative leader had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission, where he will specifically focus on how young men become radicalised.Badenoch, who hascome under pressurein the last 48 hours from individuals and organisations including the Board of Deputies of British Jews, said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”.However, the handing of a plum job to him was immediately condemned by others including Luciana Berger, a Labour member of the House of Lords who was the target of a campaign of abuse by Bonehill-Paine when she was an MP.“The decision to welcome this individual as an adviser to the Leader of the Opposition is no better than allowing him to stand as a council candidate,” she said on X. “It is a privileged and influential national role. As a victim of this man’s heinous crimes this appointment is an insult.”Both the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) had turned down the Tory party’s offer of a meeting with the former neo-Nazi, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account.Badenoch defends decision to allow man jailed for antisemitism to stand as councillorRead moreThe JLC issued a short statement on Wednesday to welcome Bonehill-Paine’s withdrawal as a Conservative candidate, but did not address his appointment as an adviser.However, the president of the Board of Deputies, Phil Rosenberg, told Times Radio it was “a good thing” that Bonehill-Paine would become an adviser to the culture and integration commission.“I think it is good to use the experiences of people who have themselves been down this track to counter radicalisation in other places,” said Rosenberg, who added that Bonehill-Pain was “probably the wrong fit” to be a councillor.Polling that was released by YouGov after news emerged that Bonehill-Paine was withdrawing found 57% of British voters thought his selection was unacceptable.Reform voters were the most likely to think he was an acceptable choice, at 36% – although they were outnumbered by the 44% of their number who deemed the decision unacceptable.Among Tory voters, 28% thought the selection was acceptable but twice that number judged it to be unacceptable (57%).​The Home Office also issued a statement on Wednesday contradicting a claim by Badenoch on Monday that Bonehill-Paine, 33, was “certified by the Home Office” to train police officers on antisemitism and countering extremism.“The Home Office does not certify individuals to deliver training,” said a spokesperson, who added that the department funds Civil Society Organisations which may use individuals to deliver training. Bonehill-Paine is understood to have worked for a time with an organisation engaging former extremists on a path to rehabilitation.Bridget ​P​hillipson, ​the equalities minister and chair of the Labour party,​ said the affair “speaks volumes” about Badenoch’s judgment.“It beggars belief that Kemi Badenoch was happy for a former neo-Nazi to stand in the first place. That she has gifted him a plum job further adds to that shame​,” she added.Badenoch’s move was also attacked by Reform UK, with a spokesperson saying the Jewish community would be alarmed that Bonehill-Paine would have a say over national Conservative party policy.Badenoch shared Bonehill-Paine’s announcement on X that he was withdrawing as a Tory candidate in next year’s elections, adding in her comments that he had been the target of a “piling on”.“If we are going to stop extremism and antisemitism, we are going to need help from those people who were part of the problem, but have now changed and are being part of the solution,” she said.Bonehill-Paine had beenselected to stand for election to Somerset councilnext year in a new Crewkerne South district, but said in a post on X on Wednesday: “Rather than standing as a local council candidate, I believe that my experience is better used supporting Kemi Badenoch in her ongoing mission to combat the antisemitism and extremism that is dividing our nation.”Hewas jailed in 2015for more than three years after posting “vile” antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally.In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, who is Jewish, which included posting messages to his blog calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”.Berger hadintervened earlier this week, telling Badenoch directly: “For the avoidance of doubt, I don’t believe this man should have *any* role in public life – because of both his racism and his view of women.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesAntisemitismKemi BadenochnewsShareReuse this content

title: Drone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior minister | Germany | The Guardian
description: Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
Content: A forensic technician works alongside a bomb disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APView image in fullscreenA forensic technician works alongside a bomb disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APGermanyDrone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior ministerInvestigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander DobrindtThe Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeDeborah Colein Berlin andAndrew Rothin WashingtonWed 5 Aug 2026 16.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s interior minister has warned that the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport marks “a new level of danger” for the country, as authorities examine whether the thwarted attack could have been planned by a foreign power.The discovery of a small drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a leading shipping and military hub, set off alarm and caused flight diversions on Wednesday morning. German police deployed a bomb disposal robot to defuse and destroy the explosive device.In public remarks on Wednesday evening, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs, and that investigators were treating it as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario”.“We are dealing here with a competition that may also include foreign powers – this will be part of the investigations – who quite obviously want to contribute to considerable uncertainty in Germany,” Dobrindt said.A DHL cargo plane that had been forced to abort its landing at the airport then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere.Dobrindt and other German officials did not explicitly mention Russia as a potential suspect in their remarks. But the airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which has previously been accused of carrying out sabotage attacks in Europe.Security experts said the incident could amount to a serious escalation in tensions withRussiaif it was determined the Kremlin played a role.Investigators said “a drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway” of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as “critical infrastructure”.“A suspected second unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft after it had taken off again following the previous closure of the runway.
