Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover,” the investigators said.View image in fullscreenFootage by News5 shows the nose of an Ukrainian Antonov plane at Leipzig-Halle airport.Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty ImagesA Nato official said: “We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate.”The drone, a quadcopter that was fitted with an explosive device, was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, according to media reports.Some of the Ukrainian aircraft are emblazoned with patriotic slogans including “Be Brave Like Kherson” and “Be Brave Like Bucha”, the site of a civilian massacre early in the full-scale Russian invasion.The tabloid Bild speculated that the explosive could have been fabricated ⁠from fertiliser and petrol, while a team from the public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche newspaper, said the device had contained pentaerythritol tetranitrate, orPETN– a primary ingredient in semtex that belongs to the same chemical family as nitroglycerin.Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, blamed Moscow. “Who else could it be but Russia?” he told the commercial broadcaster Welt TV. Moscow has not commented so far.Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called for an investigation to be conducted with the utmost urgency and also hinted at possible Russian involvement.“Should it transpire that a state is behind this action, this would constitute not merely terrorism but state terrorism directed against the federal republic of Germany and its citizens,” he told Der Spiegel.Marc Henrichmann, the CDU chair of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said the latest incident looked like “an attempt to target a company of importance for Ukraine”.If the details are confirmed, it “would represent a new level of escalation in these sorts of attacks”, he told the Rheinische Post newspaper.Several aircraft, including a passenger plane from Mallorca, were diverted because of the incident. Operations in the northern part of the airport resumed two hours later.The southern runway, where the drone was found, remained closed. Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to examine the object.View image in fullscreenGerman media reported that investigators were examining several possibilities, including that the incident was an attempt by Russia to attack Ukrainian equipment in Germany.Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice and prosecutors said: “There is no danger to the lives or safety of passengers or airport staff. Passenger air traffic is unaffected.”Germany and other European countries have had a series of suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies. They have accused Russian agents of being behind some of the flights, which Moscow has denied.Germany is the biggest single national supplier of military aid to Ukraine and has accused Russia of orchestrating a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against it, which the Kremlin has denied.Last year, a Chinese national was convicted forpassing on information about flight schedulesand cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing.Separately, Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring. Thumann is said to be under police protection.In 2024, US intelligence services reportedlyfoiled a Russian plotto assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, an apparent attempt at retaliation over the company’s role in providing a large amount of armaments for Ukraine.The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.Additional reporting by Jakub KrupaExplore more on these topicsGermanyDrones (military)Air transportRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Study finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 years | Dementia | The Guardian
description: Research suggests addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health between the ages of 45 and 65 could help reduce risk of cognitive decline
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Research suggests addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health between the ages of 45 and 65 could help reduce risk of cognitive decline
Content: Findings emphasised the importance of looking after heart health as well as brain health.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreenFindings emphasised the importance of looking after heart health as well as brain health.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyDementiaStudy finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 yearsResearch suggests addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health between the ages of 45 and 65 could help reduce risk of cognitive declineAndrew GregoryHealth editorWed 5 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScientists claim to have identified three health measures in middle age that can ward off dementia for more than a decade.Having normal blood pressure, no type 2 diabetes, and not smoking between the ages of 45 and 65 were associated with almost 13 additional years, on average, of dementia-free life, a study shows.The research also suggested that, no matter how many risk factors people had, women lived longer without dementia than men, and that white people had more dementia-free years than black people.The findings were published in the medical journal Neurology.Researchers from NYU LangoneHealthanalysed data from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (Aric) study, which began in 1986 and followed Americans for decades into late life, measuring midlife vascular risk factors and dementia.In the new analysis, researchers looked at 12,409 people with an average age of 56 who were free of dementia. Participants were assessed for three risk factors: high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and smoking. They were then followed for about three decades, with an average follow-up of 26 years.During that time, 3,008 developed dementia and 5,238 died without developing the condition.Those who had none of the three risk factors lived without developing dementia almost 13 years longer than those who had all three.Those with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke at the start of the study had an average of 30.1 more years free of dementia, the study found.Meanwhile, those with one risk factor had an extra 26.3 years, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years.“Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade,” said senior investigator Dr Josef Coresh, director of the Optimal Aging Institute at NYU Langone.“Hopefully, these results will encourage people to stop smoking and watch their vascular health closely from age 45 on.”Restricted eating hours may reduce cognitive decline in older age, researchers findRead moreThe number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But experts believe almost half of dementia cases worldwide could be prevented or delayed.Previous researchhas suggested that addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, could prevent or delay 45% of dementia cases, even as people live longer.The NYU Langone study said the three factors it identified “often emerge in midlife” and “exert lasting effects on neurodegenerative pathology”, underscoring the critical importance of early identification and management.Dr Jacqui Hanley, head of research funding at Alzheimer’s Research UK, who was not involved with the research, said: “Rather than focusing only on the chances of developing dementia, this study asks a question that matters to people: how long can we expect to live free from dementia?“This approach gives a meaningful picture of how midlife health may shape the number of years we spend living free from dementia, while also recognising that high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking are linked to a higher likelihood of dementia as well as a greater risk of dying earlier from other conditions.“These findings emphasise why it’s so important to look after your heart health as well as your brain health.”Hanley said everyone should take practical steps, including staying physically active, not smoking, and managing conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes.“While there is no guaranteed way to prevent dementia, research, including this study, suggests that addressing risk factors for poor cardiovascular health may also help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.”Explore more on these topicsDementiaMental healthHealthMedical researchnewsShareReuse this content

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their future | US politics | The Guardian
description: If the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary tale
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: If the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary tale
Content: Abdul El-Sayed speaks to his supporters in Detroit, Michigan, on Wednesday.Photograph: Dieu-Nalio Chery/EPAView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed speaks to his supporters in Detroit, Michigan, on Wednesday.Photograph: Dieu-Nalio Chery/EPAUS politicsAnalysisAbdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their futureJoseph GedeonandRachel LeingangIf the progressive wins Michigan’s general election, it could redefine the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment will call him a cautionary taleUS politics live – latest updatesWed 5 Aug 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn the final stretch of the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged voters at a small event in ruralMichiganto think about the message they could send the rest of the country when they cast their ballots.“Who are we? Who do we want to be?” El-Sayed said. “Do we want a state that’s defined by how much money corporations brought in to tell us what we couldn’t have? Or do we want to be a state where we demonstrate to the rest of the country what’s possible when you build a movement of, by and for the people?”On Tuesday, El-Sayed’s vision cleared its first hurdle:he won the primaryover moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by the party’s establishment, and tens of millions of dollars in outside spending.Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary in defining race for DemocratsRead moreHis rise, and victory, could serve as a revision to how the political establishment views swing-state politics – not requiring candidates to run from the center, but articulating how you will materially improve people’s lives as the working and middle classes struggle with affordability and rising healthcare costs.A contentious general election, in a battleground state, awaits.El-Sayed led by 48.5% to 47.5% over Stevens when the race was called. The narrow margin, in addition to more than 60,000 votes for a candidate who dropped out altogether, suggest he will have to unite the party, and convince more independent and even right-leaning voters in a swing state, to beat Republican Mike Rogers.But the race solidified a growing anti-establishment sentiment on the party’s left, where activists and supporters have sought a proactive vision that doesn’t rely on the pre-Trump status quo, apparent in a string of wins for insurgent candidates. There’s a sense that systems were already broken before Trump’s rise, and a return to those norms won’t serve everyday Americans. They’re looking for politicians who can call out their own party’s orthodoxies, and challenge the big money that hauntsUS politics.Michigan voters found it in El-Sayed, who centered his campaign around universal healthcare,and wasn’t shy about calling the war in Gaza a genocide.“It doesn’t limit us to just what we think is possible, but it changes what we think is possible,” said David Sernick, a voter in Detroit who supported El-Sayed.El-Sayed first ran for office in 2018, losing to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor of Michigan, in a Democratic primary. This time, he built a grassroots machine, barnstorming the state with in-person rallies while delivering clippable moments for social media feeds. His campaign knocked on more than 200,000 doors and made more than 1m phone calls, aided by leftwing groups such as the Working Families party and Indivisible chapters. El-Sayed held more than 500 campaign events and visited 150 churches.3:45Three key takeaways from Michigan's Democratic Senate primary – video explainerPeople like Racquel Garcia, who voted for El-Sayed in Dearborn, Michigan, said his willingness to show up underpinned their vote. El-Sayed worked as a public health official in Detroit and in Wayne county, and would show up at permit hearings and represent the people, she said.“Every time we meet with the city of Detroit officials, we’re like, ‘we need you to be like him’,” said Garcia. “You’re here to protect us, not to protect industry. So we’ve been wanting him in office. We were happy that he’s real.”Andy Levin, a former congressman from Michigan who lost to Stevens in 2022 after their districts were redrawn, said the moment rejected a “static notion of electability” that stems from a politics of anxiety and fear.“They want authenticity, they want truth telling and they want brave policy, not just proposals but action, so they can breathe in their lives,” Levintold Democracy Now. “This is a movement of Americans who are saying, enough of politics as usual.”Roy Harris, who voted in Detroit on Tuesday but wouldn’t say for whom, detailed how it was time for a change. “First-time homebuyers can’t buy a house – $400,000, first time you going out, nobody can afford that,” he said. “I’m tired of paying $4 for gas, and I am looking for a change. And I hope the new regime coming in brings that to us.”In Washington, El-Sayed’s effort to win the US Senate race in Michigan is critical for Democrats’ ambitious hopes of retaking control of the upper chamber, and will be closely watched by all factions of the left as a bellwether for the party’s future.Michigan voted for Trump, then Biden, and then Trump, in presidential elections. It is firmly a swing state. If El-Sayed, an unabashed progressive who frequently notes he has a “funny name”, can win a statewide general election, it could remake the contours of the 2028 presidential contest. If he fails, the establishment and pundit class will call him, and his ideas, too extreme – a cautionary tale for play-it-safe politics.Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-SayedRead moreIn other parts of the country, moderates won their Democratic primaries, includingblue-dog Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perezin a purple district in Washington state, who staved off a progressive challenge, and Wesley Bell, whosaw off a challengefrom Cori Bush, a former representative.Chris Rabb, a progressive whowon a contested primary for a US congressional seat in Pennsylvania, recently noted the high bar people from his branch of the party face as they seek to challenge moderates.“Nobody asks ‘centrist’ Dems to explain their losses,” Rabb wrote on X. “They lose purple districts every cycle & Beltway pundits call it ‘a tough map’. Progressives lose one major race & Dem operatives call us electoral pariahs. It’s a specious double standard.”Meanwhile, the attack lines from the right have already been drawn. Rogerspostedan AI-generated video of El-Sayed, depicting him as Odysseus among other prominent Democrats inside a Trojan horse, and saying “don’t let communism into Michigan”.A Republican has not won a US Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. The Republican National Committee called El-Sayed “Michigan’s Mamdani” and said the race “pits common sense against crazy”.El-Sayed himself remains confident.In November, he is counting on turning out people who normally turn off from politics because they’re cynical, or believe the system cannot change in a way that would make their lives better.“The goal now is not to dunk on anybody, the goal now is to come together so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026DemocratsMichigananalysisShareReuse this content

title: The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe | Germany | The Guardian
description: Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia
Content: The bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersGermanyAnalysisThe Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorInitial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from RussiaWed 5 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 22.18 EDTShareThe armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact thatit got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation.Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found inEuropefar from the Ukrainian border.Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from theUkrainewar, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery.Police from the German state of Saxony confirmed that the drone was “carrying an unknown explosive device” discovered by an employee in the “secure cargo flight operations area” near the airport’s southern runway.German media reported the attached bomb was made ofPETNand semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty.A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”.Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in Czechoslovakia, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around.A second unidentified flying object, which could well have been another drone, also collided with a DHL cargo plane in the aftermath of the first incident several hundred metres above the ground. The cargo plane only sustained minor damage.Leipzig airport is a sensitive site, the European base of Ukrainian Antonov jets, used for heavy cargo. The airport is also used by Nato and the German military for transport, as well as being a DHL hub, and the Ukrainian planes suggest it may also have been a node for supplies to Kyiv.Nato would only say it was aware of the incident on Wednesday, though it is eye-catching that the western alliance appears to have not been able to prevent drones from flying into and over a strategic airport.It is not the first time Leipzig airport has been involved in a dangerous incident. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the airport in July 2024 while a second travelled to the UK andcaught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham. Two similar packages were also found in Poland.A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who are suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. The investigation found perpetrators were recruited and given instructions online, and frequently paid in cryptocurrency, their knowledge of the full plot apparently limited.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRussia has also been behind a string of drone incursions into Europe over the past year, some more blatant than others. Around 20 unarmed Russian delta-wing Gerbera dronescrossed into Poland last September, forcing a major alert, with people in two of the country’s eastern provinces told to shelter indoors.An analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) thinktank concluded last month that the Kremlin was behind aconcerted drone surveillance campaignthat targeted the US airbase at RAF Lakenheath and other key military sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands.In the first case, Nato jets struggled to shoot down the incoming drones, most of which eventually crashed or lost power and glided to the ground. In the second, western militaries struggled to work out who were the culprits, failing to capture any of the drones or react to the surveillance efforts promptly.Russia, in sum, has so far been able to conduct other firebomb operations, as well as drone harassment and surveillance campaigns with relative impunity. Moscow is already subject to a wide range of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine, and it is likely to believe that the west has little more it is willing to punish the country with.“A drone carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition to what we have seen before,” said Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow with the IISS, adding ominously: “It is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyUkraineRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Why Spain’s EU allies turned on Pedro Sanchez over Ceuta: the hard right now sets their agenda on migration | World news | The Guardian
description: Rightwing narratives have gone mainstream, and Madrid finds itself increasingly isolated for its humane approach to migrants
Author: Katherine Butler
Headline: Rightwing narratives have gone mainstream, and Madrid finds itself increasingly isolated for its humane approach to migrants
Content: According to Spanish officials, around 2,500 migrants remain in Ceuta following last week's massive border rush from Morocco.Photograph: REDUAN/EPAView image in fullscreenAccording to Spanish officials, around 2,500 migrants remain in Ceuta following last week's massive border rush from Morocco.Photograph: REDUAN/EPAThis Is EuropeWorld newsWhy Spain’s EU allies turned on Pedro Sanchez over Ceuta: the hard right now sets their agenda on migrationRightwing narratives have gone mainstream, and Madrid finds itself increasingly isolated for its humane approach to migrantsDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKatherine ButlerAssociate editor, EuropeWed 5 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was over almost as quickly as it began. But the human cost of the mayhem in Ceuta over the last seven days, and the disunity it exposed within the EU, will take a lot longer to fix.To recap: more than 70,000 people swam or waded into the tiny Spanish enclave in north Africa from neighbouring Morocco in a matter of hours at the end of last week. The exact circumstances in which the heavily securitised border came suddenly to be open are still unclear.What is clear is that at least 88 people died. Some drowned, others were trampled in the crush. Social media hyped a distorted version of events. Far-right parties, already driving the agenda on migration across Europe,weaponised the story. And Spain’s EU allies engaged in a war of words – not over the plight of those caught up in the tragedy, but over who let them into EU territory.Italy and Denmark jointly led the way there, accusing Madrid of failing to secure the EU’s only land border with Africa. Although Ceuta is not even in the EU’s Schengen passport-free travel area, Giorgia Meloni, the far-right Italian prime minister, performatively suspended Schengen rights for travellers entering Italy fromSpain.Meloni and her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen (although a Social Democrat, is another migration hardliner),wrote to the EUdemanding emergency talks on tightening the bloc’s external borders. They enlisted the backing of all but five of the 27 EU leaders.Faced with such an unusual lack of support, Spain’sPedro Sánchezcould only protest about the “selfish, polarising and unlawful” response of his EU allies.By Monday the vast majority who arrived in Ceutahad gone back to Morocco. None attempted to reach the Spanish mainland or to abscond towards any other country’s borders. Of those leftstranded on the streets of the city, many were unaccompanied children.By then,Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Israeli ministers had weighed in to decry Europe’s “migrant invasion”, and Ceuta had begun to function, wroteJonathan Liew, “as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies”. The spectacle of left-liberal Spain facing a migration crisis of its own making was, for the European hard right and the White House “almost too good to be true”,Ruben Andersson wrote.But why the frenzy among European governments? Paul Taylor, a senior fellow with the European Policy Centre, says there was a shamelessly cynical interest for some EU leaders to pile on and isolate Madrid. The reaction was very different in the past, when Poland and Lithuania faced migrant incursions weaponised by Belarus.“Most EU governments are conservative or rightwing-led and have an interest in scapegoating Spain, which is governed by a socialist-leftist coalition, and in helping Spain’s rightwing opposition ahead of a general election due next year, and in trying to win back voters in their own countries who are defecting to rightwing populists,” Taylor said.Within the EU, Sanchez has swum against the tide, standing up to the Trump administration over Gaza, the war in Iran and Nato defence spending. During the recent wildfires he was vocal aboutclimate backsliding. In an EU where policy has been hardening since 2015, hebucks the trendon migration, too.“Spain has been an outlier, welcoming migration and actively working to integrate migrants into the economy and society,” Taylor said. “This is seen as an affront by many conservative politicians but also as a ‘pull factor’ encouraging would-be migrants to try their luck in Europe at a time when official EU policy is to combat irregular migration, crack down on abuses of the asylum system and park asylum seekers offshore in countries outside the bloc.”And this is exactly the bigger political bone Meloni, Frederiksen and others wanted to pick with Spain. In their letter to the EU, ostensibly about the immediate crisis in Ceuta, they targeted Madrid’s recent policy of allowing undocumented people working in mainland Spain toregularise their migration status, even though this was irrelevant for those involved in the Ceuta situation.What is most striking about this, Taylor said, is the hypocrisy and double standards of Spain’s critics.“Many of those criticising Spain’s amnesty allowing irregular migrants to apply for residence permits have introduced similar schemes in their own countries. Italy and Germany have both given work permits and/or the right to remain to irregular migrants already working there in programmes supported by employers plagued by labour shortages.”Why Ceuta? Why now?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat actually provoked the Ceuta surge remains unexplained.One theory is that misleading posts circulated on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook following a 29 June Spanish supreme court ruling that clarified that under international law, the state cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process.But many suspect geopoliticalmischief by Morocco– possibly to extract payback for Spain’s recent detente with its regional rival Algeria. If this is the case then the EU’s controversial strategy of outsourcing migration to regimes such as Morocco’s, looks even more problematic. Ashifa Kassam recalledin this Guardian podcasthow Morocco weaponised migrants in a previous incident in 2021,allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceutaduring a diplomatic standoff with Spain over Western Sahara.View image in fullscreenPrime minister Pedro Sánchez is increasingly under fire for his humanitarian policies towards migrants in Spain.Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/MoncloaBy Tuesday, EU justice and home affairs ministers were publicly papering over their split, although BrusselscriticisedSpain’s amnesty for undocumented migrants as “not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.Ministers endorsed a plan tostrengthen Europe’s external borders, including an early warning system and better “cooperation” with non-EU countries on migration: possibly code for more “cash for migration” deals with often unsavoury regimes.The Ceuta episode could also lead to the acceleration of ICE-style deportations from the EU. The Italian government in particular wants to see offshore migration centres, or “return hubs”, made possible under the EU’s new return regulation.Yet in a Europe devoid of safe and legal routes for asylum seekers, this is a direction that some of the most senior European legal experts havewarnedcould create a “human rights black hole”.When the European parliament voted to approve thereturn regulationlast month, there was some dismay as far-right and rightwing MEPscelebrated in the chamberwith raucous chants of “send them back!” On the evidence of the last week, it seems that Europe’s mainstream leaders have normalised the same chilling sentiment.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeSpainPedro SánchezMigrationRefugeesThe far rightnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’d want one as a pet’: the irresistibly cute solar-powered sea slug | Invertebrates | The Guardian
description: The beady-eyed, Pokémon-like leaf sheep is far more ingenious than us land mammals
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: The beady-eyed, Pokémon-like leaf sheep is far more ingenious than us land mammals
Content: The Pokémon-like leaf sheep grazes on algae and is found in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Pokémon-like leaf sheep grazes on algae and is found in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Invertebrates‘You’d want one as a pet’: the irresistibly cute solar-powered sea slugThe beady-eyed, Pokémon-like leaf sheep is far more ingenious than us land mammalsRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearInvertebrate of Year Q&A: discuss our countdown with Patrick BarkhamPatrick BarkhamWed 5 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA neon green punk sheep that lives underwater. A solar-powered slug that can perform photosynthesis. If you are seeking beauty, brains and a wonderfully innovative lifestyle, then vote leaf sheep.Invertebrate of Year Q&A: discuss our countdown with Patrick BarkhamRead moreThe leaf or sea sheep,Costasiella kuroshimae, isa sea slug about the size of a grain of rice. Like a sheep, it grazes on green stuff – certain species of algae, which it finds in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines. But its sheepy nickname does it a disservice because it is far more ingenious than us land mammals.This animal is not only powered by the algae it grazes, but by the sun. In a process called kleptoplasty, the leaf sheep steals the algae’s chloroplasts, the structures that plants use to capture sunlight and perform photosynthesis. It sequesters the intact chloroplasts within its own cells, storing them inside leaf-like branches on its back called cerata. These act like solar panels and enable the slug to power up via photosynthesis.Wisely, the beady-eyed leaf sheep lives where it feeds, on Avrainvillea, a velvety type of algae that grows in fine silts around shallow reefs.The leaf sheep’s vivid green cerata, which often feature white, pink or purple tips, provide chemical defences for this tiny animal. They give the leaf sheep its vivid green colour, which ensures it is beautifully camouflaged against the algae, which it locates via two ear-like structures above its eyes called rhinophores. These tentacles are sense and taste receptors, helping it find food and make sense of its world.View image in fullscreenThe leaf sheep’s vivid green cerata, which often feature white, pink or purple tips, provide chemical defences.Photograph: Oksana Maksymova/AlamyThe leaf sheep was onlydescribed by science in 1993and has soared in popularity in recent years thanks to advances in underwater and macro photography, which have enabled us to appreciate its irresistibly cute appearance.It must be an early favourite for invertebrate of the year 2026 because readers from around the world have nominated it, for its ingenuity and its looks, which have many echoes in popular culture from Shaun the Sheep to Pokémon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It looks like a Pokémon that you’d never want to use in battle but would definitely want as a pet,” says Matt, from Colorado. Shaymin Pokémon, to be precise, says Rei, aged nine, from Devon. Children know cool when they see it, and the leaf sheep’s inspiring example of harnessing energy from the sun certainly chimes with our times.It’sinvertebrate of the year again! From August 3-12, every day we’ll be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when you’ve got to hear about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us atenvironment.desk@theguardian.comwith Invertebrate in the subject line.Explore more on these topicsInvertebratesInvertebrate of the year 2026Marine lifeWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In Britain, we equate blackness with the working class. It’s time for a rethink | Society | The Guardian
description: In my new book, I narrate the existence, behaviours and sensibilities of the black British middle class, a social group largely ignored, until now
Author: Symeon Brown
Headline: In my new book, I narrate the existence, behaviours and sensibilities of the black British middle class, a social group largely ignored, until now
Content: Social mobility … the precariousness of Black British class structure has given rise to growing social anxiety.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSocial mobility … the precariousness of Black British class structure has given rise to growing social anxiety.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/The Guardian/Getty ImagesThe Long WaveSocietyIn Britain, we equate blackness with the working class. It’s time for a rethinkIn my new book, I narrate the existence, behaviours and sensibilities of the black British middle class, a social group largely ignored, until nowDon’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up hereSymeon BrownWed 5 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile narrating the audio version of my new book,The Good, the Black and the Boujee, came a revelatory reminder of why many black Britons see middle class status as a “white people ting”. After a recording session, I headed upstairs to see if I could find any friendly faces from my publisher before heading out into the sweltering heatwave for my cycle home. To my disappointment, I found a near-empty office floor, and left minutes later. Donning my helmet, I joined the middle class commuters who regularly left the office in cycling gear.As I approached the exit, something peculiar happened: I was met with a friendly expression of relief from the reception staff. The building had received a concerned report about a potential intruder on the top floor, they told me. The intruder was believed to be a rogue courier who had somehow passed the loading bay and made it into the editorial offices. It took me a moment to realise – the intruding courier was … me.Although I was amused rather than offended, themisunderstanding joined a chorus of similar anecdotes. In 2020,Edward Enninful, the first black editor-in-chief of Vogue, revealed thathe had also been mistaken for a courierat the publication by security. In court,black barristers say they are assumed to be defendants. Black politicians say they are assumed to be support staff in the Houses of Parliament. While these are mundane and momentaryexamples of social profiling,they reveal a more interesting truth. A black professional class has significantly expanded, but the meaning of blackness in Britain is unchanged in the public imagination.Wielding significant influenceView image in fullscreenTotem of expansion … Edward Enninful, Vogue’s first black editor-in-chief, in 2025.Photograph: Mike Coppola/MG25/Getty Images for the Met Museum/VogueIn Britain, to be black is to be assumed to be working class. This means that class differences between the black working class and the emergent black bourgeoisie are made invisible. Black British people who have gained the closest proximity to power are predominantly those who were either born middle class,or quickly initiated into it. Yet, although this social group has the power to wield significantcultural and political influence, they are a relatively young social group of barely 50 years old. As a result, their sensibility and behaviour has largely been ignored until now.Facing a data desert on this salaried group, I decided to undertake a wide ranging study of 1,460 black professionals. I gathered insights into their wealth, education and political decisions. My research revealed three groups that make up the black British middle class: a precarious “emerging black middle class” from the ends; a “traditional black middle class”, who were often racial minorities in their social lives; and a “black elite”, includinginfluential families like the Casely-Hayfords, but also those self made, such asStormzy or the business executive Dean Forbes.Whoseblack lives mattered?View image in fullscreenRevelatory … circumstances surrounding Black Lives Matter organising explains Black Britain’s class divide.Photograph: Daniel Leal-Olivas/AFP/Getty ImagesI began the odyssey of writing this book at a pivotal moment for the black middle class – the aftermath of 2020, when the Black Lives Matter movement moved from the margins to the mainstream. Many black people were beginning to demand a seat at the table. I saw a protest placard quoting the lyrics of Jay-Z, exalting the rise of black excellence. When donations poured into the coffers of BLMUK by white supporters guilted into penance, its leftist leadership faced criticism for diverting some donations to grassroots campaigns. Some demanded that the funding should have gone to black businesses. I found the criticism was perverse, but revelatory.After George Floyd’s death, black elites began to speak out in greater voice.Enninful’s story of profiling, for example, was made in a moment of public reckoning, when stories of racism were suddenlymore en vogue than anything that had graced his magazine covers. This elite also temporarily grew during this BLM boom due to a concentrated attempt to expand black representation in the upper echelons. There were successes: from thefirst black British photographer to shoot British Vogue’s front cover, to high profile appointments of privately educated black figures to the boards of major institutions like theSouthbank CentreandNational Portrait Gallery. The black middle class appear the biggest beneficiary of the BLM movement, although their success has been cyclical.Today, the black presence in these professions is facing an onslaught of political and legal challenges. A campaign to give internships to black students is being aggressively challenged, and the rightwing press currently runs pieces criticising the senior black appointments of major institutions that they believe have been “DEI hires”.I am convinced that a material opportunity for wider racial justice was hijacked by Britain’s aspirational elites who sought to consolidate their class positions. During the 2020 protests internet personalities with little historical knowledge were propelled as voices of black Britain, but had no grasp of the scholarship or activism detailing how we got here. Meanwhile, the demands of the UK BLM movement were diffuse, but many crystallised around the call for more representation in media or on boardsand higher pay for black influencers over issues like racial bias in housing that affect the black people disproportionately in poverty. The irony was the racial justice protests took place during the UK’s most diverse government in history, damaging faith in electoral politics to deliver for black voters.A precarious class positionView image in fullscreenCultivating elite taste … Racheal Broussard poses during London fashion week in February 2026.Photograph: Kirstin Sinclair/Getty ImagesIn black Britain a pervasive, underlying status anxiety has grown within the emergent middle class. A class position that once promised security, is now precarious. In 2001, about 70% of all black people in Britain lived in London; 25 years later,that figure is under 50%, despite the majority of professionals I surveyed saying they’d like to live in the city if they could afford to. Today, a generation of black professionals approaching middle age have acquired multiple degrees, earn a middle income or above and cultivate elite tastes,yet are unlikely to ever afford a house in their home borough.Middle class status anxieties even express themselves in the sphere of lifestyle and dating. When black content creators’ viral complaints are not focused on elite representation, they are often focused on social mobility through dating. Among the under-40s, there are endless discussions on the absence of suitable black men in the dating pool, reflecting the fact that black women’s social mobility has outpaced their male counterparts. Other online debates include hand-wringing over which types of black people get represented through media opportunities like book deals. Asinine questions like “are mixed-race people black” place a similar superficial emphasis on aesthetics, rather than material conditions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat’s the future of theblackandboujee?View image in fullscreenLooking for solace​ …​ most black Britons consulted for the book find relocation attractive.Photograph: blackgirlindubai/InstagramYou’d be forgiven for wanting to escape this all. Only one in three of the black professionals I surveyed wanted to remain in the UK, and this was before the rise of Reform, the latest incarnation of the nations’ anti-migrant movement. Desired destinations included Canada and Dubai. And, of course, the U.S. Despite its political turmoil, America boasts better salaries, stronger social infrastructure through black university networks, and an even more visible black elite. Just ask the new British Black Panther, David Jonsson.Black Britain itself is at an interesting crossroads,and it is hard to say which future path it will take. One road is further assimilation into white Britain, with high rates of interracial marriage between Caribbean and white families over a few short generations. I can imagine a future of mas bands at Notting Hill carnival made up of fair-skinned masqueraders with very distant Caribbean heritage, or school classrooms filled with blonde, blue-eyed children answering to Yoruba, Igbo or Ga names.Another is more global. We are increasingly connected to the transnational black diaspora identity joined by the internet. Migration and marriages across the black Atlantic might create a future marked by fluidity and cross-border movement, where Britain is a place of convergence and memory. Although black Britons have become middle class just as the entire middle is being squeezed, at no point in history has there been a black presence in Europe with greater social, cultural and economic power. The question is what will they build with it? The answer belongs to the good, the black and the boujee.Tap inAre you Black and boujee? Is middle class aspiration an abandonment of the Black struggle, or is it possible to do both? Tell us your thoughts by emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Diaspora discussesLast week,we looked at the rising costof box braids, and the social and economic pressures impacting customers and braiders. Here’s what you thought:double quotation markAs a salon owner, I see both sides every day. Clients are understandably asking why braids have become more expensive, but many don’t see what happens behind the scenes. Braiding is physically demanding work that takes years to master. Yet many talented braiders leave the industry because the pay often isn’t enough to build a sustainable career, save for a home or see a long-term future working for someone else. The shortage of experienced braiders also pushes costs up. Training takes time and salons are balancing rising business costs alongside paying people fairly. It’s a complex issue. –Fola, based in Londondouble quotation markI like to see why the least I’d pay for braids is $200 because at the end of the day, most times in New York City, it’s one lady standing for about 6/7 hours braiding my hair. I think where I started to lose connection was when the attachment (braiding extensions) started to feel like the same exact price as getting my hair done. Human hair this, human hair that; it feels like we’ve turned something as basic and simple as braids to having a bussdown. –Fayobomi Olusola-Falodun, based in New Yorkdouble quotation markI’m all for paying good, reliable braiders what they’re worth. Braiding is a skill, and skilled work deserves fair pay. But can we talk about some of these new rules? Being charged extra if your hair isn’t blow-dried bone straight? Excessive heat for what’s meant to be a protective style? The insistence on using huge amounts of gel? What happened to prioritising healthy hair? Customers should come with clean, detangled hair, absolutely. But expecting everyone to apply unnecessary heat or products that may not suit them shouldn’t be the standard. Prices have increased significantly, yet in many cases the overall service and attention to hair health haven’t improved alongside them. –Adenikè Z, based in LondonExplore more on these topicsSocietyThe Long WaveRaceClass issuesSocial mobilityInequalitynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley | Life and style | The Guardian
description: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
Content: ‘Maga is a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda’ … Gil Durán.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Maga is a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda’ … Gil Durán.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianThe ideas interviewLife and style‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyAs Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable themSteve RoseWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point“technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s“free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – byUmberto Eco,Robert Paxton,Jason Stanley– and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”By extension, he says,Silicon Valleyis fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement. That’s their vehicle for gaining power.” Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (Doge) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight.View image in fullscreenThe man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch … Peter Thiel.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesIn addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Muskmaking an apparent Nazi saluteanddescribing empathyas “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thielwriting in 2009that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggestingGreta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”View image in fullscreenMarc Andreessen has said technology must be a ‘violent assault on the forces of the unknown’.Photograph: Steve Jennings/Getty ImagesDurán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopherwith a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”.His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.View image in fullscreenCurtis Yarvin has mused about a ‘humane alternative to genocide’ to deal with unproductive citizens.Photograph: Florencia Tan Jun/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBoth of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump,in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said hespent half his time at Mar-a-Lagoin the month after Trump won the 2024 election.Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated“seasteading” movement(establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera,a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing tolongevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.He’s anti-democracy and pro-Trump: the obscure ‘dark enlightenment’ blogger influencing the next US administrationRead moreOther similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the2009 essayin which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as“America’s Hitler”to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vancetold the podcaster Jack Murphyin 2021.View image in fullscreen‘The government created these men and now these welfare kings want to destroy the very system that made them’ … Elon Musk.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesDurán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025,Bloomberg reportedthat at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated$13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recentlyjoined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX receiveda $1.6bn contractto supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day hepledged at least $100mto help Republicans inNovember’s midterm elections.“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especiallyElon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senatorDianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.He singles out the California governor,Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.View image in fullscreen‘Almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel’ … JD Vance.Photograph: Will Oliver/CNP/ShutterstockOn the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting torise up against data centresand this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future. If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). title: Stephen Libby on fashion: so many men have asked me for clothes advice since The Traitors | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Our guest columnist reveals how he found his personal style, from jumpsuits to high-waisted trousers
Author: Stephen Libby
Headline: Our guest columnist reveals how he found his personal style, from jumpsuits to high-waisted trousers
Content: Photograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanStephen Libby on men's fashionMen's fashionStephen Libby on fashion: so many men have asked me for clothes advice since The TraitorsOur guest columnist reveals how he found his personal style, from jumpsuits to high-waisted trousersStephen LibbyWed 5 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Other than the jumpsuits, I don’t think I wore anything particularly groundbreaking when I appeared onThe Traitors. I just think the bar for men’s fashion is so low that for me to come on television in a chunky mint green jumper and a pair of high-waisted jeans – which is probably one of the most neutral looks I own – seemed like a revelation. There was no styling budget, so most of what I wore came from my wardrobe.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The discovery of my personal style began when I was at primary school on the Isle of Lewis, off the north-west coast of Scotland. I realised I was different to the other boys when I began experimenting with fashion. From a young age I was turning my hems up, and I was certainly more interested in what the girls in my class were wearing.I would go so far as to say that my sexuality started to manifest in my choice of clothes. I have vivid memories of travelling to the mainland to go shopping – three hours on the ferry and then a 90-minute bus ride to Inverness. My biannual visit to Topman felt like a religious experience.One of the first things I remember buying was a grey and black striped cardigan. It was just a simple cardigan, but when I wore it to school I got ripped to shreds. Boys did not wear cardigans then. I remember feeling disheartened that this thing that I loved so much – fashion – was bringing me so much distress.double quotation markIt was never my goal to inspire an army of wide-legged trouser-wearing menBy the time I was 16 or 17, it was becoming almost impossible to hide who I was. On another trip to the mainland I bought my first pair of skinny jeans, which were very fashion forward for the Isle of Lewis in the 00s. I never showed my skinnies to my parents. When I was going out with my friends in the evening, I would put them in a bag and change into them after leaving the house. I wish I had been able to see then that I was merely doing something that a lot of my straight male counterparts would be doing years later.I went to the University of Glasgow when I was 18. Being in a city where everyone had access to all the same clothes meant I was no longer unique. That’s when I found vintage. (I was also a typical student with no money, and secondhand places were cheaper.) Everything on the high street was so flat, brown, beige, white, and I started seeing all these vintage Hawaiian shirts and incredible high-waist trousers. To me, the 60s, 70s and 80s were such a celebration of print and colour and drama. I can still remember loving this one pale blue 70s suit, but it was £50 – way out of my budget. Fifteen years on, I still wish I had bought it.Once I figured out my look, I never looked back. It’s quite distinct, and I love that I can go to a party and never have to worry about someone wearing the same thing as me. I love vintage shirts with dagger collars or billowy sleeves, and vintage trousers that have a nice flare on them to add some drama. People called me Simon Cowell when I started wearing high waists, but I just think this is how I’m supposed to look.The most stressful part of preparing to go on The Traitors had nothing to do with whether I would be a traitor or a faithful, or how far I’d get. It was: what the hell do I wear? I think people can ascertain so much about who you are through what you wear, it’s all snap judgments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving said that, it was never my goal to inspire an army of wide-legged trouser-wearing men; it was just to appear as the truest representation of myself. But since the show aired, I have had so many men message me on social media asking for clothes advice, and I’m going to use my next three columns to share my tips. So stay tuned for more, from tailoring to wedding dressing to – you guessed it – jumpsuits.Styling: Sam Deaman. Stylist’s assistant: Charlotte Gornall.
