title: Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, left, with Donald Trump at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, 17 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman, left, with Donald Trump at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, 17 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligentRafael BehrWe need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is neededWed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTShareWhen I am woken by the sound of my dog whining, I understand that she is hungry and wants me to get up. When my alarm clock goes off, I don’t consider its needs. It is following an instruction to rouse me at a certain time but it doesn’t care if I stay in bed. It doesn’t try to get me up by other means. The dog, on the other hand, will go to plan B. She barks.This capacity for autonomous action was once a difference between animals and machines. AI hasblurred the line. Advanced models devise their own strategies to reach a goal. The task might be defined by a human master, but the machine weighs its options for delivery. It can make its own choices. Given rules, it can break them.Last month, an experimental AI model run by OpenAI, the company that produces ChatGPT, broke out of a supposedly secure digital enclosure to launch asophisticated hacking attackon another company, Hugging Face. The AI had been set a test and turned criminally rogue in its determination to cheat.It is hard to describe that sort of behaviour without raiding a vocabulary conventionally reserved for sentient beings. AI models “decide” and “want” in ways that a chimpanzee can and a chair cannot.That doesn’t prove the existence of an interior process equivalent to our conscious experience of deciding and wanting. It doesn’t make the AI curious to know an answer or surprised by what it finds. It demonstrates only that we lack specific words for autonomous motive and agency in machines. And since language is the main way we get insight into other people’s minds (and one of our best indications that a mind other than our own exists at all), it takes an effort not to project mental states on to AI engines that can chat fluently in human.It is plausible that consciousness will one day emerge in robots. We know that abstract thought can arise as the end product of billions of tiny unconscious mechanical events. That is happening right now as a profusion of biochemical reactions in your body make it possible for you to read this sentence. We also know how fundamentally different that organic process is from the way a large language model would churn through a huge volume of probability equations at lightning speed to generate a sentence expressing the same idea. In the human case, meaning is shared. In the computer version, it is performed.AI pioneers muddy the distinction, speculating about the timeline for the arrival of “God-like” intelligence. They herald a new epoch of evolution. This gratifies the egos of science fiction nerds who prefer to see their business endeavours as voyages of discovery on the frontier of knowledge. It makes greed sound like philosophy and the acquisition of power by a handful of individuals sound like exploration on behalf of all humanity.We don’t need to know whether AI has crossed some theoretical threshold of self-awareness to see that it is dangerous and that its unregulated expansion is monstrously irresponsible. The OpenAI case is not isolated. Earlier this year, Anthropic limited the release of its most powerful model to a small number of hand-picked clients because it was too good at exploiting software vulnerabilities. In the wrong hands, Claude Mythoscould be a cyberweapon of mass destruction.Whose hands are the right ones? The US government will never be relaxed about the private sector having control over such awesome tools. But Donald Trump regulates by monarchical patronage, not law. He demands that companies submit to his personal authority anduses state powerto punish those that resist.There is growing clamour for less capricious regulation from within the tech sector. Engineers, and even their vainglorious bosses, are getting freaked out by the capabilities they are handling and worry about unchecked proliferation. The standard historical analogy is nuclear fission, which could be harnessed benignly, for civil power, or deployed aggressively in warheads. Except this time there are multiple Manhattan Projects all frantically competing for market share, fuelled by trillions of dollars of debt – a huge wager on future profitability – with the rest of the US economy as collateral.8:38Musk v Altman: tech bros at war over OpenAI – The LatestAnother difference: the barriers to entry for AI use, whether in research, commerce or crime, are a lot lower than for nuclear power. US labs currently have the best products, butChinese versions are not far behind. Even if the US stays at the cutting edge, second-tier models might do enough of what customers want that Silicon Valley’s output comes to look more like a luxury niche than unassailable market dominance.If that is how things play out, the geopolitical implications are vast. The US andChinahave made different bets on AI, conditioned by their different political systems. The American approach is predicated on the goal of self-training “general” AI – a system that breaks free of human limitations, improving itself on an exponential trajectory. The theory is that no rival could catch the first player to achieve that escape velocity.Beijing, accepting that it can’t build the best, has prioritised mass deployment of AI that is good enough, embedding it in schools, hospitals, factories and security forces. The American economy is great for marshalling exorbitant amounts of capital into speculative innovation. China’s one-party authoritarian state is well suited for making a cheaper version and rolling it out for data harvesting and surveillance across society in ways that would struggle to gain public consent in a democracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US is still the leader in AI. But that leadership might not be the perpetual money-spinning machine that the superintelligence gurus have advertised, in which case an uncomfortable correction is coming to a US economy kept buoyant byaerated tech stocks.The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng ZeguangRead moreA dose of enforced AI sobriety could drive demands for overdue regulation. It could even force recognition in Washington that it has to be an international process. It isn’t too late to negotiate global protocols of non-proliferation. Beijing would have incentives to sign up for the same reason that the USSR agreed to strategic arms limitation in the cold war. A moratorium or other limiting regime protects the elite status of signatories that have already mastered the technology. It would be a crowning recognition of China’s attainment of superpower parity with the US.But that scenario posits a president in the White House who is capable of strategic judgment, can summon a modicum of humility about the limits of American power and will, for humanity’s sake, see it circumscribed by international treaty. That is not Trump, who understands the ethical function of rules about as well as a rogue AI agent on a hacking spree.There is a tragic irony in the corruption of American democracy by organic stupidity as its economy comes to depend on artificial intelligence. And when the world needs leadership to confront the challenge of autonomous machines, it is presented with a US president who causes chaos with the mindless automaticity of an alarm clock and who rages against his declining power like a dog barking for attention.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicDonald TrumpChinaComputingAsia PacificcommentShareReuse this content

title: Soriot should explain the curious case of AstraZeneca’s non-deal | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: AstraZeneca’s rumoured takeover of Bristol Myers Squibb already looked weird, and was met with a lack of enthusiasm by shareholders
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: AstraZeneca’s rumoured takeover of Bristol Myers Squibb already looked weird, and was met with a lack of enthusiasm by shareholders
Content: Sir Pascal Soriot has been AstraZeneca’s chief executive for the past 14 years.Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersView image in fullscreenSir Pascal Soriot has been AstraZeneca’s chief executive for the past 14 years.Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersNils Pratley on financeBusinessSoriot should explain the curious case of AstraZeneca’s non-dealNils PratleyAstraZeneca’s rumoured takeover of Bristol Myers Squibb already looked weird, and was met with a lack of enthusiasm by shareholdersAstraZeneca falls to third-largest UK company amid US merger talksWed 5 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareHold the heartburn pills. It seems AstraZeneca is no longer contemplating a takeover of US rival Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS)to create a $400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical colossus. On Monday, the UK firm’s shares plunged 9% onthe FT’s report of preliminary talks. On Wednesday, Reuters said there are no ongoing discussions. Cue a mini-relief rally in AZ’s share price.Neither company has seen fit to tell its shareholders what was happening, so it’s impossible to know if the talks were a tentative ‘what if?’ corporate flirtation or something more substantial that has been killed, perhaps, by the lack of enthusiasm on the part of AZ’s shareholders.The deal – or non-deal – looked weird for the reasonsgiven here earlier in the week. AZ has prospered under chief executive Sir Pascal Soriot for the past 14 years by concentrating on backing its best ideas in the labs in the interests of long-term success, as opposed to playing debt-fuelled takeover games that rely on short-term cost-cutting. Since Soriotproclaims absolute confidence in hitting AZ’s revenue target of $80bn in 2030, there is no obvious reason to divert from the winning script. And, given BMS’s revenue headache in the next few years as a blockbuster cancer treatment goes off patent, the target looked odd, never mind the current quality of its cashflows.There are possible counter-arguments, naturally. Both companies are very big in oncology, so there could have been an opportunity to establish multi-year dominance in a core pharma field if competition regulators could be persuaded. Maybe the crossover meant potential cost savings would have been bigger, or easier to achieve, than is normally the case. Perhaps Soriot spotted potential in BSM’s drugs pipeline. Or just an opportunity to accelerate his ambition for AZ to generate half its revenues in the US, the world’s biggest and most lucrative market for pharma firms; the current share is 43%.Whatever it is, Soriot should shed some light on whether he sees mega-deals as any possible part of AZ’s future. It’s one thing to take a strict “no comment” approach to individual takeover tales. But most AZ shareholders surely assume they are invested in a company that doesn’t do bet-the-balance-sheet mega-deals. Rare diseases specialist Alexion,bought by AZ in 2021 for $39bn, was big – but not in BMS’s $133bn league. And the clear rationale in that case was to boost innovation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe worry is thatthe pull of the USis dominating strategic thinking as Soriot, at the age of 67, enters his final years (probably) at the helm. Or maybe there is an emerging analysis that AI is changing the pharma game. Greater transparency on corporate thinking would be useful. Soriot has always presented AZ as the last company in need of a transformative deal. If he is actually flexible on the idea, shouldn’t shareholders know?Explore more on these topicsBusinessNils Pratley on financeAstraZenecaPharmaceuticals industryMergers and acquisitionsCorporate governancecommentShareReuse this content

title: Murderous heat, an endangered food supply and no net zero: this is the life the radical right wants you to have | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: As climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like it, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: As climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like it, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Firefighters battle wildfire near Preveli on the island of Crete, Greece, 30 July 2026.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters battle wildfire near Preveli on the island of Crete, Greece, 30 July 2026.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisMurderous heat, an endangered food supply and no net zero: this is the life the radical right wants you to haveGeorge MonbiotAs climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like itWed 5 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTShareCan’t you leftists understand? Mass death is good for you. Reject the woke love of life! Welcome civilisational collapse! Watch it all burn, then dance in the ashes! This, roughly speaking, is how the dismissal of climate action is now being justified: the argument has shifted from science denial to outright nihilism.The new incendiary spirit is exemplified by that serial arsonist Allister Heath, editor of the Sunday Telegraph. In a columnin the Daily Telegraphlast week, originally titled “Britain can’t stop climate change.Scrap net zero and embrace Mediterranean life”, he argued that “climate change is real” but “the war against global warming has been lost”.This is a classic progression among those who seek to prevent a shift away from fossil fuels: first deny the problem, as theDailyandSunday Telegraphhave done for many years, then accept the problem but claim it’s now too late to act. If itistoo late, it’ll be in no small part because of the deniers. So, Heath continued, we in Britain should “ditch the despicable con that is net zero, and learn to cope with … a warmer, drier, more volatile Mediterranean climate, if that is indeed to be our fate”.Seeking to cut our emissions, he argued, shows that we suffer from an “advanced case of suicidal empathy”. I’m not qualified to diagnose people, but as a general rule, a lack of empathy, alongside callousness and an absence of guilt, is astrong indicator of a psychopath. Yes, he continued, “there will be plenty of losers, but it is pointless seeking to prevent the inevitable … Many in Britain would enjoy the kind of warmer climate predicted by modellers”.His timing was impeccable: extolling a Mediterranean climate just as the Mediterranean regiongoes up in flames. Amid general derision on social media, the editors changed the headline.Heath’s column also happened to land on the daydrought was declaredacross half of England. Nevertheless, he argued, we need universal irrigation and should construct more swimming pools. Where will the water come from? Oh, don’t get all empirical with me. He maintained we should “trust that the free market will deliver the goods on clean energy and zero-carbon transportation, but only when they are better and cheaper than existing alternatives”. Butrenewables are already cheaper, and better for us, than fossil fuelsin almost all situations. It is only through resistance to the “free market”, led by the Trump administration – which has spent billions trying tokill clean energy and sustain coal burning– that fossil fuels retain such a share of consumption. As a result of the plunging price of renewables, far from having lost the climate war, we could be about to witness a rapid turnaround. So quick, give up now, just in case we win.He dismissed cutting carbon emissions in the UK as a “moral act, an ethical imperative”, by which he appears to mean unhinged: “Down that road lies madness.” Yes, cutting our own emissionsisa moral act and an ethical imperative. It is also pragmatic. Global action on climate breakdown depends on mutual trust. If some countries refuse to play, others are also likely to refuse, and an effective global response collapses in a circle of finger-pointing. This risk is all the greater when rich nations, which tend to have the biggest fossil fuel legacies, seek to behave as free riders. If we don’t step up, why should anyone else?As for the “warmer climate predicted by modellers”, it could go quite the other way, as rising temperatures, some models suggest, could cause the Atlantic current system to stall,plunging Britain into extreme cold. Well, you’ll just have to learn to adapt to that instead.Heath’s defiance of reality is so well established that it has spawned an “Allister Heath headline generator”, which pumps out bonkers statementsnot easily distinguishablefrom the originals. In a close field, I think he takes the prize for being more wrong more often than anyone else in British journalism. This, after all, is the man who described Kwasi Kwarteng’s fiscal catastrophe as “thebest budget I have ever hearda British chancellor deliver, by a massive margin”. It’s a reliable rule: if Heath believes something, the opposite is likely to be true.But it’s not just him, and it’s not just journalism. The radical right moves as a pack, and Heath is just one of many now insisting that climate catastrophe is something we should simply suck up. Those grammar deniers Reform UK, for example, insist: “We are better to adapt to warming, rather thanpretend we can stop it.” Of course the same political tendency alsodefends austerityandprivatisation, both of which severely hamper our ability to adapt.To their credit, two Telegraph columnists,Ambrose Evans-PritchardandTim Stanley, last week broke the nihilist consensus, arguing we should rise to the challenge of climate breakdown. But they now belong to a minority, in the Telegraph andacross the rightwing press.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca SolnitRead moreWhy? Because most of the media, most of the time, provides a platform for people who say things that have the effect of serving capital, whether or not they are true, whether or not they are coherent, whether or not they may hasten disaster. While renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels in nearly all circumstances,fossil fuels are more profitable, because useful reserves are limited and can each be monopolised by a single corporation, while prices can suddenly take flight in times of war or chaos. Almost all the very rich are heavily invested in them. The result is that any attempt to restrict the use of fossil fuels is perceived as class war. Nonsensical justifications for the status quo then follow as automatically as the Allister Heath headline generator.So “embrace Mediterranean life”. But without the wine, which, as another Telegraph column laments, is becoming “smoke tainted” by all those fires triggered by some unmentioned and mysterious force. And without the food, whose production, thanks to the drought and heatwaves, isat grave riskin southern Europe, as it is here. And without your lovely gite, which might have been incinerated. Or the lush green landscape, also lost to the flames. Or the balmy summer temperatures, nowreplaced by murderous heat. Oh go on then, you know what I really mean: embrace death.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionExtreme heatWildfiresDroughtEnglandNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: What kind of society fast-tracks early release for domestic abusers? This is gambling with women’s lives | Joan Smith | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violence, says writer and campaigner for women’s rights Joan Smith
Author: Joan Smith
Headline: Andy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violence, says writer and campaigner for women’s rights Joan Smith
Content: A Million Women Rise march in London, 7 March 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Million Women Rise march in London, 7 March 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionDomestic violenceWhat kind of society fast-tracks early release for domestic abusers? This is gambling with women’s livesJoan SmithAndy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violenceWed 5 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTShareIt’s time to be blunt: the government is about to expose hundreds of vulnerable women to the risk of death or serious injury. Survivors of domestic abuse, including women who have suffered years of physical violence and intimidation, are now preparing for the moment in October when 5,000 prisoners begin to bereleased early. What are these women supposed to do? Where are they supposed to go? Their abusers know where they live. They know where their children go to school.Following an outcry, rapists and some child sex offendershave been excludedfrom the early release scheme. But by refusing to exclude men convicted of domestic violence, this government is sending a message that this category of crime – serial in nature and implicated in the deaths of one womanevery five days– is simply not a priority.In 2023,Keir Starmer promisedto cut violence against women by half in a decade. It was an eye-catching pledge, although not obviously assisted by his proposal, when he became prime minister, to allow thousands of convicted criminals back on to the streets. No one denies that Andy Burnham has inherited an overcrowding crisis in UK prisons, but his solution – in effect, accepting the previous government’s plan with a few changes – involves taking a huge gamble with women’s lives.For eight years, I was co-chair of the mayor of London’s Violence Against Women and Girls Board. I saw the devastating extent of intimate partner abuse and the chronic shortage of resources to support victims. I studied domestic homicide reviews with a shudder, seeing how one opportunity after another to save women’s lives had been missed. Now, in the midst of a justified furore, Burnham and his justice minister, Alex Norris, can’t claim they haven’t been warned.View image in fullscreenThe domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, says the decision not to exclude domestic abuse perpetrators from this scheme “puts victims’ lives at risk”, adding: “These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.” Intimate partner violence has special characteristics, including the fact that men seething with resentment towards former wives and girlfriends are all too likely to reoffend.The data is limited – reoffending rates among men convicted of domestic abuse are not listed separately but hidden among other offences, including violence against the person, criminal damage and arson. Recent incidents of public disorder have confirmed that men who abuse partners have a wider propensity for violence;most people arrestedfor violent protests after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer had previously been reported to the police for domestic abuse, for instance. In my book Home Grown: How Domestic Violence Turns Men Into Terrorists, I pointed out that many men who commit public acts of extreme violence have histories of first abusing their families.What we do know is that the proportion of released prisoners who go on to commit further offences is alarmingly high. Reoffending rates vary from about 29% if you include those with non-custodial sentences, to a “proven reoffending rate” of 43.8% for adults released from custody between January and March 2024, suggesting rehabilitation in prison is largely ineffective. The victims’ commissioner,Claire Waxman, has said“effective risk management, meaningful licence conditions, proper supervision and timely, trauma-informed communication and support remain critical” if the early release scheme goes ahead in its present form. That’s asking an awful lot of an overstretched probation service that can barely cope with its existing workload.Last month the National Audit Office revealed that almost 9,000 people required to wear an electronic tag did not have one (the governmentdisputes the figure, arguing the number is closer to 5,450). The report also delivered a damning verdict on how prisoners released on licence are monitored, concluding that “police and probation officers often lack relevant information or capacity to respond quickly to breaches”. Nearly half of alerts and breach notifications result in “no further action”.This chaotic system is what ministers are relying on when they promise survivors of domestic abuse that their attackers will be monitored and served with notices banning them from specific areas. How is that supposed to reassure a woman when the man who beat her to within an inch of her life approaches her front door? Or when he springs out as she carries groceries to her car? Some victims already report facing sceptical questioning when they report breaches of licence conditions by their former partners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen rarely commit violent crimes. We are overwhelmingly victims, not perpetrators. The criminal justice system has let us down for years, at present securing fewer than 3,000 convictions in the 70,000-plus rape cases reported to the police in England and Wales each year. We’ve been saying for a long time that rape has all but been decriminalised, which is why the original proposal to include sex offenders in the early release scheme was so insulting. Now we’re told the prime minister would have liked to go further, exempting more categories of offenders from the scheme, but the prisons crisis is so grave that victims of domestic violence will just have to put up with their abusers being released after serving only a third of their sentences.Prisons are violent, unpleasant places, understaffed and racked by crime. Their only useful effect, as far as I’m concerned, is to protect women and children from men who have already hurt them – and wouldn’t hesitate to do it again, given the opportunity. The reality of the anodyne phrase “domestic violence” is broken limbs, fractured skulls and children cowering in corners. Exposing women to more of these horrors, at the hands of men already proved to be violent, means survivors will pay the price of political failure.Joan Smith is an author, journalist and a former chair of the mayor of London’s VAWG boardDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Why waste your time on social media when you could be flicking through picture books? | Joel Snape | The Guardian
description: From histories of opera to compendiums of mosses, they’re beautiful, expertly written and don’t leave you feeling grubby, writes Joel Snape. What’s not to like?
Author: Joel Snape
Headline: From histories of opera to compendiums of mosses, they’re beautiful, expertly written and don’t leave you feeling grubby, writes Joel Snape. What’s not to like?
Content: ‘It’s quite rare that I pick one up without feeling as if I’ve improved my knowledge of the world.’Photograph: Pavlina Popovska/Getty Images (posed by a model)View image in fullscreen‘It’s quite rare that I pick one up without feeling as if I’ve improved my knowledge of the world.’Photograph: Pavlina Popovska/Getty Images (posed by a model)OpinionPicture booksWhy waste your time on social media when you could be flicking through picture books?Joel SnapeFrom histories of opera to compendiums of mosses, they’re beautiful, expertly written and don’t leave you feeling grubby. What’s not to like?Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareThere are lots of reasons not to read picture books. You can’t really mark them “done” in the same way you might, say, tick A Tale of Two Cities off your bucket list, or add them to your tally when you’re humble-bragging about what you’ve read over the past 12 months. They aren’t going to become part of the cultural zeitgeist,like MiddlemarchorThe Odyssey, and you probably won’t be able to persuade a book group to talk about them.Recently, though, I’ve been getting back into them in a big way, poking around the “oversized” shelves of my local charity shops, cooing over large-format collections ofHokusai printsin Waterstones.When I say “picture books”, by the way, I mean that in the broadest possible sense: books with lots of pictures in them. I’ve got a history of opera that I’m sure is intended for children, as well as a natural history guide that features page after page of taxonomic descriptions of moss.Picture books are a great leveller: anyone can jump into them, anywhere they like, with no need to trudge through the boring early bits to get to the juicy stuff. For some topics, they’re a requirement – maps, art and cross-sections are the obvious examples – but they make almost anything more memorable. A few years ago, I interviewed a University Challenge champion who swore by them as a way of getting an entry-level overview of nearly any subject. It’s quite rare that I pick one up without feeling as if I’ve improved my knowledge of the world.What I really like about picture books, though, is that they contain so many of the appealing features of social media and so few of the bad ones. They’re created to invite the eye, often with lots of what magazine designers call “entry points”. Perhaps you’d like to learn more about this Parasaurolophus skull? Maybethe Bayeux tapestryis more your speed? They’re written by experts and rigorously factchecked, usually without too much of the explicit political posturing that makes online life so draining.Best of all, you can deep-dive into one topic, or flit across dozens in mere moments, occasionally stopping to read an entire thread (sorry, page) when something catches your interest. Hormones, horses, Hinduism, the hundred years war: whodoesn’tfeel as if they could know more about these things?In the 21st century, it’s easy to believe that nobody needs reference books any more. All the answers, after all, are online, either on Wikipedia or ruthlessly scraped from real books by rapacious AI models. It’s just as easy to burrow down a rabbit hole on the internet as it is with the Dorling Kindersley Family Encyclopedia on your lap, except that the former goes on for ever.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCould a couch-to-5k for books get you back into reading?Read moreThe big problem is that there’s no sense of proportion on the internet: it’s more enticing to read about rollercoaster disasters than Renaissance painters – and there’s more scurrilous detail available. It’s also far too easy to click straight over to Facebook, or Bluesky, or BuzzFeed, and emerge half an hour later knowingnothingmore about the Sistine chapel.Picture books, by contrast, are one of the most soothing ways to fill spare time. They fit perfectly with a definition of “proper” reading that I’ve borrowed from the authorNaomi Alderman: the sort you wish you were doing more of, rather than the sort that makes you feel grubby afterwards. If you sit on the sofa with a picture book, preferably with your phone out of reach, you tend to emerge with a new sense of wonder about the world and our capacity to explore it and understand it.You can often pick them up cheaply, or borrow them by the half-dozen from your local library. (If you put them in a rucksack, this doubles as your workout for the day.) Even if you could live the rest of your life without needing to understand the difference between mountain fork-moss and ostrich-plume feather-moss, wouldn’t it be richer if you did?Joel Snape is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: RFK Jr has a new cooking show. Are any Trump officials doing their actual jobs? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Shouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Shouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Robert F Kennedy presenting The Real Food Show on YouTube.Photograph: hhs.gov/real-food-showView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy presenting The Real Food Show on YouTube.Photograph: hhs.gov/real-food-showOpinionRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr has a new cooking show. Are any Trump officials doing their actual jobs?Arwa MahdawiShouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare …Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTShareThe US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has got his work cut out for him.A cyclosporiasis outbreaklinked to iceberg lettuce has the entire country playing salad roulette: one bad leaf and you could become very unwell. The condition isn’t normally deadly, but, on Monday, officials in Michigan confirmed the first two fatalities. Meanwhile, it’s theworst year for measlesin the US since 1991. A disease that was once eliminated now looks as though it’s back with a vengeance – thanks in part, according to experts, to anti-vaxxers such as Kennedy himself. And this week New York officials are warning about a rare tick-borne illness calledrabbit fever (tularemia).Still, despite having rather a lot on his plate, Kennedy has found the time to front a new cooking show, hosted on YouTube. It’s called The Real Food Show and it’s supposed to help Americans prepare healthy, affordable meals at home. The first episode features the chef and TV personalityAndrew Gruel (perfect name) teachingthe US to prepare crispy salmon cakes with … salad. Which is certainly a bold way to kick things off.Of all the things that the health secretary is doing, hosting a cookery show is probably the least offensive. Still, I can’t say that the idea of Kennedy as an affordable food influencer is particularly appetising. This is a man who has boasted that he will“literally eat anything”because he doesn’t “have a gag reflex”. A man who has had to publicly clarify that the skeleton he was gnawing in a viral photo belonged toa goat and not a barbecued dog. A man who once dumped a dead bear in Central Park (after deciding not toskin it and freeze it),reportedly cut the penis offa roadkillraccoonand is said to have beenobsessed with seagull skulls. And who can forget the worm that“ate a portion of”his brain? Experts believe he may have contracted the tapeworm larva from eating undercooked pork. In short, I wouldn’t want Kennedy anywhere near my own kitchen.Kennedy, who alsohas a new podcast, is not the only Trump official who is fond of the cameras. The transportation secretary Sean Duffy (a former reality TV star) recently spent seven months filming a show calledThe Great American Road Trip, despite various crises hitting his department – including a partial government shutdown that led to Transportation Security Administration agents leaving in droves after not being paid. Duffy travelled across the US with his Fox News host wife and their nine children for the show, which was sponsored bycompanies his department regulates, such as Boeing and Shell. It seems that many Trump officials don’t really want to do the hard work that comes with being a government official; they’d rather play one on TV.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter Beinart | The Guardian
description: The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
Author: Peter Beinart
Headline: The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
Content: ‘Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionMichiganAbdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat TrumpismPeter BeinartThe candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against themWed 5 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.42 EDTShareEvery now and then, a Senate race sets the direction for an entire party. In 1991, a state official named Harris Wofford – advised by a foul-mouthed Cajun named James Carville – upset his far better-known Republican opponent to win a special election in Pennsylvania. He did it by promising to expand access to healthcare – and thus created a template for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign the following year.If Abdul El-Sayed can follow up his victory in last night’s Democratic Senate primary by winning the general election in Michigan this fall, he will have created a template of his own. Despite his closer-than-expected margin of victory, his campaign offers a model for how Democrats across the country can answer the political challenge posed byDonald Trump.By casting the Michigan Senate primary as yet another battle between progressive insurgents and establishment centrists, media coverage of El-Sayed’s campaign has tended to overlook what is innovative about it. Like Zohran Mamdani and the democratic socialists who have won House races in New York, Pennsylvania and Colorado, El-Sayed wants to end unconditional US military support for Israel. But while Mamdani sometimes discusses Israel purely through the language of human rights and international law – as he did in his recentvideoarguing that Benjamin Netanyahu should be arrested as a war criminal – El-Sayed’s message is more nationalistic. He rarely discusses the Jewish state without linking it to Washington’s failure to address problems at home.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreIn a recentinterview, the New Yorker editor, David Remnick, asked El-Sayed whether he supports one or two states in Israel-Palestine. El-Sayed did not take the bait. He replied that his focus was less on “what’s happening there rather than what’s happening here”. His primary concern, he explained, was that the US was allocating money for Israeli weapons that it could be spending on schools in Michigan. While acknowledging: “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike,” he said: “It is not my job as an American policymaker to decide what the ultimate peace should be. But it is my job to make sure that our resources are stewarded correctly for the people I’m responsible for: those kids going to those broken schools.”In relentlessly linking US military aid to Israel to unmet needs in the United States, El-Sayed is crafting a progressive version of America First. In 2016, Donald Trump exploited the resentment many Americans felt after a decade and a half of failed wars in the Middle East. Now, in the wake of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, El-Sayed is turning the tables. The difference is that Trump fused nationalism and imperialism: he said that the Iraq war was a mistake becausethe US soughtto “make western democracies out of countries that had no experience or interests in becoming a western democracy”; the US, he said, should havetaken Iraq’s oil. El-Sayed, by contrast, is fusing nationalism with progressivism. He’s not attacking the humanitarian assistance once offered by USAID. He’s condemning military aid to Israel (andalsoto Egypt, where his father was born) because it both violates human rights overseas and denies resources to Americans at home. This isn’t a message that only resonates with the American left. Last summer, the late rightwing activist Charlie Kirktweetedthat young conservatives “are skeptical about the state of America’s current relationship” with Israel “and they want to be confident America’s leaders are putting their own country first”. Apollin May by the Institute for Middle East Understanding found that by a margin of almost two-to-one, Republicans under the age of 45 prefer candidates who support reducing taxpayer-funded weapons sales to the Jewish state.But El-Sayed’s campaign offers Democrats another lesson as well. He isn’t only showing them how to reclaim nationalism from the GOP. He’s also showing them how to turn the Republican party’s financial advantage against it. In the last five weeks of El-Sayed’s primary campaign, outside Super Pacs supporting his opponent, representative Haley Stevens,spentmore than 12 times as much on television ads as did those supporting him. Most candidates can’t overcome that kind of disparity. But El-Sayed made it a source of strength. Again and again, he used Stevens’s financial support from the pro-Israel lobbying group Aipac – which contributedthe bulkof the outside money on her behalf – against her. He also linked her to other unpopular special interests. His supporters ran atelevision adhighlighting the contributions she had received from the Michigan utility, DTE Energy, which is widelydislikedfor charging high rates and allowing recurring power outages.El-Sayed’s relentless focus on the source of Stevens’s donations turned her financial advantage into an electoral albatross. When the Bulwark’s Sarah Longwellaskeda Michigan focus group why they didn’t like Stevens, “voters repeatedly brought up Aipac and the appearance of corporate influence.”El-Sayed performed this political jujitsu against a fellow Democrat. But this fall, and probably again in 2028, Democrats across the country will be badly outspent by Republicans. Donald Trump has turned the federal government into a cash cow for corporations and billionaires who profit massively from his administration and return the favor by writing campaign checks. Elon Musk alone recentlyannouncedthat he will spend at least $100m supporting Republican candidates this fall. Overall,reportedMS Now late last month, the Republican National Committee, the Republican House and Senate campaign committees and GOP-aligned Super Pacs have raised almost $600m more than their Democratic counterparts.Democrats need to hammer Trump on his unprecedented corruption | Steven GreenhouseRead moreEl-Sayed’s campaign offers a template for howDemocratscan respond: make the money the issue. El-Sayed drew a connection between Stevens’s backing from AIipac and her support for US military aid to Israel. But other Democrats can brand their Republican opponents as lackeys not just of Aipac, but of Elon Musk, big oil, big pharma or AI – and highlight the connection between their campaign funds and their support for policies that hurt ordinary people.This strategy requires Democrats to eschew corporate and special interest funding and run campaigns that rely primarily on small donors. There’s no guarantee this will work. Not all Democrats can deliver a populist message as effectively as El-Sayed. But the staggering corruption of Trump’s presidency, and the obscene wealth gap that his policies have helped create, presents them with an opportunity. Which means that El-Sayed’s model could prove effective far beyondMichigan.There are many reasons Democrats have struggled to defeat the Trump-era GOP. But among them are these: Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both. Democrats across the country should be taking notes.Peter Beinart is a contributing opinion writer atthe New York Times, editor at large atJewish Currents, a professor at theNewmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York, and the author ofThe Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter. His most recent book isBeing Jewish After the Destruction of GazaExplore more on these topicsMichiganOpinionUS politicsDemocratsDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026Super PacscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch: purging moderation is not ‘common sense’ | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A row over a local council candidate reveals a deeper problem with the Tory leader’s diagnosis of her party’s electoral predicament
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A row over a local council candidate reveals a deeper problem with the Tory leader’s diagnosis of her party’s electoral predicament
Content: ‘Mrs Badenoch said she believed in giving people a second chance.’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Mrs Badenoch said she believed in giving people a second chance.’Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersOpinionConservativesThe Guardian view on the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch: purging moderation is not ‘common sense’EditorialA row over a local council candidate reveals a deeper problem with the Tory leader’s diagnosis of her party’s electoral predicamentWed 5 Aug 2026 13.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareKemi Badenoch has been clear about the qualifying criteria for prospective Conservative MPs. They must be “serious people who understand common sense,” shehas said. The situation in local government is different, as demonstrated by Mrs Badenoch’s ill-judged support for a former neo-Nazi, selected to stand as a councillor in Somerset next year.Joshua Bonehill-Paine has convictions for racially aggravated harassment of a JewishLabour MPand assaulting a police officer among other offences. On Wednesday, as pressure grew on the party leader to repudiate him, he withdrew his candidacy.Mrs Badenoch had defended Mr Bonehill-Paine on the grounds that he had renounced his former views and was involved in anti-extremism training, using his own experience of fanatical antisemitism as a cautionary tale. The Conservative leader said she believed in giving people a second chance.That is not an ethos she has always applied. When Louise Haigh, currently first secretary of state,resignedfrom Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet over an old and minor fraud offence, Mrs Badenoch was unforgiving, declaring that “the country needs conviction politicians, not politicians with convictions”.Mrs Badenoch struggled to justify the inconsistency, claiming that a “higher threshold” applied for MPs than for councillors, whose duties are limited to “parking and bins”. That argument sat awkwardly with the defence of Mr Bonehill-Paine, based on the thoroughness of his rehabilitation. If his anti‑extremism work was exemplary, she might have wanted him to have as wide an audience as possible. Once she accepted that his offences would disqualify him from running for parliament, it was absurd to suggest thatSomersetresidents should accept a former neo-Nazi running their services. The episode raises questions about the Tory leader’s judgment.View image in fullscreenJoshua Bonehill-Paine.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YouTubeAll parties have more rigorous selection tests for MPs than council candidates. The job is more consequential and vetting resources are limited. All have been embarrassed at some point by the exposure of cranks and extremists in their election lists.But Mrs Badenoch’s contortions in this case reveal a different problem. The Conservatives are struggling to carve out a distinct identity in a fragmented political arena. The leader’s diagnosis of the Tories’ crushing 2024 defeat is that the party “talked right but governed left”. The practical application of this formula involves refusal to challenge Reform UK or its schismatic offshoot, Restore, as they drive immigration policy to ever more extreme positions, and anathematisation of the Tories’ liberal, one-nation tradition.Mrs Badenoch’s definition of the values and opinions expected of a Tory parliamentary candidate prohibits support for net zero targets or Britain remaining a signatory to the European convention on human rights. Former MPs, including senior ministers, who hold such views arenot welcome. Voters who care about the climate or believe that Britain should keep good relations with other European democracies are invited to look elsewhere.It is not surprising that a strategy of repudiating mainstream, centre-right politics in pursuit of an agenda dictated by radical nationalists has failed to lift Tory support. Since Mrs Badenoch claims to believe in the advancement of “serious people who understand common sense” in politics, she should consider applying that test more rigorously to her own candidacy to be prime minister.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on French cinema’s De Gaulle moment: present anxieties inform a new focus on the past | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A wave of films dealing with the second world war is captivating a nation facing major contemporary challenges
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A wave of films dealing with the second world war is captivating a nation facing major contemporary challenges
Content: A scene from La Bataille de Gaulle.Photograph: Malgosia Abramowska/Pathé Films - TF1 Films ProductionView image in fullscreenA scene from La Bataille de Gaulle.Photograph: Malgosia Abramowska/Pathé Films - TF1 Films ProductionOpinionCharles de GaulleThe Guardian view on French cinema’s De Gaulle moment: present anxieties inform a new focus on the pastEditorialA wave of films dealing with the second world war is captivating a nation facing major contemporary challengesWed 5 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareFor weeks now, anglophone cinephiles have been focusing their attention on the virtues and vices of Christopher Nolan’s $250madaptationof The Odyssey. Across the Channel, however, Homer’s epic tale of a flawed Greek hero has been facing stiff domestic competition. A two-partbiopicof General Charles de Gaulle, concentrating on his struggles to liberate France during the second world war, has been the word-of-mouth box office hit of the French summer.It may be that five hours’ worth of De Gaulle attracted some punters seeking air-conditioned sanctuary from the heatwaves. But there have been rave reviews both from critics andaudiences, and a notable upsurge of interest among the young. The success of the films has already had a cultural knock-on effect,boostingthe number of visitors, for example, to the Museum of the Liberation of Paris.The buzz around them is all the more striking given that the austere, aloof De Gaulle – in stark contrast to Winston Churchill – has remained a somewhat shadowy and elusive cinematic presence. Some of the cut-through has been attributed to a fast-paced, skilful screenplay, based upon British historian Julian Jackson’sacclaimedbiography. The strategy of the veteran film producerJérôme Seydouxto revitalise French historical drama through some blockbuster productions, including The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, has also been emphatically vindicated.View image in fullscreenJean Moulin.Photograph: AFP/GettyIntriguingly though, other more political factors may be playing a part. In portraying the heroic role of theFree French Forcesin north Africa – made up mostly of Black colonial troops – the De Gaulle films speak to a new generation which has grown up amid far-right-inspired controversies over nationhood and identity. And at a time when Europe’s relations with a Trump-led United States have become fraught, and the economic threat posed by China has become pressing, a resurgence of interest in Gaullist notions of leadership is perhaps unsurprising.The same might be said of a series of other high‑profile films dealing with France and the second world war. Cinemas are currently hosting, or about to host, two psychological portraits of collaboration with Marshal Philippe Pétain’sVichyregime, an account of the life of the Resistance hero Jean Moulin, and a reconstruction of a famous attempt to rescue over 100 Jewish children awaiting deportation. In the pages of Le Monde, a French historian, Henry Rousso, hasarguedthat “unlike the so-called ‘retro wave’ of the 1970s, these films do not claim to expose a repressed chapter of history … they are sounding alarm bells, with varying degrees of subtlety.”Ahead of a presidentialelectionthat could see the daughter of a notorious defender of Vichy enter the Élysée, it is not hard to see why. As Mr Rousso observes, it would be false to equate Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National party with the fascism of the 1930s. But its willingness tofloutrepublican values in relation to immigration policy, for example, carries deeply undesirable echoes of dark times.Cinematic trends often reflect back to audiences their own preoccupations. If the focus this summer and autumn inFranceis on a period defined by the stark moral choices it imposed, and the biggest homegrown hit is a film about leadership, that may tell us something about present anxieties as well as past traumas.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Missing a few days of school should not add up to a fine | Schools | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she argues that Labour should abolish fines for parents taking their children on holiday during term time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she argues that Labour should abolish fines for parents taking their children on holiday during term time
Content: ‘Time away as a family is precious and above all can be educationally valuable and enriching.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Time away as a family is precious and above all can be educationally valuable and enriching.’Photograph: AlamySchoolsLettersMissing a few days of school should not add up to a fineReaders respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she argues that Labour should abolish fines for parents taking their children on holiday during term timeWed 5 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareI am in support of Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s suggestion that we should abolish fines for holidays in school term time (I’m all for the nanny state – but we should abolish fines for holidays in term time, 2 August). She makes all the correct and logical arguments, to which I would add one more. One of the justifications for the fines is that children miss out on valuable learning, but this is simply not the case as teachers turn to movies, games and other distractions in those last weeks of term.There is very little curriculum learning happening in those periods before the main school holidays. And from what my children describe to me, over the years this “downing of tools” seems to be happening earlier each year. The argument that taking a child out of school a week before the end of term means they miss valuable learning is, frankly, laughable.Nick JohnsonDorsetIt was good to read Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett writing about the draconian policy of fining parents for taking their children out of school to go on holiday. It is indeed appallingly unfair. And unkind and small-minded – children with family overseas may never be able to see them if they are only permitted to go in the school holidays, when fares are most expensive.The reason invariably given – without evidence – is that it affects children’s education. Before the current regime, we took our daughter out of primary school every year – to see family in Scotland, or to go to friends’ weddings. It seems to have done her no harm. Twelve GCSEs with A*s, top marks in the international baccalaureate, a first at university. All despite a grim warning from the head: “If they miss a week of maths at seven, they never catch up.”Most importantly, it seems to have given her intellectual curiosity. And a healthy questioning of rules.Name and address suppliedAs a retired headteacher, I’m in total agreement with Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett. Many parents simply cannot afford to take a holiday when schools are closed, yet time away as a family is precious and above all can be educationally valuable and enriching. Never let schooling get in the way of your child’s education.Barbara FranceArnside, CumbriaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: If English devolution is to be a success, it must be done right | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Scott Hunter writes that the benefits of being a devolved authority have not yet arrived in Tees Valley, while John Hall calls for constitutional reform. Plus letters from Richard Dowling and Miland Joshi
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Scott Hunter writes that the benefits of being a devolved authority have not yet arrived in Tees Valley, while John Hall calls for constitutional reform. Plus letters from Richard Dowling and Miland Joshi
Content: Andy Burnham, left, and the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, visit a family centre in Sheffield on 31 July.Photograph: Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, left, and the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, visit a family centre in Sheffield on 31 July.Photograph: Pool PA/APDevolutionLettersIf English devolution is to be a success, it must be done rightResponding to an editorial,Scott Hunterwrites that the benefits of being a devolved authority have not yet arrived in Tees Valley, whileJohn Hallcalls for constitutional reform. Plus letters fromRichard DowlingandMiland JoshiWed 5 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareDevolution has become the flavour of the month (The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it, 31 July). The case is well argued and the need for such reform fits neatly into the situation we find in the Tees Valley – chronic underinvestment, lack of economic growth, depopulation, and so on.But the Tees Valley has had a devolved authority for 10 years and the benefits of devolution have not landed. The Tees Valley authority was issued abest value noticein April 2025, though there’s nothing to show for it.The new-age proponents of devolution, by ignoring how Tees Valley became its basket case, are missing something vital.Devolutionis discussed in economic terms in relation to the regions, and as political upheaval in relation to Westminster and the Treasury.What’s missing is acknowledgment of the political upheaval that it brings to the regions, and it is the weakness of that that the Tees Valley exemplifies. The mayor is the sole elected person in the authority. Leaders of local councils form the authority cabinet but do so in addition to their day jobs. Does the public know? No, because the only combined authority news in the local press comes from the authority’s own press releases. It’s not hard to find people on Teesside who believe that there’s been a jobs bonanza here.But the problem of political weakness within the authority remains. Devolution cannot succeed until this problem is addressed.Scott HunterEditor, Tees Valley MonitorAndy Burnhamis right to argue that England’s regions cannot deliver meaningful growth while power remains concentrated in Whitehall. Yet his intervention points to a deeper constitutional problem. England is being offered a form of devolution that remains inferior to the statutory settlements enjoyed by Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.While those nations have defined legislative frameworks setting out their powers and responsibilities, England’s regions remain dependent on piecemeal deals negotiated with central government.Burnham’s admiration for Germany’s postwarGrundgesetz(Basic Law) is therefore well placed. The law not only defines the relationship between federal and state governments but also commits the federation to equivalent living conditions across the country. It offers constitutional clarity, stability and fairness. England has no comparable settlement. Instead, its uncodified constitutional arrangements allow power to remain concentrated in Westminster, leaving regional government dependent on the centre for permission, funding and direction.If England is serious about rebalancing its economy, constitutional reform cannot stop at creating metro mayors or devolving selected powers. It requires a coherent constitutional settlement that places England’s regions on a secure and equal footing, replacing ad hoc devolution with a durable framework that disperses power by right rather than by ministerial discretion.John HallAlliance for YorkshireIf devolution is to mean anything real at all, then actual power must be devolved, which would mean it sometimes being used for purposes some would not approve of. Your editorial was arguing for devolution only for your approved purposes (transport, skills and industry, not tax giveaways). Devolution for me but not for thee?Richard DowlingLeighton Buzzard, BedfordshireRegarding the article (Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham, 2 August), we should note that the argument about inequality doesn’t hold when we regard countries with inequality just as great as ours (if not worse), which have written constitutions, such as the United States and South Africa.Regional devolution, or a written constitution, are not panaceas, because any system can only work as well as the humans operating it. If we are to have a written constitution, it might be well to make it as brief as possible, concentrating on principles rather than specific rules, so as to preserve the ability of the government to act nimbly when required, especially in crises.One possible useful ingredient might be a rotating “citizens’ jury” within the Lords for handling complex or difficult issues, with the usual peers serving as expert consultors. The result would be an influential advisory body as a collective, with the members being temporary “peers” while they serve. Primary power would remain in the Commons, as now, with MPs who have a mandate from their constituents.Miland JoshiBirminghamHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: This is your in-flight comedian speaking | Comedy | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Jimmy Cricket | Creative science | Clacton vote | Humanists and humanity | Short showers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Jimmy Cricket | Creative science | Clacton vote | Humanists and humanity | Short showers
Content: The comedian Jimmy Cricket, pictured here in 1982, passed away on Monday at age 80.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe comedian Jimmy Cricket, pictured here in 1982, passed away on Monday at age 80.Photograph: ShutterstockBrief lettersComedyLettersThis is your in-flight comedian speakingJimmy Cricket | Creative science | Clacton vote | Humanists and humanity | Short showersWed 5 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareI remember fondly Jimmy Cricket (No smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy Cricket, 4 August) taking over the intercom from the cabin crew who had just announced our flight to Manchester would be delayed. Groans from the passengers quickly gave way to laughter as Jimmy read a letter from the mammy in Ireland and the next hour passed so enjoyably that when the pilot announced take off, disappointment could be heard.Martin BrayfordAltrincham, CheshireGoodness me, Mick Foster (Letters, 3 August)! Don’t you know that “creativity” is the sole prerogative of the arts? As someone who has recently lived through Bradford City of Culture 2025, I have also learned that a “creative” is someone who paints or is a poet. No way can scientists be allowed in. What next? Engineers?Les BrookSaltaire, West YorkshireAs the byelection approaches (Report, 3 August), it might be worth reminding Clacton voters that the last comedian chosen by a European electorate turned out to be very serious indeed.Shareen CampbellBristolYears ago, I attended a humanist funeral (Letters, 2 August). I was excited to discover a form of funeral in which we didn’t have to believe in God, but this was spoiled by the celebrant explaining that we should believe in humanity. I couldn’t do that either.Stuart WaterworthTavistock, DevonTo use less water, I have reduced my shower time to one minute and 15 seconds; I’ve had no complaints so far from my nearest and dearest.Julia DraperBathHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: England’s climate is changing and our planting must change with it | Plants | The Guardian
description: Letter: We are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate, writes Richard Eltringham
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: We are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate, writes Richard Eltringham
Content: Hyde Park in London on 31 July. ‘We can keep insisting that every garden, park and verge must resemble a 1790s botanical inventory, or we can face the obvious – the climate those plants evolved for no longer exists.’Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenHyde Park in London on 31 July. ‘We can keep insisting that every garden, park and verge must resemble a 1790s botanical inventory, or we can face the obvious – the climate those plants evolved for no longer exists.’Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAPlantsLettersEngland’s climate is changing and our planting must change with itWe are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate, writesRichard EltringhamWed 5 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareYour report (Half of England officially in ‘exceptionally serious’ drought, 29 July) makes me think that perhaps it’s time to admit what horticulturists have whispered for years: the native‑plants‑only doctrine has had its day. We can keep insisting that every garden, park and verge must resemble a 1790s botanical inventory, or we can face the obvious – the climate those plants evolved for no longer exists.We are trying to keep a pre‑industrial flora alive in a post‑industrial climate. Oak saplings are crisping, beech woods are browning, and “rewilded” meadows are going from hopeful to tinderbox in a single heatwave. Meanwhile, drought‑tolerant non‑natives – Mediterranean shrubs, prairie perennials, desert grasses – sit ready to do the job: hold soil, feed pollinators, stay green, stay alive.This isn’t heresy, it’s adaptation. If the choice is plant non‑natives or watch landscapes die, then the path is obvious. Clinging to botanical nationalism while ecosystems collapse is not conservation; it’s sentimentality. England’s climate has changed. Our planting palette must change with it.Richard EltringhamLeicesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Fifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meeting | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: A Fifa statement said Gianni Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations over the World Cup sell-off
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: A Fifa statement said Gianni Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations over the World Cup sell-off
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (right), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström, appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Wafcon group game as a show of solidarity.Photograph: CAF TV/YouTubeView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (right), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström, appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Wafcon group game as a show of solidarity.Photograph: CAF TV/YouTubeGianni InfantinoFifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meetingStatement reveals Infantino wrote apologies to membersInfantino sorry for failing to consult on World Cup sell-offMatt HughesWed 5 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa on Wednesday night confirmed thatGianni Infantinowill remain as president after a meeting of its senior executives in Rabat.In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to theFifacouncil and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team.Infantino had spent the day in talks with Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, and chief legal officer, Emilio García Silvero, during which he expressed his determination to stay on in the face of mounting criticism from Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf, both of which have called for a review of Fifa’s governance.‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayRead moreIn another indication that he plans to carry on as before, Infantino will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the Fifa secretary general and members of the Fifa management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 Fifa member associations,” Fifa said in a statement. “In turn, the Fifa president reiterated his full support for the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa administration for their necessary and outstanding work in the delivery of his vision.“It was discussed and agreed that the processes, communications and interactions between the Fifa president, the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa management board that support the delivery of this vision can and should always be continuously improved in terms of their effectiveness and efficiency.“In this regard, Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will strengthen Fifa’s governance, help restore confidence in the organisation and enable us to prepare for the major events and challenges ahead in a united and transparent manner while continuing our mission to develop the game around the world.”While acknowledging that Infantino has apologised for his role in the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have seen 21% of Fifa’s commercial rights sold to private investors, the statement also insisted that Fifa will not tolerate further criticisms of its governance.Uefa is unlikely to be cowed however, with the European governing body continuing to search for a candidate to stand against Infantino in the presidential election next March, which will also take place in Rabat.“Mistakes made were acknowledged,” the statement continued. “It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently. It was further acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media.“In a separate letter to the Fifa council and Fifa member associations, an apology was made for these errors together with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again. A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the Fifa council at its next scheduled meeting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As previously communicated, the FFE proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa member associations and the Fifa council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, it was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.“There are always lessons to be learned, and Fifa will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework.“Fifa will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to examine how it can further support the development of the game through the Fifa Forward programme for the benefit of Fifa’s 211 member associations, the confederations and the regional associations.”Infantino and Grafström appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Women’s Africa Cup of Nations group game on Wednesday as a show of solidarity, having also written a jointly signed letter to Fifa council members and vice-presidents echoing the Fifa statement.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid agree club-record £115m deal for Yan Diomande and want to keep Vinícius | Real Madrid | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Content: Yan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APView image in fullscreenYan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APReal MadridReal Madrid agree club-record £115m deal for Yan Diomande and want to keep ViníciusForward becomes most expensive African playerClub are in positive talks with Vinícius JúniorEd AaronsWed 5 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of €135m (£115.7m) with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of warding off Arsenal’s interest inVinícius Júniorafter offering an improved contract to the Brazil forward.After several weeks of negotiations that saw Paris Saint-Germain pull out of the race, the deal for Diomande – the 19-year-old who joined the German side from Leganés last summer and starred for Côte d’Ivoire at the World Cup – was finally struck on Wednesday afternoon. It is understood that Madrid will pay an initial €125m plus another €10m in add-ons, a total that would eclipse the fee the Spanish side paid Borussia Dortmundto sign Jude Bellingham in 2023, believed to have been worth up to €134m including add-ons.Real Madrid ready to seal deal for Yan Diomande after PSG pull out of moveRead moreLeganés are due a 5% sell-on fee from any transfer. The teenager made only 10 appearances for their first team before being sold to Leipzig for €20m (£17.4m). Diomande, who was pictured arriving at Leipzig’s pre-season training camp in Austria on Wednesday, is expected to sign a contract until 2031 and becomes the most expensive African player in history, surpassing the £72mArsenalspent on Nicolas Pépé in 2019.His impending arrival is not thought to have any bearing on whether Vinícius stays in the Spanish capital. The Brazilian and his representatives, Roc Nation, held talks with Madrid officials on Wednesday over a contract extension, with Arsenal waiting in the wings if he decides to depart.Mikel Arteta’s side are understood to be ready to pay more than £100m for the 26-year-old who has less than a year of his contract remaining. But despite some reports that Vinícius had rejected Madrid’s latest contract offer, it is understood that he is now weighing up an improved deal closer to the €30m a season requested after what sources in Spain have described as positive talks. Vinícius said on Tuesday that Madrid’s new manager, José Mourinho, wants him to be “happy, cheerful ‌and playing my football” after returning to pre-season training following the World Cup.Arsenal, who have agreed a £75m deal to signhis Brazil teammate Bruno Guimarães from Newcastle, are believed to be exploring other options in attack should Vinícius opt to renew with Madrid.Barcelona’s sporting director, Deco, held talks with Atlético Madrid over Julián Alvarez on Wednesday in a bid to secure a deal for the Argentina forward but Arsenal are hoping that the 26-year-old could yet be persuaded to join them.Arsenal, who missed out on Morgan Rogers last month when the England forward joined Chelsea for a British record fee of £117m instead, have also been linked with PSG’s Bradley Barcola, who is wanted by Liverpool and valued at around £145m by the European champions.Explore more on these topicsReal MadridVinícius JúniorArsenalTransfer windowNewcastle UnitedRB LeipzignewsShareReuse this content

title: LIV Golf secures ‘lead investor’ until 2030 but future of star names still uncertain | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: The LIV chief, Scott O’Neil, refused to disclose the new funders of the business, but hopes Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm will stay
Author: Ewan Murray
