Headline: The LIV chief, Scott O’Neil, refused to disclose the new funders of the business, but hopes Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm will stay
Content: Scott O'Neil (right) will want top players such as Tyrrell Hatton (left) to stay with LIV after a new investor was found.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenScott O'Neil (right) will want top players such as Tyrrell Hatton (left) to stay with LIV after a new investor was found.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesLIV Golf secures ‘lead investor’ until 2030 but future of star names still uncertainLIV chief refuses to disclose new funders’ identitiesScott O’Neil hopes DeChambeau and Rahm will stayEwan MurrayWed 5 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLIVGolfhas secured a “lead investor” to safeguard its existence until 2030, although the agreement is unlikely to prevent a batch of high-profile players departing by the end of this year.Scott O’Neil, LIV’s chief executive, announced basic plans for the “next generation” of the tour on Wednesday while refusing to disclose the new funders of the business. After the withdrawal of backing from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, O’Neil has been engaged in a race against time to save his business.Cam Smith wants LIV Golf to live on but ‘100%’ would return to PGA TourRead more“We’re very fortunate that a lead investor has signed a term sheet approved by our board, which will carry and fund LIV going forward,” O’Neil said. “It’s very good news for us. At this point we are keeping the details of the deal, the investor, and much of what you might want to know in this second phase out of the media.”It is expected that this scenario could crystallise by the end of August, including with precise detail of who will play on LIV in 2027. Asked whether conclusion of the deal will protect the 2027 season, O’Neil said: “And 28 and 29 and 30.” He insisted the investor is one “of weight”.LIV’s current format involves 14 events per year and prize funds of $30m per tournament, split between individual and team prizes. Players have contracts with LIV linked to those terms. The business has lost huge sums, meaning an estimated $5bn of Saudi money was essential. From 2027, the plan is understood to involve a core of 10 events worth $10m each. Players will be given the majority of equity in the business.While generally LIV golfers have not spoken in public about potential pathways back towards the PGA Tour – partly because of contractual commitments – there is a widespread belief the change in circumstances overseen through necessity by O’Neil will trigger huge change. LIV coaxed golfers, often for hundreds of millions of dollars, from the PGA Tour from the point of its formation in 2021.Asked directly on thefutures of Bryson DeChambeauand Jon Rahm, LIV’s two star turns, O’Neil said: “I have all the time in the world for Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau. I think I’d be remiss in saying they’re not only two of the biggest, best golfers on the planet, but I think they’re some of the biggest stars in sports, let alone golf. [I] would certainly love them to come along for the ride and journey because they carry maybe more weight than anybody in the game and I have a lot of time for that.”“I think we have enough support from enough players, and we have such an interesting format and global format, I think we’ll do quite well in getting the right stars for this game.”DeChambeau’s scenario is complicated by perceived mutual indifference between him and the PGA Tour, plus the Californian’s floating of switching towards YouTube golf. Cameron Smith, Tyrrell Hatton and Dustin Johnson areother key nameswhose choice of upcoming playing domain will prove intriguing.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering victorious on stage five as Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravels | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes
Content: Demi Vollering celebrates after victory in stage five of the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering celebrates after victory in stage five of the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering victorious on stage five as Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravelsThree outstanding riders in race broke clear of pelotonPadding row intensifies after footage of male inspectionJeremy Whittlein Belleville-en-BeaujolaisWed 5 Aug 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePauline Ferrand-Prévot’s defence of herTour de France Femmestitle unravelled among the Beaujolais vineyards as the French rider lost even more ground to rivals Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Kasia Niewiadoma.The three outstanding riders in this year’s race broke clear of the peloton over the final steep gradients of Mont Brouilly, with 2023 Tour winner Vollering outsprinting overall race leader Reusser to take the fourth Tour stage win of her career.Tour de France Femmes: Demi Vollering wins stage five amid GC shake-up – live reactionRead more“Today was a really cool race,” Vollering said. “Every single rider of the team was part of it and I enjoy those victories the most. It’s even more special and beautiful because you do it all together. I thought I was not going to make it in the sprint and somehow I made it, so it was a huge relief. I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does, and I knew Marlen would gamble. I just had to try and I gave it my everything. I needed every single metre of the finishing straight.”On the unrelentingly hilly stage from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, Ferrand-Prévot’s Tour fell apart. The signs of her fading powers had comeas early as stage threeand were followed by a listless performance inTuesday’s stage four time trial.The fifth day of racing provided irrefutable confirmation of her vulnerability. “I think it’s unrecoverable,” she said of her five-minute deficit to her rivals.As Vollering, Reusser and Niewiadoma were descending from Mont Brouilly to the finish, Ferrand-Prévot was still riding up the steep climb with legs of lead. If her performance in the time trial had been unnerving, her capitulation among the vineyards was complete.Earlier in the day, Ferrand-Prévot’s hopes of reversing her overall deficit to Reusser and Vollering had been boosted by the news that, despite talk of the stagebeing rerouted due to the risk of wildfires, Friday’s stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux remains as scheduled.Although the climb to the summit of the Ventoux remains unaffected, the Vaucluse prefecture has banned public access to the nearby hills of the Dentelles de Montmirail, where two shorter climbs are routed, citing “the sensitivity of the massif and the risk of fire”. But that’s now become academic given the champion’s distance from the front of the race.After her disappointing time trial, dreams of a “PFP” bounceback were definitively shattered on the cruel slopes of the Col de Durbize, where the 2025 winner was left behind by a vicious acceleration from Vollering.View image in fullscreenPauline Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence is surely over after another disappointing stage.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesAs the lead group, containing Vollering, Reusser and the 2024 champion Niewiadoma moved further ahead, Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence crumbled in the heat of the Beaujolais afternoon. The best she can hope for now is a stage win.Meanwhile, the debate over Tuesday’s scrutiny of ridersregarding the illegal use of chest paddingto improve aerodynamics rumbled on, after riders union, the CPA, issued a statement demanding that such checks be undertaken in a “professional and respectful manner, that fully safeguards the dignity and privacy of every rider”.Tour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest paddingRead moreThe statement added that this was to “prevent any misunderstanding, controversy or unpleasant situations”.Initial reports suggested that the padding checks would be carried out by a female race commissaire, however footage screened by Flemish media showed a male commissaire making an initial inspection, in public view.The fears of illegal aerodynamic enhancement appear well founded however, as Gaël Le Bellec, a former world champion duathlete, now sports director of the Ma Petite Entreprise team competing in the Tour Femmes, acknowledged.“I’ve never had wind of it among the women,” he said, “but I know that triathletes particularly put bidons [drink bottles] under their kit on their chest to reduce aerodynamic drag.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Argentina’s Albornoz given four-match ban for intimidating referee after England defeat | Argentina rugby union team | The Guardian
description: The incident occurred after Argentina were denied a late try, with Tomás Albornoz’s ban beginning against South Africa on Saturday
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: The incident occurred after Argentina were denied a late try, with Tomás Albornoz’s ban beginning against South Africa on Saturday
Content: Tomás Albornoz accepted allegations of misconduct at a disciplinary hearing, and that his behaviour was intimidatory.Photograph: Gustavo Garello/APView image in fullscreenTomás Albornoz accepted allegations of misconduct at a disciplinary hearing, and that his behaviour was intimidatory.Photograph: Gustavo Garello/APArgentina rugby union teamArgentina’s Albornoz given four-match ban for intimidating referee after England defeatIncident occurred after Pumas were denied a late tryAlbornoz’s ban begins against South Africa on SaturdayGerard MeagherWed 5 Aug 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTomás Albornoz, the Argentina fly-half, has been banned for four matches for intimidating the referee after the full-time whistle ofEngland’s controversial victoryagainst the Pumas last month.Albornoz accepted allegations of misconduct at a disciplinary hearing, and that his behaviour was intimidatory. He will miss Argentina’s Test against South Africa on Saturday as well as their forthcoming double header with Australia and a Toulon fixture.RFU expects £10m loss off the back of England’s worst Six Nations campaignRead moreThe disciplinary committee noted that Albornoz made contact with the referee Angus Gardner and that the fly-half approached the Australian official on two occasions and had to be restrained by teammates.The incident occurred after Argentina were denied a last-gasp try against England, which would have given Albornoz a conversion attempt to draw the match, after a lengthy discussion between Gardner and the television match official Brett Cronan. Argentina felt they ought to have been awarded a penalty try, regardless of whether Bautista Delguy grounded the ball legally, for high tackles by Noah Calouri and Henry Slade as the Pumas winger went for the line.Gardner’s ultimate decision to disallow the try ensured England ran out 31-24 victors in Santiago del Estero, affording the under-fire head coach Steve Borthwick a welcome sigh of relief.While Albornoz accepted his actions amounted to intimidation of Gardner, he denied that his behaviour was abusive, insulting, offensive or threatening.World Rugbyand the disciplinary committee agreed, determining Albornoz’s actions were comparable to the low-end entry point for contact with a match official, which carries a six-match suspension.The committee determined that a four-match ban was more appropriate, having taken into consideration Albornoz’s early acceptance of the charge, his undertakings to issue public and private written apologies, and his previously clear disciplinary record. Gardner, meanwhile, will referee the third Test of South Africa’s forthcoming four-match series against New Zealand.“Tomás Albornoz has been suspended for four matches after admitting misconduct arising from interactions with match officials following Argentina’s Nations Championship match against England on 18 July,” World Rugby said in a statement. “In determining misconduct under regulation 18, the disciplinary committee noted that the Argentina fly-half accepted the misconduct allegations. In particular, he accepted that his conduct, taken as a whole, was intimidatory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The committee accepted that contact with referee Angus Gardner, although limited in nature, occurred while disputing a match official’s decision and formed part of that overall course of intimidatory conduct. The committee also noted that Albornoz approached the referee on two separate occasions and had to be restrained by teammates.”Explore more on these topicsArgentina rugby union teamEngland rugby union teamWorld RugbyRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Super League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRL | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: NRL officials are touring Super League clubs ahead of a potential investment as Wigan and Warrington announce they will face each other in Dublin next April
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: NRL officials are touring Super League clubs ahead of a potential investment as Wigan and Warrington announce they will face each other in Dublin next April
Content: Wigan Warriors’ CEO Kris Radlinski says his club is “100%” behind a potential deal with the NRL.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWigan Warriors’ CEO Kris Radlinski says his club is “100%” behind a potential deal with the NRL.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockRugby leagueSuper League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRLAustralian officials touring clubs to gauge moodWigan and Warrington set date for Dublin clashAaron BowerWed 5 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNRL officials have arrived in ­England to hold talks with clubs as the prospect of a groundbreaking deal withSuper Leaguenears completion, while two of the competition’s heavyweights, Wigan Warriors and Warrington Wolves, confirmed they will lead an on-the-road weekend to Dublin in 2027.Rugby league’s two premier club competitions have been in discussions for most of this year about a deal that would see the NRL invest a significant sum into Super League, while taking authoritative control of the competition in a bid to transform its long-term fortunes. That investment would also ensure the financial security of clubs. Both competitions put talks on hold while they finalised their broadcast details; the NRL has just completed a A$5.3bn (£2.8bn) deal for its rights, while Super League expects to confirm in the next week how its new-look broadcast deal will be shaped. Sky Sports is expected to show two or three games a week, with the rest of the fixtures streamed or broadcast elsewhere.London in a very different limbo: wins alone will not realise Broncos’ dreamRead moreBut theNRLhas now made Super League investment its number one priority. The Guardian has been told by multiple clubs that they have been visited by officials from Australia, or expect a visit in the coming days. The belief is that Australian figures are keen to get a deeper understanding of the mood among clubs as they consider a proposal from Super League to invest.That is the clearest sign yet that a deal is close, with Super League’s leading official, Rhodri Jones, saying: “We’re very hopeful that we’ll make some significant progress with the NRL over the next seven days. “We’ve been engaged with them since May but they’ve now done their TV deal, so I can say it feels like we’re their top priority.” It’s still with them to come back to us. We’re hopeful we’ll get something very soon.”View image in fullscreenWigan are likely to ask their former player and current Ireland rugby union coach, Andy Farrell, to help promote the Dublin match.Photograph: Brendan Moran/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBoth Wigan and Warrington, who became the first Super League clubs to make the trip to Las Vegas last year with the NRL, have long been advocates of Australian investment and governance. The Warriors’ CEO, Kris Radlinski, reiterated that backing on Wednesday at the announcement of their Dublin clash with Warrington at Leinster’s RDS Arena on Saturday 24 April next year. When asked if Wigan supported were still supportive of the NRL deal, Radlinski said: “100%. As we have been from the start. What they’re doing in the NRL is fantastic. I think it’s the start of a significant few months for the sport. We’re at a point where we’ll find out our broadcasting future at a time when our NRL counterparts are closing in on an offer.”Wigan and Warrington are hopeful of a capacity 20,000 crowd in Dublin, with the Warriors likely to lean on the Ireland rugby coach and Wigan legend, Andy Farrell, to help promote the game. Hull FC are in talks about moving a home game on Sunday 25 April to the same venue to make it a weekend-long event for Super League.Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueSuper LeagueNRLSport politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’ | Mohamed Salah | The Guardian
description: In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a reality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a reality
Content: Mohamed Salah has been honoured with a mural on the walls of a youth centre named after the Egyptian forward at his home village of Nagrig.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyView image in fullscreenMohamed Salah has been honoured with a mural on the walls of a youth centre named after the Egyptian forward at his home village of Nagrig.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyMohamed SalahMohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a realityMelissa ReddyWed 5 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe entrance to Al Mokawloon Al Arab’s youth sector feels imposing. At first it is confusing to pinpoint the reason. Is it the facade; a mesh of thick concrete slabs, a marble-like trim that alters in colour depending on the light, and the no-nonsense black steel gate? Perhaps it is the stately signage of white block letters in Arabic juxtaposed against the dark background, with satellite pieces of information and announcements signifying importance. But to stop and pay attention to buildings around Nasr City in eastern Cairo is to notice that the blend of functional and decorative elements of the entrance, down to even the font and array of notices, is not unique.The building’s aura can be explained by the main image above its gates, and the knowledge that to walk through them is to follow the footsteps a history-maker took from the age of 14. Mohamed Salah’s face has pride of place above the gates; it is a reminder of where he’s been, but more pertinently, of why it is important to marry talent with discipline and determination. The truth is he has achieved the impossible.Trabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talksRead moreHamdi Nouh, Salah’s first coach at Al Mokawloon and who he has referred to as a “second father”, knows that is because “he was ready to sacrifice everything, he wanted to work hard, and liked to learn”. It sounds simple, until you start drilling at the heart of what it means for a boy from Nagrig to endure a nine-hour round trip five days a week simply to train in Cairo. Salah’s route has become so well known, you can read the tale of the minimum four buses he needed to take each way in Chinese, Spanish and every other major language. One from the T-junction at the edge of his village to reach Basyoun. The transfer from there to the capital of the Gharbia Governorate, Tanta. The great slog of around 100 kilometres to reach the rush of Ramses Square. A connection from Cairo’s chaotic central transport hub to Nasr City. And, on the luckier days, a ride close to the club’s gates to spare Salah having to run almost two kilometres up a steep hill, to be on time for his training session. After four hours at the centre, he would leave to do that all again in reverse.The problem with summarising the journey in this way, as it has been done since 2017 when Salah started shifting the parameters for greatness in the Premier League, is that it omits the reality of what this daily grind truly entailed. When Nouh underlines sacrifice, part of it was Salah giving up his youth to sit shoulder slammed into shoulder, bodies filling up every available inch of the microbus and often even hanging off it, racing to the next stop and against the anxiety of missing a connection in a schedule that had no rhyme nor reason, with only enough cash for the exact journey. He was too respectful to ask his father for more, even though there was no margin for error. Salah weirdly enjoyed rather than endured the stressful odyssey. “I didn’t feel tired travelling when I was young,” he would reflect in 2022. “It’s because I was doing something I wanted, chasing a dream I had to reach. I wasn’t seeing my situation, I was seeing my goal. These are days I sit and think about, I’ll never forget them and I still smile now when I remember everything.”View image in fullscreenEgyptian boys in Nagrig look up to Mohamed Salah and hope to follow in his footsteps.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyIt is not the same for Umm Mohamed (the Mother of Mohamed), who was averse to her eldest son spending only two hours at school, between seven and nine in the morning, and venturing so far away from his village, when lanes were seen as a mere suggestion and dangerous driving was the only type. Her memories were of worry and fear prompted by the high number of crashes involving microbuses. One major accident along her son’s route provoked sheer panic, which only increased as his phone rang unanswered. She tried calling over 20 times, and while Salah insists exhaustion didn’t grip him during his great trek, he didn’t pick up because he was fast asleep. She was also concerned if he had enough money, as was her husband, Salah Ghaly, who worked as a government administrator and traded in jasmine, Nagrig’s greatest export. He funded Salah’s football path, first to Ittihad in Basyoun, which was only a half-hour trip, then on to the Othmason club in Tanta, 90 minutes away, all before he became a teenager, followed by the almighty mission to Al Mokawloon.Salah was eight when he started training there and rushed at opponents with the fearlessness of a microbus driver. “He was small, but his left foot and his shots were powerful,” Ghamri Abdel-Hameed el-Saadani, who was the juniors coach at the youth centre, says. “He was fast and could do things with the ball the other boys couldn’t.” Salah’s father knew it, and despite his own apprehensions about the big city and how it could swallow and spit out young hopefuls, he told Umm Mohamed they were doing the right thing.Back to the entrance of Al Mokawloon’s youth sector, and just behind the black steel gates, lies a story that hasn’t travelled the world like the bus trip. One of Salah’s teammates had suggested they could stay at his uncle’s house in Greater Cairo for the week. It was located in the 10th of Ramadan City and it took plenty of convincing for his parents to green-light the sleepover. Salah’s father gave him 60 Egyptian pounds and he set off. When they arrived at the house, in the black of the night, his friend’s uncle was not there. They were stuck, with not enough money or knowledge to find other lodgings.All Salah knew of Cairo were the roads through it to train at Al Mokawloon. His friend, whose name he doesn’t want to reveal to avoid the media frenzy that accompanies any detail about his life, suggested the house of someone else he knew not too far away. When they got there, Salah encountered a bigger problem. The dwelling was in a cemetery, a saddening – and scary – symptom of Cairo’s severe housing shortage and high population density. Salah was not going to stay in the necropolis. His friend had one final plan: he knew an on-site administrator at Al Mokawloon who could let them in. Right behind the steel gate, they laid out the sheets they had packed on the floor into two makeshift beds.View image in fullscreenMohamed Salah began his career at Al Mokawloon in 2010 before moving to Europe.Photograph: Courtesy of Al MokawloonSalah used his shoes as a pillow and set his alarm for 6am so the pair could be up before anyone caught them and the administrator got in trouble. They packed up their bedding and headed off, returning to the complex at 9am as though they had just arrived. The sleeping arrangement stayed secret but needed to be amended; there was too much jeopardy being so close to the entrance. The next day, the duo slept on Field 2 of the four pitches, in the open under the cold night sky. In the morning, they would again go into covert mode and Salah enjoyed that he could be early for training.Salah had already packed in a lifetime’s worth of sacrifice, effort and lessons by his 18th birthday. The moment he will never forget, however, was when he joined the first team group and moved into the Al Mokawloon’s residences. “Not everyone could stay there, so psychologically I felt like I became someone, like a star,” Salah would recall. “I used to see players finish training and go upstairs, while I would leave to take the journey back to Nagrig. I’d think, ‘One day I’ll go up there’.” He would go higher than any other Egyptian footballer in history.This is an edited extract from Only Mo Salah: An intimate portrait of the Egyptian King by Melissa Reddy, which is published by Orion Publishing and available from 13 August.Explore more on these topicsMohamed SalahLiverpoolEgypt football teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Italy to place all 27 of its major cities on highest heat alert | Italy | The Guardian
description: Move comes as fourth heatwave of summer intensifies, edging temperatures in some areas close to 40C
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Move comes as fourth heatwave of summer intensifies, edging temperatures in some areas close to 40C
Content: People cooling off near the Colosseum in Rome. Authorities have warned people to avoid direct sunlight during the hottest hours, to stay indoors where possible and drink at least 1.5 litres of water a day.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople cooling off near the Colosseum in Rome. Authorities have warned people to avoid direct sunlight during the hottest hours, to stay indoors where possible and drink at least 1.5 litres of water a day.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersItalyItaly to place all 27 of its major cities on highest heat alertMove comes as fourth heatwave of summer intensifies, edging temperatures in some areas close to 40CAngela Giuffridain RomeWed 5 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItaly is to place all of its 27 major cities, from Trieste in the north to Palermo in the south, under the highest heat alert as the fourth heatwave to hit the country this summer intensifies.A red alert means there is a higher chance of an emergency owing to the health risk posed by prolonged extreme temperatures to the entire population.Twenty-five cities were on red alert on Wednesday, with two more to be added on Thursday, the health ministry said. It is the first time this year that all 27 cities monitored by the health ministry’s heat surveillance system have been placed on maximum alert.Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis BabouliasRead moreThe cities on red alert are: Turin, Bolzano, Milan, Genoa, Venice, Verona, Trieste, Bologna, Florence, Perugia, Rome, Naples, Ancona, Pescara, Bari, Campobasso, Reggio Calabria, Palermo and Cagliari as well as Catania, Messina, Brescia, Viterbo, Latina, Rieti, Frosinone and Civitavecchia.As temperatures in some areas of Italy have edged up towards 40C in recent days, authorities have warned people to avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 6pm, to stay indoors where possible and drink at least 1.5 litres of water a day. Other guidelines include avoiding fizzy drinks, coffee, alcohol and heavy meals, wearing light clothes and never leaving children or animals in cars.The extreme heat, which scientists say is driven by the human-caused climate crisis, is not forecast to let up for at least a week.Europehas warmed about twice as fast as the global average.View image in fullscreenA tourist cools down from a misting fan in Rome.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe current heatwave has been linked to four deaths in recent days, including a 19-year-old tomato-picker and a 40-year-old carpenter, who were both working in industrial areas of the Lombardy region. A security guard in Bologna is thought to have suffered a fatal heat-related illness while in his car.This year’s heatwaves have also exacerbated a drought in the Po valley, home to Italy’s longest river, after a dry spring. More than 100 towns across Piedmont and Lombardy are dealing with water supply difficulties, with some using tanker trucks to fill drinking water reserves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe drought is putting a severe strain on Italian agriculture, with farmers saying the extreme heat is affecting crop yields. The heatwaves have also accelerated grape ripening in some areas, while milk production has fallen by 10% owing to dairy cows eating less because of heat stress.Lorenzo Giovannini, an atmospheric physicist at the University of Trento, told Ansa news agency the heatwaves this summer were already above average compared with previous years for their intensity and duration. He said that although it was difficult to predict when each heatwave would occur, the climate crisis was making them “longer and more intense”.Major tourist cities, such as Rome, are striving to mitigate the impact of the heat by providing free access to air-conditioned cinemas and cultural venues during the hottest hours of the day, and extending the opening hours of monuments including the Colosseum and Pantheon to allow for evening visits.Explore more on these topicsItalyExtreme heatClimate crisisDroughtWaterEurope weatherEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Toronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother Kindia | Toronto | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
Content: The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother.Photograph: Toronto ZooView image in fullscreenThe zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother.Photograph: Toronto ZooTorontoToronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother KindiaThe 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo saidMaya YangWed 5 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTorontoZoo has announced the birth of a female pygmy hippo calf.Kindia, the zoo’s 20-year-old pygmy hippo, started showing signs of labor at around 8.15am last Sunday, it said. Around four hours later, the calf’s feet emerged and after 1.5 hours of active labor, Kindia successfully gave birth to the baby pygmy hippo.Within 15 minutes of birth, the calf began trying to stand and was “confidently navigating the space” a few hours later, the zoo said, adding that the calf was seen nursing approximately 4.5 hours after birth.The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother. According to the zoo, the newborn is Kindia’s third calf. Kindia became pregnant after she was introduced to a 31-year-old male pygmy hippo named Harvey for eight days in January.Gene-edited beagles may offer a future option for people with dog allergiesRead more“This wonderful news comes with both hope and caution,” the zoosaid. “Kindia successfully raised her daughter Penelope in 2018, and calf survival for this species can be challenging. Our team will continue to closely monitor both mom and calf around the clock during these important first days to ensure they continue to progress well together.”Noting the species’ endangered status on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list, Dolf DeJong, the Toronto Zoo’s CEO, said: “Welcoming a pygmy hippo calf is far more than a celebration of new life. Pygmy hippos are endangered, and their wild populations continue to decline due to habitat loss and human pressures.“This birth represents the critical role modern accredited zoos play in conservation, scientific collaboration, and maintaining healthy populations that contribute to the long-term survival of the species.”Only approximately 2,000 to 3,000 pygmy hippos are believed to remain in the wild.With adult pygmy hippos weighing anywhere from 330lb to 660lb and standing around 2.5 tall, the species are native to the forests and swamps of west Africa. In recent decades however, pygmy hippos have facedgrowing threatsto their habitat including logging, mining, farming activities as well as human settlement.Explore more on these topicsTorontoAnimalsCanadaWildlifeAmericasZoosnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial records | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm
Content: BBC Broadcasting House, London.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBBC Broadcasting House, London.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial recordsPresident has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harmGaya GuptaWed 5 Aug 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s legal team is making an 11th-hour attempt to block acourt orderthat would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster.Trump claims that the BBC’s 2024 documentary on the January 6 attacks have damaged the president’s business interests. In July, a Miami-based judge ruled that the president would have to start handing over detailed financial records to theBBCby 6 August. The records would reveal details into the hundreds of businesses owned by the US president’s family trust.Trump immigration crackdown ensnares families of US troopsRead moreTrump’s attorneys asked the court on Wednesday to temporarily pause the enforcement of the court order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”.Trump’s lawyers also asked the court to amend their initial lawsuit to instead focus on the “reputation harm” that was caused by the documentary, which would keep necessary disclosures “proportional to the needs of the case”, the lawyers said.While it is unclear what Trump’s net worth is, recentfinancial disclosuresshowed that he had made more than $2.2bn during his first year back in office.The lawsuit against the BBC is one of Trump’s several recent attempts to wage legal battles against media outlets that publish critical coverage of him. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys tried to argue that a $10bndefamation suitbrought against the Wall Street Journal should go to a trial after it reported on a “bawdy” letter the president reportedly included in a birthday book for the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump’s justice department also issued and thenrecalledsubpoenas to New York Times journalists after the paper reported on security concerns with the Air Force One presidential jet.Trump’s initial lawsuit concerns a scene in the BBC documentary, entitled Trump, A Second Chance, that spliced lines from a speech the president made on 6 January 2021. The clip made it appear like Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol. The BBC has apologized for the edit but argued the defamation claims have no merit.Trump recentlyclaimedthat the BBC “used AI” to insert words into his speech, which the network has categorically denied.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpBBCnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022  | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means
Content: Of the total prosecuted, 628 had arrived by small boat.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOf the total prosecuted, 628 had arrived by small boat.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumMore than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular meansDiane TaylorWed 5 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 1,100 people, including survivors of torture and trafficking, have been convicted of illegally arriving in the UK since 2022, according to freedom of information data.TheHome Officeintroduced the offence of illegal arrival in 2022 in a bid to deter those planning to come to the UK by small boat or by other irregular means such as lorries.The decision was widely condemned at the time because the refugee convention states that those seeking sanctuary should not be criminalised for the way they travel, as they often do not have the option to move legally from an unsafe country to a safe one.FoI data obtained from theHome Officeby the criminologist Dr Victoria Taylor, a research fellow at the University of Manchester, reveals 1,109 people were prosecuted for illegal arrival between July 2022 and January 2026.The data shows 628 arrived on a small boat, 296 of whom were captured on surveillance drone footage steering a dinghy. Others had previous immigration history in the UK.Just 12 people have been convicted of the separate offence of facilitation, after steering the dinghies they arrived on. It is harder for the Home Office and Crown Prosecution Service to secure evidence that people on a dinghy were involved in organising a journey across the Channel than to prosecute them for illegal arrival.Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fireRead morePeople have been identified as having their “hand on the tiller” for many reasons, including having boating experience, steering in return for discounted passage, taking it in turns, or being under duress.In one illegal arrival case, the Home Office settled a judicial review relating to a trafficking survivor fromSouth Sudanwho was forced at gunpoint to pilot a small boat. Officials have now agreed to ensure greater protection for trafficking victims in these cases.Emily Soothill, partner at Deighton Pierce Glynn, who represented the man, said: “Unfortunately it is clear from our client’s case that potential victims of trafficking are regularly being convicted for illegal arrival and imprisoned for many months. The concessions made in our client’s case underline the need for a robust and consistent application of the UK’s modern slavery framework to prevent survivors of trafficking from being wrongly treated as criminals.”Some of those convicted of the various offences were survivors of torture and trafficking, and there were at least 30 age disputed children among them, 19 of whom had spent time in adult prisons.The organisation Captain Support UK has worked with hundreds of people imprisoned in illegal arrival cases, all of whom soughtasylumin the UK in the hours before they were arrested.A spokesperson said: “We see first-hand the negative impact these prosecutions have on people and their families. We urgently call on the government to stop imprisoning people on the move. No one should be put in prison for seeking safety and a better life.”Taylor said: “The process of who is selected for prosecution is arbitrary and cruel.”She added that the most of those imprisoned for illegal arrival since 2022 had claimed asylum in the hours before they were arrested. Many have been granted asylum since their release or have been recognised as victims of trafficking, or both.“There are serious questions about the compatibility of these prosecutions with the refugee convention, which was drafted to prevent states from penalising refugees for how they seek safety. There is no evidence to support the government’s claims that these prosecutions will ‘deter’ people from attempting to cross the Channel,” Taylor said.The Home Office has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFreedom of informationHome OfficeMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alarming surge in bluetongue disease reported among UK sheep | Farm animals | The Guardian
description: Farmers advised to vaccinate after recent hot weather provides ideal conditions for virus-carrying midges
Author: Bibi van der Zee
Headline: Farmers advised to vaccinate after recent hot weather provides ideal conditions for virus-carrying midges
Content: Bluetongue is not necessarily fatal but makes sheep ill, presenting as high fever and swelling of the lips and tongue.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenBluetongue is not necessarily fatal but makes sheep ill, presenting as high fever and swelling of the lips and tongue.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAFarm animalsAlarming surge in bluetongue disease reported among UK sheepFarmers advised to vaccinate after recent hot weather provides ideal conditions for virus-carrying midgesBibi van der ZeeWed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been an alarming surge in the number of sheep affected by an outbreak of bluetongue in the UK, and farmers whose livestock are at risk are being urged to move them out of areas where midges are plentiful.The viral disease, which does not necessarily kill sheep but makes them ill and can have a long recovery time, presents as high fever and swelling of the lips and tongue. The tongue may go blue and even protrude from the mouth.More than 590 cases were reported last week, according to the National Sheep Association (NSA).The virus is transmitted via biting midges (culicoides) and its arrival in the UK is associated with global heating. The World Organisation for Animal Health reported in 2024 that although the virus had historically “been endemic in the tropics and subtropics where temperature and humidity are ideal for biting midge survival … it began to migrate to the Mediterranean basin and southern Europe in the late 1990s” and was first recorded in the UK in 2006.The National Farmers’ Union vice-president, Robyn Munt, said: “Bluetongue is continuing to spread at an alarming rate and is a significant concern for livestock farmers across the country. The disease is creating additional uncertainty and financial pressures for many businesses, with members doing everything possible to protect their animals.“To reduce the risk, farmers are moving high-risk or non-vaccinated stock away from wet, low-lying or sheltered areas and keeping vulnerable animals housed during dawn and dusk when midge activity peaks, all of which is added pressure on farmers and forage stocks during this challenging weather period.”View image in fullscreenA sheep with bluetongue at a farm in the Netherlands in 2024.Photograph: Nick Gammon/AFP/Getty ImagesDominic Elson, who farms sheep in Devon, said he lost one of his flock on Wednesday: “I was saying goodbye to a lovely old ewe that has been on the farm for over 10 years and it’s heartbreaking to see the bluetongue virus take her down.”He said he had been frustrated by what he regards as the lack of preparedness of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), and the failure of the self-reporting system. Farmers are required to report the disease but he said the phone line appeared to be overwhelmed and it was difficult to get through.This might mean the numbers were being significantly underestimated, he said, pointing out that although the disease was not always fatal, an outbreak in the Netherlands led to the deaths of more than 4% of the national herd between September and December 2023.“With the closure of thebasic payments systemand the reduction in budget available for agri-environment schemes, upland sheep farmers are already teetering on the brink,” Elson said. “This outbreak could push some over the edge.”The NSA’s chief executive, Phil Stocker, said: “The number of reported cases shot up last week to over 590, from just 115 the previous week. The majority are being seen in the south-west ofEngland– clearly a serious hotspot for this midge-borne virus. As you would expect, calls on stocks of vaccines are increasing and stocks will be reducing but we are assured that vaccine manufacturers are doing what they can to ensure demand can be met.”He said there seemed to be some confusion over whether to vaccinate, given that full immunity took 28 days. He said: “A level of protection is likely to be reached earlier, particularly if stock were vaccinated last season. Additionally, we have several months of midge activity ahead of us and it is highly advisable that breeding males and females are vaccinated ahead of mating.”A National Audit Office report last year said the UK may be underprepared for a serious animal disease outbreak. Stocker toldFarmer’s Weeklythat surveillance had successfully identified infected premises but testing only three animals on affected holdings meant the true scale of infection was unknown.A spokesperson for Defra said: “We recognise this is an incredibly difficult time for animal keepers who are on the frontline of this disease, and we are monitoring the situation closely. We continue to work closely with industry representatives to ensure that keepers are kept up to date with developments and that issues and concerns are addressed promptly.”An Animal and Plant Health Agency spokesperson said the virus was circulating in England, particularly the south-west, and parts ofWales. They said the recent hot and humid weather had been favourable for midge populations, which had probably contributed to the increased numbers of cases.“Livestock keepers should remain vigilant and report any suspicions of disease to APHA,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage all farmers and keepers to discuss vaccination with their vet as this is the most effective way of protecting their animals.”Explore more on these topicsFarm animalsFarmingAnimalsEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in Washington state wildfire was questioned about blazes last year | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Aaron Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails fire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Aaron Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails fire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee
Content: Chimneys are seen where houses once stood in a residential community during the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington, on Tuesday.Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChimneys are seen where houses once stood in a residential community during the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington, on Tuesday.Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresSuspect in Washington state wildfire was questioned about blazes last yearAaron Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails fire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to fleeDani AnguianoWed 5 Aug 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 22.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWashington stateman accused of starting a wildfire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee around Spokane was previously questioned in connection with two fire investigations last year, according to court documents.Authorities allege that Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, started Old Trails fire, one of three major wildfires burning in Spokane county in north-eastern Washington. He was arrested on Monday and booked on suspicion of first-degree arson.Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the areaRead moreThe Old Trails fire is one of more than a dozen large blazes burning in Washington. The state has faced devastating fires in recent days amid what officials have described as an “extraordinary” fire season in the Pacific north-west due to extreme heat, drought and limited resources.Farinacci has denied that he set the Old Trails fire.The fires burning around Spokane have scorched more than 10,000 acres. Officials reported that cooler weather and higher relative humidity have aided firefighters in recent days, allowing them to establish containment lines along all three fires.Crews are now focused on strengthening containment, and preparing for the return of critical fire weather this week and over the weekend.John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, has said Farinacci was first questioned shortly after the Old Trails fire began, after he was identified by witnesses who saw him kneeling in the brush near the fire’s origin.“He was bent over in the brush, acting nervous,” Paul Child, who was driving in the area with his grandson, told the Associated Press. “You get the feeling this guy’s up to something.”Farinacci had waterproof matches, cigarettes and a butane lighter in his posession, authorities say. Police arrested him on Monday after an investigators ruled out other possible causes of the fire, and learned that he had been questioned in connection with other fires.In July 2025, there were several “bus-sized” fires in an area near the Spokane River and Farinacci’s apartment. Police searching for a wildfire suspect at a state park the following month came upon Farinacci sitting on a bench “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. Law enforcement took photos of him and according to court documents he was wearing a green T-shirt like the one he was seen in on Saturday.While he was questioned in the two investigations, he was not charged.Since Farinacci’s arrest in connection with the Old Trails fire, a clearer picture of his criminal history has emerged. He previously served roughly a decade in prison for manslaughter and aggravated assault in the 2010 killing of his father. At age 21, he shot and killed his father after an argument in a family home in Arizona.He was released from probation in early 2024, and a probation officer said he had a stable residence with his girlfriend and her family, but had not completed a mental health evaluation or domestic violence treatment.Farinacci is currently being held on $1m bail.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWildfiresWashington stateWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘Cockroach Lord’ who names new species after Tolkien and Pokémon characters | Invertebrates | The Guardian
description: Cristian Lucañas has discovered multiple species of cockroach in the Philippines, and believes there’s far more to the much-maligned insect than meets the eye
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: Cristian Lucañas has discovered multiple species of cockroach in the Philippines, and believes there’s far more to the much-maligned insect than meets the eye
Content: Entomologist Cristian Lucañas, who says cockroaches are misunderstood, with some of his specimens at the University of the Philippines Los Banos, south of Manila.Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEntomologist Cristian Lucañas, who says cockroaches are misunderstood, with some of his specimens at the University of the Philippines Los Banos, south of Manila.Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty ImagesInvertebrate of the year 2026InvertebratesThe ‘Cockroach Lord’ who names new species after Tolkien and Pokémon charactersCristian Lucañas has discovered multiple species of cockroach in the Philippines, and believes there’s far more to the much-maligned insect than meets the eyeThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 04.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Cristian Lucañas tells people about his job, their response is normally a mix of shock and confusion. “The majority would actually be questioning why,” says Lucañas, 32, who is the only entomologist specialising in cockroaches in thePhilippines, where he is known as the “Cockroach Lord”.He recalls one person, apparently perplexed at the insects’ existence, asking simply: “Did God create cockroaches?” Others seek advice on how best to kill them.Cockroaches have serious reputational issues. They haverepeatedly been rankedamong the most hated of all insects on the planet – more disliked than mosquitoes,one of the world’s deadliest creatures. The loathing dates back thousands of years: ancient Egyptians resorted to a spell to chase away “vile” cockroaches. There is even a term, katsaridaphobia, for people who are afraid of them.Lucañas says cockroaches are misunderstood. “Of course, household cockroaches are unsightly,” he says, but adds that the pests that scuttle across kitchen floors and fly out of drains arenormally Germanor American cockroaches, which make up just a fraction of the thousands of cockroach species that exist globally. “They’re not a good representative for the other cockroaches,” he adds.View image in fullscreenCristian Lucañas on a nocturnal search for cockroaches on the bark of a fallen coconut tree.Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty ImagesMost cockroach species don’t even live near humans. In the Philippines, they are found deep inside caves and forests, where Lucañas, a researcher at the University of the Philippines Los Baños, spends much of his time, observing their behaviour and searching for undescribed species. They play a crucial role in our ecosystems, recycling waste into nutrients, serving as prey for lizards or birds and, in some cases, dispersing seeds or acting as pollinators.Lucañas did not set out to be a cockroach specialist. He had hoped to study fish, he says, but his professor encouraged him to focus on insects. It was in 2013, as an undergraduate, that Lucañas went on a field trip to caves in Burdeos, Polillo Island, and spotted an undescribed species of cockroach, the gold-colouredNocticola gonzalezi.Its official name honours Juan Carlos T Gonzalez, a professor at the Institute of Biological Sciences at the University of the Philippines Los Baños. But, informally, it was called the gold cockroach, a nod to alegend in the Philippinesthat claims Japanese soldiers buried vast quantities of looted gold in the country during the second world war.View image in fullscreenNocticola gonzalezi, an undescribed species spotted by Lucañas in a cave, is known as the gold cockroach and is named after one of the entomologist’s professors.Photograph: Cristian LucañasLucañas has since described eight more Philippine cockroach species and co-described six species from other countries, naming some of them aftercharacters from Tolkien and Pokémon.Cockroaches are hugely diverse in form, he says. Different species exist in a rainbow of colours, from vivid blue and light green to metallic shades. They can also behave in unexpected ways. “There are a lot of cockroaches that look like beetles, some that can roll into balls, some can jump like crickets,” adds Lucañas.Female members of the genusPerisphaerusare particularly devoted mothers that, unusually for insects, feed their young. “The babies puncture the armpits of their mother and they stick their head inside – it’s something like breastfeeding,” he says, but rather than drinking milk, they feed on blood.Termites, a “eusocial” species of cockroach, are especially under-appreciated, despite being just as industrious and organised as ants, and living in similarly sophisticated social units.Termites are more commonly thought of as pests that damage homes, adds Lucañas. But in forest settings, their role in decomposing wood is crucial. “If those stored nutrients are not brought back to the soil, they would just be stuck in the wood. The ecosystem won’t be able to reuse those nutrients for the other organisms, for the other plants,” he adds.View image in fullscreenPerisphaerus aeneus, also known as the roly-poly cockroach. The genusPerisphaerusare devoted mothers that, unusually for insects, feed their young.Photograph: Cristian LucañasThere is a perception that cockroaches are indestructible. Pest varieties are capable of outwitting the most determined control efforts, and surviving on anything from greasy pizza to human hair.But non-household cockroaches in the Philippines are far more vulnerable, says Lucañas, who points to threats such as global heating and habitat destruction, as land is developed or exploited for mining.“There are still a lot of things that we don’t know yet [about cockroaches],” says Lucañas. “At the same time, there’s a lot of pressure on the natural environment.”Globally, invertebrates, particularly insects, are dying out at an alarming rate, though most conservationfunds go to more charismatic animals.In 2019, two cave-dwelling species, the Antipolo blind cave cockroach (Nocticola caeca) and Simon’s cave cockroach (Nocticola simoni), were listed as endangered in the Philippines, while five other cockroach species were listed as vulnerable. It was the first year that cockroaches were included on the list, as there had previously been too little information.View image in fullscreenLucañas hunting for cockroaches: there are at least 130 species in the Philippines ‘and a lot more yet to be discovered’, he says.Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty ImagesThere are at least 130 known species in the Philippines. “And a lot more yet to be discovered,” says Lucañas.There also are many unknowns about the part they play in our environment. “Do we have more of these pollinators or seed-dispersing species that we don’t know yet? What [other] roles can cockroaches play?“There’s a lot more questions that need to be answered,” he adds. “And more surprising discoveries that we will find.”It’s invertebrate of the year again! From 3-12 August, every day we’ll be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when you’ve got to hear about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us atenvironment.desk@theguardian.comwith Invertebrate in the subject line.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsInvertebratesInvertebrate of the year 2026PhilippinesEndangered speciesEndangered habitatsInsectsConservationWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Right turn on green: is the Telegraph changing its tune on the climate? | Daily Telegraph | The Guardian
description: Flurry of articles has raised eyebrows and prompted a response from Kemi Badenoch defending stance on net zero
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Flurry of articles has raised eyebrows and prompted a response from Kemi Badenoch defending stance on net zero
Content: The Conservative party leader, Kemi Badenoch, wrote her own column for the Telegraph last week defending her approach to net zero.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Conservative party leader, Kemi Badenoch, wrote her own column for the Telegraph last week defending her approach to net zero.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesDaily TelegraphAnalysisRight turn on green: is the Telegraph changing its tune on the climate?Michael SavageMedia editorFlurry of articles has raised eyebrows and drawn response from Kemi Badenoch defending stance on net zeroWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 02.42 EDTShare“Nobody can deny that the UK is getting warmer and high temperatures are becoming a clear threat to homes, nature and food security,” read the lengthy news report, which explored the devastating effect of British wildfires on families in recent years.The article’s conclusions, written after the wildfires inSuffolk last week, were no surprise given the UK’s changing climate. However, the fact that the piece appeared in the Telegraph, the rightwing title that has been a leading critic of green policies, did raise eyebrows among some readers.Praising the analysis, the independent MPRosie Duffield notedit was from an outlet “hardly known for their raging lefty/net zero/climate change agenda”.Even more intriguing was the fact that the essay came after two other notable Telegraph climate pieces. The first was by the columnist Tim Stanley, who set off a debate on the right with an article headlined: “Climate change is real – and the right needs to get serious about it.”View image in fullscreenTim Stanley’s recent column marked something of a departure for a paper better known for its climate scepticism.Photograph: Daily TelegraphThen came a piece by the Telegraph’s respected world economy editor, Ambrose Evans-Pritchard, who has long argued that the costs of climate change could not be ignored. He accusedKemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, of choosing “an abominable political moment to flirt with climate nihilism”, citing her opposition to net zero targets and purge of candidates who back them. “There comes a point when you have to conclude that the Tories have gone Trumpian on the existential issue of our time,” he wrote.Such is the Telegraph’s reputation as the Conservative party’s bible that Badenoch felt it necessary to respond directly, insisting she was opposed to the “political programme” of achieving net zero by 2050, rather than denying the climate crisis altogether.Even Allister Heath, the Sunday Telegraph editor, known for his opposition to green policies, wrote a piece concluding that “the war against global warming has been lost” – though he concluded Britain must simply adapt.View image in fullscreenThe Conservative leader offered a direct response on her climate policies.Photograph: Daily TelegraphThe flurry of pieces has caused some climate change experts to wonder whether the Telegraph’s view – and the wider debate on the right – may be shifting. It comes with the newspaper under new ownership, having been bought by the German media powerhouse Axel Springer. The owner of Politico and Die Welt has plans to make the Telegrapha global player on the centre right.“The Telegraph has got itself into a really awkward spot, especially with its new owner no doubt looking on closely,” said Leo Hickman, the editor of the specialist climate change publication Carbon Brief. “With large parts of Europe suffering an extreme summer of drought, wildfires and heat-related excess deaths, the Telegraph’s long-running history of platforming climate-sceptic commentary now looks even more badly misjudged and discordant.”In fact, Axel Springer’s approach to the issue is not unified – and its all-powerful chief executive,Mathias Döpfner, has previously said he was“all for climate change”because of the innovation it could bring.According to Telegraph insiders, the series of pieces did not come from an internal order to shift tone. One said its editor, Chris Evans, was simply “an old-school Fleet Street editor – he likes whatever is causing noise”.Most believe the pieces by Stanley and Evans-Pritchard in effect marked a Conservative party schism spilling out on to the pages of its favourite outlet, with centre-right voices speaking up after Badenoch’s decision to ban candidates who did not follow the party line on net zero.Bob Ward, the policy and communications director at the LSE’s Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, said: “We’re seeing a little bit of what has happened in the United States, where a noisy and very vocal group on the right of the right wing have been dominating the discussion about climate.“The centre right has largely disappeared from view … It is a brave piece [from Stanley], but all he’s doing is looking out the window. Actually, there are a large number of Conservative supporters who feel similar to him.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother source said the Telegraph’s own internal reader research showed many wanted action on climate change.Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George MonbiotRead moreThe pieces have been welcomed by pro-green Tories, often isolated in recent years. “It has been great to see such an active debate on the right about the best approach,” said Sam Hall, the director of Conservative Environment Network.However, others who monitor climate coverage conclude that taken as a whole, there has been no real shift in the Telegraph’s approach, with recent stories linkingrewildingand theemptying countrysideto wildfires. While the Telegraph’s editorial column noted the Stanley and Evans-Pritchard pieces, it ultimately backed Badenoch’s approach.Richard Wilson, the director of the Reliable Media campaign group, said: “We’ve seen cases before where a paper has sought to reposition itself as becoming more grounded in scientific reality around climate change – such as the Daily Express’s ‘green crusade’. Sadly, that change was not sustained.“For a credible ‘conversion’ at the Telegraph, I think we’d need to see an end to the wider pattern.”Carbon Brief’s Hickman added: “The week ended with editors giving the final word to Kemi Badenoch, who used it to simply double down on her own net zero scepticism. What on earth must the Telegraph’s readers – and new owner – make of this vertiginous rollercoaster of denial?”The Telegraph was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsDaily TelegraphTelegraph Media GroupConservativesKemi BadenochEnvironment policyNational newspapersNewspapersanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Family pay tribute to girl, nine, who died on camping trip in Scotland as man is charged | UK news | The Guardian
description: Minnie Merriman was found injured on industrial estate in Arbroath on Monday and a man has appeared in court
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Minnie Merriman was found injured on industrial estate in Arbroath on Monday and a man has appeared in court
Content: Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, was found seriously injured at an industrial estate in Arbroath and taken to hospital in Dundee, where she later died.Photograph: Police Scotland/PAView image in fullscreenMinnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, was found seriously injured at an industrial estate in Arbroath and taken to hospital in Dundee, where she later died.Photograph: Police Scotland/PAUK newsFamily pay tribute to girl, nine, who died on camping trip in Scotland as man is chargedMinnie Merriman was found injured on industrial estate in Arbroath on Monday and a man has appeared in courtHannah Al-OthmanWed 5 Aug 2026 11.50 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA girl of nine who died on a family camping trip in Scotland has been named as Minnie Merriman.In a statement released through Police Scotland, her family said: “We are devastated with the loss of our beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo. Our family asks that our privacy is respected at this extremely difficult time.”Christopher Rice, 35, was charged with murder in relation to her death when he appeared at Forfar sheriff court on Wednesday. He did not enter a plea and was committed for further examination and remanded in custody.Minnie,from West Yorkshire, was found seriously injured just after midnight on Monday at the Elliot industrial estate in Arbroath, Angus. She was taken to Ninewells hospital in Dundee where she later died.According tolocal news reportsthree other family members were also taken to hospital by ambulance. It is understood these did not include Rice, who was taken separately to hospital by officers.Police revealed that the suspect was white British after the far-right agitator Tommy Robinson shared footage from the scene of the incident, leading to speculation online about the man’s background.Police said Rice was known to Minnie and they were not looking for anyone else in connection with her death.View image in fullscreenTributes left at the Elliot industrial estate, where Minnie Merriman was found.Photograph: Rachel Keenan/PADI Mike Ness of Police Scotland’s major investigation team said: “Our thoughts remain with those affected by these events. A police presence will remain in the area while our inquiries continue. Anyone with any concerns, or information, should approach these officers or contact Police Scotland on 101.”Minnie is believed to have been camping in the area with her family. Local people said they had seen the family with a small tent in the area on Sunday afternoon.Arbroath residents left floral tributes on a grass verge at the industrial estate, which is located close to the coast.Dawn Reid, from the town,told the National: “We’re quite devastated by the news. Our kids are just not safe anywhere, it’s just heartbreaking. I just wish them all the best. She’s got a long road ahead of her, that poor mum.”Lois Speed, a councillor for Arbroath East and Lunan, said on social mediathat the incident was “heartbreaking”. Speed told local media she wanted to “express the shock within the community this morning”.“Really just my thoughts are with the little girl and her family, and those closely affected,” she said. “I don’t have much more that I can add or say, other just than express the shock and sympathies with everyone.”On Tuesday afternoon a police cordon around the scene was lifted and a green car that had been inside it had been removed.It is understood West Yorkshire police are supporting the Police Scotland investigation.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Pakistani minister on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester | UK news | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Rukhsar Ahmed was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week despite being on police bail in the UK
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Exclusive: Rukhsar Ahmed was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week despite being on police bail in the UK
Content: Rukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile.Photograph: SuppliedUK newsFormer Pakistani minister on bail over alleged child rape in 1990s ManchesterExclusive: Rukhsar Ahmed was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week despite being on police bail in the UKShah Meer Baloch,Josh Halliday,Raphael BoydandRajeev SyalWed 5 Aug 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Pakistani state minister was arrested two years ago on suspicion of raping vulnerable young girls in Manchester in the 1990s, the Guardian can reveal.Rukhsar Ahmed, who was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week after five years out of office, is on police bail in the UK after his arrest in July 2024 on suspicion of rape and trafficking children in care as part of a grooming gang.It is understood that Ahmed, 62, was expected to answer bail at a police station in Manchester last month, but failed to attend because he was “too unwell to fly”.At the same time, he was pictured on social media campaigning at various election gatherings in Mirpur in northern Pakistan.He was elected last week as an MP in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir legislative assembly for the party of Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif.Ahmed, who represents the centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021.The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024.Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area of the city, where he lived for many years.View image in fullscreenRukhsar Ahmed.Photograph: SuppliedAhmed, who has more than 17,000 followers on Facebook, was pictured with friends in Rusholme as recently as May, with associates saying he has visited regularly.He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile. One friend said people travelled for hundreds of miles to see the businessman, given his role in Pakistani politics.Detectives questioned Ahmed in July 2024 about allegations from at least two women who claimed that Ahmed was involved in raping and trafficking them when they were young girls.It is understood that detectives learned about Ahmed’s involvement in Pakistani politics when he was in custody for questioning.The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s.He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him – potentially causing a diplomatic row.A senior leader of PML-N in Pakistan-administered Kashmir said he had known Ahmed for at least two decades. but did not know about the rape allegations against him.He said: “We just heard that he was part of some groups in Manchester in 1990s. But I personally didn’t know about such severe allegations existed against Ahmed.”Ahmed did not respond to requests for comment.The revelation comes weeks after Pakistan refused the UK government’s attempts to deport a freed ringleader of a Rochdale grooming gang.Shabir Ahmed, 73, was released from jail in July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for 30 child rape offences.Friends of Rukhsar Ahmed described him as “incredibly influential” in Manchester’s Pakistani community given his political role.One associate in Rusholme said he was a “man of the people” and “one of the least corrupt people”, adding that he had visited the area recently.He is known to have visited a popular Pakistani restaurant on Stockport Road in Longsight, near Rusholme, on numerous occasions. Photos from one visit, which he posted to his Facebook account, show him and several others standing outside the restaurant.Those on Stockport Road speak highly of Ahmed. One man described him as “a man of conviction who helps people who need it”.He is particularly respected by people from the self-governing region Azad Kashmir, where his LA-4 Mirpur-IV seat is based.His influence in the community is such that people come from across the UK to meet him when he visits Manchester, which he is believed to do every few months.The Gujjar Palace was boarded up and derelict when the Guardian visited on Tuesday. One local business owner said it had been closed since at least 2009. Ahmed is the only director of the company that owns the restaurant, but it was almost struck off earlier this year after failing to file its accounts.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman arrested after four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden | UK news | The Guardian
description: Metropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assault
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Metropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assault
Content: A woman is arrested in Covent Garden after the stabbings.Photograph: SWNSView image in fullscreenA woman is arrested in Covent Garden after the stabbings.Photograph: SWNSUK newsWoman arrested after four men stabbed in London’s Covent GardenMetropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assaultCaroline DaviesandHelena HortonWed 5 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said.The Metropolitan police said the men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to a major trauma centre after the lunchtime incident on Endell Street.Two of the men were being treated for injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing and the other two had been discharged.A 47-year-old woman remained in custody after being arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, believed to be a pair of scissors, and assault.Ch Supt Jason Stewart, who leads policing in the area, said: “Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports. While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental health-related incident.“A visible police presence will remain in the area while evidence is gathered at the scene and we thank the public for their understanding.”A London ambulance service spokesperson said: “We sent an ambulance crew, a paramedic in a fast-response car and an incident response officer. We also dispatched London’s air ambulance.
