We treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road.”map of Covent GardenOne witness said the stabbing happened outside the Shaftesbury Theatre before the woman allegedly made her way down Endell Street, a popular location for eating and drinking in the area.The witness, who wanted to remain anonymous, said: “We noticed she stabbed three people with scissors by the theatre then she came down here and the police were here.”One of the victims ran into a barber shop and took his shirt off, revealing a large gash in his back, workers there said.Arjan Gjorga, who works at the Rock and Sole Plaice restaurant and witnessed the attack, said a woman involved in the incident was known to people who worked on the street.He said: “I see her all the time, she’s a homeless person. She walks up and down asking for help, she visits the church at the top of the street.”Gjorga, who did not have to close his restaurant, said: “We all saw a commotion, people were running away. It was totally random, just random people. She suddenly started stabbing them. The police reacted immediately, they arrested her right away.”View image in fullscreenEmergency services near the scene on Endell Street in Covent Garden.Photograph: James Manning/PAMatt Bishop, 42, who works at a consultancy firm next to the cordon in Covent Garden, said he had seen a woman having a “standoff” with three police officers and waving a weapon around.Andrea, the manager of Da Mario restaurant on the same street, said the attack happened in the middle of lunch service.Gesturing at a pair of men enjoying cocktails on the shaded terrace, he said: “They saw it all but they weren’t fazed. They had a police cordon right over their heads but they kept on enjoying their lunch. It’s just another day in London.”He also recognised the alleged perpetrator, saying: “She’s often on the street. We’ve seen her do things like this before, she’s recently got in an argument with a mate and thrown a bottle of vodka on the floor and it smashed outside the restaurant.”By 3.30pm, the area was calm with the cordon down.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early  | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
Content: Andrew Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by three men fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAView image in fullscreenAndrew Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by three men fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAUK criminal justiceChief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released earlyThames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jailGeraldine McKelvieSenior correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.ThePolice Federationis contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison.In August 2019, Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road inBerkshireby a car as Cole, Bowers and their accomplice Henry Long fled the scene of a quad bike theft.All three were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in prison andcould be released earlyas part of the government’s drive to free up prison places.Long, who was driving the car,was given a 16-year jail sentenceand does not qualify for early release.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers are each serving a 13-year sentence for manslaughter.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PAOn Wednesday morning, Jason Hogg, who was on duty the night Harper died, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that he would “certainly” consider joining thePoliceFederation in court action if the government refused to reverse its position, pending legal advice.“I was contacted by the Police Federation yesterday who informed me they are seeking legal advice, exploring opportunities for a judicial review against the government,” he told the Guardian on Wednesday afternoon.“So I’m watching with interest and I will be speaking to the Police Federation again.“But my hope is that we will never get there and that there is no need for the Police Federation to go down the line of a judicial review because the government will listen.”‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release schemeRead morePrison capacity in England and Wales is at critical levels. From October, the government plans to release about 5,000 prisoners who have served a third of their sentence.Harper’s widow, Lissie, successfully campaigned for a change in the law after his death.Legislation introduced four years ago – the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 – means those convicted of the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty now face mandatory life sentences. However, the law cannot be applied retrospectively.Hogg said he wrote to the prime minister,Andy Burnham, 12 days ago to express concerns that Cole and Bowers might be included in the scheme, but had not received a reply.He added that he planned to write again to Burnham, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to convey “the impact of the decision on the morale of my officers, but also on the 2,000 people who work in policing across the country”.Hogg would not be drawn on whether all prisoners convicted of manslaughter should be exempt from the scheme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThames Valley police chief constable Jason Hogg was on duty the night Harper died.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersThe government has already said those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming will not be released early, after a campaign by victims.“It isn’t my role to set government policy or set the law,” Hogg said.“But I think if you ask most people in the streets, they would probably say people who take the life of another person in our country should remain behind bars as long as possible, and I don’t think that’s particularly controversial.”However, he added that the fact Harper was an emergency services worker is a “significantly aggravating factor”.Hogg said the criminal justice system also needed “greater investment around rehabilitation”. He said the National Police Chiefs’ Council estimated it would cost about £480m to manage the freed offenders in the community.“I think there needs to be a balance between the risk caused [by] prisons being full, but also the risk of releasing people early who still pose a risk to the public,” he said.“One of the challenges around the sentencing act [is that it] releases people on the basis of the crime committed, not on the basis of how reformed they are, have they been rehabilitated, and not on the basis of the risk they pose back in the community.“So if you have somebody who still poses the risk … has felt no remorse, and they are back on the streets early, of course that risk has to be managed by the probation service and policing.”Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justicePolicePolice FederationPrisons and probationAndy BurnhamBerkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Disturbing’: TikTok faces criticism after Perez Hilton livestreams self-harm | Perez Hilton | The Guardian
description: Many online questioned how long the blogger’s broadcast remained up on the app and shared mental health resources
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Many online questioned how long the blogger’s broadcast remained up on the app and shared mental health resources
Content: Perez Hilton arrives at BOA Steakhouse grand opening at Grand Canal Shoppes at Venetian Las Vegas on 8 November 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Denise Truscello/Getty Images for BOA Steakhouse Las VegasView image in fullscreenPerez Hilton arrives at BOA Steakhouse grand opening at Grand Canal Shoppes at Venetian Las Vegas on 8 November 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Denise Truscello/Getty Images for BOA Steakhouse Las VegasPerez Hilton‘Disturbing’: TikTok faces criticism after Perez Hilton livestreams self-harmMany online questioned how long the blogger’s broadcast remained up on the app and shared mental health resourcesMaya YangWed 5 Aug 2026 16.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSocial media users have criticized TikTok after the celebrity blogger Perez Hilton livestreamed himself self-harming on the platform, prompting many to question how long the broadcast remained live and others to share mental health resources and encourage those in need to seek help.On Tuesday night, Hilton, 48, livestreamed himself engaging in self-harm as viewers pleaded for him to stop. Shortly after, local authoritiesrespondedto his home in Miami, Florida, where he was transported to a nearby hospital for medical treatment.In the aftermath, social media users and influencers have criticized TikTok for hosting the live stream. Instagram user Gina Lucianosaid: “I find it disgusting and disturbing that TikTok allowed that livestream to go on for as long as it did. It just goes to show you that that app promotes bullying.”Perez Hilton hospitalised after livestreaming self-harm on TiktokRead moreLuciano continued: “Don’t watch that video, don’t watch any clippings of that live stream. It’s not content. It’s not entertainment. It’s a cry for help.”Dana Bowling, another Instagram usersaid: “Can we file a class action suit against TikTok for exposing adults and teens to that trauma…? No one should be ok with this.”Although several users claimed the live stream lasted more than 30 minutes, aTikTokUS spokesperson disputed those reports, saying the broadcast was approximately half that length. The spokesperson said TikTok’s automated moderation systems flagged the live stream within minutes and referred it to the platform’s US moderation team for review.Several subsequent live streams were removed within 90 seconds and Hilton’s account was ultimately banned, the spokesperson added.The company said it also alerted local law enforcement officials and that the live stream violated itscommunity guidelines, which prohibit content depicting or promoting suicide or self-harm.Despite TikTok’s removal of the live stream, screen recordings of the footage have since widely circulated across other platforms including X and Instagram, in turn prompting users to advise others to turn off video autoplays and mute mentions of Hilton.“Assume every Trending Topic link with his name on it will lead you to the video. Don’t click on the link. The video is everywhere right now. To be extra sure, turn video autoplay off (it’s in Settings) and mute the phrase ‘Perez Hilton,’” one personsaidon Bluesky.Another person similarlysaid: “PLEASE mute ‘Perez Hilton’ (as a term) if images of self harm, a person in crisis… are bad for you. Please.”Other users have encouraged those struggling with mental health issues to seek support. TV personality and influencer Tefi Pessoa wrote on her Instagram story: “If Perez Hilton’s live triggered you in any way, please call 988. There is help, I promise. I love you.”The Guardian reached out to X for comment. Meta declined to comment.Many users alsocommented directlyon Hilton’s Instagram posts to express their concern, with one writing: “A lot of people care and are concerned for you. Please take care of yourself Perez. Please know that you are loved.”Someone else said: “Perez I hope you are stabilized and doing alright now, that video has us all concerned. Please heal up.”On Wednesday afternoon, Hilton’s team and familyreleased a statementconfirming that Hilton is receiving medical care.“Many of you have reached out with concern for Perez, and we are incredibly grateful for the overwhelming outpouring of love, support, and prayers. We can confirm that Perez is receiving medical care, and our family’s focus right now is on his well-being. We kindly ask that you respect Perez’s privacy, as well as the privacy of his family, during this difficult time,” the statement said.“If and when we are able to share any updates, we will do so with everyone as soon as we can. Thank you for your compassion, understanding, and continued support,” it added.Hilton, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, rose to fame in the early 2000s when he started PerezHilton.com, a celebrity gossip blog with aggressive commentary that many, including celebrities, likened to online bullying.Born inMiamito Cuban parents, Hilton graduated from New York University before working in a variety of roles, including a brief stint as an actor and later as a publicist, before finding success as a celebrity blogger under a moniker inspired by Paris Hilton.By 2007, the New York Timesreportedthat Hilton was spending 17 hours daily publishing an average of 30 blogposts every day. At the time, his website was charging $9,000 a week for a single advertisement, and as much as $45,000 for its most expensive ad package, the outlet added.Speaking tothe Guardian in 2014, Hilton described himself as being “sassy without being nasty”.In his 2021 memoir, the father of three reflected on his earlier work,writing:“I have a ton of regrets, particularly because I now see that I never needed to be so mean or cruel.”Earlier this year, Hiltonrevealedthat he underwent “emergency surgery” for deep vein thrombosis after doctors discovered the condition following a three-week hospitalization due to sepsis.Reflecting on the experience, HiltonsaidGod “presented himself to me”, adding: “I’ve been crying but happy tears … because this is just …so crazy. I’ve been reading the Bible, and so much of what is said here I had already been thinking of. It’s just overwhelming in the best, most beautiful way.”In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsPerez HiltonMental healthMiamiTikTokSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media | Mexico | The Guardian
description: César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver
Content: César Gastélum had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos.Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/ReutersView image in fullscreenCésar Gastélum had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos.Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/ReutersMexicoMexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social mediaCésar Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driverOscar Lopezin Mexico CityWed 5 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread.César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers.A motorcycle with a driver and pillion rider suddenly pulled up beside them and the driver pulled out a gun and shot Gastélum at point-blank range.A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum’sdeath to Reutersand said a major security operation was under way.The killing is the latest example of bloodshed in Culiacán, which has become an epicentre of violence as factions of the Sinaloa cartel battle for control of the city.View image in fullscreenOnlookers stand behind a police cordon at the scene of César Gastélum’s killingPhotograph: Jesús Bustamante/ReutersMexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible.Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum,said on Wednesdaythat authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer.In a war in Mexico between cartel factions, influencers become targetsRead more“The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference.At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024,according to local media.They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23,was shot and killedat a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers.Authorities announcedlast week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing.They also accused him of ordering and financing the November 2025assassination of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan, the second largest city in Michoacán state, in a killing that shocked the country.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge signals Trump’s defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal may be dismissed again | Wall Street Journal | The Guardian
description: Obama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming Murdoch
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Obama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming Murdoch
Content: Media mogul Rupert Murdoch looks on as Donald Trump speaks to members of the media during proclamation signings and appointments inside the Oval Office at the White House on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Craig Hudson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMedia mogul Rupert Murdoch looks on as Donald Trump speaks to members of the media during proclamation signings and appointments inside the Oval Office at the White House on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Craig Hudson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesWall Street JournalJudge signals Trump’s defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal may be dismissed againObama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming MurdochJeremy Barrin MiamiWed 5 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge inFloridaseemed skeptical of arguments fromDonald Trump’s legal team on Wednesday over whether the court should allow a $10bn defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal to move forward.Trump sued the Journal and the News Corp founderRupert Murdochover aJuly 2025 articleabout a “bawdy” letter reportedly from Trump that was included in a 2003 birthday book for disgraced financierJeffrey Epstein. Trump has denied authoring or signing the letter, and his attorneys have argued that the Journal published the story despite having been told it was false.US district court judge Darrin P Gayles initiallydismissedthe case in April, arguing that Trump’s attorneys had not sufficiently pleaded actual malice, the legal standard needed to win a defamation case, but he gave Trump an opportunity to refile the lawsuit. The president’s legal teamrefiled the suitin May.Representing the president, attorney Alejandro Brito, who is also handling the president’s $10bn defamationlawsuitagainst the BBC, argued that the Journal “didn’t follow journalistic standards sufficient to making the claims”.“The defendants did not and could not have [done] the investigations to make the definitive statements in this article,” Brito said in a Miami courtroom on Wednesday.Furthermore, he said that only four people could attest to the veracity of the letter: Trump, who has denied it; Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019; the bookbinder, who is also deceased; and Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell, whosaidshe does not recall who participated in the birthday book project.But the judge seemed particularly skeptical that Trump was financially harmed by the Journal’s publication, saying his lawyer’s claims seemed “rather conclusory”.Brito responded that Trump’s team did not need to specify financial harm and had “done enough at this stage”.Lawyers representing Murdoch, the Journal and parent company News Corp argued that Trump’s team had made no headway in their attempts to prove that the president was defamed by the story, headlined “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was FromDonald Trump.”“The amended complaint is no better than the original complaint,” said Andrew J Levander, an attorney representing the defendants. “It is time for this baseless lawsuit to come to an end. You gave the plaintiff a roadmap to fix this case and he couldn’t do it.”Lawyers for the defendants argued that Trump’s legal team mischaracterized the article and that the Journal could not be expected, as a matter of journalistic prerogative, to refrain from publishing an article simply because of the president’s denial.Katherine M Bolger, an attorney representing the defendants, argued that their case was actually bolstered by the Journal’s decision to include Trump’s denials – and that the reporters who authored the story, Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo, were careful to tell readers “what they know and what they don’t know”.“That’s not actual malice – that’s good journalism,” Bolger said.While Gayles did not issue a ruling from the bench, he indicated at the end of the 90-minute hearing that one would soon be coming. He also agreed to stay discovery in the case.Levander, the attorney for the Journal, argued that given Trump’s history of suing media companies, “if we get into discovery, it will be burdensome on the court and it will be burdensome on theWall Street Journal.”Explore more on these topicsWall Street JournalDonald TrumpRupert MurdochDefamation lawFloridaUS press and publishingMedia lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat | Sheikh Hasina | The Guardian
description: Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
Content: Opponents burn an effigy of Sheikh Hasina in Dhaka during her address to journalists in Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpponents burn an effigy of Sheikh Hasina in Dhaka during her address to journalists in Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersSheikh HasinaExiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threatSheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by studentsPenelope MacRaein DelhiWed 5 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBangladesh’s ousted prime ministerSheikh Hasinahas vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence.“They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government.Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence.“Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link.View image in fullscreenSheikh Hasina, the then newly elected prime minister, speaking at a press conference in Dhaka in January 2024.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersHer son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile.“She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.”The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from IndiaRead moreIndia officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed.India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition.Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia,swept to powerearlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh.View image in fullscreenSajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Sheikh Hasina, addressing the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia on Wednesday via video link.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersLast November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunalsentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanityover the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government.The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans.Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman.View image in fullscreenSheikh Hasina, right, and her former political foe, Khaleda Zia, at a wedding reception in Bangladesh in 1997.Photograph: ReutersBangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped.Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character.The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power.Explore more on these topicsSheikh HasinaBangladeshIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Big shake-up in Google’s AI team as DeepMind chief executive steps down | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Two senior engineers are leaving company to launch startup amid fears Google is falling behind in AI race
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Two senior engineers are leaving company to launch startup amid fears Google is falling behind in AI race
Content: Sir Demis Hassabis will become chair of DeepMind in a leadership overhaul.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/ReutersView image in fullscreenSir Demis Hassabis will become chair of DeepMind in a leadership overhaul.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Big shake-up in Google’s AI team as DeepMind chief executive steps downTwo senior engineers are leaving company to launch startup amid fears Google is falling behind in AI raceDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 5 Aug 2026 18.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSir Demis Hassabis is stepping down as chief executive of GoogleDeepMind, in a leadership overhaul of the UK-based AI research lab.Hassabis, aNobel prize recipient, is leaving his main managerial role to become chair of DeepMind – as well as taking on the new position of chief scientist at Alphabet, which is Google’s parent company. DeepMind will now be led by Koray Kavukcuoglu, its chief technology officer, under the title of senior vice-president.London-born Hassabis, 50, has been a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era, co-founding DeepMind in 2010 and selling it for £400m to Googlefour years later. His efforts led to him winning the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry for breakthroughs in predicting and designing the structure of proteins, via DeepMind’s AlphaFold model.Shares inAlphabet, a $4.4tn (£3.3tn) company and a leading player in the AI race, closed down 4% on Wednesday.Hassabis said on Wednesday he had been working towards artificial general intelligence (AGI) – a theoretical state where a system can match a human at any cognitive task – and felt it was “close at hand”.Adding it was critical to ensure the achievement of AGI “goes well for humanity”, he said: “I’ve decided that now is the right time for me to hand over my day-to-day operational responsibilities at GDM, so that I have the time and space to focus on the big picture and help influence what is to come to the best of my ability.”As befits a Nobel winner, Hassabis has played the more thoughtful, statesmanlike role in the AI industry in recent years. Last month he called on the US to establish a global AI watchdog to monitor the world’s most powerful models.“What we collectively do now will determine how the next phase of civilisation unfolds,” he wrote on Substack. “By safely stewarding AGI into the world, we can enter a new golden age of scientific discovery and progress, and usher in a bright future of incredible human flourishing.”Hassabis will also remain as chief executive of Isomorphic Labs, a drug discovery company that spun out of DeepMind.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeveral leaders of its Gemini model, including veteran engineer Jeff Dean, are departing the company,Googlesaid. He and Sanjay Ghemawat, another leading engineer, are leaving the company to launch a startup called Discovery Loop, which will focus on researching breakthroughs in machine learning, science and engineering.Some investors are concerned that Google is falling behind its rivals Anthropic andOpenAI, each of which hired a leading Google AI employee this summer. Both have made advances in creating coding agents.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)GoogleComputingAlphabetDeepMindOpenAIShareReuse this content

title: AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to try to trick developers | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: AI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: AI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk
Content: AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to try to trick developersAI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of riskExplainer: Should we be alarmed at AI models going rogue in tests?Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 5 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdvanced artificial intelligence models have stunned the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) by carrying out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.The institute said the incident was unprecedented and involved sending targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.The hack involved agents – AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – powered by models developed by US tech companies OpenAI andAnthropic. AISI, which was set up by the former prime minister Rishi Sunak, described the unsanctioned behaviour as a “serious incident”.The watchdog said the hack was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.AISI detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test on 28 July. It found that some of the models had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident.In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers, having decided that it would help the model pass the evaluation.In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities and used them to press the project’s human overseer into accepting the code.Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreAISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to two specific developers – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that contained harmful software. The watchdog said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented.“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” the institute said in ablogpost.In one instance, the Mythos agent signed off a message in Danish in an attempt to convince the Danish-speaking developer that they should accept the infected code. It also created fake GitHub accounts that would “agree” with its false claims that its software was not malicious.The agent had mistakenly calculated that getting the malware uploaded would trigger a sequence of events that would enable it to use the updated software to pass the AISI cyber test.The incident follows similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. Last month,OpenAI saidan agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test. Days later,Anthropic saidits Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation.AISI said the series of incidents taken together represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”.The watchdog said 17 of the 19 cases of unsanctioned behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol.AISI said the incident was not a case of a model breaking out of its “sandbox”, the term for a secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests. Mythos 5 has not been released publicly but a version of GPT-5.6 Sol with cyber safeguards in place has been launched.The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI added, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate. What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention”.AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation and said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would try to act beyond its remit.The latest safety incident with the technology came as Donald Trump said last week he was “looking at controls” for AI in the US.The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said.Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened.OpenAI said the testing occurred in “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”.The National Cyber Security Centre, part of the GCHQ intelligence agency, said the recent incidents underlined the need for AI companies to develop strong safety guardrails.Warning that detecting an incident after it had happened would not be good enough, Ollie Whitehouse, the centre’s chief technology officer, said: “These technologies must be developed and used from the outset with strong safeguards, real-time oversight, and clear plans for responding when the unexpected happens.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicTechnology sectorComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge casts doubt on future of WH Smith replacement TG Jones | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Mr Justice Hildyard, who approved rescue plan in July, said turnaround plan came with ‘very considerable’ risks
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Mr Justice Hildyard, who approved rescue plan in July, said turnaround plan came with ‘very considerable’ risks
Content: Under approved restructuring, TG Jones is closing 150 of its 450 stores.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenUnder approved restructuring, TG Jones is closing 150 of its 450 stores.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianRetail industryJudge casts doubt on future of WH Smith replacement TG JonesMr Justice Hildyard, who approved rescue plan in July, said turnaround plan came with ‘very considerable’ risksSarah ButlerWed 5 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe judge who approved a rescue plan for the formerWH Smithhigh street business – now named TG Jones – cast doubt on the future prospects of the retailer, suggesting there were “very considerable” risks in achieving a turnaround.“This has all the hallmarks of an adventurous equity play,” wrote Mr Justice Hildyard inhis judgmentpublished on Wednesday, after he last monthapproved the restructuring,which involves the closure of 150 of the books-to-paperclips retailer’s 450 stores.He added that the group’s turnaround plans “might strike the sceptic as more in the nature of generic aspirations than concrete grounds for confidence in a successful outcome”.“The execution risk is very considerable,” he said, indicating the £3m valuation of the company – compared with itsacquisition value of about £40monly a year before – reflected the potential for high losses as well as high profits.Sainsbury’s to sell Argos to three retail veterans in £120m dealRead moreThe retailer, which until recently employed about 5,000 staff, was bought last year by Modella Capital, the private equity firm which is also behind Hobbycraft and owned the UK arm of jewellery retailer Claire’s and The Original Factory Shop until they collapsed earlier this year. It recentlybought Flying Tiger, the Danish retailer known for its cut-price homewares and craft kits, which operates about 1,000 stores worldwide.The original owner of WH Smith continues to operate stores in airports, hospitals and railway stations, so Modella quicklyrebranded the high street stores as TG Jones.Sales quickly fell back after the deal, and Modella had warned it could have to call in administrators if the restructuring plan, which involves writing off debts to suppliers and cutting rent for many landlords, was not approved.The judge approved the plan despite his scepticism about potential success, because Modella had put up new investment to turn it around.Alex Willson, the chief executive of TG Jones, said last month that approval of the plan “allows us to move ahead with our turnaround strategy”.“The plan protects the substantial core of the store estate and makes TG Jones a stronger, more sustainable business,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCourt approval was needed for what is known as a “cram down” scheme, as many classes of creditor who would lose money under the scheme rejected it. The model allows courts, in certain circumstances, to impose a restructuring on dissenting classes of creditors.Fewer than a third of general creditors, who include card makers and pen brands, assented to the plan and no landlords owning unwanted stores – where rent will be cut to zero or closed – backed the plan.Small suppliers, such as toy makers, were set tolose at least half the money owed to themby the formerWH Smithhigh street chain under the restructure.Hossein Dabiri, head of courtroom reporting in Europe for credit analysis firm Debtwire, said:“Justice Hildyard’s judgment recognises the fine line UK courts must walk with restructuring plans involving cross-class cram downs, scrutinising them carefully to avoid them becoming an ‘engine of abuse’ or ‘private equity power play’, while weighing the very real danger of an imminent collapse from one of the few remaining national high street businesses.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryWH SmithnewsShareReuse this content

title: US refunds $100bn of Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: More than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegal
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: More than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegal
Content: The port of Los Angeles. Tariffs have been a key part of Donald Trump’s economic plan since he took office again.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe port of Los Angeles. Tariffs have been a key part of Donald Trump’s economic plan since he took office again.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersTrump tariffsUS refunds $100bn of Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffsMore than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegalBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaWed 5 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 05.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationhas refunded about $100bn from the tariffs it collected before the US supreme court ruled them illegal, according to reports.The $100bn (£74bn) figure, which represents 60% of the total $165bn collected from Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs, was reported by customs officials to the US court of international trade (CIT) on Tuesday, according to the Financial Times.Tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods, have been a key part of Trump’s economic plan since he took office again last year.In February, the supreme court struck down a chunk of the extra tariffs Trump had imposed, forcing the government toreturn moneyto the companies that had paid them.Trump has pitched tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.However, the deficit has grown after narrowing last year thanks to rising tax revenue and tariff income. It hit $1.37tn in the first nine months of the fiscal year, up 2% compared with the same period in 2025.Trump imposed afresh round of tariffson more than 80 countries last month to replace a 10% global duty that was due to expire. The levies range between 10% and 12.5% on countries including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the European Union’s 27 members states.The latest tariffs have been introduced under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is aimed against countries that engage in forced labour.However, this week a coalition of 25 US statessued the Trump administration over the levies, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxesstruck downby the supreme court in February.The states have asked the CIT to stop the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe states involved in the action argue that the tariffs on 59 countries and the EU cover 99.4% of US imports. Officials in the Trump administration have said the countries have not done enough to crack down on products made by forced labour.The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the Trump administration, after losing at the supreme court in February, was “once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs”.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsTariffsTrump administrationInternational tradeEconomicsGlobal economyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ted Lasso season four review – TV’s most wholesome football comedy is back | Television | The Guardian
description: It looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilled
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: It looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilled
Content: Anodyne, unreal … (from left): Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in Ted Lasso season four.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAView image in fullscreenAnodyne, unreal … (from left): Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in Ted Lasso season four.Photograph: Apple TV+/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewTed Lasso season four review – TV’s most wholesome football comedy is backIt looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilledRachel AroestiWed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving transported a flailing AFC Richmond to the upper echelons of the Premier League with his wholesome, folksy and highly simile-reliant management style, the finale of Ted Lasso’s third season saw our titular coach return to the US to spend more time with his son in Kansas. At the time (2023), the general impression was that we were waving goodbye for good. But could this intensely American protagonist really do the most British thing of all and bow out at the height of his sitcom’s popularity? Nope. Last year it was announced that its star and co-creatorJason Sudeikishad caved to market forces and was reprising his colossally popular alter ego.It was the logical thing to do: the 11-time Emmy-winning show was the most-watched streaming original of 2023. Not that logic features heavily in this fourth season. Before we discover how Ted has been lured back to south-west London, we find out what he’s been up to in the interim. Did he parlay his success into US soccer? Return triumphantly to college football? Sit back with his millions and rest on his laurels? Nope, nope and nope again. Instead, he’s working in his local supermarket, warmly greeting his customers by name, providing moral guidance to younger colleagues and generally radiating his trademark howdily-doodily energy. Why? Because he’s a good man without ego who loves to connect and make a positive difference in his community! This is Ted Lasso we’re talking about!Back to the central head-scratcher. Ted left the UK at the top of his game, ultimately choosing fatherhood over riches, professional triumph and beloved colleagues. What could possibly change his mind? Richmond’s owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham, as aspirationally imperious as ever), her deputy Higgins (Jeremy Swift, as satisfyingly square as ever) and marketing manager Keeley (Juno Temple, as unsettlingly childlike as ever) think they’ve cracked it: they fly to Kansas to offer him the job of managing the women’s team, who are languishing in the second division. Obviously, Ted declines. But then his mother – the same mother who last season convinced him to come home – encourages him to go back. So he asks his son and his estranged wife if they fancy coming with. With little explanation, they agree.If you are already a Ted Lasso ultra, you may be inclined to gloss over the twee nonsensicality of this fourth season’s setup and simply sink back into the show’s anodyne atmosphere, one that revolves around messages of positivity, togetherness and how good it is when your football team wins. If you bristle at such blatant emotional button-pushing, you might come to another conclusion: Ted Lasso is fake and phoney, to use the kind of Americanism this show loves putting into the mouths of its British characters (who calls it “the John Lewis Christmas commercial”?!). From the vague transatlanticism and fairytale London to the football-based inaccuracies and stiffly unreal vibe, Ted Lasso rarely bears any relation to reality. This is not a show for pedants.That said, the shift in focus to women’s football does at least mean entertaining some hard truths. Ted’s new assistant coach Alice Chilton (Sex Education’sTanya Reynolds) is a dour taskmaster furious at having been passed over for the top job in favour of a man. And although Ted quickly gets to work in his signature style – improving morale by drilling down into the players’ psyches – his efforts are hampered by the chronic lack of investment in women’s sport, plus injury, pregnancy, motherhood and the fact he’s barely allowed inside the changing room for propriety’s sake.Alien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens upRead moreStill, in the four episodes made available to reviewers, the tension never properly builds. Ted sees the care and industriousness behind Alice’s stony-faced exterior, which is destined to crack imminently. Rather than establishing the new team as individuals (beyond one hard-as-nails goalie and two squabbling Irish sisters), the show often falls back on comfortingly familiar dynamics: the will-they-won’t-they between Roy Kent, still manager of the men’s team, and his ex Keeley among them.For all its irritatingly ersatz qualities, the appeal of Ted Lasso is as clear as ever: the signposted comic beats, the predictable gestures towards kindness and reconciliation, the bright colours, the clean lines. A sense of quality entertainment still hangs about the whole well-oiled endeavour. Think of it as the TV equivalent of Taylor Swift: ruthlessly efficient, reassuringly dorky, blatantly basic and as monocultural as any Apple TV offering is going to get. While I suspect season four will shed some viewers – primarily those who prefer the glamour of the men’s game over the more injustice-focused angle any show about women’s sport must take – fans will be relieved to hear the show has by no means embraced gritty naturalism. Ted Lasso is still saccharine business as usual and, no doubt, still a lot of people’s cup of tea.Ted Lasso is on Apple TVExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTV comedyJason SudeikisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Gill showed theatre audiences that anywhere could be the centre of the world | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting the stories of working people
Author: Barney Norris
Headline: The playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting the stories of working people
Content: Truth teller … Peter Gill in 2015.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTruth teller … Peter Gill in 2015.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianTheatrePeter Gill showed theatre audiences that anywhere could be the centre of the worldBarney NorrisThe playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting stories of working peoplePeter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honestyWed 5 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareIwas,in Michael Coveney’s parlance, one of Peter Gill’s acolytes. I knew him in his autumn; after he’d directed his last play for the National, after he’d moved from Harriet Devine’s house in Hammersmith, where he lived for most of his adult life, into his flat a little further down the river. For 20 years we met there, or in the community centre when we held workshops with actors to help him develop material. One day he told me I should write a book about him: “I introduced postmodernism to the theatre, darling.” I was proud he’d asked me, a feeling that only slightly receded when I read an article by Nina Raine a few years later, in which she revealed he’d suggested the same thing to her. Now Peter has died, I have a strong feeling I should be writing about him again.I think the framework hasn’t yet been created to talk about Peter’s significance. When I was researchingmy book about him, I went to interview his friendBill Gaskill. What we talked about most that day was Wordsworth, and over the years I’ve come to see that as significant. It was Wordsworth who proposed that literature should speak in “the real language of men”. That project flowered a century later in the work of DH Lawrence, who broke free of the conditions of his birth to revolutionise English literature. Lawrence tore through almost every barrier he encountered, for better or worse, in every aspect of his life – but he couldn’t break into the theatre. A “vertical invader” from a peasant class, to borrow John Berger’s description of Picasso, Lawrence reshaped the artistic landscape, but the English theatre made no room in his lifetime for the stories of working people. It took another vertical invader to complete that revolution: a docker’s son from Cardiff who took Lawrence’s plays, placed them at the centre of the world and said, once and for all, “as much happens for you as for other people”. That was Peter’s achievement. He showed us anywhere could be the centre of the world.View image in fullscreenRadical compassion … Peter Gill directing Scenes from the Big Picture at the National Theatre, London, in 2003.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAnd did sobeautifully, in a Keatsian sense. When a stage direction required the baking of bread, Peter had his company bake bread, however long it took. When he ended up in hospital during tech for the Lawrence trilogy, and his assistant came to his bedside to say they were planning to use dry ice to show the bread burning, Peter asked him: “Who do you think I am, Franco Zeffirelli?” He used theatre to tell the truth.Susan Sontag wrote of Thomas Hardy that he was the only great novelist who was also a great poet. I would gently make the claim thatPeter Gillachieved a place of similar distinction: the only great playwright who was also a great director. It was his time around the Court that forged him. Allow me to get into the record what he said about the white heat of that period. He began by paraphrasing Adorno, then added something revolutionary of his own: “Once we knew about Auschwitz we didn’t know how to say anything that meant anything. The bind was that the only moral act in the light of that was to try to say something, you see?” That Beckettian second sentence – the determination to go on, not to accept humanity in ruins but to recognise it and then to seek to speak and live again – is the foundation of every good play anyone’s written since. Peter was in the room when that thought formed. Its radical compassion mustn’t leave the world with him.Explore more on these topicsTheatrePeter GillRoyal Court theatreDH LawrencecommentShareReuse this content

title: Sterling Point review – this teen drama from Gossip Girl’s creators is brilliant escapist TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Set on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mystery
Author: Micha Frazer-Carroll
Headline: Set on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mystery
Content: Summer state of mind … Bo Bragason (left) and Ella Rubin in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoView image in fullscreenSummer state of mind … Bo Bragason (left) and Ella Rubin in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoTV reviewTelevisionReviewSterling Point review – this teen drama from Gossip Girl’s creators is brilliant escapist TVSet on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mysteryMicha Frazer-CarrollWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ll be honest: I was prepared to grit my teeth through Sterling Point, Prime Video’s newest coming-of-age offering, which I dismissed as another by-the-numbers high-school drama. The show follows a type-A teen on a journey of sun-dappled self-discovery, escaping her native New York for an idyllic getaway on a picturesque Canadian island. It’s an unassuming, summer camp-style narrative, but in the style of last year’s seasonal phenomenon that was series three ofThe Summer I Turned Pretty, it manages to transcend the limits of its YA niche, revealing itself to be quite juicy.Protagonist Annie (Ella Rubin) is a highly strung 17-year-old, still reeling from a rejection from a summer business school programme when she receives the news that her estranged maternal grandfather has left her some mysterious assets. Annie, whose mother had died years ago, and her twin Connor (Keen Ruffalo), are prompted to start digging through family secrets, much to the distress of their dad (Jay Duplass of Transparent and Industry). The two learn that they’ve inherited a house in Canada – prompting Annie to take off on a secret trip in search of answers about her late mother’s life.We find ourselves on Sterling Point where Annie quickly finds herself a group of free-spirited friends, including Oona (Bo Bragason), the carefree and sexually forward linchpin of the group; Ellis (Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie), the cheeky local who flies Annie out to the island on a precarious seaplane; Rory (Daniel Quinn-Toye), a sensitive New Yorker who gets compared to Timothée Chalamet; and Ramona (Amélie Elisabeth Hoeferle), who drops a bombshell at the end of the show’s first episode. It rapidly becomes clear that the group is going to spend their leisurely time swimming in beautiful lakes, boating and crushing on each other.View image in fullscreenLake effect ... Ella Rubin and Bo Bragason in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoBeyond an intriguing central plot full of familial mysteries – which I can’t go into without entirely spoiling things – the show is doing something interesting in its generational context. Unlike the sort of timeless, placeless high-schoolers that millennial-plus screenwriters often dream up, these gen Z and gen alpha characters (from the creators ofMy Old Assand Gossip Girl) talk like actual young people, and reflect their modern preoccupations.Among this crew, there’s lots of fluidity, and an overflow of emotional literacy. Oona’s little sister, Maple (Mabel Strachan), is casually readingBessel van der Kolk’s The Body Keeps the Score: “I need to find out what the score is, and where in the body it’s being kept.” The sexualities of many of the characters are a sort of question mark, slowly emerging or shifting as the show goes on, reminiscent of coming-of-age forebears such asThe Half of ItandBooksmart. No one’s gender or queerness is turned into a major plot point, reflecting the fact that more than one in five gen Zsidentify as LGBTQ+. I laughed out loud at a quip about Oona, who, like her own mother, has repeated noncommittal flings that don’t turn into anything serious. “So she’s avoidant attached? We can work through that,” says 17-year-old Connor.The bounds of the YA genre, and of television, feel pretty flexible here. Lines get blundered a few times, and the cameras keep rolling – since the young actors were explicitly encouraged to improvise on set. There are moments where this can fall a bit flat: a punchline doesn’t quite land, or you experience the metaphorical emotional equivalent of seeing a boom in shot. But this also allows for a looser, more authentic feel. The plot and pacing take the same approach – in thespirit of Duplass’s Transparent, sometimes a plotline gets teed up and then completely disappears, subverting the usual rules of television and making things feel more frenetic.Again, there are drawbacks to this approach. More than once, the show contains what feels like a glaring plot hole. But the strangeness of these plotting and script flourishes creates an electricity that is actually more interesting than the love triangles, paternity secrets and other age-old devices at play here.In April, season three of the once boundary-pushing teen drama Euphoria was met withflop reviews. The darkness that had once distinguished and sustained the show had spiralled out of control into a nightmarish, violent and hallucinatory sex fest. The show’s first season, much like Skins, upended the glossy, sanitised teen TV of the 2010s, giving us something that felt gritty and real. Perhaps now we’re seeking an escape from this. “You turn on Netflix and it’s, like, One Tree Hill and Gossip Girl. They’re all trending again,” Canadian creator Megan Parkrecently told Teen Vogue.This feeling of refuge is enhanced by the fact that phones and social media barely feature in the show, despite the fact that teenagers now averagemore than eight hours of screen time per day. Technology is swapped for the ambient sounds and textures of nature, as well as real-life conversation, with all of its accompanying miscommunications and deceptions.If escapism is the brief, then Sterling Point fulfils it expertly. Sure, it doesn’t carry the intensity or the existentialism of its edgier counterparts. But I was surprised by how long I wanted to stay with these characters and inhabit their island bubble. It kept subverting my expectations. I didn’t want to go home.Sterling Point is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ice Cream Man review – Eli Roth’s junky slasher is one of year’s worst horrors | Horror films | The Guardian
description: The Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheap
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheap
Content: Ari Millen in Ice Cream Man.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAri Millen in Ice Cream Man.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockHorror filmsReviewIce Cream Man review – Eli Roth’s junky slasher is one of year’s worst horrorsThe Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheapJesse HassengerWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years ago, Eli Roth realized his long-held ambition to make a movie out ofThanksgiving, the horror-movie trailer he made as a gag for the Quentin Tarantino/Robert Rodriguez anthology feature Grindhouse, back in 2007. Though he didn’t actually go so far as to make the scratched-up decades-ago slasher shown in the original trailer, Thanksgiving was still Roth’s most satisfying movie in ages, replete with ridiculous gore and a side of satirical commentary – a 2020s movie fit for an old video store’s VHS horror section despite its contemporary setting.Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirRead moreNow Roth has founded a horror-focused company actually called the Horror Section, aimed at releasing movies, shows and “experiences” that appeal to the modern equivalent of those VHS-shelf gorehounds. After “presenting” a few other movies, Roth’s first direct contribution to the company is Ice Cream Man, exactly the kind of knowingly disreputable button-pusher befitting the company’s retro-sticker logo. (Indeed, Roth’s movie shares its title with a 1995 direct-to-video curiosity starring Clint Howard, though this one is unrelated.) Unfortunately, rather than a companion piece to the blackly funny murder-mystery of Thanksgiving, which riffed on Scream as much as 80s slashers, Roth’s latest feels like a demo reel for someone vastly less talented.Then again, Roth’s talent for bloody provocation has flowed and ebbed over the years, from the pointed nastiness of the Hostel movies to the snide grotesquerie of The Green Inferno. Ice Cream Man isn’t trying for the latter’s score-settling, but it retains a dim edgelord sensibility in its simple premise, bluntly executed. A mysterious, creepy-looking ice-cream man (Ari Millen) rolls into a suburban enclave, and when local kids get a taste of his cursed treats, they turn into feral, zombie-like killers. Unlike zombies, they avail themselves of whatever makeshift weapons they can find; parents, teachers and passersby are murdered by the dozen. Twelve-year-old Jared (Charlie Zeltzer), however, positioned early on as a lovable loser, is lactose-intolerant, leaving him impervious to the free ice-cream and therefore unharmed – though still in danger, as the crazed kids often force-feed those who don’t partake. Sticking with fellow non-infected kids Tommy (Shiloh O’Reilly) and Mia (Kiori Mirza Waldman), and eventually assisted by his older sister Lizzie (Sarah Abbott), Jared attempts to figure out how to stop this town-wide madness and keep it from spreading further.Early on, the winking transgression of seeing a bunch of weapon-wielding kids annihilate adults in some truly horrifying ways (and observing adults mostly too ginger to fight back occasionally summing the courage to counterattack) offers distraction from the slapdash swearing-kiddies dialogue Roth and co-writer Noah Belson lazily assign their young actors. But as inventive as some of the gore gets, the movie also never does any better than unleashing it – and when so much of that gore features bad CG blood spatter, the ugliness of the violence is eclipsed by the chintziness of the movie’s cut-rate aesthetics. The whole thing looks cheap as hell, with that sickly hyperreal digital sheen that makes so many attempts at slick indies more closely resemble a corporate training piece or amateur music video. There’s no grime or texture to anything here, rendering the gnarly kill scenes as phoney and frictionless as Roth’s half-assed-at-best characterizations.And really, those kills are all Ice Cream Man has; unlike Hostel, there aren’t any attempts made to turn the screws of suspense. The eventual backstory is a low-impact Freddy Krueger knockoff that might pass muster in an actual artifact of the 80s-slasher boom, but here feels like a rush job, the kind of thing Roth might have riffed about with his pal Tarantino in the wee hours of the morning. It’s easy to picture that conversation lasting longer than the screenplay’s eventual drafting. The whole thing is made with the swaggering confidence of someone whose friends laugh at his every joke – and the haphazard efficiency of someone who needs to get product to the marketplace for strategic Q3 growth. The Horror Section is supposed to offer edgier fare to the ravenous, enthusiastic genre fans. With this soft serve, it feels like it’s feeding them mainly contempt.Ice Cream Man is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and UK on 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Holy Days review – even Miriam Margolyes, Jacki Weaver and Judy Davis as nuns can’t save this film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Despite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far between
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Despite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far between
Content: ‘Earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie’ … Judy Davis, Elijah Tamati, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesView image in fullscreen‘Earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie’ … Judy Davis, Elijah Tamati, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesMoviesReviewHoly Days review – even Miriam Margolyes, Jacki Weaver and Judy Davis as nuns can’t save this filmDespite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far betweenLuke BuckmasterWed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 16.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree stubborn old nuns and a wide-eyed young whippersnapper head off on a mission to save the farm – sorry, convent – in this earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie. The ace up Holy Days’ sleeve is the casting, with each nun played by a legend of stage and screen: Judy Davis as Sister Agnes,Miriam Margolyesas Sister Luke and Jacki Weaver as Sister Mary Clare. It quickly becomes clear, however, that nobody is on their A-game. And the film itself is a frustrating mix of comedy and drama: not funny enough to solicit any real laughs, nor sufficiently dramatic to forge strong connections with the characters.These folk are a rather unexciting lot, despite a clear desire to present young Brian (Elijah Tamati) as the emotional glue holding things together and the habit-wearing trio as hot-blooded eccentrics. Their rundown convent, which we’re supposed to feel invested in, is a drab location both aesthetically and emotionally; it’s decaying – but not in a handsome, cinematic way. Nor is it brought to life by the people who inhabit it; in fact, the building feels borderline soulless. Maybe the developers have a point, I caught myself thinking, and this crusty old place could become a snazzy new apartment block or shopping centre.The Birthday Trip review – excellent Australian black comedy piles pressure on to privilegeRead more“Goodbye, convent!” isn’t exactly the response intended by the writer-director, Nat Boltt (adapting Dame Joy Cowley’s novel of the same name), who really needed viewers to feel invested in the characters and their circumstances. Instead, the experience feels syrupy and sentimental; less playing the heartstrings than giving them a forceful yanking.When the three sisters get wind that the convent’s land is at risk, they head off to find a property deed in the hope that they can save the day. In tow is Brian (because: fun intergenerational dynamics!) who is struggling to adapt to his father (Craig Hall) having a new romantic partner after his mother’s death. Curiously for a road movie, there aren’t many interesting locations, though the settings are picturesque – New Zealand’s magnificent landscapes providing some pretty scaffolding. The storyline is oddly threadbare and includes an unintentionally amusing revelation about halfway through that drains the central quest of its narrative purpose.View image in fullscreenJacki Weaver, Miriam Margolyes and Judy Davis in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesComedically, Boltt opts for low-hanging fruit, ie nuns behaving in mildly risque ways. In one scene, Sister Agnes lights up a cigarette (gasp!) and Sister Luke’s dentures fly out of her mouth after she takes a toke; in another, one of the nuns farts when they’re all tucked in bed together. There are also kids-say-the-darndest-things type moments, such as one in which Brian, aghast that Agnes has confessed to stealing a car, exclaims: “You did a sin! You should be prostituted!” The punchlines feel as subtle as a giant sign flashing: “LAUGH.”From early on, one can sense it’s a question ofwhenrather thanifHoly Days will dissolve into cheese and wishy-washiness. Even then it exceeds expectations, culminating in one of those cringe-inducing scenes in which the principal cast converge for a good old-fashioned dance-off, big smiles on their faces as they get jiggy with it. There are some flecks of interest en route to this non-ending, coming almost entirely from that wonderful trio of screen legends, though they are few and far between.Holy Days is out in Australian cinemas now, UK cinemas from 14 August and on digital platforms in the US nowExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsMiriam MargolyesJacki WeaverJudy DavisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Child of My Own review – barely believable true crime tale of desperation and delusion | Movies | The Guardian
description: Candy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudrama
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Candy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudrama
Content: How reliable is her version of events? … Ana Celeste in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixView image in fullscreenHow reliable is her version of events? … Ana Celeste in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixMoviesReviewA Child of My Own review – barely believable true crime tale of desperation and delusionCandy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudramaPhil HoadWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis cheekily inquisitive docudrama by Chilean director Maite Alberdi features a unique variation on the long con, and one with a precise duration: nine months. After suffering three miscarriages and under pressure from her husband and in-laws to give them a child, Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza (aka Ale, and played by Ana Celeste in re-enactments) decides to fake her next pregnancy. She is determined to have something to show at the end of it: after meeting single mother Mayra, who wants to abort her second pregnancy, at the hospital where she works, Ale agrees to take her baby once it is born.The details are hardly believable: eating copiously to gain weight, Ale manages to convince husband Arturo (Armando Espitia) and his family that this pregnancy is on track for her entire term. She reflexively tenses her muscles while he strokes her baby bump and smiles through a swirl of conflicting thoughts at her baby shower. While most con artists must dupe themselves on some level, it is true down to a physiological level in Ale’s case: a judge later testifies that her desperation to bear children may have resulted in a pseudo-pregnancy. How else to explain that the doctor signing off her maternity leave appears to hear the baby’s heartbeat?‘She wasn’t acting, she wanted to live it’: how a fake pregnancy resulted in the wildest true crime film of the yearRead moreThe first half of the film depicts this false paradise in candy-coloured reconstructions, linked up by voiceover from the real-life Ale. But as soon as she walks out of the General Hospital of Mexico with her baby hidden in a gift bag, Alberdi switches to the sobering real-life register. Arrested by the police in a motel room shortly afterwards, Ale is now finishing a 13-year prison sentence for child kidnapping. As the talking heads weigh up her degree of culpability, the film’s initial distancing device – showing the various actors auditioning to play Ale – suddenly makes sense. How reliable is her version of events, in particular her claim of the adoption arrangement? The actual Mayra, unable to forgive the abduction, insists it is total fiction.Even if Ale’s story is true, it highlights the level of her desperation, and the power of societal and biological narratives in setting our agendas. Engaging in a metaphysical parlour game of veracity-chasing, Alberdi is perhaps a little lax in resolving this central point. It allows Ale, in her fuschia-hued jail cell, to remain a broadly sympathetic protagonist – one who, in her later dealings with Arturo (who also served two years), seems to gain considerably in self-knowledge. Reminiscent ofBart Layton’s The Imposterin its portrayal of unfeasible auto-delusion, A Child of My Own is a refreshing branch-out for true crime stories into less violent, more intimate enigmas.A Child of My Own is in UK cinemas from 7 August, and on Netflix from 13 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsParents and parentingChildbirthPregnancyFamilyCrime filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Should a tech tycoon be able to pay his way into conducting a world-class orchestra? And should they really sell tickets? | Music | The Guardian
description: Elon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian tech entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical music
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Elon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian tech entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical music
