Content: Mandle Cheung, who will conduct Mahler’s Second Symphony with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at London’s Alexandra Palace.Photograph: © Shayne GreyView image in fullscreenMandle Cheung, who will conduct Mahler’s Second Symphony with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at London’s Alexandra Palace.Photograph: © Shayne GreyTom Service on musicMusicShould a tech tycoon be able to pay his way into conducting a world-class orchestra? And should they really sell tickets?Tom ServiceElon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical musicWed 5 Aug 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTShareThere are some pretty gigantic non-negotiables for an orchestral musician. You have to be able to perform the right notes in the right order, with a combination of technical expertise, artistry, skill and understanding that demands years, decades and lifetimes of devotion.But there is one figure on the orchestral concert platform who is both the most important person in the room – at least according to classical music’s hierarchies – yet who makes no sound, and whose job looks the simplest of all: the conductor, waving their arms about in time with the music and gurning at the players.Despite appearances, the professional conductor’s responsibility is to know every line of the music inside out, and to turn the performance into not only a perfected version of the rehearsal, but a one-off experience that has its own energy, shape and narrative. You want to know a trade secret? Any professional orchestra in this country could play most of the music on their programmes without a conductor. What the best professional conductors do is provide the x-factor of inspiration that allows the orchestral players to do things that they can’t achieve on their own.But still, as the Hungarian violinistCarl Flesch put it: “There is no profession which an impostor could enter more easily.”By his own admission, the 78-year-old businessman and founder of theMandle Philharmonic in Canada, Mandle Cheung, is an amateur conductor. Heresists the “maestro” tag. He loves music, he loves Mahler particularly, and he is able to conduct world-class orchestras because he is able to pay these orchestras to play for him. Last year he led the Toronto Symphony in Mahler’s Second Symphony, buthe isn’t stopping there. More Mahler, and European orchestras are in his sights. His wish becomes reality on 21 August at London’s Alexandra Palace whenCheung conducts the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, soloists Elizabeth Watts and Jennifer Johnston, and the Brighton Festival Chorus, in a performance of Mahler 2.double quotation markIt turns Mahler’s music into an expensive, ego-driven spectacle that’s all about the wish fulfilment of financially powerful peopleCheungpaid about C$500,000(£264,000) to conduct the Toronto Symphony; his representative has confirmed that Cheung is paying the RPO for the same privilege, but not the amount. “We do not disclose fees for concerts,” said an RPO spokesperson. It says something profound about the parlous state of orchestral finances on either side of the Atlantic that they need to take Cheung’s money, and risk their reputations with their players, audiences and sponsors by letting a non-professional conductor take on one of the most prestigious works in the repertoire. Mahler’s Second is a symphony of epic scale of sound and spirit. With its vast trajectory from funeral march to vision of resurrection it is one of the most complex and transcendent pieces of music you are ever likely to hear.Cheung himself acknowledged the issue,talking to the New York Timeslast year about the Toronto Symphony experience: “These are great musicians, and they work really hard all their life to become a player in a professional symphony orchestra,” he said. “And then somebody who’s not a recognized conductor just walks in and writes you a check and starts conducting you.”View image in fullscreenGilbert Kaplan conducting the New York Philharmonic in Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony at Avery Fisher Hall in 2008.Photograph: Hiroyuki Ito/Getty ImagesThere’s a wider story than one very rich person’s vanity here, and it’s far from a new one.Gilbert Kaplan, another businessman and philanthropist who was similarly obsessed with Mahler’s Second, conducted and recorded the piece with the London Symphony in 1987, and with the Vienna Philharmonic, released on Deutsche Grammophon, in 2002. There’s something about this symphony that seems to speak to the power fantasies of these men: is it that having mastered the universes of finance and technology, being in charge of orchestral and choral forces and guiding them to the radiant transcendence of the end of the symphony is the musical equivalent of building a spacecraft to go to Mars?It turns Mahler’s music into an expensive, ego-driven spectacle that’s all about the wish fulfilment of financially powerful people, curdling the spiritual message of the piece into just another commodity that can be bought and sold.Of course, one way of looking at the entire history of orchestral music and opera is that it’s always been an aristocrat’s indulgence, from the Chapel Royal of the English court to the orchestra that was Prince Esterházy’s pride and joy, and which was the laboratory for Joseph Haydn’s symphonies in the 18th century. You can extend the idea to the wealthy philanthropists of US arts from the 19th century onwards; and you could even see the state funding of the arts in Europe as a variation of the same principle: promoting an unaffordable luxury through taxation. In that context, what’s wrong with someone renting an orchestra for a night to make their dreams come true?On their own terms, you might think that none of these individual concerts that the wealthy can pay to conduct are necessarily problematic. If you’ve got the cash, and wonderful musicians will turn up to play Mahler for you, that’s up to them. But audiences deserve to know what they’re getting for the price of their tickets at Alexandra Palace - there’s nothing on the RPO’s website to say this is an event in which a professional orchestra and soloists have been privately hired by an amateur conductor.View image in fullscreenThe Royal Philharmonic Orchestra performing Mahler’s First Symphony at the Royal Albert Hall, London, last October, conducted by music director Vasily Petrenko.Photograph: Andy ParadiseThe RPO’s managing director, Sarah Bardwell, said: “The RPO takes pride in offering life-changing musical experiences to people from all walks of life, and the orchestra is looking forward to welcoming Mandle Cheung to the podium this summer.Classical musicis for everyone, and this special one-off summer concert will fulfil a dream for a great Mahler enthusiast, while materially supporting our community and education work for the new season.”I’d love to conduct the RPO myself, but am guessing that my dreams and enthusiasm for Mahler aren’t, on their own, enough; I wasn’t aware that the UK’s orchestras had a role to play in the fulfilment of businessmen’s bucket lists. The community and education work that the RPO say will be the beneficiary of Cheung’s largesse is a non-negotiable part of any orchestra’s remit and of course is vital and welcome. But if you look at how the concert is promoted on theRPO’s websiteyou might imagine you were attending a concert that belongs in the same category as performances by the RPO’s music director, Vasily Petrenko. But you’re not. You’re attending a performance that should clearly be advertised for what it is: an amateur fulfilling his most cherished fantasies. AsCheung told the New York Times: “Now that I’ve conducted in Toronto, maybe that can be sort of like a credential for approaching American orchestras, European orchestras, to see if we can work with them,” he said. “That would be nice.”double quotation markIf anyone can buy a world-class symphony orchestra to play with for one night, why not for a week, or a month, or a season?And it probably will be more than nice. The RPO’s skilled musicians will almost certainly hold the performance together, and Mahler’s music will make the radiant sounds and noises that only this symphony can; the audience will applaud and feel they have been on a massive Mahlerian journey. What’s the problem with that?Here’s the kicker: if anyone can buy a world-class symphony orchestra to play with for one night, why not for a week, or a month, or a season? Why bother with decades of specialist training to become a conductor when all you need to stand on a podium and lead a a public performance is very deep pockets? If you’re an audience member, who cares about the difference between amateurs and world-class professionals?If these currently exceptional concerts such as Cheung’s become part of an orchestra’s regular way of life, a means of generating income, the message is stark. For all those more talented musicians working away in conservatoires and opera houses and concert halls right now – those naive souls who imagine classical music is a meritocracy, not an auction – the whole principle that this is an art-form available to all is betrayed.This week Tom has been listening to:Judith Weir’s Moon and Star. I was lucky enough to be in Proms audience for Ryan Wigglesworth, the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra and BBC Singers’ performance of this work. Based on Emily Dickinson’s poetry, it’s music that charms and beguiles.Listen again hereExplore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicRoyal Philharmonic OrchestraLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like Backstreet Boys, but less sultry’: how the Jonas Brothers notched up 20 years of pop stardom against the odds | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Unlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appeal
Author: Claudia Efemini
Headline: Unlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appeal
Content: ‘They’re committed to their art’ … (L-R): Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas, AKA the Jonas Brothers.Photograph: Pamela LittkyView image in fullscreen‘They’re committed to their art’ … (L-R): Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas, AKA the Jonas Brothers.Photograph: Pamela LittkyPop and rock‘Like Backstreet Boys, but less sultry’: how the Jonas Brothers notched up 20 years of pop stardom against the oddsUnlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appealClaudia EfeminiWed 5 Aug 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jonas Brothers appeared in the mid-00s in a blaze of smiles, dressed in shirts, suspenders and ties, singing sappy love songs that won the hearts of girls who quickly became obsessed with this Disney-signed band. Many assumed the fraternal trio would fade away, overtaken by whatever new act replaced them in the whims of teenagers. Yet this week marks 20 years since the release of their debut album,It’s About Time, and the toothsome threesome are bigger than ever.Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas started out with danger-free pop-punk, evolving into a kind of broad-brush feelgood pop. Their true breakthrough was in 2008 with US No 5 hitBurnin’ Up, teeing up three back-to-back US No 1 albums as they became the youngest group to appear on the cover of Rolling Stone. The usual dreaded “creative differences” precipitated a six-year hiatus and the pursuit of solo careers and acting. But they reformed in 2019 in spectacular style, getting their first US No 1 hit withSucker, and by last year they had the clout to sell out the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the World Cup final was later hosted.This evolution from Disney cornballs to legacy act is as unexpected as it is remarkable. “They’re slick, and sometimes over-produced,” says Nate Sloan, co-host of the podcast Switched on Pop. “But they genuinely love making and playing music and that’s what draws me to their continued work.”Sloan argues that the key to their success is dogged devotion to honing their craft. “They’re committed to their art in a way that people may not realise,” he says. “They were writing their own songs from when they were preteens, and even when they sought out professional songwriting collaborators they opted for more daring voices.” He cites Jon Bellion, the hip-hop leaning singer-songwriter who co-wrote and co-produced 2023’s The Album.View image in fullscreen‘They were great, sweet kids’ … the band in their early daysAnother collaborator who was there right at the beginning is Michael Mangini, co-producer of their debut album. “They do what every artist that has a 20-year career has to do: evolve,” he says. Rock-leaning tunes about adolescence – including a cover of Busted’s dumb time-travel anthem Year 3000, with the original’s horniness significantly dialled down – have given way to mature music about fatherhood. “They’re not the same people that they were when they were teenagers, so it would be ridiculous to make a record that has those types of lyrics,” continues Mangini. “Some artists don’t deviate but I think the ones that have true longevity, they grow.”Mangini witnessed the band’s formation in person during a 2005 meeting with Steve Greenberg, then president of Columbia Records, who would end up co-producing It’s About Time with Mangini. “I was hired to come and meet Nick” – the only brother signed to the label at the time – “and somehow in a meeting the conversation turned into: ‘You should become a group,’” says Mangini, after learning that Joe had done some work on Broadway and Kevin played guitar and could sing background vocals. “They certainly weren’t thinking of themselves as a group called the Jonas Brothers. As a matter of fact, they hated the name,” Mangini laughs. But they signed a deal with Columbia after a demo impressed other execs.At the time, Nick was just 12 years old, while Joe was 15 and Kevin was 17. “It required me to remember what it was like to be that young again,” Mangini says. “It was fun and they were great, sweet kids. I’ve worked with tons of other young people but Nick had a point of view when writing songs. He, at 12, could sit down with me, who had been writing songs for 20 or 25 years at that point, and have something to say and be able to articulate it.”Their brotherhood contains “the blend of complementary roles that powers the most successful bands”, Sloan says. “Nick is the youngest but also seems to have the strongest creative vision; Kevin is the eldest but seems most comfortable in a supporting role; Joe is the most entertaining, and the greatest frontman in many ways.”View image in fullscreenHaven’t strayed far … Joe Jonas in Camp Rock.Photograph: John Medland/Disney ChannelColumbia envisaged them as a classic boyband. “Then when we got into the studio and we started working through writing songs, it sort of took a more edgier, rock, pop-punk leaning vibe.” But debut album It’s About Time flopped at No 91 in the US charts, and Columbia dropped them.Disney’s recording label, Hollywood Records, saw the potential revenue in these three unthreateningly handsome young lads and snapped them up in 2007. They featured as themselves on sitcom series Jonas, and starred as fictional band Connect 3 in teen movies Camp Rock and Camp Rock 2: The Final Jam.While Disney-schooled stars such asBritney Spears,Miley CyrusandSabrina Carpentermoved away from the brand with deliberately racy material, the brothers have hardly drifted from wholesome cheesiness. “How do Disney Channel stars show the world that they’re adults? A really sexy video,” says Shasta Smedsrud, a millennial fan from near Seattle. The Jonas Brothers, though, “broke off from Disney gracefully and just kept going”, though they are returning to that era with Camp Rock 3, premiering on 13 August.For many of their fans, predominantly millennials and older gen Zs, it comes as a shock that their debut album is turning 20. “Wow, I feel old,” says Smedsrud. She remembers watching the music video forSOSon Disney Channel in 2007. “It was almost like the Backstreet Boys but less sultry. I think that’s why they did so well for us,” she said. She now gets a hit of nostalgia from songs like this: “When you hear Joe do his usual on the guitar or Nick’s little riff, you get really excited.”Back in the 2000s, physical media was thriving and magazines and fanzines dominated the fandom; Smedsrud recalls having a diary solely dedicated to Nick Jonas, who she obsessed over. “I would cut pictures out, and be like: this song is about me, or when I see Nick he’s going to recognise me and we’re going to get married,” she laughs.View image in fullscreenA spectacular comeback … performing at the Grammy awards in 2020.Photograph: John Shearer/Getty Images for the Recording AcademyThe boys’ clean-cut looks meant they initially appealed more to girls than boys, though there are some male fans, too. “My girlfriend and her family were my gateway,” says 30-year-old Jordan Corman, who got into them in his late teens and remains a fan. “The teenage boy mindset was if you like the Jonas Brothers, there’s something wrong with you,” he says. “But they actually just make good music.”‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starRead moreSmedsrud describes her three children under six as “little fans” of a band who “don’t really use profanity, so it’s kind of safe for your kids”. Monica Andre, a 27-year-old teacher from Oregon, told her kindergarten class about seeing a Jonas Brothers concert the previous weekend, and the children asked who they were. “So I was like, let’s draw Joe, just for fun,” she says. Andre shared the drawings on TikTok, which circulated online, with the brothers themselves commenting on her post. Since then, her class has become infatuated, and particularly inspired by Kevin’s journey from having a more supporting role to launching a solo career alongside the band in 2025. “If you’re sharing something you love and it makes you happy, it makes them happy,” she says.Will the Jonas Brothers still be around 10 years from now? “Certainly,” Mangini says. “I don’t know if they’ll still be making records, but 30 years from now, they’re going to be touring and people will still be showing up. Because once something’s part of your growing up, there’s a special love for it.”Explore more on these topicsPop and rockDisney ChannelWalt Disney CompanyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocation | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoil
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoil
Content: Emotional turmoil … Phoebe Bridgers.Photograph: Olof Grind/PR handoutView image in fullscreenEmotional turmoil … Phoebe Bridgers.Photograph: Olof Grind/PR handoutPhoebe BridgersReviewPhoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocation(Dead Oceans)After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoilAlexis PetridisWed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last time Phoebe Bridgers put out a solo album was six years ago, at the height of the Covid pandemic:Punishernot only ended 2020 near the top of many critics’ best-of lists, it made the UK Top 10 and sold half a million copies in the US. The intervening period has proved just as commercially triumphant. With the release of their debut album The Record,Boygenius– the band she had formed with Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker – went from a kind of supergroup for Pitchfork readers to a genuine mainstream phenomenon: the album won three Grammys. Another win, for Bridgers’ collaboration with SZA, Ghost in the Machine, meant Bridgers left the 2024 ceremony the night’s biggest winner. Other pop stars called on her services: she sang on Taylor Swift’s re-recorded version of Red (and supported on the Eras tour), Lorde’s Solar Power and on Paul McCartney’s McCartney III Imagined.View image in fullscreenPhoebe Bridgers: Lost WeekendBut to judge by Lost Weekend’s opening track, all was not well. The Outside depicts the singer crowd-surfing at a gig in Ohio – “they never let me hit the ground, way beyond the barricade” – and ending a song with her fist triumphantly raised. Then it adds a qualifier. “But I was on the outside, watching,” she sings, the sense of dislocation heightened by the fact that her voice is smothered by a vocoder, and the musical accompaniment – a sweet fingerpicked acoustic guitar figure – keeps vanishing into an ambient backing that sounds like static.It acts as a signpost to the rest of Lost Weekend, musically and lyrically. There is a lot of emotional turmoil in the latter, largely occasioned by the death of her father, with whom Bridgers had a strained relationship – though the album is dedicated “For Dad” – and the collapse of her high-profile relationship with actor Paul Mescal: the title track confirms that they were, as rumoured, engaged (“I’m supposed to be married but I called it off”). If you’re the kind of person who gets their kicks combing new albums for celebrity gossip, there’s plenty here to occupy you, not least a line in The Governor’s Waltz that could be interpreted as a swipe at Mescal’s current partner, Gracie Abrams (“she can pretend to be me / Since she took my place in my bed, on that stage”).Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Boys – videoThat said, you certainly don’t need to have a prurient interest in the vacillations of celebrity romance to feel the album’s emotional impact. The Governor’s Waltz would be an acutely drawn and genuinely affecting portrait of a relationship in its clingy death throes regardless of who the protagonists were; the clattering, chaotic Bobby is equally impactful in its depiction of the heady early days of a love affair, complete with a line about no longer requiring the services of a vibrator, or rather “a thing in a box I don’t fuck any more”. Still Standing, meanwhile, describes the disquieting sensation of being unable to muster the emotions you’re supposed to feel at the death of a parent: digging around for fond memories, Bridgers instead comes up with recollections of spousal abuse, distance and irrational behaviour and ends up “feeling indifferent, wearing black”. “I am my old man’s oldest son,” she sings at the album’s conclusion. “I fought the wall and the wall won.”Bridgers’ lyrics are brilliant throughout, but they’re matched by the individuality of Lost Weekend’s sound. At heart it’s a well-written Americana-infused indie singer-songwriter album, complete with the yearning melodies, acoustic guitars, mandolins and melancholy violin you might expect, made by people well-versed in such things: the cast list features Jack Antonoff, Bridgers’ Boygenius bandmates, Jon Brion, Alex G and Conor Oberst. But perhaps the most telling credits are those for “sound design”: for huge swathes of Lost Weekend, the standard indie singer-songwriter instruments struggle to make themselves heard amid waves of droning electronics, splinters of feedback and eerie wordless vocals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPhoebe Bridgers on Taylor Swift, her boyfriend Paul Mescal and speaking out on Roe v Wade: ‘I want to show everybody what I believe in’Read moreSongs suddenly plunge into silence, or are drenched in swirling, dreamlike echo or subject to unexpected codas that often pull in different emotional directions. Kill Me’s closing desire to vanish – the lyrics reference the case of the Somerton Man, an unidentified body found in late 1940s Adelaide – is far more aggressive than the rest of the song; the title track explodes into chattering euphoria. The overall effect is disorientating, occasionally disturbing and really thrilling: there’s something really daring about the sound of Panorama, where a beautiful melody and a rustic banjo figure are almost completely buried under occasionally discordant murk.The result is a heady, potent, occasionally wrenching album, albeit one flecked with optimism. The most straightforward thing here is Never Going Back!, which repeats the line “the way it used to be is not the way it is” over and over to a charging indie-rock backing. As Above looks ahead to the point where the first flush of romance fades into familiarity, and gives it a positive spin: “You’re gonna take me for granted but I can handle it.”“The past is looking brighter all the time,” sings Bridgers on Liberty Tree. The path to get to that point has evidently been a trying one: Lost Weekend transforms it into a rich and rewarding journey.Lost Weekend is released on 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Ghost of the Mountains by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi review – the secrets of the snow leopard | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: An Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animal
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: An Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animal
Content: A snow leopard.Photograph: Edo Schmidt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA snow leopard.Photograph: Edo Schmidt/AlamyBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewThe Ghost of the Mountains by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi review – the secrets of the snow leopardAn Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animalEdward PosnettWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen bored, try the following game – I call it “Purr or Roar?”. Take any feline and guess whether it can purr or roar (it cannot do both because purring and roaring require different anatomical structures). Some candidates are easy: any child knows that lions and tigers roar and that a tabby does not. But between the great cats and our pets are numerous other species, from lynxes to panthers, whose anatomy is not so easy to infer. A leopard, for instance? Roar (or growl). The discreet, mountain-dwelling snow leopard? Purr.The snow leopard is the protagonist of Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi’s first book, a compelling and intimate look at this elusive mountain specialist. An Indian conservationist and mountaineer, Suryawanshi pursues the creature through the Himalayas and Gobi desert. This is a gritty and detailed portrait of an often misunderstood and endangered species in an increasingly hostile, crowded and hot environment.Suryawanshi grew up in Aurangabad in the Deccan Peninsula – far away from the snow leopard’s habitat – and decided to pursue ecology after reading biologist George Schaller’s The Year of the Gorilla in the city’s public library. He writes of his admiration for western conservationists, mountaineers and explorers – Schaller, Reinhold Messner, and British imperial adventurer Francis Younghusband – and yet he is an Indian writer, writing about the ecology of his own country. As much as his book is about snow leopards, it also asks us to consider their biographers: who is it who gets to tell the story of the nonhuman lives around us?Despite its name, the snow leopard has little in common with the leopard (its closest living relative is the tiger). And, unlike the leopard, it is adapted to the harsh and rugged terrain of the highest ranges, from India to Russia. It has an absurdly bushy tail, used both as extra limb and voluminous shawl, and large paws which act like snow shoes. What it lacks in power (it does not have a particularly strong bite), it makes up for in agility and guile (snow leopards can chase their prey down steep cliff faces; and have been known to drive horses into deep snow where they can be picked off). They are extremely difficult to spot; Suryawanshi observes that their “ochre-and-dust-colour coat with its irregular rosettes looks exactly like a rock covered with lichens”. Indeed, he muses, they should really be called “rock leopards”.I have read much about the snow leopard, or rather books by writers searching for some ideal version of them. Suryawanshi’s book is very different, and can almost be read in opposition to the quest narratives of, say, Peter Matthiessen or Sylvain Tesson. Much like a conservationist’s diary, his book is shorn of romance, and recounts the grind of observing and counting snow leopards in remote parts of the world, far away from his wife and young daughter. He wades through snow, sets up camera traps, and tries to defuse tensions with local herders. His snow leopards are part of an ecosystem, just like any other animal; they are hated and loved, as well as being objects of indifference.According to Suryawanshi, although snow leopards prefer to hunt wild animals, up to 70% of their diet is livestock, a recipe for conflict with local people. He talks to one herder in the Spiti Valley of the Indian Himalayas who nonchalantly relates that he shot a snow leopard after it attacked his goats, and dumped its corpse in a river. Here is no sacred object of veneration, then, but a potential pest, the equivalent of European fox (other locals speak of their fondness for the cats: a community in the village of Kibber ended up adopting and feeding a sick snow leopard, even naming him Rancho after a character in a Bollywood film).Much of Suryawanshi’s work is dedicated to mediating conflict between the cats and locals. He assists in the design of a livestock enclosure that can deter the claws and ingenuity of a hungry snow leopard; and makes recommendations on schemes to compensate herders whose animals have been killed. Interestingly, he notes that women are the most hostile to snow leopards as they are the ones who look after livestock (and do not necessarily benefit from compensation schemes). One local woman asks: “why don’t you marry one of your snow leopards?”The most painful section in the book relates to the bitter dispute regarding the The International Union forConservationof Nature’s 2017 decision to downgrade the animal’s from “endangered” to “vulnerable”. Suryawanshi and his colleagues at the Snow Leopard Trust bitterly opposed the move, arguing that the decision was based on flawed science and driven by the political considerations of large NGOs in the west. In his eyes, “racial power dynamics and colonial legacies of conservation and research” were at play. As of today, the snow leopard is still classed as vulnerable.There is a critique here of the stories that we have told ourselves about the snow leopard, an attempt to wrest it back from literary and metropolitan writers. In one section, Suryawanshi retraces Matthiessen’s steps in Nepal, but it seems as though his heart isn’t really in it. Along the way, he notices the effects of mass tourism, and learns that Nepal’s richest man, who owns an instant noodle company, had sought to build a resort in a remote village for tourists hoping to spot snow leopards. He takes a gentle swipe at Matthiessen: did the American writer ever stop to think about the consequences of mythologising the creature?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI think it’s a push to blame Matthiessen for the plight of the snow leopard, in the same way that Melville shouldn’t be held accountable for the decline in sperm whales. But Suryawanshi’s point is that stories matter: the snow leopard has become a commodity in the way that Everest has, a mountain to be summited. The effect of this book is a gradual stripping away of mystification, revealing the snow leopard to be fragile and beautiful just like any other inhabitant of high mountain ranges – the pika, the wild yak, the Pallas’s cat – but no less wondrous for it, and no less deserving of our attention and respect.The Ghost of the Mountains: Unravelling the Secrets of the Snow Leopard by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi is published by Grant (£20). title: A Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin review – a surprising and darkly funny debut | Books | The Guardian
description: A dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novel
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novel
Content: Wry humour … Brodie Crellin.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenWry humour … Brodie Crellin.Photograph: PRBooksReviewA Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin review – a surprising and darkly funny debutA dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novelElla Fox-MartensWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of us come upon our family’s dysfunctions gradually, like a door that opens a little wider each year. This uncle, you find out, has had an affair; grandma has a hoarding problem. The cremation of the nuclear family illusion is a cornerstone of literature, especially when it’s hastened by one of those unavoidable core gatherings: weddings, births, funerals. But what happens when there was never any illusion to start with; when the story begins in the ashes?The delight of Brodie Crellin’s accomplished, surprising debut lies in the way it wrestles with this question, and in its depiction of a family that fails to meet any conventional definition of the word. With a cutting eye and wry humour, Crellin finds fantastic power in the story of three maladjusted people reeling in the face of death, whose relationships to one another are endlessly confronting and complex.There is friendless Patch, riddled with anxiety, who bursts into tears at the memory of the postman’s suicide and falls victim to a terrible haircut. There is Patch’s father, Robin, who is “gay, yes, mostly, but mutable”. And there is Jude, her domineering, malevolently competent cousin, a playwright who “loves to make an entrance”. They’re bound by the newly deceased Mary: Robin’s ex, Patch’s mother, and Jude’s aunt – a woman who “[didn’t] have a problem with gay men” but was lukewarm on lesbians. Orbiting this “isosceles”, as Jude calls it, is Juliette, Jude’s gleefully moneyed mother, and Mel, Mary’s neighbour. Various other characters swing in and out, all fully realised no matter how brief their appearances, my favourite of which was Mary’s poor, forgotten “empath” labrador, Leonard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt’s a joy to read fiction that understands sex so well, and is neither sentimental nor sleazyThe stage is set, as Jude cruises in from Naples, for a fraught collision of past and present. As the funeral draws closer and tensions simmer, Crellin juggles the minutiae of death – chopping vegetables, arranging memorial photos – with fragmented recollections of messy family history. It’s rare to read a novel that can skip in and out of so many points of view and keep the different styles of narration intact. Yet even with regular flashbacks, A Sense of Occasion feels remarkably natural thanks to Crellin’s light touch, especially in the arch, zippy dialogue. There are shades of classic mid-century stories, particularly Dorothy Baker’s Cassandra at the Wedding, and some of the caustic social wit of Edward St Aubyn’s Melrose chronicles, but the boldness feels entirely modern.It’s a joy, too, to read fiction that understands sex so well, and is neither sentimental nor sleazy. Crellin conveys the importance of sex as a vehicle for each character’s foibles and desires; as a shadowy place where so much can be manipulated and communicated. The book summons up a kaleidoscope of erotic experience across the spectrum, sometimes hot and sometimes ridiculous, including a quasi-incestuous relationship rendered with nuance and consideration.If the novel leans a little hard on Jude and her mother, Juliette, for its class critiques, it’s easily forgiven on account of just how much fun it is to watch these characters crash into each other, and for the deftly nasty one-liners that they toss out. “Patch lacked the confidence conferred by a private education,” Jude thinks smugly. “But she could also say that Patch was simply less intelligent.” And yet the story never veers into mean-spirited satire, largely thanks to Patch herself, the grief-stricken daughter, who is the heartbeat of the novel. Perennially misunderstood and underestimated – including by her own mother, when she was alive – Patch is awkward but raw, a keen observer of herself and others.There is immense pleasure and vitality – and ultimately a great deal of tenderness – in A Sense of Occasion’s depiction of flawed, strange people who love badly, and can’t help but get in the way of themselves over and over again. After all, as George Bernard Shaw wrote, “If you cannot get rid of the family skeleton, you may as well make it dance.”A Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin is published by Jonathan Cape (£16.99). title: The ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talent | Games | The Guardian
description: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesThe ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talentBig developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playingDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Last week, Asha Sharma, the new head of Xbox, laid outher vision for the future of the consoleand interestingly, the two titles she picked out as potential areas of growth were Minecraft and Candy Crush Saga – games that don’t exactly scream next-generation entertainment. Neither relies on hyper-realistic visuals, which is the north star that games consoles and gaming PCs have been aiming at for the past 40 years. They are, instead, well-designed, well-loved franchises that you can play and enjoy on almost any PC, console or phone.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The fact is, the quest for visual hyperrealism is breaking the games industry. It’s becoming more and more expensive to put high-end graphics hardware into machinesthanks to demand from the AI sector; at the same time, creating superrealistic visuals is an incredibly expensive and complex part of game development, leading to longer development periods. GTA VI, for example, has taken at least eight years to develop and is rumoured to have cost between $1bn and $2bn. By my back-of-an-envelope calculations, that’s around four times more than GTA V. Admittedly, the detail on everything, from the characters’ faces, to the cars, to the cityscapes, is astonishing. But will it be four times better than GTA V? Will it be four times more fun?It’s very clear from the shameful number of redundancies the industry has processed in the last two years that its model isn’t working. An increased focus on graphical fidelity leads to greater costs, which in turn leads to creative caution. Everyone is chasing a teeny number of slots in the big genres, and most of them are falling short. WasConcord– an OK entry into the grossly over-burdened hero shooter genre – really worth the $400m that Sony put into it, or would that money have been better spent on a few more games likeAstro Bot, or even a freshRatchet and Clankor two?View image in fullscreenWe don’t need no fancy graphics … Minecraft.Photograph: MojangI’m convinced that only a small minority of gamers now care about how many beautifully lit, ray-traced, frame-injected polygons a machine can fling around. I feel a wave of despondency any time a game asks me to choose between performance or fidelity modes. Sometimes I don’t even notice if I’m playing at 30 or 60 frames per second.Visual fidelity isn’t where the art happens. The art is in the style and substance of the game. Titles such asOkami,Journeyor Cuphead wouldn’t look better with more detailed graphics. I didn’t enjoyThe Last of Usmore on PS5 than I did on PS4 – or PS3, for that matter. We’re at a stage where developers have nailed the production of beautiful open worlds filled with lifelike characters. So what do we do with those worlds now? That is the question of the artist – and there are still plenty of artists left in this troubled business.Lets remind ourselves of the most important shift in visual clarity in the home video business: VHS to DVD. The latter format arrived in the late 1990s and still accounts for 50-60% of disc sales – 4K Blu-ray discs, the most visually detailed offering, come in at about 20%. This is an unfair comparison, of course, because the home video business has faced a very different range of competitors and market challenges. But the fact is, when people want to buy a film, half of those people will still buy it on a format that’s been around for almost 30 years.What have been some of the best games this year?Pokopia,Mixtape, Cairn, Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight,Mina the Hollower, Denshattack!,Mewgenics, Titanium Court … None would have been made more compelling by detailed graphics. Sure, these are mostly indie titles – they don’t have to shift hardware units, and they don’t have to showcase the prowess of first-party studios to shareholders – but it’s interesting, isn’t it, that the two games Xbox’s Sharma referenced for her road ahead had comparatively humble origins. So did Roblox, the title that Minecraft must contend with; as did Fortnite, possibly the most popular game in the world.If social media platforms have taught us anything, it’s that we live in an age that values rapidly dispersed ideas over “perfect” realisation. If digital TV platforms have taught us anything, it’s that people struggle to wait two years for a new instalment in a beloved franchise. And yet the market is saturated with high-end content; it is everywhere, and it is losing. TS Eliot once wrote: “Humankind cannot bear very much reality” – in art, in games, in real-life, we like to stop just short. That is the sweet spot. An ultra-high-end graphics chipset is not required to get us there.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat we do in life echoes in eternity … How Many Dudes?Photograph: Butterscotch ShenanigansIt’s an age-old philosophical question: how many men would it take to defeat a lion in combat? Or a gorilla? Or a duck the size of a horse? Well, thanks toHow Many Dudes?we can now answer that question. In this roguelike auto-battler, you build and command a group of differently skilled dudes – some are wizards, some are zombies, some are knights, but all must enter the arena together and fight whatever fate throws at them. The experience is a chaotic and ridiculous maesltrom of flailing limbs – there is tactical depth beneath the daft premise. The game isa cult hit on Steamand, dude, after only a few hours of play, I can totally see why.Available on:PC, AndroidEstimated playtime:Five hours plusWhat to readView image in fullscreenSupport your local games makers … A Short Hike is included part of a fundraiser for laid-off developers.Photograph: AdamgryuAnindie game bundleput together to raise money for laid-off game developers in North America hasraised more than $100,000in three days. The bundle, organised by the Communication Workers Union, isavailable on Itch.iofor $10 (though you can pay more) – it includes 127 games, including acclaimed titles such as A Short Hike and SkateBird. The offer is running until 13 August.Electronic Artshas been bought by Saudi Arabia’s wealth fundand a group of investors for $55bn (£41bn). It is the second-biggest gaming acquisition, and ends EA Games’s 36-year history as a publicly traded company.Microsoft has increasedprices forXbox consolesin Europe and the UK. At the lowest price point, the Xbox Series S 512GB model is going up from £299.99 to £429.99, while the Xbox Series X 1tb model will be rising from £499.99 to £669.99. The company has blamed higher storage and memory costs. Hoping things will improve next year? Nope.Samsung expectsthe situation to worsen through 2027.Sega has created a five-hour playlist featuring the music ofSonic composer Jun Senoue, asVGC reports. Available on Apple Music and Spotify, it contains 100 tracks and runs for just over five hours. Perfect for your next hike across the Pennines (or, indeed, any Green Hill Zone).OurSummer Games previewis in full swing, with pieces aboutClean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim, A Line Held Tight, about worker’s rights and lives, and the adorableTanuki: Pon’s Summer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ’em all after 30 yearsWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleyMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Dominik DiamondSingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video gamesHalo: Campaign Evolved – they don’t make ’em like this any more | ★★★★☆Big Walk – larking around with mates elevated to an artform | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenWhat if I’m becoming bad? … Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix game.Photograph: APHere’s a timely question fromMaddie, via email:“Whatever happened to the movie tie-in video game? As someone who first got into games by playing the Harry Potter titles on PlayStation, I miss these often derided treasures. Did they just go out of fashion?”Conveniently for me, the answer to this question is tied in with the essay above: movie games simply became too expensive and took too long to make, so the risks outweighed the potential rewards. What we tend to see now are more limited tie-ins, such as mini VR “experiences” along the lines ofStranger Things VRorProject Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, a forthcoming mixed-reality tie-in with the film. With the really big movie brands, meanwhile, we’re getting standalone offshoots –Indiana Jones and the Great Circle,Alien: Isolation,Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order… I think this is good, as all of those titles were very good – which is more than can be said for most tie-in games throughout history. Let’s be honest, for every GoldenEye, Lego Star Wars or Disney’s Aladdin, there were a hundred Charlie’s Angels, Top Guns and ETs. This is one example where technological progress has brought inarguable benefits.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VIMinecraftXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew Valley | Games | The Guardian
description: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Author: Nicole Clark
Headline: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Content: Charming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioView image in fullscreenCharming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioGamesWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleySince Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touchesNicole ClarkWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarming simulator games deliver on an escapist fantasy: going off-grid from the modern work grind, in exchange for charming small-town life and a farm to call your own. While these games have had dedicated fans since the days of Harvest Moon, the most popular today,Stardew Valley, contemporised the genre with a larger range of activities and lovable townspeople to befriend and romance. Created in 2016 by independent developer Eric Barone, it has now sold more than 50m copies and become the mould for so many other indie farming sims.Fields of Mistria is one of these farming sims in a post-Stardewworld – though it updates the core formula. Created by independent developer NPC Studio, Fields of Mistria has already proven popular: it debuted in early access (a pre-release version of the game meant for early players to find bugs and give feedback) forPCplayers on Steam in August 2024, and in the first month the game racked up more than 4m player hours. It’s for a good reason: Mistria satisfies all of those same farming sim desires but with more expansive character creation and a story steeped in magic.What is Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenAlready popular in its first month of early access … Fields of Mistria.Illustration: NPC StudioFields of Mistria is a farming and life simulator game with fantasy themes. You play as the new farmer in Mistria, a lovable small town in recovery from an earthquake, whose inhabitants hope you’ll fulfil their requests for various produce and supplies. Over the four seasons you grow crops, raise barn animals and attend events: from regular Saturday markets to the annual Shooting Star festival. Choose between a cat or a dog as a pet and accumulate toys and accessories for all your animals. My personal favourite is watching a duck and a rabbit play together on a seesaw.You’ll repair structures and buildings in town, such as the bridge or the Sleeping Dragon Inn. Donate supplies and funds, raise your renown level and town rank, and restore Mistria to its former glory. Along the way you’ll make friends with the townspeople: like Ryis the carpenter, who is shockingly quick at those repairs, or Hayden, the owner of Sweetwater Farm who has a haughty prize-winning chicken called Henrietta (and yes, you can befriend her, too).You can also fish, catch bugs and explore the mines; just be careful about selling anything immediately, because you might want to hold on to it to donate to the museum, or use it to craft cute furniture for your home. Your character evolves along with you: the more you do, the more you’ll be able to level up skills such as cooking, ironmongery, and archaeology.How is Fields of Mistriadifferent fromStardewValley?Fields of Mistria may sound like aclassic farming sim– but there’s a twist: you gain magical powers, thanks to the mysterious dragon Caldarus, who you can talk to by visiting a shrine on your farm. One spell lets you create rain, so you don’t have to painstakingly water all of your crops. Another lets you fully restore stamina, so you can get back to fishing for that golden eel. It seems the earthquake may have unearthed some unexpected parts of Mistria’s history.And while Stardew Valley – despite its lauded queer relationship options – has thus far only offered two choices forgender expression, in Mistria, character gender options also include “they/them”, “she/they,” “he/they,” and more.There are also some great accessibility features. In particular, you can make a day longer by slowing down time, giving yourself a truly leisurely pace to play. It’s an antidote to how frantic Stardew Valley can feel, especially during special events when you’re trying to pack as much into a day as you can.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre there romance-friendly characters in Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenEagerly awaited romance arcs … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioMistria is full of potential suitors, and you can woo any eligible villager regardless of gender. There’s Juniper, the sorceress who owns the local bathhouse, and who wouldn’t look out of place with the cast of Sailor Moon. Or maybe you’d like to romance March, the grumpy blacksmith who is a tough nut to crack – he’s atsundere, an anime archetype for someone who’s abrasive at first – until you know him better.Early accesscappedthe number of hearts you could unlock with each villager, and players have been eagerly awaiting the extended romance arcs in the full game. Without spoiling too much, let’s just say there’s also at least once romance option who isn’texactlyhuman.This lively cast of characters and love interests is ultimately what makes Fields of Mistria a standout in its genre. The town is always alive and bustling, encouraging you to spend time there – Friday nights at the Inn, where everyone gathers, being a highlight. Some of the villagers play Dungeons and Dragons, while others try out new desserts. You can ask socialite Elsie for gossip, or even join the kids in an adventuring club. There’s a real sense of place and kinship that makes playing Fields of Mistriafeel like a lovely escape.Explore more on these topicsGamesPCSimulation gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dog Man: The Musical review – Dav Pilkey’s megastar mutt sniffs out the spotlight in a barking show | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stage
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: A part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stage
Content: Throwing it all together … Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenThrowing it all together … Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorTheatreReviewDog Man: The Musical review – Dav Pilkey’s megastar mutt sniffs out the spotlight in a barking showSouthbank Centre, LondonA part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stageTim JonzeWed 5 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps, if you don’t have a child in primary school, you will be blissfully unaware of Dog Man, Dav Pilkey’s series of graphic novels about a cop who – after a terrible injury – has his dog’s head sewn on to his own body, thereby creating a crime-fighting canine/human crossbreed. But if you’ve been swept up by the phenomenon – and Dog Manisa phenomenon, selling more than 70m copies in the decade since the first book was published – then you will know that this mutt has some serious star power: there’s aDog Man film, video game, board game … and now a musical,arriving in the UKafter off-Broadway success.The Dog Man books are chaotic, hilarious and full of pathos, but writer/lyricist Kevin Del Aguila and composer Brad Alexander’s show leans largely on the former. There’s slapstick humour and jokes about butt-sniffing. When Dog Man is asked how his day is going, he replies: “Ruff!” It’s aimed at the younger end of Pilkey’s readership, which is confusing as there are also Dickens references.The plot – based on several early Dog Man books in the 14-strong series – is actually a musical within a musical: George and Harold, the fictional writers of the Dog Man comics, have decided to put on a musical to prove to their teacher how easy that would be. Because they’re throwing it all together using whatever they can find in their cupboard, Timothy R Mackabee’s set is charmingly DIY – skyscrapers are made from cardboard and gaffer tape, characters shapeshift across soft toy/glove puppet/human actor form.View image in fullscreenSuper-powers from brain dust … Vanessa Dumatey as Flippy in Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorOur hero hound (Renan Teodoro) is pitted against Petey (Sam Kipling), the villainous cat, and Flippy (Vanessa Dumatey), a psychokinetic butterflyfish who has gained super-powers from eating “brain dust”. But there’s a twist! To help achieve his evil aims, Petey clones himself, expecting a similarly twisted replica to emerge – instead he mistakenly creates Li’l Petey (Rebecca-Jo Roberts), a super-cute and naive kid who insists on calling Petey “papa” (cue much “I’m NOT your papa!!”).Li’l Petey is the books’ emotional core and no doubt parents will relate to the idea of suddenly having a mini-me in their world who annoyingly doesn’t behave as instructed. But as the energetic cast dance, sing and bark their way around the set like CBeebies presenters after three pints of Skittles, these more moving moments get buried in the production, directed and choreographed by Jen Wineman. There’s also a slight disconnect in seeing people act out these roles – would children not get more excited at seeing Pilkey’s cutesy characters come to life with big furry heads rather than, say, an orange beanie?Translating a graphic novel into a musical was always going to throw up such hurdles. At one point the hyperactive George and Harold, played by Ricardo Mendes and Peter Lavery, bring a board onstage to try to replicate the “animated” flip-o-ramas from the series. “This isn’t working the way it does in the comics!” they complain. It’s a joke, but still – perhaps musicals aren’t quite as easy to pull off as George and Harold thought.AtSouthbank Centre, London, until 16 August. title: I’m Every Woman: The Chaka Khan Musical review – Queen of Funk’s jukebox epic lacks the X factor | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Alexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven show
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Alexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven show
Content: Nimble staging … Alexandra Burke as Chaka Khan in I’m Every Woman.Photograph: Danny KaanView image in fullscreenNimble staging … Alexandra Burke as Chaka Khan in I’m Every Woman.Photograph: Danny KaanTheatreReviewI’m Every Woman: The Chaka Khan Musical review – Queen of Funk’s jukebox epic lacks the X factorTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, LondonAlexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven showAmmar KaliaWed 5 Aug 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the pantheon of soul divas,Chaka Khanis surely one of the fiercest. With a soaring, multioctave vocal range that earned accolades from Aretha Franklin and Miles Davis, as well as a chequered personal life and a stint in the Black Panthers alongside Fred Hampton, Khan’s story has long felt ripe for immortalisation in a jukebox musical.I’m Every Woman features X Factor winnerAlexandra Burkein the lead role, with a book by Khan’s own creative director, Nia T Hill. Running just shy of three hours, it is a gargantuan undertaking of two uneven parts.The opening half sprints through a remarkable girlhood and young adulthood. Khan’s father leaves the family owing to a drug problem, she joins the local Black Panther party chapter in Chicago, falls in love, decides to become a singer and witnesses Hampton’s murder – all in a matter of minutes. Celebrity impersonations pop up in case the frenetic pace isn’t enough to hold the audience’s attention – from a spirited Joni Mitchell to vapid parodies of Prince, Stevie Wonder and Miles Davis.View image in fullscreenOver too quick … Burke as Chaka Khan and Teddy Wills as Fred Hampton.Photograph: Danny KaanBurke plays Khan with an energetic youthfulness – but when it comes to vocals faces a sisyphean task. She makes a valiant effort of singalong hits like Ain’t Nobody and Tell Me Something Good, but lacks the resonance to replicate Khan’s power. Nowhere is this clearer than during the ballad Through the Fire, which employs three singers to replicate Khan’s performance and still falls short of her key-jumping agility.Director Racky Plews’ staging is nimble, making use of immersive projections, while the ensemble boasts a comic star in Ashley Stroud, as Khan’s bolshie younger sister, Taka Boom. Yet when the second half arrives and Khan finds herself the “Queen of Funk” in the 1980s, the show runs entirely out of pace and music.The Prince-penned I Feel for You is a raucous post-interval opener, but the remaining hour meanders through Khan’s 90s and 00s years, choosing to focus on her charitable foundation work and efforts to go independent, rather than her artistry. When it comes time for a harried emotional reunion with her estranged daughter in rehab, the pathos refuses to land. Instead, I’m Every Woman becomes a musical in service to somewhat sparse music, rather than a clearly astounding story.AtTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, London, until 27 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsChaka KhanAlexandra BurkereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Getting old is no fun’: Game of Thrones author George RR Martin speaks out about depression amid further book delays | George RR Martin | The Guardian
description: A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series
Content: ‘There have been nightmares’ … George RR Martin in 2019.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘There have been nightmares’ … George RR Martin in 2019.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverGeorge RR Martin‘Getting old is no fun’: Game of Thrones author George RR Martin speaks out about depression amid further book delaysA new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire seriesEmma LoffhagenWed 5 Aug 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge RR Martin has opened up about experiencing depression during a “stressful” and “overwhelming” year, as readers continue to await the long-delayed sixth instalment of his A Song of Ice and Fire series.The 77-year-old American author, whose fantasy novels shaped and inspired the hit HBO television seriesGame of Thrones,wrote candidly about his recent difficulties in his first personal blog post for almost six months.“This year has been … stressful, to say the least,” he wrote ina post titled Better Late Than Never. “So much has been happening, it’s been overwhelming. Some great things, exciting things. Dreams coming true. But there have been nightmares too. I have lost friends. Battled sadness and depression. The worst may be yet to come.”He explained that posts published on his website since February had been written by his assistants because he had continued to fall behind despite their help.Martin, who turns 78 in September, also reflected on ageing; “getting old is no fun”, he wrote, although he added that the year had contained “amazing times” alongside its difficulties.“I suppose that’s just life. Of course, I knew that. If you’ve read my stories, you know that.”A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms has saved the Game of Thrones universeRead moreAmong the year’s highlights, Martin noted thatA Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,HBO’s Game of Thrones prequel based on his Tales of Dunk and Egg novellas, had received nine Emmy nominations, including for outstanding drama series.His comments come amidcontinued speculation about The Winds of Winter,the planned sixth and penultimate novel in A Song of Ice and Fire. The book has been in progress since the publication of the fifth instalment, A Dance with Dragons, in 2011, and has become one of the most eagerly awaited novels in modern publishing. No publication date has been announced.Martin has faced sustained criticism from some readers over the delay, and has previously referred to the book as “the curse of my life”. The Game of Thrones TV show eventually overtook its source material, with its later seasons following a separate narrative that receiveda mixed response from critics and viewers,especially after its final season in 2019.In ablog post in May 2025, Martin directly addressed those who believed he had abandoned the series, sarcastically listing the accusations levelled against him: “I will never finish Winds. If I do, I will never finish A Dream of Spring. If I do, it won’t be any good.”Continuing the charges, he wrote: “I am going to die soon anyway, because I am so old. I lost all interest in A Song of Ice and Fire decades ago. I don’t give a shit about writing any longer, I just sit around and spend my money.”But Martin insisted that he remained invested in Westeros and its characters. “I care about them all,” he wrote. “More than you can ever imagine.”In an interview withthe Hollywood Reporter in January, Martin said he had completed about 1,100 manuscript pages of The Winds of Winter. He said leaving the series unfinished would feel like “a total failure”, adding: “I do think if I can just get some of these other things off my back, I could finish The Winds of Winter pretty soon … It’s been made clear to me that Winds is the priority, but … I don’t know. Sometimes I’m not in the mood for that.”In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsGeorge RR MartinFantasy booksGame of ThronesFictionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Analogue evil: why today’s horror film-makers are obsessed with obsolete tech | Horror films | The Guardian
description: From Obsession to Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a new wave of movies are ditching minimalism for retro settings
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Obsession to Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a new wave of movies are ditching minimalism for retro settings
Content: Hannah Einbinder in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Mubi/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHannah Einbinder in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: Mubi/Everett/ShutterstockHorror filmsAnalogue evil: why today’s horror film-makers are obsessed with obsolete techFrom Obsession to Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a new wave of movies are ditching minimalism for retro settingsJames McClellanWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe indie-horror hit filmsObsessionandBackroomsopened this summer’s movie season with a bang, each grossing hundreds of millions of dollars and turning out legions of younger moviegoers. Many have pointed out the similarity between the films: both were made for comparatively minuscule budgets by gen Z directors –Curry Barkerand Kane Parsons – who first rose to prominence on YouTube.Fewer people are talking about the other quality the two movies share: a steady stream of analogue props and production design that plunges you into some bygone pre-digital era. Obsession’s lead characters Bear and Nikki work at a mom-and-pop music store, take rides in Bear’s vintage station wagon and the plot centers around a kitschy, old-fashioned gag gift. InBackrooms, Mary hawks her self-help cassette tapes on late-night infomercials, Clark smacks his TV to adjust the fuzzy signal – in the HDTV age, no one has done this for decades – and the wall-to-wall carpeted, ceiling-tiled backrooms look straight out of a long-abandoned office park on the side of the highway.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma review – Gillian Anderson superb in queer slasher spectacularRead moreJane Schoenbrun’s new filmTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasmatakes this trend to another level, following a young director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) trying to reboot an 80s slasher film franchise, who’d like to cast the original film’s starlet, Billy (Gillian Anderson) in the remake. Kris must go to the films’ now-deserted summer camp set to recruit Billy, whose star has since faded and now lives a reclusive existence there. The film blends the past and present into a funny and freaky, yet also emotional and cathartic, acid-trip of a movie.But why exactly are all of these movies leaning into this vintage vibe? There’s no doubt that nostalgia has always had a powerful pull for film-makers and audiences alike. But there is also a functional reason: modern aesthetics lack the texture that horror movies need to thrive, texture that can be more easily found in past eras.Think of the sleek, minimalist style that sums up post-2010s interior design: the vaguely Scandinavian surfaces and rounded edges that you might find at an Apple Store or a Blank Street Coffee. There’s nothing lurking around those squeaky-clean corners, and that’s a problem for a genre that relies on suspense. Horror film settings are basically haunted houses, after all – and haunted houses need those long shadows cast by that weird, old hatstand, the warped floorboards that creak and groan and that creepy old portrait that may or may not be watching as you tiptoe across the room. So many of our household items have been sucked up into the cloud: a grandfather clock, record player and stack of dusty tomes can now be replaced by one, compact smart home speaker on the countertop. It’s all gotten a bit too ordered and empty.Obsessed with Obsession: how a low-budget horror changed the game in HollywoodRead moreAll three of these films feature their own spin on the haunted house. At the start of Obsession, Bear’s apartment is fairly ordinary, if a bit old-fashioned. But as Nikki begins to unravel, so too does the apartment, morphing into a grotesque sort-of nest for whatever Nikki is becoming – bodily fluids ooze into the carpet, windows and doors are haphazardly boarded up, casting the place in darkness; the only light emanates from the snowy picture on Bear’s bulky TV console.The eponymous backrooms in Parsons’s film have mystery and monsters around every corner. Characters are constantly clambering over piles of broken furniture, sliding down chutes, and climbing up vertigo-inducing staircases. Meanwhile, things get even more meta in Camp Miasma, which largely takes place on the set of a horror film – a campground full of empty cabins and even a cinema. And within these haunted houses, there need to be ample objects for the characters to interact with: the rubber bats and bowls of cold spaghetti – err, I mean brains – that make us squirm.View image in fullscreenMichael Johnston, Megan Lawless and Cooper Tomlinson in Obsession.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesThe One Wish Willow in Obsession looks like the type of gag gift I loved as a kid, like those little red fortune-telling fish or a Magic 8 Ball. Camp Miasma also literally opens with a montage of toys: trading cards, board games and other collectibles from the fictitious film franchise. Many of these objects have been digitized in recent years, however, which doesn’t always serve a horror movie’s best interests; it’s like watching a toddler play with a set of Lincoln Logs versus an iPad – one’s just more interesting to watch than the other.Similarly, these films seem to be happiest with some electronic devices, just not our current iPhone era. It’s as if technology froze around the year 2000 – when station wagons roamed the streets, the Yellow Pages hung from pay phones, and of course, physical media were everywhere, with floppy disks and desktops, VHS tapes and VCRs, CDs, records, radios and more.It’s worth remembering that these technologies weren’t always used for quaint or peculiar effect – they were once quite cutting edge. The Ring (a remake of the 1998 Japanese filmRingu) was powered brilliantly by a cursed videotape, creepy footage and an ominous telephone call with news of your impending death. None of this would work today – no one has a VCR, let alone a landline. A few years before,The Blair Witch Project’s fuzzy, jittery camcorder POV-style cinematography gave the film a frantic, unsettled feel – we never quite have the full picture of what is going on. And certainly less than if it was shot on the crystal-clear video we now have access to on our phone cameras. Backrooms opens with a very similar scene – the videographer is running from something, terrified, before it cuts out. What happened to the videographer? We don’t know. But if we keep watching, we might find out.View image in fullscreenRenate Reinsve in Backrooms.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWhen a film sprinkles in these little totems from another time, it also creates a powerful feeling of surrealism. “I was a fifth grader hanging around in the horror section at the local video store, obsessively renting and watching and just dreaming,”Schoenbrun said in an interviewabout their inspiration for Camp Miasma. Horror plays with a dream-like state more than other genres, since they often feature supernatural elements and ask the viewer to suspend disbelief.But this also allows film-makers to explore other realities aspirationally, which may sound counterintuitive given the genre’s depravity. And just like Schoenbrun tries to recreate a feeling from their childhood, maybe a part of us all yearns for the past – and these physical souvenirs remind us of these simpler times. Even the concept of “yearning” has become a gen Z buzzword; longing for something – in this case for a world that Barker and Parsons can’t even remember.Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is out on 7 August in the US and Australia, and 21 August in the UKExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsGillian AndersonThrillersBackroomsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Prisoners killed each other’s kittens. So now they’re forbidden inside’: Vladimir Karamazov’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’
Content: Stray cats on Belene Island by Vladimir Karamazov, from his photobook For the Grace of God.Photograph: Vladimir KaramazovView image in fullscreenStray cats on Belene Island by Vladimir Karamazov, from his photobook For the Grace of God.Photograph: Vladimir KaramazovMy best shotArt and design‘Prisoners killed each other’s kittens. So now they’re forbidden inside’: Vladimir Karamazov’s best photograph‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 5 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBelene prison, in northernBulgariaon the border with Romania, is the most heavily guarded facility of its type in my country. It is on an island, so escape is near impossible, and has the largest number of people serving life sentences for murder in any Bulgarian prison.This image describes a sad, terrible story. There are a lot of stray cats on the island, as well as pigeons and mosquitoes. The prisoners used to adopt stray kittens and keep them as pets. When I started my project, For the Grace of God, at the prison, many prisoners had pet cats. But in a prison, this can become a problem – prisoners kill each other’s pets as punishment or for revenge. So now it’s forbidden. It’s even the same with flowers – some think of the flowers as friends, they nurture and grow them in the sun, but then other prisoners destroy them. Anything a prisoner can create a relationship with can be destroyed. Part of their punishment is to be alone, without any family, or any attachments to anything.double quotation markI host the Bulgarian version of The Traitors. But I was curious about life inside prisonIt’s another world with a different set of rules, another language, and even money is different – cigarettes are currency. There are a lot of rules. I spent a lot of time in Belene, living like the prisoners, spending all day with them, listening to their stories. I am a well-known television and theatre actor here in my country. I’ve hosted the Bulgarian edition of Survivor for five seasons; I host the Bulgarian version of The Traitors. I have a lot of work, but I don’t like the people in my industry, and my work as an actor is boring for me now. I started this project out of curiosity about life inside: people in my country have no idea how prisoners live. It was difficult to get permission as I wanted to access the prison for a year and to be allowed to shoot everywhere and anywhere with no limitations.Talking to the prisoners, I discovered that everything begins in their childhood: 99% grew up in a family without love, money, or with abuse; something was broken. This is a problem in society, not only for these people. Most people just want prisoners dead; they would prefer funding to go to old people or children. When I presented this work at the National Gallery in Sofia, people were crying – it was the first time they saw prisoners as people like us. They saw human beings.
