We are all the same, but some people don’t have the opportunity for a good life.At the beginning, I was scared of the prisoners who were sentenced without parole. I thought these people had nothing to lose and could kill me as a joke. I said to the director to please alert me if any of them were in my vicinity. One day he introduced Milchu, and told me to spend the day with him. I asked Milchu to please tell me if we came across any of the prisoners without parole. He laughed and asked me how I expected them to look? I said I don’t know – in chains? But I begged him to warn me. The next day I asked him the same thing. Eventually he told me: “I’m one of them. I have a 26-year life sentence without parole.” My mind was blown – I didn’t expect that this man I had spent two days with was a killer. I couldn’t sleep that night.double quotation markCan you be friends with a killer? The hard truth is yesThe first three months were very difficult, I had a lot of nightmares. There are a lot of terrible stories, but I didn’t want to explain the stories in my photographs. I wanted to think about how a criminal life begins, to ask questions, not judge. “Can you be friends with a killer?” I was asked once. The hard truth is yes. Today I am good friends with three prisoners sentenced without parole.My life has changed a lot in the last two years because of this experience. Forgiveness is a simple word, but it’s very hard. Milchu has three children, and when he killed someone, he also destroyed his whole family, his world. I met one of his daughters who told me that for 15 years after her father’s crime she hated him every day for destroying their life. Then one day she understood that hating this man her whole life was terrible for her, so she decided to forgive him.I related this story to Milchu – he started to cry. He said it was the most important moment of his life. He never knew his daughter had forgiven him. He said he would die happy.For the Grace of God is published by Gost books(£60)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: KaramazovfotoVladimir Karamazov’s CVBorn:Bulgaria, 1979High point:My greatest achievement is that I had the courage, after 20 successful years as an actor – playing major roles in film, theatre and television – to turn to photography and start from scratch. To leave one life and set out to pursue another – for me more interesting – where I confront the truth of our lives. As an actor I am an interpreter, recreating reality. As a photographer I am a creator who captures and preserves reality. Within six years I managed to pass through many levels of photography, I won many awards, held major exhibitions and have created the projects that excite me. Through my projects I try to open a door for society to places they do not want to look, do not know what is there, and are afraid of. When they peek through my open door, they see that it is not so frightening there, that people like us live there, too.Top tip:I constantly urge people to think a little more. When we hear something bad about someone, we are immediately inclined to condemn them. But we do not know their story, we do not know why they committed a certain act, yet we judge. If we give ourselves time and get to know that person, we will learn the reason why they are the way they are. This happened to me with people convicted of murder. The act itself is horrifying. But when you learn the whole story of that person, when you understand that they grew up without family, without love, in terrible squalor and hunger, you understand why they are that way.Explore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotPhotographyBulgariafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Film posters for The Mummy banned from public display in UK | Movies | The Guardian
description: Watchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Watchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’
Content: Part of the poster for The Mummy that provoked 30 complaints after appearing in London tube stations.Photograph: ASA/PAPart of the poster for The Mummy that provoked 30 complaints after appearing in London tube stations.Photograph: ASA/PAMoviesFilm posters for The Mummy banned from public display in UKWatchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 09.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm posters for The Mummy have been banned from outdoor public display in the UK because they include realistic depictions of a dead child.The UK’sAdvertising Standards Authority(ASA) received 30 complaints over the promotional campaign in London tube stations for the new Lee Cronin film.The adverts included a poster showing a closeup image of a female with a mummified appearance and one eye swollen shut. The text said: “Some things are meant to stay buried.”TV and livestreaming services trailed scenes of a body being removed from a sarcophagus and a woman looking distressed as a greying hand with long brittle nails brushes her cheek. The advert, which ends with the mother saying “I just want my daughter back”, was approved by the Clearcast vetting agency for post-7.30pm broadcasts.Many of the complainants said the ads were distressing for children and adults alike.Warner Bros defended the campaign, saying it had been prepared with “due responsibility to consumers and society” and was not designed to create fear or offence.It said the character depicted in the posters was a “living mummy” who was returned to her parents many years after been kidnapped as a child.Warner said the posters used a face with a neutral expression and reduced the risk of distress by avoiding elements of violence, threat or intimidation.The studio added that the design had been submitted to Transport for London’s advertising partner Global and had been accepted for display on theLondon Undergroundnetwork.It said the horror themes in the trailer were implied rather than shown explicitly and contained no “jump scares, no violence or gore” and no graphic imagery.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUpholding complaints about the posters, the ASA said the grey and ashen appearance of the female’s skin, the dry and cracked lips and mouth, one eye swollen shut and the other fixed and vacant, together with the sunken and lifeless appearance of the face, gave a “realistic impression of a dead child”.It said that while the ads were not placed within 100 metres of any schools, one billboard was visible from a children’s nursery.The watchdog said: “In any case, we considered the image was likely to distress young children and that it was unsuitable for display where it was likely to be seen by them. We therefore concluded that the ads were unsuitable for outdoor display and therefore breached the code.”Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsAdvertising Standards AuthorityAdvertisingLondonLondon UndergroundShareReuse this content

title: ‘Web puppies’: how these tiny jumping spiders became a social media sensation | Pets | The Guardian
description: The new stars of TikTok have eight furry legs and eight soulful eyes. But are they quite as adorable as real puppies?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The new stars of TikTok have eight furry legs and eight soulful eyes. But are they quite as adorable as real puppies?
Content: Now you see it …Photograph: Donny Hughes/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNow you see it …Photograph: Donny Hughes/Getty ImagesPass notesPets‘Web puppies’: how these tiny jumping spiders became a social media sensationThe new stars of TikTok have eight furry legs and eight soulful eyes. But are they quite as adorable as real puppies?Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Web puppies.Age:Pet jumping spiders typically live for one to three years.Jumping spiders?Yikes!I thought we were talking about puppies?They’re called that because they’re cute. They are also known as spooders and spoods.OK, but they’ve still goteight legs.Eight eyes, too, as it happens.And, judging by the name, they can jump.Actually, there are more than 6,000 species of jumping spiders (from the familySalticidae) in the world. Relax, though, they’re not big.We’re not talkingAragog, the giant spider from Harry Potter, then?No, they can easily fit on your fingernail. Guess where theyarebig, though?I’m hoping it’s not in my bed.Nope. On the internet.I supposethe web would bewhere you’dfind spiders.Yes, they’re a craze, with videos of tiny pet jumping spiders popping up on social media.Doing what?Well, in one TikTok with more than 2m views,a spider called Violetappears to hug a little clay human figure before retiring to its little pink cottage.I suppose that is kind of sweet.Violet sadly died earlier this year, but her owner, a 33-year-old South Carolina woman, has other pet spiders including Tinkerbell and Pebbles, both with strong online presences.So you can buy these things?Creatures, please. Yes, theNew York Timesspoke to Lauren Taylor, a graphic designer who has about 2,000 in her Nevada house, including a playful one-year-old canopy jumping spider named Harry. Lauren breeds them and charges from $60 to $100 (£45-£75) for one, depending on the breed.That’s cheaper than an actual puppy.And double the legs.But can you create that bond?“You would never think it’s possible until you do it,” says Lauren. Also, meet Opal …Who’s that?She’s another TikTok star, who went viral in 2021 after she was filmed “tucking in” her babies to their silken egg sack, with the caption: “Gotta protek dem.”Yuck (and not because I’m scared of spiders).You’re not alone: not everyone approves of this arachnophilic anthropomorphism for clicks. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) is one example.What does Peta say?Thatit’s a “cruel social media fad”and “these complex, sensitive animals belong in their natural habitats – not in a glass prison”. And last year, after a couple of pet retail chains began selling jumping spiders in the US, more than 2,000 people signed apetition demanding they stop.Wasn’t it Peta who, in a campaign to try to stop people eating them, once referred to fish as “sea kittens”?Very true. Which some might say disqualifies them from being taken seriously about anything, ever.Do say:“Daddy, get me a web puppy! Now!”Don’t say:“Where is she? She was right here a second ago … Tinkerbell!”Explore more on these topicsPetsPass notesSpidersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The herbicide haunting a New York farm town | Herbicides | The Guardian
description: Paraquat is banned in over 70 countries. Some farmers and their families in Hebron believe the pesticide is causing Parkinson’s disease and are demanding that New York ban it
Author: Amudalat Ajasa
Headline: Paraquat is banned in over 70 countries. Some farmers and their families in Hebron believe the pesticide is causing Parkinson’s disease and are demanding that New York ban it
Content: Gordan Chaplin and his wife, Sarah Teale, at their home in Hebron, New York.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusView image in fullscreenGordan Chaplin and his wife, Sarah Teale, at their home in Hebron, New York.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusHerbicidesThe herbicide haunting a New York farm townParaquat is banned in over 70 countries. Some farmers and their families in Hebron believe the pesticide is causing Parkinson’s disease and are demanding that New York ban itAmudalat Ajasain New York for New York FocusWed 5 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGordon Chaplin gingerly stepped out of the car at the top of the steep hill behind his farmhouse, sporting a bandage on his hand from a fall the day before. He gripped his cane as he shuffled through the knee-high grass. He stopped every few feet to catch his breath, leaning on his caregiver for support.Looking out at the distant Adirondacks and Catskill mountains, he thought back to the years when he could run up the hill with ease.“Things just don’t work as well as they used to. In fact, sometimes they don’t work at all,” said Chaplin, 81, who has owned the farm for over 40 years. “There’s nothing worse than having your whole life … falling apart.”Nearly a decade ago, he began experiencing symptoms he couldn’t explain. His once-pristine handwriting became unreadable,his face took on a permanent look of worry, and he acted out his dreams while he slept. After years of inconclusive test results from various doctors, he received a diagnosis: he had Parkinson’s disease, an incurable degenerative brain disease that affects motor functions and causes cognitive impairment. He had no family history or genetic predisposition to the disease.Chaplin and his wife, Sarah Teale, believe the cause lay hidden under the idyllic hills of their 200-acre cattle and corn farm. For decades, a tenant farmer sprayed the land with paraquat, a herbicide that’s used to kill broadleaf weeds and grasses – and that research has linked to Parkinson’s.The couple lives in Hebron, a rural farming town of about 1,800 residents in Washington county. After Chaplin’s diagnosis, Teale discovered that 14 people near their home had the disease, too. She calls the seven-mile stretch of highway between east and west Hebron “Parkinson’s Valley”. In nearby towns, she found dozens more. And she believes there’s a common culprit.Paraquat is banned in dozens of countries and is coming under heavier scrutiny in the US. This year, 14 states introduced bills to restrict or ban its use. Vermont was the only state to pass a ban. New York lawmakers sought to be the second, butthe billdied on the floor amid a prolonged budget standoff that crowded out other legislation.“Hundreds of bills that we would normally pass never got a vote because we ran out of time,” said assembly member and bill sponsor Linda Rosenthal. “More people will suffer between now and when this bill becomes law. You can bet I’m going to work really hard to make sure it passes the next session.”View image in fullscreenSarah Teale calls the seven-mile stretch of highway between east and west Hebron, ‘Parkinson’s Valley’.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusParaquat was first registered for use in the 1960s. Since then, its popularity has ballooned.Between 2014 and 2018, paraquat use across the country doubled to at least 11m pounds a year, according to the latest available data from theUS Geological Survey. It’s most commonly sprayed on crops including corn, soybeans, cotton and grapes.In some years in the early 2000s, New York’s paraquat use ranked in the top 10 nationally. According to 2018 USGS data, the latest available, growers inNew Yorksprayed a total of nearly 149,000lb of paraquat, ranking 31st in the country.The scientific debate over paraquat’s safety has been building for decades. Studies dating back to the late 1990s have linked paraquat exposure to Parkinson’s disease. A 2002studyfound that mice injected with paraquat lost dopamine neurons, a hallmark of Parkinson’s. A 2011studyfound that farmers who sprayed paraquat were 2.5 times as likely to develop Parkinson’s as those who did not.A 2024 studyfoundthat people living or working near areas sprayed with paraquat had double the risk of developing Parkinson’s.Research linking paraquat to Parkinson’s is “one of the strongest databases out there linking a chemical exposure to a disease”, said Deborah Cory-Slechta, a University of Rochester neurotoxicologist.Ray Dorsey, a neurologist at the Atria Research and Global Health Institute, said it’s a common misconception that people with Parkinson’s developed it primarily because of ageing or genetics. About 85% of Americans with Parkinson’s carry no known genetic risk factor for the disease, he said.“The principal causes of Parkinson’s disease are not inside of us, not in our DNA, but outside of us, in our environment,” said Dorsey, who published abookon the disease last year that identified Hebron as a hotspot. “The continued use of paraquat is likely sowing the future seeds of Parkinson’s disease.”The herbicide has been banned in over 70 countries, including China, Brazil and the entire European Union. But not the United States.Under Joe Biden’s administration, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) determined that it needed more time to examine the health risks of paraquat use. The agency has warned about the herbicide’s toxicity, noting that “one small accidental sip can be fatal”, and requires sprayers to undergo special training. The agency has stopped short of linking exposure to Parkinson’s disease, as other government health bodies have done abroad.View image in fullscreenChaplin and Teale believe the cause of Chaplin’s Parkinson’s disease is the pesticide paraquat, which a tenant farmer sprayed on their land for a decade.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusLast November, the agencysaidit would require paraquat manufacturers to study how far paraquat vapors travel from the initial spray site. That announcement came after Syngenta, one of the world’s largest producers of paraquat,submitted new datathat suggested vapors maytravel miles fartherthan previously thought.The company, based in Switzerland, stood by the product’s safety.“While Syngenta has great sympathy for those suffering from Parkinson’s, we reject the claim that our product is the cause,” said a Syngenta spokesperson, Dimitri Houtart, in a statement to New York Focus. The Guardian additionally invited comment from Syngenta and did not receive a response.Houtart pointed toa 2013 studyconducted by the company’s scientists that found that paraquat did not cause the neuron damage associated with Parkinson’s, even with high doses in the brain. He also cited recent research conducted by theCaliforniaandAustraliangovernments that did not find a causal link between Parkinson’s and paraquat exposure.Just about everyone in Hebron knows someone touched by Parkinson’s, residents told New York Focus during a visit to the town last month.In 2024, Teale hosted a town hall for families in the area affected by the disease. The room had a maximum occupancy of 60 people. About 85 people piled in.“They just started coming in, and coming in, and coming in,” Teale recalled. “They didn’t know all the people that had it. They were really shocked.”Sharon “Sally” Giambatista was among them.Growing up, summers in Hebron for Giambatista often meant hours in her family’s strawberry fields, plucking and munching her way through row after row of fruit.No one in her family dreamed pesticides could be toxic. Her father mixed them with his bare hands, and cropdusters sprayed them overhead from their cabs.View image in fullscreenSharon ‘Sally’ Giambatista, who is a part of the Liebig family, and her husband Paul Giambatista, at their home in Hebron, New York. Ms Giambatista has Parkinson’s disease, as does her sister, which they attribute to the chemical Paraquat being sprayed in the area. The women picked strawberries for the family business, Liebig Berries, when they were children.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York Focus“The pilot would tip the wings and wave and spray us with his poison,” Giambatista remembered.That exposure, she believes, changed the course of her life. Hours after getting engaged in the fall of 2009, imagining the future ahead of her, she received a call: she had Parkinson’s disease. She was 56 years old.A few years later, one of her older sisters was diagnosed, too. They had no family history of the disease. Of her four siblings, Giambatista and that older sister spent the most time in the fields.“We thought we are lucky to live out here in the fresh air,” Giambatista said, her shoulders and arms trembling in waves that never fully stop. “We just didn’t know.”New York state doesn’t publish town-level Parkinson’s data. But Brian Campbell, Hebron’s town supervisor, said there were far more cases than there should be. His own father died of Parkinson’s after living with the disease for more than 30 years.Campbell believes a herbicide or pesticide is the culprit, though he’s not sure which. “I’ve got to believe it’s things we sprayed that were in the valley,” he said.“[I’m] fortunate at this point that I don’t have it yet. That’s about all you can say,” he added with an uneasy laugh.View image in fullscreenBrian Campbell, Hebron’s town supervisor, at the Hebron town court and meeting hall. Mr Campbell lost his father from Parkinson’s disease, which he attributes to the chemical Paraquat being sprayed in the area.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusThousands of Americans have filed lawsuits against Syngenta, which sells paraquat under the brand name Gramoxone, alleging that the company failed to warn consumers about paraquat’s substantial health risks. Neither Chaplin nor Giambatista is currently seeking damages.In 2025,Syngenta stated in its financial report that it had raised $792m to cover settlement costs. Without going into detail about any individual cases, the company said its goal was to “end the cost and distraction of lawsuits which Syngenta believes are without merit”.In 2022, the Guardian and the New Lede published internal documents revealing that Syngenta wasaware of the mounting researchlinking the herbicide to Parkinson’s disease. The company monitored scientists studying the links,lobbied the EPAto bar critical scientists from sitting on advisory panels,strategizedways to “influence academia, and regulatory and NGO environments”, and created ateamto respond to external scientific publications.The overall goal, the internal documents revealed, was “to protect people and our reputation”.This March, Syngenta announced that it would stop making paraquat by the end of June. The companycited“significant competition from generic producers” as the reason; a spokesperson said that the change was not made in response to litigation or safety concerns.View image in fullscreenA keepsake of the 2007/2008 Granville community guide featuring Liebig Berries on the cover at the Giambastista home in Hebron, New York.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusGeneric paraquat produced by other companies poses similar risks.“Without a ban, there’s nothing stopping another company from swooping in and filling the void,” said Nathan Donley, a senior scientist and pesticide expert at the Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group.When New York lawmakers try to enact a ban next year, they will go up against the New York Farm Bureau, the state’s largest agriculture advocacy group and one of the lead opponents of the bill. The group did not respond to repeated requests for comment.A week before the legislative session ended, Renée St Jacques, the Farm Bureau’s director of public policy,told The Capitol Pressroom, a radio show,that if paraquat is “used with the safety precautions in place, farmers are safe”.Now 73 years old, Giambatista wonders what her life would be like if Parkinson’s hadn’t taken the things she loved most. Would she still be singing if the disease hadn’t reduced her voice to just above a whisper? Would she paint more if her trembling hands could hold a brush?She struggles to understand why manufacturers continue to sell something so seemingly toxic, and why lawmakers haven’t done more to stop them.“Knowing what you know now, how can you not fight against that? How can you not strive to find something better, or give up some of the big profit?” Giambatista asked.View image in fullscreenGordan Chaplin, center, receives help getting into the car from his aide at their home in Hebron, New York, in June 2026.Photograph: Cindy Schultz for New York FocusThe disease’s slow creep has touched every corner of Chaplin’s life, too. He gave up his cows when running and walking became too difficult. He used to roam the woods for hours on end; he now depends on a cane and a caregiver, after a fall left him with 60 stitches. He was a writer and wanted to finish his sixth book; he now struggles to hold a pen or remember his thoughts.“It’s stripped me of half of my life or more,” Chaplin said. “There’s always a hope that I’ll beat it and be able to come back. I don’t think it’s hopeless, but then, I’m pretty sure it is hopeless.”On the eve of Teale’s birthday in early June, the couple sat at a picnic table in their backyard.She thought about the year to come. She looked at Chaplin, who coughed after taking a bite of food, and wished simply that he would get better.The sun dropped behind the trees, and the pet goats retreated. Chaplin pointed at the edge of the woods.“Look at that tractor coming out,” he said.There was no tractor.He spent the next few hours at the table with a pair of binoculars, watching a party unfold in the garden. No one was there.This story originally appeared in New York Focus, a nonprofit news publication investigating power in New York.Sign up for their newsletter here.Explore more on these topicsHerbicidesNew YorkUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best coffee machines in 2026 for every home and budget, tested by our expert | Coffee | The Guardian
description: From capsule to bean-to-cup, espresso to filter, these are the coffee makers our aficionado rates the highest from his test of 30
Author: Sasha Muller
Headline: From capsule to bean-to-cup, espresso to filter, these are the coffee makers our aficionado rates the highest from his test of 30
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterCoffeeReviewThe best coffee machines in 2026 for every home and budget, tested by our expertFrom capsule to bean-to-cup, espresso to filter, these are the coffee makers our aficionado rates the highest from his test of 30The best espresso machines to release your inner baristaSasha MullerWed 5 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.When it comes to something as earth-shatteringly important as coffee, everyone has an opinion. Some crave a single perfect shot of espresso, while others seek the milkiest latte; some love Starbucks and others, well, don’t. That’s why the idea of there being a single best coffee machine is fanciful – everyone’s idea of the perfect coffee couldn’t be more different.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.As a selfless service to coffee drinkers everywhere, I’ve spent the past two years researching and trialling coffee machines to produce a shortlist of tried-and-tested recommendations. The list spans all the main types of coffee maker: manual espresso, filter, bean-to-cup and capsule. (Not sure what all of this means? Read our dedicated guide tothe different types of coffee machine.)I’ve aimed this guide at everyday coffee lovers who want to up their game without spending a fortune or losing hours to perfecting their craft. Ease of use, simplicity and relative affordability play just as important a role as the quality of the coffee. If you love coffee and need help choosing, then read on – you’ll brewbetter coffeewith one of these machines on your worktop.At a glanceBest budget manual coffee machineDe’LonghiStilosa EC230£104 at AmazonBest budget bean-to-cup coffee machineDe’LonghiMagnifica Evo One Touch£369 at Peter TysonBest capsule coffee machineL’orBarista Sublime£69.99 at AmazonBest bean-to-cup coffee machineDe’LonghiRivelia£599 at AmazonBest filter coffee machineFellowAiden£365 at HealfBest manual machineLelitAnna PL41TEM£509.95 at Origin CoffeeBest manual machine for beginnersSageBambino Plus£399 at John LewisWhy you should trust meHaving spent more than seven years as the resident coffee bore at a product-testing publication, I’ve wiled away countless hours in the search for better-tasting coffee. I’ve tested every type of machine, from capsule, filter and fully automated bean-to-cup models all the way through to fully manualespresso machines.Sadly, though, I have had to accept defeat in my pursuit of latte art mastery – despite the occasional happy accident, most of my attempts resemble indecent cave drawings. I apologise in advance for any incriminating photo evidence.How I testedView image in fullscreenThe coffee machines were tested across criteria such as taste and usability.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianI tested (or retested) 30 machines, several of which I’ve reviewed previously and three of which have a permanent place on my kitchen worktop. I’ve also pored over user reviews and forums, and consulted the recommendations of trusted coffee experts online and on YouTube in the search for other models to test.Every machine has been run alongside either my own go-to machines or a curated selection of rivals for side-by-side taste and usability testing. Several kilos of fresh coffee beans and a pile of Nespresso-compatible pods have been sourced directly from my go-to roaster,Craft House Coffee. I’ve used the manufacturers’ official pods where applicable, too.For the filter and espresso machines that don’t have an integrated coffee grinder, I’ve used my own: aBaratza Vario W+and aKingrinder K6 hand grinder. I consumed so much coffee during the testing process that my blood type is now skinny macchiato.After testing, any coffee machines sourced for this article are either being returned to their sources or donated to charity.The best coffee machines in 2026View image in fullscreen‘A beginner’s dream’: the Sage Bambino Plus.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianBest budget manual coffee machine:De’Longhi Stilosa EC230De’LonghiStilosa EC230from£104£105 at Argos£104 at AmazonWhat we loveTasty espresso; low priceWhat we don’t lovePlasticky buildView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The Guardian£105 at Argos£104 at AmazonNo, it’s not a typo: the Stilosa EC230 really is that affordable. With some takeaway coffees commanding £4 a pop, you could forgo just one month of paper cups of coffee and save enough to buy your own espresso machine. And boy, does the Stilosa make a great espresso.Why we love itThe price is obviously a big part – after all, we love a bargain – but it would be a false economy if it didn’t deliver the espresso-based goods. Connoisseurs may want more features and control, but they’ll probably be pretty surprised, too. Feed the Stilosa with great-quality, well-ground beans from a good grinder, and it’ll serve stunning coffee.I got great results from the medium-light roast beans I had to hand, and pairing the Stilosa with myKingrinder K6 grinderwas a match made in heaven. Espresso was flavourful and well balanced. Although the steam wand lacks oomph, with a bit of practice it serves up silky hot milk with a dense microfoam. The result? Great espresso, wonderful flat whites, moreish cappuccinos.Make sure you check the model number before buying, though. TheEC235and EC260 look almost identical, but swap the manual steam wand for an automatic steam wand and pressurised coffee baskets. That means easier but inferior milk frothing and middling espresso – if you’re planning to feed the Stilosa good, freshly ground coffee, then buy the EC230.It’s a shame that …you don’t get everything you need in the box. The water tank feels cheap, and there’s no option to fit a water filter – although that can be fixed by buying a separate water filter jug.It comes with a piece of plastic that resembles a plastic tamper and coffee scoop, but it’s useless at the former and merely OK at the latter. My advice?Buy a proper metal tamper for under a tenner.The spouts also tend to drip as there’s no pressure valve, so have a cloth handy. Maybe an apron, too.Machine type:manual espressoDimensions:21x 34 x 29cm (WDH)Time to heat up:1min 30secsMakes milk-based drinks?YesPeak noise level:80dB (61dB average)Warranty:one-year repair or replaceDe’LonghiStilosa EC230from£104£105 at Argos£104 at AmazonWhat we loveTasty espresso; low priceWhat we don’t lovePlasticky buildBest budget bean-to-cup coffee machine:De’Longhi Magnifica Evo One TouchDe’LonghiMagnifica Evo One Touchfrom£369£369 at Peter Tyson£417 at AOWhat we loveMilk-based coffees at the touch of a buttonWhat we don’t loveSmall milk carafeView image in fullscreen£369 at Peter Tyson£417 at AOI’ve tested several De’Longhi bean-to-cup machines over the years, all the way up to its range-topping £2,299.99Maestosa, but the Magnifica Evo One Touch is the best-value pick by a margin. It serves up tasty espressos, americanos and lattes with minimum fuss.Why we love itThe machine is fairly compact by bean-to-cup standards, although you’ll need to leave a little room around and above the machine. Bright, illuminated icons along the top edge evoke the glow of touchscreens on pricier models, but these are simple buttons. You can choose from seven different drinks, and the built-in milk carafe allows you to craft cappuccinos and creamy lattes with zero hassle.The quality of the drinks isn’t as immaculate as the pricier Jura C8, but it’s not far off. Espresso is rich and flavourful, hitting about 68C, and cappuccinos and latte macchiatos are topped with a pleasingly dense layer of creamy foam. The MyLatte drink option will prove popular: fill the carafe with the right amount of milk for your preferred coffee cup, and the machine will drain the carafe and add a shot of coffee.It’s a shame that …it’s not quiet. The grinder’s whines peak at 75dB, and the average noise level of 60dB is markedly louder than the Jura. The lack of a dedicated hot-milk function feels like an oversight.Machine type:bean-to-cupDimensions:24 x 44 x 36cm (WDH)Time to heat up:35 secondsMakes milk-based drinks?YesPeak noise level:75dB (average 60dB)Warranty:two-year repair or replace at De’Longhi’s discretionDe’LonghiMagnifica Evo One Touchfrom£369£369 at Peter Tyson£417 at AOWhat we loveMilk-based coffees at the touch of a buttonWhat we don’t loveSmall milk carafeFor more, read the Filter’s guide to thebest bean-to-cup coffee machinesBest capsule coffee machine:L’or Barista SublimeL’orBarista Sublimefrom£69.99£69.99 at Robert Dyas£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGood results with Nespresso and L’or capsulesWhat we don’t loveDrip tray too smallView image in fullscreen£69.99 at Robert Dyas£69.99 at AmazonBuilt by Philips, this L’or-branded machine makes a huge range of coffees thanks to its compatibility with official Nespresso, Nespresso-compatible and L’or’s own range of pods. It doesn’t support the latest Vertuo pods, but this machine looks great and works well.Why we love itThe compact dimensions are a big plus, and the design is (mostly) sensible. There’s a removable 0.8-litre water tank at the rear, and the drip tray and pod bin slide out together.It’s easy to use, too. Simply lift the large curved handle on top, pop in a capsule and close the lid. You can also pour two normal-size cups simultaneously.I wasn’t a fan of some of the more potent XXL L’or espresso pods – although the high-street chain flavour may be to some tastes – but there are more than 100 options from which to choose.It’s a shame that …the drip tray, lid and pod bin separate with minimal encouragement, so it’s easy to send their contents scattering across your kitchen floor if you’re not paying attention. Nor is it the quietest machine, although it’s unlikely to wake up the household.Some users have reported that the machine doesn’t play nicely with all Nespresso-compatible capsules. I had no such problems during my testing, but it’s worth buying a handful of capsules to test before buying in bulk.Opinions are mixed on thesustainability of capsule coffee, butL’orandNespresso’sstandard aluminium capsules can be sent back for recycling – both companies provide free postage options for returning capsules in bulk. L’or doesn’t yet offer compostable options, but Nespresso and Nespresso-compatible compostable capsules are available.Machine type:capsuleDimensions:16 x 40 x 28cm (WDH)Time to heat up:4 secondsMakes milk-based drinks?NoPeak noise level:60dB (average 45dB)Warranty:two yearsL’orBarista Sublimefrom£69.99£69.99 at Robert Dyas£69.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGood results with Nespresso and L’or capsulesWhat we don’t loveDrip tray too smallBest bean-to-cup coffee machine:De’Longhi RiveliaDe’LonghiRiveliafrom£599£599.99 at De’Longhi£599 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent coffee, helpful touchscreen; two hoppersWhat we don’t loveGrinder is noisy; awkwardly positioned controlsView image in fullscreen£599.99 at De’Longhi£599 at AmazonAlthough most automatic bean-to-cup machines look broadly similar, the Rivelia attempts to do things a little differently. It still makes black and white coffees, with adjustable levels of froth no less, but the big appeal is the swappable bean hoppers.Why we love itIf you love the idea of having decafandcaffeinated coffee ready to go, then the Rivelia answers your prayers. You get two 250g bean hoppers in the box, and you swap between them with a quick twist and a click. The touchscreen pipes up as you do so: you can choose to brew one last coffee from the beans in the chute, or purge them into the internal bin. If the choice of two bean varieties isn’t enough, you can buyextra hoppersfor about £18 a pop.Flexibility goes hand in hand with an unconventional design. Eschewing the usual big, black cuboid template, the Rivelia has a smaller, more slender footprint. The 1.4-litre water tank protrudes out of the side, and the hopper pokes out of the top, but the smaller main unit looks much less imposing.The touchscreen interface is a joy. It’s slick and helpful, and deftly guides users throughout the process of making and customising drinks with friendly, helpful, onscreen messages. You can create up to four user profiles, too, so everyone can have their preferred drinks and settings loaded and ready to brew.The Rivelia also brews a superb coffee. You get a huge choice of short and long coffee drinks, both with and without milk. Espresso, the bedrock of many milk-based coffees, is superb. The grinder offers 14 steps of adjustment and is capable of grinding so finely that it chokes the machine. This is an asset: dial it in carefully, and it rewards with the kind of rich, unctuous espresso that most bean-to-cups can only dream of.There’s oodles of adjustability, too. The Bean Adapt feature adjusts brewing settings to suit the beans you’re using, and it can be effective with a little tweaking. However, you can easily adjust strength and volume to suit your tastes – and the size of your cups – and being able to adjust the level of milk froth is something you don’t always get on cheaper machines.It’s impressive to see how much De’Longhi has packed in for the money. The touchscreen interface is top-notch, and the coffee is among the best I’ve tasted from a bean-to-cup machine at any price. If you’re looking for a step up from budget machines, then the Rivelia will show you what you’re missing.It’s a shame that …the Rivelia’s design sacrifices practicality in one key area. The touchscreen interface is undoubtedly brilliant, but as it’s positioned on the Rivelia’s top panel and faces upwards, it’s poorly positioned for shorter or seated users. A front-facing touchscreen would ruin the look, but it would be far more usable.Machine type:assisted espresso machineDimensions:24.5 x 43 x 38.5cm (WDH)Time to heat up:38 secondsMakes milk-based drinks?Yes, automaticPeak noise level:51dB (brew), 51dB (steam), 68dB (grind)Warranty:two-year repair or replace at De’Longhi’s discretionDe’LonghiRiveliafrom£599£599.99 at De’Longhi£599 at AmazonWhat we loveExcellent coffee, helpful touchscreen; two hoppersWhat we don’t loveGrinder is noisy; awkwardly positioned controlsBest filter coffee machine:Fellow AidenFellowAidenfrom£365£365 at Healf£365 at AmazonWhat we loveGets the best from any coffee; highly customisableWhat we don’t loveExpensive; swapping filter basketsView image in fullscreen£365 at Healf£365 at AmazonThe Fellow Aiden promises “barista-quality results without the learning curve”. And it delivers. In the months I’ve had this filter coffee machine on my worktop, it’s made glorious brews with everything from light to dark roast coffees – and with minimal effort.Why we love itThe Aiden’s magic touch is that it leads beginners by the hand and allows tinkerers to tweak water temperature and flow down to seconds and degrees centigrade. It’s versatile: you can brew a single cup of coffee directly into a cup, or fill the metal insulated jug with up to 1.5 litres of coffee. It tells you exactly how much ground coffee to use, and it’ll even do cold brew.It’s easy to get to grips with, too. The little clickable dial scrolls through simple text-based menus on the round OLED screen. The superbly minimalist user guide gives useful tips. Built-in wifi means you can use the Aiden app for iOS and Android, too, and tweak every recipe from your smartphone screen – or schedule brews to be ready the moment you wake up.The Aiden tailors its settings to suit the type of coffee and the amount you’re brewing. There are preset brew recipes for light, medium and dark roast coffee, each adjusting the water temperature and flow for the best results. They’re a great starting point. Some coffees can become bitter or sour on machines with set brewing temperatures, but the Aiden creates a more refined cup.It’s a shame that …there’s no integrated water filter. Using a water filter jug is a simple solution, but it’s preferable to be able to pour in tap water and just hit the brew button.The dual filter baskets are fiddly. As much as I love the convenience of brewing a single cup – or a big jug – it’s annoying having to keep flat-bottomed and cone-shaped paper filters stocked in the cupboard.Machine type:filterDimensions:23 x 23 x 30cm (WDH)Time to heat up:not applicableMakes milk-based drinks?NoPeak noise level:63dB (average 48dB)Warranty:two yearsFellowAidenfrom£365£365 at Healf£365 at AmazonWhat we loveGets the best from any coffee; highly customisableWhat we don’t loveExpensive; swapping filter basketsBest manual machine:Lelit Anna PL41TEMLelitAnna PL41TEMfrom£509.95£509.95 at Origin Coffee£509.95 at Coffee FriendWhat we loveBrilliant coffee; adjustable brew temperatureWhat we don’t loveFinicky; non-standard 57mm portafilterView image in fullscreen£509.95 at Origin Coffee£509.95 at Coffee FriendIf you want to get serious about espresso, then the Anna PL41TEM deserves a place on your shortlist. The stainless-steel build is reminiscent of the Gaggia Classic, but the big upgrade is the adjustable PID temperature controller that puts you in charge of the brewing and steaming temperatures.Why we love itIt’s the Anna’s mixture of talents that makes it so appealing. Value is foremost: its closest rival, theGaggia Classic, is a similar price but lacks a PID for temperature control – a £200+ aftermarket upgrade. The two-year warranty is welcome, too, and Lelit is also confident enough to warranty it for a full year of commercial (ab)use.Once you’ve primed the boiler (note: read the instructions carefully), you can get brewing in about three minutes. The Anna PL41TEM lets you adjust the brew and steam temperatures from 80C to 130C. Set to the specific brew temperature recommended for your coffee, or just start with the default 95C.The control is invaluable: I remedied a slight bitterness to my first shots by dropping the brew temperature down a single degree. If, like me, you love globe-trotting one far-flung coffee plantation at a time, this adjustability ekes out amazing results from exotic light roasts through to classic Italian espresso.It’s a shame that …getting started may be daunting for beginners. The text-only, bullet-point instructions are unwelcoming;YouTube videosare a friendlier place to start. The manual fill boiler requires a little care, so it’s essential to get the hang of.The solid, basic design is reassuring for longevity, but refined it is not. The water tank just clunks into place with rubber pipes feeding from the top, and the top cover and drip tray are rattly. What’s more, the 57mm portafilter is a non-standard size, so upgrades to the portafilter, basket and various accessories are slightly harder to come by.One final minor moan from my long-term testing: the plastic window is just a tad too opaque, so it’s not very clear how much water is remaining.Machine type:manual espressoDimensions:23x 38 x 34cm (WDH)Time to heat up:3 minutesMakes milk-based drinks?YesPeak noise level:79dB (64dB average)Warranty:two-year repair or replace at Lelit’s discretionLelitAnna PL41TEMfrom£509.95£509.95 at Origin Coffee£509.95 at Coffee FriendWhat we loveBrilliant coffee; adjustable brew temperatureWhat we don’t loveFinicky; non-standard 57mm portafilterBest manual machine for beginners:Sage Bambino PlusSageBambino Plusfrom£399£399 at John Lewis£399 at ArgosWhat we loveEasy to use; automatic milk frothing works wellWhat we don’t loveBrew temperature isn’t adjustableView image in fullscreen£399 at John Lewis£399 at ArgosThe Bambino Plus’s balance of coffee-brewing talent and beginner-friendly features can’t be beaten for the money. It welcomes even complete newcomers with its friendly, informative user manual and helpful YouTube tutorials, and it’s capable of brewing brilliant coffee.Why we love itIt’s a neat little machine, and the modest dimensions mean it will slot unobtrusively on to most kitchen worktops. Sage supplies almost everything you need in the box, too. I say almost everything: you’ll also need some good, fresh coffee beans and something to grind them with.The quality of the coffee seals the deal here, however. In something of a rarity at this price, the Bambino Plus has a temperature controller, ensuring the brewing water hits the coffee grounds at a consistent temperature. Combine that with a decent-quality coffee bean and a capable grinder, and you’ve got a recipe for routinely good espresso with a minimum of faff.Factor in the automatic milk texturing, which crafts wonderfully hot, silky, frothed milk at the press of a button, and it’s invigoratingly easy to whip up superb flat whites and cappuccinos. It’s a beginner’s dream.It’s a shame that …the manual mode doesn’t feel quite right without a proper physical dial, so budding baristas may hanker for a fully manual espresso machine. As you can’t adjust the brew temperature, you’re better off sticking with medium- to dark-roast coffee beans (lighter roasts require higher brew temperatures, so they may taste a little sour).Machine type:assisted manual espressoDimensions:19.5 x 32 x 31cm (WDH)Time to heat up:6 secondsMakes milk-based drinks?YesPeak noise level:63dB (50dB average)Warranty:two-year repair, replace or refund at Sage’s discretionRead our fullSage Bambino Plus reviewSageBambino Plusfrom£399£399 at John Lewis£399 at ArgosWhat we loveEasy to use; automatic milk frothing works wellWhat we don’t loveBrew temperature isn’t adjustableThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Makes consistently enjoyable coffee’: the Lavazza Jolie Evo.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianKitchenAid KF4KitchenAidKF4from£899£899 at KitchenAid£899 at John LewisWhat we loveSlender footprint; great coffee; easy to useWhat we don’t loveRear-mounted water tank; poor carafe designView image in fullscreen£899 at KitchenAid£899 at John LewisBest for:smaller kitchensThe KF4 packs a capable fully automatic bean-to-cup machine into a smaller package than most. Measuring just 19.5cm wide, the KF4 will slot into even small kitchens without hogging worktop space.The £899 price is fairly steep, but this machine feels classier and more solid than the cheaper De’Longhi Rivelia – it’s on a par with four-figure machines. And while similarly priced rivals such as theJura C8make do with a basic display, the KF4 has a large 8.8cm front-facing touchscreen.The upmarket look and feel go hand in hand with refined brewing. Espresso was gorgeous from the off, and the strength and body controls are invaluable for dialling in the perfect shot.Milk-based coffees are impressive, too – milk froth is tight and creamy, and among the best here. The froth level isn’t adjustable, though: it’s frothed milk or flat steamed milk, and nothing in between.It didn’t make the final cut because …with prices dipping towards £600, the De’Longhi Rivelia remains better value. Don’t discount the KF4, though: its trump card is the slimmer design, more upmarket look and feel, and the more convenient front-facing touchscreen and controls.Machine type:bean-to-cup;dimensions:19.5 x 47.5 x 36cm (WDH);time to heat up:60 seconds;makes milk-based drinks?Yes;peak noise level:63dB (average 43dB);warranty:two years (five-year parts/service availability commitment for burr grinder, 10 for the rest of the machine)KitchenAidKF4from£899£899 at KitchenAid£899 at John LewisWhat we loveSlender footprint; great coffee; easy to useWhat we don’t loveRear-mounted water tank; poor carafe designNinja Cafe Luxe ES601UKNinjaCafe Luxe ES601UKfrom£449£549 at John Lewis£449 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value for assisted machine; lots of optionsWhat we don’t loveFiddlier than fully assisted modelsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The Guardian£549 at John LewisFrom £449 at AmazonBest for:sublime espresso and milk-based coffees without the effort – or the expenseImagine a manual espresso machine that does all the hard work for you – that’s the Cafe Luxe in a nutshell. Pour coffee beans into the hopper on top, and it’ll grind, measure and adapt the settings automatically to produce the perfect espresso, long black and beyond.Indeed, espresso is just the beginning. Press a button on the shiny fascia, and it’ll whip milk into a hot, silken froth perfect for a cappuccino or flat white. But what if you fancy something more akin to a filter coffee? Or a cold brew coffee, for that matter? Not a problem: cold or hot, milk or coffee, the Cafe Luxe will brew, steam or froth it to perfection. Take a little time to decipher the busy control panel, and a whole world of coffee lies at your fingertips.If you’re wondering why you’d pick this over a fully automatic bean-to-cup machine, then the answer is the coffee quality. As this is a portafilter machine, the Ninja draws out a depth of flavour and complexity from good coffee beans that fully automatic machines can only dream of. The downside is more effort, but if you want manual espresso quality without the faff, this is as good as it gets for about £500 – Sage’s superior assisted machines cost twice as much.It didn’t make the final cut because …if you have the money to spend but don’t want a fully manual machine, the question is whether this will be automatic enough for you. If you’d prefer to simply press a button and get on with the washing-up, then a fully automatic bean-to-cup machine such as theDe’Longhi Magnifica Evo One Touchabove will be a better pick.Machine type:assisted;dimensions:37 x 33 x 37cm (WDH);time to heat up:35 seconds;makes milk-based drinks?Yes;peak noise level:66dB (average 57dB);warranty:two yearsNinjaCafe Luxe ES601UKfrom£449£549 at John Lewis£449 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value for assisted machine; lots of optionsWhat we don’t loveFiddlier than fully assisted modelsMoccamaster KBG SelectMoccamasterKBG Selectfrom£268£268 at Selfridges£268 at AmazonWhat we loveSimple to use; brews a tasty jug of coffeeWhat we don’t loveExpensive; no adjustable brew temperatureView image in fullscreen£268 at Selfridges£268 at AmazonBest for:simple filter coffeeSpending more than £200 on a filter coffee machine may seem extravagant, but the KBG Select is anything but ordinary. Built to last a lifetime, it’s one of a few select machines to earn an accreditation from the Specialty Coffee Association and the European Coffee Brewing Centre for its brewing prowess.That the machine is designed and handbuilt in the Netherlands goes some way towards explaining the high price. As does the five-year warranty and the promise of lifelong repairability. It certainly doesn’t hurt that you can pick from more than 20 kitchen-matching colours.And it couldn’t be simpler to use: pop in a paper filter, add the ground coffee to the filter, and wait patiently. You can brew anything between four and 10 125ml cups of coffee – admittedly closer to five normal-size mugs – and a full jug takes a consistent six minutes to brew.If you’re making fewer cups, you can flick the half-jug switch to slow the brewing process and eke every last drop of flavour from smaller doses of coffee. However much you brew, the hotplate then stays on for 40 minutes, keeping coffee warm without stewing it.The quality of the coffee it makes, and the consistency with which it does so, is what sets the KBG Select apart. I’ve had surprisingly pleasant results from preground supermarket coffee, but routinely enjoy wonderful cups from freshly ground beans. Feed the KBG Select with great coffee and it quietly does the rest.It didn’t make the final cut because …the machine feels lightweight, and the glass carafe doesn’t feel especially solid. That said, my unit has been used daily for almost two years now, and nothing has broken. Yet.One final word of caution for any coffee perfectionists: you may prefer a machine with more adjustability, such as the excellentFellow Aiden.Machine type:filter;dimensions:32 x 17 x 36cm (WDH);time to heat up:25 seconds;makes milk-based drinks?No;peak noise level:59dB (average 44dB);warranty:five years (excluding carafe)MoccamasterKBG Selectfrom£268£268 at Selfridges£268 at AmazonWhat we loveSimple to use; brews a tasty jug of coffeeWhat we don’t loveExpensive; no adjustable brew temperatureDe’Longhi Magnifica StartDe’LonghiMagnifica Startfrom£320£339.99 at De’Longhi£320 at AmazonWhat we loveFrothy coffee at the touch of a buttonWhat we don’t loveNoisy; not quite as refined as the Evo modelView image in fullscreen£339.99 at De’Longhi£320 at AmazonBest for:a cheap bean-to-cup machineThe Start isn’t as fancy-looking as the step-up Evo family. You can pick from plain gloss black plastics and glossy grey. But the quality of coffee it makes is just as good as the Magnifica Evo – internally, they’re pretty much identical.It’s really easy to use. Fill the 250g hopper with beans, slot the supplied water filter into the 1.8-litre tank, and after a 40-second warmup and initial rinse, it’s ready to brew.The little touch-sensitive buttons brew cappuccino, espresso, coffee (AKA a long black) or hot water. You can pick from three coffee strength levels, or choose to add your own preground coffee via the chute.Hold down any drink button, and you can preset how much milk or how much coffee is poured. That means you can transform the cappuccino preset into more of a latte, if you prefer – or just ensure that the machine fills your favourite mug or cup just so.The coffee spouts slide up and down easily, too, so you can just about squeeze in a 15cm-tall cup, or slide them down to pour neatly into a tiny espresso cup.Itdidn’t make the final cut because …it’s rather noisy. The grinder chunters at 75dB, and the milk frother sputters up to 78dB. And talking of milk, there’s still no dedicated hot milk button. Thankfully, there is a trick: select the preground coffee option and don’t add any coffee. Voilà! Hot, frothy milk.Do be careful when buying: there are several Magnifica Start models. Cheaper models swap the milk carafe for a steam wand, so check before you buy. And if you see a similarly specifiedMagnifica Evo(above) discounted for a similar or lower price – buy that instead. It’s slightly nicer looking, marginally easier to use, and some of its models have more drink options.Machine type:fully automatic bean to cup;dimensions:24 x 44 x 35cm (WDH);time to heat up:40 seconds;makes milk-based drinks?Yes;peak noise level:78dB (average 66dB);warranty:two-year repair or replace at De’Longhi’s discretionDe’LonghiMagnifica Startfrom£320£339.99 at De’Longhi£320 at AmazonWhat we loveFrothy coffee at the touch of a buttonWhat we don’t loveNoisy; not quite as refined as the Evo modelLavazza Jolie EvoLavazzaJolie Evofrom£66.48£99 at Lavazza£66.48 at AmazonWhat we loveBrews strong Italian espresso or black coffeeWhat we don’t loveDesign a little rough around the edgesView image in fullscreen£99 at Lavazza£66.48 at AmazonBest for:hassle-free Italian espresso and tasty black coffeeThere are cheaper capsule machines and there are far fancier ones, but the £99 Jolie Evo earns a recommendation by making consistently enjoyable coffee. Lavazza’sA Modo Miocapsule range is small, but each gives a pleasingly brash, nutty Italian espresso flavour with minimal hassle, and the machine is compact and uncomplicated.The Jolie Evo is small, so it fits into tiny gaps on a kitchen worktop. The removable 0.6-litre water tank saves you from carrying jugs of water across the kitchen, and the little bin holds five caps.The machine heats up in 30 to 35 seconds, then you drop a capsule in the slot, pull down the lever (which has a rather satisfying action) and press the button. The Jolie Evo will keep pouring until you press the button a second time, so you can have any amount of coffee from the shortest ristretto to a longer 160ml brew. It’s reasonably quiet, too: I measured a peak sound level of 45dB from a metre away.It didn’t make the final cut because …the water tank can be fiddly to slot back into place. Also, the capsule drawer doesn’t always push back flush with the surround.Machine type:capsule;dimensions:12 x 33 x 21cm (WDH);time to heat up:35 seconds;makes milk-based drinks?No;peak noise level:45dB (average 35dB);warranty:two-year repair or replace at Lavazza’s discretionLavazzaJolie Evofrom£66.48£99 at Lavazza£66.48 at AmazonWhat we loveBrews strong Italian espresso or black coffeeWhat we don’t loveDesign a little rough around the edgesSage Barista Touch Express Impress with cold extractionSageBarista Touch Express Impress with cold extractionfrom£1,199.95£1,199.95 at Sage£1199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveWelcoming touchscreen; quality of drinks is superbWhat we don’t loveExpensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The Guardian£1,199.95 at Sage£1199.99 at CurrysBest for:stunning espresso and cold coffee without the manual slogSage’s recently upgraded Barista Touch Impress with cold extraction takes everything I loved about the old model and adds cold-brew coffee and cold espresso to its drinks list. It’s basically identical in every other way – and that’s a very good thing.As ever, it makes consistently great coffee with minimal to zero faff. There’s not as much assistance asSage’s £1,699 Oracle Jet– norits £2,449.95 Oracle Dual Boilerfor that matter – but it’s a darn sight simpler than a manual machine. And as long as you don’t mind getting involved, it’s no slower than a fully automatic model. It just requires you to move the portafilter from left to right, slide a jug of milk under the steam wand and prod the touchscreen occasionally.The bright colour touchscreen is the gamechanger here – it gently introduces users to the machine, and the simple icon-based interface is easy to grasp even for complete beginners. Swipe through the wide selection of drinks, tap the one you want and then work through the process of grinding, brewing and steaming with a few taps of the touchscreen and a few twists of the portafilter.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s an awful lot of money to spend on a coffee machine. If you have the money burning a hole in your pocket, then a manual espresso machine and separate grinder will make better-tasting coffee (with a bit of skill and effort), and similarly priced automatic machines are far easier to use. And if the assisted espresso concept has caught your eye, you don’t have to spend four figures: the Ninja scratches that itch for half the price.Machine type:assisted manual espresso;dimensions:36 x 34 x 42cm (WDH);time to heat up:six seconds;makes milk-based drinks?Yes;peak noise level:73dB (average 60dB);warranty:two-year repair, replace or refund at Sage’s discretionSageBarista Touch Express Impress with cold extractionfrom£1,199.95£1,199.95 at Sage£1199.99 at CurrysWhat we loveWelcoming touchscreen; quality of drinks is superbWhat we don’t loveExpensiveWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenDaily cleaning is non-negotiable for machines with built-in milk-frothing systems.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianWhat type of coffee machine is best for you?Buying the right coffee machine for you – and your wider household – boils down to two questions: how much coffee do you drink, and how much effort are you willing to put in? Here, I’ll cover the quick pros and cons of each type of machine.For more, read our full guide onhow to choose the right type of coffee machine for youFilter coffee machinesBest for:brewing big batches of coffeeIf you have multiple coffee drinkers in the house, or a slightly excessive daily coffee intake, a filter coffee machine will brew a big jug of black coffee in well under 10 minutes. Add (ideally freshly) ground coffee and water. Press a button. Wait for the smell of freshly brewed coffee to waft. If you like to drink coffee throughout the day, opt for a model with a thermal jug.Capsule coffee machinesBest for:quick cups of half-decent coffeeMany capsule brands exist, but simplicity and consistency are a universal selling point. Add a capsule, press a button, and a coffee pours into your cup. For one or two quick coffees, these are a godsend. However, even the tastiest capsules are fairly average compared with good, fresh coffee in other machine types.Automatic bean-to-cupBest for:good coffee with zero effortKeep the water tank and bean hopper topped up, and these do the rest. Press a button, and everything from short shots to long blacks pours forth. Opt for a model with a milk carafe, and lattes, flat whites and cappuccinos are on the menu. Use good coffee and you’ll get good results, but even the best automatic machines pale in comparison with a good, cheap manual espresso alternative.Assisted espresso machineBest for:great coffee with minimal effortA halfway house between the automatic bean-to-cup models and a manual espresso machine. A robot barista, if you like. The fully assisted models guide every step of the process – the grind, dosage, brew and milk steaming is all optimised for you. More effort than an auto machine, but the vastly improved coffee may be worth it.Manual espresso machineBest for:the best possible coffee with lots of effortThese are the fiddliest machines to use and the hardest to master – yet they make the best coffee. Some include an integrated grinder, but it’s up to you to optimise the grind size, dosage, brew time and milk steaming yourself. Get it right, however, and affordable manual machines will trounce four-figure automatic models.For more, read our guide to thebest espresso machinesManual brewersBest for:great coffee on a budgetEven if you do have a coffee maker on your worktop, it’s great to have a simple, low-effort brewer close to hand for when you just can’t be bothered. Or for when you want to brew a big batch for a gathering. AHario V60 filter (£7.53 at the time of writing), which you can just throw on top of a cup or carafe, makes a lovely coffee. And don’t discount the humble cafetière, either – it’s the low-effort king of coffee brewing. Buy an eight- or 12-cup model, and you can caffeinate a whole table of guests. My favourite is theBodum Chambord (£38 at time of writing).For more, read our guide tothe best cafetièresWarrantyWhen things go wrong with your coffee machine, the first port of call is the manufacturer’s warranty. Most have a two-year repair-or-replace warranty as standard, but pricier models may increase that to three years or – in the rare case of Moccamaster – five years.For the most part, these will be a repair-or-replace warranty, which means the machine will have to be shipped back to the manufacturer, sometimes at its expense but not always (as ever, it pays to read the small print). It will then be at the company’s discretion as to whether a repair or a replacement is the best course of action.Before you buy, it’s advisable to shop around and check whether different retailers provide free extended cover or offer sensibly priced upgrades to the standard warranty – or alternatively, you can consider third-party appliance insurance. This is unlikely to be cost-effective for cheaper machines, though: even a small monthly outlay will quickly add up to more than the price of a new machine.RepairabilityWhen you’re out of warranty, things can get tricky. Generally speaking, the cheaper the machine, the less likely it is that repairs will be economical. Some machines, such as capsule, filter and low-end espresso models, are just not designed to be easily serviceable. Screws and bolts are often replaced by plastic clips, which generally aren’t designed to be unclipped once fastened. Spare parts are hard to come by, too, if they exist at all. And a repair is unlikely to be worthwhile anyway: labour charges will be in the region of £40 an hour.If you want to buy once – or like the popular Reddit communityr/Buy It For Life– you’ll need to spend more upfront for a machine with a repairable design and a healthy supply of spare parts.Everything you need to make great coffee – and the kit that’s not worth your moneyRead moreHow often should you clean your coffee machine?The oils in coffee are brilliant at creating sticky, hard-to-remove stains – and dried-on milk does a pretty good job, too. That’s why regular, light cleaning is always better than letting grime build up. A quick wipe with a wet cloth and a rinse of the machine’s washable or removable parts after every use can save a lot of hassle.If you’re not sure what the best approach is for your machine, then always consult your user manual as the first port of call. Some parts will be dishwasher friendly – or sink and soapy water friendly – while others may require dedicated cleaning products. You can read tips from coffee experts inour guide to making your coffee machine last longer.How to recycle your old coffee machineView image in fullscreenRepair shops can breathe new life into old coffee machines.Photograph: YakobchukOlena/Getty Images/iStockphotoIf you’re tempted to just sling your old coffee machine in the bin, hang on. There are sustainable options you can consider.Repair:If you were happy with your coffee machine before it went kaput, the first option is to repair it. Have a look on Google to see if there are any coffee machine repair shops or technicians nearby. These experts may be able to give you some general advice about the viability and cost-effectiveness of a repair.Donate:Another option is to offer it for free onFreecycle,Freegleor a similar service. If the machine doesn’t work, you can state that it’s supplied on a spares or repair basis. Someone may relish the challenge of bringing it back to life.Refurbish:Some manufacturers provide the option to return your broken machine for repair, even if it’s out of warranty. In the event a repair isn’t possible or cost-effective, they may recycle or refurbish your machine for resale – and possibly offer you another refurbished machine for less. If in doubt, it’s always worth emailing or phoning your manufacturer.Reuse:If you’re replacing your machine with another from the same manufacturer, some parts may be interchangeable, so it could be useful to keep it for spares. Many espresso machines have similarly sized portafilters and filter baskets, and the same goes for other types of coffee machines: many manufacturers use compatible parts across multiple models in their ranges.Recycle:For the parts or machines you can’t reuse, most coffee machines – and most small appliances, for that matter – can be recycled. If you’re unsure about your nearest options, try the Recycling Locator onRecycle Your Electricals. Type in your postcode, the type of appliance and whether you want to recycle, donate or repair it, and you’ll find a list of your nearest options.For my postcode, this gave me the location and contact details for my local recycling centre, in addition to branches of Argos, Tesco, Asda and Currys. It also gave a list of which products would be accepted at each location. This, however, is worth taking with a pinch of salt; I’d contact the location before turning up with a trolley full of old appliances.For example, not all of those stores will provide free recycling for non-customers. Currys is a notable exception, accepting most small electrical items for free in-store recycling. Asda recycles goods only when customers are buying a replacement in-store, unless they are less than 30cm on their longest edge. And although it said my local Tesco would accept coffee machines, the staff member I spoke to said that while they’d accept anything with a battery, they weren’t aware of an equivalent service for bigger items.The best bet is your local recycling centre, as it will be more likely to accept appliances, especially bulkier ones. Some centres also have dedicated repair boxes where items that may be repairable can be left – in my local borough, these are then taken to prison repair programmes so they can be donated to charity or other good causes.If you can’t get to your local centre, your council may collect smaller appliances alongside your bin collections. For reference, my council stipulates that the items be no larger than 35 x 40cm, fit in a carrier bag and not include any glass. Those dimensions cover most coffee machines, so the only challenge may be finding a carrier bag that’s big enough.Read our guide onhow to make your coffee machine last longerSasha Muller is atech and consumer journalist, avid coffee drinker and craft beer enthusiast with more than two decades of experience in testing products and avoiding deadlines. If he’s not exploring the local woods with his kids, boring people talking about mountain bike tyres or spending ill-advised amounts on classicdrum’n’bassvinyl, he’s probably to be found somewhere swearing at an inanimate objectThis article was originally published on 2 March 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page.
