title: How to turn unwanted anchovy tin oil into salsa verde – recipe | Fish | The Guardian
description: This powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: This powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!
Content: Tom Hunt’s anchovy oil salsa verdePhotograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s anchovy oil salsa verdePhotograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFishHow to turn unwanted anchovy tin oil into salsa verde – recipeThis powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!Tom HuntWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe oil from a tin of anchovies is a powerhouse larder ingredient that you possibly never knew existed. It’s a flavour bomb that carries all the delicious flavour compounds of the fish themselves, especially if you want to add their wonderful flavour to a dish but want to save the anchovies to serve separately or as a garnish.This salsa verde is based on Giorgio Locatelli’s in his bookMade in Italy, and it’s made with a knife rather than a blender. Chopping by hand gives it a much better texture, especially when you’re also using the stalks, which a blender can turn fibrous. The boiled egg is optional but traditional, and helps emulsify the sauce. Locatelli uses just the yolk, but I’ve used the whole egg, not least to avoid the faff of finding a use for the spare white. This sauce is incredible with lamb or mutton and very good with grilled fish.Anchovy oil salsa verdeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appNever throw fat down the sink. In fact, never throw fat awayat all– it can be repurposed to use in cooking and is a wonderful ingredient in its own right that you never even knew you had. Anchovy oil specifically adds umami and a wonderful depth of flavour to a dish without overpowering it, and works brilliantly in salsa verde. (If need be, put the drained anchovies in a sterilised jar, top with extra-virgin olive oil – which can also be reused – seal and store in the fridge for up to two weeks.This is my first time adding boiled egg to the classic sauce, and I was really impressed with the results: it made a huge difference to the texture, and helped emulsify and fortify the sauce. It’s traditional to add just the hard-boiled egg yolk, but the whole egg, including the white, worked really well and disappeared into the salsa.100g flat-leaf parsley, leaves and stalks, or a mix of whatever soft herbs you have to hand1 small garlic clove, peeledSea salt and black pepper2 tbsp capers, drained and finely chopped1 hard-boiled egg(optional)2 tbsp caper brine, or white-wine vinegarOil from a standard tin of anchovies(roughly 15-30ml)30-50ml extra virgin olive oilFinely chop the parsley, stalks and all, then cross-chop with a rocking motion until evenly and very finely chopped. Pound the garlic and a pinch of sea salt in a mortar, to make a smooth paste, then add the capers and pound again to make a rough puree. Add the chopped herbs and an optional chopped hard-boiled egg, and pound to an smooth, emulsified paste.Stir in the caper brine and the anchovy oil, then work in enough extra-virgin olive oil to create a loose, spoonable sauce. Season to taste, then serve straight away or leave to rest for an hour. Store any excess in a clean jar in the fridge for up to two days, or freeze in an ice-cube tray to use later.Explore more on these topicsFishWaste notFoodFood wasteSauces and graviesHerbs and spicesItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Angela Hartnett’s Italian summer recipes: grilled peaches, green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in tomato sauce | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Two inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine
Author: Angela Hartnett
Headline: Two inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine
Content: Angela Hartnett’s grilled peaches mozzarella and green beansPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenAngela Hartnett’s grilled peaches mozzarella and green beansPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.Italian food and drinkAngela Hartnett’s Italian summer recipes: grilled peaches, green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in tomato sauceTwo inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine: grilled peaches with green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in a roast tomato sauceAngela HartnettWed 5 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtCicoria, peaches, green beans and tomatoes are among our favourites ingredients right now, inspiring dishes that celebrate freshness and flavour. The restaurant is perched at the top of the Royal Opera House in London, so our dining room is flooded with sunlight throughout the day, which is just as well because these vibrant, simple dishes are best enjoyed in the sunshine.Grilled peaches, mozzarella and green beans (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minCook15 minServes4Sea salt and black pepper200g fine green beans, trimmed250g buffalo mozzarella4 ripe peaches, halved and stonedExtra-virgin olive oil1 small shallot, peeled and finely sliced1 tbsp balsamic vinegar, or good white-wine vinegar1 small handfulbasil leavesToasted almonds or hazelnuts, to serve (optional)A little grated lemon zest, to serve (optional)Bring a pan of salted water to a boil, then blanch the beans for two to three minutes, until just tender. Drain, refresh in iced water, then drain again and set aside. Meanwhile, tear the mozzarella into large pieces, and leave it to come up to room temperature.Heat a griddle pan until it’s properly hot. Rub the flesh sides of the peach halves lightly with olive oil, then grill cut side down for two to three minutes, until charred and slightly softened, but still holding their shape.Put the beans and sliced shallot in a bowl, then dress them with olive oil, the vinegar, salt and black pepper. Taste and adjust the seasoning – it should be fresh and sharp.Arrange the grilled peaches, mozzarella and dressed beans on a platter, spoon over any dressing left in the bowl, then scatter over the basil leaves, toasted nuts and a little lemon zest, if using. Finish with a final drizzle of olive oil and a little sea salt, and serve slightly warm or at room temperature.Gnudi with roast tomato sauceWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenPrep10 minChill8 hr+Cook1 hr 10 minServes4For the roast tomato sauce500g ripe plum tomatoes2garlic cloves,peeled and lightly crushedA few thyme sprigsSea salt and black pepperExtra-virgin olive oil1 small splashred-wine vinegarFor the gnudi250g good-quality ricotta, well-strained50g finely grated parmesan,plus extra for servingFresh nutmeg250g semolinaWhite pepperTo finishBasil leavesGood olive oilTo make the tomato sauce, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the tomatoes in a roasting tray with the garlic and thyme, season well and drizzle generously with good olive oil. Roast for 35-40 minutes, until the tomatoes collapse and lightly caramelise. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs, then blend or crush the tomatoes to your preferred consistency. Add a dash of vinegar to sharpen the flavour, then check the seasoning and keep warm in a bowl.Meanwhile, to make the gnudi, beat the ricotta until smooth and light, then stir in the parmesan and grate in a little nutmeg to taste. Season generously, then chill for 30 minutes.Spread half the semolina on an oven tray and the rest on a clean work surface. Roll spoonfuls of the ricotta mixture into short, roughly 1½cm-thick sausages, then cut into smallpieces and shape gently into balls. Roll the gnudi lightly in the semolina on the work surface as you work, then arrange them on the semolina-covered tray.When all the gnocchi are on the tray, cover them generously with the remaining semolina, so they’re almost buried. Cill overnight, if possible, or for at least several hours.Bring a large pan of salted water to a gentle simmer, then, working in batches, drop in the gnudi and cook for three to four minutes, until they float to the surface. Lift out carefully with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.Spoon the warm tomato sauce on to plates, arrange the gnudi on top and finish with basil leaves, more parmesan and a final drizzle of olive oil.Angela Hartnett heads upCicoria at The Royal Opera House, LondonExplore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkSummer food and drinkFoodSaladAngela HartnettVegetablesCheeserecipesShareReuse this content

title: Better off together: could combining pension pots boost your retirement income? | Pensions | The Guardian
description: Many UK workers have cash in multiple schemes – should you roll them into one? There are pros and cons
Author: Sandra Haurant
Headline: Many UK workers have cash in multiple schemes – should you roll them into one? There are pros and cons
Content: Many Britons have several pension pots that they might benefit from combining.Illustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMany Britons have several pension pots that they might benefit from combining.Illustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianPensionsBetter off together: could combining pension pots boost your retirement income?Many UK workers have cash in multiple schemes – should you roll them into one? There are pros and consSandra HaurantWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow many pensions do you have? In the days of a job for life, many people had just two: the state pension and the one offered by their employer. But a combination of people changing jobs more often and rules that force employers to enrol workers into schemes automatically, means you are likely to end up with more.The number of people saving into a private sector workplace pension has doubled since 2012 to reach 23 million, according to thePensionsRegulator, largely because of “auto-enrolment”. On top of that, millions of people have personal pensions and self-invested private pensions (Sipps). And some will have all three.“Every time we change jobs, we are likely to begin a new pension,” says Alistair McQueen, the head of savings and retirement at Aviva. “With average [job] tenure at about five years, we may end our working lives with many pension pots.”As a result, he says, there is growing interest in consolidation: combining some or all of your pensions, except those that you get from the state.Pros and consOne big benefit of consolidation is it arguably makes things a lot simpler. “There is quite a strong argument to say that if you’ve got all your pensions in one place, it’s less of a daunting task to try to engage more with how it’s invested rather than having four or five little pots all over the place, which doesn’t feel as meaningful,” says Kirsty Stone, a partner and chartered financial planner at The Private Office.Combining pension pots, whether workplace schemes or Sipps, into a fund with lower annual management fees can save you thousands of pounds. Moving money out of an underperforming fund into one providing better returns can also add thousands.double quotation markHaving your pensions in one place can be beneficial if you want to access your money through ‘flexible drawdown’There are potential post-retirement benefits, too. Having your pensions in one place can be beneficial if you want to access your money through “flexible drawdown” – whereby, instead of buying an annuity, you take out chunks of your pension to live on.Stone says: “If you want to pay yourself £500 a month, say, that is much easier to do if you access it all from one provider.” If the pension pots remain separate, you need to deal with each provider individually, which, says Stone, “will just be messy in retirement”.There are, however, situations where combining pensions could make you worse off.“It’s definitely not a no-brainer,” says Steve Webb, a partner at the consultancy firm LCP and a former pensions minister. “If someone is thinking about consolidating pensions, the question is always why? What is the problem you are trying to solve?”He adds: “If you leave pensions where they are, they are not frozen or lost – they will continue growing. And, depending on the pensions, leaving them there might be the best choice.”View image in fullscreenYou need to weigh up whether combining your pensions will make you better off in retirement.Photograph: John Hopkins/AlamyBefore deciding to combine your retirement savings, it is important to be aware of the implications and, crucially, understand the benefits offered by your existing pension. These could include guaranteed annuity rates and the right to take more than the standard 25% as a tax-free lump sum. In certain cases, where the contract stipulates you can take the tax-free lump sum at the age of 55 rather than saying the “normal minimum age”, this will override changes coming in 2028 that raise it to 57.If you have a defined benefit pension, also known as a final salary pension, you would almost certainly lose money by moving it. There is legislation to protect people from this: anyone with a cash equivalent transfer value of more than £30,000 is obliged to take financial advice before transferring out. Most experts would advise taking advice even if its value is below that amount.FeesIf you have built up a number of very small pension pots while job-hopping, the earlier you are in your career, the more you could benefit from grouping those small pensions together and getting them working harder for you.But if you are approaching retirement, you may get more flexibility by keeping them separate.There are specific rules for pension pots worth less than £10,000 that allow you to withdraw the money in a way that you cannot for larger pensions.View image in fullscreenIf you have built up small pension pots while job-hopping, the earlier you are in your career, the more you could benefit from grouping them together.Photograph: Fredrick Kippe/AlamyThen there is the question of fees. Not all providers charge exit or transfer fees for moving your pension, but if they do, these fees will eat into your savings.And you will want to avoid a situation where you move all your pensions into one private pension or Sipp, only to find yourself paying higher management fees than previously. Annual management fees on workplace schemes have been negotiated with providers based on bulk membership, so they are typically lower than on private schemes, Webb says.So while there are plenty of online services offering to consolidate your pension, you always need to check the fees. If they are charging twice as much as your workplace pension, your investments would need to work very hard to better your returns.The processCombining defined contribution pensions, also known as money purchase pensions, is usually straightforward, largely thanks to the fact that providers will be very pleased to take your money.Typically, you would begin by contacting the scheme into which you want to pool the funds.“They will ask for the details of the pensions you are transferring, and they take it from there. It is normally a fairly simple process you can request online,” Stone says. “However, on occasion, you’ll be asked to complete paper forms or answer questionnaires as part of this process.”Importantly, while the provider will oversee the process and take care of much of the admin, they will not offer advice and will just follow your instructions.How to trace old pensionsMake a list of your former employers and the dates you worked there, as well as the pension providers for each employer, if you know the names. If any of the companies have closed since you left, you may be able to track down the pension scheme they used through thePension Protection Fundwebsite.If you can’t find the contact details, try thegovernment’s search service. You will need employers’ or providers’ names, and it will only tell you how to get in touch with the pension provider, not whether you have a pension. You can also tryGretel, a free online service that traces dormant accounts including pensions, using your own address history rather than the details of former employers or providers.Next, contact the providers to find out if you have a pension, and how much is saved. The more information you can give (such as employment dates, former names and your national insurance number), the better. Once you have tracked them down, you can decide whether consolidating retirement savings is the right plan for you.Four pension scenariosAnita, 59View image in fullscreenIllustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianStarted her career as a teacher in secondary schools and paid into the Teachers’ Pension Scheme (TPS) until she left to work in the private sector 15 years ago. She has worked for three different employers since, and has workplace pensions with each. She checked recently and has £95,000, £77,500 and £83,000 in these schemes, all of which have annual charges of 0.3%. She is interested in using flexible drawdown to take her pension money as and when she needs.What should Anitaconsider?The TPS is sometimes considered the “gold standard” in pensions. There are different versions of this scheme depending on the date of membership. Anita’s pension will be based on her final salary, because she was teaching before changes to the system in 2015.“It’s likely Anita has built up significant benefits in the TPS, and the pension she will get in retirement is based on length of service and earnings as a teacher,” says Charlene Young, a senior pensions and savings expert at the investment platform AJ Bell.Anita may be able to start taking this pension from as young as 60. So she should leave this one where it is.Kirsty Stone at The Private Office says it is worth considering consolidating the other pensions, particularly if Anita decides she wants to use flexible drawdown. “It’s much easier to do this with one pension rather than taking small amounts from different pots,” Stone adds.Gemma, 33View image in fullscreenIllustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianHas had several jobs. She did not opt out of auto-enrolment and so has four or five workplace pensions. She would like to put everything in one place as she feels a bit confused by all the different providers, and has even lost some of their details in house moves.What should Gemmaconsider?It would be best to take direct action to track down and combine her pensions before things get harder to manage. Gemma can begin by using a tracing service to find her old pensions.“She next needs to decide whether it’s best to combine what she has built up so far into her current active workplace pension, or into another scheme running alongside it, so that there are no more than one or two plans to manage,” Young says.This could also help Gemma to engage with her retirement savings because it is often easier to understand what is there when it is all in one place. Stone suggests Gemma should look beyond a scheme’s default fund to maximise the growth. “You want to be sure you’re making your investments work as hard as possible while you’re younger, and the default strategy is very rarely the best strategy from an investment standpoint,” Stone says.Phil, 51View image in fullscreenIllustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianHas five different pensions, one of which allows him to take a tax-free lump sum at 55. One is a Sipp that he set up when he was briefly self-employed. He has left it in the default fund and knows the charges are 1%, which is higher than for his workplace schemes. The other pensions are defined contribution schemes – all are worth more than £10,000.What should Philconsider?That the older pension allows him to take a tax-free lump sum at 55, rather than 57 under the new rules, is a benefit he probably will not want to lose, and it would be wise to move the Sipp into a lower-cost pension, as those fees will eat into his savings.“The three other pots might still be good candidates for combining, so that Phil can focus on the investment strategy in one additional pot rather than all three,” Young says.Because of the benefits and decisions to make around lump sums, Phil should consider financial advice, she suggests. “He will need to pay a fee, but advice can help avoid costly mistakes, and a recommendation based on personal circumstances should give greater peace of mind with retirement planning.”Sam, 27View image in fullscreenIllustration: Yufei Yang/The GuardianHas had a few jobs since graduation and has three pension pots worth a lot less than £10,000 each. He is not currently working but is applying for jobs. He could do with the cash, so wonders if he could access funds from his pensions.What should Samconsider?“Unfortunately, you cannot usually access pension pots until age 55, rising to 57 from 6 April 2028,” Young says. Since the money is tied up, “it’s worth considering combining the existing small pots into the lowest-cost suitable scheme”.Stone says: “What combining does is provide you with simplicity. And even if the pensions are worth £10,000 in total, say, you can get that working harder and get into a stronger place by the time he retires.”With decades to go until retirement, she also says Sam should opt for higher-risk investments to benefit from more growth.Explore more on these topicsPensionsOccupational pensionsAuto-enrolment pensionsConsumer affairsRetirement planningfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get | Beauty | The Guardian
description: ‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users
Content: Illustration: Sara Andreasson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sara Andreasson/The GuardianBeauty‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to usersLaura O'ConnorWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTShareDanielle, 37, didn’t always have issues with body image: she used to be a model and recalls receiving positive attention from men. However, when two years of unemployment plunged her into a period of financial insecurity, her confidence faded. “It was easy to wonder, if I was prettier, if some of my features were different, would that help?” she said.So, when Danielle saw videos on TikTok about a “facial analysis” service that claimed it could provide her with “science-backed” glow-up advice, she bought it without hesitation. Three-hundred and thirty dollars later, after sending in selfies to be analyzed, Danielle received her personalized 30-page report from the company Qoves.Qoves scored everything from Danielle’s ear shape to the femininity of her features. It recommended she get a rhinoplasty, a lowerblepharoplasty, acanthopexy, chin implants and amalarplasty. Additionally: microblading, lash enhancements, filler in her temples and cheeks, a mixture of filler and Botox in her chin and jaw, and Botox around her mouth.double quotation markI do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollarsDanielleDanielle, who now works in tech in Colorado, is delaying any cosmetic surgery until she pays off the credit card debt accrued from her two years without a paycheck; once it is, she is interested in traveling to Mexico for procedures on her nose and eyelids. She also recently consulted a Botox and filler injector.Qoves states that attractive people “get better treatment everywhere, from the hospital to the courtroom” and claims it is easier for them to find jobs and earn money. There is some truth to this: the “halo effect” is adocumented phenomenonof good-looking people being perceived as smarter and more sociable than their average-looking counterparts, andstudieshave linked attractiveness tobetter pay. For Danielle, who asked to go by first name only for privacy, this promised material advantage was a selling point: “It gave me a motivation that I didn’t have in the past, which was seeing it as potentially helping my career and financial security.”From bone smashing to chin extensions: how ‘looksmaxxing’ is reshaping young men’s facesRead morePlastic surgery andnonsurgical cosmetic enhancementssuch as Botox haveunambiguously increasedin popularity over the past two decades, to the point that the aesthetics of bought beauty have become inescapable on social media. This has opened the door for“looksmaxxing” influencers, who take fixation with appearance to the extreme. Coalescing around the language of science and “self-improvement”, looksmaxxers claim that attractiveness can be quantified – that individual features should be analyzed and empirically scored, and physical improvements are made where necessary. The ultimate goal is to achieve “facial harmony”, or the ideal proportions of nose, eyes and other features in relationship to one another.Now, a slew of facial analysis services are benefitting from the looksmaxxing ethos, capitalizing on people’s insecurities about appearance under the guise of helping them become their best selves. Qoves, which Danielle used, cites peer-reviewed research to lend credibility to its idea of quantifiable beauty. It provides analyses for men and women, and for $150 recommends “nonsurgical” changes, such as injectables, with an optional $180 upgrade for surgical recommendations. Cheaper tools such as Facemaxify and Epica use AI to score the components of a user’s face against an opaque metric of facial harmony. In addition to recommending expensive procedures, the services often offer paid subscriptions. Epica’s specialty is skin and makeup plans for women, and it directs users to affiliate links for cosmetics and grooming products.“I do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollars,” Danielle said, noting that her confidence decreased when she started using TikTok. “All of the people that I look at [on social media] and think are beautiful have gotten plastic surgery.”Océane, 25, discovered Qoves via one of its beauty videos on YouTube, where it has more than 1m subscribers. Self-image was a longstanding concern for her: “I’ve always loved beauty, makeup and physical appearance, but I’ve never really liked my own image. I was always put down by my parents,” she said. “My mom wanted to pay for a nose job for me when I turned 18.” At school, kids bullied her. “They called me a dolphin because of my nose.”Océane, who lives in France, paid an additional $80 for express delivery and received her results from Qoves in two days. It provided her a sense of relief: the report didn’t recommend any changes to her nose and otherwise “confirmed what I already knew about my flaws”, she said.double quotation markThese sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disordersDr Tracy VaillancourtDr Tracy Vaillancourt is a professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa and one of the many scholars Qovescitesin promotional materials. She expressed concern about the negative psychological impact of facial analysis services on self-esteem. “This is what women are most insecure about: their appearance,” she said. “There are going to be some who are told they look better than they thought and that’s great. Is that really going to be sustained over time?” In other words, can a service that emphasizes appearance as a metric of self-worth ever provide someone with lasting peace of mind, or does it perpetuate a cycle of self-criticism?Moreover, though Qoves and Epica limit their services to adults aged 18 and up, the age restrictions are easy for minors to bypass. Qoves users are expected to self-report issues with self-image, with few guardrails in place to deter anyone with body dysmorphia disorder before they are presented with a menu of their flaws. “You can circumvent that so easily, it’s just going to give them the appearance of due diligence and making sure they’re not exploiting people who are vulnerable – but ultimately, they will be exploiting people who are vulnerable,” Vaillaincourt said. “These sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disorders and people with low self-esteem.”Qoves referenced Vaillancourt’s work in a video called The Cost of Being Too Pretty to show thatbeautiful women face jealousy from others. But Vaillancourt isn’t a scholar of beauty: she researches bullying, mental health and violence prevention. Though Qoves correctly interpreted her research on physical appearance and hostility, she is uneasy about research like hers being used for paid services like Qoves, that she believes have the capacity to harm women’s mental health.Beyond Vaillancourt’s research, the applications of “science” used to back up these facial analysis services are shaky at best.‘The face doesn’t move’: Hollywood’s obsession with cosmetic surgeries has led to stiffer looks – and performancesRead moreQoves breaks down customers’ features based on “masculine and feminine facial qualities”, it explains in avideoreferencing a 2018bulletinin the journal Frontiers of Psychology. Dr Justin Mogilski, psychology professor at the University of South Carolina Salkehatchie, co-authored the bulletin. However, his research was a limited view of how a group of primarily college-aged Americans perceived certain features as masculine or feminine.“Do findings like mine generalize to every single population that makes up the world or a country? Or within every context where the attractiveness of a given feature can vary based on local ecology or culture? They do not,” Mogilski said. “So, would I make suggestions [for facial enhancements] based on our or anyone else’s data? I would not.”Some services do not make any pretense of considering location or cultural standards in how they quantify beauty. On its website, Epica reports a commitment to diversity and inclusion, though it is unclear how its methodology reflects this – particularly as AI tools are increasingly criticized for perpetuating racial bias. Qoves insists its analyses are appropriate for all ethnicities, and says it will “consider unique facial traits and characteristics common to your demographic” when creating a report. In reality, as some people have pointed out online, its promotional materials often replicate Eurocentric conceptions of beauty: slim noses and large, double-lidded eyes for women, for example. As one person commented on a Qoves video breaking down Bangladeshi women’s faces: “What’s shown here seems to reflect a beauty ideal rather than the real diversity of Bangladeshi women.”double quotation markI don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to [measure attractiveness and sell recommendations]Dr Mitch BrownThe lack of transparency around the methods and metrics the services use to measure attractiveness is its own issue. “These services owe it to their clients and themselves – if they want to be seen as credible – to be able to demonstrate scientifically” what their methods are, said Dr Mitch Brown, an assistant professor of psychological science at the University of Arkansas who has studied the science of attraction for over a decade. According to experts such as Brown, the available literature on attractiveness is too heterogenous, making any universal, population-wide generalizations questionable. And, even if we know certain features are deemed as attractive by a specific community, are these findings lasting enough to justify changing one’s appearance? Are they sound enough to support a paid service’s recommendation?“I don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to do that. I would caution anyone against that,” Brown said.In an email to the Guardian, Epic said: “We are unable to disclose proprietary information regarding our algorithmic methodologies, technical frameworks, or internal product development details.” It continued: “We continually review and refine our platform to ensure our services provide a supportive, fair and positive experience for all users.”Qoves did not respond to a request for comment.I purchased my own report with Qoves and uploaded my selfies to Epica to see what these tools really offered.For Qoves, I was asked to check boxes confirming that I did not have “concerns related to body dysmorphic disorder” and would be comfortable receiving weight loss recommendations, and then asked to upload pictures of my face and side profile.A couple of days later, Qoves presented me with an 18-tab analysis of each of my features, along with a 16-page “aesthetic protocol”, complete with a disturbing mockup of what my face would look like should I implement its recommendations: a healthy dose of lip filler, makeup and the overly tweezed eyebrows I sported in 10th grade.‘Anti-ageing is anti-life’: why longevity culture is just ageism in a lab coatRead moreFor Epica, I was asked: how often do I use makeup? Do I want more control over my appearance? Instantly, I received a “skin health” score of 61%, with uneven texture highlighted as the main concern and a flood of serums advertised across my screen to fix it. I then moved to my couch, retook a selfie in the new lighting, and saw my skin health score jump to 81%.Before receiving these reports, I had never considered whether my mouth was upturned or wide, or whether or not Botox at my ripe age of 26 would be beneficial. I had not considered “dark feminine” makeup styles as being my look. But now I found myself second-guessing what I saw in the mirror. Just how downturned did my mouthreallylook to those around me? How would Botox or a haul of new makeup change features I hadn’t previously been concerned about?The language of looksmaxxing was in my head, and I didn’t like it.“Ultimately, there are going to be implications for mental health,” Vaillancourt said, “and it’s going to be about social comparison: never feeling good enough, never achieving enough.”In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: the best undereye concealers for over-35s | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Want to brighten dark circles without accentuating wrinkles? You’re not alone – this is the most-asked makeup question and here is the answer
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Want to brighten dark circles without accentuating wrinkles? You’re not alone – this is the most-asked makeup question and here is the answer
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianSali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: the best undereye concealers for over-35sWant to brighten dark circles without accentuating wrinkles? You’re not alone – this is the most-asked makeup question and here is the answerSali HughesWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The most common makeup question asked by women over 35 is this: what’s a good undereye concealer that won’t make lines and wrinkles look cakey and dry? I’m getting to them, I promise. But first, I must say that prep is key – dry, flaky skin will only look more so under makeup, so undereyes should first be hydrated and smoothed with a good, moisturising skincare routine. Only then can a concealer get on with the business of brightening and camouflaging.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Givenchy’sPrisme Libre Skin-Caring Concealer(£37) is my most recommended for fortysomethings and beyond, regardless of skin type. It’s perfectly balanced in that it’s moisturising and softening, but not so much so that it slips and slides and doesn’t deliver on lasting coverage – it has just enough heft. It works as well on the face as it does under eyes and stays fresh looking all day.double quotation markGlossier’s balm has a texture so buttery and comforting that it almost feels like eye creamMore moisturising for drier types is Dior’sForever Skin Correct(£35). I’ve used this for years and it’s a rare beast: a concealer offering full, lasting coverage without exacerbating dryness. The shade range is particularly well considered, too. If you’d like the coverage/moisture ratio weighted towards the latter, Glossier’sStretchBalm Concealer(£22) has a texture so buttery and comforting that it almost feels likeeye cream. It has less pigment than those above, but if dark circles aren’t a huge issue for you, that won’t matter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: behold the power of the long-wearing liquid eyeshadowRead moreOffering a little more in the way of both coverage and moisture is NYX’s excellentBare With Me Concealer Serum(£9.99). If you don’t mind the pump bottle (not my favourite), the texture is gorgeous – lightweight, fluid and spreadable. The finish is smooth, flattering and very natural-looking. It’s a great and well-priced concealer for anyone.Those blessed with natural oil around the eyes may find these unduly moisturising and wish to focus more on blur. Charlotte Tilbury’sAirbrush Flawless Blur Concealer(£31) is superb (and by far her best to date), packing in heaps of coverage – a little goes a very long way – and a soft, matte finish without heaviness or dryness. The effect is pretty on all but especially, in my view, on mature skins with a little more texture to contend with.Finishing is very important. I reject the outmoded preaching around never using powder on ageing skin. Nonsense. Modern powders help not hinder the effort. Coat a small, fluffy brush lightly in powder and tap over concealer to set and prevent creasing.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Catch of the day: a seafood safari on France’s culinary coast | France holidays | The Guardian
description: From Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafood
Author: Mary Novakovich
Headline: From Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafood
Content: A fish stall in Le Touquet.Photograph: Michael Juno/AlamyView image in fullscreenA fish stall in Le Touquet.Photograph: Michael Juno/AlamyFrance holidaysCatch of the day: a seafood safari on France’s culinary coastFrom Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafoodMary NovakovichWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStellio Lestienne, chef atLa Matelotein Boulogne’s harbour, shows me his shopping list as we browse the city’s daily morning fish market. He wants to pick up some crab and sole, which are in season, but his usual lobster fisher is still out on his boat, so he’ll have to wait a bit for that. Although I’ve been a regular visitor to both Boulogne and the surrounding Hauts-de-France region for about 30 years, this is my first time in the fish market. Now I’m kicking myself for all that lost time.It’s not very big, nor is it remotely picturesque, stretching along a nondescript car park in the port. But it does have a fantastic selection of fish and seafood, both from fishers (pêcheurs artisansin light-blue stalls) and retailers (commerçantsin dark blue). And it’s considerably cheaper than other fish markets I’ve seen. “People come here from the UK with cool bags to do their shopping,” Stellio says, pointing to a man doing that very thing. I spot filletedroussettes(dogfish) going for €2 each. At another stall, a man deftly slices through a grotesque-looking monkfish, cutting out the prized cheeks.View image in fullscreenBoulogne harbour.Photograph: Anthony Hucks/AlamyBoulogne-sur-Mer is France’s largest fishing port and all of this bounty is just a short jaunt across the Channel. This makes the idea of a seafood safari along the Côte d’Opale – whose chalky cliffs, sand dunes and forests stretch south from Calais to Le Touquet and beyond – impossible for me to resist.I start in the fishing village of Audresselles, a pleasant 45-minute pootle along the coast road fromLeShuttle’s terminal.La Marie Galante, run by cheerful and talented sisters Béatrice and Godeleine Cuvellier, has a cosy interior and razor clams on the menu. Accustomed to seeing empty razor-clam shells on my favourite Norfolk beach but not on restaurant menus (too much of a faff to collect, a local fishmonger told me), I pounce on these shellfish smothered in garlic and parsley. This is followed by a typical plate offruits de mer– oysters, whelks, giant juicy prawns and half a crab. Around me echoes the sound of people studiously pounding their crab claws open, soon joined by my own. The sound of a happy restaurant.View image in fullscreenMary Novakovich tackles crab at La Marie Galante in Audresselles.Photograph: Adam BatterbeeOne of my favourite French towns awaits a little further along the coast – Wimereux, with its wonderfully whimsical 19th-century architecture and long expanse of beach. Its art deco grande dame,Hotel l’Atlantic, has had a major makeover since I last stayed. Chef Benjamin Delpierre, co-owner with his wife Aurélie, has also since handed back the restaurant’s Michelin star, throwing off the constraints that came with it. In a relaxed yet sophisticated atmosphere, I dip prawn croquettes into a curried beetroot puree before revelling in a fillet of roast cod with an addictive celery cream and rich chicken jus. All the while, I watch mesmerised as the sun dips across the Channel.Le Touquet, with its long sandy beaches, pine forests and golf courses loved by Channel-hopping Brits, is my next stop. But first I make a detour to its neighbour across the River Canche, Étaples-sur-Mer. This is another first for me: a visit toMaréis, an exhibition centre and aquarium telling the story of French sea fishing in the North Sea and Channel. And what an utterly fascinating story it turns out to be. What is caught in the sea and how it’s caught are vividly brought to life thanks to clever immersive and interactive exhibits (in French and English). Fish swim in an aquarium above my head, while another large tank holds enormous rays gliding through the water.double quotation markAround me echoes the sound of people studiously pounding their crab claws open. The sound of a happy restaurantThat evening in Le Touquet, the shouts of England fans from the Globe Trotter pub keep me abreast of the World Cup score while, across the lane atPérard, I dine on a whole grilled sea bream. I can’t remember the last time I could fillet a fish so effortlessly, such was the perfection of the grilling and freshness of the fish. On the way back to my hotel,Novotel Thalassa Le Touquet, I’m treated to the same sunset spectacle as in Wimereux, the sands and the sea glowing in the warm light.I spend an agreeable morning wandering through Le Touquet’s sprawling market, most of whose food stalls are under soaring wooden vaulted ceilings within the semicircular covered market. Not surprisingly, the fishmongers have their own section, where they’ve set up abar àhuitresso you can sit at high tables and orderfruits de merand a glass of wine. It’s tempting, but I go for a bowl of mussels covered in oozing maroilles cheese in nearbyLa Chope. The restaurant’s soundtrack of death metal isn’t exactly conducive to a relaxing lunch, but the food just about makes up for it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWimereux seafront and sea pool.Photograph: Yann Avril/AlamyI still have an evening in Boulogne to look forward to, but first a stroll around the Old Town near the imposing basilica. My B&B is here too, theStay Well Hôtel de Fiennes, an elegant 1732 townhouse with a courtyard made for unwinding. But the prospect of dinner at La Matelote drags me out of the comfy chairs and down to the port. Delicious flavours follow: langoustine with cauliflower cream; white asparagus with smoked salmon, caviar, basil cream and hummus; hake with pea puree and thyme-roasted carrots. And it’s all crowned by a quite stupendous lemon souffle. I’m not a dessert person, but this makes me want to applaud whoever made this divine creation.I have a final stop before the end of my little seafood safari – back to Audresselles, but this time to my regular haunt,Chez Mimi. Trying to be sensible after days of indulgence, I opt for a small plate of crustaceans instead of my usual calorific “crabe mimi” (stuffed crab with fries). My husband orders it instead, making me wish I were less sensible. In the village square, everything is being set up for that weekend’s annual crab festival, now in its 50th year and an event I enjoyed years ago. I might be missing the party, but I have my own seafood celebration to savour.The trip was provided byHauts-de-France tourismandPas-de-Calais tourism.Hotel l’Atlantichas doubles from €129room only,Novotel Le Touquetfrom €128 room only andThe Stay Well Hôtel de Fiennesfrom €160 B&BExplore more on these topicsFrance holidaysFood and drinkRestaurantsDay tripsShort breaksCalais holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I found a forbidden novel – it led to a dangerous, lasting love | Uyghurs | The Guardian
description: Growing up in the Chinese region of Xinjiang, romance was frowned upon – as was much of my Uyghur culture. But one day, exploring a strange house, I found a gateway to both worlds
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Growing up in the Chinese region of Xinjiang, romance was frowned upon – as was much of my Uyghur culture. But one day, exploring a strange house, I found a gateway to both worlds
Content: ‘Something innocent yet dangerous emerged’ … Yalkun and Rabia on their honeymoon in Mardin, Turkey, October 2020.Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun UluyolView image in fullscreen‘Something innocent yet dangerous emerged’ … Yalkun and Rabia on their honeymoon in Mardin, Turkey, October 2020.Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun UluyolA moment that changed meUyghursA moment that changed me: I found a forbidden novel – it led to a dangerous, lasting loveGrowing up in the Chinese region of Xinjiang, romance was frowned upon – as was much of my Uyghur culture. But one day, exploring a strange house, I found a gateway to both worldsYalkun UluyolWed 5 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany people have a book that changes their life. For me and my wife, one book in particular changed our destinies for ever. We have been in love since we were teenagers, and today we are happily married – all because I accidentally discovered a forbidden novel in someone else’s house.It was a hot summer’s evening in 2009, in Kumul,Xinjiang. I was 16 and my father insisted I accompany him to visit a distant relative, where they would spend hours chatting about the old days and feasting as if they hadn’t eaten in years. As the well-behaved teenager I tried to be, I sat politely, nodding at their stories and pretending to absorb their “life lessons”, attempting to hide my boredom. The living room, with its small windows and bright lighting, was unbearable.Desperate to escape, I asked for permission to explore the host’s study, a room lined with hundreds of books. As I browsed the neatly arranged shelves, a seven-volume Uyghur novel caught my eye. Hidden in a corner, perhaps intentionally concealed, it seemed to call to me. I asked if I could borrow it. The host lowered his voice. “It’s a well-written book about the brutalities of the Cultural Revolution,” he said quietly. “It’s banned by the government. Don’t show it to anyone, don’t take it to school, and return it when you’re done.” It was titled Leyighan Bulaq (The Muddy Spring) and written by the famous Uyghur novelist Jalalidin Băhram.We arrived home around midnight, but curiosity consumed me. I opened the first volume and couldn’t stop reading. I became obsessed with its characters – teachers in a rural area of my homeland – who endured forced labour, assimilation and political indoctrination. Centred on three young couples, the story was all about friendship, love and resilience.View image in fullscreenYalkun Uluyol in Kumul, Xinjiang, China, in December 2009.Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun UluyolDespite my promise, I decided to share the book with another bookworm in my class – Rabia, my closest academic rival and secret friend. We exchanged handwritten notes about books, our only way of “talking” in a conservative Muslim town where friendships between boys and girls were unwelcome. Rabia was very shy, avoiding me at school, but the notebooks we wrote to each other in created a private world.I couldn’t keep this precious novel from her. Ignoring all warnings, I smuggled it into school and slipped it into her bag along with my notebook. “The friendship in this book is so pure,” I wrote. “I cherish our friendship the same way.”We had exchanged notes before, but this time something shifted, something innocent yet dangerous emerged: love. Through our notes, we talked about the characters and events, gradually blending our own feelings into the discussions, writing as though we ourselves were characters in the story. One day, citing the book’s main characters, I wrote: “I think I have feelings for you, just as Hikmet had for Gulziba.” And with that single sentence, our love story began.About a year later, I left home to study abroad. Our relationship went through ups and downs but survived through phone calls and online messages. But for us to reunite and build a life, Rabia needed a passport, which was a nearly impossible task as the Xinjiang authorities tightly control the issuing of passports forUyghurs. After being denied the chance to sit a university entrance exam because she wore a headscarf – another everyday indignity Uyghurs endured as the Chinese government tightened its social control in the region – she moved to Beijing for a language course.View image in fullscreenThe seven volumes of Leyighan Bulaq by Jalalidin Băhram, in Yalkun and Rabia’s library in Istanbul, Turkey.Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun UluyolThat move turned out to be a blessing in disguise as it allowed her to bypass strict passport controls in our home town. Four years after I left home, she finally reached Istanbul, where I was studying, in 2014, and we got married in 2020. Many of our loved ones could not attend, including Rabia’s parents and siblings, and my father.China has renamed hundreds of Uyghur villages and towns, say human rights groupsRead moreMost newly married couples are happy. We were, too, but we were also forced into exile as horrible things were happening back home. As part of Xi Jinping’s “strike hard” campaign, Chinese authorities arbitrarily detainedhundreds of thousands of Uyghur peoplewithout due process, including my father.Because the Chinese governmentpunishes Uyghurs for contacting others abroad, we could not share important milestones of our lives with loved ones. When our two-year-old daughter died in November 2023 due to an incurable illness, we buried her – along with all the great memories she could have had with her grandparents back in our homeland – at a graveyard in Istanbul.In late 2024, we moved to London and opened a new chapter of our lives. As we unpacked, we sorted through our old school notebooks – over a dozen of them – and sat reading the letters we had written to each other in secret more than a decade earlier. We realised that, like the plot of Leyighan Bulaq, our lives have always been full of tragedy but also friendship, love and resilience. We celebrate the love story we have created and the wounds we have healed together, all thanks to a forbidden book.Explore more on these topicsUyghursA moment that changed meChinaXinjiangRelationshipsMarriagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘This isn’t some vendetta’ – Tulisa Contostavlos on taking on the tabloids, sex tapes and shame | Tulisa Contostavlos | The Guardian
description: The N-Dubz and X Factor star’s career went into freefall after an elaborate sting by the Sun on Sunday, and she’s still campaigning for tougher press regulation. But will it work?
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The N-Dubz and X Factor star’s career went into freefall after an elaborate sting by the Sun on Sunday, and she’s still campaigning for tougher press regulation. But will it work?
Content: ‘I’m that girl that’s rough around the edges’ … Tulisa Contostavlos.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m that girl that’s rough around the edges’ … Tulisa Contostavlos.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTulisa ContostavlosInterview‘This isn’t some vendetta’ – Tulisa Contostavlos on taking on the tabloids, sex tapes and shameEmine SanerThe N-Dubz and X Factor star’s career went into freefall after an elaborate sting by the Sun on Sunday, and she’s still campaigning for tougher press regulation. But will it work?Wed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLate last year,Tulisa Contostavlostook a good look at her life. Her relationship had come to an end and she found herself in her late 30s (she’s 38 now), wondering what next. “I started thinking about all the things I’d never done,” she says. At 20, life had got weird – Contostavlos was in the successful hip-hop group N-Dubz and became an adult just as the fame and money started coming in. By 24, she was a judge on the Saturday night TV show X Factor. If that hadn’t happened, she thinks she might have become an archaeologist – she’s obsessed with ancient history. And so last year she went travelling, to Egypt to see the pyramids, and to Peru to visit Machu Picchu.There were other, bigger changes. She gave up smoking and started having therapy for the first time. Contostavlos sat down, she says, and “I wrote a list of what my ‘greatest self’ looked like – where she’d go, how she thought, how she felt, the things she would do. I started implementing every single thing on that list and I found through doing that, you just become her – it is actually that simple. It just takes effort and discipline.” Her greatest self, she says, “is a person of action, and she turns lemons into lemon cake”. It got her thinking about the criminal trial that left her career in freefall. “I was like, right, let’s try to do something.”In 2013, Contostavlos was the subject ofa tabloid stingby Mazher Mahmood, the reporter known as the Fake Sheikh. He had posed as a Bollywood turned Hollywood producer, and was dangling the prospect of a £3.5m movie role for her. The front page story of the Sun on Sunday alleged that she had arranged to sell him cocaine. She denied it and the evidence seemed shaky – essentially she had put Mahmood in touch with someone she thought may know how to get hold of drugs – but she was charged. It went to trial, collapsing when itemerged that Mahmood had liedin pre-trial evidence; he would later be sentenced to15 months in prisonfor conspiring to pervert the course of justice. Still, she lost her house, and her job. “It was gone – the dream, the work, everything I strived for. That kid that used to bang her head against the wall at 12 years old, going, ‘I’ve got to make it.’ Everything she fought for was just down the drain.”View image in fullscreenN-Dubz in 2009, from left: Dappy, Contostavlos and Fazer.Photograph: Dave Hogan/Getty ImagesHer career never really recovered. Contostavlos remained in the public eye – she appeared on I’m A Celebrity, and there was a 2022N-Dubzreunion – but there is still judgment, she says. “No matter what level of normality I get back to or acceptance, I’m always going to be that chick that certain brands don’t want to touch. I’m that girl that’s rough around the edges,” she says. “Which for me is why I’m like, all right, fuck you. I’m gonna do things my way.”Contostavlos always appeared tough, but she’s also warm and funny when we talk in the Guardian’s offices. She’s unexpected, in lots of ways. She’s writing a fantasy novel, and is obsessed with The Lord of the Rings – she thinks she’s seen the films possibly thousands of times. “I’m actually a super-nerd,” she says. She devours books by spiritual leaders, and is given to spotting signs and taking note of the premonitions in her dreams. She has a lot of interests – one being the growing medical use of psychedelics (she took part in an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru). Another longstanding one is the matter of tougher press regulation, for which she is a prominent campaigner.Contostavlos is involved with Hacked Off, the campaign group that includes Hugh Grant and has called for tighter regulation of the press. Now, she has also launched her own campaign and petition calledFix the Press, in which she calls for an “independent press regulator – one the press does not control, fund, or appoint” with powers to investigate and fine newspapers. At the time of writing, it had nearly 25,000 signatures and Paramount+ are making a three-part documentary following her life and the campaign.The Independent Press Standards Organisation (Ipso), a rival to the government-backed regulator that no major media organisation would join, was set up after the dissolution of the Press Complaints Commission (PCC). The PCC was dissolved during the Leveson inquiry, held in 2011 and 2012, which found it was ineffective as a regulator and had failed to investigate ethical breaches such as phone hacking. Many of the biggest publishers signed up to Ipso (some, including the Guardian and theFinancial Times, did not). However, Contostavlos argues that, as the organisation is funded by its member publications, and former journalists and editors are on the board, it is not independent enough. “I don’t want to have any cap on freedom of speech,” she says. But she believes Ipso is “marking its own homework”.View image in fullscreenContostavlos at the Royal Courts of Justice in London, July 2012, after taking legal action against her ex over the publication of a private video tape.Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty ImagesHacked Off is also calling for the second part of the Leveson inquiry – which would have looked at the relationships between the press and the police – to be reinstated. She hasn’t met Andy Burnham (she adds: “yet”) but she hopes the new prime minister will be more sympathetic to the cause than Keir Starmer. Ten years ago, as a shadow minister, Burnham said the second stage of the Leveson inquiry, which was cancelled in 2018 by then culture secretary Matt Hancock, was “non-negotiable” . A lot has happened since then, includinglast month’s high court rulingagainst Prince Harry and other celebrities in their legal battle against Associated Newspapers Limited, the publishers of the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday. It remains to be seen where the press reform movement goes now.It is understandable that Contostavlos would have a personal grievance against the press, but she insists, “This isn’t some vendetta. I didn’t wake up one day and go, ‘I want to take you down.’” She pauses, and says: “It’s just about fairness.” She has dealt with what happened to her, but says she wants “to prevent the same thing from happening to other people”.You can be sympathetic to the people whose lives have been ruined by press intrusion and criminal activity, and also think any creeping state regulation of the pressis a bad and potentially dangerous idea. Contostavlos says the concern comes down to similar things: “It’s the worry that certain people have certain powers to do certain things. Right now, mine is there are certain members that are high up in the press that have control, and your argument is: what if someone within the government has control? It’s all about it being truly independent, picking the right regulation to oversee it.”Another criticism of Hacked Off, and by extension Contostavlos’s campaign, is that the target – newspapers – seems so out of date. However uncontrolled the tabloids were in the era of phone hacking, surely their current influence pales in comparison with social media, where people are subject to gross invasions of privacy and vitriol? “I agree that socials should be addressed. I feel like that is a whole separate campaign,” she says. But that’s not a reason not to also tackle the tabloids, she says. “I don’t really see social media breaking big news. I see the press break the news, and then social media runs with it. The source remains the same. So what do you do? Nothing at all, or start where you can?”As a child, fame and money were always her target – money meant freedom from her childhood poverty, and fame meant love. Contostavlos grew up in Camden, north London, an only child, although she was close to her cousin Dappy, with whom she would go on to form N-Dubz, with his schoolfriend Fazer. Her parents had been musicians, but separated. Contostavlos lived with her mother, who had schizoaffective disorder, which meant caring for her during low episodes. “It’s very much shaped my personality, and it affects every area of my life – my day to day, my work, my friendships, my love life. Sometimes it can seem like I’m quite detached because I’m so independent.” She knew she wanted to be rich, “so I could get out. I used to fantasise about having my own home where I didn’t have to deal with all the shit.” If you go to her house now, she says with a laugh, everything is pristine and in its place. “That brings me peace as an adult.”View image in fullscreen‘Before it was just a name. Now it’s real life’ … Contostavlos, with the words ‘female boss’ tattooed on her arm.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe adoration that fame brought fulfilled another need, she says. “We all walk around day to day, searching for validation in everything that we do, and I’m really trying to work on needing zero validation, knowing that all the love and light that I need is right here, inside of me. Now I’m aware of it more than ever; I have such a disinterest in fame.” She smiles. “Don’t get me wrong. I’ll do things if I get a massive cheque for it and if I don’t feel like I’m selling my soul for something.” Contostavlos is starting a property company, and ploughing money into that. It will, she hopes, “give me more freedom to never have to work in entertainment if I don’t want to”.For a while, fame and money did make her happy. Then, in 2012, an ex-boyfriend sold a video of Contostavlos in an intimate act. “It destroyed such a huge part of my mental health, and it still affects me, and my love life, to this day.” It’s hard to remember now, post-#MeToo and sex positivity, but at the time, instead of seeing her as a victim, Contostavlos was shamed. “Back then: slag. It was, like, whore, low-class chav, all of that.”Then, in 2013, the sting happened. Contostavlos thinks about £300,000 was spent on making her believe Mahmood was a film producer, including flying her first-class to Las Vegas and booking meetings in five-star hotels. To Contostavlos, acting represented escape. She was disillusioned with the X Factor. “I was getting really bad depression,” she says. In acting, she thought, “You can pretend to be someone else every day.”She describes the role she was being seen for as an “urban British lead”, and says she was encouraged by one of Mahmood’s assistants to play up her Camden bad girl image. They asked her to source drugs for them, even though she says she wasn’t into drugs and had no idea how to do it. During the trial, Contostavlos was in “fighting mode, I had purpose”. It was afterwards, her career in shreds, that she struggled. She had made a suicide attempt just before she was charged, and made another after the trial. “I started to realise my life was never going to be the same, and I felt like I couldn’t change it either.”Getting N-Dubz back together in 2022 helped, not least financially. She had been kept afloat from royalties, including from a song she had co-written which was released by Britney Spears, but there were still months, she says, “when I had to sell my Rolex to pay my rent”. In Contostavlos’s reframing, it has all been a valuable learning experience. “Going through the years of shit put me through financial difficulties that made me start valuing my money, valuing the way that I spend it … Now I have the business mind.” She used to call herself the Female Boss – she had it tattooed on her arm, and it was the title of her 2012 solo album. “Before it was just a name. Now it’s real life.”Contostavlos has taken control in other ways. She has frozen her eggs and isn’t ruling out using a surrogate if she ever decides she would like to have a child. With the time pressure off, “I do not revolve my life around finding a man whatsoever.”She has been through such a lot since childhood. Why has it taken her this long to start counselling? “I’ve always been someone that has been like, what the fuck can some Oxford University bookworm tell me about life when I’ve lived it?” But she says it came down to being her “greatest self”. That person is “not too big for her boots when it comes to taking outside advice”.View image in fullscreenTulisa at Manchester Pride in August 2025.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockDoes she feel grief, or bitterness, for the career and life she might have had? “Not in the slightest,” she says. “If I’d have carried on as I was, I would have been way less self-aware. I wouldn’t be who I am right now – and I love who I am.” Contostavlos talks a lot about alignment and the “inner work” she’s done on herself. It sounds woo-woo, but it clearly works for her. “That emptiness, that depression I’ve had all my life, that anxiety, it’s taken me to get to 38 to nail it. I’m, like, 80% sweet. Because what more luxury is there in life than having peace of mind and inner happiness, and lack of need for validation? What could be more important than that?”She seems to be getting there, from finding financial stability to doing the things that make her happy and, in the case of her press regulation campaign, what she considers important. “Even if I’m just sparking the fire and starting the conversations, at least it can feel worth it. That’s all it is – positive meaning and purpose.”Tulisa isfilming athree-part documentary series for Paramount+, charting her campaign for stronger press regulationExplore more on these topicsTulisa ContostavlosN-DubzMental healthReality TVNewspapersThe SunNational newspapersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
Content: The closures are the latest in a process of cutbacks overseen by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe closures are the latest in a process of cutbacks overseen by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyUS to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuumState department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and CameroonRobert Taitin WashingtonWed 5 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and theCaribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the departmentfired more than 1,300 employees,including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to theAmerican Foreign Service Association.Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” saidJeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places whereChinais present?”The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism inCanada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years,told the Canadian broadcaster CBCthe closure could harm US interests.“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island ofGrenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyChinaCameroonIndonesiaJapanGrenadaCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year  | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity
Content: A maize crop affected by lack of rain in Zimbabwe. ‘The biggest food security impact, in southern Africa, will be during the 2027 to 2028 lean season,’ one expert said.Photograph: Aaron Ufumeli/EPAView image in fullscreenA maize crop affected by lack of rain in Zimbabwe. ‘The biggest food security impact, in southern Africa, will be during the 2027 to 2028 lean season,’ one expert said.Photograph: Aaron Ufumeli/EPAEl Niño southern oscillationEl Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next yearUN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurityFiona HarveyEnvironment editorWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by therapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting.This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts ofAfricaand pressure on food prices from the war in Iran.Even ifthe forecast El Niñois less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries currently in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Wednesday.Central and South America, theCaribbeanand southern Africa are likely to be worst affected, according to the analysis. In south and south-east Asia there is likely to be less rainfall than usual, which would cause serious problems for agriculture and farmers.India’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’Read moreThis year’s El Niño –a weather system that develops every few years in the Pacific Oceanand brings changes to rainfall patterns around the world – is shaping up to be the strongest in at least 70 years. Some are calling it a “super El Niño”, though this term is not officially recognised.GraphicWhat is certain is thatits impacts and strength are being strongly affected by the climate crisis. Earlier this year, experts said a strong El Niño could work in tandem with global heating todeliver the hottest year on recordeither this year or, more likely, in 2027.Private sector forecasters havealready warned of the impact of the gathering El Niño on global food prices, but the report published by the WFP is the first to look closely at global hunger. The WFP said it was hoping to reduce the effects of the extreme weather through early warning systems and “anticipatory” relief efforts, for which at least $80m (£60m) is budgeted.Theconsequences will still be far-reaching, as farmers may take more than one season to exhaust their food supplies. In southern Africa, for instance, the main growing season stretches from October this year to March 2027, but it will be about nine months later, during the lean season following the harvest, that the worst impacts will bite.“The biggest food security impact, in southern Africa, will be during the 2027 to 2028 lean season,” said Richard Choularton, the WFP’s director of the climate and resilience service.Farmers should be somewhat cushioned by the lingering benefits of last year’s harvest, which was an unusually good one. “At the end of 2025, food prices were in favourable ranges, though there has been upward pressure from the war in the Middle East,” said Jean-Martin Bauer, the WFP’s director of food security.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDuring the 2015-16 El Niño, about 60 million to 100 million people were affected by acute food insecurity, theterm WFP uses to denote hunger that falls below the level of famine. In those years, the WFP was not yet rolling out its updated anticipatory actions, so its experts hope this year’s extreme weather will have a lower impact even if the El Niño is more severe.However, Choularton said efforts had been hampered by a lack of data, as some collection efforts had been cut for lack of funding.The WFP’s data covers the 45 countries it works in where baseline estimates for food insecurity are available. There could be additional impacts outside these hard-hit areas.Food prices could come under pressure across the world, as well as in the 45 countries examined, said Bauer. “This will also depend on the choices that exporting countries make. It’s very important to avoid a situation where large countries stop food exports,” he said. “At the regional level, there could certainly be high prices and [problems with] food access.”In the UK and Europe, farmers have beenwarning of the impact of extreme heatand lack of rainfall on their harvests, with retailersbraced for higher prices.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationHungerFood securityUnited NationsAmericasCaribbeanAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Wednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpoint  | Morocco | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the ground
Author: Hettie O'Brien
Headline: In today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the ground
