Content: The pictures were more dramatic than the reality on the ground.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPAView image in fullscreenThe pictures were more dramatic than the reality on the ground.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPAFirst Edition newsletterMoroccoWednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpointIn today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the groundHettie O'BrienWed 5 Aug 2026 01.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 01.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. Last week, an estimated 72,000 migrants began crossing into a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Morocco. Within 24 hours, most of them hadheaded home. At least 88 people died after attempting the crossing, according to local officials. This isn’t the whole story of what happened over the last week, but the facts are worth remembering.At an emergency meeting yesterday, EU interior ministers sought to draw a line under Ceuta, insisting that the passport-free Schengen area had never been at risk from the arrival of migrants at this scale. Despite this, much of the media coverage has suggested that events in Ceuta represent a territorial threat toEurope, sparking calls for greater security across the region’s borders.It’s a pattern that has become familiar since the 2015 refugee crisis. As Europe has created fewer opportunities for migrants to legally cross its borders, people have tried to cross them illegally, resulting in dangerous bottlenecks, human tragedies, and a slew of spectacular images that the right has seized upon to justify draconian policies.For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke toDaniel Trilling, a journalist who writes about refugees and migration, about the political actors trying to capitalise on Ceuta, and why tragedies like this are bound to keep happening. That’s after the headlines.Five big storiesEnvironment| Eight of the biggest oil companiesamassed profits of morethan $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.UK politics| Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said,promising a root-and-branch reformof standards after several damning maternity scandals.Middle East| Jordan is convening an emergency meeting over an “imminent”threat of an Israeli takeoverof the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”.Ukraine| Russian strikes in and around Kyivkilled at least 14 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Some reports put the death toll at 15.Ceuta| Hundreds of peoplehave gatheredin the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.In depth: ‘The claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue’View image in fullscreenMigrants who crossed into Spain via Ceuta are escorted by the Spanish army back to Morocco.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APOn Thursday, a group of people roughly the size of Guildford’s population began crossing into Ceuta. Many of them swam around the border fence. Some drowned; others were crushed. Dozens died. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you,”one toldthe Guardian.Most of these people were young men searching for work and hoping to build a better life for themselves. There are no reports suggesting any of them reached mainland Europe. “It’s very difficult for people without the right documents to travel from Ceuta to mainland Europe, andSpainhas lots of experience returning people who cross without permission,” Trilling says. “So the claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue.”Although Spain was reportingon Fridaythat most of these migrants had returned to Morocco, videos of men clambering on rocks and walking through Ceuta’s streets had already gone viral on social media, where they were amplified by right-wing voices. “Ceuta has been turned into a third world city in only 48 hours,” Tommy Robinson posted on X. Elon Musk, no stranger to sticking his oar into the politics of foreign nations, posted: “all military age males means it is an invasion”.“By the time the images started circulating, the so-called crisis was over. But the political damage was already done,” Trilling says.Why did so many people make the crossing?A social media hoax, which hinged ona Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, seems to have played a pivotal role in encouraging the crossings. Instagram posts suggested Spain’s border with Morocco was opening up, TikTok videos showed people where to swim, and Facebook users began tracking coast guard patrols. It’s unclear who was behind these accounts, as several of them weredeletedsoon after the crossings. At a crisis meeting on Saturday, EU member states speculated that the events may have been coordinated.As the hoax spread, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum, allowing thousands of people to cross into Ceuta. Some analysts have suggested that Rabat, Morocco’s administrative capital, deliberately opened the border to protest Pedro Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria (Morocco has a territorial dispute with the country). Others have pointed to Rabat’s increasingly toasty relationship with the Trump administration, which has clashed with Sánchez during the Iran war.Hasn’t this happened before?“The central problem is that European border policies have given countries like Morocco a means of exerting pressure on European states,” Trilling says. The EU has increasingly outsourced (“externalised,” in the policy lingo) border policing to non-EU countries, which have the power to loosen their borders whenever they choose. We’ve seen versions of Ceuta happen before: in 2021, Morocco allowed10,000 peopleto cross into the territory during a diplomatic row with Spain. Turkey tried something similar onGreece in 2020, and Poland has long accused Belarus (a close ally of Russia) of encouraging migrants to cross into the Schengen area.The EU has taken an increasingly hardline stance on migration since 2015. This has paradoxically helped to create some of the problems that politicians say they’re trying to solve. The fortification of security means that people are forced into taking illegal and unsafe routes where there might have been safe, legal routes previously. When border security is breached, it results in a sudden influx of people, and the kind of alarming images that we’ve seen this week, which are then used to justify even further restrictions. “The performance of control very often leads to precisely the sense in which things are out of control,” says Trilling.How is the right capitalising on this?Following the events in Ceuta, Nigel Farage wasted no time in resurrecting his pernicious “Breaking Point” poster from 2016, and he and Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson, have described those who made the crossing as “fighting-age males.”The term is one of the right’s favourite new ways to frame peoplecrossing borders, depicting them as threats, while giving little thought to those who lose their lives or don’t fit the brief. By Monday afternoon, Farage had alighted on a new policy that would use the Royal Navy to “stop the boats once and for all”. We published auseful explaineron why this would probably violate international law.It would be possible to dismiss this announcement as a last-ditch attempt to change the subject, considering the£5m giftthat Farage currently seems to want to avert eyes from(and his impending byelection bin fight). But that would be missing the bigger picture. Ceuta has given the right a powerful new argument for why hardline immigration policies are common sense, and, by contrast, why a more pragmatic and humane approach to migration is foolish, harmful or, as one Spectator piece put it recently, the result of “luxury” beliefs.This sort of language encourages centre-left parties to accept the right’s logic. Take, for example, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who was among22 signatories to a letteron Saturday that suggested Spain’s liberal migration policies compromise Europe’s security. These policies have no application in Ceuta, but Merz will soon be trying to fight off the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in state elections.What happens next?In a speech delivered from the White Cliffs of Dover on Monday, Andy Burnham pledged to be “relentless” in curbing small boats while building a system that offers “safe routes”. It marked a change from Starmer, whose attempts to appease would-be Reform voters culminated in his infamous “Island of strangers” speech. Still, it’s too early to say how Burnham will approach migration, and whether he will reopenroutesthat his predecessor closed.“Time and again, the right has tried to claim that you can basically shut yourself off from the rest of the world and make these things go away,” Trilling says. “But they don’t go away. And Ceuta is a perfect example of that.”What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenHouse leaders Blanco and Samantha Escandón present laurel crowns to their campers during the opening ceremony.Photograph: Salgu Wissmath/The GuardianI was really moved bythese imagesfrom a summer camp forLGBTQ+kids in Texas, a state where trans people have been regularly targeted and demonised.MichaelWhat do Feast, Viennetta, Magnum, Calippo, Twister and Cornetto have in common? They wereall inventedin the 15-year golden age ofBritish ice-cream.HettieAs a fair weather cyclist, I’ve had a smug summer, avoiding sardines-in-a-sauna style public transport on my bike. Reading aboutcommuterson theheaving 17:46 from Eustonhas only confirmed this.Michael“In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence”, the authorEmily Kenwaywrites in this thoughtful opinion piece about the family members who sustain ourcare system.HettieI for one have (obviously)alwaysbeen a fan of the Turritopsis dohrnii, but at last the immortal jellyfish is gettingproper recognitionin this year’s Guardianinvertebrate of the yearcompetition.Michaelskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser shows her time trial pedigree on stage four.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesCycling| The world time-trial champion, Marlen Reusser,took the overall leadin the Tour de France Femmes after winning the fourth stage from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon.Football| Gianni Infantino’s authority was dealt a further blow after his No 2, the Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafström, called the failed World Cup private investment plan a“sad and reproachable series of events”.Football| The Manchester United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will“stick together”and be ready for the new Women’s Super League season, despite their head coach Marc Skinner departing.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian“Oil giants make $90bn from price surge as climate crisis engulfs Europe”, is theGuardian’s front page.TheTelegraphsays “Setting free Pc Harper’s killers is ‘not justice’”, theMailwrites “9,300 domestic abusers set to be released”,Metrohas “Jailed just last year … but my son’s killer already set freedom”, and theSun’s take is “See you in court, PM”.TheFTsplashes “Google assembles $200bn Wall Street machine to supply chips for Anthropic”, thei Paperhas “Private firms may face ban on profiteering to make care homes cheaper” and theExpresswrites “How many more lives will you risk by doing nothing?” TheTimes, on fiscal rules, says “Borrowing splurge in bid to boost economy”.The LatestPhotograph: The GuardianIs Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president?Gianni Infantino’s reign as Fifa president is in severe peril after the collapse of his plans to sell off parts of the World Cup to private investment. Many Concacaf countries are considering following Europe’s lead by formally removing their support for Infantino, and there are widespread calls to remove him from his post.Lucy Houghspeaks to columnistJonathan Liew.Watch it on YouTube.Cartoon of the day | Ella BaronView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ella Baron/The GuardianThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenA biama dancer performing in Abidjan.Photograph: Miléquêm DiarassoubaOnce the soundtrack to postwar optimism and excess, Côte d’Ivoire’s dance music scene is evolving, thanks to TikTok and street dance battles.Seven years after the death of its biggest star, DJ Arafat, a new generation of artists and dancers are reinventing the coupé-décalé genre, with the new high-energy biama movement winning over young fans and social media users alike.Eromo Egbejule visitsa 400-strong neighbourhood dance arena in Abidjan, where a local rapper calls the craze “a dance for the immature”.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsMoroccoFirst Edition newsletterSpainMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones | Morocco | The Guardian
description: People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100
Content: Spain estimates 70,000 people who made the crossing have been returned, leaving about 2,000 still in Ceuta.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpain estimates 70,000 people who made the crossing have been returned, leaving about 2,000 still in Ceuta.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesMoroccoHundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved onesPeople hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100Soraya Aybar Laafou in Fnideq andAshifa Kassamin MadridWed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged ofabout 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.On Tuesday, as interior ministers from across the EUjoined an emergency videoconferenceto grapple with the lingering tensions, the focus on the Moroccan side of the border with Ceuta was on the harrowing death toll.At least 88 people have died in Ceuta, according to local officials, and another 11 inMorocco, while dozens of others remain missing.“I have just one son,” said Hadijja, who had been waiting at the border since Saturday, scanning the steady stream of returnees for any sign of her 23-year-old son. “I haven’t had any news of him; he’s not answering his mobile phone.”She had travelled to the border from her home in Tangier, surmising that her unemployed son was among those who had made the crossing. “He didn’t tell me he was going to cross,” she said. “This is a tragedy.”View image in fullscreenPeople in Fnideq wait at the Ceuta border hoping to see their missing friends or relatives.Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty ImagesAn estimated 70,000 people who arrived late last week in Ceuta had been returned to Morocco in recent days, Spain’s interior minister said Tuesday.Referencing posts on TikTok, Facebook and WhatsApp that had claimed Morocco wasletting peoplecross the border, people arrived at Fnideq by foot or packed into buses and cars as they joined the surge of people crossing into Spain.Madrid sprang into action, working with Rabat to return the vast majority of those who crossed within 48 hours, even as it fended offa political crisissparked by calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left | Jonathan LiewRead moreAs they returned to Moroccan soil, some said they had come home voluntarily. “I was hungry for days and filled with fear,” said Abselam, 19, from Kenitra in north-western Morocco.A Ceuta resident had eventually taken him in, giving him food and a place to sleep, before he decided to return home. “It’s not worth it, there aren’t jobs for everyone.”Others said they had been forced out of the Spanish territory. “The police surrounded a group of us and escorted us all the way towards the border,” said Simo, 21, from Tetuan. “We didn’t really have a choice.”In recent days, NGOs across Spain havevoiced concernsthat some of those who crossed into Ceuta and who were eligible for international protection were being returned before being allowed to exercise their right to request asylum.On Tuesday the Spanish government estimated that 2,000 people who had made the crossing were still in Ceuta. The tally includes at least 862 children who have been registered as unaccompanied minors, as Unicef Spain warned that dozens more could still be wandering the city’s streets unprotected.“Many small children crossed over; we don’t know how many have disappeared,” Susana Hidalgo, a migration expert for the organisation, told the broadcaster TVE. The result was a “tremendously difficult” situation in Ceuta.“There are many families on the other side of the border looking for their sons and daughters,” she said, while in Ceuta “there are 10- and 12-year-old children asking for phones so they can call their mothers and tell them they’re OK.”Spanish police said on Tuesday they had set up an office in Ceuta to gather reports of missing people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe concerns over the fate of unaccompanied children in Ceuta were heightened on Tuesday afterSpanish media published a videothat appeared to show a boy age 12 crying as he begged a soldier not to send him back to Morocco. After several bystanders intervened, pointing out that Spanish law impeded children from being deported alone, the operation – which played out just metres from the border – was halted.Days after the sudden influx, questions continue to linger as to what led to the mass crossing. Morocco hasfaced mounting accusationsover the role it may have played. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of Ceuta, said earlier this week.The insinuation was rejected by a senior Moroccan official. “It’s simplistic to say that Morocco should just have used force to stop them. That is to completely misunderstand this phenomenon,” the official told AFP.“At a certain point, the Moroccan law enforcement forces could no longer confront the migrants because the numbers were very large” and because “the pull effect was very strong,” he added. “Could Spain, seeing them coming, have done something to stop them simply using weapons and security forces? That’s not possible.”In a statement published on Sunday, Morocco’s interior ministry laid blame with the “exploitation of the digital sphere” and “the spread of misinformation” to explain the mass crossing.Spanish intelligence sources have suggested the influx could be traced to a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported.The Moroccan official said Rabat had sought to warn Madrid about the repercussions of the ruling. “We started engaging with the Spanish side around 22-23 July, when the networks began talking about this,” the official told AFP. “We explained that this ruling was going to create a problem. And it did create a problem.”The claim was rejected by Spain’s migration minister, Elma Saiz. “At no point was there any evidence, any report that alerted us to the magnitude of this unprecedented event,” she told reporters in Madrid.The uncertainty hovering over what exactly transpired extended to Fnideq, where the relatives gathered at the border spoke in hushed tones of what could have happened to their loved ones.Many held on to hope, citing the trickle of good-news stories that had emerged in recent days, such as that of Fatima, who had spent the day waiting at the border with her family for a glimpse of her brother, who had crossed into Ceuta days earlier.“My brother’s phone had run out of battery, but yesterday he borrowed the phone of a Spaniard to call me,” she said. “He told me he would come back this morning, so here we are waiting. I’m sure he’ll arrive soon.”Explore more on these topicsMoroccoSpainMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Toronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother Kindia | Toronto | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
Content: The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother.Photograph: Toronto ZooView image in fullscreenThe zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother.Photograph: Toronto ZooTorontoToronto zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother KindiaThe 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo saidMaya YangWed 5 Aug 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTorontoZoo has announced the birth of a female pygmy hippo calf.Kindia, the zoo’s 20-year-old pygmy hippo, started showing signs of labor at around 8.15am last Sunday, it said. Around four hours later, the calf’s feet emerged and after 1.5 hours of active labor, Kindia successfully gave birth to the baby pygmy hippo.Within 15 minutes of birth, the calf began trying to stand and was “confidently navigating the space” a few hours later, the zoo said, adding that the calf was seen nursing approximately 4.5 hours after birth.The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother. According to the zoo, the newborn is Kindia’s third calf. Kindia became pregnant after she was introduced to a 31-year-old male pygmy hippo named Harvey for eight days in January.Gene-edited beagles may offer a future option for people with dog allergiesRead more“This wonderful news comes with both hope and caution,” the zoosaid. “Kindia successfully raised her daughter Penelope in 2018, and calf survival for this species can be challenging. Our team will continue to closely monitor both mom and calf around the clock during these important first days to ensure they continue to progress well together.”Noting the species’ endangered status on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list, Dolf DeJong, the Toronto Zoo’s CEO, said: “Welcoming a pygmy hippo calf is far more than a celebration of new life. Pygmy hippos are endangered, and their wild populations continue to decline due to habitat loss and human pressures.“This birth represents the critical role modern accredited zoos play in conservation, scientific collaboration, and maintaining healthy populations that contribute to the long-term survival of the species.”Only approximately 2,000 to 3,000 pygmy hippos are believed to remain in the wild.With adult pygmy hippos weighing anywhere from 330lb to 660lb and standing around 2.5 tall, the species are native to the forests and swamps of west Africa. In recent decades however, pygmy hippos have facedgrowing threatsto their habitat including logging, mining, farming activities as well as human settlement.Explore more on these topicsTorontoAnimalsCanadaWildlifeAmericasZoosnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media | Mexico | The Guardian
description: César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver
Content: César Gastélum had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos.Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/ReutersView image in fullscreenCésar Gastélum had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos.Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/ReutersMexicoMexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social mediaCésar Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driverOscar Lopezin Mexico CityWed 5 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread.César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers.A motorcycle with a driver and pillion rider suddenly pulled up beside them and the driver pulled out a gun and shot Gastélum at point-blank range.A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum’sdeath to Reutersand said a major security operation was under way.The killing is the latest example of bloodshed in Culiacán, which has become an epicentre of violence as factions of the Sinaloa cartel battle for control of the city.View image in fullscreenOnlookers stand behind a police cordon at the scene of César Gastélum’s killingPhotograph: Jesús Bustamante/ReutersMexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible.Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum,said on Wednesdaythat authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer.In a war in Mexico between cartel factions, influencers become targetsRead more“The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference.At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024,according to local media.They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23,was shot and killedat a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers.Authorities announcedlast week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing.They also accused him of ordering and financing the November 2025assassination of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan, the second largest city in Michoacán state, in a killing that shocked the country.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Peruvian cardinal hails $150m lead poisoning settlement for 1,300 people as a ‘historic milestone’  | Mining | The Guardian
description: Cardinal Pedro Barreto received death threats and harassment during his almost 20-year campaign against a US mining company’s operations in the Andes
Author: Dan Collyns
Headline: Cardinal Pedro Barreto received death threats and harassment during his almost 20-year campaign against a US mining company’s operations in the Andes
Content: A child plays at a playground next to the smelting complex of La Oroya in the Peruvian Andes, 2016.Photograph: Mariana Bazo/ReutersView image in fullscreenA child plays at a playground next to the smelting complex of La Oroya in the Peruvian Andes, 2016.Photograph: Mariana Bazo/ReutersSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanMiningPeruvian cardinal hails $150m lead poisoning settlement for 1,300 people as a ‘historic milestone’Cardinal Pedro Barreto received death threats and harassment during his almost 20-year campaign against a US mining company’s operations in the AndesSupported byAbout this contentDan Collynsin LimaWed 5 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Peruvian cardinal who received a barrage of death threats when he challenged the firm behind a toxic smelter has called a $150m (£111m) out-of-court settlement to more than 1,000 people who were allegedly poisoned by the plant as children “a historic milestone”.Cardinal Pedro Barreto, 82, was in Rome meetingPope Leo XIVand other cardinals in June when he received news that the firm that ran the smelter, the Doe Run Company, a subsidiary of Renco Group,would pay $150m to 1,373 Peruvianswho have suffered health impacts since childhood.View image in fullscreenCardinal Pedro Barreto led a campaign for justice for the Andean town of La Oroya.Photograph: Andrew Medichini/APThe news came as Barreto – the former archbishop of Huancayo, a city in the Peruvian Andes – was preparing to travel to the US to testify in the first of four civil trials in St Louis, Missouri, as part of a 19-year legal battle against Doe Run, which is owned by US billionaire Ira Rennert, who also serves as chair of the Renco Group.“This is a historic milestone,” said Barreto, speaking to the Guardian. “But this long-awaited justice doesn’t solve the problem faced by many children who were personally affected, especially neurologically. The money will not compensate for the harm they have suffered, but it is a sign that justice has been served.”Barreto led a nearly two-decade campaign to hold the US company to account for the severe health impacts on the population of the Andean town of La Oroya, which the Blacksmith Institute,a US-based environmental NGO now known as Pure Earth, in 2007listed asone of the world’s 10 most polluted places.The settlement brought to a close one of the longest-running civil lawsuits against a multinational corporation in one country for environmental pollution or toxic exposure that caused injury or damage in another country.Schlichter Bogard, a St Louis-based law firm,alleged that Doe Run failed to reduce lead emissionsat the Peruvian multi-metal smelter, resulting in permanent injuries and harm. Doe Run Resources Corporation, which has its headquarters in St Louis, did not admit wrongdoing in agreeing to the settlement.What began in 2007 in state court on behalf of 17 Peruvian children grew into a federal court case withmore than 1,373 plaintiffs, now young adults. Each could receive at least $100,000 from the payout.Jerry Schlichter, the founder and co-managing partner of the law firm, described the payout as a “historic tipping point in that the American companies in this case have been held responsible for their actions in another country to foreign citizens who are not US residents”.View image in fullscreenAn aerial image of the Doe Run complex and the town of La Oroya in 2022.Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesSchlichter said his team of lawyers and religious leaders such as Barreto won the settlement because of their “passion and conviction that this was a just cause, this was a righteous battle”, and that the individuals deserved their compensation for the exposure to lead emissions.“This will be a life-changing event for every one of these 1,373 children,” Schlichter said. “It will enable them to have a new path in their life, whatever that might be.”During his time as archbishop of Huancayo, Barreto had contacted the Saint Louis University College for Public Health and Social Justice, which sent researchers to assess theaffected children in La Oroya in 2005and found they hadamong some of the highest blood lead levels ever recorded. The university also found that lead, arsenic, cadmium and sulphur dioxide emissions had increased since Doe Run took over the smelting complex in 1997.Nearly 100% of children under the age of six in La Oroyahad blood-lead levels above 10 μg/dL(10 micrograms of lead in every tenth of a litre of blood), well in excess of levels that can cause growth impairment and lower IQs in children, according to a 2004 study by Peru’s environmental health office.Barreto faced death threats and harassment, often from employees at the smelter who feared losing their livelihoods, after he began his activism in 2004, soon after taking on the archdiocese of Huancayo that includes La Oroya.“It was an irrefutable fact that I was threatened in various ways,” said Barreto, one of three Peruvian cardinals. He said it was often done publicly and through messages that indicated that “if I kept speaking out, they were going to take much more drastic measures”.But he stressed that it was the local population who deserved recognition.“We have had to endure just a little of the immense suffering they constantly face,” he said.“Before settlement, it was the longest-running case in the federal court system,” said Schlichter, who said it had been a David v Goliath fight against Rennert. “Tens of thousands of attorney hours were spent on the case and we had five national law firms who were opposing us,” he said.View image in fullscreenMothers wait with their children for a medical examination at La Oroya’s health clinic, 2013.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThe Department of Justice joined the defendants in asking that the lawsuit be transferred to Peru, but Schlichter resolutely opposed. “If the case had gone to Peru, the children would have got nothing,” he said. Winning the settlement was “very gratifying after such a long and risky fight”, he added.The New York-based Renco Group and its founder, Rennert, 92, made a fortune in the 1980s junk-bond market before developing an empire of mining companies, smelting plants and industrial firms. According to Forbes in 2024,his worth is estimated at $3.8bn(£2.8bn).In a statement, Doe Run’s chief executive, Matt Wohl, said: “We elected to put this behind us and focus on what matters – running our business, serving our customers and investing in new technologies.”Explore more on these topicsMiningSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanPeruAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mexico’s top university orders 58,000 students to resit entrance exam after suspected cheating | Mexico | The Guardian
description: National Autonomous University of Mexico says applicants must take test in person after online debacle
Author: Oscar Lopez
Headline: National Autonomous University of Mexico says applicants must take test in person after online debacle
Content: Applicants protest outside the National Autonomous University of Mexico against the institution’s decision to force a resit.Photograph: Mario Guzman/EPAView image in fullscreenApplicants protest outside the National Autonomous University of Mexico against the institution’s decision to force a resit.Photograph: Mario Guzman/EPAMexicoMexico’s top university orders 58,000 students to resit entrance exam after suspected cheatingNational Autonomous University of Mexico says applicants must take test in person after online debacleOscar Lopezin Mexico CityWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMexico’s largest and most prestigious university has announced that about 58,000 students will have to resit their entrance exam after abnormally high test results raised suspicions of widespread cheating.The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam) said the exam would take place in person after its first attempt at a fully remote online version led to a debacle and thousands of annulled results.“The Unam, the home of science, humanities and understanding, knows how to recognie mistakes and self-correct,” the university’s rector, Leonardo Lomelí, said on Monday. “There is no evasion or complacency. There is responsibility and we act accordingly.”Nearly 160,000 students took the entrance exam earlier this summer. The at-home test included an AI-powered webcam to monitor candidates with voice and facial recognition to ensure no cheating took place. But the results indicated that the checks had failed to stop fraud.Between 2021 and 2025 only 3.5% of applicants obtained a score of 100 or more out of 120, but this year the figure was 16%. The proportion of students who achieved a score of 110 or more increased sixfold from 0.9% to 5.5%.Almost 30% of candidates for the medicine programme, among the most competitive undergraduate tracks in the region, obtained a score of 100 or more, compared with 9% last year.View image in fullscreenUnam’s central library in Mexico City.Photograph: David R Frazier Photolibrary, Inc./AlamyThe results sparked a national scandal, leading the country’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, to suggest the country’s attorney general may have to investigate. “Support is always available, but in any case if a crime has been committed it is a matter for the prosecutor’s office,” she said.Hundreds of Unam applicants protested in Mexico City on Monday against having to take the control exam, blocking major thoroughfares in the south of the capital.Lomelí said: “I offer an apology to the candidates who, having been fairly accepted, will be called upon to take the control exam. However, it is necessary to ensure certainty and guarantee equity in access.”Calls grow ‘to flunk’ Portugal’s education minister amid exam marking fiascoRead moreThe drive for more equitable access led the university to offer the exam online for the first time this year. Students previously had to travel to Mexico City from their home states, sometimes many hundreds of miles away.The entrance exam is notoriously competitive. The more than 150,000 applicants this year were competing for 21,962 places.Just before the results were to be publicly released, theuniversity announcedit had annulled the results of 2% of tests – 3,174 exams – after detecting irregularities such as identity impersonation, external assistance and the use of AI.A technical expert who reviewed the resultstold the New York Times(NYT) that nearly half of the exams – 75,000 tests – could have involved some degree of cheating. AI may have played a role, but test questions were also leaked and even sold online while the exam was open in May and June.Cheating tips were also widely passed around before the test went live, according to the NYT.The Unam announced in July that it hadfiled a criminal complaintafter detecting the alleged irregularities. It said authorities would investigate potential misconduct involving individuals or companies that allegedly offered fraudulent services to applicants and their families.The cheating scandal compelled the institution to halt all admissions and appoint a technical committee to decide the fate of the 158,712 young people who took the exam, anunprecedented measurein the university’s 115-year modern history.Lomelí also announced that the academic year for new students would begin on 31 August, rather than 10 August as originally scheduled.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
Author: David Smith
Headline: Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
Content: Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti has not been expelled but if she were to leave the US she would have to reapply for a visa, according to the state department.Photograph: Wolfgang Kumm/DPA/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti has not been expelled but if she were to leave the US she would have to reapply for a visa, according to the state department.Photograph: Wolfgang Kumm/DPA/AFP/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyUS revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feudMove is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in BrasíliaDavid SmithWashington bureau chiefTue 4 Aug 2026 21.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 21.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s administration hasrevoked the visaof Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.The US state department saidMaria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassadorDaniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.Lula says Brazil will not be treated like ‘tinpot country’ after US designates gangs as terroristsRead more“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said.The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.”The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term againstSenator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump.Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.”Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before thefirst round of the election, on 4 October.The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country.“President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.”The latest confrontation followsBrazil’s refusal last monthto issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides.The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression.Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time.Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”.The row is particularly sensitive becauseJair Bolsonaroand his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series ofclashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region.Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met.Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration hasimposed tariffsof up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family.The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government.Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyUS politicsBrazilDonald TrumpAmericasLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvanewsShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand capital delights in rare snowfall as southern city residents ski down world’s steepest street | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Snow falls in Wellington for the first time in 15 years while snow blanketed Dunedin and Christchurch on the country’s south island
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Snow falls in Wellington for the first time in 15 years while snow blanketed Dunedin and Christchurch on the country’s south island
Content: Snow in the New Zealand city of Dunedin.Photograph: Mark StevensonView image in fullscreenSnow in the New Zealand city of Dunedin.Photograph: Mark StevensonNew ZealandNew Zealand capital delights in rare snowfall as southern city residents ski down world’s steepest streetSnow falls in Wellington for the first time in 15 years while snow blanketed Dunedin and Christchurch on the country’s south islandEva Corlettin WellingtonTue 4 Aug 2026 23.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemperatures have plummeted acrossNew Zealandas an Antarctic cold snap hovers over the country, delighting the capital, Wellington, which experienced snow for the first time in 15 years, while giving a southern city’s residents a chance to ski through the streets.The front moved in on Tuesday, with much of the country waking to freezing conditions, frosts, snowfall, hail and bitingly cold wind.Conditions persisted on Wednesday morning, with three South Island locations reaching -9C. Some highways were closed, while parts of the North Island’s east coast woke to thick hail storms.Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three yearsRead moreInWellington, a mix of sleet and snow fell to sea level just after midday on Tuesday, for the first time in 15 years. Office workers rushed out of their buildings to stand in the flurries and elated residents expressed shock and joy as they flooded social media with footage.It was a “winter wonderland”, wrote one social media user.“Snow in Wellington?! Amazing! What a way to turn a day around,” wrote another.“Finding the excitement around this so wholesome. I went to my office window and every window in the building opposite was filled with people watching too,” someone wrote on Reddit.Students inDunedin, the South Island’s second largest city, were sent home on Tuesday, after snow blanketed the city and many took the opportunity to make the most of the weather.Video footage in local media outlets showed residents snowboarding down the city’s streets, with one daring skier flying down Baldwin Street – recognised by the Guinness World Records as theworld’s steepest street.Skier flies down world’s steepest street after snowfall in New Zealand – video“The thing I love about Dunedin is you get half an inch of snow maybe twice a year and everyone loses their minds,” wrote one social media user.Further north, Christchurch’s New Brighton Beach was covered in a dusting of snow and a plane had to abort its landing into the Christchurch International Airport due to wind and rain.View image in fullscreenSnow on Dunedin streets on Tuesday.Photograph: Mark StevensonPolice responded to multiple incidents of cars sliding off icy roads, and urged the public to avoid travel.Temperatures were set to warm on Wednesday but would plunge again overnight, with Thursday likely to be the coldest morning of the year in parts of the country, Metservice, New Zealand’s weather bureau, said.Meanwhile, Transpower, the national grid operator, said it recorded the highest-ever electricity use during Wednesday morning’s peak and warned there may be an energy shortfall on Friday morning.Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandSnowAsia PacificWellingtonDunedinnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our new champion’: Philippines swept up in tennis fever after Alex Eala’s historic win  | Philippines | The Guardian
description: WTA event win earns 21-year-old a presidential reception in the Philippines as interest in tennis surges in home country
Author: Natasha May
Headline: WTA event win earns 21-year-old a presidential reception in the Philippines as interest in tennis surges in home country
Content: Alexandra Eala of the Philippines after beating Jessica Pegula at the Washington DC Open tennis tournament.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAView image in fullscreenAlexandra Eala of the Philippines after beating Jessica Pegula at the Washington DC Open tennis tournament.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAPhilippines‘Our new champion’: Philippines swept up in tennis fever after Alex Eala’s historic winWTA event win earns 21-year-old a presidential reception in the Philippines as interest in tennis surges in home countryNatasha Mayin BangkokTue 4 Aug 2026 22.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThePhilippineshas been swept up in tennis fever after 21-year-old rising star Alex Eala delivered a historic win, drawing praise from the president who hosted a reception in her honour.On Monday, Eala became thefirst player from the Philippinesto win a Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Tour-level singles title.Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos released a message on social media on Tuesday congratulating Eala on “yet another historic achievement”, adding: “You continue to redefine what is possible for Philippine tennis and inspire countless young Filipinos to dream without limits.”Eala not only beat the top-ranked player, Jessica Pegula, to win the title in Washington DC, but also did so coming back from behind in a match spread over two days due to rain delays.Pegula said after the match: “This is the best Monday final crowd I’ve seen ... To all the Filipino fans that came out, and have supported, you guys are helping to grow tennis around the world, and I appreciate that. Being a female athlete, being in tennis, we love to see that growth.”Signs in the stadium during the match expressed what Eala means to the country, including one reading: “Alex you make us proud to be Filipino”.View image in fullscreenAlexandra Eala poses with her trophy after beating Jessica Pegula.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAFilipinos had already been celebrating Eala’s historic run at Wimbledon in July, going farther than any Filipino woman at a grand slam championship andupsetting the defending champion, Iga Swiatek, in straight sets on Centre Court.Eala came home to a hero’s welcome, with Marcos hosting a reception in her honour at Malacanang Palace in Manila, and a nation that had previously paid little attention to the sport now obsessed with it.Soy sauce refills and reused jars: can Philippines’ tingi culture hold back deluge of plastic waste?Read moreShe has inspired droves of Filipinos to take up tennis, which has seen classes, camps and courts fully booked, leading clubs to upgrade old courts, and increased support for the tennis federation.Speaking about this rise in popularity at a press conference, Eala said: “Everyone comes up to me whenever I go back to Manila saying it’s so hard to get courts … that’s a good thing because when I was younger the courts were empty, nobody was playing.”The Philippines’ sporting interests have historically been all about the“three Bs”: basketball, billiards and boxing. But now fans and supporters of Eala have been packing local venues and public spaces with watch parties, often staying up to cheer through the night on the other side of the world.The Philippines has not had a prominent sporting superstar to throw its support behind since boxing champion Manny Pacquiao, who applauded Eala as “our new champion” on social media, lauding her Washington comeback for showing the “Filipino heart” .Washington’s tournament director Mark Ein said interest in Eala had been unmatched. He told a media conference, “over the last month the ticketing team says at least 80%, if not more, of the requests in this tournament are about when is Alex Eala playing?”View image in fullscreenAlexandra Eala thanks her fans after losing the Women’s Singles fourth round match against Jasmine Paolini at the Wimbledon Championships in July.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPATennis is a sport often dominated by players whose home countries – the United States, Great Britain, and France – can afford the tens of millions of dollars annually it takes to develop young talent. The Philippines does not have that infrastructure, and tennis remained a sport for the elite, with courts mostly found in wealthy areas.Eala comes from a prominent family, but shelearned to play tennis on painted-over basketball courtsin Quezon City before moving to Spain to attend the Rafa Nadal Academy on a scholarship at the age of 13.Eala is inspiring young Filipinos from more modest backgrounds to find the means to play but has spoken about the need to improve access to public courts and equipment, as well as the condition of those that are available.It was only during her Wimbledon she truly appreciated the impact she is having on millions of Filipinos, she told the palace reception according to the state news agency.“I’m so grateful that I am able to share my triumphs … with the country,” Eala said. “As we say, tagumpay nating lahat (this is our victory).”This article was amended on 5 August 2026 to correct a misspelling of Jessica Pegula’s surname.Explore more on these topicsPhilippinesTennisAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: News Corp subscriptions fall in Australia as company takes aim at ‘slimy’ AI slop | News Corporation | The Guardian
description: Chief executive Robert Thomson says ‘crass kleptomaniac’ AI companies are ‘in possession of stolen goods’
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: Chief executive Robert Thomson says ‘crass kleptomaniac’ AI companies are ‘in possession of stolen goods’
Content: Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, has reported robust international results but attacked AI companies for ‘pilfering’ their work.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRobert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, has reported robust international results but attacked AI companies for ‘pilfering’ their work.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesNews CorporationNews Corp subscriptions fall in Australia as company takes aim at ‘slimy’ AI slopChief executive Robert Thomson says ‘crass kleptomaniac’ AI companies are ‘in possession of stolen goods’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorWed 5 Aug 2026 19.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNews Corp has reported a slight slide in digital subscriptions at its Australian mastheads, erasing recent gains, among otherwise robust financials at the Rupert Murdoch-backed global conglomerate.Digital subscribers at News Corp Australia – a division that includes the Australian, the Daily Telegraph and the Herald Sun, among others – fell from 1,166,000 to 1,162,000 during the financial year, according to the company’s internal data published in its full year results on Thursday morning.The figures represent a reversal in momentum. The Australian division has grown digital subscriptions in recent years, as it transitions away from its traditional newspaper base.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNews Corp’s broader news media unit, which includes the Sun and the Times in London and the New York Post, recorded mixed results, with advertising revenue still under pressure, falling 2% during the year to 30 June.The news media division also recorded costs linked to the launch of News Corp’s latest newspaper, the California Post, which is the Los Angeles outpost of the New York Post andedited by Australian News Corp veteranNick Papps.The News Corp chief executive, Robert Thomson, used the release of the company’s financial results to hit out at AI models that “pilfer and profit from our work”, as media companies around the world seek compensation for the use of their content.“Without our journalists, our authors, our data, our brands and our professional expertise, users would be drowning in a slimy sea of AI slop,” Thomson said.“We will pursue those pilferers and companies that are clients of these crass kleptomaniacs should know they are patently in possession of stolen goods.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNews Corp has commercial agreements in place with OpenAI and Meta.The comments come amidcontested plans by the Albanese governmentto expand its news bargaining incentive, which would require tech giants to compensate media outlets for the news on their platforms, either through making commercial deals or paying a higher levy.Explore more on these topicsNews CorporationMedia businessAustralian medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Labor MP Ed Husic taken to hospital with fractures and concussion after car crash | Labor party | The Guardian
description: Husic to take ‘short’ period of leave after collision on Sydney motorway on Tuesday
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Husic to take ‘short’ period of leave after collision on Sydney motorway on Tuesday
Content: Labor member for Chifley, Ed Husic, was taken to hospital with significant injuries after his car was hit by a truck on a Sydney motorwayView image in fullscreenLabor member for Chifley, Ed Husic, was taken to hospital with significant injuries after his car was hit by a truck on a Sydney motorwayLabor partyLabor MP Ed Husic taken to hospital with fractures and concussion after car crashHusic to take ‘short’ period of leave after collision on Sydney motorway on TuesdayFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorWed 5 Aug 2026 18.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabor MP Ed Husic was hospitalised this week after his car was involved in an accident with a truck and another car travelling on Sydney’s M7 motorway.The incident happened at Dean Park, as the Chifley MP was travelling home from his electorate office, around 6.20pm on Tuesday, according to a spokesperson.Husic was treated by paramedics at the scene and taken to Westmead Hospital for assessment and treatment. He was in a stable condition.Husic was discharged on Wednesday with minor abrasions, fractures and a concussion.A spokesperson for the MP said he was providing a statement to police about the incident.“On medical advice, Mr Husic will take a short period of leave from parliamentary duties while he recovers.“Mr Husic thanked the doctors, nurses and paramedics at Westmead Hospital for providing him with outstanding care and thanked his friends and family for their support, especially during his hospital stay.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailPhotos of the Tesla sedan show serious damage to the back driver’s side, with windows and windscreens smashed and airbags deployed.A NSW Police spokesman said the crash at Dean Park involved a Kenworth B Double truck and a Mazda ute. All three vehicles were towed from the scene of the crash, at Richmond Road.A 70-year-old man in the ute and the 43-year-old truck driver were not injured.“Officers from Riverstone Police Area Command have commenced an investigation into the circumstances of the incident,” the spokesman said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnyone with information or dashcam and mobile phone footage should contact Riverstone Police Station or Crime Stoppers.View image in fullscreenThe car Labor MP Ed Husic was driving in during Tuesday’s accident in SydneyHusic, the former industry minister, is expected to return to parliamentary duties soon. Parliament resumes in Canberra on Tuesday after the July winter break.“Mr Husic was extremely grateful to walk away from the accident without more serious injury,” his spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsLabor partyAustralian politicsSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 1,500 properties bought using first home buyers’ 5% deposit scheme converted into investments | Housing | The Guardian
description: New data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: New data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000
Content: Australia’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers ‘shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors’, the Greens say.Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralia’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers ‘shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors’, the Greens say.Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAPHousingNearly 1,500 properties bought using first home buyers’ 5% deposit scheme converted into investmentsNew data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniWed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 17.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of nearly 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, new data shows.The scheme is also helping hundreds of Australians earning more than $300,000 a year, after Labor stopped excluding high-income borrowers.First-time buyers can borrow 95% of a property’s value and have the government guarantee the loan, waiving costly lenders’ mortgage insurance, under the scheme.Housing Australia, which runs the program, provided the data in response to a Senate estimates question on notice in June.House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to biteRead moreFrom its launch in 2020 until May 2026, the scheme released 1,485 homes because they were converted into investment properties, the agency said.The conversions were a small proportion of the 208,000 total guarantees issued over that time.Barbara Pocock, the Greens’ housing spokesperson, said the scheme was supposed to help first home buyers on lower incomes to get a roof over their heads.“It shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors,” Pocock said.Guardian Australia asked the housing minister, Clare O’Neil, whether investment purchases were undermining the scheme’s intention.A spokesperson said: “When a participant transitions out of the scheme, and the government is no longer guaranteeing their mortgage, the owner is entitled to decide what they do with their home.”If buyers stop living in the property, they are no longer covered by the guarantee and must negotiate with their bank but are not forced to sell or refinance.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBob Tasevski, a Mortgage Choice broker, said buyers would typically try to avoid being forced off the guarantee as their bank would probably charge them the unpaid lender’s mortgage insurance.“Banks generally wouldn’t waive that unless there’s a special reason for it,” Tasevksi said.NAB’s executive for home ownership, Lin Lu, said the bank asked customers to advise if their circumstances changed.“When this occurs, we’ll work with them to understand their individual situation and discuss the options available to them,” Lu said.The government did not directly answer when asked if it could rule out the prospect of more 5% scheme buyers fraudulently renting out their purchases without notifying lenders or the government.A spokesperson said Housing Australia monitored rental listings, property datasets, participants’ transaction activity and changes to addresses to ensure properties remained owner-occupied.Booming popularityThe Albanese government amended the scheme so it no longer excluded high-income earners in October 2025. Since then, it had enabled more than 5,600 home purchases each month on average, compared with just over 3,400 the year before.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMore than 5,000 homes a month bought with 5% deposit scheme graphPrices of homes eligible for the scheme have sincerisen faster – and fallen more slowly– than the rest of the market.Guardian Australiain July revealedone in three new participants was earning above the scheme’s previous annual income caps of $125,000 for singles and $200,000 for couples.The new data shows the scheme had been used by 155 singles earning more than $300,000 and 92 couples earning over $400,000. The highest-earning recipient was a couple on more than $674,000.The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, dismissed criticism of high earners’ access on the ABC on Monday.“There are some markets around the country, where people, even on relatively good incomes, have found it difficult to get a toehold in the market,” Chalmers said.Australia has had housing crises before: what can we learn from them? | Anne O’BrienRead moreParticipants in the scheme are in strong financial positions, with 89% ahead on their repayments, according to Housing Australia’s data. They were less likely to fall behind on loans than the average homebuyer.Since the scheme began, 1,392 guarantees of the 207,000 had fallen more than 90 days behind on their loan and 436 of those were still in arrears by May.Of the 45,300 homes bought under the scheme from its expansion up to May, just two households were in arrears, a separate answer revealed.The government has only had to foot the bill on 13 defaults over the lifetime of the scheme, at a total cost of $604,537. Most of those claims emerged in the past 12 months.While rising interest rates and falling house prices have added to the risk of defaults, fewer than 1% of all home borrowersacross the countryare in negative equity.Do you know more? title: Drone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior minister | Germany | The Guardian
description: Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
Content: A forensic technician works alongside a bomb disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APView image in fullscreenA forensic technician works alongside a bomb disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APGermanyDrone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior ministerInvestigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander DobrindtThe Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeDeborah Colein Berlin andAndrew Rothin WashingtonWed 5 Aug 2026 16.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s interior minister has warned that the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport marks “a new level of danger” for the country, as authorities examine whether the thwarted attack could have been planned by a foreign power.The discovery of a small drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a leading shipping and military hub, set off alarm and caused flight diversions on Wednesday morning. German police deployed a bomb disposal robot to defuse and destroy the explosive device.In public remarks on Wednesday evening, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs, and that investigators were treating it as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario”.“We are dealing here with a competition that may also include foreign powers – this will be part of the investigations – who quite obviously want to contribute to considerable uncertainty in Germany,” Dobrindt said.A DHL cargo plane that had been forced to abort its landing at the airport then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere.Dobrindt and other German officials did not explicitly mention Russia as a potential suspect in their remarks. But the airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which has previously been accused of carrying out sabotage attacks in Europe.Security experts said the incident could amount to a serious escalation in tensions withRussiaif it was determined the Kremlin played a role.Investigators said “a drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway” of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as “critical infrastructure”.“A suspected second unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft after it had taken off again following the previous closure of the runway. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover,” the investigators said.View image in fullscreenFootage by News5 shows the nose of an Ukrainian Antonov plane at Leipzig-Halle airport.Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty ImagesA Nato official said: “We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate.”The drone, a quadcopter that was fitted with an explosive device, was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, according to media reports.Some of the Ukrainian aircraft are emblazoned with patriotic slogans including “Be Brave Like Kherson” and “Be Brave Like Bucha”, the site of a civilian massacre early in the full-scale Russian invasion.The tabloid Bild speculated that the explosive could have been fabricated ⁠from fertiliser and petrol, while a team from the public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche newspaper, said the device had contained pentaerythritol tetranitrate, orPETN– a primary ingredient in semtex that belongs to the same chemical family as nitroglycerin.Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, blamed Moscow. “Who else could it be but Russia?” he told the commercial broadcaster Welt TV. Moscow has not commented so far.Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called for an investigation to be conducted with the utmost urgency and also hinted at possible Russian involvement.“Should it transpire that a state is behind this action, this would constitute not merely terrorism but state terrorism directed against the federal republic of Germany and its citizens,” he told Der Spiegel.Marc Henrichmann, the CDU chair of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said the latest incident looked like “an attempt to target a company of importance for Ukraine”.If the details are confirmed, it “would represent a new level of escalation in these sorts of attacks”, he told the Rheinische Post newspaper.Several aircraft, including a passenger plane from Mallorca, were diverted because of the incident. Operations in the northern part of the airport resumed two hours later.The southern runway, where the drone was found, remained closed. Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to examine the object.View image in fullscreenGerman media reported that investigators were examining several possibilities, including that the incident was an attempt by Russia to attack Ukrainian equipment in Germany.Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice and prosecutors said: “There is no danger to the lives or safety of passengers or airport staff. Passenger air traffic is unaffected.”Germany and other European countries have had a series of suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies. They have accused Russian agents of being behind some of the flights, which Moscow has denied.Germany is the biggest single national supplier of military aid to Ukraine and has accused Russia of orchestrating a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against it, which the Kremlin has denied.Last year, a Chinese national was convicted forpassing on information about flight schedulesand cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing.Separately, Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring. Thumann is said to be under police protection.In 2024, US intelligence services reportedlyfoiled a Russian plotto assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, an apparent attempt at retaliation over the company’s role in providing a large amount of armaments for Ukraine.The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.Additional reporting by Jakub KrupaExplore more on these topicsGermanyDrones (military)Air transportRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe | Germany | The Guardian
description: Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia
Content: The bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersGermanyAnalysisThe Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeDan SabbaghDefence and security editorInitial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from RussiaWed 5 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 22.18 EDTShareThe armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact thatit got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation.Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found inEuropefar from the Ukrainian border.Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from theUkrainewar, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery.Police from the German state of Saxony confirmed that the drone was “carrying an unknown explosive device” discovered by an employee in the “secure cargo flight operations area” near the airport’s southern runway.German media reported the attached bomb was made ofPETNand semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty.A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”.Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in Czechoslovakia, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around.A second unidentified flying object, which could well have been another drone, also collided with a DHL cargo plane in the aftermath of the first incident several hundred metres above the ground. The cargo plane only sustained minor damage.Leipzig airport is a sensitive site, the European base of Ukrainian Antonov jets, used for heavy cargo.
