The airport is also used by Nato and the German military for transport, as well as being a DHL hub, and the Ukrainian planes suggest it may also have been a node for supplies to Kyiv.Nato would only say it was aware of the incident on Wednesday, though it is eye-catching that the western alliance appears to have not been able to prevent drones from flying into and over a strategic airport.It is not the first time Leipzig airport has been involved in a dangerous incident. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the airport in July 2024 while a second travelled to the UK andcaught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham. Two similar packages were also found in Poland.A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who are suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. The investigation found perpetrators were recruited and given instructions online, and frequently paid in cryptocurrency, their knowledge of the full plot apparently limited.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRussia has also been behind a string of drone incursions into Europe over the past year, some more blatant than others. Around 20 unarmed Russian delta-wing Gerbera dronescrossed into Poland last September, forcing a major alert, with people in two of the country’s eastern provinces told to shelter indoors.An analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) thinktank concluded last month that the Kremlin was behind aconcerted drone surveillance campaignthat targeted the US airbase at RAF Lakenheath and other key military sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands.In the first case, Nato jets struggled to shoot down the incoming drones, most of which eventually crashed or lost power and glided to the ground. In the second, western militaries struggled to work out who were the culprits, failing to capture any of the drones or react to the surveillance efforts promptly.Russia, in sum, has so far been able to conduct other firebomb operations, as well as drone harassment and surveillance campaigns with relative impunity. Moscow is already subject to a wide range of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine, and it is likely to believe that the west has little more it is willing to punish the country with.“A drone carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition to what we have seen before,” said Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow with the IISS, adding ominously: “It is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyUkraineRussiaEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy calls for more air defences as Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17 | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukraine shoots down most drones but no ballistic missiles in overnight attack that mainly targeted civilian facilities
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Ukraine shoots down most drones but no ballistic missiles in overnight attack that mainly targeted civilian facilities
Content: The attack set off fires in warehouses and storage areas.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/APView image in fullscreenThe attack set off fires in warehouses and storage areas.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/APUkraineZelenskyy calls for more air defences as Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17Ukraine shoots down most drones but no ballistic missiles in overnight attack that mainly targeted civilian facilitiesOliver HolmesWed 5 Aug 2026 12.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 01.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has blamed allies for not delivering air defences fast enough after Ukraine failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in a deadly overnight attack that killed at least 17 people and ⁠injured dozens more.Preliminary data from the Ukrainian air force showed its defences shot down 98 of the 115 drones fired byRussiaovernight, but no ballistic missiles.“Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today,” the Ukrainian president said on social media. “It is very important that our partners understand that delays in supplying them, or an unwillingness to provide anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction.”There is a global shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles after demand soared with theUkraineand Iran wars. Supplies of air defence missiles for Ukraine in the first half of this year fell to a third of their 2025 level, Zelenskyy said.Kyiv has been pleading for months for more Patriot interceptors while under intensifying attack. Last month Donald Trump suggested the US might grant Ukraine alicence to manufacture Patriots, but later he appeared to backtrack, telling reporters the underlying technology was“a hard thing to give away”.9:02Russia exploits Ukraine’s air defence shortage in deadly attack on Kyiv - The LatestUkraine’s military administration said seven sites were hit in Wednesday’s assault that began after midnight. Zelenskyy said the main targets were civilian facilities, including a brewing company, construction materials warehouses and a railway station.Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Partners who are not yet ready to play a more active role in supplying interceptors can help by implementing new sanctions. A significant share of Russia’s ballistic missile production is still not under sanctions. Even now.“New steps are needed – from the G7, the European Union, and everyone who supports the protection of life. Thank you to those who are willing to help in this way.”Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said on social media on Wednesday that Moscow had committed more atrocities in its “illegal war”. “Once again we wake up to the news of horrible atrocities by Russia through its aerial attacks on Ukraine. Russia must pay for the destruction it has caused,” she said.France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, accused Russia of choosing to target civilians. “This policy of terror, carried out with missiles and drones, is unacceptable,” he said. “Each new attack reinforces an obvious truth: Russia must pay the price for its aggression and answer for its crimes.”He added that the EU would implement new sanctions while “strengthening military support for Ukraine so that it can defend itself and protect its population”.Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said there may still be people under the rubble left by the attack on the city.Rescuers pulled two people from the ruins of a warehouse near the city centre. An ambulance driver was among the injured and four people were in a critical condition, Klitschko added.He ‌said the attack set off fires in warehouses and storage areas. A ​large fire broke out on the city’s outskirts and debris from a fallen missile landed beside a residential building.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine war briefing: Russian soldier in Crimea shoots comrades and civiliansRead moreThe Kyiv military administration said the attack caused an ammonia leak that emergency crews were tackling.Witnesses heard explosions throughout the city. One journalist reported dark smoke and the acrid smell of burning lingering in the air hours later.Natalia Reutska, who lives in Kyiv, told Agence France-Presse: “The night was so terrifying, so hard. We’ve gotten used to waking up thinking: ‘We were lucky today’, and that’s very scary.”Russian attacks on Kyiv also struck Epicentr, Ukraine’s largest home improvement and DIY retail chain. Two key logistics facilities and a factory were destroyed within minutes.The Russian defence ministry said it hit logistic hubs and supply centres in Kyiv and surrounding areas, claiming they were for being used for military purposes. Russia’s military has a history of striking civilian targets in Ukraine andcommitting atrocities.Officials in Ukraine were also monitoring Russian advances in the east. On Wednesday, authorities ordered hundreds of families with children to leave the stronghold city of Kramatorsk because of intensifying Russian strikes.“This is a difficult but necessary decision,” said the Donetsk region governor, Vadym Filashkin. “The security situation is deteriorating, so it is unacceptable to leave children under the constant threat of Russian attacks.”Kramatorsk is one of the major cities Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region​, but Moscow’s forces are close by.On Tuesday, Ukraine hit Russian logistics hubs for the online retailer Wildberries, adding to ​more than a dozen ​it had attacked.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaVolodymyr ZelenskyyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Head of drone manufacturer critically injured in car bomb in Russia | Russia | The Guardian
description: Assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory
Content: Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside a restaurant in central Moscow.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APView image in fullscreenRussia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside a restaurant in central Moscow.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APRussiaHead of drone manufacturer critically injured in car bomb in RussiaAssassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territoryPjotr SauerWed 5 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of a leading Russian drone manufacturer has been critically injured in a car bomb near Ekaterinburg, in what appears to be the latest ina series of assassination attemptstargeting figures linked to the country’s war in Ukraine.Vladimir Tkachuk, the founder of the private drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, was rushed to intensive care on Wednesday after a bomb planted beneath his Mercedes exploded, according to Russian state media, citing emergency services. His bodyguard was killed in the explosion.The Russian news agency Tass reported that Tkachuk was in a critical condition and doctors were “fighting [to save] his life”.Images circulating on social media showed the charred wreckage of a Mercedes, with blood stains visible on the pavement nearby.Uraldronzavod is one of several private drone manufacturers that sprang up in Russia after the full-scale invasion ofUkraine. The company is best known for producing the Upyr (Ghoul), a low-cost first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drone manufactured using 3D-printing technology at its facility in Ekaterinburg and widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine.In 2024, Vladimir Putin visited the factory, where he was given a tour by Tkachuk.Uraldronzavod and Tkachuk have been hit with sanctions by western governments for their role in supporting Russia’s war.Tkachuk is also the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Obsessed with War, which has more than 500,000 followers and has been used to raise funds and procure military equipment for Russian soldiers fighting on the frontline.Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after anexplosion outside an upmarket restaurantin central Moscow that killed five people.Russian authorities have not identified the intended target of that attack, but pro-Kremlin bloggers and independent Russian media suggested it was aimed at Col Gen Aleksandr Chayko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly celebrating his birthday at the restaurant.Among those killed was Chayko’s son-in-law Daniil Peredrya, the independent outlet Agentstvo reported on Wednesday, citing government records.Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes.Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics in operations inside Russia, including planting explosive devices beneath vehicles that can be detonated remotely.The latest assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue its clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory, and is likely to intensify scrutiny of Russia’s internal security apparatus and its inability to protect senior officials and pro-war figures.Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran and Oman agree on coordinates of route through strait of Hormuz, says Iranian foreign ministry – as it happened  | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Joint announcement for geographic coordinates being finalised, says spokesperson, adding that it would not guarantee security in waterway
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: Joint announcement for geographic coordinates being finalised, says spokesperson, adding that it would not guarantee security in waterway
Content: 11.18 EDTIran and Oman agreed on coordinates of route through Hormuz, Iran's foreign ministry saysThe ⁠geographic coordinates for a shipping ⁠route ⁠through the ​straitof Hormuz⁠have been agreed byIranand ⁠Oman, and ​a ‌joint announcement ‌is being ‌finalised, provided no third parties interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokespersonEsmaeil Baghaei ‌said on Wednesday.Baghaei added ​that any such agreement betweenIranand ⁠Oman would not, ​by itself, ​guarantee security ​in the ​strategic waterway.Share

title: Understanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran says | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Joint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Joint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: ReutersStrait of HormuzUnderstanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran saysJoint statement with Oman is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s securityAndrew Rothin Washington and agenciesWed 5 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran andOmanhave reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is ​being finalised provided certain third parties do not interfere,Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail ⁠Baghaei said on Wednesday.Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran andOmanwould not, by ⁠itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway.The proposed deal between ​Iran and Oman would ‌give Tehran control ‌over ships entering the gulf through the strait of Hormuz, ‌a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, in one of the biggest concessions yet toIran.The deal appears to be a stepping stone toward a broader ceasefire agreement with the US that would reopen the strait of Hormuz for marine traffic and lift a US blockade on Iranian ports that has brought upheaval to global energy markets. It comes as Donald Trump has claimed there could be an announcement as soon as Wednesday on a separate US-Iran peace deal.But the sources pushed backagainst assertions ‌byTrumpthat a deal reopening the strait was imminent, saying important details ​still had to be agreed.If endorsed by the US, the Iran-Oman deal would mark a significant concession by handing partial control over the waterway to Tehran. The strait of Hormuz was a neutral waterway before the US and Israel launched joint strikes in February, prompting Iran to attack shipping in the region.Baghaei described the negotiations between Tehran and Muscat as “professional” and “moving forward”, saying “the two sides had reached a mutual understanding ⁠on the geographical parameters of the route under discussion”.Baghaei ​added ​that, if some third ​parties do not obstruct the process, the joint ​statement between ‌the two ​countries, containing the ​main considerations and key points of understanding, was in the final stages of review and drafting.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzIranOmanMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel strikes southern Lebanon killing one and injuring 11  | Israel | The Guardian
description: Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefire
Author: William Christou
Headline: Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefire
Content: A Lebanese boy removes his damaged bicycle from his destroyed home in south Lebanon on Wednesday after an Israeli airstrike.Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/APView image in fullscreenA Lebanese boy removes his damaged bicycle from his destroyed home in south Lebanon on Wednesday after an Israeli airstrike.Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/APIsraelIsrael strikes southern Lebanon killing one and injuring 11Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefireWilliam Christouin BeirutWed 5 Aug 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Israeli airstrike in southLebanonkilled one person and injured 11, the Lebanese ministry of health said, in one of Israel’s deadliest bombings since the start of the June ceasefire.Israel carried out an airstrike in the town of Tebnine, south Lebanon hitting a cemetery, the Lebanese health ministry said. It said the town of al-Mansouri, also in south Lebanon, was bombed too, forcing families to flee.The Israeli military issued a displacement order about 30 minutes before the strike, saying it was destroying Hezbollah’s infrastructure in the area in response to the group’s “violation of the ceasefire”.Two Israeli troops were killed and seven wounded in an explosion in south Lebanon on Wednesday, with the origin unknown. In recent weeks, Israeli troops have been wounded by booby-trapped vehicles and mines laid by Hezbollah in south Lebanon.View image in fullscreenIsraeli tanks in south Lebanon on Wednesday.Photograph: EPAWednesday was the first time Israel has issued a displacement order since the start of the June ceasefire. Such orders were a near daily occurrence during the most recent round of Hezbollah-Israel fighting, which started on 2 March and displaced more than 1 million people in Lebanon.Since the June ceasefire, Israel has occupied swathes of Lebanon as part of a so-called security zone. It has continued bombing parts of the area and killing people who have come near.It is a similar approach to in Gaza, where Israel occupies more than 60% of the strip under what it calls its “yellow line”, and continues to carry out bombings there. Earlier this year, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he had ordered the army to seizecontrol of 70% of the Gaza strip.Gaza 'yellow zone'More than 1,200 people have been killed in Gaza since the beginning of the October ceasefire. At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes in the strip over the past weekend.In Lebanon, Israel has continued mass demolitions in areas it occupies, including a blast last week that used 700 tons of explosives around Beaufort Castle, outside Nabatieh. Israel has said it is targeting Hezbollah infrastructure, but rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, say the indiscriminate nature of the explosives could comprise the war crime of wanton destruction.Talks between the Lebanese government and Israel for a more permanent peace are continuing, with the two sides meeting in Rome on Tuesday. The Lebanese government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal, while Israel wants the disarmament of Hezbollah.View image in fullscreenA woman and child stand next to Lebanese military vehicles in Zawtar al Gharbiya, southern Lebanon, one of the pilot zones.Photograph: EPAThe meetings in Rome are the seventh between the two sides, with talks expected to focus on the Ali Taher area in south Lebanon, where Israeli troops have been conducting detonations.So far, negotiations have resulted three “pilot zones” in south Lebanon where the Lebanese army has assumed control. The two sides are using these as tests of whether the Lebanese army can prevent Hezbollah from entering and can continue to dismantle the group’s infrastructure there.Progress in the pilot zones is slow and the Lebanese government has asked for a quicker Israeli withdrawal, which Israel is unlikely to agree to.The fighting this year started after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. Israel then began a bombing campaign and invaded south Lebanon. Israel has since killed 4,321 people in Lebanon, while at least 40 Israelis, 38 of them troops, were killed by Hezbollah.Explore more on these topicsIsraelLebanonHezbollahMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat | Sheikh Hasina | The Guardian
description: Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
Author: Penelope MacRae
Headline: Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
Content: Opponents burn an effigy of Sheikh Hasina in Dhaka during her address to journalists in Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpponents burn an effigy of Sheikh Hasina in Dhaka during her address to journalists in Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersSheikh HasinaExiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threatSheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by studentsPenelope MacRaein DelhiWed 5 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBangladesh’s ousted prime ministerSheikh Hasinahas vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence.“They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government.Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence.“Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link.View image in fullscreenSheikh Hasina, the then newly elected prime minister, speaking at a press conference in Dhaka in January 2024.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersHer son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile.“She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.”The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from IndiaRead moreIndia officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed.India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition.Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia,swept to powerearlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh.View image in fullscreenSajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Sheikh Hasina, addressing the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia on Wednesday via video link.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersLast November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunalsentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanityover the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government.The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans.Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman.View image in fullscreenSheikh Hasina, right, and her former political foe, Khaleda Zia, at a wedding reception in Bangladesh in 1997.Photograph: ReutersBangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped.Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character.The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power.Explore more on these topicsSheikh HasinaBangladeshIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistani authorities ban international media from reporting in most of country | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Rules brought in soon after killing of dozens of protesters, news of which was reported only by overseas outlets
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Rules brought in soon after killing of dozens of protesters, news of which was reported only by overseas outlets
Content: Even before the current crackdown on protests, Pakistan was already ranked low on the World Press Freedom Index.Photograph: Sohail Shahzad/EPAView image in fullscreenEven before the current crackdown on protests, Pakistan was already ranked low on the World Press Freedom Index.Photograph: Sohail Shahzad/EPAPakistanPakistani authorities ban international media from reporting in most of countryRules brought in soon after killing of dozens of protesters, news of which was reported only by overseas outletsShah Meer Balochin IslamabadWed 5 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePakistani authorities have imposed severe new restrictions on international media, including barring them from reporting in most of the country, in a move that has provoked a significant backlash from journalist organisations.According to the new rules anyone, including Pakistani nationals, should seek permission first if they want to report from anywhere Pakistan except three cities – Islamabad, Karachi and Lahore.Pakistan is ranked 153 out of 180 on the World Press Freedom Index. Successive regimes there haveimposed restrictions and censorshipon local media. But this is the first time they have put restrictions on international media.The sudden announcement of new rules came afterthe killing of dozens of protesters in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which was only reported by international media.Al Jazeera’s website was restricted in Pakistan after it reported on the bloody protests and the news that people were boycotting regional elections from Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistan’s Kashmir.Pakistan’s information ministry derided Al Jazeera’s reporting as “yellow journalism”, a derogatory term used for sensationalised reporting.Authorities have not publicly announced a ban of the news website, but it remains inaccessible without a VPN.The BBC reported from Pakistan-administered Kashmir and quoted protesters and people who accused Pakistani security forces of firing at unarmed protesters. Pakistani authorities issued a strongly worded denial and asked all journalists to immediately leave Kashmir.UK journalists ‘self-censoring stories about Trump and the right over safety fears’Read moreThe new rules, which the ministry of information called the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026, do not specify a timeframe for how long it would take for journalists to be granted permission to report.Nasir Zaidi, a former general secretary at the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists and a senior journalist, said that international media has been objectively reporting on protest movements, crackdowns on opposition parties and the repressive political situation in Pakistan.“For decades, various governments have always tried to kill the news and they failed because of the reporting of international media and now it came up with these repressive rules to curb the movement of journalists. They don’t want the truth to be reported,” said Zaidi.The government denies that the new rules are a blanket restriction on the movement of journalists or constrict media.Zaidi, who was subjected to public flogging during the military dictatorship of Gen Zia ul-Haq for raising his voice for media rights, said that he had never witnessed such times before.“Despite the fact I have worked during martial laws, but, such curbs and restrictions on international media were unseen. It is worse than martial law,” he added.According to the new guidelines, the accreditation and registration is mandatory for international media outlets and journalists in the country.The new rules also state that journalists can lose their accreditation for “acts against ideology, sovereignty, security or public order of Pakistan”.Legal experts and journalists have said that these stipulations are vague and difficult to interpret.“Pakistan is sending a very wrong message to the world with all these rules curbing free speech and freedom of international media,” said Zaidi.Explore more on these topicsPakistanPress freedomCensorshipSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police station | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station
Author: Haroon Janjua
Headline: Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station
Content: A street in Lahore, where the incident occured.Photograph: Rahat Dar/EPAView image in fullscreenA street in Lahore, where the incident occured.Photograph: Rahat Dar/EPARights and freedomPakistanPakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police stationLahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at stationSupported byAbout this contentHaroon Janjuain IslamabadWed 5 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in a police station in Lahore,Pakistan, has prompted authorities to suspend all 78 police officers and staff at the precinct, in one of the country’s biggest ever disciplinary actions against its police force.The woman alleges that an assistant sub-inspector apprehended her, took her to Ghaziabad police station and raped her in a room on the second floor. The woman’s family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating that she had been sexually assaulted at the station.The accused officer has been arrested and is now facing a criminal investigation for rape. All 78 police officials and staff members of Lahore’s Ghaziabad police station were suspended on Tuesday.Lahore’s deputy inspector general of police (operations), Faisal Kamran, told the Guardian that the officers were suspended because, under police rules, all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing within the station and they had failed to do so.“No officer questioned why the assistant sub-inspector had brought the woman to the station without any female police personnel present,” Kamran said.“I suspended all 78 police officials, and the gender crime wing is investigating the case, and we will dismiss the culprits, and we will ensure the safety of all police stations in the city,” he added.The case has sparked outrage in Pakistan, where rights groups have long claimed many women are reluctant to report sexual violence because of stigma and a lack of confidence in law enforcement. Allegations of misconduct by police officers have further eroded public trust, activists say.“This is an extremely disturbing incident and reflects the longstanding lack of accountability within the police,” said Farzana Bari, a women’s rights activist. “It is a stark example of the abuse of power. Allegations of police misconduct and custodial rape are not new, and we have seen such cases over the years.“We campaigned relentlessly in the 1990s for women’s police stations because survivors often did not feel safe reporting abuse to male officers. While the police’s record on protecting women remains poor, the fact that this case has been reported offers some hope that justice will be served.”Convictions for rape remain rare despite legal reforms in recent years.The Sustainable Social Development Organisation saidthe national conviction rate was about 0.5% in 2024, whileofficial datashowed the rate in Punjab, where the incident occurred, was 4% in 2025.Rights groups attribute the low rates to weak investigations, poor evidence collection, delays in prosecutions and the stigma surrounding sexual violence.According to police data, there were more than 20,000 crimes against women in Punjab province in the first half of 2026, up from the same period in 2025.“Unless state institutions are held accountable, such crimes will continue. What is needed is structural reform and stronger oversight to ensure justice for ordinary people,” Bari said.Explore more on these topicsPakistanRights and freedomSouth and central AsiaWomen's rights and gender equalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I just want to find them’: deadly cloudbursts devastate Kashmir’s mountain communities | Kashmir | The Guardian
description: Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock
Content: Rescue teams search for missing people in Murrah village after the cloudburst-triggered landslide. Photograph: Ishtayaq RasoolIncreasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestockByIshtayaq Rasool in Indian-administered KashmirWed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 05.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administeredKashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, acloudburstsent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.Murrah is perched high in thePir Panjalrange above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.View image in fullscreenRescue teams search for missing people in Murrah village after the cloudburst-triggered landslide.Photograph: Ishtayaq RasoolLatief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.View image in fullscreenA photograph on a phone of 16-year-old Sajjad Ahmed, whose body remains missingPhotograph: Ishtayaq RasoolAs mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmirthis month, killingat least 28 people.Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities.View image in fullscreenWomen gather on a rooftop as the funeral procession of the fourth recovered victim arrives in Murrah villagePhotograph: Ishtayaq RasoolThe destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station.Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced.About 180 miles north, inGurez Valleynear the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road.Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads.“People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.”Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across thewestern Himalayas.The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (Icimod) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades.“The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.”ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns.View image in fullscreenLower Murrah village in Poonch district.Photograph: Ishtayaq RasoolDr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration.“For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.”For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.”Explore more on these topicsKashmirIndiaNatural disastersClimate crisisSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarism | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career
Author: Lanre Bakare
Headline: Sociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and career
Content: Jason Arday is the youngest black person to be appointed a professor at the University of Cambridge.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday is the youngest black person to be appointed a professor at the University of Cambridge.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianUniversity of CambridgeCambridge professor Jason Arday resigns amid accusations of plagiarismSociology professor to stand down after university announces investigation into his qualifications and careerPlaybooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: the claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRichard AdamsandLanre BakareWed 5 Aug 2026 16.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Arday, theCambridgeprofessor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, has resigned after the university announced he was to face new investigations into his qualifications and career.Arday, who had been dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials, issueda statementon Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.In the statement, published on the Good Law Project website, he wrote: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at theUniversity of Cambridgeand Jesus College.“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreHowever, after days of detailed scrutiny of his previous work and statements, which highlighted apparent discrepancies, Arday said he had “concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away”.Simon & Schuster had been preparing to publish Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, later this month. His resignation may pause or even halt its publication and planned publicity tours.Cambridge had initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions multiplied over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.The Guardian publishedits own investigationuncovering discrepancies in Arday’s public accounts involving prodigious fundraising feats as well as claims he had been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders.Arday first faced allegations that he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and other academic research late last year, and has rejected the claims. An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded his PhD in 2015, did not uphold the charges of plagiarism but said they were probably caused by “honest and reasonable error”.Arday has denied all accusations of plagarism, telling the Guardian last week: “There have been multiple thorough investigations across several institutions as a result of the allegations, and immense scrutiny, including with an academic misconduct panel who concluded that there was no plagiarism or academic misconduct.”On Wednesday evening, Cambridge announcedit would launch an investigationafter it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.It said in a statement: “The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Prof Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.“Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our misconduct in research policy. This is consistent withour previous statement on the matter.“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.“We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”A spokesperson for Jesus College, Cambridge, said it was launching its own parallel “process”.“Prof Arday’s college fellowship is linked to his university role and we will fully support the university.“Prof Arday remains a fellow during this process. We recognise that this is a very difficult time for him and his family, and ask that they are treated with compassion and respect.”The new investigations may have been triggered by Arday’s claims that he held a string of prestigious visiting fellowships and professorships at other universities, including statements in published biographies dating back to 2018 that he was a visiting fellow or visiting professor at Ohio State University in the US. Ohio State hasdenied that Arday was ever employedin any role.Biographies linked to Arday have also claimed he had visiting professorships at Durham, Glasgow, Coventry and London Metropolitan universities as well as Nelson Mandela University in South Africa.Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology at Cambridge, at the comparatively young age of 37, received wide publicity through Arday’s life story, which includes a diagnosis of autism at the age of three, being unable to speak until he was 11, or read or write until he was 18.Despite those factors, Arday went on to university and swiftly climbed the academic ladder. After receiving his PhD in 2015 he held academic posts at Leeds Beckett, Roehampton and Durham universities, including a brief stint at Warwick University, before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Glasgow University in 2021. By early 2023 he had sought and won appointment to a professorship at Cambridge.Arday also claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days as well as running 600 miles in six days, and raising £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions he revised some of those claims, and instead said he was part of a funding raising group that he cannot name for legal reasons.Arday told the Guardian he had been the target of multiple threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.Jason Arday’s resignation statement in fullDear colleagues,It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming Professor of Sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life. To become the youngest Black professor in the University’s history was something I could scarcely have imagined as a child growing up with a diagnosis of autism, unable to speak until I was eleven years old.The response from so many people across the world was overwhelming. Thousands celebrated not simply my appointment, but what it represented: that talent, perseverance and hope can triumph over even the greatest adversity. It has been the privilege of my life to teach my students, to learn alongside them, and to witness their curiosity, kindness and ambition. They have given me far more than I could ever have given them.Sadly, the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack. While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.I have tried to continue because I believe deeply in the values of higher education, in rigorous scholarship, and in the transformative power of universities. I have tried because of my students, my colleagues and the countless people who have written to tell me that my journey gave them hope.But there comes a point when the personal cost becomes too great.I have a family. I want to be present for them. I want to reclaim some peace, some privacy and some semblance of an ordinary life. I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement.For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away.This decision should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship or in the values that first brought me to Cambridge. Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me. It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.To my students: thank you. Teaching you has been the greatest honour of my academic career. Your brilliance, compassion and determination give me enormous hope for the future.To my colleagues and to the many thousands of people, from every corner of the world, who have supported me, defended me, written to me, and believed in me when it mattered most, I offer my deepest gratitude. Your kindness has carried me through some of the darkest moments of my life.This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.I need time to heal. I need time to simply be myself again.And when that time comes, I will return.I will return stronger, wiser and with the same determination that has always defined my journey. There is still so much work to do, and I look forward to doing it alongside so many of you in the years ahead.For now, however, I ask only for understanding, for compassion, and for the space to begin again.With gratitude,Professor Jason ArdayExplore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgePlagiarismHigher educationAcademicsUniversity careersCambridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper | NHS | The Guardian
description: Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand
Content: Yvette Cooper says climate change requires ‘some immediate acute responses’ by health services in the UK.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYvette Cooper says climate change requires ‘some immediate acute responses’ by health services in the UK.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesNHSNHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette CooperHealth secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demandAdapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?Jessica Elgot,Alexandra ToppingandFiona HarveyWed 5 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNHShas been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.The health secretary,Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.Doctors and other medical professionals have warned of the impact that repeated heatwaves are having on the NHS in England, including advice from the Royal College of GPs to cancel surgeries in extreme weather. Radiotherapy machines and MRI scanners have failed in hot weather, wards have overheated and cooling units serving hospitals have broken down.England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, with an estimated 2,877 people dying in the May and June heatwaves.Summers are likely to become increasingly hot in the future, with temperatures topping 40C likely to become more frequent instead of being outliers as the climate crisis takes further hold.chart showing rising UK summer temperatures 1900s-2020sCooper told the Guardian that rising global temperatures were causing challenges for the NHS that it had not encountered before. “This is a new thing for the NHS to have to deal with. There is a remarkable determination of the NHS to respond, but we need much greater resilience.”She said that in her new role as health secretary she had visited her local A&E in Yorkshire where staff described the overcrowding caused by heatwaves. “It would be normal during the winter weeks and months, but not in the summer, to have the very high attendances that they have had,” she said.She said she had discussed a public health awareness campaign with the chief medical officer, Sir Chris Whitty, warning people to look out for elderly relatives and those with young babies to ensure they were coping in the heat.Climate change meant “some immediate acute responses”, Cooper said, adding: “I’ve been clear we now need to prepare for summer pressures in the way that the NHS for a long time has prepared for winter pressures.“We need a much clearer assessment now of what that means, what the pressures are going to be, what management needs to be in place to cope.”The Climate Change Committee, the government’s statutory advisers on net zero, published alandmark report in Maywarning that the UK’s infrastructure was not built for such a climate, and calling for all hospitals and care homes to have air conditioning within the next decade, with all schools to follow by 2050. The CCC advised the government to plan for at least 2C of global heating by 2050, and potentially further rises.Farmers this summer have also warned about how the extreme temperatures caused by the climate crisis were affecting the UK’s food security and ability to cope with drought.No 10 said that improving the UK’s resilience to extreme heat was high on the agenda of the government – including building more reservoirs – saying the focus on tackling climate change must be on “practical resilience alongside cutting emissions”.Cooper said that she and Whitty agreed there needed to be more public information about who was most at risk from extreme heat, because of the “distressing” number of heat deaths.Days each year when temperatures of 30C or more were recorded in Greater London“There is a need for all of us to look out for our elderly neighbours and family members in the heat of summer, exactly as you would if it was freezing cold weather and you would be checking on elderly family members or relatives. We need to do the same thing now, in the summer, in the heatwaves and also for the very young.”She said that cooling hospitals and other facilities would be a key part of the major investment in NHS infrastructure. “That is a new thing we are now having to address and to plan for. That obviously takes time as well to address that. But it is one of the things that’s being looked at now as part of the capital programme,” she said.The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, told a press conference in London on Wednesday that tackling the climate crisis should be higher on the agenda. “I think we need to sit with that reality: 3,000 people have died because of extreme heat,” he said.“The scenes we have seen play out on our television screens are frankly apocalyptic. And yet the response from our government is to pretend none of this is happening. It’s an astonishing dereliction of duty from those whose first responsibility is to keep us safe.”The Royal College of Physicians’ clinical vice-president, Dr Hilary Williams, has said the NHS currently had very little built-in resilience to cope with extreme heat. “The impact of heatwaves on staff cannot be overstated,” she said. “There is a sense of foreboding when we see the weather forecast, because we know what is to come, and there is very little staff can do.”The government has also been urged by MPs to do more to allow people to cool their own homes. More than 50 MPs have written to the UK’s certification agencies to urge them to speed up a process to get air conditioning on to theboiler upgrade scheme, which offers grants for replacing gas boilers with greener alternatives like heat pumps.Despite the governmentexpanding the scheme to air-coolers last year, accreditation agencies have not yet given a stamp of approval.“If people worried about a future of extreme temperatures know they can get a heat pump which will also act as air conditioning they will be more motivated to make the switch – that’s good news for energy bills and the planet,” said Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for Hitchin, who organised the letter. “The agencies accrediting this scheme just really need to get on with it now.”July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England, with no significant rainfall expected in the area for some time.The summer has already seen two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June, fuelling drought and wildfires. About 23 million people across England and Wales areunder a hosepipe ban.The National Farmers’ Union warned earlier this week that Britain could face shortages of certain foods after punishing drought in parts of England. Farms across the country were affected by floods over the winter, making planting extremely difficult.This year’s El Niño, fuelled by global heating, is also supercharging temperatures:the World Meteorological Organisation confirmedthis week that the weather system developing in the Pacific was likely to be unusually strong.Andy Burnham has been criticised for failing to mention the climate crisis, net zero or the drought and heatwaves in his first weeks in No 10 – though he has promised the government will ramp up efforts to improve the state’s resilience.A spokesperson for the prime minister said: “We recognise that climate change is already affecting communities across the country, through extreme heat, drought and pressure on food production. That’s why we’re focused on practical resilience alongside cutting emissions.”He said the government would put “record investment in water infrastructure, including new reservoirs, while backing farmers to improve water security and strengthen the resilience of British food production.“Planning reforms are also making it easier to deliver on-farm infrastructure, including reservoirs and other productivity improvements.”Explore more on these topicsNHSYvette CooperClimate crisisHealthEnglandHospitalsGPsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather? | Environment | The Guardian
description: As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming
Content: Farmers have warned that Britain could face food shortages as a result of this year’s droughts. Pictured: Waddenhall Farms in Kent.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFarmers have warned that Britain could face food shortages as a result of this year’s droughts. Pictured: Waddenhall Farms in Kent.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesEnvironmentAdapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farmingNHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette CooperFiona HarveyEnvironment editorWed 5 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NHS has been told it must become more resilient to increasingly frequent heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis, as the UK government puts adaptation to extreme heat high on its agenda. But what other public services are already feeling the strain?TransportLondon bus driversplan to go on strikelater this month over their working conditions, as many have been experienced cab temperatures reaching close to 40C in the recent heat. Most London buses are fitted with air-flow cooling systems rather than air conditioning. Sadiq Khan, the mayor, has said drivers should not be working in unsafe hot conditions, but Arriva, the private operator, has said it will take time to update its fleet.Rail services have also been disrupted as theshrinkage of soil due to the dry weather has made embankments unsafein the south of England because sleepers, part of the tracks, can move or drop out of position. Heat can also warp rails, leading operators to impose lower speed limits for safety.On the roads,the RAC has reported that breakdowns have soared by a fifth, often owing to engines overheating, or tyre blowouts on overheated road surfaces.View image in fullscreenA London bus driver takes a break in the shade on a day the weather exceeded 30C.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesFarming and foodThis year’s harvest could be the worst on record, analysis published on Wednesday found, as thethird year running of drought in Englandleft farmers with dry soil and damaged crops. Cereals and oilseed yields could be down as much as 2.5m tonnes across the UK, worth £390m in lost revenue for arable farmers, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank. Livestock farmers are also under pressure: grass growth has halved, forcing some to use feed they had hoped to save for winter.This followedan unusually wet start to the yearbut most farms are not in a position to store water adequately on their farms. The Country Land and Business Association (CLA), representing landowners, is calling for planning reforms to make small reservoirs on farms easier, while some regenerative farming practices can also help to store more water on land.If dry conditions persist into autumn,farmers will have further problems preparing for next year. Tom Lancaster, the food and farming analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, said: “At the start of spring, farmers were hopeful of a better year, but the dry April and July and record-breaking heat have left farmers facing down the barrel of a third awful harvest in a row.“Farming is now the sector most exposed to climate change and the risks and damage that it brings. From the wettest winter on record in 2024, to the hottest summer in 2025 and now unprecedented heat and drought this year, we are in danger of UK farming entering a climate doom loop, as repeated impacts undermine the capacity of farmers to drill next year’s crop.”As farmers have struggled, theprice of fresh food has risen. The wholesale price of tomatoes is up by more than 60%, iceberg lettuce by 90% and potatoes by more than 40%. The outlook abroad is gloomy too, with a super El Niño increasingly possible, so relying on imports to make up the shortfall may bring more problems with it.Working conditionsThe UK does not have a maximum legal temperature for workers, and employees have struggled, particularly those working in poorly repaired public buildings. Court cases have been disrupted, with onejudge in Bristol telling a jury in July they had to listen to a defendant through a virtual linkbecause the dock was unusable in the heat.Some public libraries that are already equipped with air conditioning are operating as “cool spaces” for communities. Maps can be found online showingwhere they are available.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA construction worker in the sun during a heatwave this summer.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/AFP/Getty ImagesPaul Nowak, secretary general of the TUC, told the Guardian: “After a summer of heatwaves, it is clear we need to adapt to the climate crisis.”Employers need to keep staff working indoors and outdoors safe, with regular breaks or flexible working, proper equipment and access to water, he said, but legislation was also needed.“As heatwaves become our new normal, we need to find ways to work and live with hot weather,” he said. “That means new laws on maximum working temperatures, adapting buildings and workplaces to keep them cool, and ambitious climate action to tackle the problem at its root.”SchoolsPupils are off at the moment, escaping the stuffy classrooms thatreduced some to tears in the summer term, but some of the inequalities in the UK’s education system continue: the Guardian revealed thatprivate schools were continuing to water their lawns, despitehosepipe banscovering close to half of England and some of Wales.The heat should be less severe when most return in September, butthe Climate Change Committee has called for all schools to have air conditioning by 2050, and for a rethink of the traditional school year. It suggested that having exams in June may no longer be the most sensible way of arranging the academic timetable, given evidence that heat can affect pupils’ test performance.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentFarmingExtreme heatClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early  | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail
Content: Andrew Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by three men fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAView image in fullscreenAndrew Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by three men fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft.Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PAUK criminal justiceChief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released earlyThames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jailGeraldine McKelvieSenior correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.ThePolice Federationis contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison.In August 2019, Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road inBerkshireby a car as Cole, Bowers and their accomplice Henry Long fled the scene of a quad bike theft.All three were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in prison andcould be released earlyas part of the government’s drive to free up prison places.Long, who was driving the car,was given a 16-year jail sentenceand does not qualify for early release.View image in fullscreenJessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers are each serving a 13-year sentence for manslaughter.Photograph: Thames Valley police/PAOn Wednesday morning, Jason Hogg, who was on duty the night Harper died, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that he would “certainly” consider joining thePoliceFederation in court action if the government refused to reverse its position, pending legal advice.“I was contacted by the Police Federation yesterday who informed me they are seeking legal advice, exploring opportunities for a judicial review against the government,” he told the Guardian on Wednesday afternoon.“So I’m watching with interest and I will be speaking to the Police Federation again.“But my hope is that we will never get there and that there is no need for the Police Federation to go down the line of a judicial review because the government will listen.”‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release schemeRead morePrison capacity in England and Wales is at critical levels. From October, the government plans to release about 5,000 prisoners who have served a third of their sentence.Harper’s widow, Lissie, successfully campaigned for a change in the law after his death.Legislation introduced four years ago – the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 – means those convicted of the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty now face mandatory life sentences. However, the law cannot be applied retrospectively.Hogg said he wrote to the prime minister,Andy Burnham, 12 days ago to express concerns that Cole and Bowers might be included in the scheme, but had not received a reply.He added that he planned to write again to Burnham, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to convey “the impact of the decision on the morale of my officers, but also on the 2,000 people who work in policing across the country”.Hogg would not be drawn on whether all prisoners convicted of manslaughter should be exempt from the scheme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThames Valley police chief constable Jason Hogg was on duty the night Harper died.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersThe government has already said those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming will not be released early, after a campaign by victims.“It isn’t my role to set government policy or set the law,” Hogg said.“But I think if you ask most people in the streets, they would probably say people who take the life of another person in our country should remain behind bars as long as possible, and I don’t think that’s particularly controversial.”However, he added that the fact Harper was an emergency services worker is a “significantly aggravating factor”.Hogg said the criminal justice system also needed “greater investment around rehabilitation”. He said the National Police Chiefs’ Council estimated it would cost about £480m to manage the freed offenders in the community.“I think there needs to be a balance between the risk caused [by] prisons being full, but also the risk of releasing people early who still pose a risk to the public,” he said.“One of the challenges around the sentencing act [is that it] releases people on the basis of the crime committed, not on the basis of how reformed they are, have they been rehabilitated, and not on the basis of the risk they pose back in the community.“So if you have somebody who still poses the risk … has felt no remorse, and they are back on the streets early, of course that risk has to be managed by the probation service and policing.”Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justicePolicePolice FederationPrisons and probationAndy BurnhamBerkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge announces investigation into professor accused of plagiarism | University of Cambridge | The Guardian
description: University says it has ‘new information’ about academic career of Jason Arday, the youngest black professor in its history
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: University says it has ‘new information’ about academic career of Jason Arday, the youngest black professor in its history
Content: Jason Arday insists portraying him as a liar and fantasist is ‘totally unacceptable’.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday insists portraying him as a liar and fantasist is ‘totally unacceptable’.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianUniversity of CambridgeCambridge announces investigation into professor accused of plagiarismUniversity says it has ‘new information’ about academic career of Jason Arday, the youngest black professor in its historyRichard AdamsandLanre BakareWed 5 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Arday, theCambridgeprofessor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, is to face investigation by the university after it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.Cambridge initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions mounted over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.The Guardian publishedits own investigationuncovering discrepancies in Arday’s public accounts involving prodigious fundraising feats as well as claims he had been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders.Arday first faced allegations that he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and other academic research late last year, and has rejected the claims. An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded his PhD in 2015, did not uphold the charges of plagiarism but said they were probably caused by “honest and reasonable error”.Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreArday has denied plagarism, telling the Guardian last week: “There have been multiple thorough investigations across several institutions as a result of the allegations, and immense scrutiny, including with an academic misconduct panel who concluded that there was no plagiarism or academic misconduct.”The statement from the university on Wednesday evening said: “TheUniversity of Cambridgehas begun an investigation following new information about Prof Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.“Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our misconduct in research policy. This is consistent withour previous statement on the matter.“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.“We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”A spokesperson for Jesus College, Cambridge, said it was launching its own parallel “process”. “Prof Arday’s college fellowship is linked to his university role and we will fully support the university.“Prof Arday remains a fellow during this process. We recognise that this is a very difficult time for him and his family, and ask that they are treated with compassion and respect.”The new investigations may have been triggered by Arday’s claims that he held a string of prestigious visiting fellowships and professorships at other universities, including statements in published biographies dating back to 2018 that he was a visiting fellow or visiting professor at Ohio State University in the US. Ohio State hasdenied that Arday was ever employedin any role.Biographies linked to Arday have also claimed he had visiting professorships at Durham, Glasgow, Coventry and London Metropolitan universities as well as Nelson Mandela University in South Africa.Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology at Cambridge, at the comparatively young age of 37, received wide publicity through Arday’s life story, which includes a diagnosis of autism at the age of three, being unable to speak until he was 11, or read or write until he was 18.Despite those factors, Arday went on to university and swiftly climbed the academic ladder. After receiving his PhD in 2015 he held academic posts at Leeds Beckett, Roehampton and Durham universities, including a brief stint at Warwick University, before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Glasgow University in 2021. By early 2023 he had sought and won appointment to a professorship at Cambridge.Arday also claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days as well as running 600 miles in six days, and raising £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions he has revised some of those claims, and instead says he was part of a funding raising group that he cannot name for legal reasons.Arday told the Guardian he had been the target of multiple threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home.
