Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.The controversy comes as Simon & Schuster prepares to publish Arday’s memoir later this month, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of CambridgeUniversitiesPlagiarismHigher educationCambridgeAcademicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Winner of Florida python hunting contest nabs 96 snakes: ‘I was on a mission’ | Florida | The Guardian
description: Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove them
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove them
Content: Tom Rahill holding a Florida-native water snake as he searches for Burmese pythons in August 2022.Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTom Rahill holding a Florida-native water snake as he searches for Burmese pythons in August 2022.Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty ImagesFloridaWinner of Florida python hunting contest nabs 96 snakes: ‘I was on a mission’Burmese pythons are an invasive species in the Everglades, and the challenge is part of initiative to remove themLucy CampbellWed 5 Aug 2026 19.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe winner of this year’s annualFloridaPython Challenge hunted down and eliminated 96 invasive Burmese pythons from the Everglades national park, as part of an initiative to remove hundreds of the snakes from the area every year.The challenge invites hunters to participate in 10 days of capturing and humanely euthanizing as many of the invasive snakes as possible across eight designated hunting locations, with the winner taking home a cash prize of $10,000. The event is hosted by Florida fish, wildlife and conservation (FWC), the south Florida water management district, the National Park Service and others.This year’s competition drew 907 participants from 30 US states, as well as Canada and Vietnam. The winner, Tom Rahill, harvested 96 Burmese pythons, all from the Everglades. A python hunter by trade, Rahill founded an organization called SwampApes in Broward county that takes veterans suffering from PTSD on python hunts in Florida’s wetlands.Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000Read moreIn commentsreported by Naples Daily News, Rahill told an FWC meeting in Panama City on Wednesday: “I was on a mission to get one of our veterans a big snake. I did it. And we wrestled this thing … The veteran was just over the moon.”Once that was achieved, he said he went deeper into the Everglades, where he found the 96 snakes. Over the course of 10 days in July, 280 snakes in total were removed. Before the competition began, 1,400 pythons had been taken out this year.The challenge also awards several other cash prizes, including $1,000 for the longest python killed, which this year went to Rahm Levinson, who hunted a snake measuring 16ft 5in.Burmese pythons are native to south-east Asia, and have wreaked havoc since they were first found in the Everglades ecosystem in the 1990s, consuming resources andwiping outa significant portion of the area’s native wildlife. The apex predators are incredibly hard to detect, contributing to the population ballooning to a number that conservative estimates put in the tens of thousands.Females can lay dozens of eggs, sometimes up to 100 annually, and although many hatchlings do not survive to adulthood, there are fears the pythons are reproducing faster than they can be caught. The annual challenge is therefore now held during the summer hatching season in a bid to boost the number captured.Aimed at raising public awareness of invasive species, and getting the public involved in conservation and efforts to protect the Everglades ecosystem by controlling the number of Burmese pythons, the event has seen more than 1,600 of the snakes removed from the area since 2017. Combined with FWC contractors, who hunt the reptiles year-round, that figure rises to more than 19,000 snakes removed since 2017.Sarah Funck, program coordinator at the FWC, told Wednesday’s meeting that there is no “silver bullet” to solve Florida’s python invasion, but stressed that the elimination of just one python “is a win for Florida’s native wildlife”.Explore more on these topicsFloridaSnakesReptilesWildlifeAnimalsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial: toxicologist testifies about medications found in defendant’s blood | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Variety of prescriptions were found in blood of mother accused of strangling her three children, court hears
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Variety of prescriptions were found in blood of mother accused of strangling her three children, court hears
Content: Lindsay Clancy awaits the start of proceedings at Plymouth superior court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 30 July 2026.Photograph: CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via APView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy awaits the start of proceedings at Plymouth superior court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 30 July 2026.Photograph: CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via APMassachusettsLindsay Clancy murder trial: toxicologist testifies about medications found in defendant’s bloodVariety of prescriptions were found in blood of mother accused of strangling her three children, court hearsSign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailEdward HelmoreWed 5 Aug 2026 19.27 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trial of Lindsay Clancy, theMassachusettswoman accused of killing her three children in January 2023, continued on Wednesday with a forensic toxicologist testifying to the variety and concentration of medications found in the defendant’s blood.Justin Brower,a forensic toxicologist with NMS Laboratories, testified that his lab examined the levels of four psychiatric medications detected in Clancy’s blood after she allegedly strangled her children and attempted to take her own life.Those drugs included the antidepressant mirtazapine, the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, the antidepressant trazodone and quetiapine, a drug used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Brower noted that quetiapine could also be prescribed in low doses to treat insomnia.Postpartum psychosis or murder? Trial of mother who killed her kids spotlights mental healthRead moreAsked if the concentrations of each drug were different from what was prescribed, Brower said the only drug that appeared slightly elevated was quetiapine, but noted that it was not at a “toxic concentration” or “suicidal concentration”.“Usually people take handfuls of pills when they’re trying to harm themselves and take their own life, and this is not consistent with that,” Brower testified.He later testified, upon questioning from Clancy’s defense attorney, that the toxicology results “don’t tell the entire story”.Prosecutors say Clancy acted intentionally when she killed her children Callan, eight months old; Dawson, three years old; and Cora, five years old. Clancy’s defense team says she was a loving mother who was overcome by postpartum psychosis, had undiagnosed bipolar disorder and was on problematic medications.The court has heard from a range of experts for the prosecution, with testimony at times halted when witnesses, including Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, or the defendant have become overwhelmed.On Wednesday, the family’s nanny, Elaine Rossi, was asked on the stand if she’d ever had concerns about Clancy’s care for her children.“Not at all. She was a wonderful mom,’ she said. “I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids.”If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. A not-guilty verdict by reason of a lack of criminal responsibility could lead to her being placed in a state mental health facility.On Monday, jurors heard excerpts from Clancy’s journals that revealed her mental struggles including thoughts of suicide and her feeling overwhelmed with motherhood, including her struggles to get her newborn to sleep, going back to work as a labor and delivery nurse, not being able to breastfeed, and feeling disconnected from her children and husband.“I’m so desperate to get a mental break from taking care of everyone that my mind is trying to find something physically wrong with me,” she wrote in an entry on 18 November 2022.The trial has shone a light on significant gaps in the diagnosis and treatment of postpartum psychosis and postpartum depression. Clancy’s attorneys say her condition seemed to worsen on an ever-shifting lineup of psychiatric prescriptions.In the three months before the killings, clinicians prescribed a range of antidepressants, sleep aids, an antipsychotic and other medications while Clancy reported increasingly profound insomnia, anxiety, despair and confusion about what was real, according to a civil lawsuit filed against caregivers that claims they should have recognized that Clancy and her children were at risk.In her diaries, Clancy wrote, “I want help. I want to be well,” and described feeling “incredibly sad and guilty” about not breastfeeding. She also wrote that she was “obsessed” with managing Callan’s sleep and nap schedule.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I have crazy brain fog. I feel like I can’t make a plan,” she wrote in another, undated entry. “I live moment to moment waiting for the next nap time. I’m terrified of Cal getting overtired now because I feel can’t help him.”“Hearing him cry for 1 plus hours and not intervening just about killed me,” Clancy wrote, adding that she had told her husband, Patrick, “I want to die.” She also wrote: “I now have horrible insomnia and anxiety which is causing depression. I have no appetite. I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I want help. I want to be well.”Clancy first sought help from a postpartum depression program in late December 2022. She went on to check herself into a psychiatric hospital and later told a psychiatrist that she heard a “man’s voice” in her head telling her to “kill the children so you can kill yourself”. Nineteen days later, after being discharged, she carried out the killings.The defendant is now paralyzed from her attempt to take her own life. When she woke up in hospital and was asked by a forensic psychologist how she felt, she responded: “Horrified.” Dr Jhilam Biswas of Brigham and Women’s hospital testified that Clancy asked “can she have visitors, and where her family is”.The court has also heard from Patrick Clancy, who recounted the medications his former wife was taking, her health and demeanor, and the destructive thoughts she was having. He has said he forgives Lindsay and believes that the killings were motivated purely by her mental health.When the jury heard the anguished 911 call Patrick Clancy made on the night of the killings, several members could be seen holding back tears. He described returning home after collecting medications and a takeout meal to find their home “quiet”.Patrick Clancy went upstairs to find found the door to their bedroom locked. After breaking in, the room was covered in blood and the window was open. His wife was lying on the ground below. She told him she had tried to take her own life. He asked where the children were, and she told him they were in the basement.When emergency services arrived, he ventured downstairs to find their three children with exercise resistance bands around their necks. Duxbury police officer Brian Josephine testified that he heard Patrick scream: “She killed the fucking kids.”In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsMental healthUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge signals Trump’s defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal may be dismissed again | Wall Street Journal | The Guardian
description: Obama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming Murdoch
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Obama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming Murdoch
Content: Media mogul Rupert Murdoch looks on as Donald Trump speaks to members of the media during proclamation signings and appointments inside the Oval Office at the White House on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Craig Hudson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMedia mogul Rupert Murdoch looks on as Donald Trump speaks to members of the media during proclamation signings and appointments inside the Oval Office at the White House on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Craig Hudson for The Washington Post via Getty ImagesWall Street JournalJudge signals Trump’s defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal may be dismissed againObama-appointed judge seemed unmoved by Trump attorneys’ arguments in case also naming MurdochJeremy Barrin MiamiWed 5 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge inFloridaseemed skeptical of arguments fromDonald Trump’s legal team on Wednesday over whether the court should allow a $10bn defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal to move forward.Trump sued the Journal and the News Corp founderRupert Murdochover aJuly 2025 articleabout a “bawdy” letter reportedly from Trump that was included in a 2003 birthday book for disgraced financierJeffrey Epstein. Trump has denied authoring or signing the letter, and his attorneys have argued that the Journal published the story despite having been told it was false.US district court judge Darrin P Gayles initiallydismissedthe case in April, arguing that Trump’s attorneys had not sufficiently pleaded actual malice, the legal standard needed to win a defamation case, but he gave Trump an opportunity to refile the lawsuit. The president’s legal teamrefiled the suitin May.Representing the president, attorney Alejandro Brito, who is also handling the president’s $10bn defamationlawsuitagainst the BBC, argued that the Journal “didn’t follow journalistic standards sufficient to making the claims”.“The defendants did not and could not have [done] the investigations to make the definitive statements in this article,” Brito said in a Miami courtroom on Wednesday.Furthermore, he said that only four people could attest to the veracity of the letter: Trump, who has denied it; Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019; the bookbinder, who is also deceased; and Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell, whosaidshe does not recall who participated in the birthday book project.But the judge seemed particularly skeptical that Trump was financially harmed by the Journal’s publication, saying his lawyer’s claims seemed “rather conclusory”.Brito responded that Trump’s team did not need to specify financial harm and had “done enough at this stage”.Lawyers representing Murdoch, the Journal and parent company News Corp argued that Trump’s team had made no headway in their attempts to prove that the president was defamed by the story, headlined “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was FromDonald Trump.”“The amended complaint is no better than the original complaint,” said Andrew J Levander, an attorney representing the defendants. “It is time for this baseless lawsuit to come to an end. You gave the plaintiff a roadmap to fix this case and he couldn’t do it.”Lawyers for the defendants argued that Trump’s legal team mischaracterized the article and that the Journal could not be expected, as a matter of journalistic prerogative, to refrain from publishing an article simply because of the president’s denial.Katherine M Bolger, an attorney representing the defendants, argued that their case was actually bolstered by the Journal’s decision to include Trump’s denials – and that the reporters who authored the story, Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo, were careful to tell readers “what they know and what they don’t know”.“That’s not actual malice – that’s good journalism,” Bolger said.While Gayles did not issue a ruling from the bench, he indicated at the end of the 90-minute hearing that one would soon be coming. He also agreed to stay discovery in the case.Levander, the attorney for the Journal, argued that given Trump’s history of suing media companies, “if we get into discovery, it will be burdensome on the court and it will be burdensome on theWall Street Journal.”Explore more on these topicsWall Street JournalDonald TrumpRupert MurdochDefamation lawFloridaUS press and publishingMedia lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’re selling the safety of the traveling public’: TSA workers decry Trump privatization push | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Union exploring options to oppose program that would put US airport screening into hands of private contractors
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Union exploring options to oppose program that would put US airport screening into hands of private contractors
Content: Airport travelers queue in San Francisco.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAirport travelers queue in San Francisco.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTrump administration‘They’re selling the safety of the traveling public’: TSA workers decry Trump privatization pushUnion exploring options to oppose program that would put US airport screening into hands of private contractorsMichael SainatoWed 5 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe labor union representing workers at the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) is raising alarms over a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports.The agency informed the union last month of plans to enact the TSA Gold+ program, which would shift security and control of the screening technology into the hands of private contractors at airports in Tampa, Charleston and Des Moines. Union workers are expected to lose their union contract and benefits once a contractor takes over.“This is a major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001 and the deadly bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Scotland in 1988,” Everett Kelley, national president of the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) said instatement.“Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities and TSA employees themselves.”The AFGE iscurrently reviewinglegal options to fight back against the privatization push from the Trump administration.Before the TSA wascreatedin November 2001 by the Bush administration after the 9/11 attacks, airport security was operated by private contractors with less stringent standards.Chris Finlay, a TSA worker in Tampa and president of AFGE local 556, recounted his experience working at another Florida airport where, 12 years ago, a private contractor took over screening. At the time, TSA agents were told their salary would remain the same – only for the contractor to cut pay a few weeks into employment.“For a private contract company, they’re not doing it out of duty for the traveling public or the constitution or anything. They’re doing it because it’s a business decision,” Finlay said.“As a business, their primary goal is to be profitable, and staffing is the most expensive part of that contract, so if they can reduce how much they have to pay staff, they’re going to.”He also noted concerns over security quality. In 2015, an employee working for the private contractor at the Florida airport outside Orlando wasfired after they reporteda steak knife made it through security to the contractor.“A private company is going to be concerned with being profitable,” Finlay said. “They’re selling the safety of the traveling public for corporate greed. That’s what is happening.”Gold+ is the latest TSA privatization effort, adding on to other initiatives, including an expansion of thescreening partnership programthat uses private contractors, overseen by the TSA, to handle security screenings at small and non-hub airports. The TSA plans to eliminate roughly 4,500 positions as the program expands to 220 US airports.While the program has private contractors managing screening, unlike Gold+, it does not allow the contractors to own and operate security equipment.In May, the TSA deputy administrator, Adam Stahl,saidthat the Gold+ privatization push could eventually include artificial intelligence replacing some security officers.The changes come in the wake of the Trump administration’sproposed TSA budget cutsfor fiscal year 2027, which would entail eliminating 8,400 transportation security officer positions, about 14% of the TSA screening workforce.Last year, the Trump administrationtriedto eliminate collective bargaining agreements for 47,000 TSA employees – first in March and again in December, though the efforts were blocked by federal judges.“The Trump administration’s clear objective is to ultimately privatize all aviation security screening functions, and we don’t have to theorize about what that may look like because we have been through this before and witnessed the devastating and deadly consequences,” Kelley said.TSA officers will have first right of refusal to move their employment, and affected employees will either receive severance or retirement based on their years of service with agency.“TSA Gold+ presents a new way for TPA [Tampa international airport] to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience. Throughout this transition, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees,” said a TSA spokesperson in an email.“We look forward to working closely with TPA to implement enhancements that will benefit everyone who travels through this airport.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US refunds $100bn of Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: More than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegal
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: More than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegal
Content: The port of Los Angeles. Tariffs have been a key part of Donald Trump’s economic plan since he took office again.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe port of Los Angeles. Tariffs have been a key part of Donald Trump’s economic plan since he took office again.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersTrump tariffsUS refunds $100bn of Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffsMore than half of tariff income refunded after supreme court ruled Trump’s levies were illegalBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaWed 5 Aug 2026 06.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 05.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationhas refunded about $100bn from the tariffs it collected before the US supreme court ruled them illegal, according to reports.The $100bn (£74bn) figure, which represents 60% of the total $165bn collected from Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs, was reported by customs officials to the US court of international trade (CIT) on Tuesday, according to the Financial Times.Tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods, have been a key part of Trump’s economic plan since he took office again last year.In February, the supreme court struck down a chunk of the extra tariffs Trump had imposed, forcing the government toreturn moneyto the companies that had paid them.Trump has pitched tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.However, the deficit has grown after narrowing last year thanks to rising tax revenue and tariff income. It hit $1.37tn in the first nine months of the fiscal year, up 2% compared with the same period in 2025.Trump imposed afresh round of tariffson more than 80 countries last month to replace a 10% global duty that was due to expire. The levies range between 10% and 12.5% on countries including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the European Union’s 27 members states.The latest tariffs have been introduced under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is aimed against countries that engage in forced labour.However, this week a coalition of 25 US statessued the Trump administration over the levies, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxesstruck downby the supreme court in February.The states have asked the CIT to stop the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe states involved in the action argue that the tariffs on 59 countries and the EU cover 99.4% of US imports. Officials in the Trump administration have said the countries have not done enough to crack down on products made by forced labour.The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the Trump administration, after losing at the supreme court in February, was “once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs”.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsTariffsTrump administrationInternational tradeEconomicsGlobal economyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meeting | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: A Fifa statement said Gianni Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations over the World Cup sell-off
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: A Fifa statement said Gianni Infantino has sent written apologies to the Fifa council and the 211 member associations over the World Cup sell-off
Content: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (right), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström, appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Wafcon group game as a show of solidarity.Photograph: CAF TV/YouTubeView image in fullscreenThe Fifa president, Gianni Infantino (right), and secretary general, Mattias Grafström, appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Wafcon group game as a show of solidarity.Photograph: CAF TV/YouTubeGianni InfantinoFifa insists Gianni Infantino will remain president after Rabat crisis meetingStatement reveals Infantino wrote apologies to membersInfantino sorry for failing to consult on World Cup sell-offMatt HughesWed 5 Aug 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa on Wednesday night confirmed thatGianni Infantinowill remain as president after a meeting of its senior executives in Rabat.In a statement which also revealed that Infantino has sent written apologies to theFifacouncil and the 211 member associations for failing to consult them over the World Cup sell-off, the world governing body said that he retains the full support of his leadership team.Infantino had spent the day in talks with Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, and chief legal officer, Emilio García Silvero, during which he expressed his determination to stay on in the face of mounting criticism from Uefa and the North American confederation Concacaf, both of which have called for a review of Fifa’s governance.‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayRead moreIn another indication that he plans to carry on as before, Infantino will fly to Colombia on Thursday to attend the inauguration of the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in the city of Cali.“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the Fifa secretary general and members of the Fifa management board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 Fifa member associations,” Fifa said in a statement. “In turn, the Fifa president reiterated his full support for the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa administration for their necessary and outstanding work in the delivery of his vision.“It was discussed and agreed that the processes, communications and interactions between the Fifa president, the Fifa secretary general and the Fifa management board that support the delivery of this vision can and should always be continuously improved in terms of their effectiveness and efficiency.“In this regard, Fifa’s top management is fully confident that the outcomes of today’s meeting will strengthen Fifa’s governance, help restore confidence in the organisation and enable us to prepare for the major events and challenges ahead in a united and transparent manner while continuing our mission to develop the game around the world.”While acknowledging that Infantino has apologised for his role in the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have seen 21% of Fifa’s commercial rights sold to private investors, the statement also insisted that Fifa will not tolerate further criticisms of its governance.Uefa is unlikely to be cowed however, with the European governing body continuing to search for a candidate to stand against Infantino in the presidential election next March, which will also take place in Rabat.“Mistakes made were acknowledged,” the statement continued. “It was agreed that it was not the intention for the Fifa council and Fifa member associations to feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently. It was further acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media.“In a separate letter to the Fifa council and Fifa member associations, an apology was made for these errors together with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again. A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the Fifa council at its next scheduled meeting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As previously communicated, the FFE proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the Fifa member associations and the Fifa council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, it was agreed that Fifa will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.“There are always lessons to be learned, and Fifa will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework.“Fifa will work closely with the relevant stakeholders to examine how it can further support the development of the game through the Fifa Forward programme for the benefit of Fifa’s 211 member associations, the confederations and the regional associations.”Infantino and Grafström appeared together at the Malawi v Zambia Women’s Africa Cup of Nations group game on Wednesday as a show of solidarity, having also written a jointly signed letter to Fifa council members and vice-presidents echoing the Fifa statement.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Game, set, Chat: how tennis players use AI to scout opponents and run their lives | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The emergence of GenAI has led to a generational shift with tennis stars conflicted on the impact of technology on their sport
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The emergence of GenAI has led to a generational shift with tennis stars conflicted on the impact of technology on their sport
Content: Emma Raducanu uses ChatGPT a lot: ‘One minute it’s history. One minute it’s art.’Photograph: Ella Ling/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmma Raducanu uses ChatGPT a lot: ‘One minute it’s history. One minute it’s art.’Photograph: Ella Ling/ShutterstockTennisGame, set, Chat: how tennis players use AI to scout opponents and run their livesThe emergence of GenAI has led to a generational shift with stars conflicted on the impact of technology on their sportTumaini CarayolWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot so long ago, Emma Raducanu was on her phone when she found herself wondering what her comprehensive usage of ChatGPT said about her own character. “I use Chat a lot,” Raducanu says, laughing. “Every small thing I do it and I got this idea. So, you know how Spotify do a Spotify Wrapped? I asked ChatGPT to make me a Chat Wrapped, and it was giving me a rundown on my personality.“I was like: ‘It’s a little bit too accurate.’ It was very clear, very concise. No nonsense, straight into the question. I thought: ‘OK, I can relate maybe. Some of that is true.’”Pat Rafter: ‘Why aren’t we producing players like Spain? I don’t know’Read moreThe emergence of generative AI has led to a shift in society and changed the way many people seek information. Like everyone, this generation of tennis players must figure outwhere these tools fitinto their lives. There are some who believe AI can provide them with an advantage on the court.Jessica Pegula, whose husband sometimes makes AI-generated reports of her opponents solely for his own amusement, learned recently that someone on the tour, whom she declines to name, is drawing on ChatGPT and similar tools to scout the playing styles of future opponents. “I don’t know if they fully 100% listen to it, but I think maybe they cross-reference to see how accurate it is,” she says. “It’s not bad. It just summarises everything and you can make it maybe very simplified or make it complicated.”Bianca Andreescu,the 2019 US Open champion, explains how she recently found herself on ChatGPT before a match with a completely unfamiliar opponent after dropping down to compete on the lower-level ITF circuit. “There weren’t many videos on her,” she says. “So I was curious. Because Chat will scout other sources, right? And I was like: ‘Please be specific. Please do your research.’ And I think it worked out well.”AI has quietly aided several of the top players for some time. Most recently, the ATP has developed a platform calledTennisIQ that processes a massive amount of in-match data to define a player’s performance rating and shot quality. However, in a sport where athletes invest significant sums into employing coaches, many find the concept of directly seeking out generative AI platforms questionable at best.Zizou Bergs, the top-ranked Belgian male, immediately shakes his head in disgust. “I heard of someone [scouting with ChatGPT], and he showed me the result of it,” he says. “It was two or three years ago and I thought it was completely trash.”View image in fullscreenBianca Andreescu used ChatGPT to scout an unfamiliar opponent recently.Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/APDaniil Medvedev has found himself on ChatGPT with friends and his team members as they jokingly try to solve the most pressing question in men’s tennis:how to beat Jannik Sinnerand Carlos Alcaraz. He describes AI as a true armchair coach: “[It] says some things [about Sinner and Alcaraz] and I’m: ‘OK great, how do I do it?’ Like: ‘OK, I see what you mean and it’s not bad things, but how do I go on court and do it?’”A bored Coco Gauff once asked an AI platform about the best strategy for playing herself. “It didn’t say anything I didn’t already know,” she says. Then she comically rolls her eyes. “Newsflash: everybody plays me the same way – hit to my forehand and hope I double-fault.”Many of these conversations about the use of AI in tennis shift quickly to a discussion on the use of AI in life outside the court. For Raducanu, there is no common theme to the types of questions with which she peppers ChatGPT: “It’s as random as my brain. One minute it’s history. One minute it’s art. One minute it’s some random fact. One minute it’s translations. So different questions.”Players in general, however, are a far more cautious group. For now, Frances Tiafoe wants nothing to do with GenAI. “I don’t have ChatGPT. I don’t have the other one. I haven’t used much AI-generated stuff. I’m going against the grain. I’m still Google searching,” he says.Jelena Ostapenko,the 2017 French Open champion, says her perspective towards ChatGPT has been coloured by a ridiculous tale she once heard. “Somebody came to some country, they thought they didn’t need a visa. Then they came and they were stuck in the airport because ChatGPT told them they didn’t need a visa even though they did. So no offending ChatGPT, but I still think you still have to check stuff yourself. Because it’s making us lazy. It’s not a good thing.”Ostapenko does use ChatGPT, but only when she is too lazy to search for things herself. “I don’t have the plus version, because I don’t want to pay €20,” she says, laughing. “Not because I … obviously I can pay that. Just to push myself to do more than using ChatGPT to do stuff for me.”View image in fullscreenDaniil Medvedev is not a fan of AI and believes it leads to laziness.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APLaziness is a common reason for some players’ disdain for AI, including Medvedev. “In general I don’t like AI,” he says. “Because even if I’m someone who can be a bit lazy sometimes, I do believe we need to do something sometimes. With AI it feels like so many people are going to just stay on the sofa and make their life through AI. I don’t think it is nice.”For others, such as Naomi Osaka, the environmental cost of AI gives them pause. “I just heard it takes up a lot of water, and I like the water we have on Earth,” she says. Gauff concurs: “AI, I think it is cool, but also I don’t like what it does to the environment, so I don’t think I’m going to waste my clicks on that.“The last time I had to use AI was for an emergency because we had to go to the hospital,” she says, smiling, before urgently clarifying her statement. “But not for me! It was for my friend.”There are others who do consult it. Andreescu says she has taken a deep interest in the subject, listening to countless AI-related podcasts. “I’m trying not to become too obsessed with it because it can control our life,” she says. “You can ask him anything, talk about anything, won’t talk back. It’ll ask you questions and seem interested in what you’re talking about.”Iga Swiatek grins sheepishly as she explains how she uses AI. “He’s writing emails for me sometimes,” she says. Elina Svitolina, meanwhile, bursts out laughing when explaining her last ChatGPT prompt. “What colours are suiting me the most,” she says, cackling. “It was pastel colours. Cold summer.”Above all, uncertainty rules the locker room. Tiafoe has long been known for his carefree outlook on life, but on the subject of AI he is something of an old soul. “I just can’t get with it. I’m looking outside. In my backyard, there’s a golf course there and no one’s sitting in the seat [while it is] lawn mowing the whole course. I’m struggling: this can’t be reality,” he says, theatrically shaking his head. “At one point I will [embrace AI] but I don’t like so much information. It’s just crazy.”Explore more on these topicsTennisAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: NWSL sets plans for early start, summer break next season to account for 2027 World Cup | NWSL | The Guardian
description: The Women’s World Cup and MLS’s calendar shift will offer the NWSL presented the NWSL with a host of challenges and opportunities for its 2027 plans
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The Women’s World Cup and MLS’s calendar shift will offer the NWSL presented the NWSL with a host of challenges and opportunities for its 2027 plans
Content: Commissioner Jessica Berman speaks at a press conference on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Jordan Tovin/ReutersView image in fullscreenCommissioner Jessica Berman speaks at a press conference on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Jordan Tovin/ReutersNWSLNWSL sets plans for early start, summer break next season to account for 2027 World CupOpening day is 11 February, in line with LA Super BowlWorld Cup, MLS shift offer opportunities and challengesLeague explores options after Victory+ streamer collapseElla Brockwayin New YorkWed 5 Aug 2026 16.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 16.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNWSLon Wednesday revealed the schedule footprint for its 2027 season, which will feature a seven-week summer break for the Women’s World Cup and a February start, the earliest in the league’s history.The regular season will begin on 11 February with a match hosted by Angel City in Los Angeles, three days before Super Bowl LXI is played in the same city. The annual Challenge Cup, which pits the reigning champion against the Shield winner, will be played on 6 February at a location to be determined.Continuity, chaos and Rodman: how Washington Spirit are thriving in NWSLRead moreEach team will play a 30-game schedule. The break will cover the entirety of the World Cup, which runs from 24 June to 25 July in Brazil. The regular season concludes with a Decision Day on 31 October, with playoffs in the first two weekends of November and the championship on 20 November.During the 2023 Women’s World Cup, the NWSL paused regular season play for five weeks but continued playing the Challenge Cup, at the time an in-season tournament. In the three years since, the league has expanded from 12 teams to 16 and increased its overall regular-season match calendar from 132 to 240.The decision to open the regular season in Los Angeles during Super Bowl week was intentional, commissioner Jessica Berman said at a midseason press conference on Wednesday. The Super Bowl is being broadcast on ESPN, which is also an NWSL media partner, and Berman said the league will be working closely with ESPN to make sure that the NWSL is woven into the weekend’s coverage.Such a move is part of the league’s ongoing effort to integrate into the broader American sports landscape. The NWSL has played tentpole games at baseball stadiums, including atthe New York Mets’ Citi Fieldlast month; its matches have been featured in ESPN doubleheaders alongside the WNBA this year; it staged an outreach campaign during the men’s World Cup and resumed play this season as the men’s tournament ended.“Inevitably, we will have overlap with competing properties,” Berman told the Guardian. “So it’s finding the places where we feel like we can find synergy and lean in, but then also carving out the spaces and times that we feel like are ownable.”Berman said she has heard from media executives who believe the NWSL could “own the summer”. The 2027 campaign will be one of the first tests of that theory.In the wake of Major League Soccer’sdecision to switchto a fall-to-spring schedule beginning in 2027, the NWSL’s board of governors planned to vote on the same change to align with much of the global soccer world. The players’ association voiced its opposition to a switch, citing weather and facility concerns, and in April the league saidit had postponed the voteand would maintain its spring-to-fall schedule through 2030.MLS is playing a 14-game sprint season from February to May before starting its new cadence in mid-to-late July. The change has “benefits and challenges” for the NWSL, Berman said, given many of the teams in the two leagues share venues. NWSL dates will overlap with the MLS sprint schedule and the start of the 2027-28 regular season, and few NWSL teams own their home venues to have priority in scheduling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStars, stakes and still some controversy: Gotham’s record-setting night sums up state of NWSLRead moreThe leagues won’t play their postseasons at the same times, which should stand to benefit future NWSL championship weekends. Carlin Hudson, the league’s vice-president of strategy, told the Guardian she doesn’t foresee the league changing from a neutral-site location in the short term – MLS stages its final at the home venue of the higher seed – and acknowledged that more markets could be in contention to stage the championship.“The neutral site allows us to do things like the Skills Challenge the same week, and have a fanfest that’s really planned well in advance, so I don’t see us necessarily navigating away from that,” she said. “But there will certainly be an opportunity there for us to be more proactive in our championship scheduling.”Media rights updateBerman also addressed the league’s short-lived partnership with free streamer Victory+, which came to an abrupt end last week.The league terminated its partnership with Victory+ after the streamer missed payments, according to reports from Awful Announcing and Sports Business Journal. Victory+ was slated to air more than 50 matches this season and had accumulated a roster of former players and media personalities to appear on game broadcasts.The games intended to air on Victory+ will air on NWSL+, the league’s free direct-to-consumer platform, for the rest of this season and next.Victory+ was among the league’s five media partners for the 2026 and 2027 season. The NWSL began its current media deal in 2024 for a record $240m, but it has received criticism for its fragmentation, with games scattered across CBS, ABC/ESPN, Prime Video, Ion, Victory+ and NWSL+. The league will begin negotiations for a new deal after the 2027 World Cup.Explore more on these topicsNWSLWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Washington Commanders to sign four-time Pro Bowl receiver Stefon Diggs | Washington Commanders | The Guardian
description: The 32-year-old receiver is reportedly joining Washington on a one-year contract after recording his seventh 1,000-yard season in eight years
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 32-year-old receiver is reportedly joining Washington on a one-year contract after recording his seventh 1,000-yard season in eight years
Content: New England released Stefon Diggs in March after he played one season ⁠on a three-year, $63.5m contract.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenNew England released Stefon Diggs in March after he played one season ⁠on a three-year, $63.5m contract.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APWashington CommandersWashington Commanders to sign four-time Pro Bowl receiver Stefon DiggsVeteran reportedly agrees to deal worth up to $12mWideout joins Jayden Daniels and Terry McLaurinDiggs cleared by court and NFL after allegationsField Level Media ReutersWed 5 Aug 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheWashington Commandersare set to sign four-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Stefon Diggs, multiple ⁠outlets reported on Wednesday.Diggs, 32, played last season with theNew England Patriots, in which he ⁠posted his seventh 1,000-yard ⁠campaign in ​the past eight years.ESPN reported Diggs is getting a one-year deal with the Commanders worth ⁠up to $12m with incentives.Falcons make Bijan Robinson highest-paid running back in NFL history with deal worth up to $75mRead moreNew England released Diggs on 4 March after he played one season ⁠on a three-year, $63.5m contract.On 5 May, Diggs was acquitted ​by a jury in Dedham (Massaschusetts) ‌district court of strangling ‌or assaulting his private chefin an alleged incidentfrom December.The ‌following month, theNFLreportedly determined that there was insufficient evidence of any violations by Diggs of the league’s personal conduct policy. That means he is not facing a suspension for the 2026 season.Returning from a torn ACL, Diggs caught 85 ‌passes for 1,013 yards and four touchdowns in 17 games last season. He added 110 yards and ​a touchdown on 14 receptions over four playoff games as the Patriots reached Super Bowl LX, losing 29-13 to the Seattle Seahawks.The Maryland product was a four-time Pro Bowl selection with the Buffalo ⁠Bills from 2020-23.Diggs played five seasons for the Minnesota Vikings (2015-19) ​before joining the ​Bills. He also played for ​the Houston Texans in 2024 before signing with the ​Patriots and ‌has 942 catches ​for 11,504 ​yards and 74 touchdowns in 161 regular-season games (153 starts).Diggs would provide a quarterback-friendly target for third-year Commanders star Jayden Daniels, whose current wide receivers include veteran Terry McLaurin, Antonio Williams, Luke McCaffrey and Dyami Brown.Explore more on these topicsWashington CommandersNFLUS sportsNew England PatriotsShareReuse this content

title: LIV Golf secures ‘lead investor’ until 2030 but future of star names still uncertain | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: The LIV chief, Scott O’Neil, refused to disclose the new funders of the business, but hopes Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm will stay
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The LIV chief, Scott O’Neil, refused to disclose the new funders of the business, but hopes Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm will stay
Content: Scott O'Neil (right) will want top players such as Tyrrell Hatton (left) to stay with LIV after a new investor was found.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenScott O'Neil (right) will want top players such as Tyrrell Hatton (left) to stay with LIV after a new investor was found.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesLIV Golf secures ‘lead investor’ until 2030 but future of star names still uncertainLIV chief refuses to disclose new funders’ identitiesScott O’Neil hopes DeChambeau and Rahm will stayEwan MurrayWed 5 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLIVGolfhas secured a “lead investor” to safeguard its existence until 2030, although the agreement is unlikely to prevent a batch of high-profile players departing by the end of this year.Scott O’Neil, LIV’s chief executive, announced basic plans for the “next generation” of the tour on Wednesday while refusing to disclose the new funders of the business. After the withdrawal of backing from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, O’Neil has been engaged in a race against time to save his business.Cam Smith wants LIV Golf to live on but ‘100%’ would return to PGA TourRead more“We’re very fortunate that a lead investor has signed a term sheet approved by our board, which will carry and fund LIV going forward,” O’Neil said. “It’s very good news for us. At this point we are keeping the details of the deal, the investor, and much of what you might want to know in this second phase out of the media.”It is expected that this scenario could crystallise by the end of August, including with precise detail of who will play on LIV in 2027. Asked whether conclusion of the deal will protect the 2027 season, O’Neil said: “And 28 and 29 and 30.” He insisted the investor is one “of weight”.LIV’s current format involves 14 events per year and prize funds of $30m per tournament, split between individual and team prizes. Players have contracts with LIV linked to those terms. The business has lost huge sums, meaning an estimated $5bn of Saudi money was essential. From 2027, the plan is understood to involve a core of 10 events worth $10m each. Players will be given the majority of equity in the business.While generally LIV golfers have not spoken in public about potential pathways back towards the PGA Tour – partly because of contractual commitments – there is a widespread belief the change in circumstances overseen through necessity by O’Neil will trigger huge change. LIV coaxed golfers, often for hundreds of millions of dollars, from the PGA Tour from the point of its formation in 2021.Asked directly on thefutures of Bryson DeChambeauand Jon Rahm, LIV’s two star turns, O’Neil said: “I have all the time in the world for Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau. I think I’d be remiss in saying they’re not only two of the biggest, best golfers on the planet, but I think they’re some of the biggest stars in sports, let alone golf. [I] would certainly love them to come along for the ride and journey because they carry maybe more weight than anybody in the game and I have a lot of time for that.”“I think we have enough support from enough players, and we have such an interesting format and global format, I think we’ll do quite well in getting the right stars for this game.”DeChambeau’s scenario is complicated by perceived mutual indifference between him and the PGA Tour, plus the Californian’s floating of switching towards YouTube golf. Cameron Smith, Tyrrell Hatton and Dustin Johnson areother key nameswhose choice of upcoming playing domain will prove intriguing.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: From media deals to roster rules: five priorities for MLS’s new commissioner | MLS | The Guardian
description: Larry Berg will have plenty of things on his to-do list when he officially starts as the league’s commissioner in January
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Larry Berg will have plenty of things on his to-do list when he officially starts as the league’s commissioner in January
Content: A view from MLS Cup 2025, won by Inter Miami over the Vancouver Whitecaps.Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA view from MLS Cup 2025, won by Inter Miami over the Vancouver Whitecaps.Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Getty ImagesMLSFrom media deals to roster rules: five priorities for MLS’s new commissionerLarry Berg will have plenty of things on his to-do list when he officially starts as the league’s commissioner in JanuaryJeff RueterWed 5 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Larry Berg fielded his first wave of questions asMLScommissioner-elect, he tried to make clear his ambitious vision to take the league to another level. Until a question about the league’s broadcasting plans came up, that is. To his right sat Don Garber, whose 28-year tenure in the role will conclude at year’s end.“Well, as the incoming commissioner, I’m allowed to kick it to the current commissioner to answer that question,” Berg said with a laugh as he briefly reclined in his chair at the league’s headquarters in Manhattan. “Only for a few months,” Garber said.To follow MLS is to following a sprawling soccer league as well as a self-proclaimed “challenger brand”. Every action is contextualized by MLS’s ongoing search for greater relevance and respect. On 1 January, that project will be Berg’s to helm – and there are plenty of items on his to-do list.New MLS commissioner says promotion and relegation won’t be coming ‘anytime soon’Read moreChart a broadcast futureBerg will eventually be looked to for answers about what MLS will do when its current pact with Apple concludes after the 2028-29 season.From the beginning, MLS’s streaming deal with Apple looked like a gamble, netting an initial $250m per year to partner with one of the most trusted innovators in any arena, albeit one that had limited experience broadcasting sports and whose adoption was (and remains) not nearly as widespread as more traditional networks. Now in their fourth year together, the platform’s offering of ancillary content beyond matches and occasional pregame shows has nearly run dry altogether. Multiple sources throughout the landscape have acknowledged the decrease in cameras at MLS matches compared to the first year in 2023.Evidence of how the audience is responding to their partnership is scarce. In July 2025, Garber said MLS broadcasts were “averaging 120,000 unique viewersper” game, a rare bit of hard data in an era where streamers obscure specifics of their viewership. While MLS will never command comparable interest to a World Cup, the fact the 2026 installment set multiple records for soccer viewership is a reminder that there are plenty more eyeballs to be won.It’s impossible to underemphasize the importance of media rights deals. They represent a significant chunk of any sports league’s revenue stream, which is shared among the teams. A wimpy broadcast deal can complicate the path ahead for even the greatest of leagues: Ligue 1 haslearned that the hard way. MLS can’t afford to take a step back, but is another streaming-only solution its best option?View image in fullscreenLarry Berg gave his first press conference as the incoming commissioner on Tuesday.Photograph: Dustin Satloff/MLS/Getty ImagesClarify how the league will evolve on the pitchBerg’s candidacy was boosted by his work leading the sporting and competition committee, with Garber affirming he was hand-picked well before showing aspirations to become a commissioner. It’s a powerful board which works to gradually evolve MLS’s roster rules to improve the standard of play. On Tuesday, he wasn’t shy about stating his ambitions.“Look, we have a lot to do. Obviously, the foundation’s terrific, but I think it all starts with quality on the field,” Berg said. “Everyone wants to take advantage of this rocket fuel from the World Cup, but they have different views of how to do so. … It’s my job to take all these things in and come up with a plan going forward. And sometimes it’s just a question of being a little bit creative.”The current framework isn’t lacking for creativity, a charitable way to describe much-maligned rules like discovery rights and strict squad designations. Those mechanisms have limited more ambitious teams’ abilities to spend across their entire rosters as they’d wish, while aspiring “selling teams” can only reinvest so much of their transfer windfalls into the next wave of talent.The league’s upcoming calendar switch will put it on the same player transfer schedule as the world’s other top leagues, so owners have already begun talks about how to evolve the roster rulebook. The main case for “flipping” the calendar wasled by sporting cues. Anything short of a radical reinvention in how MLS’s roster construction would make one wonder why the calendar was flipped in the first place.All 45 Major League Soccer players at the 2026 World Cup, rankedRead moreKeep strides with Liga MX, then Americas, then the worldLate in his availability, Berg alluded to needing to try to get more people aware of the Leagues Cup, the annual summer showcase tournament pitting MLS teams against foes from Liga MX. Its broadening into a proper competition coincided with MLS’s deal with Apple, and four years have done little to make it a must-watch.If there’s still a benefit for MLS to take from the Leagues Cup, still largely being played on a lopsided field with most games in MLS venues, it’s to test its mettle against Liga MX’s best. An MLS team has reached the final of the region’s top competition, the Concacaf Champions Cup, every year since 2022, bucking a longtime trend of outright Mexican dominance. Still, the balance of squads usually leaves MLS’s best at a disadvantage compared to giants like Monterrey, Club América, Chivas and others.This all scales beyond North America, too, as Conmebol president Alejandro Domínguez hasleft the door ajarfor future Libertadores participation from MLS and Liga MX sides. But with MLS’s restrictions to squad-building, it’s difficult to see even one of their best sides contending with the likes of River Plate, Palmeiras, or Flamengo.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd then there’s the scaling effect beyond the Americas. Inter Miami grabbed the kind of attention and respect that MLS yearns to make regular with a win over Porto: MLS’s first competitive triumph over a European opponent. But it wasn’t all good; Berg’s LAFC struggled at the Club World Cup, having been the final team into the field by way of a late play-in game.Even just regularly making the Club World Cup ought to be a priority given the ludicrous prize pool on offer simply for showing up. But in order to get there, Berg and the MLS front office need to find ways for teams to raise their quality enough to make regional titles more attainable.View image in fullscreenCruz Azul deafeated the Vancouver Whitecaps in the 2025 Champions Cup final.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersIncrease clubs relevant in their marketsIt was no small feat for Berg and his now-former ownership peers to make a second team stick in Los Angeles, especially in the immediate aftermath of Chivas USA.The owners also deserve some measure of commendation for fostering a rapport with their supporters, collectively called the 3252, who create singular and engaging matchday atmospheres. LAFC found a stadium site in the city proper, built a great facility there, and has become an established part of the city’s sports landscape. Their support feels authentic to the region and the scenes in the supporters bank are often used by MLS in advertisements.The league needs more teams to enjoy such a strong overall picture. For the successes of LAFC, there are also longtime struggles to become prominent in major markets like Colorado, Houston, New England, and Dallas – legacy MLS clubs who have improved along with the league in some ways but not in others. Fixing these issues was a priority under Garber as well, but the work here is far from over.How does MLS pick up the World Cup mantle? Casemiro helps, but it’ll take much moreRead moreThe next CBAAll of these factors will be considered during the most immediate of these headline items: looming labor negotiations. MLS and the MLS Players Association renegotiated their previous terms in 2021 in light of the Covid-19 pandemic, extending the deal to the end of 2027. That endpoint is approaching with haste, and how Berg handles his first bargaining process taking cues from all 30 ownership groups, rather than being one of 30 voices weighing in, will set a tone between the entities that will have ramifications throughout the rest of his tenure.MLS has evolved alotsince that re-worked deal was ratified in 2021. There are the aforementioned changes: the calendar flip, the Leagues Cup, and now a new commissioner. The league has also changed its playoff format to include a best-of-three first round and a wild card round (though berg hinted this would change in his press conference), launched developmental MLS Next Pro to link MLS academies to their first teams, and seen another four teams debut.Much of the mid-2020s will be remembered in the background of Lionel Messi’s stateside exploits, but the 39-year-old won’t be touring MLS venues forever. These talks will clarify and codify the priorities and framework for the league’s next chapter – one stewarded, officially, by Berg. There is no indication that a work stoppage of any type is coming, but a long, drawn-out CBA fight could bring one about, and that would be a disastrous scenario for the league’s overall momentum.Explore more on these topicsMLSUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How the ABA changed basketball forever: Dr J, George Gervin and the league that dared to be different | Basketball | The Guardian
description: Fifty summers after the ABA-NBA merger, George Gervin, Ralph Simpson and others reflect on the league whose swagger and innovations changed basketball forever
Author: Jacob Uitti
Headline: Fifty summers after the ABA-NBA merger, George Gervin, Ralph Simpson and others reflect on the league whose swagger and innovations changed basketball forever
Content: The Spurs’ George Gervin (left) boxes out the Pacers’ George McGinnis during a 1975 ABA playoff game in Indianapolis.Photograph: Heinz Kluetmeier/Sports Illustrated/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Spurs’ George Gervin (left) boxes out the Pacers’ George McGinnis during a 1975 ABA playoff game in Indianapolis.Photograph: Heinz Kluetmeier/Sports Illustrated/Getty ImagesBasketballHow the ABA changed basketball forever: Dr J, George Gervin and the league that dared to be differentFifty summers after the ABA-NBA merger, George Gervin, Ralph Simpson and others reflect on the league whose swagger and innovations changed basketball foreverJacob UittiWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter practice, George Gervin wanted to go home. He was a rookie playing for the Virginia Squires of the upstart AmericanBasketballAssociation, and the sleek, Detroit-born hooper didn’t yet know what being a pro quite meant. He didn’t know that the real workouts often startedafterpractice. But his teammate Julius “Dr J” Erving quickly showed him the ropes.“Doc would say, ‘Hey, young fella! Where you going? Me and you ain’t done!’” Gervin tells the Guardian. “Me and him would play one-on-one after practice. It was beautiful, probably one of the most beautiful experiences I had as a young pro.”Today, Gervin is remembered as being one of basketball’s great scorers. Known as the Iceman, his finger roll is still studied by the best in the game. A Hall of Famer, Gervin led the National Basketball Association in scoring four out of five years from 1978 to 1982. But before that, he was considered damaged goods.A fistfight in college saddled Gervin with a bad reputation. And though he averaged nearly 30 points per game for Eastern Michigan University as a sophomore in college, he was not anNBAprospect. So, he played a year in the CBA before earning a tryout in the ABA.Still thought of as a subpar league in the 1970s, the fledgling ABA was hoping to force a merger with the more established NBA. The ABA needed all the talent it could get, so guys like Gervin got a shot. Gervin wasn’t drafted – instead, he impressed in his tryout and the Squires signed him. “Because I shot the ball well,” Gervin remembers.Turns out, the ABA was just the step the scoring wing needed. “I came in a little young, inexperienced,” Gervin says. “Coming into a world that I needed to have some kind of guidance.” But those one-on-one games between the Iceman and Dr J proved to be beneficial for both mind and body.View image in fullscreenJulius Erving (32), Larry Kenon (35), George Gervin (44), Artis Gilmore (53) and David Thompson (33) look on before the 1976 ABA slam dunk contest in Denver.Photograph: Carl Iwasaki/Sports Illustrated/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJulius Erving from the line in 1976.Photograph: Manny Millan/Sports Illustrated/Getty Images“He’d throw me the ball and say, ‘Me and you are playing one-on-one,’” Gervin says. “At the same time, he wasn’t really competing against me. He was getting me ready. Seeing what I was made of. I tell him today that I owe him. Because he helped build my self-confidence and self-esteem. He helped me understand I had the ability to play in the league.”Fifty years after the ABA merged with the NBA, ending the upstart league’s nine-year run, players like Gervin remain living reminders of its enduring influence. The merger, finalized in the summer of 1976, brought only four ABA franchises into the NBA, but many of the league’s innovations – and some of its brightest stars – would permanently reshape professional basketball.Even now, Gervin and Erving remain close friends. Their paths have crossed countless times since those one-on-one practices in Virginia. But one day that especially stands out is 27 January 1976 – the day of the first modern pro basketball dunk contest.The ABA, which was founded in the late 1960s as a rival to the NBA, soon became known as the more flamboyant and fun of the two. Though it didn’t have the national TV contracts and history the NBA did, what the ABA offered fans was high-flying dunks, a red-white-and-blue basketball, the three-point shot, and fashion out the wazoo,from muttonchop sideburns to afros. And no one symbolized the ABA’s cultural heft quite like Dr J.A star on and off the court, Erving and the ABA made history on that January night in 1976. With no money for a half-time performer at the ABA All-Star game, officials organized a dunk contest, which featured, among others, Erving, Gervin, and leaper David Thompson. In the end, it was Dr J who won the trophy,flying from the free-throw linelike Superman.“Awful!” says Gervin, laughing, thinking about the contest. “I was awful! I couldn’t beat them. You’re going into a contest knowing you can’t win. I knew I couldn’t beat David Thompson or Doc. So, it was just being a part of the show. I was brave enough to accept defeat – part of something that was bigger than I ever thought.”Julius Erving made history in winning the 1976 ABA slam dunk contest.Still, despite the lack of hope to win, Gervin knew his name attached to the contest would draw eyeballs, even if he wasn’t known as a creative dunker as his peers. “I’m thankful that I said OK,” he says. “The game is basically entertainment. Being ABA, that’s what we were all about – entertaining.”The NBA in the early 1970s was largely resistant to change. So, the ABA took on the job of pushing the game forward. Though the NBA did have high-wattage players like Walt “Clyde” Frazier, Lew Alcindor (laterKareem Abdul-Jabbar), Wilt Chamberlain, Oscar Robertson and others, it was nevertheless known as being slower, stodgier.It also didn’t allow underclassmen to join its ranks –until Spencer Haywood.Despite the NBA’s self-imposed four-year rule, the ABA drafted the 1968 Olympic gold medalist before he’d graduated from college. And Haywood, whose mother was working in poverty picking cotton in Mississippi, suited up. As a first-year player, he won both the Rookie of the Year and MVP trophies in Denver. His success opened the doors for other underclassmen like Ralph Simpson.“Spencer and I played high school ball together in Detroit,” Simpson tells the Guardian. In college, Simpson starred for a season at Michigan State, averaging nearly 30 points. But then his father had a heart-attack and got sick. “Spencer said, ‘Well, why don’t you come out here with me.’ We didn’t have any money and things were getting kind of hard. I wanted to stay at school, but I got offered a little money and that’s how I got to Denver.”A sweet-scoring swingman with a knack for rebounding, Simpson became a five-time ABA All-Star playing for coaches like Hall of Famer Larry Brown. “The ABA gave us a chance to develop,” says Simpson, who is also the father of Grammy-winning artistIndia Arie. “I probably wasn’t ready to play in the NBA, but after a year or two, I started to develop.”Thompson was one of Simpson’s teammates in Denver. And Simpson was with his friend at the 1976 dunk contest. “I told Julius I thought David would beat him!” Simpson remembers. “But I think David got a little nervous looking at Dr. J and his status. Going into the last round, David was leading and missed a 360-degree dunk. And Julius—he didn’t miss any.”Dr J capped the competition with that leaping dunk from the foul line. “Julius ended up winning it, taking off from the free-throw line,” says Simpson, with a laugh. “I thought his foot was on the line. But I wouldn’t tell Julius that! He’d get mad, probably.”View image in fullscreenThe San Antonio Spurs’ Baseline Bums fans look on before a 1975 game agains the Denver Nuggets.Photograph: John Iacono/Sports Illustrated/Getty ImagesThe ABA’s restless existence meant teams came and went, from the Miami Floridians, the San Diego Conquistadors and other oddball franchises. But if the teams were fleeting, the personalities were unforgettable. Every season seemed to introduce another larger-than-life figure, from the troubled Marvin “Bad News” Barnes to the politically minded Warren Jabali.But Simpson remembers the strong camaraderie the league offered its workforce. Players were friends, despite the heated competitions. “Warren Jabali, he taught me a lot when he was in Denver for those two years,” Simpson says. “He probably was the best all-around guard.”Jabali was a fire hydrant of a man. He was also militant in his political convictions. Simpson remembers going to an All-Star game in Virginia. The hotel they stayed at required the ABA players to room in the basement. “Warren really got upset about it and wanted us to boycott,” Simpson says. “We didn’t end up boycotting, but the owners got ahold of it, and when we got back to Denver, they cut Warren.”Jabali later moved to Africa, phoning Simpson just before his plane took off to offer some last words of praise before the journey. “He told me, ‘Ralph, you’re the best one-on-one player in the ABA,’” Simpson says. “That came out of his mouth. That was exciing to me, he knew ball.”In the summer of 1976, some 50 years ago, the ABA merged with NBA. Four of the remaining seven ABA teams were absorbed – the Indiana Pacers, San Antonio Spurs, New York Nets and Denver Nuggets. Simpson says part of the condition of Denver’s acceptance into the NBA was that he be shipped to Detroit to play for the Pistons. Whether that’s fact, he also says one of the greatest thrills of his career was putting on his hometown uniform.“That brought tears to my eyes,” Simpson says. “I saw up in the stands, my dad was crying, too.”For Gervin, the 1976 merger between the ABA and NBA was ultimately good. While there were downsides – dozens of players were left without jobs – pro basketball benefited from the union. The ABA had put people like Gervin and Simpson on the big stage, but after the merger, there was still more to prove on the hardwood. “We played with chips on our shoulder,” Gervin says. “We played to let the NBA fans know that we were for real and that we could play.”But it worked. Among the 24 roster spots at the NBA All-Star game in 1977, just a year after the merger, half were filled by former ABA players, including Erving, Gervin, Thompson, and more. “I think that’s an indication of we wasn’t lying,” says Gervin.Explore more on these topicsBasketballNBAUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Vollering victorious on stage five as Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravels | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Race favourite Demi Vollering won a three-way sprint to claim stage five at the Tour de France Femmes
Content: Demi Vollering celebrates after victory in stage five of the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemi Vollering celebrates after victory in stage five of the Tour de France Femmes.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Vollering victorious on stage five as Ferrand-Prévot’s defence unravelsThree outstanding riders in race broke clear of pelotonPadding row intensifies after footage of male inspectionJeremy Whittlein Belleville-en-BeaujolaisWed 5 Aug 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePauline Ferrand-Prévot’s defence of herTour de France Femmestitle unravelled among the Beaujolais vineyards as the French rider lost even more ground to rivals Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Kasia Niewiadoma.The three outstanding riders in this year’s race broke clear of the peloton over the final steep gradients of Mont Brouilly, with 2023 Tour winner Vollering outsprinting overall race leader Reusser to take the fourth Tour stage win of her career.Tour de France Femmes: Demi Vollering wins stage five amid GC shake-up – live reactionRead more“Today was a really cool race,” Vollering said. “Every single rider of the team was part of it and I enjoy those victories the most. It’s even more special and beautiful because you do it all together. I thought I was not going to make it in the sprint and somehow I made it, so it was a huge relief. I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does, and I knew Marlen would gamble. I just had to try and I gave it my everything. I needed every single metre of the finishing straight.”On the unrelentingly hilly stage from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, Ferrand-Prévot’s Tour fell apart. The signs of her fading powers had comeas early as stage threeand were followed by a listless performance inTuesday’s stage four time trial.The fifth day of racing provided irrefutable confirmation of her vulnerability. “I think it’s unrecoverable,” she said of her five-minute deficit to her rivals.As Vollering, Reusser and Niewiadoma were descending from Mont Brouilly to the finish, Ferrand-Prévot was still riding up the steep climb with legs of lead. If her performance in the time trial had been unnerving, her capitulation among the vineyards was complete.Earlier in the day, Ferrand-Prévot’s hopes of reversing her overall deficit to Reusser and Vollering had been boosted by the news that, despite talk of the stagebeing rerouted due to the risk of wildfires, Friday’s stage to the summit of Mont Ventoux remains as scheduled.Although the climb to the summit of the Ventoux remains unaffected, the Vaucluse prefecture has banned public access to the nearby hills of the Dentelles de Montmirail, where two shorter climbs are routed, citing “the sensitivity of the massif and the risk of fire”. But that’s now become academic given the champion’s distance from the front of the race.After her disappointing time trial, dreams of a “PFP” bounceback were definitively shattered on the cruel slopes of the Col de Durbize, where the 2025 winner was left behind by a vicious acceleration from Vollering.View image in fullscreenPauline Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence is surely over after another disappointing stage.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesAs the lead group, containing Vollering, Reusser and the 2024 champion Niewiadoma moved further ahead, Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence crumbled in the heat of the Beaujolais afternoon.
