The best she can hope for now is a stage win.Meanwhile, the debate over Tuesday’s scrutiny of ridersregarding the illegal use of chest paddingto improve aerodynamics rumbled on, after riders union, the CPA, issued a statement demanding that such checks be undertaken in a “professional and respectful manner, that fully safeguards the dignity and privacy of every rider”.Tour de France Femmes cyclists face checks for aerodynamic-boosting chest paddingRead moreThe statement added that this was to “prevent any misunderstanding, controversy or unpleasant situations”.Initial reports suggested that the padding checks would be carried out by a female race commissaire, however footage screened by Flemish media showed a male commissaire making an initial inspection, in public view.The fears of illegal aerodynamic enhancement appear well founded however, as Gaël Le Bellec, a former world champion duathlete, now sports director of the Ma Petite Entreprise team competing in the Tour Femmes, acknowledged.“I’ve never had wind of it among the women,” he said, “but I know that triathletes particularly put bidons [drink bottles] under their kit on their chest to reduce aerodynamic drag.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakaway | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: A document has shown how Fifa staff were involved in the European breakaway and that the global governing body was prepared to sideline member associations
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: A document has shown how Fifa staff were involved in the European breakaway and that the global governing body was prepared to sideline member associations
Content: The proposed European Super League caused widespread revulsion among fans, including this protest outside Stamford Bridge in 2021.Photograph: Rob Pinney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe proposed European Super League caused widespread revulsion among fans, including this protest outside Stamford Bridge in 2021.Photograph: Rob Pinney/Getty ImagesGianni Infantino‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayDocument shows Fifa staff were involved in projectFifa was prepared to sideline member associationsExclusive byNick AmesWed 5 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino held talks about rebranding the ill-fated European breakaway competition the “Fifa Super League”, with negotiations going as far as the term sheet for an agreement that would have changed the face of European football.The term sheet, whose full contents can be revealed for the first time, is dated October 2020 and proposes renaming any new competition under Fifa’s branding. It outlines the extent to which Infantino’s administration were implicated in a scheme that caused widespread revulsion among fans and excluded clubs in April 2021. It also reveals thatFifawas prepared to sideline its member associations in pushing plans to cut back the number of international windows and outlines how global football’s governing body would have been given special governance and political rights with a “golden share”.Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreIn a week when football is reeling from the fallout after Infantino scrappedhis plan to sell chunks of the World Cupto private investors, the document shows Fifa’s leadership was deeply involved in another attempt to put the sport’s major competitions under corporate control. It sets out a partnership of at least 12 years between Fifa and the Super League and proposes a joint venture that would have run its commercial operations.The document also proposes that an iteration of Fifa’s expanded Club World Cup, referred to as the “global club competition”, would be held annually over an enshrined three-week period and tied directly to the Super League. That tournament would have been a straight knockout competition rather than the group-based version that relaunched in 2025. While the term sheet states that the new tournaments would have to be passed by Fifa’s annual congress and the Fifa council, federations around the world are understood to have been bypassed in the plan’s formation.Infantino was among a number of Fifa staff involved in the project and is understood to have been fully aware of its progression. The term sheet says the founding clubs “want to agree the terms of a partnership” between the Super League and Fifa, leading to the creation of the two competitions. It follows an initial proposal to Fifa by the breakaway clubs, also seen by the Guardian, that sketches the framework for a potential agreement. While non-binding, a term sheet is generally the precursor to a definitive contract and suggests discussions between Fifa and the Super League’s creators were nearing a conclusion at the time.It is unclear whether Infantino and Fifa progressed their role in the project beyond the term-sheet stage. After a version of the scheme was infamously launched without Fifa’s direct involvement in April 2021,ultimately scrappedfollowing large-scale protests, Infantino addressed Uefa’s congress in Montreux saying his organisation could “only strongly disapprove the creation of the Super League”. Multiple sources have stated that an earlier conversation with the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, convened by a third party, hastened Fifa’s president distancing himself from the new venture. Infantino is understood to have told associates afterwards that he had no wish to work against football’s institutions.Yet the evidence of Fifa’s outline agreement with the Super League, coupled with Infantino’s disastrous Football Forward Enterprise scheme, casts doubt on that assertion and suggests multiple attempts to reshape the game without consulting its most important stakeholders. The league would have contained 15 permanent members and five clubs qualifying from existing competitions. It also commits to creating a women’s equivalent, using the same clubs, by an unspecified date. The term sheet refers to Fifa under the name “WO1”, which is also the name used in the British army for a high-ranking officer.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino later changed tack in relation to a European breakaway.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersIn a section outlining the agreement’s key components, it says the Super League “is open to discuss naming the competition WO1 SL”. It also confirms Fifa would be “granted a preferred equity stake in the Super League”, which would give it decision-making capability on format changes, calendar alterations, distribution of solidarity money and the appointment of a chief executive for the competition.Senior figures within European football are understood to have been shocked by the plan to drastically shrink the number of international windows, squeezing them into two fortnight-long spaces each year. Member associations, many of whom are being courted for support by Infantino as he battles to save his tenure this week, may have lost the commercial opportunities available from added visibility for their national teams and found themselves at the behest of a privately run club competition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA separate point in the earlier proposal also notes “reduction of leagues” as a point for discussion. The term sheet states that “a new international match calendar” devised by Fifa, the Super League and “other relevant stakeholders” would be reviewed and implemented with Fifa’s agreement.Clubs participating in the Super League would have been required to join the World Football Club Association (WFCA), which was a short-lived representative body launched by the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez, in 2019. Real were key drivers of the Super League scheme and only closed the door on the project when announcing an agreement with Uefa in February this year.Fifa’s close proximity to the Super League proposal adds to the growing number of privately backed ventures brought to the table by Infantino during his 10-year reign. In 2018 he pressed the case for a $25bn offer from SoftBank, the Japanese institution, to create an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. Close allies within Fifa are understood to have cautioned him against the plan, which failed to gain support after opposition from Europe.Fifa was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoEuropean Super LeagueFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid agree club-record £115m deal for Yan Diomande and want to keep Vinícius | Real Madrid | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Content: Yan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APView image in fullscreenYan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APReal MadridReal Madrid agree club-record £115m deal for Yan Diomande and want to keep ViníciusForward becomes most expensive African playerClub are in positive talks with Vinícius JúniorEd AaronsWed 5 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of €135m (£115.7m) with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of warding off Arsenal’s interest inVinícius Júniorafter offering an improved contract to the Brazil forward.After several weeks of negotiations that saw Paris Saint-Germain pull out of the race, the deal for Diomande – the 19-year-old who joined the German side from Leganés last summer and starred for Côte d’Ivoire at the World Cup – was finally struck on Wednesday afternoon. It is understood that Madrid will pay an initial €125m plus another €10m in add-ons, a total that would eclipse the fee the Spanish side paid Borussia Dortmundto sign Jude Bellingham in 2023, believed to have been worth up to €134m including add-ons.Real Madrid ready to seal deal for Yan Diomande after PSG pull out of moveRead moreLeganés are due a 5% sell-on fee from any transfer. The teenager made only 10 appearances for their first team before being sold to Leipzig for €20m (£17.4m). Diomande, who was pictured arriving at Leipzig’s pre-season training camp in Austria on Wednesday, is expected to sign a contract until 2031 and becomes the most expensive African player in history, surpassing the £72mArsenalspent on Nicolas Pépé in 2019.His impending arrival is not thought to have any bearing on whether Vinícius stays in the Spanish capital. The Brazilian and his representatives, Roc Nation, held talks with Madrid officials on Wednesday over a contract extension, with Arsenal waiting in the wings if he decides to depart.Mikel Arteta’s side are understood to be ready to pay more than £100m for the 26-year-old who has less than a year of his contract remaining. But despite some reports that Vinícius had rejected Madrid’s latest contract offer, it is understood that he is now weighing up an improved deal closer to the €30m a season requested after what sources in Spain have described as positive talks. Vinícius said on Tuesday that Madrid’s new manager, José Mourinho, wants him to be “happy, cheerful ‌and playing my football” after returning to pre-season training following the World Cup.Arsenal, who have agreed a £75m deal to signhis Brazil teammate Bruno Guimarães from Newcastle, are believed to be exploring other options in attack should Vinícius opt to renew with Madrid.Barcelona’s sporting director, Deco, held talks with Atlético Madrid over Julián Alvarez on Wednesday in a bid to secure a deal for the Argentina forward but Arsenal are hoping that the 26-year-old could yet be persuaded to join them.Arsenal, who missed out on Morgan Rogers last month when the England forward joined Chelsea for a British record fee of £117m instead, have also been linked with PSG’s Bradley Barcola, who is wanted by Liverpool and valued at around £145m by the European champions.Explore more on these topicsReal MadridVinícius JúniorArsenalTransfer windowNewcastle UnitedRB LeipzignewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dream come true’: Eva Olid delighted after being named Manchester United’s new head coach | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: Manchester United have announced two-year deal for the ‘progressive and innovative leader’ after the Spanish coach led Hearts to glory last season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester United have announced two-year deal for the ‘progressive and innovative leader’ after the Spanish coach led Hearts to glory last season
Content: Eva Olid shows off her new colours after becoming the new Manchester United head coach.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEva Olid shows off her new colours after becoming the new Manchester United head coach.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester United Women‘Dream come true’: Eva Olid delighted after being named Manchester United’s new head coachUnited impressed by her ability to develop playersSpaniard signs two-year deal after guiding Hearts to gloryTom GarryWed 5 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEva Olid has described being appointed as theManchester United Womenhead coach as a dream come true after signing a two-year contract until 2028 with the option of a further year.The Spanish coach will replace Marc Skinner,whose surprise departure came on Monday.Marc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thin | Tom GarryRead moreOlid led Hearts to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title last season and departing the Edinburgh club by mutual agreement in a five-year spell during which she oversaw a remarkable period of progress.The 40-year-old’s arrival comes as United are understood to be prioritising developing homegrown players rather than spending large transfer fees rather than spending large fees.In a statement, the club said: “Olid’s appointment marks the start of an exciting new era for Manchester United Women as the club embarks on a clear vision for long-term, sustainable growth and success.“Important foundations have already been put in place to further support the development of homegrown talent and young players, as well as senior internationals, and establish a clear football identity. Significant investment has been made into the academy infrastructure and facilities, underlining the ambition to build the leading youth development system in the country.”Olid told the club’s website yesterday: “The opportunity to become head coach of Manchester United Women is a dream come true. The club has outstanding infrastructure and everything we need to achieve our ambitions. We have an excellent training facility, an academy that is already producing players capable of performing in a competitive first team, and an exceptional group of support staff.View image in fullscreenEva Olid signs up for Manchester United.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty Images“There is already so much talent within our squad and I am excited to work with the players to support them to fulfil their immense potential. I am joining Manchester United at a really exciting time. There is a clear alignment in our shared vision for long-term success. I cannot wait to begin preparing a team that will make our incredible supporters proud.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited finished fourth in the Women’s Super League last season and reached the quarter-finals of the Women’s Champions League, as well as the League Cup final.Matt Johnson, United’s director of women’s football, said: “Eva is an outstanding coach with an incredible determination to succeed. Her remarkable achievements at Heart of Midlothian showcased her ability to maximise the potential of individual players, whilst also implementing an exciting style of football.“Eva is the perfect coach to lead us into an exciting new era. She shares our commitment to developing exciting homegrown and young players, a tradition deeply embedded in our club’s history and culture, as well as improving established senior internationals, both of which form an integral part of our vision for long-term, sustainable success.”Explore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Football federation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World Cup
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Football federation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World Cup
Content: According to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been ‘holed up’ in Salé, Morocco, this week as he tries to save his presidency.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenAccording to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been ‘holed up’ in Salé, Morocco, this week as he tries to save his presidency.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAFifaInfantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa?Jonathan LiewFederation leaders are massing forces at the gates, but years after the first proposed selling off of its commercial legacy and the Qatar World CupWed 5 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn recent decades the city of Salé, just across the river from Rabat on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, has undergone a remarkable transformation. At the start of this century it was a gritty working-class area, whose old town was still weathered enough to serve as a body double for the Somali capital Mogadishu in the film Black Hawk Down. But in recent decades, under the country’s autocratic government, the area has been transformed beyond measure, and largely beyond control.The population has trebled in the space of 40 years. Slums have been cleared, often forcibly, to make way for grand megaprojects: a new tram system, luxury tourist spaces, a sparkling marina, a blue-chip business park called Technopolis, and – since last July – the African headquarters ofFifa. And in a way, this hub of disruption and avarice, unshakeable volition and rampant capitalism, feels like the perfect location from which a besieged warlord might choose to make his desperate last stand.Gianni Infantino scrambling for his future in Morocco with Colombia nextRead moreAccording to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been “holed up” in Salé this week as he tries to save his presidency. Apparently Infantino’s aides have been feverishly calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer Infantino their public support. On Wednesday one of them, Luís Figo,decided to break his silence. “Infantino must go,” he said, condemning his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup to private investors as “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed.” That’ll be a no, then.Meanwhile, the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation are massing forces at the gates. A “governance boycott”, in which members refuse to attend meetings or ratify Fifa decisions, is one idea. A rival World Cup-style competition – which would in effect translate to secession – is the nuclear option. And yes, in the moment this feels good, stirring, cathartic, karmic. We should all take a certain satisfaction in seeing Infantino get his long-deserved kicking. For all this, a pertinent question should also pose itself. Why now? And why like this?It is, after all, almost eight years since Fifa first proposed selling off a slice of its commercial legacy. In 2018 Infantino agreed in principle a deal with the Japanese firm SoftBank – whose main financial backer just so happened to be the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia – for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. The scheme eventually sputtered to a halt, but with virtually none of the screaming and apocalyptic threats seen over the past fortnight.It is four years since the soiled, blood-soaked Qatar World Cup, and the“today I feel gay”speech that turned the sport’s most important administrator into a figure of ridicule. Two years since Saudi Arabia were handed the 2034 tournament in a bidding process no other country appeared to be prepared for. Three years since the Club World Cup was coerced into existence over a chorus of player welfare concerns. Two months sinceOmar Artan was summarily denied entryto a World Cup in which he was supposed to be refereeing. One month sinceFolarin Balogun had his suspension overturnedin a supposedly independent process.View image in fullscreenApparently Gianni Infantino’s aides have been calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer the president their public support.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFor the men and women who – as it turned out – held Infantino’s fate in their hands all along, none of this appeared to be a red line. For years the injustices, the indignities, the reputational and environmental damage, the ruptures to rules and structures, the stitch-ups and dead migrant workers, have been waved through by acclamation. And so it is worth wondering whether anything has materially changed here, beyond the fleeting opportunity for ambitious footballing executives to claim the keys to Infantino’s empire.It is more than a decade since the late Lord Triesman, the former FA chair, described Fifa as a “mafia family”, and nothing about that description feels less true today. This is in many ways a supralegal body operating beyond the boundaries of conventional politics or economics, operating under its own rules and its own moral code, tied together not through popular consent but through a feudal system of tribute and protection, which changes not through legislation or overthrow but by occasional mob-style decapitation.The moral objections to Infantino’s investment plan are manifest, but perhaps more striking still – for a president who has staked everything on his ability to drive revenue – is the economic illiteracy. One hand-picked buyer (Joshua Kushner), one made-up number ($20 billion) and an artificial countdown clock (19 September). Is this really how to fetch the best price for your asset? Or is it how you act when you want to secure a bigger piece of the largesse you have so selflessly created, but are statutorily bound to one more term in your current job?‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayRead moreAnd in hindsight, it seems clear that Infantino’s thirst for bending rules and breaking conventions was a kind of loyalty test, his Yakuza tattoo, a way of demonstrating to the billionaire investor class that he truly was one of them. No wonder his first instinct on finding himself cornered was reportedly to appeal to Donald Trump: his roof, his protection, his kindred spirit.It is often said that Infantino is the symptom and Fifa is the disease. In fact Fifa too is the symptom; the disease is capitalistic fascism, a simple disdain for humanity, a belief that some are born to rule and others are bound to follow. And this is a cancer that will remain embedded in so many of our institutions long after Infantino has taken his last celebrity selfie, long after “45/47” has chowed down his last Oval Office Big Mac, long after the new Fifa regime has swept in through the door wearing the pageant sash of reform.Football, the greatest mass pursuit ever invented, will of course endure. In a way its ingenuity, its ability to adapt and not be crushed by adaptation, is its beauty and its curse. Like the Salé skyline, it warps and shifts and grows and gentrifies and swells beyond recognition. This is still recognisably the same land, the same turf, upon which its ancestors once stood. But the old waterfront is gone for ever.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is a clear vision’: Matthias Jaissle installed as Newcastle head coach | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: The German has been officially announced as Eddie Howe’s successor at St James’ Park on the day they allowed Bruno Guimarães to leave
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: The German has been officially announced as Eddie Howe’s successor at St James’ Park on the day they allowed Bruno Guimarães to leave
Content: ‘When Newcastle United come your way you take notice,’ says the new head coach Matthias Jaissle.Photograph: Florian Schroetter/APView image in fullscreen‘When Newcastle United come your way you take notice,’ says the new head coach Matthias Jaissle.Photograph: Florian Schroetter/APNewcastle United‘There is a clear vision’: Matthias Jaissle installed as Newcastle head coachGerman officially announced as Howe’s successor‘This an incredibly compelling place to be’Louise TaylorWed 5 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthias Jaissle has described Newcastle “as an incredibly compelling place to be” after finally formalising his managerial move from Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli.The 38-year-old German has been with his new players at their training camp in La Manga, southern Spain, since last Saturday but, despite also falling under the ownership of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Al-Ahli took time to provide Newcastle with some vital paperwork regarding the release of a head coach they were extremely reluctant to lose.Arsenal agree £75m fee with Newcastle for Bruno Guimarães as clubs reach compromiseRead moreJaissle won two Asian Champions Leagues at the Jeddah-based club and, having enjoyed earlier success during a much-vaunted stint in charge of RB Salzburg, is regarded as one of the brightest young coaches in football. He will be installed as the head coach at St James’ Park.Nonetheless, the task of succeeding Eddie Howe with the start of the new season only a fortnight away is considerable – and particularly as Newcastle have lost three key players this summer in Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and, now,the Arsenal-bound Bruno Guimarães.Jaissle remains undaunted. “WhenNewcastle Unitedcome your way you take notice,” he said. “The ambition of the club, the vision for the future and the opportunity ahead made this an incredibly compelling place to be.“I am incredibly excited about the future. I fully and unreservedly believe in this project, the ambition and the direction the club is taking. There is a clear vision, strong leadership and an exceptional platform to build on.”Under Howe, Newcastle’s motto was “intensity is our identity” and Jaissle suggested he would be following a similar path. “My teams are built on togetherness, hard work and a passion to improve every single day,” he said.“I believe there is enormous potential within this squad and throughout this football club. I give my complete commitment and total energy to bringing further success to Newcastle.”With Howe’s coaching staff having departed with him, Jaissle is assembling a new backroom team but it seems David Hopkinson, Newcastle’s chief executive, and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, have full faith in his ability to revive the fortunes of a club that finished a disappointing 12th in the Premier League last season. “Matthias is one of the most exciting and highly regarded young coaches in football and I’m thrilled to welcome him to Newcastle,” Hopkinson said.Wilson said: “Matthias’s leadership style and football philosophy are strongly aligned with our sporting vision. His teams play high-energy football and we could feel his passion during all our discussions throughout the recruitment process.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Punch to the gut’: Indian football thrown into chaos with Jamshedpur withdrawal from ISL | Soccer | The Guardian
description: In a blow for the league, Tata Steel has pulled the plug on the club saying it wants to ‘focus more intensely on grassroots development’
Author: John Duerden
Headline: In a blow for the league, Tata Steel has pulled the plug on the club saying it wants to ‘focus more intensely on grassroots development’
Content: Players from Jamshedpur FC gather for a team photo during the 2025-26 season.Photograph: Courtesy of ISLView image in fullscreenPlayers from Jamshedpur FC gather for a team photo during the 2025-26 season.Photograph: Courtesy of ISLSoccer‘Punch to the gut’: Indian football thrown into chaos with Jamshedpur withdrawal from ISLIn a blow for the league, Tata Steel has pulled the plug on the club saying it wants to ‘focus more intensely on grassroots development’John DuerdenWed 5 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Please don’t let this be the final whistle for Jamshedpur FC,” the defender Pratik Chaudharisaid, looking into the cameraas teammates looked on disconsolately. “We would like to say on behalf of all the players, please do rethink about this. Because if this happens, this is not just a loss for Indian football … this is a big loss for all of India.”In addition, fans of the Indian Super League club marched in protest, petitions were launched, and the Indian football legend Sunil Chhetri said it was a “punch to the gut” and joined others in begging for a rethink.‘Trabzon, are you ⁠ready?’: Mohamed Salah lands in Turkey to sign for TrabzonsporRead moreThe target of all these pleas was the Jamshedpur owner Tata Steel, which surprisingly pulled the plug on the club on 31 July. After the problems of the 2025-26 campaign, which started five months late and lasted just 13 games, the new season’s big kick-off on 4 September was to be a new start. The positivity and optimism before the new season, fragile though it was, disappeared along with JFC.And understandably so as it is a huge blow, for players, staff and fans but also for the league. Jamshedpur had solid support and won the ISL shield in 2022, five years after the club was formed. Steve Coppell was the first head coach with Scott Cooper, Aidy Boothroyd and Owen Coyle all following in his footsteps.Baljit Rihal of Inventive Sports was the agent who took Coppell to the city in the eastern state of Jharkhand. “To be quite frank, after all the uncertainty Indian football has faced over the last couple of seasons, Jamshedpur FC would have been one of the last clubs I expected to pull out,” he told the Guardian.The club was founded by the Tata Group, which has been involved with Indian football at various levels for decades. “When an institution with that history decides it can no longer continue at the highest level, it says something very serious about the current state of the game,” Rihal said.The league is also losing a major corporate backer, one which insists, however, that the decision is not about money. “At Tata Steel, sports have never been evaluated through a profit-and-loss lens,” the company’s vice-president and the club’s chairman, Sundara Ramam, told the Guardian.View image in fullscreenJamshedpur FC won the Indian Super League shield in 2022Photograph: Courtesy of ISL“Our decision to exit professional club football has nothing to do with Tata Steel’s financial position. In fact, the resources that would have been spent on the club will continue to be invested in grassroots sports development. Our sports budget is not decreasing. It will continue to grow. As chairman of Jamshedpur FC, I can say clearly that this decision was driven by our desire to focus more intensely on grassroots development and not by financial considerations.”Yet if others follow suit then there may not be much of a professional pathway for young talent. This latest episode shines a light on the league once more. In the club’s original letter sent to the All India Football Federation, concerns were expressed about the financial model of the ISL, which recently changed. Reliance Industries was the federation’s commercial partner from 2010 but, when that agreement expired in 2025, a new deal was not made and a new partner not found, hence the shortened season.This time,the AIFF looks after governance and administrationwith the clubs taking on the commercial and marketing side. “The old model meant clubs had very little say in how the league was packaged and sold,” Ravi Puskur, the chief executive of Goa FC, said last month.“Now the clubs hold the broadcast and sponsorship rights directly. It puts the incentive to grow the league’s commercial value in the hands of the people who are most invested in it growing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA member of Jamshedpur’s staff told the Guardian that the decision was because of concerns over the new arrangements. “I believe Tata are not interested in the club-led model,” he says. “There had to be a commitment of four years and the AIFF was asking for an initial payment of around £43,000 from all 14 clubs to be made by 31 July. Tata might have thought it’s better to stop rather than get dragged into unknown waters.”View image in fullscreenThe former Crystal Palace manager Steve Coppell was the club’s first head coach in 2017.Photograph: The India Today Group/Getty ImagesIt is a worrying exit as this is not the only corporate departure from Indian football of late. “Reliance stepping away from its central role was significant,” Rihal says. “City Football Group leaving Mumbai City was another warning.” That happened in December,in the middle of the problems last season.“Tata now withdrawing from Jamshedpur FC feels different again because of the group’s deep-rooted history in Indian football. These departures have happened for different reasons, but collectively they represent a major loss of confidence in the professional game.”Now there is fear that others may follow and there will be some relief if all 13 remaining clubs kick off the season. “Indian football can recover, but we should not underestimate the scale of the challenge,” Rihal says.“The priority now must be the people affected, followed by urgent clarity over the league’s structure and future. Players, staff and supporters cannot continue living from one period of uncertainty to the next. They deserve much better.”There is still hope that Tata could have a rethink. “I understand that some tough decisions in sport are down to what makes sense in the boardroom,” Chhetri said. “But I can only request and hope that the thinktank at Tata picks their heart over head and reconsiders this call. It might be a poor business decision, but it will be the one Indian football needs the most at this hour.”Explore more on these topicsFootballIndiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’ | Mohamed Salah | The Guardian
description: In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a reality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a reality
Content: Mohamed Salah has been honoured with a mural on the walls of a youth centre named after the Egyptian forward at his home village of Nagrig.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyView image in fullscreenMohamed Salah has been honoured with a mural on the walls of a youth centre named after the Egyptian forward at his home village of Nagrig.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyMohamed SalahMohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’In this exclusive book extract, Melissa Reddy documents the Egyptian King’s sacrifice and dedication to make his vision a realityMelissa ReddyWed 5 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe entrance to Al Mokawloon Al Arab’s youth sector feels imposing. At first it is confusing to pinpoint the reason. Is it the facade; a mesh of thick concrete slabs, a marble-like trim that alters in colour depending on the light, and the no-nonsense black steel gate? Perhaps it is the stately signage of white block letters in Arabic juxtaposed against the dark background, with satellite pieces of information and announcements signifying importance. But to stop and pay attention to buildings around Nasr City in eastern Cairo is to notice that the blend of functional and decorative elements of the entrance, down to even the font and array of notices, is not unique.The building’s aura can be explained by the main image above its gates, and the knowledge that to walk through them is to follow the footsteps a history-maker took from the age of 14. Mohamed Salah’s face has pride of place above the gates; it is a reminder of where he’s been, but more pertinently, of why it is important to marry talent with discipline and determination. The truth is he has achieved the impossible.Trabzonspor aim to sign Mohamed Salah this week after opening transfer talksRead moreHamdi Nouh, Salah’s first coach at Al Mokawloon and who he has referred to as a “second father”, knows that is because “he was ready to sacrifice everything, he wanted to work hard, and liked to learn”. It sounds simple, until you start drilling at the heart of what it means for a boy from Nagrig to endure a nine-hour round trip five days a week simply to train in Cairo. Salah’s route has become so well known, you can read the tale of the minimum four buses he needed to take each way in Chinese, Spanish and every other major language. One from the T-junction at the edge of his village to reach Basyoun. The transfer from there to the capital of the Gharbia Governorate, Tanta. The great slog of around 100 kilometres to reach the rush of Ramses Square. A connection from Cairo’s chaotic central transport hub to Nasr City. And, on the luckier days, a ride close to the club’s gates to spare Salah having to run almost two kilometres up a steep hill, to be on time for his training session. After four hours at the centre, he would leave to do that all again in reverse.The problem with summarising the journey in this way, as it has been done since 2017 when Salah started shifting the parameters for greatness in the Premier League, is that it omits the reality of what this daily grind truly entailed. When Nouh underlines sacrifice, part of it was Salah giving up his youth to sit shoulder slammed into shoulder, bodies filling up every available inch of the microbus and often even hanging off it, racing to the next stop and against the anxiety of missing a connection in a schedule that had no rhyme nor reason, with only enough cash for the exact journey. He was too respectful to ask his father for more, even though there was no margin for error. Salah weirdly enjoyed rather than endured the stressful odyssey. “I didn’t feel tired travelling when I was young,” he would reflect in 2022. “It’s because I was doing something I wanted, chasing a dream I had to reach. I wasn’t seeing my situation, I was seeing my goal. These are days I sit and think about, I’ll never forget them and I still smile now when I remember everything.”View image in fullscreenEgyptian boys in Nagrig look up to Mohamed Salah and hope to follow in his footsteps.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyIt is not the same for Umm Mohamed (the Mother of Mohamed), who was averse to her eldest son spending only two hours at school, between seven and nine in the morning, and venturing so far away from his village, when lanes were seen as a mere suggestion and dangerous driving was the only type. Her memories were of worry and fear prompted by the high number of crashes involving microbuses. One major accident along her son’s route provoked sheer panic, which only increased as his phone rang unanswered. She tried calling over 20 times, and while Salah insists exhaustion didn’t grip him during his great trek, he didn’t pick up because he was fast asleep. She was also concerned if he had enough money, as was her husband, Salah Ghaly, who worked as a government administrator and traded in jasmine, Nagrig’s greatest export. He funded Salah’s football path, first to Ittihad in Basyoun, which was only a half-hour trip, then on to the Othmason club in Tanta, 90 minutes away, all before he became a teenager, followed by the almighty mission to Al Mokawloon.Salah was eight when he started training there and rushed at opponents with the fearlessness of a microbus driver. “He was small, but his left foot and his shots were powerful,” Ghamri Abdel-Hameed el-Saadani, who was the juniors coach at the youth centre, says. “He was fast and could do things with the ball the other boys couldn’t.” Salah’s father knew it, and despite his own apprehensions about the big city and how it could swallow and spit out young hopefuls, he told Umm Mohamed they were doing the right thing.Back to the entrance of Al Mokawloon’s youth sector, and just behind the black steel gates, lies a story that hasn’t travelled the world like the bus trip. One of Salah’s teammates had suggested they could stay at his uncle’s house in Greater Cairo for the week. It was located in the 10th of Ramadan City and it took plenty of convincing for his parents to green-light the sleepover. Salah’s father gave him 60 Egyptian pounds and he set off. When they arrived at the house, in the black of the night, his friend’s uncle was not there. They were stuck, with not enough money or knowledge to find other lodgings.All Salah knew of Cairo were the roads through it to train at Al Mokawloon. His friend, whose name he doesn’t want to reveal to avoid the media frenzy that accompanies any detail about his life, suggested the house of someone else he knew not too far away. When they got there, Salah encountered a bigger problem. The dwelling was in a cemetery, a saddening – and scary – symptom of Cairo’s severe housing shortage and high population density. Salah was not going to stay in the necropolis. His friend had one final plan: he knew an on-site administrator at Al Mokawloon who could let them in. Right behind the steel gate, they laid out the sheets they had packed on the floor into two makeshift beds.View image in fullscreenMohamed Salah began his career at Al Mokawloon in 2010 before moving to Europe.Photograph: Courtesy of Al MokawloonSalah used his shoes as a pillow and set his alarm for 6am so the pair could be up before anyone caught them and the administrator got in trouble. They packed up their bedding and headed off, returning to the complex at 9am as though they had just arrived. The sleeping arrangement stayed secret but needed to be amended; there was too much jeopardy being so close to the entrance. The next day, the duo slept on Field 2 of the four pitches, in the open under the cold night sky. In the morning, they would again go into covert mode and Salah enjoyed that he could be early for training.Salah had already packed in a lifetime’s worth of sacrifice, effort and lessons by his 18th birthday. The moment he will never forget, however, was when he joined the first team group and moved into the Al Mokawloon’s residences. “Not everyone could stay there, so psychologically I felt like I became someone, like a star,” Salah would recall. “I used to see players finish training and go upstairs, while I would leave to take the journey back to Nagrig. I’d think, ‘One day I’ll go up there’.” He would go higher than any other Egyptian footballer in history.This is an edited extract from Only Mo Salah: An intimate portrait of the Egyptian King by Melissa Reddy, which is published by Orion Publishing and available from 13 August.Explore more on these topicsMohamed SalahLiverpoolEgypt football teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns in Chelsea defeat as Real Betis see off Arsenal | Friendlies | The Guardian
description: Chelsea were beaten 1-0 by Juventus in a friendly in Hong Kong, while Premier League champions Arsenal succumbed to a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis in Dublin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chelsea were beaten 1-0 by Juventus in a friendly in Hong Kong, while Premier League champions Arsenal succumbed to a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis in Dublin
Content: Mykhailo Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute in Chelsea’s defeat.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMykhailo Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute in Chelsea’s defeat.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesFriendliesMykhailo Mudryk returns in Chelsea defeat as Real Betis see off ArsenalChelsea beaten 1-0 by Juventus in Hong Kong friendlyArsenal defeated 3-1 by Real Betis in DublinAgenciesWed 5 Aug 2026 18.13 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleXabi Alonso hailed Mykhailo Mudryk’s “emotional” return from a doping ban as the winger played for Chelsea for the first time in nearly two years in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Juventus in Hong Kong on Wednesday.Mudryk came on as a substitute for Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute, drawing applause from his teammates and loud cheers fromChelseafans in the 43,575 crowd at Kai Tak Sports Park.Luís Figo blasts ‘deceitful’ Infantino and says Fifa president must quit to ‘save football’Read moreThe Ukraine international has not played a competitive match since November 2024,having been provisionally suspendedafter returning an “adverse finding” for the banned substance meldonium.However, the 25-year-old was cleared to return to action after resolving the case with the Football Association. Despite a lively cameo on the left side, Mudryk was unable to stopJuventustaking the spoils courtesy of a wonderful second-half strike from the Kosovo international Edon Zhegrova.“Really pleased for him. It was emotional for everyone from the club to see him back,” Alonso said of Mudryk.Arsenal were punished for defensive errors as they slipped to a 3-1 friendly defeat byReal Betisat the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.The Premier League champions fell behind to first-half goals from Rodrigo Riquelme and Nelson Deossa and although the Gunners hit back through Piero Hincapié, Pablo Fornals struck a third for Betis before the break. Mikel Arteta named an unchanged lineup after his side won Saturday’s opening friendly match 4-1 in Spain against Girona, but they fell behind in the ninth minute when goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga failed to make contact with a corner and Riquelme lashed home at the back post.View image in fullscreenPiero Hincapié scored for Arsenal but could not prevent their defeat against Real Betis.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAChristos Tzolis failed to take advantage forArsenalwhen Betis goalkeeper Álvaro Valles passed the ball straight to the Gunners’ summer signing before Deossa put the visitors 2-0 up with a 30-yard thunderbolt into the top corner.Arsenal reduced the deficit when Valles misjudged a corner from Tzolis for Hincapié to head home, but Betis restored their two-goal advantage before the break as former West Ham midfielder Fornals swept the ball beyond a stationary Arrizabalaga following Kai Havertz’s misplaced pass.Arteta made wholesale changes at half-time, with the 16-year-old Marli Salmon appearing at centre-half, and neither side created a clearcut scoring chance as the game lost its momentum.Explore more on these topicsFriendliesChelseaJuventusArsenalReal BetisXabi AlonsonewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Carney has ‘no confidence’ in Infantino as Luís Figo calls for Fifa president to resign | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The Canadian prime minister called Infantino’s abortive sell-off scheme ‘fatal’, while the Portuguese legend Figo said he should stand down ‘to save football’
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: The Canadian prime minister called Infantino’s abortive sell-off scheme ‘fatal’, while the Portuguese legend Figo said he should stand down ‘to save football’
Content: The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney (left), and the Portuguese legend Luís Figo have hit out at Gianni Infantino.Composite: Canadian Press/Shutterstock; AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney (left), and the Portuguese legend Luís Figo have hit out at Gianni Infantino.Composite: Canadian Press/Shutterstock; AFP/Getty ImagesGianni InfantinoMark Carney has ‘no confidence’ in Infantino as Luís Figo calls for Fifa president to resignCanadian prime minister calls abortive sell-off plan ‘fatal’Figo says Infantino should stand down ‘to save football’Matt HughesandEd AaronsWed 5 Aug 2026 17.49 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said on Wednesday that he had no confidence in Gianni Infantino’s leadership of Fifa afteranother bruising dayfor the beleaguered president during which the Portugal legend Luís Figo also called for him to resign.Figo had described Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors as “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed”. Although more measured, Carney’s intervention could be more significant, as the former governor of the Bank of England is close to the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, who is being urged to run against Infantino in next year’sFifapresidential election.‘Fifa Super League’: Infantino discussed having governing body’s name on European breakawayRead moreMontagliani has yet to commit to standing, but Concacaf have called for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance with many of their members ready to withdraw their support for Infantino. “It should be fatal,” Carney said of the abortive sell-off scheme. “Certainly I don’t have confidence in Mr Infantino.”Infantino was forced to scrap hiscontroversial proposalafter a fierce backlash that was led by Uefa, with the 56-year-old now battling for his future having called an emergency meeting of Fifa staff on Wednesday as pressure on him mounts.On Tuesday the Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, accused Fifa of blackmail by threatening to withhold financial assistance from his federation if it refused to back the president’s bid for re-election. That came after the former Arsenal manager Arsène Wenger, who is Fifa’s chief of global football development, issued a statement distancing himself from the plan that said the decision to withdraw it was “absolutely necessary and beyond question”.Figo, the former Barcelona and Real Madrid winger who won 127 caps for Portugal, joined the chorus of criticism and accused Infantino of having “debased the office of Fifa president that he promised to elevate” since taking over in 2016.“I could write 10,000 words on the problems at Fifa. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go,”he wrote in the Daily Mail.“He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve. He has lost the support of his senior staff, his closest advisers, the vast majority of people who devote their lives to this sport and even, it would seem, the Fifa Peace Prize winner [Donald Trump]. It is too late to save his dignity but it is not too late to save football. He should go. Now.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInfantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreFigo, who has been a football adviser to Uefa since 2017, cited Infantino’s lack of transparency over his attempts to push through the private equity deal that would have reportedly led to an increase in his salary to $30m a year as more evidence he is unfit to govern world football.“It’s not honest when you fail to mention that, after you have delivered the head of the World Cup on a platter to your mates in DC, they are going to give you a job worth five times your current salary,” he wrote.“None of this comes as a surprise when you consider the litany of abuses he has inflicted on football’s reputation; from suspending and reversing disciplinary decisions to breaking the laws of the game over a half-time show, nothing gets in the way of pleasing his friends.”Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaMark CarneyFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Super League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRL | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: NRL officials are touring Super League clubs ahead of a potential investment as Wigan and Warrington announce they will face each other in Dublin next April
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: NRL officials are touring Super League clubs ahead of a potential investment as Wigan and Warrington announce they will face each other in Dublin next April
Content: Wigan Warriors’ CEO Kris Radlinski says his club is “100%” behind a potential deal with the NRL.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWigan Warriors’ CEO Kris Radlinski says his club is “100%” behind a potential deal with the NRL.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockRugby leagueSuper League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRLAustralian officials touring clubs to gauge moodWigan and Warrington set date for Dublin clashAaron BowerWed 5 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNRL officials have arrived in ­England to hold talks with clubs as the prospect of a groundbreaking deal withSuper Leaguenears completion, while two of the competition’s heavyweights, Wigan Warriors and Warrington Wolves, confirmed they will lead an on-the-road weekend to Dublin in 2027.Rugby league’s two premier club competitions have been in discussions for most of this year about a deal that would see the NRL invest a significant sum into Super League, while taking authoritative control of the competition in a bid to transform its long-term fortunes. That investment would also ensure the financial security of clubs. Both competitions put talks on hold while they finalised their broadcast details; the NRL has just completed a A$5.3bn (£2.8bn) deal for its rights, while Super League expects to confirm in the next week how its new-look broadcast deal will be shaped. Sky Sports is expected to show two or three games a week, with the rest of the fixtures streamed or broadcast elsewhere.London in a very different limbo: wins alone will not realise Broncos’ dreamRead moreBut theNRLhas now made Super League investment its number one priority. The Guardian has been told by multiple clubs that they have been visited by officials from Australia, or expect a visit in the coming days. The belief is that Australian figures are keen to get a deeper understanding of the mood among clubs as they consider a proposal from Super League to invest.That is the clearest sign yet that a deal is close, with Super League’s leading official, Rhodri Jones, saying: “We’re very hopeful that we’ll make some significant progress with the NRL over the next seven days. “We’ve been engaged with them since May but they’ve now done their TV deal, so I can say it feels like we’re their top priority.” It’s still with them to come back to us. We’re hopeful we’ll get something very soon.”View image in fullscreenWigan are likely to ask their former player and current Ireland rugby union coach, Andy Farrell, to help promote the Dublin match.Photograph: Brendan Moran/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBoth Wigan and Warrington, who became the first Super League clubs to make the trip to Las Vegas last year with the NRL, have long been advocates of Australian investment and governance. The Warriors’ CEO, Kris Radlinski, reiterated that backing on Wednesday at the announcement of their Dublin clash with Warrington at Leinster’s RDS Arena on Saturday 24 April next year. When asked if Wigan supported were still supportive of the NRL deal, Radlinski said: “100%. As we have been from the start. What they’re doing in the NRL is fantastic. I think it’s the start of a significant few months for the sport. We’re at a point where we’ll find out our broadcasting future at a time when our NRL counterparts are closing in on an offer.”Wigan and Warrington are hopeful of a capacity 20,000 crowd in Dublin, with the Warriors likely to lean on the Ireland rugby coach and Wigan legend, Andy Farrell, to help promote the game. Hull FC are in talks about moving a home game on Sunday 25 April to the same venue to make it a weekend-long event for Super League.Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueSuper LeagueNRLSport politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’ | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)
Content: A Wayve autonomous car on a London street.Photograph: WayveView image in fullscreenA Wayve autonomous car on a London street.Photograph: WayveSelf-driving cars‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first)Jasper JollyWed 5 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe taxi app company Uber and the autonomous technology developer Wayve have been granted the first minicab licences inLondonallowing them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now.The companies said they would start trips in the UK “later this summer” before the full public launch.The San Francisco-headquartered Uber and London-based Wayve are racing against the Google-owned Waymo and itsChinese equivalent Baidu’s Apollo Goto launch self-driving taxi services in London. Theirprogress is being watched closelybecause the British capital will be one of the first cities in the world to have American and Chinese tech firms operating on the same roads.Uber and Wayve said more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for the self-driving taxis.Transport for London (TfL), the capital’s licensing authority, granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar. The companies said TfL had confirmed they reached the required safety standards.A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.The next step, of operating the taxis without a driver, will require Uber and Wayve to seek approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency.TfL said it would monitor the use of the vehicles, and was ready to intervene if passenger safety was compromised. A spokesperson said: “Safety is our top priority. Any new vehicle licensed to carry passengers on London’s roads must align with our Vision Zero goal of eliminating all deaths and serious injuries from collisions on London’s streets by 2041.”Wayve, which wasco-founded by the New Zealand-born Alex Kendall, has been testing its tech in London since 2018 with safety drivers. In previous demonstrations to the Guardian the car has navigated most of the obstacles of north London’s busy roads, although the safety driver was forced to intervene at one point.Sarah Gates, Wayve’s vice-president for global affairs and assurance, said: “This licence is an important step towards giving Londoners the chance to experience autonomous driving technology.“The responsible deployment of these vehicles will bring us safer, cleaner and quieter streets, and we’re proud to continue working alongside regulators, communities and the public as we take the next steps towards making autonomous rides a reality in the capital.”View image in fullscreenAutonomous driving systems usually incorporate surround cameras and radar. Wayve also utilises AI.Photograph: The Lightwriter/AlamyThe licence approval was not welcomed by minicab drivers, who fear the threat to their livelihood. Matthew Wright, a regional organiser for the GMB union, raised concerns about job losses, increased unemployment and liability for accidents, and said “extreme caution” was warranted from TfL.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This is a worrying development for our private hire driver members,” he said. “We can’t go charging ahead with new technologies without considering the implications of autonomous vehicles on all parties.”Driverless taxi services are already operating in several cities around the world, although mainly in the US and China, where most of the software developers are based. However, US companies are essentially blocked from China, and vice versa, meaning they have not had to compete directly.Uberabandoned its own effortsto develop self-driving technology in 2020, but it is working with several partners around the world who are in turn using different systems. That includes the Chinese company WeRide, which is operating driverless taxis in Abu Dhabi, UAE.Wayve is alsoworking with the Japanese manufacturer Nissanon integrating its tech in private cars.The news came as Uber reported better than expected second-quarter gross bookings of $58.02bn (£43bn), but said earnings for the next quarter would fall below Wall Street forecasts.The company also outlined ‌plans to spend more than $10bn on autonomous vehicles over the coming years, although it did not provide a specific ‌timeline.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsUberAutomotive industryRoad transportTransport policyTransportLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley | Life and style | The Guardian
description: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: As Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable them
Content: ‘Maga is a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda’ … Gil Durán.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Maga is a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda’ … Gil Durán.Photograph: Winni Wintermeyer/The GuardianThe ideas interviewLife and style‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyAs Elon Musk, Peter Thiel and their peers have grown richer and more influential, Gil Durán argues they have all but abandoned democracy – and found the perfect government to enable themSteve RoseWed 5 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn April, Gil Durán was permanently banned from Elon Musk’s X for posting just two words. Durán was responding to a post from the tech company Palantir outlining its 22‑point“technological manifesto”, which praised American “hard power”, western culture and AI weapons, denounced inclusivity and called for compulsory national service. Durán responded: “TLDR: Fascism” (TLDR is short for “too long, didn’t read”).Durán didn’t break any of X’s written rules, he points out over a video call from San Francisco – so much for Musk’s“free-speech absolutism”. His ban might just have had something to do with his preceding tweet, showing the cover of his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy. The book’s central argument is that big tech is no longer our friend, as many of its billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions.Fascism is no exaggeration, Durán asserts. He researched multiple definitions – byUmberto Eco,Robert Paxton,Jason Stanley– and decided that Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement ticks all the boxes. “It’s a cult of grievance that seeks to purge its enemies by demonising them through absurd and surreal propaganda that exploits fears over law and order and gender and sexuality in order to seize power and install a permanent hierarchy that fascists consider the moral order of the world and the universe. In addition, you also have this sort of nationalistic, militaristic vibe.”By extension, he says,Silicon Valleyis fascist “because they have wholly aligned with a fascist movement. That’s their vehicle for gaining power.” Few could dispute this alignment after seeing the bosses of Meta, Google, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI line up behind Trump at his second inauguration, or Musk’s now shuttered “department of government efficiency” (Doge) being given free rein to conduct mass firings of federal employees, or Palantir’s AI-driven surveillance technology enabling deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It’s a cosy relationship, Durán says: the tech titans have helped Trump and his family become billionaires through cryptocurrency and have been given government contracts and freedom from regulation or oversight.View image in fullscreenThe man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch … Peter Thiel.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesIn addition, Durán believes, “Silicon Valley has gone fascist because they have adopted an extreme ideology of tech supremacy.” While Maga promises a return to a mythical glorious past, he says, the “technofascists” are promising a mythical glorious future: “We’re going to be in the stars. We’re going to be in space. And all we need is to get rid of anybody who stands in our way as we seek to accelerate technology toward this speedy, violent, God-like transcendence that we will achieve if we can only burn enough energy and enough compute to bring our boom loop into existence.”It sounds almost like a conspiracy theory, but Durán is not short of evidence. Muskmaking an apparent Nazi saluteanddescribing empathyas “the fundamental weakness of western civilisation”. Palantir’s Peter Thielwriting in 2009that “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible” and giving a lecture series suggestingGreta Thunberg could be the antichrist. Marc Andreessen, the CEO of the tech investment company Andreessen Horowitz, paraphrasing Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, the co-author of Mussolini’s Fascist Manifesto, in his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto”: “Technology must be a violent assault on the forces of the unknown, to force them to bow before man.”Durán, a journalist and former political adviser, lays out the narrative in exacting detail, outlining the connections between these men (and it is all men) and the origins of their often deeply weird beliefs, many of which view everyone outside their circle or opposed to their agenda as expendable.Unpacking all their overlapping philosophies would take some time, but TLDR: “It’s the idea that what matters more is the billions or trillions of people yet unborn in the future. And the only way they’re going to get to be born is if this elite group of white tech figures and gazillionaires makes the right decisions to make the human race transhuman and multiplanetary through AI and technology,” says Durán. “By becoming a billionaire, they all have this idea that they’re superior to everyone else. They are susceptible to this kind of thinking.”View image in fullscreenMarc Andreessen has said technology must be a ‘violent assault on the forces of the unknown’.Photograph: Steve Jennings/Getty ImagesDurán, 50, is almost the opposite: the son of working-class Mexican immigrants in California. He was the first in his family to go to college, having grown up in relative poverty: “It made me tough and gave me an unyielding loyalty to regular people over the many rich and powerful people I’ve spent a lot of my time around.”Durán’s book traces the roots of this movement to two important sources. One is the 1997 book The Sovereign Individual, written by the American investor James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg, the former Times editor and BBC grandee (and father of Jacob). Their book prophesied how digital tools such as the internet and cryptocurrency would pave the way for a privatised, corporatised, unregulated, post-democratic future ruled by rich, powerful, unaccountable individuals. Two decades later, this led to the idea of “network states” – digital realms beyond the jurisdiction of nation states – as popularised by Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz.The other source is Curtis Yarvin, a former software developer and armchair philosopherwith a penchant for psychedelics, sometimes referred to as the godfather of the “dark enlightenment”. In pseudonymous blogs in the late 2000s, Yarvin outlined a worldview in which liberal democracy had failed to deliver progress, partly because institutions such as education and the media had been captured by what he called “the Cathedral”.His proposed solution was a mass firing of government employees (he coined the acronym “Rage”, “retire all government employees”) and the installation of a “national CEO, [or] what’s called a dictator”. Yarvin also mused about a “humane alternative to genocide” to deal with unproductive citizens and has had to deny accusations that he is a white supremacist or supports racist ideologies. Scratch the surface, Durán suggests, and Yarvin’s ideas have much in common with Nazi ideologies, “but updated as rightwing dogma for the blogging age”.View image in fullscreenCurtis Yarvin has mused about a ‘humane alternative to genocide’ to deal with unproductive citizens.Photograph: Florencia Tan Jun/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBoth of these sources might have languished in obscurity had it not been for Thiel, the man at the heart of Silicon Valley’s rightward lurch. He has amassed enormous wealth through a series of investments in tech startups – first PayPal, then Facebook, Spotify, LinkedIn, Palantir and OpenAI, among others. He was the first major tech figure to back Donald Trump,in July 2016, and persuaded others to follow, including Andreessen, who said hespent half his time at Mar-a-Lagoin the month after Trump won the 2024 election.Thiel liked The Sovereign Individual so much that he wrote a new introduction when it was reprinted in 2020. He has also made steps to found his own network state – first via the ill-fated“seasteading” movement(establishing floating countries in international waters) then via Próspera,a “special economic zone” on an island in Honduras. Incorporated in 2017 with permission from the Honduran government and reportedly co-funded by Srinivasan, Andreessen and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Próspera has sought to attract digital startups with loose regulations (appealing tolongevity researchers), low taxes and a crypto-friendly economy.He’s anti-democracy and pro-Trump: the obscure ‘dark enlightenment’ blogger influencing the next US administrationRead moreOther similar projects have sprung up. In 2021, the president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, hailed the mooted creation of a “Bitcoin City”. In 2023, Trump announced plans to build 10 “Freedom Cities” on government land across the US, with input from Próspera representatives. In 2024, Srinivasan founded a “Network School” in Johor, Malaysia.Thiel also began to absorb Yarvin’s theories about how the political order was preventing progress. In the2009 essayin which Thiel declared the incompatibility of freedom and democracy, he also said “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” made capitalist democracy impossible, which did not win him many mainstream supporters. But Yarvin backed up Thiel and the two became friends and allies. “While The Sovereign Individual provided the foundation for the billionaire’s political vision, Yarvin created a blueprint for turning that vision into reality,” Durán writes.Thiel was instrumental in injecting these ideas, and people, into the US government – not least JD Vance, whom Durán describes as “almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel”. It was Thiel who set up Vance as a venture capitalist, giving him a role at his firm Mithril Capital, then investing in Vance’s own fund, Narya Capital (Tolkien-derived names are a theme with these people). It was Thiel who backed Vance’s move into politics, where he went from condemning Trump as“America’s Hitler”to supporting him and parroting Yarvin’s ideas. “I think that what Trump should do, if I was giving him one piece of advice: fire every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, replace them with our people,” Vancetold the podcaster Jack Murphyin 2021.View image in fullscreen‘The government created these men and now these welfare kings want to destroy the very system that made them’ … Elon Musk.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesDurán had observed this Silicon Valley takeover developing and began writing about it in 2024. “I thought this would be a problem in five to 10 years, but when JD Vance got on the ticket, it suddenly took on a new urgency,” he says. Now, it almost feels too late. In 2025,Bloomberg reportedthat at least 16 men connected to Thiel and his companies occupied positions of power in the Trump administration, including David Sacks, who is now a special adviser for AI and crypto. Musk’s Doge has swung its chainsaw at the government, crypto and AI regulation has all but disappeared, the Trump family are now billionaires and the tech oligarchs have become the Republicans’ largest donors.At the same time, they have become substantial beneficiaries of the very government they once sought to dismantle. Palantir has an estimated$13.7bn in US government contracts; last year, its stock price rose more than90% in six months. Andreessen is backing dozens of defence companies scooping up government contracts and recentlyjoined the Pentagon’s advisory board. Last week, Musk’s SpaceX receiveda $1.6bn contractto supply rockets to the US Space Force – on the same day hepledged at least $100mto help Republicans inNovember’s midterm elections.“It’s a severe cautionary tale about the hazards of privatisation,” says Durán. “The government created these men, especiallyElon Musk. And now these welfare kings want to pull up the ladder, want to destroy the very system that made them. This is a massive failure by the US intelligence apparatus – to not see this threat forming from the inside.”Durán, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, as well as for the late Democratic senatorDianne Feinstein, blames the Democrats as much as the Republicans. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.He singles out the California governor,Gavin Newsom, as a prime example of a “Silicon Valley Democrat”: “You don’t see him criticising these guys. He only goes after Trump, Trump, Trump and Vance, Vance, Vance … You want some viral content? Why don’t you go off on Peter Thiel’s weird antichrist obsession?” Even if the Democrats take control after the midterms or the 2028 presidential election, Durán is worried that “these tech fascists will win … because Democrats will not hold them accountable”.View image in fullscreen‘Almost entirely a creation of Peter Thiel’ … JD Vance.Photograph: Will Oliver/CNP/ShutterstockOn the plus side, the Silicon Valley takeover has not been going that well lately. Network states around the world are losing ground. In 2021, Próspera’s special economic status was repealed by the new president, Xiomara Castro (it is suing the Honduran government for $10.8bn). Two weeks ago, Srinivasan’s Network School was ordered to close (Srinivasan says he is moving it to Kazakhstan). Trump’s Freedom Cities remain unbuilt.One saving grace, says Durán, is that “a lot of these people don’t really have a great grasp of on-the-ground realities”. Nobody really wants to live in a soulless network state, he says: “Why would you be in Kazakhstan instead of San Francisco, which is the global capital of tech?” On the other hand, he points out, the tech billionaires have effectively turned the US into a de facto network state.But they may well have overplayed their hand. “Silicon Valley oligarchs are really vulnerable right now,” says Durán. “People don’t like them. People are starting torise up against data centresand this vision of an AI apocalypse that kills all the jobs and potentially kills all of humanity. You’re scaring the hell out of people and now they don’t like you. Into that could step a politician to take advantage of that trend and come up with a message that speaks to the concerns of people and against the dark fantasies of the oligarchs.”The question now, he says, “is how we turn the momentum in our favour and against the billionaires. Because they have a plan to win. They think they’re going to succeed.” This could be a radicalising moment: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”If not, he says, we’ll find ourselves in a situation where “we don’t have democracy, we don’t have an economy and we don’t have a future.
