If that doesn’t radicalise people, then we deserve what we’re going to get.”The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy is published on 18 August (Simon & Schuster, £25). title: AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to try to trick developers | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: AI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: AI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk
Content: AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AI models shock UK testers by using fake identities to try to trick developersAI Security Institute says OpenAI and Anthropic models went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of riskExplainer: Should we be alarmed at AI models going rogue in tests?Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 5 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdvanced artificial intelligence models have stunned the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) by carrying out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.The institute said the incident was unprecedented and involved sending targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.The hack involved agents – AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – powered by models developed by US tech companies OpenAI andAnthropic. AISI, which was set up by the former prime minister Rishi Sunak, described the unsanctioned behaviour as a “serious incident”.The watchdog said the hack was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.AISI detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test on 28 July. It found that some of the models had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident.In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers, having decided that it would help the model pass the evaluation.In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities and used them to press the project’s human overseer into accepting the code.Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael BehrRead moreAISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to two specific developers – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that contained harmful software. The watchdog said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented.“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” the institute said in ablogpost.In one instance, the Mythos agent signed off a message in Danish in an attempt to convince the Danish-speaking developer that they should accept the infected code. It also created fake GitHub accounts that would “agree” with its false claims that its software was not malicious.The agent had mistakenly calculated that getting the malware uploaded would trigger a sequence of events that would enable it to use the updated software to pass the AISI cyber test.The incident follows similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. Last month,OpenAI saidan agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test. Days later,Anthropic saidits Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation.AISI said the series of incidents taken together represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”.The watchdog said 17 of the 19 cases of unsanctioned behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol.AISI said the incident was not a case of a model breaking out of its “sandbox”, the term for a secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests. Mythos 5 has not been released publicly but a version of GPT-5.6 Sol with cyber safeguards in place has been launched.The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI added, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate. What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention”.AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation and said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would try to act beyond its remit.The latest safety incident with the technology came as Donald Trump said last week he was “looking at controls” for AI in the US.The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said.Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened.OpenAI said the testing occurred in “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”.The National Cyber Security Centre, part of the GCHQ intelligence agency, said the recent incidents underlined the need for AI companies to develop strong safety guardrails.Warning that detecting an incident after it had happened would not be good enough, Ollie Whitehouse, the centre’s chief technology officer, said: “These technologies must be developed and used from the outset with strong safeguards, real-time oversight, and clear plans for responding when the unexpected happens.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicTechnology sectorComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Darth Vader to become a TikTok star as Disney strikes deal on short video | TikTok | The Guardian
description: Characters and memorable scenes from back catalogue made available to group of creator fans
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Characters and memorable scenes from back catalogue made available to group of creator fans
Content: Darth Vader could find himself transformed into a vertical video star after TikTok struck its first pact with a traditional media company.Photograph: Taschen/LFLView image in fullscreenDarth Vader could find himself transformed into a vertical video star after TikTok struck its first pact with a traditional media company.Photograph: Taschen/LFLTikTokDarth Vader to become a TikTok star as Disney strikes deal on short videoCharacters and memorable scenes from back catalogue made available to group of creator fansMichael SavageMedia editorWed 5 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe likes of Darth Vader, Spider-Man and Moana are about to becomeTikTokstars for the first time – at least now on an official basis – after Walt Disney struck a “first of its kind” deal with the booming short-video platform.In an acknowledgment of the influence fan-made content now has in the entertainment industry, a select group of creators will be allowed to use characters and memorable scenes from Disney’s back catalogue.It is the latest sign of the irresistible rise of short-form vertical video, where users consume content via their phone screens without flipping it round to watch in a wider landscape format.Some of the creator content will be featured on Disney’s own attempt to break into vertical video, its Disney+ Verts platform, which is currently available only in the US.It confirms the powerful status of creator “fandom” and the power of TikTok, which has surpassed 200 million US users, including about six in 10 adults under 30, according to the Pew Research Center. The platform launched internationally less than a decade ago.The rise of short-form video and the resulting fan content means big entertainment companies have had to become more relaxed about the use of their intellectual property.Disney said that under a US pilot, creators would be given access to “an expansive collection of thoughtfully curated” content featuring characters and stories from across Disney’s brands, including Pixar,Marveland Star Wars.Dawn Yang, the global head of entertainment at TikTok, said: “Creators are at the heart of everything we do at TikTok. Their creativity extends the life of films and shows into conversations that fans discover and share.“Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful.”View image in fullscreenMoana. Big entertainment companies have had to become more relaxed about the use of their intellectual property.Photograph: Disney/APIt marks Disney’s latest attempt to sanction the use of its characters by a high-profile third party, after ashort-lived arrangementthat allowed OpenAI’s Sora video-generation tool to use figures from its back catalogue.The decision, announced late last year, was controversial in Hollywood, given that Sora was seen as posing a threat to some in the creative industry, and longstanding issues around protecting copyright.Just a few months later, OpenAI abruptly closed down Sora after a backlash over some of theviolent and racistcontent produced using the tool, as well as deepfakes and misinformation. The closure was also seen as part of OpenAI’s attempts to streamline its operations before taking the company public.Disney’s announcement came as it revealed that the success of Toy Story 5 had helped it beat earnings forecasts. Its shares jumped 4.6% ⁠in premarket trading.Revenues from its parks and experiences were up 10% from a year ago, helped by a 4% increase in visits to its theme parks. Revenues in that portion of the business reached nearly $10bn.Rivals season 2 became the biggest original premiere in the UK and Ireland on Disney+.Explore more on these topicsTikTokDisney+PixarMarvelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Teachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big tech | Schools | The Guardian
description: Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy
Content: Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWithout guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedSchoolsTeachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big techPartnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversySupported byAbout this contentLee V GainesWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDarius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it.As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it.“It’s killing our jobs, it’s changing our society, it’s replacing humans,” said Saczuk, who teaches English as a new language at Long Island City high school in Queens. “In order to retain my job, I need to know how to use AI because it’s not going away.”So he turned to training offered by the American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US with roughly 1.8 million members, at its new National Academy for AI Instruction. Last year, the academy began offering in-person and virtual AI training across the country. The goal is to train 400,000 educators over the span of five years, helping them understand AI’s benefits and potential harms and also shape how it’s used in the classroom.Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Though the AFT’s $23m training initiative is one of the few structured programs for teachers, its funding, provided entirely by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, is stirring controversy. Supporters say the training is necessary for the future, but critics argue the academy pushes AI into classrooms, steering teachers toward tools that undermine students’ learning.Chasing new skills, going back to basics and pushing for collective action: how software engineers are adapting to AIRead more“It’s handing more political power over” to big tech, said Audrey Watters, author of Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. It’s really “dangerous” for educators to partner with companies that “seem opposed” to the goal of education, she said.AI has become a ubiquitous force in classrooms, despite the lack of official guidance. More than half of polled teens say they use AI for help with schoolwork and nearly six in 10 think using AI to cheat is a regular occurrence at their schools, according to aPew Research Center surveyconducted last fall. Meanwhile only about four in 10 teachers say their schools offer professional development or training related to AI, according to arecent NPR/Ipsos poll. And about half of all teachers polled say their school hasn’t offered any guidance on AI, or they’re unclear on what it is.Teaching educators about AI is a “moral imperative”, said Randi Weingarten, the AFT president. She argues that AI training empowers teachers to make informed decisions about how, when or whether to use AI in their instruction. And without outside funding, it was a choice between taking big tech’s money or doing nothing, she said.“There was no fairy godmother philanthropist that was sprinkling millions of dollars on us to actually create a mechanism to educate,” Weingarten said. “I am not promoting the use of AI. Educators need to know the tool.”For Microsoft, which is contributing the largest share of funding at $12.5m, the goal is to give educators a voice in shaping how AI products are used, said Justin Spelhaug, leader of Microsoft’s education, workforce and nonprofit programs.“By partnering with teachers’ unions … we believe we can learn directly from teachers on what they want and need in their classroom,” he said in a statement.But Watters asserts that AI’s presence in the classroom is not a foregone conclusion.“The industry would very much like us to believe that it’s not going away,” Watters said. “But the future is unwritten.”The classroom AI debateTech company leaders have largely painted AI as beneficial to education, some even claimingAI could replace teachers. But experts say there’s stilla lack of researchproving whether AI actually improves learning outcomes.In a 2024blog post, Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said he envisioned a future where “children will have virtual tutors”. AI could replicate some of the meaningful experiences teachers provide, such as making students feel understood and inspired, Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president, said in 2023 onthe Possible podcast, hosted by Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn co-founder, and Aria Finger, his chief of staff.View image in fullscreenThe Khanmigo chatbot, an AI-powered guide developed by Khan Academy, is seen during a math and science class at Khan Lab School in Palo Alto, California.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images“Imagine if you could give that kind of teacher to every student 24/7 … for free,” Brockman said.Microsoft believes “AI can help reduce administrative burdens, personalize learning and create more time for students”, Spelhaug said. “But there is no substitute for the role of a teacher.”OpenAI, which pledged $10m to the academy, and Anthropic, which committed $500,000 to the first year, did not respond to a request for comment.AI companies are already making their way into classrooms. Over the last two years, Miami-Dade county public schools, one of the largest US districts, began rolling out Google’s Gemini chatbotto teachers and high school students. Last fall,Microsoft announcedAI tools for teachers at no additional cost for educational customers. AndOpenAIandAnthropicoffer K-12 teachers free use of versions of their chatbots designed for educators.There’s been a longstanding playbook in which tech companies provide free training and resources to teachers in exchange for feedback and product advocacy, said Justin Reich, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor and author of Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can’t Transform Education.Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said.“Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”.The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said. By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said.“It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said.The concern is “understandable” though not accurate, Spelhaug said.“This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.”The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here.View image in fullscreenPilar Cuevas, a social studies teacher, looks up at her interactive whiteboard during her class in Inglewood, California. Cuevas gives her students homework in a Cornell notes format, which makes it more difficult for them to input their homework into an AI program.Photograph: Juliana Yamada/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesIna May speechat the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added.“They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.”Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal.Teaching without a guideThere’s no established approach for training teachers on AI. The technology is simply too new. But the academy’s leaders hope to work with teachers to find ways to use the technology without compromising students’ cognitive development, independent thinking, data privacy and mental health.“The sad thing is there is no map, and the terrain is changing every single day,” John Holleran, an AI academy trainer said to teachers assembled at a May session. “So, it’s going to be difficult for us to sort of figure out where we’re going.”Demand for the academy’s training is strong. A May training sold out within hours, leaving about 150 people on the waitlist, according to staff. The session focused on two key points: AI can’t replace teachers. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up.For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts.Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges.Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities.“Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.”Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves.To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning.The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian.“As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said.Saczuk, the teacher from Queens, considered the training “necessary”. Still, he left with more questions than answers.“What is the role of the teacher?” he asked. “It’s a big question mark.”Explore more on these topicsSchoolsReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)US educationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Palantir paid just £2m corporation tax in UK in 2024 despite lucrative public sector contracts | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Software group benefits from global systems and accounting practices ‘that enable tax to be shirked’, says union boss
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Software group benefits from global systems and accounting practices ‘that enable tax to be shirked’, says union boss
Content: Palantir expects its worldwide revenues to almost double this year to $8bn (£5.95bn), its CEO has said.Photograph: Juan Marcos Borsatto/AlamyView image in fullscreenPalantir expects its worldwide revenues to almost double this year to $8bn (£5.95bn), its CEO has said.Photograph: Juan Marcos Borsatto/AlamyPalantirPalantir paid just £2m corporation tax in UK in 2024 despite lucrative public sector contractsSoftware group benefits from global systems and accounting practices ‘that enable tax to be shirked’, says union bossJuliette GarsideWed 5 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe software groupPalantirpaid just £2m in corporation tax in the UK in 2024, despite holding public sector contracts worth hundreds of millions, thanks to tax breaks that are likely to reduce its contributions to governments around the world for years to come.The US-headquartered company, which has harnessed AI to securelucrative work for the NHSand the Ministry of Defence, is growing exponentially.Palantir’s shares bounced 17% in early trading on Tuesday after its chief executive, Alex Karp, forecast worldwide revenues would almost double this year to $8bn (£5.95bn), a result that hedescribed as “otherworldly”.But the amount of tax Palantir pays compared to profits earned – its effective tax rate – is just 1.4% globally, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research (Cictar).In the US last year, the company paid nothing in federal taxes and just over $2.5m in state taxes, the report states.Andrea Egan, general secretary at the trade unionUnison, which commissioned the report, said: “Systems that enable tax to be shirked on an industrial scale clearly have to change. The likes of Palantir need to stump up what’s due. Tech giants raking off billions in profit shouldn’t be free to pay what they please. Ministers shouldn’t award contracts to run public services to firms that are starving them of cash.”View image in fullscreenAlex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, right, signs a deal with the UK’s then defence secretary, John Healey, in September last year. Palantir was awarded a three-year, £240m contract with the MoD last December.Photograph: Lucy North/PAThe UK is Palantir’s biggest market outside the US, with £247m of revenues declared by the company for 2024, the most recent year covered by the report, while the majority of its non-US workforce – about 750 employees – are based in Britain.As of 2026, Palantir holds an estimated £670m in government contracts. A three-year, £240m deal with the MoD was awarded last December without a competitive tender.In 2024 the company paid just £2.1m in UK corporation tax, despite declaring profits of over £25m, giving an effective tax rate of just over 8%, researchers found. The UK corporation tax rate was 25% that year and remains at that level.Despite the size of the UK market, tax collected here was less than in South Korea, Japan, France or Germany.One reason, according to the researchers, is that Palantir is accounting for its UK revenues in the US, a practice sometimes referred to as transfer pricing. “A major pattern emerges of Palantir shifting revenues and profits from contracts in Europe to the US parent company to take advantage of the massive tax shelter it has created there,” they said.While 26% of all Palantir revenue is sourced from customers outside the US, only 4% of revenue is booked abroad. The reason for this is not clear, but researchers said they believed contracts with customers were signed with Palantir’s US companies, which in turn paid a service fee to local country subsidiaries to deliver the work.For example, Palantir disclosed £159m of revenues in its UK company filings for 2024, but disclosed £247m of UK revenues in its stock market filings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for Palantir said the company complied with the tax regimes in the jurisdictions in which it operated.Photograph: Kristoffer Tripplaar/AlamyA spokesperson for Palantir said the company complied with the tax regimes in the jurisdictions in which it operated, andcriticising its use of transfer pricing was “simply not credible”. They said: “Transfer pricing, which allocates a company’s profits among entities within the Palantir group of companies, is an entirely standard practice that is virtually universal for large multinational companies.”They said accounting practices could lead to different filings in different countries, and it was common for US parent companies, as the ultimate owners of the products sold, to record revenues earned abroad.Another way in which Palantir cuts its tax bill is by granting share options to staff. The company can reduce what it owes by the amount the shares are worth when they vest.Employees are liable for income tax on their share options, often at higher rates, but the use of shares rather than cash to pay staff shifts the tax burden from the company to its employees.A Palantir spokesperson said this was “a completely standard tax measure established under the previous Labour government [in the UK]”, designed to give employees a real stake in a business. “Crucially, it means that more tax is paid because corporation tax is 25%, whereas for these shares, income tax, which is higher, is due.”In the US, Palantir has stored up billions in tax credits from share options, and losses carried forward from previous years, meaning that at the current rate of profit, it would not be liable for US federal income tax payments for “nearly a decade”, the report states.Like other US companies, Palantir is also a beneficiary of tax cuts implemented under Donald Trump, who reduced the rate for corporations from 35% to 21% during his first term as president. In his second term, he negotiated a carve-out from an international agreement to impose a minimum tax rate of 15% on large multinationals.“While profits are earned in European markets, much of that income is returned to the US in the form of related party payments,” the report states. “While some level of related party payments may be justified, it appears that Palantir’s efforts are intentionally and artificially reducing taxable income and income tax payments across its European operations.”Palantir said it paid $148m in UK employment taxes last year, a figure that included employer national insurance contributions and some income tax paid on behalf of staff.Explore more on these topicsPalantirTax and spendingOutsourcingUnisonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get | Beauty | The Guardian
description: ‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to users
Content: Illustration: Sara Andreasson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sara Andreasson/The GuardianBeauty‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get‘Looksmaxxing’ culture has led to the rise of facial analysis services – but experts warn they aren’t backed by science and can be harmful to usersLaura O'ConnorWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTShareDanielle, 37, didn’t always have issues with body image: she used to be a model and recalls receiving positive attention from men. However, when two years of unemployment plunged her into a period of financial insecurity, her confidence faded. “It was easy to wonder, if I was prettier, if some of my features were different, would that help?” she said.So, when Danielle saw videos on TikTok about a “facial analysis” service that claimed it could provide her with “science-backed” glow-up advice, she bought it without hesitation. Three-hundred and thirty dollars later, after sending in selfies to be analyzed, Danielle received her personalized 30-page report from the company Qoves.Qoves scored everything from Danielle’s ear shape to the femininity of her features. It recommended she get a rhinoplasty, a lowerblepharoplasty, acanthopexy, chin implants and amalarplasty. Additionally: microblading, lash enhancements, filler in her temples and cheeks, a mixture of filler and Botox in her chin and jaw, and Botox around her mouth.double quotation markI do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollarsDanielleDanielle, who now works in tech in Colorado, is delaying any cosmetic surgery until she pays off the credit card debt accrued from her two years without a paycheck; once it is, she is interested in traveling to Mexico for procedures on her nose and eyelids. She also recently consulted a Botox and filler injector.Qoves states that attractive people “get better treatment everywhere, from the hospital to the courtroom” and claims it is easier for them to find jobs and earn money. There is some truth to this: the “halo effect” is adocumented phenomenonof good-looking people being perceived as smarter and more sociable than their average-looking counterparts, andstudieshave linked attractiveness tobetter pay. For Danielle, who asked to go by first name only for privacy, this promised material advantage was a selling point: “It gave me a motivation that I didn’t have in the past, which was seeing it as potentially helping my career and financial security.”From bone smashing to chin extensions: how ‘looksmaxxing’ is reshaping young men’s facesRead morePlastic surgery andnonsurgical cosmetic enhancementssuch as Botox haveunambiguously increasedin popularity over the past two decades, to the point that the aesthetics of bought beauty have become inescapable on social media. This has opened the door for“looksmaxxing” influencers, who take fixation with appearance to the extreme. Coalescing around the language of science and “self-improvement”, looksmaxxers claim that attractiveness can be quantified – that individual features should be analyzed and empirically scored, and physical improvements are made where necessary. The ultimate goal is to achieve “facial harmony”, or the ideal proportions of nose, eyes and other features in relationship to one another.Now, a slew of facial analysis services are benefitting from the looksmaxxing ethos, capitalizing on people’s insecurities about appearance under the guise of helping them become their best selves. Qoves, which Danielle used, cites peer-reviewed research to lend credibility to its idea of quantifiable beauty. It provides analyses for men and women, and for $150 recommends “nonsurgical” changes, such as injectables, with an optional $180 upgrade for surgical recommendations. Cheaper tools such as Facemaxify and Epica use AI to score the components of a user’s face against an opaque metric of facial harmony. In addition to recommending expensive procedures, the services often offer paid subscriptions. Epica’s specialty is skin and makeup plans for women, and it directs users to affiliate links for cosmetics and grooming products.“I do believe that the standard I’ve acquired for what’s beautiful is impossible to achieve without spending thousands of dollars,” Danielle said, noting that her confidence decreased when she started using TikTok. “All of the people that I look at [on social media] and think are beautiful have gotten plastic surgery.”Océane, 25, discovered Qoves via one of its beauty videos on YouTube, where it has more than 1m subscribers. Self-image was a longstanding concern for her: “I’ve always loved beauty, makeup and physical appearance, but I’ve never really liked my own image. I was always put down by my parents,” she said. “My mom wanted to pay for a nose job for me when I turned 18.” At school, kids bullied her. “They called me a dolphin because of my nose.”Océane, who lives in France, paid an additional $80 for express delivery and received her results from Qoves in two days. It provided her a sense of relief: the report didn’t recommend any changes to her nose and otherwise “confirmed what I already knew about my flaws”, she said.double quotation markThese sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disordersDr Tracy VaillancourtDr Tracy Vaillancourt is a professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa and one of the many scholars Qovescitesin promotional materials. She expressed concern about the negative psychological impact of facial analysis services on self-esteem. “This is what women are most insecure about: their appearance,” she said. “There are going to be some who are told they look better than they thought and that’s great. Is that really going to be sustained over time?” In other words, can a service that emphasizes appearance as a metric of self-worth ever provide someone with lasting peace of mind, or does it perpetuate a cycle of self-criticism?Moreover, though Qoves and Epica limit their services to adults aged 18 and up, the age restrictions are easy for minors to bypass. Qoves users are expected to self-report issues with self-image, with few guardrails in place to deter anyone with body dysmorphia disorder before they are presented with a menu of their flaws. “You can circumvent that so easily, it’s just going to give them the appearance of due diligence and making sure they’re not exploiting people who are vulnerable – but ultimately, they will be exploiting people who are vulnerable,” Vaillaincourt said. “These sorts of things are so destructive to people who have body dysmorphia, dysphoria, a history of eating disorders and people with low self-esteem.”Qoves referenced Vaillancourt’s work in a video called The Cost of Being Too Pretty to show thatbeautiful women face jealousy from others. But Vaillancourt isn’t a scholar of beauty: she researches bullying, mental health and violence prevention. Though Qoves correctly interpreted her research on physical appearance and hostility, she is uneasy about research like hers being used for paid services like Qoves, that she believes have the capacity to harm women’s mental health.Beyond Vaillancourt’s research, the applications of “science” used to back up these facial analysis services are shaky at best.‘The face doesn’t move’: Hollywood’s obsession with cosmetic surgeries has led to stiffer looks – and performancesRead moreQoves breaks down customers’ features based on “masculine and feminine facial qualities”, it explains in avideoreferencing a 2018bulletinin the journal Frontiers of Psychology. Dr Justin Mogilski, psychology professor at the University of South Carolina Salkehatchie, co-authored the bulletin. However, his research was a limited view of how a group of primarily college-aged Americans perceived certain features as masculine or feminine.“Do findings like mine generalize to every single population that makes up the world or a country? Or within every context where the attractiveness of a given feature can vary based on local ecology or culture? They do not,” Mogilski said. “So, would I make suggestions [for facial enhancements] based on our or anyone else’s data? I would not.”Some services do not make any pretense of considering location or cultural standards in how they quantify beauty. On its website, Epica reports a commitment to diversity and inclusion, though it is unclear how its methodology reflects this – particularly as AI tools are increasingly criticized for perpetuating racial bias. Qoves insists its analyses are appropriate for all ethnicities, and says it will “consider unique facial traits and characteristics common to your demographic” when creating a report. In reality, as some people have pointed out online, its promotional materials often replicate Eurocentric conceptions of beauty: slim noses and large, double-lidded eyes for women, for example. As one person commented on a Qoves video breaking down Bangladeshi women’s faces: “What’s shown here seems to reflect a beauty ideal rather than the real diversity of Bangladeshi women.”double quotation markI don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to [measure attractiveness and sell recommendations]Dr Mitch BrownThe lack of transparency around the methods and metrics the services use to measure attractiveness is its own issue. “These services owe it to their clients and themselves – if they want to be seen as credible – to be able to demonstrate scientifically” what their methods are, said Dr Mitch Brown, an assistant professor of psychological science at the University of Arkansas who has studied the science of attraction for over a decade. According to experts such as Brown, the available literature on attractiveness is too heterogenous, making any universal, population-wide generalizations questionable. And, even if we know certain features are deemed as attractive by a specific community, are these findings lasting enough to justify changing one’s appearance? Are they sound enough to support a paid service’s recommendation?“I don’t think the science is anywhere clear enough to do that. I would caution anyone against that,” Brown said.In an email to the Guardian, Epic said: “We are unable to disclose proprietary information regarding our algorithmic methodologies, technical frameworks, or internal product development details.” It continued: “We continually review and refine our platform to ensure our services provide a supportive, fair and positive experience for all users.”Qoves did not respond to a request for comment.I purchased my own report with Qoves and uploaded my selfies to Epica to see what these tools really offered.For Qoves, I was asked to check boxes confirming that I did not have “concerns related to body dysmorphic disorder” and would be comfortable receiving weight loss recommendations, and then asked to upload pictures of my face and side profile.A couple of days later, Qoves presented me with an 18-tab analysis of each of my features, along with a 16-page “aesthetic protocol”, complete with a disturbing mockup of what my face would look like should I implement its recommendations: a healthy dose of lip filler, makeup and the overly tweezed eyebrows I sported in 10th grade.‘Anti-ageing is anti-life’: why longevity culture is just ageism in a lab coatRead moreFor Epica, I was asked: how often do I use makeup? Do I want more control over my appearance? Instantly, I received a “skin health” score of 61%, with uneven texture highlighted as the main concern and a flood of serums advertised across my screen to fix it. I then moved to my couch, retook a selfie in the new lighting, and saw my skin health score jump to 81%.Before receiving these reports, I had never considered whether my mouth was upturned or wide, or whether or not Botox at my ripe age of 26 would be beneficial. I had not considered “dark feminine” makeup styles as being my look. But now I found myself second-guessing what I saw in the mirror. Just how downturned did my mouthreallylook to those around me? How would Botox or a haul of new makeup change features I hadn’t previously been concerned about?The language of looksmaxxing was in my head, and I didn’t like it.“Ultimately, there are going to be implications for mental health,” Vaillancourt said, “and it’s going to be about social comparison: never feeling good enough, never achieving enough.”In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978

title: The ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talent | Games | The Guardian
description: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesThe ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talentBig developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playingDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Last week, Asha Sharma, the new head of Xbox, laid outher vision for the future of the consoleand interestingly, the two titles she picked out as potential areas of growth were Minecraft and Candy Crush Saga – games that don’t exactly scream next-generation entertainment. Neither relies on hyper-realistic visuals, which is the north star that games consoles and gaming PCs have been aiming at for the past 40 years. They are, instead, well-designed, well-loved franchises that you can play and enjoy on almost any PC, console or phone.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The fact is, the quest for visual hyperrealism is breaking the games industry. It’s becoming more and more expensive to put high-end graphics hardware into machinesthanks to demand from the AI sector; at the same time, creating superrealistic visuals is an incredibly expensive and complex part of game development, leading to longer development periods. GTA VI, for example, has taken at least eight years to develop and is rumoured to have cost between $1bn and $2bn. By my back-of-an-envelope calculations, that’s around four times more than GTA V. Admittedly, the detail on everything, from the characters’ faces, to the cars, to the cityscapes, is astonishing. But will it be four times better than GTA V? Will it be four times more fun?It’s very clear from the shameful number of redundancies the industry has processed in the last two years that its model isn’t working. An increased focus on graphical fidelity leads to greater costs, which in turn leads to creative caution. Everyone is chasing a teeny number of slots in the big genres, and most of them are falling short. WasConcord– an OK entry into the grossly over-burdened hero shooter genre – really worth the $400m that Sony put into it, or would that money have been better spent on a few more games likeAstro Bot, or even a freshRatchet and Clankor two?View image in fullscreenWe don’t need no fancy graphics … Minecraft.Photograph: MojangI’m convinced that only a small minority of gamers now care about how many beautifully lit, ray-traced, frame-injected polygons a machine can fling around. I feel a wave of despondency any time a game asks me to choose between performance or fidelity modes. Sometimes I don’t even notice if I’m playing at 30 or 60 frames per second.Visual fidelity isn’t where the art happens. The art is in the style and substance of the game. Titles such asOkami,Journeyor Cuphead wouldn’t look better with more detailed graphics. I didn’t enjoyThe Last of Usmore on PS5 than I did on PS4 – or PS3, for that matter. We’re at a stage where developers have nailed the production of beautiful open worlds filled with lifelike characters. So what do we do with those worlds now? That is the question of the artist – and there are still plenty of artists left in this troubled business.Lets remind ourselves of the most important shift in visual clarity in the home video business: VHS to DVD. The latter format arrived in the late 1990s and still accounts for 50-60% of disc sales – 4K Blu-ray discs, the most visually detailed offering, come in at about 20%. This is an unfair comparison, of course, because the home video business has faced a very different range of competitors and market challenges. But the fact is, when people want to buy a film, half of those people will still buy it on a format that’s been around for almost 30 years.What have been some of the best games this year?Pokopia,Mixtape, Cairn, Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight,Mina the Hollower, Denshattack!,Mewgenics, Titanium Court … None would have been made more compelling by detailed graphics. Sure, these are mostly indie titles – they don’t have to shift hardware units, and they don’t have to showcase the prowess of first-party studios to shareholders – but it’s interesting, isn’t it, that the two games Xbox’s Sharma referenced for her road ahead had comparatively humble origins. So did Roblox, the title that Minecraft must contend with; as did Fortnite, possibly the most popular game in the world.If social media platforms have taught us anything, it’s that we live in an age that values rapidly dispersed ideas over “perfect” realisation. If digital TV platforms have taught us anything, it’s that people struggle to wait two years for a new instalment in a beloved franchise. And yet the market is saturated with high-end content; it is everywhere, and it is losing. TS Eliot once wrote: “Humankind cannot bear very much reality” – in art, in games, in real-life, we like to stop just short. That is the sweet spot. An ultra-high-end graphics chipset is not required to get us there.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat we do in life echoes in eternity … How Many Dudes?Photograph: Butterscotch ShenanigansIt’s an age-old philosophical question: how many men would it take to defeat a lion in combat? Or a gorilla? Or a duck the size of a horse? Well, thanks toHow Many Dudes?we can now answer that question. In this roguelike auto-battler, you build and command a group of differently skilled dudes – some are wizards, some are zombies, some are knights, but all must enter the arena together and fight whatever fate throws at them. The experience is a chaotic and ridiculous maesltrom of flailing limbs – there is tactical depth beneath the daft premise. The game isa cult hit on Steamand, dude, after only a few hours of play, I can totally see why.Available on:PC, AndroidEstimated playtime:Five hours plusWhat to readView image in fullscreenSupport your local games makers … A Short Hike is included part of a fundraiser for laid-off developers.Photograph: AdamgryuAnindie game bundleput together to raise money for laid-off game developers in North America hasraised more than $100,000in three days. The bundle, organised by the Communication Workers Union, isavailable on Itch.iofor $10 (though you can pay more) – it includes 127 games, including acclaimed titles such as A Short Hike and SkateBird. The offer is running until 13 August.Electronic Artshas been bought by Saudi Arabia’s wealth fundand a group of investors for $55bn (£41bn). It is the second-biggest gaming acquisition, and ends EA Games’s 36-year history as a publicly traded company.Microsoft has increasedprices forXbox consolesin Europe and the UK. At the lowest price point, the Xbox Series S 512GB model is going up from £299.99 to £429.99, while the Xbox Series X 1tb model will be rising from £499.99 to £669.99. The company has blamed higher storage and memory costs. Hoping things will improve next year? Nope.Samsung expectsthe situation to worsen through 2027.Sega has created a five-hour playlist featuring the music ofSonic composer Jun Senoue, asVGC reports. Available on Apple Music and Spotify, it contains 100 tracks and runs for just over five hours. Perfect for your next hike across the Pennines (or, indeed, any Green Hill Zone).OurSummer Games previewis in full swing, with pieces aboutClean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim, A Line Held Tight, about worker’s rights and lives, and the adorableTanuki: Pon’s Summer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ’em all after 30 yearsWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleyMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Dominik DiamondSingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video gamesHalo: Campaign Evolved – they don’t make ’em like this any more | ★★★★☆Big Walk – larking around with mates elevated to an artform | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenWhat if I’m becoming bad? … Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix game.Photograph: APHere’s a timely question fromMaddie, via email:“Whatever happened to the movie tie-in video game? As someone who first got into games by playing the Harry Potter titles on PlayStation, I miss these often derided treasures. Did they just go out of fashion?”Conveniently for me, the answer to this question is tied in with the essay above: movie games simply became too expensive and took too long to make, so the risks outweighed the potential rewards. What we tend to see now are more limited tie-ins, such as mini VR “experiences” along the lines ofStranger Things VRorProject Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, a forthcoming mixed-reality tie-in with the film. With the really big movie brands, meanwhile, we’re getting standalone offshoots –Indiana Jones and the Great Circle,Alien: Isolation,Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order… I think this is good, as all of those titles were very good – which is more than can be said for most tie-in games throughout history. Let’s be honest, for every GoldenEye, Lego Star Wars or Disney’s Aladdin, there were a hundred Charlie’s Angels, Top Guns and ETs. This is one example where technological progress has brought inarguable benefits.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VIMinecraftXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew Valley | Games | The Guardian
description: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Author: Nicole Clark
Headline: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Content: Charming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioView image in fullscreenCharming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioGamesWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleySince Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touchesNicole ClarkWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarming simulator games deliver on an escapist fantasy: going off-grid from the modern work grind, in exchange for charming small-town life and a farm to call your own. While these games have had dedicated fans since the days of Harvest Moon, the most popular today,Stardew Valley, contemporised the genre with a larger range of activities and lovable townspeople to befriend and romance. Created in 2016 by independent developer Eric Barone, it has now sold more than 50m copies and become the mould for so many other indie farming sims.Fields of Mistria is one of these farming sims in a post-Stardewworld – though it updates the core formula. Created by independent developer NPC Studio, Fields of Mistria has already proven popular: it debuted in early access (a pre-release version of the game meant for early players to find bugs and give feedback) forPCplayers on Steam in August 2024, and in the first month the game racked up more than 4m player hours. It’s for a good reason: Mistria satisfies all of those same farming sim desires but with more expansive character creation and a story steeped in magic.What is Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenAlready popular in its first month of early access … Fields of Mistria.Illustration: NPC StudioFields of Mistria is a farming and life simulator game with fantasy themes. You play as the new farmer in Mistria, a lovable small town in recovery from an earthquake, whose inhabitants hope you’ll fulfil their requests for various produce and supplies. Over the four seasons you grow crops, raise barn animals and attend events: from regular Saturday markets to the annual Shooting Star festival. Choose between a cat or a dog as a pet and accumulate toys and accessories for all your animals. My personal favourite is watching a duck and a rabbit play together on a seesaw.You’ll repair structures and buildings in town, such as the bridge or the Sleeping Dragon Inn. Donate supplies and funds, raise your renown level and town rank, and restore Mistria to its former glory. Along the way you’ll make friends with the townspeople: like Ryis the carpenter, who is shockingly quick at those repairs, or Hayden, the owner of Sweetwater Farm who has a haughty prize-winning chicken called Henrietta (and yes, you can befriend her, too).You can also fish, catch bugs and explore the mines; just be careful about selling anything immediately, because you might want to hold on to it to donate to the museum, or use it to craft cute furniture for your home. Your character evolves along with you: the more you do, the more you’ll be able to level up skills such as cooking, ironmongery, and archaeology.How is Fields of Mistriadifferent fromStardewValley?Fields of Mistria may sound like aclassic farming sim– but there’s a twist: you gain magical powers, thanks to the mysterious dragon Caldarus, who you can talk to by visiting a shrine on your farm. One spell lets you create rain, so you don’t have to painstakingly water all of your crops. Another lets you fully restore stamina, so you can get back to fishing for that golden eel. It seems the earthquake may have unearthed some unexpected parts of Mistria’s history.And while Stardew Valley – despite its lauded queer relationship options – has thus far only offered two choices forgender expression, in Mistria, character gender options also include “they/them”, “she/they,” “he/they,” and more.There are also some great accessibility features. In particular, you can make a day longer by slowing down time, giving yourself a truly leisurely pace to play. It’s an antidote to how frantic Stardew Valley can feel, especially during special events when you’re trying to pack as much into a day as you can.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre there romance-friendly characters in Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenEagerly awaited romance arcs … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioMistria is full of potential suitors, and you can woo any eligible villager regardless of gender. There’s Juniper, the sorceress who owns the local bathhouse, and who wouldn’t look out of place with the cast of Sailor Moon. Or maybe you’d like to romance March, the grumpy blacksmith who is a tough nut to crack – he’s atsundere, an anime archetype for someone who’s abrasive at first – until you know him better.Early accesscappedthe number of hearts you could unlock with each villager, and players have been eagerly awaiting the extended romance arcs in the full game. Without spoiling too much, let’s just say there’s also at least once romance option who isn’texactlyhuman.This lively cast of characters and love interests is ultimately what makes Fields of Mistria a standout in its genre. The town is always alive and bustling, encouraging you to spend time there – Friday nights at the Inn, where everyone gathers, being a highlight. Some of the villagers play Dungeons and Dragons, while others try out new desserts. You can ask socialite Elsie for gossip, or even join the kids in an adventuring club. There’s a real sense of place and kinship that makes playing Fields of Mistriafeel like a lovely escape.Explore more on these topicsGamesPCSimulation gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Video game maker EA bought by Saudi-led group for $55bn | Games | The Guardian
description: Company acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Company acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner
Content: Electronic Arts is known for video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield.Photograph: EA GamesView image in fullscreenElectronic Arts is known for video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield.Photograph: EA GamesGamesVideo game maker EA bought by Saudi-led group for $55bnCompany acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared KushnerJoanna PartridgeWed 5 Aug 2026 02.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectronic Arts, the maker of video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield, has been bought by Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund and a group of investors for $55bn (£41bn).The company announced the completion of the deal on Tuesday evening, only days after the EU gave its approval, the final regulatory green light needed.EA is best known for its blockbuster sports games including EA Sports FC (previously called Fifa). In what is one of the biggest buyouts on record, EAGamesis being taken private, ending its 36-year history as a publicly traded company.The company has been bought by Saudi Arabia’s PIF along with Affinity Partners, a private equity company run by Donald Trump’s son-in-lawJared Kushnerand the private equity firm Silver Lake Partners.“EA has created stories, characters, and communities that have become part of everyday life for hundreds of millions of people,” Kushner said. “We’re excited to support the company as it continues to reach new audiences, inspire the next generation of creators, and expand the ways people around the world connect through play.”The Saudi royal family has been investing in video games and esports for some time, alongside sports, media andcomedy, while the Saudi crown prince,Mohammed bin Salman, has a reputation for being a gamer.EA was founded by the former Apple employee William “Trip” Hawkins in 1982. Hawkins began playing analog versions of baseball and football made by Strat-O-Matic as a teenager during the 1960s. The company has been run by its current chief executive, Andrew Wilson, since 2013.EA’s games still have a dedicated fanbase, although its annual revenues have stagnated in recent years, hovering between $7.4bn and $7.6bn.Competition from mobile video game makers, such as Epic Games, has intensified in recent years, and one of EA’s biggest rivals, Activision Blizzard, was bought by Microsoft foralmost $69bnin 2023.As a private company, EA will no longer be required to report its financial results each quarter, freeing it from some scrutiny, which some analysts say can remove some pressure to meet targets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, there are often job cuts and cost-cutting at formerly public companies when they are taken private, although there has not been any suggestion that this will happen at EA.The company laid off about 5% of its workforce in 2024 but had 14,500 employees in March 2025 and cut several hundred jobs in May.On Monday, EA reported lower than expected revenues in the last quarter, blamed on a decline in engagement with its latest Battlefield game.Explore more on these topicsGamesMergers and acquisitionsSaudi ArabiaJared KushnerPrivate equityEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter Beinart | The Guardian
description: The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
Author: Peter Beinart
Headline: The candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against them
Content: ‘Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionMichiganAbdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat TrumpismPeter BeinartThe candidate has crafted a progressive nationalism and shown his party how to turn Republicans’ financial advantage against themWed 5 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.42 EDTShareEvery now and then, a Senate race sets the direction for an entire party. In 1991, a state official named Harris Wofford – advised by a foul-mouthed Cajun named James Carville – upset his far better-known Republican opponent to win a special election in Pennsylvania. He did it by promising to expand access to healthcare – and thus created a template for Bill Clinton’s presidential campaign the following year.If Abdul El-Sayed can follow up his victory in last night’s Democratic Senate primary by winning the general election in Michigan this fall, he will have created a template of his own. Despite his closer-than-expected margin of victory, his campaign offers a model for how Democrats across the country can answer the political challenge posed byDonald Trump.By casting the Michigan Senate primary as yet another battle between progressive insurgents and establishment centrists, media coverage of El-Sayed’s campaign has tended to overlook what is innovative about it. Like Zohran Mamdani and the democratic socialists who have won House races in New York, Pennsylvania and Colorado, El-Sayed wants to end unconditional US military support for Israel. But while Mamdani sometimes discusses Israel purely through the language of human rights and international law – as he did in his recentvideoarguing that Benjamin Netanyahu should be arrested as a war criminal – El-Sayed’s message is more nationalistic. He rarely discusses the Jewish state without linking it to Washington’s failure to address problems at home.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreIn a recentinterview, the New Yorker editor, David Remnick, asked El-Sayed whether he supports one or two states in Israel-Palestine. El-Sayed did not take the bait. He replied that his focus was less on “what’s happening there rather than what’s happening here”. His primary concern, he explained, was that the US was allocating money for Israeli weapons that it could be spending on schools in Michigan. While acknowledging: “I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike,” he said: “It is not my job as an American policymaker to decide what the ultimate peace should be. But it is my job to make sure that our resources are stewarded correctly for the people I’m responsible for: those kids going to those broken schools.”In relentlessly linking US military aid to Israel to unmet needs in the United States, El-Sayed is crafting a progressive version of America First. In 2016, Donald Trump exploited the resentment many Americans felt after a decade and a half of failed wars in the Middle East. Now, in the wake of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, El-Sayed is turning the tables. The difference is that Trump fused nationalism and imperialism: he said that the Iraq war was a mistake becausethe US soughtto “make western democracies out of countries that had no experience or interests in becoming a western democracy”; the US, he said, should havetaken Iraq’s oil. El-Sayed, by contrast, is fusing nationalism with progressivism. He’s not attacking the humanitarian assistance once offered by USAID. He’s condemning military aid to Israel (andalsoto Egypt, where his father was born) because it both violates human rights overseas and denies resources to Americans at home. This isn’t a message that only resonates with the American left. Last summer, the late rightwing activist Charlie Kirktweetedthat young conservatives “are skeptical about the state of America’s current relationship” with Israel “and they want to be confident America’s leaders are putting their own country first”. Apollin May by the Institute for Middle East Understanding found that by a margin of almost two-to-one, Republicans under the age of 45 prefer candidates who support reducing taxpayer-funded weapons sales to the Jewish state.But El-Sayed’s campaign offers Democrats another lesson as well. He isn’t only showing them how to reclaim nationalism from the GOP. He’s also showing them how to turn the Republican party’s financial advantage against it. In the last five weeks of El-Sayed’s primary campaign, outside Super Pacs supporting his opponent, representative Haley Stevens,spentmore than 12 times as much on television ads as did those supporting him. Most candidates can’t overcome that kind of disparity. But El-Sayed made it a source of strength. Again and again, he used Stevens’s financial support from the pro-Israel lobbying group Aipac – which contributedthe bulkof the outside money on her behalf – against her. He also linked her to other unpopular special interests. His supporters ran atelevision adhighlighting the contributions she had received from the Michigan utility, DTE Energy, which is widelydislikedfor charging high rates and allowing recurring power outages.El-Sayed’s relentless focus on the source of Stevens’s donations turned her financial advantage into an electoral albatross. When the Bulwark’s Sarah Longwellaskeda Michigan focus group why they didn’t like Stevens, “voters repeatedly brought up Aipac and the appearance of corporate influence.”El-Sayed performed this political jujitsu against a fellow Democrat. But this fall, and probably again in 2028, Democrats across the country will be badly outspent by Republicans. Donald Trump has turned the federal government into a cash cow for corporations and billionaires who profit massively from his administration and return the favor by writing campaign checks. Elon Musk alone recentlyannouncedthat he will spend at least $100m supporting Republican candidates this fall. Overall,reportedMS Now late last month, the Republican National Committee, the Republican House and Senate campaign committees and GOP-aligned Super Pacs have raised almost $600m more than their Democratic counterparts.Democrats need to hammer Trump on his unprecedented corruption | Steven GreenhouseRead moreEl-Sayed’s campaign offers a template for howDemocratscan respond: make the money the issue. El-Sayed drew a connection between Stevens’s backing from AIipac and her support for US military aid to Israel. But other Democrats can brand their Republican opponents as lackeys not just of Aipac, but of Elon Musk, big oil, big pharma or AI – and highlight the connection between their campaign funds and their support for policies that hurt ordinary people.This strategy requires Democrats to eschew corporate and special interest funding and run campaigns that rely primarily on small donors. There’s no guarantee this will work. Not all Democrats can deliver a populist message as effectively as El-Sayed. But the staggering corruption of Trump’s presidency, and the obscene wealth gap that his policies have helped create, presents them with an opportunity. Which means that El-Sayed’s model could prove effective far beyondMichigan.There are many reasons Democrats have struggled to defeat the Trump-era GOP. But among them are these: Republicans have owned nationalism and populism. If Abdul El-Sayed can win this fall, he’ll have handed his party a roadmap for how to reclaim both. Democrats across the country should be taking notes.Peter Beinart is a contributing opinion writer atthe New York Times, editor at large atJewish Currents, a professor at theNewmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York, and the author ofThe Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter.
