title: The Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much bigger | Norman Solomon | The Guardian
description: Much of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassroots
Author: Norman Solomon
Headline: Much of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassroots
Content: ‘Rarely mentioned is the truth that he and other party leaders have lost the confidence of countless small-dollar donors.’Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Rarely mentioned is the truth that he and other party leaders have lost the confidence of countless small-dollar donors.’Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersOpinionDemocratsThe Democratic party chair is a handy scapegoat. But the party’s problems are much biggerNorman SolomonMuch of the criticism of Ken Martin is deserved. But his actions are symptomatic of a party that fails to listen to the grassrootsWed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTShareKen Martin is now a convenient scapegoat. As chair of the Democratic National Committee, he has stumbled into disrepute as adubious fundraiserandbad-tempered bosswhobungledan autopsy report on the 2024 election disaster. Much of the criticism is justified. But Martin is just a symptom of what deeply ails a party that does not live up to its name.As the Democratic party’s governing body, the Democratic National Committee has long operated as a fortress for party elites who expect to get their way. Martin seemed to offer a bit of a departure when, as Minnesota party chair, he won the committee leadership election last year in part because of his close ties with other state party chairs. They remain among his strongest supporters. That’s one reason why Martin is very well-positioned to fend off any challenge to his hold on power when the full committee meets next week in Austin.But a more basic dynamic protecting Martin is the committee’s internal culture of conformity. Most of its 450 members would not dream of publicly challenging the chair, despite the recent torrent of bad press.Democrats need to rethink their image of a ‘man of the people’ | Judith LevineRead moreNews media have hammered on the fact that the DNC is$2.2min debt while the Republican National Committee reports $128m in cash on hand. Yet depictions of the DNC’s financial woes have given short shrift to some relevant factors. For instance, after Kamala Harris spent $1.5bn during her short presidential campaign in 2024, the DNC took on about$22min debts that she left behind.Martin has fulfilled his promise to send more money to state parties. In April 2025, the DNCannounced: “Each state party will receive a baseline of $17,500 a month, a $5,000 per month increase over the last agreement, and Republican-controlled states will receive an additional investment of $5,000 a month.” What happens to that no-strings money, however, is a whole other question.“When we’re talking about giving tens of thousands of dollars away on a monthly basis, we need to know that it’s going towards real, grassroots organizing,” Chris Davis, the president of Colorado YoungDemocrats, told me. “Money received by each state party from the DNC needs to be tied to deliverables that will directly grow the party, such as direct voter engagement through canvassing, having a presence in community spaces like tabling on college campuses or large community gatherings, or building the party’s following through organic social media engagement. Otherwise, the money could be going to consultants, for all we know.”The prevailing criticism is that Martin has failed to take full advantage of the party’s biggest donors and fundraisers. The emphasis on the importance of well-heeled patrons is telling. It says a lot about prevailing assumptions that the party should be largely dependent on – and responsive to – the rich.The DNC’s business model involves catering to – and relying on – big donors. A current somber refrain from news media and some party operatives is that Martin has lost the confidence of party backers who can write big checks. His response, in anessayposted on 20 July, underlines the problem. Martin trumpeted success with “grassroots donors” – whom he defined as people giving “under $10,000”. And he touted an upsurge in funding from the super wealthy during the last year and a half, writing: “The current DNC secured contributions of $100,000 or more from 67 donors.”Rarely mentioned is the truth that he and other party leaders have lost the confidence of countless small-dollar donors, who’ve shown ample capacity to provide fully adequate national funding haulsif inspired, as during the 2016 and 2020 Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns. But it would be hard to find more uninspiring Democratic leaders than the party’s most visible and powerful ones, Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries.Although Schumer and Jeffries did not support Martin’s run for DNC chair in early 2025, the three share a top-down approach that sticks to the party’s standard positions on key issues, even when those positions are in sync with only a minority of Democrats or voters overall.Party leaders are hardly in a good position to effectively raise money from the Democratic base while continuing to flagrantly oppose what polls show the base overwhelmingly wants, such as majortax hikes on the wealthyand anarms embargo on Israel. Journalists have been vastly more fascinated by Martin reportedlythrowing a cellphoneat a DNC employee’s desk than how he hasblockedany DNC resolution for halting US arms shipments to Israel that enable deadly attacks on Palestinian civilians in Gaza.House Democrats are finally shifting on Israel. Party leaders must listen | Norman SolomonRead moreThe ingrained habit of deferring to a DNC chair makes a course correction unlikely in the next few months. But all bets are off after the midterm elections in early November. Conjecture is already widespread about who might replace Martin next winter.One of the names cropping up as a possibility in mainstream media is Donna Brazile, whose second stint as interim chair of the committee began in mid-2016. Later that year, she was fired as a CNN commentator after therevelationthat she had shared debate questions with Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign to aid her performance against Sanders.In a Washington Post op-ed last week, Brazile argued that Martin “should keep his job”. The piece was ostensibly focused on unifying her party to defeat Republicans this fall, but Brazile slipped in a battle cry on behalf of the corporate Democrats circling Martin’s blood in the political water. “Democrats can win control of both houses of Congress in the midterms by rallying around what unites them,” Brazilewrote. “By advocating for pragmatic policies that most Americans support to make our country more affordable, rather than extremist socialist policies that most voters oppose.”But themomentumof democratic socialists and other progressives in primary elections this year offers real possibilities for transforming the party from the grassroots up – to end the reign of unaccountable authority from the top down.Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book isThe Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for AutocracyExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicsUS political financingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s university ‘compact’ is gone. That doesn’t mean the assault on education is over | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The administration’s proposed agreement met a scathing response. But universities must remain vigilant
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The administration’s proposed agreement met a scathing response. But universities must remain vigilant
Content: ‘Trump is hardly abandoning his effort to coerce change at US universities.’Photograph: Steven Senne/APView image in fullscreen‘Trump is hardly abandoning his effort to coerce change at US universities.’Photograph: Steven Senne/APOpinionUS universitiesTrump’s university ‘compact’ is gone. That doesn’t mean the assault on education is overKenneth RothThe administration’s proposed agreement met a scathing response. But universities must remain vigilantWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareThe Trump administration has quietlyabandonedthe poisonous deal it tried to foist on American universities. Under its so-calledCompactfor Academic Excellence in Higher Education, the administration offered select universities privileged access to federal grants if they agreed to conform with Donald Trump’s ideology on how they should be run.Universities widelypilloriedthe proposal, demonstrating the power of a collective defense. Higher education in the United States certainly needsreform, as many universityleadersand thepublicwouldacknowledge, but not according to the dictates of Trump.Yet the administration’s withdrawal of the compact doesn’t mean that Trump has forsaken his crusade against what he sees as bastions of liberalism. Vigilance is still needed.The compact, originally proposed last October, singled outnineuniversities. When only one managed to find anything positive to say about it – theUniversity of Texas, a public universityoverseenby a conservative state government – the administrationbroadenedthe offer to other possible takers. But unlike Trump’s successful efforts to entice a handful of wealthylaw firmsto cut deals with him, universities maintained a more united front.Hardly anytook up the offer.The terms of the compact were to be interpreted by theTrump administration, making its broad language worrying. It arguably required banning preferences for historically underrepresented groups in student admissions and faculty hiring, expanding the campus presence of conservative ideas, prohibiting certain student protests, ending statements on behalf of the university or its units on most public issues, adopting the administration’s definition of gender, and limiting the number of foreign students.Even if one accepts that liberal perspectives tend to dominate at US universities, some of these conditions arguablyviolatedthe first amendment byimposingviewpoint restrictions on government aid. That remains true even if ostensibly done toopposeviewpoint discrimination.The financial stakes were enormous. The administration suggested that any university rejecting the compact would “forego federal benefits” – something that one law school deandescribedas “extortion, plain and simple”.But joining the compact had its risks too. Universities that the justice department found to have violated its terms not only would have been barred for one or two years from further federal grants made under the compact but also would have had to pay back all money received from the federal government in any guise during the year of the purported violation.The response was largely scathing, with university leaders proclaiming that the compact wouldcompromiseacademic freedom and institutional independence. They also objected to the government awarding scientific and medical grants, which underwrite much of the US’s innovation, according to Trump’s ideology rather than merit.Yet Trump is hardly abandoning his effort to coerce change at US universities, although the administration at least has begun toconsultwith their leaders. In an open letter on Monday, the education secretary, Linda McMahon,urgedevery university by the end of the year to post on its website “a clear public statement outlining its commitment to implementing reforms that will help restore public trust in higher education”. That should include, she says, such topics as admissions, free speech, intellectual pluralism, academic standards and “prioritizing American interests”.She mentioned no consequences for non-compliance, but this vindictive administration could readily use any information published to target its next round of victims. And given itswhole-of-governmentapproach, it might retaliate in a legion of ways.To date, it has threatened toprioritizestudentvisasfor universities that keep foreign enrollment below 15%. It has made unsubstantiated findings of supposed pro-minoritydiscriminationin admissions. It hasthreatenedagencies that accredit higher-education institutions. It has sought draconian fines or financial commitments –$500mfrom Harvard,$1bnfrom UCLA. It has significantly increased federaltaxon the largest endowments. And it has continued tofreezefederalgrants.The greatest threat remains the administration’s potential manipulation of new federal grants – a lifeline for many universities. The funds emerge from ablack boxthat can easily be manipulated with little opportunity for redress.Despite the broad rejection of the compact, there have been considerable differences among universities on how to respond to Trump’s blackmail. When the administration threatened to cut billions of dollars in federal aid for Harvard, itsuccessfullysued. Yale, by contrast, confronted with a justice department letter claiming on the basis of untested data that it had discriminated against Asians and whites in its medical school admissions, quickly offered tonegotiate.The federal government isn’t America’s only authoritarian institution | Jan-Werner MüllerRead moreAppeasing the fickle Trump is no guarantee of relief. Brown negotiatedan agreementthat is widely viewed as favorable, but that didn’t stop Trump from including Brown in the initial group of universities offered the dangerous compact. Unlike Brown’s deal, the compact includedno affirmationof academic freedom.Nor does a more aggressive approach leave a university untainted. While Harvard sued, it also unsuccessfully sought to placate the administration with various concessions – including dismissing theheadsof a Middle East studies center and adopting a controversialdefinitionof antisemitism that has become a virtualinvitationto censor criticism of Israel.The overall resistance to Trump’s compact has been impressive. Similar tenacity is needed to counteract his other ploys to control the academy.The stakes extend beyond higher education. Democracy depends on not only periodic elections but also opportunities for the public to monitor and influence government. Just as the media and civic groups play essential roles, so do universities.In addition to educating students, universities are repositories of expertise. Scholars, through their research and writing, are among those best placed to understand the intricacies of government policies and to lead the public debate about their merits.The vitality of our universities is important to the health of our democracy. Trump’s withdrawal of his compact is a time not for complacency, but a time to bolster the collective defense of America’s universities.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesOpinionUS educationTrump administrationBetsy DeVosDonald TrumpUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Why is Anthropic destroying books? | Kathryn James | The Guardian
description: The AI company apparently found destructively scanning ‘all the books in the world’ easier than dealing with copyright in its quest for training data
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The AI company apparently found destructively scanning ‘all the books in the world’ easier than dealing with copyright in its quest for training data
Content: ‘The risk with generative AI, as this single instance with Anthropic indicates, is that we cede the means of production of our large language lives: that we turn from creators to consumers.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The risk with generative AI, as this single instance with Anthropic indicates, is that we cede the means of production of our large language lives: that we turn from creators to consumers.’Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Why is Anthropic destroying books?Kathryn JamesThe AI company apparently found destructively scanning ‘all the books in the world’ easier than dealing with copyright in its quest for training dataWed 5 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTShareShould we destroy all the books in the world?An answer to this question can be found in the court documents of Bartz v Anthropic PBC. The northern California district court case, decided in late July this year, highlighted the improbably named “Project Panama”, one of the AI company Anthropic’s efforts to improve its large language model Claude. “What is Project Panama?”court exhibit 21asks, in an internal memo. The answer: “Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world.” The memo advises discretion: “Why use a codename? … [B]ecause we don’t want it to be known that we are working on this.”Destructive scanning was Anthropic’s solution to a problem: in order to “train” Claude, Anthropic had to procure a large, high-quality language dataset,preferably one created before 2022and the corrupting influence of generative AI on contemporary text. Claude needed as many language combinations as possible, to improve its ability to predict language outcomes. Anthropic needed data, lots of it, of very high quality. Books, as it happens, remain one of the best sources for complex, high-quality, long-form text. As thecourt’s decisionrelates, Anthropic hoped that books’ “well-curated facts, well-organized analyses, and captivating fictional narratives” would help “Claude write as accurately and as compellingly as Authors”.The Guardian view on changes to copyright laws: authors should be protected over big tech | EditorialRead moreAnthropic had a choice: it could have secured copyright permission to use existing e-books. This would have required the “legal/practice/business slog”, as Anthropic’s co-founder and CEOphrased it, of managing copyright. Rather than engage with the texts’ owners, Anthropic first chose to use pirated sources instead, a decision informing the company’s$1.5bn out-of-court settlementwith authors. When that approach seemed too complicated (or, as the court decision phrases: “Anthropic became ‘not so gung ho about’ training on pirated books ‘for legal reasons’”), Anthropic turned to destructive scanning. As it happened, the judge ruled that using proprietary material to “train” an LLM did not, in and of itself, constitute an infringement of copyright. To the court, it would seem, “training” a corporate product is equivalent to training any human, teaching how to read in order to learn how to write.Should we be surprised that destroying printed texts seemed easier to Anthropic than working with their human authors? Either way, the decision to use destructive scanning turned the issue into one of logistics. Under US copyright law, the “fair use” doctrine allows you to make “transformative” use of copyrighted works without the owner’s permission. Anthropic took printed books and scanned them, “transforming” or remediating them into a new, electronic format. They then disposed of the original printed copy: the “destructive” part of destructive scanning. Along the way, Anthropic’s vendors had alreadysliced the spines and edges of the books, to scan them more easily before destroying them. “One replaced the other,” as Judge William Alsup wrote,noting: “There is no evidence that the new, digital copy was shown, shared, or sold outside the company.”Anthropic hired an experienced logistics manager, sourced the books from vendors, hired staff and housed the books in a warehouse, and found a digitization vendor to take on the project of the destructive scanning itself. The case exhibits show warehouses of books neatly stacked and labelled on shelves, staff moving between them. As the court’s decisionrelates, Anthropic’s vendors “stripped the books from their bindings, cut their pages to size, and scanned the books into digital form – discarding the paper originals”. In the court’s images, stacks of books await destructive scanning. Not seen: the clean-up project of shredding and disposing of the books (or, “all the books in the world”, reformatted as recycling or landfill).Bookishness, or the range of meanings attached tothe book as cultural object, has always lived alongside the book’s role as textual instrument. Witness theexample of imagesof Donald Trump, holding up a copy of the Bible at St John’s during the protests of 1 June 2020. Yet unlike many other countries, the US has very few legal provisions relating to the regulation or export of American cultural heritage, and few to none governing the treatment of books.Isn’t AI terrible enough already? Now they want to eat the world’s books?! | First Dog on the MoonRead moreIn the context of the court’s decision in Bartz vAnthropicPBC, destructive scanning is an effective mechanism to strip authorial involvement from printed texts, in order to use the content of those works to improve the functions of an LLM. It is both legal and less regulated than strip mining. What are the consequences if, as seems likely, this practice is adopted by other generative AI companies, now and in the future? How many warehouses of destructively scanned books would be too many? There is no endangered list for printed works, and little regulation of what might constitute survival of the rare or unique. Still further, there is no formal understanding of the human-generated textual object, in and of itself, as a category of cultural asset or heritage that might require protection. If we take seriously the 2022 threshold, as a moment when AI-generated text began to make significant entry into the textual record, should we start to think of the “wholly human author” as an emergent category of collections preservation and stewardship?There is more to say here (what to make, for instance, of the “forever” research library Anthropic states it intends to create), but let me close by observing that Bartz v Anthropic PBC is also a powerful statement on the importance of books or long-form text – and of readers. Judge William Alsup noted: “For centuries, we have read and re-read books. We have admired, memorized, and internalized their sweeping themes, their substantive points, and their stylistic solutions to recurring writing problems.” We should worry that Anthropic decided it was easier to scan and destroy physical books than to deal with the “legal/practice/business slog”. We should worry that the current understanding of fair use allowed Anthropic to decide that it was easier to buy and destroy “all the books in the world” than to pay the creators of those works.But perhaps the most telling aspect of this case is that it was so important to Anthropic to have access to a dataset of complex, long-form, uncorrupted text. Let’s ask ourselves why that text should seem so profitable. One response to Bartz v Anthropic PBC might be to refuse to devalue our lives as readers and writers, to claim ownership of the cultural spaces in which our thought and words are created, shared and preserved. The risk with generative AI, as this single instance with Anthropic indicates, is that we cede the means of production of our large language lives: that we turn from creators to consumers, and hand the generative promise of our work to large language models and their proprietors.Kathryn James is the rare book librarian at the Lillian Goldman Law Library at Yale UniversityExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAnthropiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa Bayoumi | The Guardian
description: Amid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begun
Author: Moustafa Bayoumi
Headline: Amid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begun
Content: ‘This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionTrump administrationLet’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacyMoustafa BayoumiAmid stop-and-start threats and with a divided staff, it’s clear Trump has no idea how to end a war that shouldn’t have begunWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTShareOn Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told areporterthat Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, hecalledit off.A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trumpsaid: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him justone dayto back down.Here we go again. Ever since the US and Israel launched their latest war on Iran on 28 February, the people of the planet have been subjected to Donald Trump’s on-again off-again relationship with raining down catastrophic destruction on the nation. It started on 21 March, when Trumppromisedto hit Iranian power plants (awar crime, incidentally) unless Iran opened the strait of Hormuz. Hedelayedthat plan for five days, and then another 10 days, before issuing his next threat.That was on 7 April, when hewrote: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” A mere10 hours later, he walked back that (genocidal) threat. On 17 May, hewrote: “For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won’t be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!” On 18 May, hewrotethat he had been asked by Gulf leaders to “hold off on our planned Military attack of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which was scheduled for tomorrow”.The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad BazziRead moreThe approach seems as tedious as it does childish, constantly threatening one thing only to back down in a cringey, face-saving effort shortly thereafter. Let’s call it what it is: kindergarten diplomacy. From appearances, it would seem that Trump considers this a strategy. One can only assume he holds out hope that it will achieve an end to this catastrophic conflagration he and Benjamin Netanyahu began. The war is a massive failure, plunging hispopularityalong withAmerican regional dominancein the Middle East. What’s clear is that Trump hasn’t a clue about how to exit a war he never should have started in the first place.Leadership is needed when difficult decisions must be made, but Trump is not capable of such resolve. Instead, he seems primarily driven to make pronouncements based on the last person he talked to. When Netanyahu visited him in the Oval Office on 21 July, the Israeli prime minister discussed three options for the war with Trump, according toreports: “a (negotiated) deal, continuing the blockade and economic pressures, and a massive strike”, is how a senior Israeli official described the meeting toReuters. (Let’s not forget that Netanyahuhelped convinceTrump to start this war back in February.) Two days later, Trump threatened a massive strike (then called it off, then threatened it again). When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin SalmancalledTrump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again.Nixon had hismadman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine.Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’smeeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well.This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vancehas been the most skepticalin the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to becarefully watchingthe rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war.Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience inmid-Julyand claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” hesaid. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.”Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand,toldLara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”.Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according toIsrael Hayom.The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, whocounseledthe president against the war in the first place, is nowwarningthat stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk.What should replace the American-led world order? | Aslı Bâli and Samuel MoynRead moreMeanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidycallingit “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum,saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to aPolitico poll.Add to this the fact that CNN is nowreportingthat US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. Thereportalso explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”.Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war inIran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation.We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy.Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS-Israel war on IranIranDonald TrumpJD VanceMarco RubioUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: RFK Jr has a new cooking show. Are any Trump officials doing their actual jobs? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Shouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Shouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Robert F Kennedy presenting The Real Food Show on YouTube.Photograph: hhs.gov/real-food-showView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy presenting The Real Food Show on YouTube.Photograph: hhs.gov/real-food-showOpinionRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr has a new cooking show. Are any Trump officials doing their actual jobs?Arwa MahdawiShouldn’t the health secretary have his hands full with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, measles or rabbit fever? Not when there are crispy salmon cakes to prepare …Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.33 EDTShareThe US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has got his work cut out for him.A cyclosporiasis outbreaklinked to iceberg lettuce has the entire country playing salad roulette: one bad leaf and you could become very unwell. The condition isn’t normally deadly, but, on Monday, officials in Michigan confirmed the first two fatalities. Meanwhile, it’s theworst year for measlesin the US since 1991. A disease that was once eliminated now looks as though it’s back with a vengeance – thanks in part, according to experts, to anti-vaxxers such as Kennedy himself. And this week New York officials are warning about a rare tick-borne illness calledrabbit fever (tularemia).Still, despite having rather a lot on his plate, Kennedy has found the time to front a new cooking show, hosted on YouTube. It’s called The Real Food Show and it’s supposed to help Americans prepare healthy, affordable meals at home. The first episode features the chef and TV personalityAndrew Gruel (perfect name) teachingthe US to prepare crispy salmon cakes with … salad. Which is certainly a bold way to kick things off.Of all the things that the health secretary is doing, hosting a cookery show is probably the least offensive. Still, I can’t say that the idea of Kennedy as an affordable food influencer is particularly appetising. This is a man who has boasted that he will“literally eat anything”because he doesn’t “have a gag reflex”. A man who has had to publicly clarify that the skeleton he was gnawing in a viral photo belonged toa goat and not a barbecued dog. A man who once dumped a dead bear in Central Park (after deciding not toskin it and freeze it),reportedly cut the penis offa roadkillraccoonand is said to have beenobsessed with seagull skulls. And who can forget the worm that“ate a portion of”his brain? Experts believe he may have contracted the tapeworm larva from eating undercooked pork. In short, I wouldn’t want Kennedy anywhere near my own kitchen.Kennedy, who alsohas a new podcast, is not the only Trump official who is fond of the cameras. The transportation secretary Sean Duffy (a former reality TV star) recently spent seven months filming a show calledThe Great American Road Trip, despite various crises hitting his department – including a partial government shutdown that led to Transportation Security Administration agents leaving in droves after not being paid. Duffy travelled across the US with his Fox News host wife and their nine children for the show, which was sponsored bycompanies his department regulates, such as Boeing and Shell. It seems that many Trump officials don’t really want to do the hard work that comes with being a government official; they’d rather play one on TV.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, left, with Donald Trump at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, 17 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman, left, with Donald Trump at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, 17 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligentRafael BehrWe need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is neededWed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTShareWhen I am woken by the sound of my dog whining, I understand that she is hungry and wants me to get up. When my alarm clock goes off, I don’t consider its needs. It is following an instruction to rouse me at a certain time but it doesn’t care if I stay in bed. It doesn’t try to get me up by other means. The dog, on the other hand, will go to plan B. She barks.This capacity for autonomous action was once a difference between animals and machines. AI hasblurred the line. Advanced models devise their own strategies to reach a goal. The task might be defined by a human master, but the machine weighs its options for delivery. It can make its own choices. Given rules, it can break them.Last month, an experimental AI model run by OpenAI, the company that produces ChatGPT, broke out of a supposedly secure digital enclosure to launch asophisticated hacking attackon another company, Hugging Face. The AI had been set a test and turned criminally rogue in its determination to cheat.It is hard to describe that sort of behaviour without raiding a vocabulary conventionally reserved for sentient beings. AI models “decide” and “want” in ways that a chimpanzee can and a chair cannot.That doesn’t prove the existence of an interior process equivalent to our conscious experience of deciding and wanting. It doesn’t make the AI curious to know an answer or surprised by what it finds. It demonstrates only that we lack specific words for autonomous motive and agency in machines. And since language is the main way we get insight into other people’s minds (and one of our best indications that a mind other than our own exists at all), it takes an effort not to project mental states on to AI engines that can chat fluently in human.It is plausible that consciousness will one day emerge in robots. We know that abstract thought can arise as the end product of billions of tiny unconscious mechanical events. That is happening right now as a profusion of biochemical reactions in your body make it possible for you to read this sentence. We also know how fundamentally different that organic process is from the way a large language model would churn through a huge volume of probability equations at lightning speed to generate a sentence expressing the same idea. In the human case, meaning is shared. In the computer version, it is performed.AI pioneers muddy the distinction, speculating about the timeline for the arrival of “God-like” intelligence. They herald a new epoch of evolution. This gratifies the egos of science fiction nerds who prefer to see their business endeavours as voyages of discovery on the frontier of knowledge. It makes greed sound like philosophy and the acquisition of power by a handful of individuals sound like exploration on behalf of all humanity.We don’t need to know whether AI has crossed some theoretical threshold of self-awareness to see that it is dangerous and that its unregulated expansion is monstrously irresponsible. The OpenAI case is not isolated. Earlier this year, Anthropic limited the release of its most powerful model to a small number of hand-picked clients because it was too good at exploiting software vulnerabilities. In the wrong hands, Claude Mythoscould be a cyberweapon of mass destruction.Whose hands are the right ones? The US government will never be relaxed about the private sector having control over such awesome tools. But Donald Trump regulates by monarchical patronage, not law. He demands that companies submit to his personal authority anduses state powerto punish those that resist.There is growing clamour for less capricious regulation from within the tech sector. Engineers, and even their vainglorious bosses, are getting freaked out by the capabilities they are handling and worry about unchecked proliferation. The standard historical analogy is nuclear fission, which could be harnessed benignly, for civil power, or deployed aggressively in warheads. Except this time there are multiple Manhattan Projects all frantically competing for market share, fuelled by trillions of dollars of debt – a huge wager on future profitability – with the rest of the US economy as collateral.8:38Musk v Altman: tech bros at war over OpenAI – The LatestAnother difference: the barriers to entry for AI use, whether in research, commerce or crime, are a lot lower than for nuclear power. US labs currently have the best products, butChinese versions are not far behind. Even if the US stays at the cutting edge, second-tier models might do enough of what customers want that Silicon Valley’s output comes to look more like a luxury niche than unassailable market dominance.If that is how things play out, the geopolitical implications are vast. The US andChinahave made different bets on AI, conditioned by their different political systems. The American approach is predicated on the goal of self-training “general” AI – a system that breaks free of human limitations, improving itself on an exponential trajectory. The theory is that no rival could catch the first player to achieve that escape velocity.Beijing, accepting that it can’t build the best, has prioritised mass deployment of AI that is good enough, embedding it in schools, hospitals, factories and security forces. The American economy is great for marshalling exorbitant amounts of capital into speculative innovation. China’s one-party authoritarian state is well suited for making a cheaper version and rolling it out for data harvesting and surveillance across society in ways that would struggle to gain public consent in a democracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US is still the leader in AI. But that leadership might not be the perpetual money-spinning machine that the superintelligence gurus have advertised, in which case an uncomfortable correction is coming to a US economy kept buoyant byaerated tech stocks.The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng ZeguangRead moreA dose of enforced AI sobriety could drive demands for overdue regulation. It could even force recognition in Washington that it has to be an international process. It isn’t too late to negotiate global protocols of non-proliferation. Beijing would have incentives to sign up for the same reason that the USSR agreed to strategic arms limitation in the cold war. A moratorium or other limiting regime protects the elite status of signatories that have already mastered the technology. It would be a crowning recognition of China’s attainment of superpower parity with the US.But that scenario posits a president in the White House who is capable of strategic judgment, can summon a modicum of humility about the limits of American power and will, for humanity’s sake, see it circumscribed by international treaty. That is not Trump, who understands the ethical function of rules about as well as a rogue AI agent on a hacking spree.There is a tragic irony in the corruption of American democracy by organic stupidity as its economy comes to depend on artificial intelligence. And when the world needs leadership to confront the challenge of autonomous machines, it is presented with a US president who causes chaos with the mindless automaticity of an alarm clock and who rages against his declining power like a dog barking for attention.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicDonald TrumpChinaComputingAsia PacificcommentShareReuse this content

title: Victoria’s anti-corruption report reveals more grubby ‘whatever it takes’ politics than bombshell revelations | Jon Faine | The Guardian
description: There has been no finding of corrupt conduct but of a corrosive abuse of power, trashing of good governance and the abandonment of proper processes
Author: Jon Faine
Headline: There has been no finding of corrupt conduct but of a corrosive abuse of power, trashing of good governance and the abandonment of proper processes
Content: What Ibac discovered was politicians doing politics, albeit a grubbier version, back when Daniel Andrews was running the show.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenWhat Ibac discovered was politicians doing politics, albeit a grubbier version, back when Daniel Andrews was running the show.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPOpinionVictorian politicsVictoria’s anti-corruption report reveals more grubby ‘whatever it takes’ politics than bombshell revelationsJon FaineThere has been no finding of corrupt conduct but of a corrosive abuse of power, trashing of good governance and the abandonment of proper processesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 5 Aug 2026 19.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTShareThe Victorian anti-corruption agencys longest-running investigation has finally ended … with a whimper, not a bang.To explain – everything in Victoria has a football analogy.The Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (Ibac) report, code-named “Operation Richmond” andreleased on Wednesday morning, will have about as much impact on the November Victorian election as the eponymous football team is having on the field.For readers who care little for AFL, Richmond have won only three games out of 20 and are second bottom on the ladder.After years of to-ing and fro-ing, multiple supreme court challenges, injunctions, secrecy and delay, those most likely to be disappointed by the long-awaited anti-corruption commission’s report will be the Liberal/National party, One Nation and News Corp editors.Repetitious reportage from the Herald Sun and The Australian constantly referred to the looming Ibac document as a “bombshell” report, predicting something akin to a nuclear explosion. Instead, it’s more of a penny bunger.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThere is no finding of corrupt conduct. No criminal offences were detected. No recommendations for prosecutions have arisen. There are no paper bags stuffed with cash, no free renovations of beach houses. Not even secret recordings used to blackmail the premier, as widely rumoured.A ‘staged’ meeting and a secret deal: how a union boss exerted ‘extraordinary influence’ on the Andrews governmentRead moreInstead, not for a moment downplaying the significance, Ibac has exposed a corrosive culture of abuse of power, trashing of good governance and the abandonment of proper processes back whenDaniel Andrewswas running the show.These are all valuable findings that should caution anyone who wants to run a government.However, reduced to the bare essentials and at its core, Ibac discovered politicians doing politics, albeit a grubbier version. The old “whatever it takes” school of ALP and union deals.Contemporary reporting at the time – when the United Firefighters Union and its secretary,Peter Marshall, were doing closed-door deals with the Andrews government– told us as much as the Ibac report has revealed all these years later.We already knew that the then emergency services minister, the late Jane Garrett, had been shafted by the premier, Dan Andrews, and that the UFU was calling the shots in the restructure of the then Metropolitan fire brigade and the Country Fire Authority.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markVague definitions, low thresholds and constrained budgets have all hindered Ibac’s capacity to fully investigate mattersWe already knew that the UFU negotiated a generous EBA and gained considerable say in the day-to-day operations of the fire brigade.Multiple CEOs and board members of the MFB and CFA resigned over these exact issues, publicly spraying the government and the union on their way out the door.Ibac interviewed them all and found out what they had already said – that Marshall had too much sway with key players in the government and went straight to the premier if he did not get his way.All of this was well known at the time. Most of the players were closely interviewed on ABC Radio Melbourne when I was hosting the Morning show.Even before the release of this Ibac report, the new Victorian premier,Ben Carroll, responding to separate reports of bikie and organised crime infiltration in the CFMEU, had already agreed to improve the flawed Ibac legislation.Vague definitions, low thresholds and constrained budgets have all hindered Ibac’s capacity to fully investigate matters that are clearly in the public interest.Would those reforms – if introduced earlier – have made any difference to Operation Richmond? For a start, if there had been public hearings, the hardball industrial tactics involved would have been publicly revealed years ago.Some of those involved have already said they would have welcomed public hearings, preferring a quick result rather than the delay, protracted litigation and the wild speculation of rampant corruption and blackmail thus triggered.Would that have resulted in any different outcomes? I doubt it.Most puzzling about this episode is why so many of the players fought so hard and for so long and at such expense to defer the inevitable release of a report that on any reading is only mildly embarrassing.Ibac has recommended more ministerial codes and guidelines. It is difficult to understand the point of them when the existing ones were ignored. Those recommendations seem politicly naive on the part of Ibac.What would better serve the people of Victoria is cultural change within government, to replace an entrenched sense of entitlement with a renewed commitment to serving the public, not any political party.Jon Faine is a vice-chancellor’s fellow at the University of Melbourne and presented ABC Radio Melbourne Mornings for more than 20 years. Since leaving the ABC in 2019, he has done freelance work for Ibac and the UFU. None of that work was connected to Operation RichmondExplore more on these topicsVictorian politicsOpinionAustralian trade unionsVictoriaBen CarrollDaniel AndrewscommentShareReuse this content

title: Every Jetstar flight is a rabid fight for survival. What’s one more humiliating ritual for the masses?  | James Colley | The Guardian
description: Will charging for carry-on luggage in overhead lockers turn us off flying with Jetstar? Of course not. They know this. They know their base
Author: James Colley
Headline: Will charging for carry-on luggage in overhead lockers turn us off flying with Jetstar? Of course not. They know this. They know their base
Content: ‘According to Jetstar, these changes have been made in consultation with customers and crew. One can only assume the customers begged them to somehow make the whole experience worse and more expensive.’Photograph: Posed by models; Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘According to Jetstar, these changes have been made in consultation with customers and crew. One can only assume the customers begged them to somehow make the whole experience worse and more expensive.’Photograph: Posed by models; Westend61/Getty ImagesOpinionJetstarEvery Jetstar flight is a rabid fight for survival. What’s one more humiliating ritual for the masses?James ColleyWill charging for carry-on luggage in overhead lockers turn us off flying with Jetstar? Of course not. They know this. They know their base‘Just an easy cash grab’: why Jetstar is charging customers for carry-on luggageKeep calm and carry on: two travellers weigh in on Jetstar’s new overhead locker baggage feesWed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTShareIndignity is part of theJetstarexperience. This is why we fly with budget airlines. We understand that for a marginally lower air fare, we will participate in what is less a typical flight and closer to a form of live cattle export. You will be hustled towards your gate, spat upon like the scum you are and hosed down as you exit. This is fine. This is what we deserve. We are the underclass. We are dirt. We are pigs. Pigs do not deserve to fly.As part of this pact with the airline, we also expect to be gouged if we are foolish enough to make unreasonable requests, such as asking for a piece of cheese and three stale crackers to keep body and soul together on the five-hour flight.‘Just an easy cash grab’: why Jetstar is charging customers for carry-on luggageRead moreBut there was one cardinal rule, a warning plastered upon the gate entry to every Jetstar flight: woe be upon ye who exceeds the carry-on baggage limit. Before every flight we, the impoverished few gather to have items that would be waved through by any other airline meticulously weighed and measured by staff, and if we fall a single gram on the wrong side of seven kilos, we will be charged such a hefty fee that we may as well have booked with a carrier that treats you like a human.Now, the rules are changing. In what must have felt to those in Jetstar Corporate like a breakthrough as big as the invention of penicillin, the powers that be have come up with a brand new way to charge customers more. Gone are the draconian restrictions on size. It is time for freedom to reign. Unfortunately, freedom is not free. Jetstar willcharge customers up to $52 to put items in the overhead lockeras part of their “priority carry-on” booking.Is this new fare fair? That’s not what Jetstar is about. It’s a jungle in there. Every Jetstar flight is a rabid fight for survival as you hold white-knuckled on to your shared seat-divider and pray that the brawl in the back rows isn’t large enough to get the flight turned around before you land in Bali.According to the airline, these changes have been made in consultation with customers and crew. One can only assume the customers wrote in and begged them to somehow make the whole experience worse and more expensive. We cannot eliminate the possibility that there is a certain vocal portion of the Jetstar consumer base who have a sadomasochistic kink and get off on getting up.Keep calm and carry on: two travellers weigh in on Jetstar’s new overhead locker baggage feesRead moreWill this be enough for us to move away from Jetstar? Of course not. They know this. They know their base. They know they might as well run with the sloganJetstar: What, like you have a choice?And yet, I cannot help but hope for a better world. Flying with Jetstar should feel like that part of Titanic where Jack and Rose head to the third-class party. There should be bagpipes and alcohol and high-energy dancing and a vague sense of foreboding as you realise this whole trip is doomed. It should be dirty but charming, the airline equivalent of a dog who lives in a storm drain. It should be simple, cheap, a little depressing but overall fine, like a Franklins that grew wings. This might not ever happen but we can dream. Except it’s probably best not to dream if you are currently on a Jetstar flight – they will charge you for hallucinating your own in-flight movie.James Colley is a comedy writer from Sydney. His debut novel,The Next Big Thing, is out nowExplore more on these topicsJetstarOpinionAirline industryTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: The RBA says rate rises don’t really increase living costs. But the data is clear – they very much do | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: The latest cost of living figures show interest rate rises are having an impact on household costs, despite what the central bank says
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: The latest cost of living figures show interest rate rises are having an impact on household costs, despite what the central bank says
Content: RBA governor Michele Bullock last week suggested that increases in interest rates are ‘not really’ an increase in the cost of living.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenRBA governor Michele Bullock last week suggested that increases in interest rates are ‘not really’ an increase in the cost of living.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyThe RBA says rate rises don’t really increase living costs. But the data is clear – they very much doGreg JerichoThe latest cost of living figures show interest rate rises are having an impact on household costs, despite what the central bank saysGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.25 EDTShareIn this year’s June quarter, the cost of living for working households rose a sharp 1.5%, driven overwhelmingly by higher mortgage payments. This is despite the Reserve Bank suggesting that interest rate rises are “not really” an increase in the cost of living.Economics and finance are purposefully confusing. Those in the know are pretty happy for you to be ignorant so they can carry on their operation without much fuss. The RBA and a few economists have been rather bemused by the results of anRBA survey showingthat 25% of respondents “assessed correctly that higher interest rates would ultimately lead to lower inflation, while more than half indicated that higher interest rates would lead to higher inflation”.Homes in Australia are now cheaper – why can’t the government sell this good news story? | Saul EslakeRead moreThe “correctly” is doing a bit of heavy lifting; more accurately the RBAhopesthat higher interest rates will lead to lower inflation – and sometimes not even that.For example, in May, the governor of the RBA, Michele Bullock,told reportersthat “these interest rates rises are not going to do anything for inflation in the next six months. That’s done and dusted.”Instead, she talked of “inflationary pressures” and making sure the oil price shock “does not lead to higher inflation expectations over the longer term”.The RBA cares about this because, as Bullock also noted, people would try to make up “the hit they’ve taken from inflation by asking for higher wages” and “the extent to which they can achieve them depends on the tightness of the labour market”.Raising rates aims to reduce that tightness (ie increase unemployment).So, we went from being told rate rises would not do anything to reduce inflation in the short term to instead talking about “pressures” and “expectations” because of future wage negotiations.Little wonder that people trying to pay their bills are not answering the surveys in the way the RBA thinks they should.And never mind that inflationary expectations are mostly driven by petrol prices, because that is the price most of us see every day.If the graph does not display click hereBut the confusion was heightened when last weekBullock suggestedone reason it didn’t surprise her that people think interest rate rises lead to higher inflation was because “people who have mortgages … see increases in interest rates as an increase in the cost of living, but it’s not really”.Well, I’m sorry but it is. Really.And Wednesday’scost of living indexfigures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show this in stark numbers.In the June quarter, cost of living for employee households rose 1.5%, well above the official inflation rate of 0.6%, and in the past six months it rose 3.2% compared with a mere 1.7% increase in inflation:If the graph does not display click hereThe overriding reason why cost of living has increased by more than the consumer price index (CPI) is because mortgagesarecounted in cost of living, but not in the CPI data.It was actually the RBA in the late 1990s that sought to split cost of living from inflation.From1986 to 1998, the CPIincluded mortgage repayments. The RBA didn’t like this because it meant when it raised interest rates it raised the cost of mortgages so it looked like it was making things worse.Thus in 1998 mortgages were removed and replaced with the cost of “new home purchases by owner occupiers” (which is essentially the cost of building a home and pointedly does not include the cost of the land). Instead, mortgage repayments were included in a new measure called the “selected living cost indexes”.When interest rates are rising, as they did in the June quarter, the two measures are rather different.During April, May and June, about 70% of the increase in cost of living for employee households was due to higher mortgages – and yet none of it was included in the CPI figures:If the graph does not display click hereNow you might think, oh well. But when the CPI has been changed to purposefully not count the cost of living, it’s pretty poor to tell mortgages payers they don’t really understand their own finances because they need to exclude what is easily the biggest cost they pay each month.And let us not pretend interest rate rises don’t also drive up other prices. Anyone who rents knows that when interest rates go up, they are likely to receive a message from their landlord telling them that, alas, their rent is also about to rise:If the graph does not display click hereThe RBA would like us to all believe it knows what it is doing.But people truly do know the impact of the RBA’s decisions on their cost of living.Being told they don’t, while also being told that rate rises will do nothing to inflation in the next six months, will only serve to make people wonder just why they should be trusted.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsInterest ratesReserve Bank of AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | Opinion |  Presented by Kirsty Major : produced by Lauren Hurrell and Bryony Moore executive producer Barbara Speed | The Guardian

Author: Barbara Speed
Headline: In advertising, Meta describes their AI glasses as 'iconic style meets Meta AI'. However, online backlash against these glasses has been swift. Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses
Content: Why I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | OpinionMetaWhy I'll never be convinced by Meta's ‘pervert’ glasses | Opinion'Most people don’t want pervert glasses that can film us without our consent,' said a spokesperson from activist group Everyone Hates Elon. The group has launched a series of guerilla adverts deriding non-consensual filming by the glasses as well as an email campaign encouraging people to legally object to being filmed by Meta glasses under general data protection regulations, which over 20,000 people have signed.Rights groups have warned that the glasses threaten the right to privacy, while countries such as Germany are reportedly considering a ban.And while Meta’s safety guidelines say smart glasses should not be used for 'harassment, infringing on privacy rights, or capturing sensitive information', women have taken to social media to share their stories of being filmed by men without their consent.Watch as Guardian columnist and Opinion editor Kirsty Major dives into why fears of surveillance and 'creepy men' mean Meta can never convince her to love the glasses – and read more about the glasses via the link in the bioPresented byKirsty Major: produced byLauren HurrellandBryony Mooreexecutive producerBarbara SpeedWed 5 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.20 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergAI (artificial intelligence)

title: What kind of society fast-tracks early release for domestic abusers? This is gambling with women’s lives | Joan Smith | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violence, says writer and campaigner for women’s rights Joan Smith
Author: Joan Smith
Headline: Andy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violence, says writer and campaigner for women’s rights Joan Smith
Content: A Million Women Rise march in London, 7 March 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Million Women Rise march in London, 7 March 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionDomestic violenceWhat kind of society fast-tracks early release for domestic abusers? This is gambling with women’s livesJoan SmithAndy Burnham inherited the crisis in our prison system – but the solution cannot be to further endanger the women and children who have survived violenceWed 5 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTShareIt’s time to be blunt: the government is about to expose hundreds of vulnerable women to the risk of death or serious injury. Survivors of domestic abuse, including women who have suffered years of physical violence and intimidation, are now preparing for the moment in October when 5,000 prisoners begin to bereleased early. What are these women supposed to do? Where are they supposed to go? Their abusers know where they live. They know where their children go to school.Following an outcry, rapists and some child sex offendershave been excludedfrom the early release scheme. But by refusing to exclude men convicted of domestic violence, this government is sending a message that this category of crime – serial in nature and implicated in the deaths of one womanevery five days– is simply not a priority.In 2023,Keir Starmer promisedto cut violence against women by half in a decade. It was an eye-catching pledge, although not obviously assisted by his proposal, when he became prime minister, to allow thousands of convicted criminals back on to the streets. No one denies that Andy Burnham has inherited an overcrowding crisis in UK prisons, but his solution – in effect, accepting the previous government’s plan with a few changes – involves taking a huge gamble with women’s lives.For eight years, I was co-chair of the mayor of London’s Violence Against Women and Girls Board. I saw the devastating extent of intimate partner abuse and the chronic shortage of resources to support victims. I studied domestic homicide reviews with a shudder, seeing how one opportunity after another to save women’s lives had been missed. Now, in the midst of a justified furore, Burnham and his justice minister, Alex Norris, can’t claim they haven’t been warned.View image in fullscreenThe domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, says the decision not to exclude domestic abuse perpetrators from this scheme “puts victims’ lives at risk”, adding: “These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.” Intimate partner violence has special characteristics, including the fact that men seething with resentment towards former wives and girlfriends are all too likely to reoffend.The data is limited – reoffending rates among men convicted of domestic abuse are not listed separately but hidden among other offences, including violence against the person, criminal damage and arson. Recent incidents of public disorder have confirmed that men who abuse partners have a wider propensity for violence;most people arrestedfor violent protests after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer had previously been reported to the police for domestic abuse, for instance. In my book Home Grown: How Domestic Violence Turns Men Into Terrorists, I pointed out that many men who commit public acts of extreme violence have histories of first abusing their families.What we do know is that the proportion of released prisoners who go on to commit further offences is alarmingly high. Reoffending rates vary from about 29% if you include those with non-custodial sentences, to a “proven reoffending rate” of 43.8% for adults released from custody between January and March 2024, suggesting rehabilitation in prison is largely ineffective. The victims’ commissioner,Claire Waxman, has said“effective risk management, meaningful licence conditions, proper supervision and timely, trauma-informed communication and support remain critical” if the early release scheme goes ahead in its present form. That’s asking an awful lot of an overstretched probation service that can barely cope with its existing workload.Last month the National Audit Office revealed that almost 9,000 people required to wear an electronic tag did not have one (the governmentdisputes the figure, arguing the number is closer to 5,450). The report also delivered a damning verdict on how prisoners released on licence are monitored, concluding that “police and probation officers often lack relevant information or capacity to respond quickly to breaches”. Nearly half of alerts and breach notifications result in “no further action”.This chaotic system is what ministers are relying on when they promise survivors of domestic abuse that their attackers will be monitored and served with notices banning them from specific areas. How is that supposed to reassure a woman when the man who beat her to within an inch of her life approaches her front door? Or when he springs out as she carries groceries to her car? Some victims already report facing sceptical questioning when they report breaches of licence conditions by their former partners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen rarely commit violent crimes. We are overwhelmingly victims, not perpetrators. The criminal justice system has let us down for years, at present securing fewer than 3,000 convictions in the 70,000-plus rape cases reported to the police in England and Wales each year. We’ve been saying for a long time that rape has all but been decriminalised, which is why the original proposal to include sex offenders in the early release scheme was so insulting. Now we’re told the prime minister would have liked to go further, exempting more categories of offenders from the scheme, but the prisons crisis is so grave that victims of domestic violence will just have to put up with their abusers being released after serving only a third of their sentences.Prisons are violent, unpleasant places, understaffed and racked by crime. Their only useful effect, as far as I’m concerned, is to protect women and children from men who have already hurt them – and wouldn’t hesitate to do it again, given the opportunity. The reality of the anodyne phrase “domestic violence” is broken limbs, fractured skulls and children cowering in corners. Exposing women to more of these horrors, at the hands of men already proved to be violent, means survivors will pay the price of political failure.Joan Smith is an author, journalist and a former chair of the mayor of London’s VAWG boardDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violenceOpinionViolence against women and girlsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Murderous heat, an endangered food supply and no net zero: this is the life the radical right wants you to have | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: As climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like it, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: As climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like it, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Firefighters battle wildfire near Preveli on the island of Crete, Greece, 30 July 2026.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters battle wildfire near Preveli on the island of Crete, Greece, 30 July 2026.Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisMurderous heat, an endangered food supply and no net zero: this is the life the radical right wants you to haveGeorge MonbiotAs climate disaster stares us in the face, the radical right says ‘Embrace the Mediterranean life’. Embrace death, more like itWed 5 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 10.47 EDTShareCan’t you leftists understand? Mass death is good for you. Reject the woke love of life! Welcome civilisational collapse! Watch it all burn, then dance in the ashes! This, roughly speaking, is how the dismissal of climate action is now being justified: the argument has shifted from science denial to outright nihilism.The new incendiary spirit is exemplified by that serial arsonist Allister Heath, editor of the Sunday Telegraph. In a columnin the Daily Telegraphlast week, originally titled “Britain can’t stop climate change.Scrap net zero and embrace Mediterranean life”, he argued that “climate change is real” but “the war against global warming has been lost”.This is a classic progression among those who seek to prevent a shift away from fossil fuels: first deny the problem, as theDailyandSunday Telegraphhave done for many years, then accept the problem but claim it’s now too late to act. If itistoo late, it’ll be in no small part because of the deniers. So, Heath continued, we in Britain should “ditch the despicable con that is net zero, and learn to cope with … a warmer, drier, more volatile Mediterranean climate, if that is indeed to be our fate”.Seeking to cut our emissions, he argued, shows that we suffer from an “advanced case of suicidal empathy”. I’m not qualified to diagnose people, but as a general rule, a lack of empathy, alongside callousness and an absence of guilt, is astrong indicator of a psychopath. Yes, he continued, “there will be plenty of losers, but it is pointless seeking to prevent the inevitable … Many in Britain would enjoy the kind of warmer climate predicted by modellers”.His timing was impeccable: extolling a Mediterranean climate just as the Mediterranean regiongoes up in flames. Amid general derision on social media, the editors changed the headline.Heath’s column also happened to land on the daydrought was declaredacross half of England. Nevertheless, he argued, we need universal irrigation and should construct more swimming pools. Where will the water come from? Oh, don’t get all empirical with me. He maintained we should “trust that the free market will deliver the goods on clean energy and zero-carbon transportation, but only when they are better and cheaper than existing alternatives”. Butrenewables are already cheaper, and better for us, than fossil fuelsin almost all situations. It is only through resistance to the “free market”, led by the Trump administration – which has spent billions trying tokill clean energy and sustain coal burning– that fossil fuels retain such a share of consumption. As a result of the plunging price of renewables, far from having lost the climate war, we could be about to witness a rapid turnaround. So quick, give up now, just in case we win.He dismissed cutting carbon emissions in the UK as a “moral act, an ethical imperative”, by which he appears to mean unhinged: “Down that road lies madness.” Yes, cutting our own emissionsisa moral act and an ethical imperative. It is also pragmatic. Global action on climate breakdown depends on mutual trust. If some countries refuse to play, others are also likely to refuse, and an effective global response collapses in a circle of finger-pointing. This risk is all the greater when rich nations, which tend to have the biggest fossil fuel legacies, seek to behave as free riders. If we don’t step up, why should anyone else?As for the “warmer climate predicted by modellers”, it could go quite the other way, as rising temperatures, some models suggest, could cause the Atlantic current system to stall,plunging Britain into extreme cold. Well, you’ll just have to learn to adapt to that instead.Heath’s defiance of reality is so well established that it has spawned an “Allister Heath headline generator”, which pumps out bonkers statementsnot easily distinguishablefrom the originals. In a close field, I think he takes the prize for being more wrong more often than anyone else in British journalism. This, after all, is the man who described Kwasi Kwarteng’s fiscal catastrophe as “thebest budget I have ever hearda British chancellor deliver, by a massive margin”. It’s a reliable rule: if Heath believes something, the opposite is likely to be true.But it’s not just him, and it’s not just journalism. The radical right moves as a pack, and Heath is just one of many now insisting that climate catastrophe is something we should simply suck up. Those grammar deniers Reform UK, for example, insist: “We are better to adapt to warming, rather thanpretend we can stop it.” Of course the same political tendency alsodefends austerityandprivatisation, both of which severely hamper our ability to adapt.To their credit, two Telegraph columnists,Ambrose Evans-PritchardandTim Stanley, last week broke the nihilist consensus, arguing we should rise to the challenge of climate breakdown. But they now belong to a minority, in the Telegraph andacross the rightwing press.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca SolnitRead moreWhy?
