Because most of the media, most of the time, provides a platform for people who say things that have the effect of serving capital, whether or not they are true, whether or not they are coherent, whether or not they may hasten disaster. While renewables are cheaper than fossil fuels in nearly all circumstances,fossil fuels are more profitable, because useful reserves are limited and can each be monopolised by a single corporation, while prices can suddenly take flight in times of war or chaos. Almost all the very rich are heavily invested in them. The result is that any attempt to restrict the use of fossil fuels is perceived as class war. Nonsensical justifications for the status quo then follow as automatically as the Allister Heath headline generator.So “embrace Mediterranean life”. But without the wine, which, as another Telegraph column laments, is becoming “smoke tainted” by all those fires triggered by some unmentioned and mysterious force. And without the food, whose production, thanks to the drought and heatwaves, isat grave riskin southern Europe, as it is here. And without your lovely gite, which might have been incinerated. Or the lush green landscape, also lost to the flames. Or the balmy summer temperatures, nowreplaced by murderous heat. Oh go on then, you know what I really mean: embrace death.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionExtreme heatWildfiresDroughtEnglandNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous | Yiannis Baboulias | The Guardian
description: Droughts that were once a century now happen every year, and the impact on wildlife, industrial output and culture itself is catastrophic, says Yiannis Baboulias, a Greek writer based in London
Author: Yiannis Baboulias
Headline: Droughts that were once a century now happen every year, and the impact on wildlife, industrial output and culture itself is catastrophic, says Yiannis Baboulias, a Greek writer based in London
Content: The dry Danube, in Rasova, Romania, 3 August.Photograph: Vadim Ghirdă/APView image in fullscreenThe dry Danube, in Rasova, Romania, 3 August.Photograph: Vadim Ghirdă/APOpinionRiversEurope’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrousYiannis BabouliasDroughts that were once a century now happen every year, and the impact on wildlife, industrial output and culture itself is catastrophicWed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTShareLast week, 186 passengers had to be evacuated from the cruise ship Viking Ullur,after it ran aground on a sandbankin the Danube. Others have beenleft stranded, unable to move between Vienna and Budapest. Passengers stood on deck, the Habsburg splendour around them out of reach as the river fell to 41cm in Budapest, within 8cm of its 2018 all-time low. Elsewhere on the Hungarian stretch of the river, new record lows were recorded.Farther east inRomania, the Danube recorded its lowest water levels since 1996. A river’s flow is measured in cubic metres per second, and at Baziaș, where the river enters the country, it stood at 1,700m³/s, against a July average of 4,700m³/s. Ferry services were suspended, as were grain barges.While providing the most glamorous images, the Danube is just one of the major rivers veining throughEuropethat has been suffering through this summer’s drought. Farther north, the Rhine, perhaps the most vital fresh-water transport route in the continent, broke its own records, with levels at Kaub dropping to about 40cm, the level at which shipping runs in emergency mode, with barges loading as little as a fifth of normal capacity.The extent and frequency of these summer droughts has surprised even the most pessimisticexpert observers. In 2018, Germany’s weather service designated that year aJahrhundertsommer– a once-in-a-century summer – as the Rhine spent 132 days at low water. “The events of 2018 can’t be allowed to be repeated,” said Andreas Scheuer, then the federal transport minister. But they were.In 2022, EU scientists described the drought gripping the continent asthe worst in at least 500 years. Then in 2025, Germany logged its driest March on record and another low-water summer. And this July, the Danube’s water level was at a low it didn’t reach until October during the 2018 drought. The crisis is now happening every year, and it’s arriving earlier.A study led by Dr Sehrish Usman at the University of Mannheim, working with European Central Bank economists, found that last summer’s heatwaves, droughts and floods hit a quarter of all EU regions,causing short-term lossesof at least €43bn, with the total expected to reach €126bn by 2029. On the Rhine alone, the Kiel Institute has shown that a single month of low watercuts German industrial productionby about 1%.The immense wildfires we’re seeing across the continent are not separate from this phenomenon, as the same mechanism is driving both: a hotter atmosphere is soaking up soil moisture faster than the rain can replenish it. That dry soil can’t feed the rivers, or the plants, which end up feeding the fires instead. France has recorded more than three times its annual average number of wildfires already this summer, assoil moisture is the lowest Météo-France has ever recordedthis early in the season. The fires, like the river crisis, are arriving ahead of schedule.The damage these events inflict on the natural world is harder to put into numbers. In 2018, Swiss authoritiespulled about a tonneof dead grayling from the Rhine (about 30% of the annual catch), as water temperatures surpassed 25C. By 2022, the reintroduced Atlantic salmon the river had spentdecades nursing backcould no longer reach their spawning grounds. Pollutant concentrations rise as water levels fall. On the Danube that year,oxygen levels fellclose to the threshold below which trout can’t survive. Dredging was banned, and wastewater plants were placed on standby. Then this month, water levels dropped to the point where Romania was forced to shut down nuclear plants beside the Danube for the first time, as the reactors use river water to cool their cores, and if the river drops too far they can’t run safely. The country declared a nationwide state of emergency and detonated 180kg of explosives on the Bala canal to clear a rock obstructing the flow, buying the remaining reactor a few more days. Meanwhile in Hungary, the Paks nuclear plant, which normally supplies almost half of the country’s electricity, could be fully shut down within days.View image in fullscreenUnderwater explosives are used to clear rocks and improve water flow to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant in Izvoarele, Romania, 3 August.Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/APAbout seven years ago, when I first started looking into what’s happening to Europe’s great waterways, I contactedChristina Gruber, a freshwater ecologist and artist based in Vienna, who has been watching this longer than most. I wanted to understand the effects these events have on the societies that have built big parts of their identity and culture around these rivers. She told me about an island her friends used to swim out to in the summer, to get away from the grownups. By 2019, people could walk to it. We’re also seeing theslow disappearanceof the Danube’s fishers, all but gone from a river that has fed them since at least 300BC. The people who knew the river best were gone, as the water went with them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 1986, the Italian polymath Claudio Magris travelled the Danube from source to delta andwrote a bookabout what a river means. The Danube was the connecting tissue of Mitteleuropa. Vienna’s concert halls, Budapest’s parliament, the Ottoman and Habsburg and Byzantine sediment accumulated along its banks over centuries, into much that we understand as a shared civilisation. The Rhine is Germany’s industrial spine, the artery that carried the coal and iron ore on which a particular idea of the country was built.Magris was already writing about a river in cultural decline before the water levels started being a central part of the question. “Century event” has disappeared from the official vocabulary, as seven consecutive years of records made it ridiculous, and replaced by superlatives such as “all-time low”, “historic”, “30-year low”. The problem is that this language still treats each summer as an exceptional incident, with hope for a recovery attached. But this assumption too, that Europe’s great rivers will keep being what they were, regardless of what we do to the climate that feeds them, should also be abandoned.Yiannis Baboulias is a Greek writer based in London. His work focuses on European politics, the environment and the far rightExplore more on these topicsRiversOpinionDroughtEuropeWildfiresWaterFishHungarycommentShareReuse this content

title: Keep calm and carry on: two travellers weigh in on Jetstar’s new overhead locker baggage fees | Nick Miller and Warren Murray | The Guardian
description: Is the budget airline’s plan to charge for carry-on bag storage a tax on bad behaviour, or just plain old price gouging? Two Guardian staffers check in
Author: Warren Murray
Headline: Is the budget airline’s plan to charge for carry-on bag storage a tax on bad behaviour, or just plain old price gouging? Two Guardian staffers check in
Content: Will extra luggage fees discourage shoving massive bags into the overhead compartments, or is it all a massive gouge?Photograph: aquaArts studio/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill extra luggage fees discourage shoving massive bags into the overhead compartments, or is it all a massive gouge?Photograph: aquaArts studio/Getty ImagesOpinionJetstarKeep calm and carry on: two travellers weigh in on Jetstar’s new overhead locker baggage feesNick MillerandWarren MurrayIs the budget airline’s plan to charge for carry-on bag storage a tax on bad behaviour, or just plain old price gouging? Two Guardian staffers check inTue 4 Aug 2026 23.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTShareIn significant news for budget travellers, Jetstar will charge its passengersup to $52 to put carry-on baggage in the overhead locker. Will the new rules finally bring an end to the entitled carry-on culture, where people hold up the airline just to jam their oversized suitcase into the overhead locker? Or is it just another way for cut-price airlines to gouge passengers?Two well-travelled Guardian staffers battle it out.The case for: ‘The carry-on arms race has gotten insufferable’Tax the behaviour you hate, right? Can I hear it from the economists here? Is someone being awful? Make them pay for it and maybe they will reconsider.Jetstar to charge fees up to $52 to put carry-on baggage in overhead lockersRead moreAnd the behaviour I hate on planes (OK,oneof the behaviours I hate on planes, I have a list), is the Entitled Carry-On.Apologies to those who indulge: I have silently raged at you for years. You bought an unnecessarily huge suitcase, and you probably put another bag on top of it that you smuggled past the gate.You congratulated yourself at the prospect of not having to wait a few minutes at the carousel after debarkation. And you jammed the lot in the overhead locker, leaving no space for travellers (moi) with more modest and sensible needs, perhaps nappies and food for children, or jocks and a shirt for a quick overnight stay.Perhaps you didn’t get to the gate early enough, so after you boarded you squeezed up and down the aisle with your overpacked monstrosity in search of someone else’s locker space to colonise. Perhaps your baggage has left no space for mine, and I am the poor wanderer: apologising, blameless, bereft.View image in fullscreen‘Jetstar have made the overhead into the overhead,’ writes Nick Miller.Photograph: ozgurcankaya/Getty ImagesSo pay up. If you hadn’t been so obsessed with squeezing everything in, if this carry-on arms race hadn’t gotten so insufferable, perhaps we wouldn’t have to have come to this. Civilisation is a social compact, and we all pay the price when free-riders abuse the environment (METAPHOR!).Jetstar have made the overhead into the overhead. I applaud you for this,Jetstar. For this, and absolutely nothing else (refers to aforementioned list).– Nick MillerThe case against: ‘I can foresee having to stare at someone’s arse crack indefinitely’For years we were led to believe that only having carry-on baggage, and no checked baggage, was the best way to ensure your flight would depart on time. Now, apparently, this solution has morphed into a problem, with passengers supposedly blocking the aisles and stressing out while they try to heft their cases into the overhead bins.The new solution is to cram your carry-on bag under the seat in front, or – surprise surprise – be charged for it.Jetstar promises that as a fringe benefit, the weigh-and-shame procedure at the departure gates will be a thing of the past. At the same time, the airline announces those underseat bags will have to fit within certain dimensions. So now, instead of having your overhead bag weighed – what, you’ll have your under-seat bag put to the tape measure in the event of a line call? How will that make things quicker?On board, instead of people holding up the aisle to stow their bags into the overhead bins – frustrating, yes, but a task in which, if there’s a genuine struggle, neighbouring passengers usually pitch in – I can foresee having to stare at someone’s arse crack indefinitely while they bend over and try to ram their bags under the seat in front. Unlike the overhead scenario, no one is going to get down and grub around on the floor of a Jetstar plane to help you; nor is there room to do so.This will also extend the knees-in-back-of-seat phenomenon to the feeling of having your bum rummaged when someone tries to get their headphones out of their wedged-in bag from under your pew.This reasonably well-seasoned air traveller, along with many others I’m sure, has long since adapted to going a week or so interstate or overseas with only carry-on luggage, sized to fit the overhead lockers – no checked bags. An investment in well designed, lightweight pull-aboard luggage soon pays off in terms of paying less to fly.Now, any such luggage becomes a write-off if it fails to conform to the underseat stowage dimensions.I seriously doubt this has anything to do with speeding up boarding and departure – Jetstar never seem to have given much of a shit about keeping to schedule – and much more to do with finding a new way to gouge passengers for their luggage again, in an age when many have learned to fly light and save.– Warren MurrayExplore more on these topicsJetstarOpinionTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Homes in Australia are now cheaper – why can’t the government sell this good news story?  | Saul Eslake | The Guardian
description: Ministers love to claim credit for things like cheaper petrol and cheaper pharmaceuticals – why not cheaper housing?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ministers love to claim credit for things like cheaper petrol and cheaper pharmaceuticals – why not cheaper housing?
Content: Falling property prices are ‘the most effective antidote to the problems of deteriorating housing affordability and declining access to home ownership,’ Saul Eslake writes.Photograph: Jesse Thompson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFalling property prices are ‘the most effective antidote to the problems of deteriorating housing affordability and declining access to home ownership,’ Saul Eslake writes.Photograph: Jesse Thompson/Getty ImagesOpinionHousingHomes in Australia are now cheaper – why can’t the government sell this good news story?Saul EslakeMinisters love to claim credit for things like cheaper petrol and cheaper pharmaceuticals – why not cheaper housing?Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 4 Aug 2026 20.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 01.21 EDTShareResidential property prices in Australia’s eight capital cities have fallen by an average of 2.5% from their most recent peak in March, according to data published earlier this week by bothCotalityandProptrack. The declines have been somewhat greater in Sydney and Melbourne – 5.6% and 5.7% respectively – where they started earlier, than in other cities. Indeed, prices have not yet begun to fall in Perth, Hobart or Darwin, nor have they (on average) declined outside the capital cities.Those falls are likely to continue, and to become more widespread, for some time yet. Themajor banksare predicting that capital city prices will be flat to down 5% over the course of 2026, with larger declines of between 3 and 10% in Sydney and Melbourne.Others have forecastthat prices could fall by between 5 and 10% this year.House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to biteRead moreIt’s important to put these numbers in context. On average, property prices in Australia’s eight capital cities are stillupby 47.7% from their lows in the early stages of the pandemic, by 144% from their lows during the global financial crisis of 2008-09, by 365% since the turn of the century, and by 1,007% (yes, more than 1,000%) over the past 40 years. Even a decline of 10% – the most currently being forecast – would leave the vast majority of property owners ahead, and in most cases substantially ahead, of whatever their property initially cost them.The same context needs to be kept in mind when assessing figures tossed around to describe the home values “destroyed” by falling property prices. The 1.6% fall in the average value of all residential properties (including those in regional areas) since the most recent peak will have lowered the total value of Australian residential property by close to $200bn. That sounds like a lot of money – and of course to any individual Australian, it is. But the total value of Australian residential land and buildings, according to the most recent estimates from theAustralian Bureau of Statistics, was $12.3tn (yes,trillion) as at 31 March.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEven if prices were to fall by 10% from their peak, the total value of Australian residential real estate would still be more than $11tn.And that is well in excess of the $2.6tn of mortgage debt which is secured against Australian residential property.All of that may be of little comfort to the approximately 45,000 people who have used the government’s 5% deposit scheme to become first home buyers since October last year. Some – although by no means all – of them may now be in a position where their home is, for now at least, worth less than the mortgage they took on in order to buy it (that is, in “negative equity”). That’s an uncomfortable position to be in.double quotation markEven if prices were to fall by 10% from their peak, the total value of Australian residential real estate would still be more than $11tnBut it’s only really a practical problem for those who find themselves having to sell their recently purchased home at a loss – which is likely to only be a small proportion. More likely, through a combination of remaining in their home for up to eight years (the “norm” for first-time buyers) and paying down their mortgage, possibly by more than they’re contractually obliged to (as a large proportion of homebuyers do), they will eventually return to a positive equity position.Those Australians whose only exposure to residential property prices is through their own home – the vast majority of property owners – will, in reality, be little affected by a 5-10% fall in property prices. Yes, their home may realise a smaller amount if and when they sell it than it would have had they sold it late last year (although it will still be worth a lot more than when they originally bought it). But if they are selling in order to “trade up” to a larger home, or one in a more “desirable location”, that home will also likely cost them less than it would have last year. And if they’re “downsizing”, the smaller home that they’re buying will also cost them less.Of course, a much larger decline in property prices (which no one is currently forecasting) could create broader problems for the economy and, potentially, the financial system.A very large – say, 20% or more – decline in residential property prices could result in a bigger proportion of borrowers finding themselves in a negative equity position, which would probably prompt them to curb their discretionary spending – and in some cases, also to cut back on what are ordinarily regarded as “essentials” – in order to pay down their mortgage more quickly. That could in turn materially dampen overall consumer spending, with potential consequences for employment and unemployment.A very large decline in property prices could also prompt concerns about the stability of the Australian financial system, given that mortgages represent more than 40% of the total assets of banks operating in Australia – although historically Australian borrowers have been vastly less likely to default on mortgages than their American counterparts.But, it’s important to once again note, no one is forecasting declines in property prices of anywhere near this magnitude.More modest declines, of the sort which arenow beingwidely anticipated, are for the most part a Good Thing.In particular, they represent the most effective antidote to the problems of deteriorating housing affordability and declining access to home ownership which have been slowly metastasising in Australia for more than four decades.House prices are falling in Australia. That’s a good thing – if you believe housing is a basic human need | Saul EslakeRead moreThis year the government has been claiming credit for cheaper petrol – via the temporary cut in fuel excise – and for cheaper pharmaceuticals – via its changes to the PBS. If any other expenses listed on the consumer price index were to exhibit meaningful declines over the next year or so, ministers would be falling over themselves trying to claim credit for it.But somehow they seem reluctant to embrace the idea that the solution to the problems caused by “expensive housing” is “cheaper housing” – even though in the most recent budget they implemented reforms which are likely to contribute to housing becoming more affordable – that is to say, cheaper.Perhaps if they were more willing to do that, they’d find it easier to “sell” these changes as a Good Thing for most Australians.Saul Eslake is a vice-chancellor’s fellow at the University of Tasmania and an independent consulting economistExplore more on these topicsHousingOpinionAustralian economycommentShareReuse this content

title: Thar she blows! Hull Maritime Museum resurfaces with a walk-in whale and a ‘monkey mermaid’ | Architecture | The Guardian
description: The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring city
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring city
Content: She sounds! … the skeleton of a 40ft-long North Atlantic right whale dominates Hull Maritime Museum’s Age of Sail gallery.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowView image in fullscreenShe sounds! … the skeleton of a 40ft-long North Atlantic right whale dominates Hull Maritime Museum’s Age of Sail gallery.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowArchitectureThar she blows! Hull Maritime Museum resurfaces with a walk-in whale and a ‘monkey mermaid’The £20m reboot shows off exhibits ranging from a giant whale skeleton to tiny ‘scrimshaws’ of carved bone to a very strange mermaid, all telling a gripping tale of a great seafaring cityCatherine SlessorWed 5 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe star attraction of Hull’s revamped and revitalised Maritime Museum is a colossal 40ft-long skeleton of an North Atlantic right whale, beached more than a century ago. The remains of this leviathan dominate an exhibition space scarcely large enough to contain its stupendous bulk. Children can crawl into its ribcage, like junior Jonahs, popping up in a clear plastic dome as digital images of swimming whales slowly unspool across the ceiling.Docile, leisurely and extremely blubbery – which meant that harpooned carcasses conveniently floated, as well as yielding copious quantities of valuable oil – the North Atlantic right whale was hunted almost to extinction during the whaling era. Today, it’s estimated that there are fewer than 400 left.View image in fullscreenExhibits ahoy … exterior of the revamped Hull Maritime Museum.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowAt the other end of the cetacean scale is a delicately carved whale that can fit into the palm of your hand, studded with miniature harpoons designed for use as toothpicks. It forms part of the museum’s world class collection of scrimshaw, the niche and intensely fiddly folk art of carving and decorating pieces of ivory or bone. Crewmen would while away the long hours “scrimshandering”, inscribing whales’ teeth and walrus tusks with images of ships and patriotic Britannias, or tableaux from their travels and portraits of loved ones. Other bounties on display include the spiralled rapiers of narwhal tusks, surreally fashioned into hatstands and bedposts.Hull’s geography ensured that its history was indisputably maritime. Set at the confluence of the River Hull and Humber estuary, it prospered, successively, through trading, whaling and fishing. Latterly, its historic relationship with the sea has been renewed through the production of wind turbine blades for offshore arrays at the city’s Alexandra Dock. And Hull and the Humber remain one of the UK’s busiest port complexes.View image in fullscreenScrimshandered … sperm whale tooth engraving of the Phoenix of London by Burdett Phoenix, 1820s.Photograph: © Hull Maritime MuseumNonetheless, the sense of city out on a limb, and one that has seen better days, still persists. Hull’s centre is pockmarked with vacant shops, and its docklands, which took a pounding during the second world war, remain apologetically gap-toothed in places, despite the crowded marina and upscale warehouse conversions.The poet Philip Larkin, Hull’s most infamous adopted son, who measured out his life in coffee spoons as head librarian of the city’s university, wrote of “the surprise of a large town … where only salesmen and relations come, within a terminate and fishy-smelling pastoral of ships up streets ...” Larkin had an ambivalent relationship with Hull, but a statue of him, erected in 2010, now greets you at the city’s Paragon station.View image in fullscreenThis Place Called Hull gallery at the refurbished Hull Maritime Museum.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowWhen the dock offices first opened in 1871, Larkin’s “pastoral of ships up streets” would have been an even more emphatic reality. At that time, Hull’s skyline was more ships’ masts than church spires, with vessels crammed into a network of docks. Set on a prominent site overlooking the now infilled Queen’s Dock, the dock offices exude a chest-puffing, Victorian mercantile bombast. Originally designed by Christopher Wray, whose career encompassed a spell in Calcutta’s public works department, the building’s florid and fruity neoclassical style is embellished with Neptunian details such as sea monsters, fishing nets and trident-like railings. An unconventional triangular plan was crowned by chunky pepperpot cupolas at its three corners.Now listed Grade II*, it was converted into the city’s Maritime Museum in 1975. (The museum itself began life in 1912 as the more prosaic Museum of Fisheries and Shipping in the city’s Pickering Park.) Over time, however, the Museum of Hull, as it was known, became tired, shabby and ripe for a reboot. Only two of its four floors were publicly accessible and the main exhibition space was painted shiny grey and lurid Germolene pink.“You also couldn’t read the whole room as a volume because there was this big ramp in the middle going up to a mezzanine level,” says Claire Humphrey, senior architect with conservation specialist Purcell, which oversaw the remodelling. The intrusive ramp has been removed and the colour scheme toned down to a more historically accurate and visually palatable palette: subtle marine blues set against a glacially white ceiling.The £20.4m project follows on from Hull’s successful stint as City of Culture in 2017. Funding came jointly from Hull city council, which contributed £11.8mn, along with the National LotteryHeritageFund, which allocated £7.7m. The remainder was raised through private donations. The rebooting has enabled the museum to double its public space and show 50% more objects from its expansive collection. Around 1,300 artefacts are now on display across the galleries and open storage spaces, many being seen by the public for the first time.View image in fullscreen‘The best room in Hull’ … the museum’s Court Room.Photograph: ©Hufton+CrowUnderscored by a reframed approach to curation, new display systems bring Hull’s maritime cornucopia more vividly to life, from dockers’ tools and a stuffed polar bear, to Inuit bootees and a so-called “mermaid” (actually a rather hideous chimera of a monkey fused with a fish). A veritable regatta of model ships, pedantically accurate to the last detail, illustrates the shift from sail to steam, an advance that supercharged the shipping and fishing industries. One of the museum’s most cherished artefacts is a carved wooden figurehead of a bounding dog from the Sirius, the first steamship to complete a transatlantic crossing entirely under steam power in 1838.Other sections explore the rich currents of migration that flowed through Hull, propitiously poised between Old and New Worlds. You can also learn about Lillian Bilocca, the “headscarf revolutionary” who doughtily campaigned to improve safety on fishing fleets in the 1960s. In 150 years of commercial trawling out of Hull, more than 6,000 crewmen were lost, now commemorated in the museum’s simple and dignified memorial space. Yet despite Bilocca’s success, which undoubtedly saved lives, she was ostracised and blacklisted.View image in fullscreenDeep dive … A scrimshaw of a jolly sailor waving the Royal Navy’s flag, from the ship the Cornelia, early 1800s.Photograph: © Hull Maritime MuseumThroughout, the aim has been to carefully restore, repair and and revive, a strategy involving, at times, heroic feats of painstaking toil. The setpiece space of the Court Room, with its heraldic shields of Hanseatic League ports and columns of red and pink scagliola resembling an Italian delicatessen counter, has been renovated to serve as an events venue. Restoring the intricate ceiling decorations of intertwined foliage and starfish required a team of eight conservators working aloft on scaffolding platforms for six weeks, hand-cleaning the plaster with cotton buds to remove decades of accumulated grime. “We were aiming to create the best room in Hull,” says Humphrey, “and I think we achieved it.”The deep dive into Hull’s 800-year-old maritime history does not end with the museum. The remodelled building forms part of a wider circuit that takes in the re-landscaped Queen’s Gardens, originally designed by modernist architect Frederick Gibberd, and a new visitor centre for the Arctic Corsair, a historic trawler (think of it as Hull’s Cutty Sark) that will be permanently berthed in a cavernous dry dock within the North End Shipyard. Associated urban realm improvements literally pave the way for a more structured and civilised experience for both tourists and locals, with a vibe that aims to be more Copenhagen than Humberside.In leveraging Hull’s maritime history in an unsentimental way – after all, the mechanisms of trade and extraction are notoriously unsentimental – these initiatives suggest the possibility of a different kind of civic future. In this context, the museum’s deftly handled and uplifting restoration will surely help to turn the tide.Hull Maritime Museum opens on 8 AugustExplore more on these topicsArchitectureMuseumsHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Prisoners killed each other’s kittens. So now they’re forbidden inside’: Vladimir Karamazov’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’
Content: Stray cats on Belene Island by Vladimir Karamazov, from his photobook For the Grace of God.Photograph: Vladimir KaramazovView image in fullscreenStray cats on Belene Island by Vladimir Karamazov, from his photobook For the Grace of God.Photograph: Vladimir KaramazovMy best shotArt and design‘Prisoners killed each other’s kittens. So now they’re forbidden inside’: Vladimir Karamazov’s best photograph‘The men in this jail in Bulgaria used to adopt these stray kittens. But pets can be a problem. They get killed as punishment or for revenge’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 5 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBelene prison, in northernBulgariaon the border with Romania, is the most heavily guarded facility of its type in my country. It is on an island, so escape is near impossible, and has the largest number of people serving life sentences for murder in any Bulgarian prison.This image describes a sad, terrible story. There are a lot of stray cats on the island, as well as pigeons and mosquitoes. The prisoners used to adopt stray kittens and keep them as pets. When I started my project, For the Grace of God, at the prison, many prisoners had pet cats. But in a prison, this can become a problem – prisoners kill each other’s pets as punishment or for revenge. So now it’s forbidden. It’s even the same with flowers – some think of the flowers as friends, they nurture and grow them in the sun, but then other prisoners destroy them. Anything a prisoner can create a relationship with can be destroyed. Part of their punishment is to be alone, without any family, or any attachments to anything.double quotation markI host the Bulgarian version of The Traitors. But I was curious about life inside prisonIt’s another world with a different set of rules, another language, and even money is different – cigarettes are currency. There are a lot of rules. I spent a lot of time in Belene, living like the prisoners, spending all day with them, listening to their stories. I am a well-known television and theatre actor here in my country. I’ve hosted the Bulgarian edition of Survivor for five seasons; I host the Bulgarian version of The Traitors. I have a lot of work, but I don’t like the people in my industry, and my work as an actor is boring for me now. I started this project out of curiosity about life inside: people in my country have no idea how prisoners live. It was difficult to get permission as I wanted to access the prison for a year and to be allowed to shoot everywhere and anywhere with no limitations.Talking to the prisoners, I discovered that everything begins in their childhood: 99% grew up in a family without love, money, or with abuse; something was broken. This is a problem in society, not only for these people. Most people just want prisoners dead; they would prefer funding to go to old people or children. When I presented this work at the National Gallery in Sofia, people were crying – it was the first time they saw prisoners as people like us. They saw human beings. We are all the same, but some people don’t have the opportunity for a good life.At the beginning, I was scared of the prisoners who were sentenced without parole. I thought these people had nothing to lose and could kill me as a joke. I said to the director to please alert me if any of them were in my vicinity. One day he introduced Milchu, and told me to spend the day with him. I asked Milchu to please tell me if we came across any of the prisoners without parole. He laughed and asked me how I expected them to look? I said I don’t know – in chains? But I begged him to warn me. The next day I asked him the same thing. Eventually he told me: “I’m one of them. I have a 26-year life sentence without parole.” My mind was blown – I didn’t expect that this man I had spent two days with was a killer. I couldn’t sleep that night.double quotation markCan you be friends with a killer? The hard truth is yesThe first three months were very difficult, I had a lot of nightmares. There are a lot of terrible stories, but I didn’t want to explain the stories in my photographs. I wanted to think about how a criminal life begins, to ask questions, not judge. “Can you be friends with a killer?” I was asked once. The hard truth is yes. Today I am good friends with three prisoners sentenced without parole.My life has changed a lot in the last two years because of this experience. Forgiveness is a simple word, but it’s very hard. Milchu has three children, and when he killed someone, he also destroyed his whole family, his world. I met one of his daughters who told me that for 15 years after her father’s crime she hated him every day for destroying their life. Then one day she understood that hating this man her whole life was terrible for her, so she decided to forgive him.I related this story to Milchu – he started to cry. He said it was the most important moment of his life. He never knew his daughter had forgiven him. He said he would die happy.For the Grace of God is published by Gost books(£60)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: KaramazovfotoVladimir Karamazov’s CVBorn:Bulgaria, 1979High point:My greatest achievement is that I had the courage, after 20 successful years as an actor – playing major roles in film, theatre and television – to turn to photography and start from scratch. To leave one life and set out to pursue another – for me more interesting – where I confront the truth of our lives. As an actor I am an interpreter, recreating reality. As a photographer I am a creator who captures and preserves reality. Within six years I managed to pass through many levels of photography, I won many awards, held major exhibitions and have created the projects that excite me. Through my projects I try to open a door for society to places they do not want to look, do not know what is there, and are afraid of. When they peek through my open door, they see that it is not so frightening there, that people like us live there, too.Top tip:I constantly urge people to think a little more. When we hear something bad about someone, we are immediately inclined to condemn them. But we do not know their story, we do not know why they committed a certain act, yet we judge. If we give ourselves time and get to know that person, we will learn the reason why they are the way they are. This happened to me with people convicted of murder. The act itself is horrifying. But when you learn the whole story of that person, when you understand that they grew up without family, without love, in terrible squalor and hunger, you understand why they are that way.Explore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotPhotographyBulgariafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Should a tech tycoon be able to pay his way into conducting a world-class orchestra? And should they really sell tickets? | Music | The Guardian
description: Elon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian tech entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical music
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Elon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian tech entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical music
Content: Mandle Cheung, who will conduct Mahler’s Second Symphony with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at London’s Alexandra Palace.Photograph: © Shayne GreyView image in fullscreenMandle Cheung, who will conduct Mahler’s Second Symphony with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at London’s Alexandra Palace.Photograph: © Shayne GreyTom Service on musicMusicShould a tech tycoon be able to pay his way into conducting a world-class orchestra? And should they really sell tickets?Tom ServiceElon Musk may be able to buy a trip to Mars, but when the super wealthy pay to be conductors – as Canadian entrepreneur Mandle Cheung is doing – it makes a mockery of a meritocracy in classical musicWed 5 Aug 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTShareThere are some pretty gigantic non-negotiables for an orchestral musician. You have to be able to perform the right notes in the right order, with a combination of technical expertise, artistry, skill and understanding that demands years, decades and lifetimes of devotion.But there is one figure on the orchestral concert platform who is both the most important person in the room – at least according to classical music’s hierarchies – yet who makes no sound, and whose job looks the simplest of all: the conductor, waving their arms about in time with the music and gurning at the players.Despite appearances, the professional conductor’s responsibility is to know every line of the music inside out, and to turn the performance into not only a perfected version of the rehearsal, but a one-off experience that has its own energy, shape and narrative. You want to know a trade secret? Any professional orchestra in this country could play most of the music on their programmes without a conductor. What the best professional conductors do is provide the x-factor of inspiration that allows the orchestral players to do things that they can’t achieve on their own.But still, as the Hungarian violinistCarl Flesch put it: “There is no profession which an impostor could enter more easily.”By his own admission, the 78-year-old businessman and founder of theMandle Philharmonic in Canada, Mandle Cheung, is an amateur conductor. Heresists the “maestro” tag. He loves music, he loves Mahler particularly, and he is able to conduct world-class orchestras because he is able to pay these orchestras to play for him. Last year he led the Toronto Symphony in Mahler’s Second Symphony, buthe isn’t stopping there. More Mahler, and European orchestras are in his sights. His wish becomes reality on 21 August at London’s Alexandra Palace whenCheung conducts the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, soloists Elizabeth Watts and Jennifer Johnston, and the Brighton Festival Chorus, in a performance of Mahler 2.double quotation markIt turns Mahler’s music into an expensive, ego-driven spectacle that’s all about the wish fulfilment of financially powerful peopleCheungpaid about C$500,000(£264,000) to conduct the Toronto Symphony; his representative has confirmed that Cheung is paying the RPO for the same privilege, but not the amount. “We do not disclose fees for concerts,” said an RPO spokesperson. It says something profound about the parlous state of orchestral finances on either side of the Atlantic that they need to take Cheung’s money, and risk their reputations with their players, audiences and sponsors by letting a non-professional conductor take on one of the most prestigious works in the repertoire. Mahler’s Second is a symphony of epic scale of sound and spirit. With its vast trajectory from funeral march to vision of resurrection it is one of the most complex and transcendent pieces of music you are ever likely to hear.Cheung himself acknowledged the issue,talking to the New York Timeslast year about the Toronto Symphony experience: “These are great musicians, and they work really hard all their life to become a player in a professional symphony orchestra,” he said. “And then somebody who’s not a recognized conductor just walks in and writes you a check and starts conducting you.”View image in fullscreenGilbert Kaplan conducting the New York Philharmonic in Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony at Avery Fisher Hall in 2008.Photograph: Hiroyuki Ito/Getty ImagesThere’s a wider story than one very rich person’s vanity here, and it’s far from a new one.Gilbert Kaplan, another businessman and philanthropist who was similarly obsessed with Mahler’s Second, conducted and recorded the piece with the London Symphony in 1987, and with the Vienna Philharmonic, released on Deutsche Grammophon, in 2002. There’s something about this symphony that seems to speak to the power fantasies of these men: is it that having mastered the universes of finance and technology, being in charge of orchestral and choral forces and guiding them to the radiant transcendence of the end of the symphony is the musical equivalent of building a spacecraft to go to Mars?It turns Mahler’s music into an expensive, ego-driven spectacle that’s all about the wish fulfilment of financially powerful people, curdling the spiritual message of the piece into just another commodity that can be bought and sold.Of course, one way of looking at the entire history of orchestral music and opera is that it’s always been an aristocrat’s indulgence, from the Chapel Royal of the English court to the orchestra that was Prince Esterházy’s pride and joy, and which was the laboratory for Joseph Haydn’s symphonies in the 18th century. You can extend the idea to the wealthy philanthropists of US arts from the 19th century onwards; and you could even see the state funding of the arts in Europe as a variation of the same principle: promoting an unaffordable luxury through taxation. In that context, what’s wrong with someone renting an orchestra for a night to make their dreams come true?On their own terms, you might think that none of these individual concerts that the wealthy can pay to conduct are necessarily problematic. If you’ve got the cash, and wonderful musicians will turn up to play Mahler for you, that’s up to them. But audiences deserve to know what they’re getting for the price of their tickets at Alexandra Palace - there’s nothing on the RPO’s website to say this is an event in which a professional orchestra and soloists have been privately hired by an amateur conductor.View image in fullscreenThe Royal Philharmonic Orchestra performing Mahler’s First Symphony at the Royal Albert Hall, London, last October, conducted by music director Vasily Petrenko.Photograph: Andy ParadiseThe RPO’s managing director, Sarah Bardwell, said: “The RPO takes pride in offering life-changing musical experiences to people from all walks of life, and the orchestra is looking forward to welcoming Mandle Cheung to the podium this summer.Classical musicis for everyone, and this special one-off summer concert will fulfil a dream for a great Mahler enthusiast, while materially supporting our community and education work for the new season.”I’d love to conduct the RPO myself, but am guessing that my dreams and enthusiasm for Mahler aren’t, on their own, enough; I wasn’t aware that the UK’s orchestras had a role to play in the fulfilment of businessmen’s bucket lists. The community and education work that the RPO say will be the beneficiary of Cheung’s largesse is a non-negotiable part of any orchestra’s remit and of course is vital and welcome. But if you look at how the concert is promoted on theRPO’s websiteyou might imagine you were attending a concert that belongs in the same category as performances by the RPO’s music director, Vasily Petrenko. But you’re not. You’re attending a performance that should clearly be advertised for what it is: an amateur fulfilling his most cherished fantasies. AsCheung told the New York Times: “Now that I’ve conducted in Toronto, maybe that can be sort of like a credential for approaching American orchestras, European orchestras, to see if we can work with them,” he said. “That would be nice.”double quotation markIf anyone can buy a world-class symphony orchestra to play with for one night, why not for a week, or a month, or a season?And it probably will be more than nice. The RPO’s skilled musicians will almost certainly hold the performance together, and Mahler’s music will make the radiant sounds and noises that only this symphony can; the audience will applaud and feel they have been on a massive Mahlerian journey. What’s the problem with that?Here’s the kicker: if anyone can buy a world-class symphony orchestra to play with for one night, why not for a week, or a month, or a season? Why bother with decades of specialist training to become a conductor when all you need to stand on a podium and lead a a public performance is very deep pockets? If you’re an audience member, who cares about the difference between amateurs and world-class professionals?If these currently exceptional concerts such as Cheung’s become part of an orchestra’s regular way of life, a means of generating income, the message is stark. For all those more talented musicians working away in conservatoires and opera houses and concert halls right now – those naive souls who imagine classical music is a meritocracy, not an auction – the whole principle that this is an art-form available to all is betrayed.This week Tom has been listening to:Judith Weir’s Moon and Star. I was lucky enough to be in Proms audience for Ryan Wigglesworth, the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra and BBC Singers’ performance of this work. Based on Emily Dickinson’s poetry, it’s music that charms and beguiles.Listen again hereExplore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musicRoyal Philharmonic OrchestraLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Peter Gill showed theatre audiences that anywhere could be the centre of the world | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting the stories of working people
Author: Barney Norris
Headline: The playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting the stories of working people
Content: Truth teller … Peter Gill in 2015.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTruth teller … Peter Gill in 2015.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianTheatrePeter Gill showed theatre audiences that anywhere could be the centre of the worldBarney NorrisThe playwright and director, who has died aged 86, completed DH Lawrence’s revolution in spotlighting stories of working peoplePeter Gill: a theatrical visionary with an unsparing honestyWed 5 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTShareIwas,in Michael Coveney’s parlance, one of Peter Gill’s acolytes. I knew him in his autumn; after he’d directed his last play for the National, after he’d moved from Harriet Devine’s house in Hammersmith, where he lived for most of his adult life, into his flat a little further down the river. For 20 years we met there, or in the community centre when we held workshops with actors to help him develop material. One day he told me I should write a book about him: “I introduced postmodernism to the theatre, darling.” I was proud he’d asked me, a feeling that only slightly receded when I read an article by Nina Raine a few years later, in which she revealed he’d suggested the same thing to her. Now Peter has died, I have a strong feeling I should be writing about him again.I think the framework hasn’t yet been created to talk about Peter’s significance. When I was researchingmy book about him, I went to interview his friendBill Gaskill. What we talked about most that day was Wordsworth, and over the years I’ve come to see that as significant. It was Wordsworth who proposed that literature should speak in “the real language of men”. That project flowered a century later in the work of DH Lawrence, who broke free of the conditions of his birth to revolutionise English literature. Lawrence tore through almost every barrier he encountered, for better or worse, in every aspect of his life – but he couldn’t break into the theatre. A “vertical invader” from a peasant class, to borrow John Berger’s description of Picasso, Lawrence reshaped the artistic landscape, but the English theatre made no room in his lifetime for the stories of working people. It took another vertical invader to complete that revolution: a docker’s son from Cardiff who took Lawrence’s plays, placed them at the centre of the world and said, once and for all, “as much happens for you as for other people”. That was Peter’s achievement. He showed us anywhere could be the centre of the world.View image in fullscreenRadical compassion … Peter Gill directing Scenes from the Big Picture at the National Theatre, London, in 2003.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAnd did sobeautifully, in a Keatsian sense. When a stage direction required the baking of bread, Peter had his company bake bread, however long it took. When he ended up in hospital during tech for the Lawrence trilogy, and his assistant came to his bedside to say they were planning to use dry ice to show the bread burning, Peter asked him: “Who do you think I am, Franco Zeffirelli?” He used theatre to tell the truth.Susan Sontag wrote of Thomas Hardy that he was the only great novelist who was also a great poet. I would gently make the claim thatPeter Gillachieved a place of similar distinction: the only great playwright who was also a great director. It was his time around the Court that forged him. Allow me to get into the record what he said about the white heat of that period. He began by paraphrasing Adorno, then added something revolutionary of his own: “Once we knew about Auschwitz we didn’t know how to say anything that meant anything. The bind was that the only moral act in the light of that was to try to say something, you see?” That Beckettian second sentence – the determination to go on, not to accept humanity in ruins but to recognise it and then to seek to speak and live again – is the foundation of every good play anyone’s written since. Peter was in the room when that thought formed. Its radical compassion mustn’t leave the world with him.Explore more on these topicsTheatrePeter GillRoyal Court theatreDH LawrencecommentShareReuse this content

title: Himmler’s ‘anti-Nazi’ masseur: Claes Bang stars as SS chief’s ‘magic Buddha’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: Felix Kersten, the personal therapist of Hitler’s principal enforcer, claimed to have saved countless lives from the Holocaust. A new feature film exposes him as a narcissist prone to myth-making
Author: Geoffrey Macnab
Headline: Felix Kersten, the personal therapist of Hitler’s principal enforcer, claimed to have saved countless lives from the Holocaust. A new feature film exposes him as a narcissist prone to myth-making
Content: Martin Müller as Heinrich Himmler (left) and Claes Bang as Felix Kersten in I Is Another.Photograph: Anke Neugebauer/©Anke Neugebauer / Ostlicht Filmproduktion GmbH / Wega FilmView image in fullscreenMartin Müller as Heinrich Himmler (left) and Claes Bang as Felix Kersten in I Is Another.Photograph: Anke Neugebauer/©Anke Neugebauer / Ostlicht Filmproduktion GmbH / Wega FilmMoviesHimmler’s ‘anti-Nazi’ masseur: Claes Bang stars as SS chief’s ‘magic Buddha’Felix Kersten, the personal therapist of Hitler’s principal enforcer, claimed to have saved countless lives from the Holocaust. A new feature film exposes him as a narcissist prone to myth-makingGeoffrey MacnabWed 5 Aug 2026 05.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years ago, German writer-director Felix Randau was approached by French producers who wanted him to make a miniseries about Felix Kersten, the former massage therapist to Nazi SS head Heinrich Himmler.When the producers first pitched the project, there was one sentence which leapt out. “They said that if Steven Spielberg had known about Felix Kersten, he would have shot a film about him, not about Oskar Schindler.” Who was this intriguing, largely overlooked figure, who claimed to have saved countless Jews and other concentration camp prisoners from certain death?View image in fullscreenHeinrich Himmler with Felix Kersten in 1944.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyRandau went on to make his own movie about Kersten, but it certainly does not portray the Gestapo chief’s personal therapist as a hero. In I Is Another, which has its world premiere at the Locarno film festival this week, he is played by Danish actor Claes Bang (once a Dracula for the BBC), as a mercurial, charming but very slippery figure.The myth the masseur promoted in his postwar memoirs was that he had used his influence over Himmler to save many people from being sent to the gas chambers.A biography by French journalist Joseph Kessel, The Man With the Miraculous Hands, reinforced the idea that Kersten had helped “entire populations escape the terror of deportation” and that he “prevented the crematory ovens from receiving their full quota of corpses”. Randau now dismisses the book as “full of lies”.In the film, Kersten is shown on a long train journey to Oslo where he hopes he will be awarded the Nobel prize. During the journey, he is accosted by a fictional investigative journalist Hedda Wohmann (Valerie Pachner) who strongly suspects he is liar and hopes to catch him out.In preparation for the movie, Randau did extensive research of his own and discovered the masseur’s SS membership card in an archive in Berlin. Kersten had always concealed his SS membership but Randau found a letter in the archive in which the masseur asked if he was allowed to wear the SS uniform in public, undermining his later claims that he was an avowed anti-Nazi. There was also plentiful evidence that Kersten forged several of the documents which showed him in the best light.However, when it comes to establishing whether or not Kersten really was spying on behalf of the Swedes, as many have claimed, he hit a dead end. For reasons no one could explain, all the files still remain classified (although Randau can’t help but notice how well connected the masseur was with Swedish government sources).View image in fullscreen‘He wanted to save his own reputation’ … Claes Bang as Felix Kersten in I Is Another.Photograph: Anke Neugebauer/©Anke Neugebauer / Ostlicht Filmproduktion GmbH / Wega Film Vienna“I think he definitely saved some people’s lives but not thousands,” Randau concludes. “I am sure he did it only because he wanted to save his own reputation, maybe even his own life.“He was a narcissist, and like all narcissists, his self-confidence was really weak. For him, it wasn’t enough to be a hero, he wanted to be a superhero and that was his mistake.”The writer-director believes that after the Nazi defeat in Stalingrad in 1943, Kersten realised that the ship was sinking. “He had to jump off somehow. At that point, he started to manipulate Himmler and there was this mutual whitewashing with other guys involved. A lot of letters and documents are definitely fake, letters saying things like, ‘thank you for being such an enemy of the Nazi system like I am’ and stuff like that.”One fact was incontrovertible. Kersten, who died in 1960, was a brilliant masseur. He provided instant relief for Himmler from his excruciating intestinal spasms. The SS chief called him “a magic Buddha who cures everything” and was extremely indulgent toward him as a consequence.View image in fullscreenFelix Randau, the German director of I Is AnotherPhotograph: Oscar Gonzalez/Getty ImagesKersten was personable too. People tended to like him. He was, the director says, “a skirt chaser, a ladies’ man” and he is rumoured to have lived in a menage a trois with his wife and his secretary.This wasn’t an easy film to cast or finance, partly because the director didn’t want to portray Himmler as a grotesque comic book villain. The SS chief was “sadistic and completely nuts”, he says, but he was “still a human being”.“Some actors turned it down because they said I would provide a stage for evil. I think that is really ridiculous because if you cancel evil, it will grow in the dark.” (Himmler was eventually played by Martin Müller, an unsung actor best known for his TV work.)View image in fullscreen‘Some actors turned it down because they said I would provide a stage for evil’ … on the set of I Is Another.Photograph: Anke Neugebauer/©Anke Neugebauer / Ostlicht Filmproduktion GmbH / Wega FilmAsk Randau about the rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland and he says he finds it “terrifying”. “Of course, this is a period movie but I think it has a lot of connections to our present time. There are no more fundamental agreements about what is true and what is not true. This is one of our main problems – and that was the thing I was interested in.“I think it’s because all the people who experienced war are dead now. My father died some months ago. He was 86 and his first memory was of him and his mother running with bombs falling down, streets burning and piles or corpses. But this generation doesn’t exist any more.”Kersten doesn’t emerge well from the movie. For all his surface charm, he is eventually revealed as overbearing, thin-skinned, dishonest and prey to tantrums. Nonetheless, having spent so long researching and making the movie, Randau retains a certain sympathy for him.“I think he did good things but for bad reasons. He was maybe bored with his life and so tried to stage it. But he was still deeply involved in all the shit.”I Is Another premieresat the Locarno film festival on 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsSecond world warNazismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dog Man: The Musical review – Dav Pilkey’s megastar mutt sniffs out the spotlight in a barking show | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stage
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: A part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stage
Content: Throwing it all together … Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenThrowing it all together … Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorTheatreReviewDog Man: The Musical review – Dav Pilkey’s megastar mutt sniffs out the spotlight in a barking showSouthbank Centre, LondonA part-canine cop, a villainous cat and a psychokinetic butterflyfish burst into song as the wildly popular children’s books are adapted for the stageTim JonzeWed 5 Aug 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps, if you don’t have a child in primary school, you will be blissfully unaware of Dog Man, Dav Pilkey’s series of graphic novels about a cop who – after a terrible injury – has his dog’s head sewn on to his own body, thereby creating a crime-fighting canine/human crossbreed. But if you’ve been swept up by the phenomenon – and Dog Manisa phenomenon, selling more than 70m copies in the decade since the first book was published – then you will know that this mutt has some serious star power: there’s aDog Man film, video game, board game … and now a musical,arriving in the UKafter off-Broadway success.The Dog Man books are chaotic, hilarious and full of pathos, but writer/lyricist Kevin Del Aguila and composer Brad Alexander’s show leans largely on the former. There’s slapstick humour and jokes about butt-sniffing. When Dog Man is asked how his day is going, he replies: “Ruff!” It’s aimed at the younger end of Pilkey’s readership, which is confusing as there are also Dickens references.The plot – based on several early Dog Man books in the 14-strong series – is actually a musical within a musical: George and Harold, the fictional writers of the Dog Man comics, have decided to put on a musical to prove to their teacher how easy that would be. Because they’re throwing it all together using whatever they can find in their cupboard, Timothy R Mackabee’s set is charmingly DIY – skyscrapers are made from cardboard and gaffer tape, characters shapeshift across soft toy/glove puppet/human actor form.View image in fullscreenSuper-powers from brain dust … Vanessa Dumatey as Flippy in Dog Man: The Musical.Photograph: Mark SeniorOur hero hound (Renan Teodoro) is pitted against Petey (Sam Kipling), the villainous cat, and Flippy (Vanessa Dumatey), a psychokinetic butterflyfish who has gained super-powers from eating “brain dust”. But there’s a twist! To help achieve his evil aims, Petey clones himself, expecting a similarly twisted replica to emerge – instead he mistakenly creates Li’l Petey (Rebecca-Jo Roberts), a super-cute and naive kid who insists on calling Petey “papa” (cue much “I’m NOT your papa!!”).Li’l Petey is the books’ emotional core and no doubt parents will relate to the idea of suddenly having a mini-me in their world who annoyingly doesn’t behave as instructed. But as the energetic cast dance, sing and bark their way around the set like CBeebies presenters after three pints of Skittles, these more moving moments get buried in the production, directed and choreographed by Jen Wineman. There’s also a slight disconnect in seeing people act out these roles – would children not get more excited at seeing Pilkey’s cutesy characters come to life with big furry heads rather than, say, an orange beanie?Translating a graphic novel into a musical was always going to throw up such hurdles. At one point the hyperactive George and Harold, played by Ricardo Mendes and Peter Lavery, bring a board onstage to try to replicate the “animated” flip-o-ramas from the series. “This isn’t working the way it does in the comics!” they complain. It’s a joke, but still – perhaps musicals aren’t quite as easy to pull off as George and Harold thought.AtSouthbank Centre, London, until 16 August. Thentouringuntil 13 June 2027.Explore more on these topicsTheatreChildren's books: 8-12 yearsChildren and teenagersSouthbank CentreMusicalsChildren's theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like Backstreet Boys, but less sultry’: how the Jonas Brothers notched up 20 years of pop stardom against the odds | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Unlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appeal
Author: Claudia Efemini
Headline: Unlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appeal
Content: ‘They’re committed to their art’ … (L-R): Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas, AKA the Jonas Brothers.Photograph: Pamela LittkyView image in fullscreen‘They’re committed to their art’ … (L-R): Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas, AKA the Jonas Brothers.Photograph: Pamela LittkyPop and rock‘Like Backstreet Boys, but less sultry’: how the Jonas Brothers notched up 20 years of pop stardom against the oddsUnlike their Disney peers, the toothesome trio didn’t pivot to being sexy – and they’re now at their stadium-filling peak. Fans and collaborators explain their unique, cheesy appealClaudia EfeminiWed 5 Aug 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jonas Brothers appeared in the mid-00s in a blaze of smiles, dressed in shirts, suspenders and ties, singing sappy love songs that won the hearts of girls who quickly became obsessed with this Disney-signed band. Many assumed the fraternal trio would fade away, overtaken by whatever new act replaced them in the whims of teenagers. Yet this week marks 20 years since the release of their debut album,It’s About Time, and the toothsome threesome are bigger than ever.Kevin, Joe and Nick Jonas started out with danger-free pop-punk, evolving into a kind of broad-brush feelgood pop. Their true breakthrough was in 2008 with US No 5 hitBurnin’ Up, teeing up three back-to-back US No 1 albums as they became the youngest group to appear on the cover of Rolling Stone. The usual dreaded “creative differences” precipitated a six-year hiatus and the pursuit of solo careers and acting. But they reformed in 2019 in spectacular style, getting their first US No 1 hit withSucker, and by last year they had the clout to sell out the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the World Cup final was later hosted.This evolution from Disney cornballs to legacy act is as unexpected as it is remarkable. “They’re slick, and sometimes over-produced,” says Nate Sloan, co-host of the podcast Switched on Pop. “But they genuinely love making and playing music and that’s what draws me to their continued work.”Sloan argues that the key to their success is dogged devotion to honing their craft. “They’re committed to their art in a way that people may not realise,” he says. “They were writing their own songs from when they were preteens, and even when they sought out professional songwriting collaborators they opted for more daring voices.” He cites Jon Bellion, the hip-hop leaning singer-songwriter who co-wrote and co-produced 2023’s The Album.View image in fullscreen‘They were great, sweet kids’ … the band in their early daysAnother collaborator who was there right at the beginning is Michael Mangini, co-producer of their debut album. “They do what every artist that has a 20-year career has to do: evolve,” he says. Rock-leaning tunes about adolescence – including a cover of Busted’s dumb time-travel anthem Year 3000, with the original’s horniness significantly dialled down – have given way to mature music about fatherhood. “They’re not the same people that they were when they were teenagers, so it would be ridiculous to make a record that has those types of lyrics,” continues Mangini. “Some artists don’t deviate but I think the ones that have true longevity, they grow.”Mangini witnessed the band’s formation in person during a 2005 meeting with Steve Greenberg, then president of Columbia Records, who would end up co-producing It’s About Time with Mangini. “I was hired to come and meet Nick” – the only brother signed to the label at the time – “and somehow in a meeting the conversation turned into: ‘You should become a group,’” says Mangini, after learning that Joe had done some work on Broadway and Kevin played guitar and could sing background vocals. “They certainly weren’t thinking of themselves as a group called the Jonas Brothers. As a matter of fact, they hated the name,” Mangini laughs. But they signed a deal with Columbia after a demo impressed other execs.At the time, Nick was just 12 years old, while Joe was 15 and Kevin was 17. “It required me to remember what it was like to be that young again,” Mangini says. “It was fun and they were great, sweet kids. I’ve worked with tons of other young people but Nick had a point of view when writing songs. He, at 12, could sit down with me, who had been writing songs for 20 or 25 years at that point, and have something to say and be able to articulate it.”Their brotherhood contains “the blend of complementary roles that powers the most successful bands”, Sloan says. “Nick is the youngest but also seems to have the strongest creative vision; Kevin is the eldest but seems most comfortable in a supporting role; Joe is the most entertaining, and the greatest frontman in many ways.”View image in fullscreenHaven’t strayed far … Joe Jonas in Camp Rock.Photograph: John Medland/Disney ChannelColumbia envisaged them as a classic boyband. “Then when we got into the studio and we started working through writing songs, it sort of took a more edgier, rock, pop-punk leaning vibe.” But debut album It’s About Time flopped at No 91 in the US charts, and Columbia dropped them.Disney’s recording label, Hollywood Records, saw the potential revenue in these three unthreateningly handsome young lads and snapped them up in 2007. They featured as themselves on sitcom series Jonas, and starred as fictional band Connect 3 in teen movies Camp Rock and Camp Rock 2: The Final Jam.While Disney-schooled stars such asBritney Spears,Miley CyrusandSabrina Carpentermoved away from the brand with deliberately racy material, the brothers have hardly drifted from wholesome cheesiness. “How do Disney Channel stars show the world that they’re adults? A really sexy video,” says Shasta Smedsrud, a millennial fan from near Seattle. The Jonas Brothers, though, “broke off from Disney gracefully and just kept going”, though they are returning to that era with Camp Rock 3, premiering on 13 August.For many of their fans, predominantly millennials and older gen Zs, it comes as a shock that their debut album is turning 20. “Wow, I feel old,” says Smedsrud. She remembers watching the music video forSOSon Disney Channel in 2007. “It was almost like the Backstreet Boys but less sultry. I think that’s why they did so well for us,” she said. She now gets a hit of nostalgia from songs like this: “When you hear Joe do his usual on the guitar or Nick’s little riff, you get really excited.”Back in the 2000s, physical media was thriving and magazines and fanzines dominated the fandom; Smedsrud recalls having a diary solely dedicated to Nick Jonas, who she obsessed over. “I would cut pictures out, and be like: this song is about me, or when I see Nick he’s going to recognise me and we’re going to get married,” she laughs.View image in fullscreenA spectacular comeback … performing at the Grammy awards in 2020.Photograph: John Shearer/Getty Images for the Recording AcademyThe boys’ clean-cut looks meant they initially appealed more to girls than boys, though there are some male fans, too. “My girlfriend and her family were my gateway,” says 30-year-old Jordan Corman, who got into them in his late teens and remains a fan. “The teenage boy mindset was if you like the Jonas Brothers, there’s something wrong with you,” he says. “But they actually just make good music.”‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starRead moreSmedsrud describes her three children under six as “little fans” of a band who “don’t really use profanity, so it’s kind of safe for your kids”. Monica Andre, a 27-year-old teacher from Oregon, told her kindergarten class about seeing a Jonas Brothers concert the previous weekend, and the children asked who they were. “So I was like, let’s draw Joe, just for fun,” she says. Andre shared the drawings on TikTok, which circulated online, with the brothers themselves commenting on her post. Since then, her class has become infatuated, and particularly inspired by Kevin’s journey from having a more supporting role to launching a solo career alongside the band in 2025. “If you’re sharing something you love and it makes you happy, it makes them happy,” she says.Will the Jonas Brothers still be around 10 years from now? “Certainly,” Mangini says. “I don’t know if they’ll still be making records, but 30 years from now, they’re going to be touring and people will still be showing up. Because once something’s part of your growing up, there’s a special love for it.”Explore more on these topicsPop and rockDisney ChannelWalt Disney CompanyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocation | Phoebe Bridgers | The Guardian
description: After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoil
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoil
Content: Emotional turmoil … Phoebe Bridgers.Photograph: Olof Grind/PR handoutView image in fullscreenEmotional turmoil … Phoebe Bridgers.Photograph: Olof Grind/PR handoutPhoebe BridgersReviewPhoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocation(Dead Oceans)After sweeping the Grammys and being scrutinised by the press, Bridgers deploys electronics and unsettling sound design to brilliantly evoke emotional turmoilAlexis PetridisWed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last time Phoebe Bridgers put out a solo album was six years ago, at the height of the Covid pandemic:Punishernot only ended 2020 near the top of many critics’ best-of lists, it made the UK Top 10 and sold half a million copies in the US. The intervening period has proved just as commercially triumphant. With the release of their debut album The Record,Boygenius– the band she had formed with Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker – went from a kind of supergroup for Pitchfork readers to a genuine mainstream phenomenon: the album won three Grammys. Another win, for Bridgers’ collaboration with SZA, Ghost in the Machine, meant Bridgers left the 2024 ceremony the night’s biggest winner. Other pop stars called on her services: she sang on Taylor Swift’s re-recorded version of Red (and supported on the Eras tour), Lorde’s Solar Power and on Paul McCartney’s McCartney III Imagined.View image in fullscreenPhoebe Bridgers: Lost WeekendBut to judge by Lost Weekend’s opening track, all was not well. The Outside depicts the singer crowd-surfing at a gig in Ohio – “they never let me hit the ground, way beyond the barricade” – and ending a song with her fist triumphantly raised. Then it adds a qualifier. “But I was on the outside, watching,” she sings, the sense of dislocation heightened by the fact that her voice is smothered by a vocoder, and the musical accompaniment – a sweet fingerpicked acoustic guitar figure – keeps vanishing into an ambient backing that sounds like static.It acts as a signpost to the rest of Lost Weekend, musically and lyrically. There is a lot of emotional turmoil in the latter, largely occasioned by the death of her father, with whom Bridgers had a strained relationship – though the album is dedicated “For Dad” – and the collapse of her high-profile relationship with actor Paul Mescal: the title track confirms that they were, as rumoured, engaged (“I’m supposed to be married but I called it off”). If you’re the kind of person who gets their kicks combing new albums for celebrity gossip, there’s plenty here to occupy you, not least a line in The Governor’s Waltz that could be interpreted as a swipe at Mescal’s current partner, Gracie Abrams (“she can pretend to be me / Since she took my place in my bed, on that stage”).Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Boys – videoThat said, you certainly don’t need to have a prurient interest in the vacillations of celebrity romance to feel the album’s emotional impact. The Governor’s Waltz would be an acutely drawn and genuinely affecting portrait of a relationship in its clingy death throes regardless of who the protagonists were; the clattering, chaotic Bobby is equally impactful in its depiction of the heady early days of a love affair, complete with a line about no longer requiring the services of a vibrator, or rather “a thing in a box I don’t fuck any more”.
