Still Standing, meanwhile, describes the disquieting sensation of being unable to muster the emotions you’re supposed to feel at the death of a parent: digging around for fond memories, Bridgers instead comes up with recollections of spousal abuse, distance and irrational behaviour and ends up “feeling indifferent, wearing black”. “I am my old man’s oldest son,” she sings at the album’s conclusion. “I fought the wall and the wall won.”Bridgers’ lyrics are brilliant throughout, but they’re matched by the individuality of Lost Weekend’s sound. At heart it’s a well-written Americana-infused indie singer-songwriter album, complete with the yearning melodies, acoustic guitars, mandolins and melancholy violin you might expect, made by people well-versed in such things: the cast list features Jack Antonoff, Bridgers’ Boygenius bandmates, Jon Brion, Alex G and Conor Oberst. But perhaps the most telling credits are those for “sound design”: for huge swathes of Lost Weekend, the standard indie singer-songwriter instruments struggle to make themselves heard amid waves of droning electronics, splinters of feedback and eerie wordless vocals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPhoebe Bridgers on Taylor Swift, her boyfriend Paul Mescal and speaking out on Roe v Wade: ‘I want to show everybody what I believe in’Read moreSongs suddenly plunge into silence, or are drenched in swirling, dreamlike echo or subject to unexpected codas that often pull in different emotional directions. Kill Me’s closing desire to vanish – the lyrics reference the case of the Somerton Man, an unidentified body found in late 1940s Adelaide – is far more aggressive than the rest of the song; the title track explodes into chattering euphoria. The overall effect is disorientating, occasionally disturbing and really thrilling: there’s something really daring about the sound of Panorama, where a beautiful melody and a rustic banjo figure are almost completely buried under occasionally discordant murk.The result is a heady, potent, occasionally wrenching album, albeit one flecked with optimism. The most straightforward thing here is Never Going Back!, which repeats the line “the way it used to be is not the way it is” over and over to a charging indie-rock backing. As Above looks ahead to the point where the first flush of romance fades into familiarity, and gives it a positive spin: “You’re gonna take me for granted but I can handle it.”“The past is looking brighter all the time,” sings Bridgers on Liberty Tree. The path to get to that point has evidently been a trying one: Lost Weekend transforms it into a rich and rewarding journey.Lost Weekend is released on 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsPhoebe BridgersIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Film posters for The Mummy banned from public display in UK | Movies | The Guardian
description: Watchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Watchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’
Content: Part of the poster for The Mummy that provoked 30 complaints after appearing in London tube stations.Photograph: ASA/PAPart of the poster for The Mummy that provoked 30 complaints after appearing in London tube stations.Photograph: ASA/PAMoviesFilm posters for The Mummy banned from public display in UKWatchdogs say adverts in London tube stations broke its rules with ‘realistic impression of a dead child’Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 5 Aug 2026 09.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm posters for The Mummy have been banned from outdoor public display in the UK because they include realistic depictions of a dead child.The UK’sAdvertising Standards Authority(ASA) received 30 complaints over the promotional campaign in London tube stations for the new Lee Cronin film.The adverts included a poster showing a closeup image of a female with a mummified appearance and one eye swollen shut. The text said: “Some things are meant to stay buried.”TV and livestreaming services trailed scenes of a body being removed from a sarcophagus and a woman looking distressed as a greying hand with long brittle nails brushes her cheek. The advert, which ends with the mother saying “I just want my daughter back”, was approved by the Clearcast vetting agency for post-7.30pm broadcasts.Many of the complainants said the ads were distressing for children and adults alike.Warner Bros defended the campaign, saying it had been prepared with “due responsibility to consumers and society” and was not designed to create fear or offence.It said the character depicted in the posters was a “living mummy” who was returned to her parents many years after been kidnapped as a child.Warner said the posters used a face with a neutral expression and reduced the risk of distress by avoiding elements of violence, threat or intimidation.The studio added that the design had been submitted to Transport for London’s advertising partner Global and had been accepted for display on theLondon Undergroundnetwork.It said the horror themes in the trailer were implied rather than shown explicitly and contained no “jump scares, no violence or gore” and no graphic imagery.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUpholding complaints about the posters, the ASA said the grey and ashen appearance of the female’s skin, the dry and cracked lips and mouth, one eye swollen shut and the other fixed and vacant, together with the sunken and lifeless appearance of the face, gave a “realistic impression of a dead child”.It said that while the ads were not placed within 100 metres of any schools, one billboard was visible from a children’s nursery.The watchdog said: “In any case, we considered the image was likely to distress young children and that it was unsuitable for display where it was likely to be seen by them. We therefore concluded that the ads were unsuitable for outdoor display and therefore breached the code.”Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsAdvertising Standards AuthorityAdvertisingLondonLondon UndergroundShareReuse this content

title: ‘Getting old is no fun’: Game of Thrones author George RR Martin speaks out about depression amid further book delays | George RR Martin | The Guardian
description: A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: A new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire series
Content: ‘There have been nightmares’ … George RR Martin in 2019.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘There have been nightmares’ … George RR Martin in 2019.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverGeorge RR Martin‘Getting old is no fun’: Game of Thrones author George RR Martin speaks out about depression amid further book delaysA new blog post by the fantasy writer has outlined his recent difficulties, as fans continue to speculate on the elusive sixth book in his A Song of Ice and Fire seriesEmma LoffhagenWed 5 Aug 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge RR Martin has opened up about experiencing depression during a “stressful” and “overwhelming” year, as readers continue to await the long-delayed sixth instalment of his A Song of Ice and Fire series.The 77-year-old American author, whose fantasy novels shaped and inspired the hit HBO television seriesGame of Thrones,wrote candidly about his recent difficulties in his first personal blog post for almost six months.“This year has been … stressful, to say the least,” he wrote ina post titled Better Late Than Never. “So much has been happening, it’s been overwhelming. Some great things, exciting things. Dreams coming true. But there have been nightmares too. I have lost friends. Battled sadness and depression. The worst may be yet to come.”He explained that posts published on his website since February had been written by his assistants because he had continued to fall behind despite their help.Martin, who turns 78 in September, also reflected on ageing; “getting old is no fun”, he wrote, although he added that the year had contained “amazing times” alongside its difficulties.“I suppose that’s just life. Of course, I knew that. If you’ve read my stories, you know that.”A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms has saved the Game of Thrones universeRead moreAmong the year’s highlights, Martin noted thatA Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,HBO’s Game of Thrones prequel based on his Tales of Dunk and Egg novellas, had received nine Emmy nominations, including for outstanding drama series.His comments come amidcontinued speculation about The Winds of Winter,the planned sixth and penultimate novel in A Song of Ice and Fire. The book has been in progress since the publication of the fifth instalment, A Dance with Dragons, in 2011, and has become one of the most eagerly awaited novels in modern publishing. No publication date has been announced.Martin has faced sustained criticism from some readers over the delay, and has previously referred to the book as “the curse of my life”. The Game of Thrones TV show eventually overtook its source material, with its later seasons following a separate narrative that receiveda mixed response from critics and viewers,especially after its final season in 2019.In ablog post in May 2025, Martin directly addressed those who believed he had abandoned the series, sarcastically listing the accusations levelled against him: “I will never finish Winds. If I do, I will never finish A Dream of Spring. If I do, it won’t be any good.”Continuing the charges, he wrote: “I am going to die soon anyway, because I am so old. I lost all interest in A Song of Ice and Fire decades ago. I don’t give a shit about writing any longer, I just sit around and spend my money.”But Martin insisted that he remained invested in Westeros and its characters. “I care about them all,” he wrote. “More than you can ever imagine.”In an interview withthe Hollywood Reporter in January, Martin said he had completed about 1,100 manuscript pages of The Winds of Winter. He said leaving the series unfinished would feel like “a total failure”, adding: “I do think if I can just get some of these other things off my back, I could finish The Winds of Winter pretty soon … It’s been made clear to me that Winds is the priority, but … I don’t know. Sometimes I’m not in the mood for that.”In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsGeorge RR MartinFantasy booksGame of ThronesFictionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Video game maker EA bought by Saudi-led group for $55bn | Games | The Guardian
description: Company acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Company acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner
Content: Electronic Arts is known for video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield.Photograph: EA GamesView image in fullscreenElectronic Arts is known for video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield.Photograph: EA GamesGamesVideo game maker EA bought by Saudi-led group for $55bnCompany acquired in deal involving Affinity Partners, a firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared KushnerJoanna PartridgeWed 5 Aug 2026 02.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectronic Arts, the maker of video games such as The Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield, has been bought by Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund and a group of investors for $55bn (£41bn).The company announced the completion of the deal on Tuesday evening, only days after the EU gave its approval, the final regulatory green light needed.EA is best known for its blockbuster sports games including EA Sports FC (previously called Fifa). In what is one of the biggest buyouts on record, EAGamesis being taken private, ending its 36-year history as a publicly traded company.The company has been bought by Saudi Arabia’s PIF along with Affinity Partners, a private equity company run by Donald Trump’s son-in-lawJared Kushnerand the private equity firm Silver Lake Partners.“EA has created stories, characters, and communities that have become part of everyday life for hundreds of millions of people,” Kushner said. “We’re excited to support the company as it continues to reach new audiences, inspire the next generation of creators, and expand the ways people around the world connect through play.”The Saudi royal family has been investing in video games and esports for some time, alongside sports, media andcomedy, while the Saudi crown prince,Mohammed bin Salman, has a reputation for being a gamer.EA was founded by the former Apple employee William “Trip” Hawkins in 1982. Hawkins began playing analog versions of baseball and football made by Strat-O-Matic as a teenager during the 1960s. The company has been run by its current chief executive, Andrew Wilson, since 2013.EA’s games still have a dedicated fanbase, although its annual revenues have stagnated in recent years, hovering between $7.4bn and $7.6bn.Competition from mobile video game makers, such as Epic Games, has intensified in recent years, and one of EA’s biggest rivals, Activision Blizzard, was bought by Microsoft foralmost $69bnin 2023.As a private company, EA will no longer be required to report its financial results each quarter, freeing it from some scrutiny, which some analysts say can remove some pressure to meet targets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, there are often job cuts and cost-cutting at formerly public companies when they are taken private, although there has not been any suggestion that this will happen at EA.The company laid off about 5% of its workforce in 2024 but had 14,500 employees in March 2025 and cut several hundred jobs in May.On Monday, EA reported lower than expected revenues in the last quarter, blamed on a decline in engagement with its latest Battlefield game.Explore more on these topicsGamesMergers and acquisitionsSaudi ArabiaJared KushnerPrivate equityEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sterling Point review – this teen drama from Gossip Girl’s creators is brilliant escapist TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Set on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mystery
Author: Micha Frazer-Carroll
Headline: Set on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mystery
Content: Summer state of mind … Bo Bragason (left) and Ella Rubin in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoView image in fullscreenSummer state of mind … Bo Bragason (left) and Ella Rubin in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoTV reviewTelevisionReviewSterling Point review – this teen drama from Gossip Girl’s creators is brilliant escapist TVSet on an idyllic Canadian island, this coming-of-age series is juicy stuff. It swaps the darkness of recent YA TV for warmth, humour and a surprisingly compelling mysteryMicha Frazer-CarrollWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ll be honest: I was prepared to grit my teeth through Sterling Point, Prime Video’s newest coming-of-age offering, which I dismissed as another by-the-numbers high-school drama. The show follows a type-A teen on a journey of sun-dappled self-discovery, escaping her native New York for an idyllic getaway on a picturesque Canadian island. It’s an unassuming, summer camp-style narrative, but in the style of last year’s seasonal phenomenon that was series three ofThe Summer I Turned Pretty, it manages to transcend the limits of its YA niche, revealing itself to be quite juicy.Protagonist Annie (Ella Rubin) is a highly strung 17-year-old, still reeling from a rejection from a summer business school programme when she receives the news that her estranged maternal grandfather has left her some mysterious assets. Annie, whose mother had died years ago, and her twin Connor (Keen Ruffalo), are prompted to start digging through family secrets, much to the distress of their dad (Jay Duplass of Transparent and Industry). The two learn that they’ve inherited a house in Canada – prompting Annie to take off on a secret trip in search of answers about her late mother’s life.We find ourselves on Sterling Point where Annie quickly finds herself a group of free-spirited friends, including Oona (Bo Bragason), the carefree and sexually forward linchpin of the group; Ellis (Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie), the cheeky local who flies Annie out to the island on a precarious seaplane; Rory (Daniel Quinn-Toye), a sensitive New Yorker who gets compared to Timothée Chalamet; and Ramona (Amélie Elisabeth Hoeferle), who drops a bombshell at the end of the show’s first episode. It rapidly becomes clear that the group is going to spend their leisurely time swimming in beautiful lakes, boating and crushing on each other.View image in fullscreenLake effect ... Ella Rubin and Bo Bragason in Sterling Point.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Prime VideoBeyond an intriguing central plot full of familial mysteries – which I can’t go into without entirely spoiling things – the show is doing something interesting in its generational context. Unlike the sort of timeless, placeless high-schoolers that millennial-plus screenwriters often dream up, these gen Z and gen alpha characters (from the creators ofMy Old Assand Gossip Girl) talk like actual young people, and reflect their modern preoccupations.Among this crew, there’s lots of fluidity, and an overflow of emotional literacy. Oona’s little sister, Maple (Mabel Strachan), is casually readingBessel van der Kolk’s The Body Keeps the Score: “I need to find out what the score is, and where in the body it’s being kept.” The sexualities of many of the characters are a sort of question mark, slowly emerging or shifting as the show goes on, reminiscent of coming-of-age forebears such asThe Half of ItandBooksmart. No one’s gender or queerness is turned into a major plot point, reflecting the fact that more than one in five gen Zsidentify as LGBTQ+. I laughed out loud at a quip about Oona, who, like her own mother, has repeated noncommittal flings that don’t turn into anything serious. “So she’s avoidant attached? We can work through that,” says 17-year-old Connor.The bounds of the YA genre, and of television, feel pretty flexible here. Lines get blundered a few times, and the cameras keep rolling – since the young actors were explicitly encouraged to improvise on set. There are moments where this can fall a bit flat: a punchline doesn’t quite land, or you experience the metaphorical emotional equivalent of seeing a boom in shot. But this also allows for a looser, more authentic feel. The plot and pacing take the same approach – in thespirit of Duplass’s Transparent, sometimes a plotline gets teed up and then completely disappears, subverting the usual rules of television and making things feel more frenetic.Again, there are drawbacks to this approach. More than once, the show contains what feels like a glaring plot hole. But the strangeness of these plotting and script flourishes creates an electricity that is actually more interesting than the love triangles, paternity secrets and other age-old devices at play here.In April, season three of the once boundary-pushing teen drama Euphoria was met withflop reviews. The darkness that had once distinguished and sustained the show had spiralled out of control into a nightmarish, violent and hallucinatory sex fest. The show’s first season, much like Skins, upended the glossy, sanitised teen TV of the 2010s, giving us something that felt gritty and real. Perhaps now we’re seeking an escape from this. “You turn on Netflix and it’s, like, One Tree Hill and Gossip Girl. They’re all trending again,” Canadian creator Megan Parkrecently told Teen Vogue.This feeling of refuge is enhanced by the fact that phones and social media barely feature in the show, despite the fact that teenagers now averagemore than eight hours of screen time per day. Technology is swapped for the ambient sounds and textures of nature, as well as real-life conversation, with all of its accompanying miscommunications and deceptions.If escapism is the brief, then Sterling Point fulfils it expertly. Sure, it doesn’t carry the intensity or the existentialism of its edgier counterparts. But I was surprised by how long I wanted to stay with these characters and inhabit their island bubble. It kept subverting my expectations. I didn’t want to go home.Sterling Point is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ted Lasso season four review – TV’s most wholesome football comedy is back | Television | The Guardian
description: It looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilled
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: It looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilled
Content: Anodyne, unreal … (from left): Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in Ted Lasso season four.Photograph: Apple TV+/PAView image in fullscreenAnodyne, unreal … (from left): Brendan Hunt, Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds in Ted Lasso season four.Photograph: Apple TV+/PATV reviewTelevisionReviewTed Lasso season four review – TV’s most wholesome football comedy is backIt looked like it was gone forever, but Jason Sudeikis’s hugely popular show returns with a premise that’s all twee nonsensicality. If you love messages of positivity and togetherness, you’ll be thrilledRachel AroestiWed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving transported a flailing AFC Richmond to the upper echelons of the Premier League with his wholesome, folksy and highly simile-reliant management style, the finale of Ted Lasso’s third season saw our titular coach return to the US to spend more time with his son in Kansas. At the time (2023), the general impression was that we were waving goodbye for good. But could this intensely American protagonist really do the most British thing of all and bow out at the height of his sitcom’s popularity? Nope. Last year it was announced that its star and co-creatorJason Sudeikishad caved to market forces and was reprising his colossally popular alter ego.It was the logical thing to do: the 11-time Emmy-winning show was the most-watched streaming original of 2023. Not that logic features heavily in this fourth season. Before we discover how Ted has been lured back to south-west London, we find out what he’s been up to in the interim. Did he parlay his success into US soccer? Return triumphantly to college football? Sit back with his millions and rest on his laurels? Nope, nope and nope again. Instead, he’s working in his local supermarket, warmly greeting his customers by name, providing moral guidance to younger colleagues and generally radiating his trademark howdily-doodily energy. Why? Because he’s a good man without ego who loves to connect and make a positive difference in his community! This is Ted Lasso we’re talking about!Back to the central head-scratcher. Ted left the UK at the top of his game, ultimately choosing fatherhood over riches, professional triumph and beloved colleagues. What could possibly change his mind? Richmond’s owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham, as aspirationally imperious as ever), her deputy Higgins (Jeremy Swift, as satisfyingly square as ever) and marketing manager Keeley (Juno Temple, as unsettlingly childlike as ever) think they’ve cracked it: they fly to Kansas to offer him the job of managing the women’s team, who are languishing in the second division. Obviously, Ted declines. But then his mother – the same mother who last season convinced him to come home – encourages him to go back. So he asks his son and his estranged wife if they fancy coming with. With little explanation, they agree.If you are already a Ted Lasso ultra, you may be inclined to gloss over the twee nonsensicality of this fourth season’s setup and simply sink back into the show’s anodyne atmosphere, one that revolves around messages of positivity, togetherness and how good it is when your football team wins. If you bristle at such blatant emotional button-pushing, you might come to another conclusion: Ted Lasso is fake and phoney, to use the kind of Americanism this show loves putting into the mouths of its British characters (who calls it “the John Lewis Christmas commercial”?!). From the vague transatlanticism and fairytale London to the football-based inaccuracies and stiffly unreal vibe, Ted Lasso rarely bears any relation to reality. This is not a show for pedants.That said, the shift in focus to women’s football does at least mean entertaining some hard truths. Ted’s new assistant coach Alice Chilton (Sex Education’sTanya Reynolds) is a dour taskmaster furious at having been passed over for the top job in favour of a man. And although Ted quickly gets to work in his signature style – improving morale by drilling down into the players’ psyches – his efforts are hampered by the chronic lack of investment in women’s sport, plus injury, pregnancy, motherhood and the fact he’s barely allowed inside the changing room for propriety’s sake.Alien erotica, football coaching and making Meryl Streep cry: Ted Lasso’s new star Tanya Reynolds opens upRead moreStill, in the four episodes made available to reviewers, the tension never properly builds. Ted sees the care and industriousness behind Alice’s stony-faced exterior, which is destined to crack imminently. Rather than establishing the new team as individuals (beyond one hard-as-nails goalie and two squabbling Irish sisters), the show often falls back on comfortingly familiar dynamics: the will-they-won’t-they between Roy Kent, still manager of the men’s team, and his ex Keeley among them.For all its irritatingly ersatz qualities, the appeal of Ted Lasso is as clear as ever: the signposted comic beats, the predictable gestures towards kindness and reconciliation, the bright colours, the clean lines. A sense of quality entertainment still hangs about the whole well-oiled endeavour. Think of it as the TV equivalent of Taylor Swift: ruthlessly efficient, reassuringly dorky, blatantly basic and as monocultural as any Apple TV offering is going to get. While I suspect season four will shed some viewers – primarily those who prefer the glamour of the men’s game over the more injustice-focused angle any show about women’s sport must take – fans will be relieved to hear the show has by no means embraced gritty naturalism. Ted Lasso is still saccharine business as usual and, no doubt, still a lot of people’s cup of tea.Ted Lasso is on Apple TVExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTV comedyJason SudeikisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Ghost of the Mountains by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi review – the secrets of the snow leopard | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: An Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animal
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: An Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animal
Content: A snow leopard.Photograph: Edo Schmidt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA snow leopard.Photograph: Edo Schmidt/AlamyBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewThe Ghost of the Mountains by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi review – the secrets of the snow leopardAn Indian mountaineer follows in the footsteps of explorers and conservationists in search of an enigmatic animalEdward PosnettWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen bored, try the following game – I call it “Purr or Roar?”. Take any feline and guess whether it can purr or roar (it cannot do both because purring and roaring require different anatomical structures). Some candidates are easy: any child knows that lions and tigers roar and that a tabby does not. But between the great cats and our pets are numerous other species, from lynxes to panthers, whose anatomy is not so easy to infer. A leopard, for instance? Roar (or growl). The discreet, mountain-dwelling snow leopard? Purr.The snow leopard is the protagonist of Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi’s first book, a compelling and intimate look at this elusive mountain specialist. An Indian conservationist and mountaineer, Suryawanshi pursues the creature through the Himalayas and Gobi desert. This is a gritty and detailed portrait of an often misunderstood and endangered species in an increasingly hostile, crowded and hot environment.Suryawanshi grew up in Aurangabad in the Deccan Peninsula – far away from the snow leopard’s habitat – and decided to pursue ecology after reading biologist George Schaller’s The Year of the Gorilla in the city’s public library. He writes of his admiration for western conservationists, mountaineers and explorers – Schaller, Reinhold Messner, and British imperial adventurer Francis Younghusband – and yet he is an Indian writer, writing about the ecology of his own country. As much as his book is about snow leopards, it also asks us to consider their biographers: who is it who gets to tell the story of the nonhuman lives around us?Despite its name, the snow leopard has little in common with the leopard (its closest living relative is the tiger). And, unlike the leopard, it is adapted to the harsh and rugged terrain of the highest ranges, from India to Russia. It has an absurdly bushy tail, used both as extra limb and voluminous shawl, and large paws which act like snow shoes. What it lacks in power (it does not have a particularly strong bite), it makes up for in agility and guile (snow leopards can chase their prey down steep cliff faces; and have been known to drive horses into deep snow where they can be picked off). They are extremely difficult to spot; Suryawanshi observes that their “ochre-and-dust-colour coat with its irregular rosettes looks exactly like a rock covered with lichens”. Indeed, he muses, they should really be called “rock leopards”.I have read much about the snow leopard, or rather books by writers searching for some ideal version of them. Suryawanshi’s book is very different, and can almost be read in opposition to the quest narratives of, say, Peter Matthiessen or Sylvain Tesson. Much like a conservationist’s diary, his book is shorn of romance, and recounts the grind of observing and counting snow leopards in remote parts of the world, far away from his wife and young daughter. He wades through snow, sets up camera traps, and tries to defuse tensions with local herders. His snow leopards are part of an ecosystem, just like any other animal; they are hated and loved, as well as being objects of indifference.According to Suryawanshi, although snow leopards prefer to hunt wild animals, up to 70% of their diet is livestock, a recipe for conflict with local people. He talks to one herder in the Spiti Valley of the Indian Himalayas who nonchalantly relates that he shot a snow leopard after it attacked his goats, and dumped its corpse in a river. Here is no sacred object of veneration, then, but a potential pest, the equivalent of European fox (other locals speak of their fondness for the cats: a community in the village of Kibber ended up adopting and feeding a sick snow leopard, even naming him Rancho after a character in a Bollywood film).Much of Suryawanshi’s work is dedicated to mediating conflict between the cats and locals. He assists in the design of a livestock enclosure that can deter the claws and ingenuity of a hungry snow leopard; and makes recommendations on schemes to compensate herders whose animals have been killed. Interestingly, he notes that women are the most hostile to snow leopards as they are the ones who look after livestock (and do not necessarily benefit from compensation schemes). One local woman asks: “why don’t you marry one of your snow leopards?”The most painful section in the book relates to the bitter dispute regarding the The International Union forConservationof Nature’s 2017 decision to downgrade the animal’s from “endangered” to “vulnerable”. Suryawanshi and his colleagues at the Snow Leopard Trust bitterly opposed the move, arguing that the decision was based on flawed science and driven by the political considerations of large NGOs in the west. In his eyes, “racial power dynamics and colonial legacies of conservation and research” were at play. As of today, the snow leopard is still classed as vulnerable.There is a critique here of the stories that we have told ourselves about the snow leopard, an attempt to wrest it back from literary and metropolitan writers. In one section, Suryawanshi retraces Matthiessen’s steps in Nepal, but it seems as though his heart isn’t really in it. Along the way, he notices the effects of mass tourism, and learns that Nepal’s richest man, who owns an instant noodle company, had sought to build a resort in a remote village for tourists hoping to spot snow leopards. He takes a gentle swipe at Matthiessen: did the American writer ever stop to think about the consequences of mythologising the creature?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI think it’s a push to blame Matthiessen for the plight of the snow leopard, in the same way that Melville shouldn’t be held accountable for the decline in sperm whales. But Suryawanshi’s point is that stories matter: the snow leopard has become a commodity in the way that Everest has, a mountain to be summited. The effect of this book is a gradual stripping away of mystification, revealing the snow leopard to be fragile and beautiful just like any other inhabitant of high mountain ranges – the pika, the wild yak, the Pallas’s cat – but no less wondrous for it, and no less deserving of our attention and respect.The Ghost of the Mountains: Unravelling the Secrets of the Snow Leopard by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi is published by Grant (£20). title: A Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin review – a surprising and darkly funny debut | Books | The Guardian
description: A dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novel
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novel
Content: Wry humour … Brodie Crellin.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenWry humour … Brodie Crellin.Photograph: PRBooksReviewA Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin review – a surprising and darkly funny debutA dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novelElla Fox-MartensWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of us come upon our family’s dysfunctions gradually, like a door that opens a little wider each year. This uncle, you find out, has had an affair; grandma has a hoarding problem. The cremation of the nuclear family illusion is a cornerstone of literature, especially when it’s hastened by one of those unavoidable core gatherings: weddings, births, funerals. But what happens when there was never any illusion to start with; when the story begins in the ashes?The delight of Brodie Crellin’s accomplished, surprising debut lies in the way it wrestles with this question, and in its depiction of a family that fails to meet any conventional definition of the word. With a cutting eye and wry humour, Crellin finds fantastic power in the story of three maladjusted people reeling in the face of death, whose relationships to one another are endlessly confronting and complex.There is friendless Patch, riddled with anxiety, who bursts into tears at the memory of the postman’s suicide and falls victim to a terrible haircut. There is Patch’s father, Robin, who is “gay, yes, mostly, but mutable”. And there is Jude, her domineering, malevolently competent cousin, a playwright who “loves to make an entrance”. They’re bound by the newly deceased Mary: Robin’s ex, Patch’s mother, and Jude’s aunt – a woman who “[didn’t] have a problem with gay men” but was lukewarm on lesbians. Orbiting this “isosceles”, as Jude calls it, is Juliette, Jude’s gleefully moneyed mother, and Mel, Mary’s neighbour. Various other characters swing in and out, all fully realised no matter how brief their appearances, my favourite of which was Mary’s poor, forgotten “empath” labrador, Leonard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt’s a joy to read fiction that understands sex so well, and is neither sentimental nor sleazyThe stage is set, as Jude cruises in from Naples, for a fraught collision of past and present. As the funeral draws closer and tensions simmer, Crellin juggles the minutiae of death – chopping vegetables, arranging memorial photos – with fragmented recollections of messy family history. It’s rare to read a novel that can skip in and out of so many points of view and keep the different styles of narration intact. Yet even with regular flashbacks, A Sense of Occasion feels remarkably natural thanks to Crellin’s light touch, especially in the arch, zippy dialogue. There are shades of classic mid-century stories, particularly Dorothy Baker’s Cassandra at the Wedding, and some of the caustic social wit of Edward St Aubyn’s Melrose chronicles, but the boldness feels entirely modern.It’s a joy, too, to read fiction that understands sex so well, and is neither sentimental nor sleazy. Crellin conveys the importance of sex as a vehicle for each character’s foibles and desires; as a shadowy place where so much can be manipulated and communicated. The book summons up a kaleidoscope of erotic experience across the spectrum, sometimes hot and sometimes ridiculous, including a quasi-incestuous relationship rendered with nuance and consideration.If the novel leans a little hard on Jude and her mother, Juliette, for its class critiques, it’s easily forgiven on account of just how much fun it is to watch these characters crash into each other, and for the deftly nasty one-liners that they toss out. “Patch lacked the confidence conferred by a private education,” Jude thinks smugly. “But she could also say that Patch was simply less intelligent.” And yet the story never veers into mean-spirited satire, largely thanks to Patch herself, the grief-stricken daughter, who is the heartbeat of the novel. Perennially misunderstood and underestimated – including by her own mother, when she was alive – Patch is awkward but raw, a keen observer of herself and others.There is immense pleasure and vitality – and ultimately a great deal of tenderness – in A Sense of Occasion’s depiction of flawed, strange people who love badly, and can’t help but get in the way of themselves over and over again. After all, as George Bernard Shaw wrote, “If you cannot get rid of the family skeleton, you may as well make it dance.”A Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin is published by Jonathan Cape (£16.99).
