title: Holy Days review – even Miriam Margolyes, Jacki Weaver and Judy Davis as nuns can’t save this film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Despite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far between
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Despite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far between
Content: ‘Earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie’ … Judy Davis, Elijah Tamati, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesView image in fullscreen‘Earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie’ … Judy Davis, Elijah Tamati, Miriam Margolyes and Jacki Weaver in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesMoviesReviewHoly Days review – even Miriam Margolyes, Jacki Weaver and Judy Davis as nuns can’t save this filmDespite the movie’s stacked cast, an oddly threadbare storyline and comedy that targets low-hanging fruit leaves the laughs few and far betweenLuke BuckmasterWed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 16.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree stubborn old nuns and a wide-eyed young whippersnapper head off on a mission to save the farm – sorry, convent – in this earnestly made but emotionally lukewarm road movie. The ace up Holy Days’ sleeve is the casting, with each nun played by a legend of stage and screen: Judy Davis as Sister Agnes,Miriam Margolyesas Sister Luke and Jacki Weaver as Sister Mary Clare. It quickly becomes clear, however, that nobody is on their A-game. And the film itself is a frustrating mix of comedy and drama: not funny enough to solicit any real laughs, nor sufficiently dramatic to forge strong connections with the characters.These folk are a rather unexciting lot, despite a clear desire to present young Brian (Elijah Tamati) as the emotional glue holding things together and the habit-wearing trio as hot-blooded eccentrics. Their rundown convent, which we’re supposed to feel invested in, is a drab location both aesthetically and emotionally; it’s decaying – but not in a handsome, cinematic way. Nor is it brought to life by the people who inhabit it; in fact, the building feels borderline soulless. Maybe the developers have a point, I caught myself thinking, and this crusty old place could become a snazzy new apartment block or shopping centre.The Birthday Trip review – excellent Australian black comedy piles pressure on to privilegeRead more“Goodbye, convent!” isn’t exactly the response intended by the writer-director, Nat Boltt (adapting Dame Joy Cowley’s novel of the same name), who really needed viewers to feel invested in the characters and their circumstances. Instead, the experience feels syrupy and sentimental; less playing the heartstrings than giving them a forceful yanking.When the three sisters get wind that the convent’s land is at risk, they head off to find a property deed in the hope that they can save the day. In tow is Brian (because: fun intergenerational dynamics!) who is struggling to adapt to his father (Craig Hall) having a new romantic partner after his mother’s death. Curiously for a road movie, there aren’t many interesting locations, though the settings are picturesque – New Zealand’s magnificent landscapes providing some pretty scaffolding. The storyline is oddly threadbare and includes an unintentionally amusing revelation about halfway through that drains the central quest of its narrative purpose.View image in fullscreenJacki Weaver, Miriam Margolyes and Judy Davis in Holy Days.Photograph: Kismet MoviesComedically, Boltt opts for low-hanging fruit, ie nuns behaving in mildly risque ways. In one scene, Sister Agnes lights up a cigarette (gasp!) and Sister Luke’s dentures fly out of her mouth after she takes a toke; in another, one of the nuns farts when they’re all tucked in bed together. There are also kids-say-the-darndest-things type moments, such as one in which Brian, aghast that Agnes has confessed to stealing a car, exclaims: “You did a sin! You should be prostituted!” The punchlines feel as subtle as a giant sign flashing: “LAUGH.”From early on, one can sense it’s a question ofwhenrather thanifHoly Days will dissolve into cheese and wishy-washiness. Even then it exceeds expectations, culminating in one of those cringe-inducing scenes in which the principal cast converge for a good old-fashioned dance-off, big smiles on their faces as they get jiggy with it. There are some flecks of interest en route to this non-ending, coming almost entirely from that wonderful trio of screen legends, though they are few and far between.Holy Days is out in Australian cinemas now, UK cinemas from 14 August and on digital platforms in the US nowExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsMiriam MargolyesJacki WeaverJudy DavisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Child of My Own review – barely believable true crime tale of desperation and delusion | Movies | The Guardian
description: Candy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudrama
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Candy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudrama
Content: How reliable is her version of events? … Ana Celeste in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixView image in fullscreenHow reliable is her version of events? … Ana Celeste in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixMoviesReviewA Child of My Own review – barely believable true crime tale of desperation and delusionCandy-coloured recreations of one woman’s pregnancy unravel as dark truths are revealed in Maite Alberdi’s intimate docudramaPhil HoadWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis cheekily inquisitive docudrama by Chilean director Maite Alberdi features a unique variation on the long con, and one with a precise duration: nine months. After suffering three miscarriages and under pressure from her husband and in-laws to give them a child, Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza (aka Ale, and played by Ana Celeste in re-enactments) decides to fake her next pregnancy. She is determined to have something to show at the end of it: after meeting single mother Mayra, who wants to abort her second pregnancy, at the hospital where she works, Ale agrees to take her baby once it is born.The details are hardly believable: eating copiously to gain weight, Ale manages to convince husband Arturo (Armando Espitia) and his family that this pregnancy is on track for her entire term. She reflexively tenses her muscles while he strokes her baby bump and smiles through a swirl of conflicting thoughts at her baby shower. While most con artists must dupe themselves on some level, it is true down to a physiological level in Ale’s case: a judge later testifies that her desperation to bear children may have resulted in a pseudo-pregnancy. How else to explain that the doctor signing off her maternity leave appears to hear the baby’s heartbeat?‘She wasn’t acting, she wanted to live it’: how a fake pregnancy resulted in the wildest true crime film of the yearRead moreThe first half of the film depicts this false paradise in candy-coloured reconstructions, linked up by voiceover from the real-life Ale. But as soon as she walks out of the General Hospital of Mexico with her baby hidden in a gift bag, Alberdi switches to the sobering real-life register. Arrested by the police in a motel room shortly afterwards, Ale is now finishing a 13-year prison sentence for child kidnapping. As the talking heads weigh up her degree of culpability, the film’s initial distancing device – showing the various actors auditioning to play Ale – suddenly makes sense. How reliable is her version of events, in particular her claim of the adoption arrangement? The actual Mayra, unable to forgive the abduction, insists it is total fiction.Even if Ale’s story is true, it highlights the level of her desperation, and the power of societal and biological narratives in setting our agendas. Engaging in a metaphysical parlour game of veracity-chasing, Alberdi is perhaps a little lax in resolving this central point. It allows Ale, in her fuschia-hued jail cell, to remain a broadly sympathetic protagonist – one who, in her later dealings with Arturo (who also served two years), seems to gain considerably in self-knowledge. Reminiscent ofBart Layton’s The Imposterin its portrayal of unfeasible auto-delusion, A Child of My Own is a refreshing branch-out for true crime stories into less violent, more intimate enigmas.A Child of My Own is in UK cinemas from 7 August, and on Netflix from 13 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsParents and parentingChildbirthPregnancyFamilyCrime filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ice Cream Man review – Eli Roth’s junky slasher is one of year’s worst horrors | Horror films | The Guardian
description: The Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheap
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheap
Content: Ari Millen in Ice Cream Man.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAri Millen in Ice Cream Man.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockHorror filmsReviewIce Cream Man review – Eli Roth’s junky slasher is one of year’s worst horrorsThe Hostel and Thanksgiving director takes a massive stumble with a rushed retro horror made on the cheapJesse HassengerWed 5 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years ago, Eli Roth realized his long-held ambition to make a movie out ofThanksgiving, the horror-movie trailer he made as a gag for the Quentin Tarantino/Robert Rodriguez anthology feature Grindhouse, back in 2007. Though he didn’t actually go so far as to make the scratched-up decades-ago slasher shown in the original trailer, Thanksgiving was still Roth’s most satisfying movie in ages, replete with ridiculous gore and a side of satirical commentary – a 2020s movie fit for an old video store’s VHS horror section despite its contemporary setting.Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirRead moreNow Roth has founded a horror-focused company actually called the Horror Section, aimed at releasing movies, shows and “experiences” that appeal to the modern equivalent of those VHS-shelf gorehounds. After “presenting” a few other movies, Roth’s first direct contribution to the company is Ice Cream Man, exactly the kind of knowingly disreputable button-pusher befitting the company’s retro-sticker logo. (Indeed, Roth’s movie shares its title with a 1995 direct-to-video curiosity starring Clint Howard, though this one is unrelated.) Unfortunately, rather than a companion piece to the blackly funny murder-mystery of Thanksgiving, which riffed on Scream as much as 80s slashers, Roth’s latest feels like a demo reel for someone vastly less talented.Then again, Roth’s talent for bloody provocation has flowed and ebbed over the years, from the pointed nastiness of the Hostel movies to the snide grotesquerie of The Green Inferno. Ice Cream Man isn’t trying for the latter’s score-settling, but it retains a dim edgelord sensibility in its simple premise, bluntly executed. A mysterious, creepy-looking ice-cream man (Ari Millen) rolls into a suburban enclave, and when local kids get a taste of his cursed treats, they turn into feral, zombie-like killers. Unlike zombies, they avail themselves of whatever makeshift weapons they can find; parents, teachers and passersby are murdered by the dozen. Twelve-year-old Jared (Charlie Zeltzer), however, positioned early on as a lovable loser, is lactose-intolerant, leaving him impervious to the free ice-cream and therefore unharmed – though still in danger, as the crazed kids often force-feed those who don’t partake. Sticking with fellow non-infected kids Tommy (Shiloh O’Reilly) and Mia (Kiori Mirza Waldman), and eventually assisted by his older sister Lizzie (Sarah Abbott), Jared attempts to figure out how to stop this town-wide madness and keep it from spreading further.Early on, the winking transgression of seeing a bunch of weapon-wielding kids annihilate adults in some truly horrifying ways (and observing adults mostly too ginger to fight back occasionally summing the courage to counterattack) offers distraction from the slapdash swearing-kiddies dialogue Roth and co-writer Noah Belson lazily assign their young actors. But as inventive as some of the gore gets, the movie also never does any better than unleashing it – and when so much of that gore features bad CG blood spatter, the ugliness of the violence is eclipsed by the chintziness of the movie’s cut-rate aesthetics. The whole thing looks cheap as hell, with that sickly hyperreal digital sheen that makes so many attempts at slick indies more closely resemble a corporate training piece or amateur music video. There’s no grime or texture to anything here, rendering the gnarly kill scenes as phoney and frictionless as Roth’s half-assed-at-best characterizations.And really, those kills are all Ice Cream Man has; unlike Hostel, there aren’t any attempts made to turn the screws of suspense. The eventual backstory is a low-impact Freddy Krueger knockoff that might pass muster in an actual artifact of the 80s-slasher boom, but here feels like a rush job, the kind of thing Roth might have riffed about with his pal Tarantino in the wee hours of the morning. It’s easy to picture that conversation lasting longer than the screenplay’s eventual drafting. The whole thing is made with the swaggering confidence of someone whose friends laugh at his every joke – and the haphazard efficiency of someone who needs to get product to the marketplace for strategic Q3 growth. The Horror Section is supposed to offer edgier fare to the ravenous, enthusiastic genre fans. With this soft serve, it feels like it’s feeding them mainly contempt.Ice Cream Man is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and UK on 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Queens of the Dead review – drag performers slay on the party scene in playful zombie comedy  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Tina Romero’s queer spin on the horror genre delivers plenty of laughs and splattery fun – even if the storytelling occasionally stumbles
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Tina Romero’s queer spin on the horror genre delivers plenty of laughs and splattery fun – even if the storytelling occasionally stumbles
Content: Larger than life … Nina West in Queens of the Dead.Photograph: Shannon Madden/Independent Film Company/ShudderView image in fullscreenLarger than life … Nina West in Queens of the Dead.Photograph: Shannon Madden/Independent Film Company/ShudderMoviesReviewQueens of the Dead review – drag performers slay on the party scene in playful zombie comedyTina Romero’s queer spin on the horror genre delivers plenty of laughs and splattery fun – even if the storytelling occasionally stumblesCatherine BrayWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAzombie epidemic taking place in the LGBTQ+ warehouse party scene is the fun premise of this wobbly but often endearing comedy-horror. The film’s biggest ace is its cast, with charismatic screen presences such as Katy M O’Brian (Love Lies Bleeding) and Cheyenne Jackson (30 Rock) sparking off larger-than-life comedy types including Nina West (RuPaul’s Drag Race) and Jaquel Spivey (2024’s Mean Girls). Slay, queen, boots the house down, etc.Meanwhile, director Tina Romero has some large boots to fill: she’s the daughter ofGeorge A Romero, the man who more or less created the zombie movie as we know it. In some ways that’s unfortunate: it’s difficult to watch Queens of the Dead without thinking about the seminal 1968 classic Night of the Living Dead and its variable sequels and imitators. To its credit, QOTD realises that it would be futile to deny its House of Romero heritage; instead, the script calls attention to its venerable ancestor with that film’s most famous quote repurposed as a sassy catcall: “They’re coming to get you Barbara!” It’s a moment that works pretty well.Indeed, there are many moments scattered throughout the film – one-liners, set-pieces, character intros, dance-offs – that would work nicely in a skit in a nightclub show or on TikTok. There’s a lack of overall storytelling momentum, though: like the zombies themselves, events mostly just kind of shuffle along. The production values are a bit of a letdown, too: visually, Queens of the Dead has a cheap, bright, flat quality.Notable exceptions are the clothes and makeup department (of course) and the gore effects, which are nicely squishy, but the script doesn’t give the practical effects team anything memorably horrible to get their teeth into – hardened gorehounds may leave feeling short-changed. The target audience is probably moreDragRace with a soft spot for silly horror than horror aficionados per se, so those fans should have a good time.Queens of the Dead is on Shudder and AMC from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsLGBTQ+ rightsDragreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie review – plucky pups do their thing on Jurassic-style island  | Animation in film | The Guardian
description: Stranded on an island full of prehistoric animals, the Paw Patrol squad get stuck in in a remarkably charmless animation
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Stranded on an island full of prehistoric animals, the Paw Patrol squad get stuck in in a remarkably charmless animation
Content: Baffling … Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie.Photograph: Paramount PicturesView image in fullscreenBaffling … Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie.Photograph: Paramount PicturesAnimation in filmReviewPaw Patrol: The Dino Movie review – plucky pups do their thing on Jurassic-style islandStranded on an island full of prehistoric animals, the Paw Patrol squad get stuck in in a remarkably charmless animationCatherine BrayWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Paw Patrol pups – that’s Chase, Marshall, Skye, Rocky, Rubble and Zuma – are engaged in a rescue mission as this latest film instalment of the puppy rescue team series opens. A family on a yacht are in danger of being burned alive, and the plucky dogs are all that stands between them and a crispy fried demise. Unfortunately, it’s a little difficult to root for this family, the annoying teenaged son in particular, who is either an influencer or wannabe influencer. Obviously nobody deserves to die on the basis of their being an influencer, but building a rescue sequence around one feels a bit like if Jurassic Park were about trying to save dino-embryo-thief Dennis Nedry, instead of having him meet his demise at the hands and claws and teeth of a dilophosaurus with impeccable comic timing.Speaking of Jurassic Park, that’s more or less where the plucky pups end up after the yacht rescue: a storm blows them off course to a mysterious island that boasts a T rex and other assorted prehistoric beasties. None of what transpires as a result is particularly entertaining, and we can only urge families to vote with their wallets and hand over their hard-earned to higher quality children’s entertainment.No child will be missing out if you omit Paw Patrol from their lives. Children love to watch things over and over – those multiple repeat viewings may as well be of decent stuff. Bluey, In the Night Garden, Duggee, the Aardman films – there is so much available, it is baffling that the slop finds such a huge market. Children deserve charm and at least some degree of wit from their entertainment – and Paw Patrol: The Dino Mov ie has neither.Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie is in UK cinemas on 7 August and Australian cinemas on 10 September.Explore more on these topicsAnimation in filmFamily filmsChildren's TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I’m Every Woman: The Chaka Khan Musical review – Queen of Funk’s jukebox epic lacks the X factor | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Alexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven show
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Alexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven show
Content: Nimble staging … Alexandra Burke as Chaka Khan in I’m Every Woman.Photograph: Danny KaanView image in fullscreenNimble staging … Alexandra Burke as Chaka Khan in I’m Every Woman.Photograph: Danny KaanTheatreReviewI’m Every Woman: The Chaka Khan Musical review – Queen of Funk’s jukebox epic lacks the X factorTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, LondonAlexandra Burke is valiant in the leading role but the superstar’s story is squandered in this sprawling and uneven showAmmar KaliaWed 5 Aug 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the pantheon of soul divas,Chaka Khanis surely one of the fiercest. With a soaring, multioctave vocal range that earned accolades from Aretha Franklin and Miles Davis, as well as a chequered personal life and a stint in the Black Panthers alongside Fred Hampton, Khan’s story has long felt ripe for immortalisation in a jukebox musical.I’m Every Woman features X Factor winnerAlexandra Burkein the lead role, with a book by Khan’s own creative director, Nia T Hill. Running just shy of three hours, it is a gargantuan undertaking of two uneven parts.The opening half sprints through a remarkable girlhood and young adulthood. Khan’s father leaves the family owing to a drug problem, she joins the local Black Panther party chapter in Chicago, falls in love, decides to become a singer and witnesses Hampton’s murder – all in a matter of minutes. Celebrity impersonations pop up in case the frenetic pace isn’t enough to hold the audience’s attention – from a spirited Joni Mitchell to vapid parodies of Prince, Stevie Wonder and Miles Davis.View image in fullscreenOver too quick … Burke as Chaka Khan and Teddy Wills as Fred Hampton.Photograph: Danny KaanBurke plays Khan with an energetic youthfulness – but when it comes to vocals faces a sisyphean task. She makes a valiant effort of singalong hits like Ain’t Nobody and Tell Me Something Good, but lacks the resonance to replicate Khan’s power. Nowhere is this clearer than during the ballad Through the Fire, which employs three singers to replicate Khan’s performance and still falls short of her key-jumping agility.Director Racky Plews’ staging is nimble, making use of immersive projections, while the ensemble boasts a comic star in Ashley Stroud, as Khan’s bolshie younger sister, Taka Boom. Yet when the second half arrives and Khan finds herself the “Queen of Funk” in the 1980s, the show runs entirely out of pace and music.The Prince-penned I Feel for You is a raucous post-interval opener, but the remaining hour meanders through Khan’s 90s and 00s years, choosing to focus on her charitable foundation work and efforts to go independent, rather than her artistry. When it comes time for a harried emotional reunion with her estranged daughter in rehab, the pathos refuses to land. Instead, I’m Every Woman becomes a musical in service to somewhat sparse music, rather than a clearly astounding story.AtTroubadour Wembley Park theatre, London, until 27 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsChaka KhanAlexandra BurkereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talent | Games | The Guardian
description: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Big developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playing
Content: Grand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto VI: Vintage Vice City pack.Photograph: Rockstar GamesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesThe ​games industry’s obsession with ​visual fidelity is costing them money and talentBig developers are discovering that the technical progress of photorealism doesn’t always translate into the creative spark that gives gamers joy – and keeps them playingDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 5 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Last week, Asha Sharma, the new head of Xbox, laid outher vision for the future of the consoleand interestingly, the two titles she picked out as potential areas of growth were Minecraft and Candy Crush Saga – games that don’t exactly scream next-generation entertainment. Neither relies on hyper-realistic visuals, which is the north star that games consoles and gaming PCs have been aiming at for the past 40 years. They are, instead, well-designed, well-loved franchises that you can play and enjoy on almost any PC, console or phone.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The fact is, the quest for visual hyperrealism is breaking the games industry. It’s becoming more and more expensive to put high-end graphics hardware into machinesthanks to demand from the AI sector; at the same time, creating superrealistic visuals is an incredibly expensive and complex part of game development, leading to longer development periods. GTA VI, for example, has taken at least eight years to develop and is rumoured to have cost between $1bn and $2bn. By my back-of-an-envelope calculations, that’s around four times more than GTA V. Admittedly, the detail on everything, from the characters’ faces, to the cars, to the cityscapes, is astonishing. But will it be four times better than GTA V? Will it be four times more fun?It’s very clear from the shameful number of redundancies the industry has processed in the last two years that its model isn’t working. An increased focus on graphical fidelity leads to greater costs, which in turn leads to creative caution. Everyone is chasing a teeny number of slots in the big genres, and most of them are falling short. WasConcord– an OK entry into the grossly over-burdened hero shooter genre – really worth the $400m that Sony put into it, or would that money have been better spent on a few more games likeAstro Bot, or even a freshRatchet and Clankor two?View image in fullscreenWe don’t need no fancy graphics … Minecraft.Photograph: MojangI’m convinced that only a small minority of gamers now care about how many beautifully lit, ray-traced, frame-injected polygons a machine can fling around. I feel a wave of despondency any time a game asks me to choose between performance or fidelity modes. Sometimes I don’t even notice if I’m playing at 30 or 60 frames per second.Visual fidelity isn’t where the art happens. The art is in the style and substance of the game. Titles such asOkami,Journeyor Cuphead wouldn’t look better with more detailed graphics. I didn’t enjoyThe Last of Usmore on PS5 than I did on PS4 – or PS3, for that matter. We’re at a stage where developers have nailed the production of beautiful open worlds filled with lifelike characters. So what do we do with those worlds now? That is the question of the artist – and there are still plenty of artists left in this troubled business.Lets remind ourselves of the most important shift in visual clarity in the home video business: VHS to DVD. The latter format arrived in the late 1990s and still accounts for 50-60% of disc sales – 4K Blu-ray discs, the most visually detailed offering, come in at about 20%. This is an unfair comparison, of course, because the home video business has faced a very different range of competitors and market challenges. But the fact is, when people want to buy a film, half of those people will still buy it on a format that’s been around for almost 30 years.What have been some of the best games this year?Pokopia,Mixtape, Cairn, Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight,Mina the Hollower, Denshattack!,Mewgenics, Titanium Court … None would have been made more compelling by detailed graphics. Sure, these are mostly indie titles – they don’t have to shift hardware units, and they don’t have to showcase the prowess of first-party studios to shareholders – but it’s interesting, isn’t it, that the two games Xbox’s Sharma referenced for her road ahead had comparatively humble origins. So did Roblox, the title that Minecraft must contend with; as did Fortnite, possibly the most popular game in the world.If social media platforms have taught us anything, it’s that we live in an age that values rapidly dispersed ideas over “perfect” realisation. If digital TV platforms have taught us anything, it’s that people struggle to wait two years for a new instalment in a beloved franchise. And yet the market is saturated with high-end content; it is everywhere, and it is losing. TS Eliot once wrote: “Humankind cannot bear very much reality” – in art, in games, in real-life, we like to stop just short. That is the sweet spot. An ultra-high-end graphics chipset is not required to get us there.What to playView image in fullscreenWhat we do in life echoes in eternity … How Many Dudes?Photograph: Butterscotch ShenanigansIt’s an age-old philosophical question: how many men would it take to defeat a lion in combat? Or a gorilla? Or a duck the size of a horse? Well, thanks toHow Many Dudes?we can now answer that question. In this roguelike auto-battler, you build and command a group of differently skilled dudes – some are wizards, some are zombies, some are knights, but all must enter the arena together and fight whatever fate throws at them. The experience is a chaotic and ridiculous maesltrom of flailing limbs – there is tactical depth beneath the daft premise. The game isa cult hit on Steamand, dude, after only a few hours of play, I can totally see why.Available on:PC, AndroidEstimated playtime:Five hours plusWhat to readView image in fullscreenSupport your local games makers … A Short Hike is included part of a fundraiser for laid-off developers.Photograph: AdamgryuAnindie game bundleput together to raise money for laid-off game developers in North America hasraised more than $100,000in three days. The bundle, organised by the Communication Workers Union, isavailable on Itch.iofor $10 (though you can pay more) – it includes 127 games, including acclaimed titles such as A Short Hike and SkateBird. The offer is running until 13 August.Electronic Artshas been bought by Saudi Arabia’s wealth fundand a group of investors for $55bn (£41bn). It is the second-biggest gaming acquisition, and ends EA Games’s 36-year history as a publicly traded company.Microsoft has increasedprices forXbox consolesin Europe and the UK. At the lowest price point, the Xbox Series S 512GB model is going up from £299.99 to £429.99, while the Xbox Series X 1tb model will be rising from £499.99 to £669.99. The company has blamed higher storage and memory costs. Hoping things will improve next year? Nope.Samsung expectsthe situation to worsen through 2027.Sega has created a five-hour playlist featuring the music ofSonic composer Jun Senoue, asVGC reports. Available on Apple Music and Spotify, it contains 100 tracks and runs for just over five hours. Perfect for your next hike across the Pennines (or, indeed, any Green Hill Zone).OurSummer Games previewis in full swing, with pieces aboutClean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim, A Line Held Tight, about worker’s rights and lives, and the adorableTanuki: Pon’s Summer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ’em all after 30 yearsWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleyMy family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Dominik DiamondSingStar Take That anyone? The strange joy of charity shop video gamesHalo: Campaign Evolved – they don’t make ’em like this any more | ★★★★☆Big Walk – larking around with mates elevated to an artform | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenWhat if I’m becoming bad? … Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix game.Photograph: APHere’s a timely question fromMaddie, via email:“Whatever happened to the movie tie-in video game? As someone who first got into games by playing the Harry Potter titles on PlayStation, I miss these often derided treasures. Did they just go out of fashion?”Conveniently for me, the answer to this question is tied in with the essay above: movie games simply became too expensive and took too long to make, so the risks outweighed the potential rewards. What we tend to see now are more limited tie-ins, such as mini VR “experiences” along the lines ofStranger Things VRorProject Hail Mary: Journey Among the Stars, a forthcoming mixed-reality tie-in with the film. With the really big movie brands, meanwhile, we’re getting standalone offshoots –Indiana Jones and the Great Circle,Alien: Isolation,Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order… I think this is good, as all of those titles were very good – which is more than can be said for most tie-in games throughout history. Let’s be honest, for every GoldenEye, Lego Star Wars or Disney’s Aladdin, there were a hundred Charlie’s Angels, Top Guns and ETs. This is one example where technological progress has brought inarguable benefits.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGrand Theft AutoGrand Theft Auto VIMinecraftXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew Valley | Games | The Guardian
description: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Author: Nicole Clark
Headline: Since Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touches
Content: Charming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioView image in fullscreenCharming small-town life … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioGamesWhat is Fields of Mistria? A magical new obsession for fans of Stardew ValleySince Stardew Valley rejuvenated the farming sim genre a decade ago, games like Fields of Mistria are capitalising on its popularity with their own special touchesNicole ClarkWed 5 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarming simulator games deliver on an escapist fantasy: going off-grid from the modern work grind, in exchange for charming small-town life and a farm to call your own. While these games have had dedicated fans since the days of Harvest Moon, the most popular today,Stardew Valley, contemporised the genre with a larger range of activities and lovable townspeople to befriend and romance. Created in 2016 by independent developer Eric Barone, it has now sold more than 50m copies and become the mould for so many other indie farming sims.Fields of Mistria is one of these farming sims in a post-Stardewworld – though it updates the core formula. Created by independent developer NPC Studio, Fields of Mistria has already proven popular: it debuted in early access (a pre-release version of the game meant for early players to find bugs and give feedback) forPCplayers on Steam in August 2024, and in the first month the game racked up more than 4m player hours. It’s for a good reason: Mistria satisfies all of those same farming sim desires but with more expansive character creation and a story steeped in magic.What is Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenAlready popular in its first month of early access … Fields of Mistria.Illustration: NPC StudioFields of Mistria is a farming and life simulator game with fantasy themes. You play as the new farmer in Mistria, a lovable small town in recovery from an earthquake, whose inhabitants hope you’ll fulfil their requests for various produce and supplies. Over the four seasons you grow crops, raise barn animals and attend events: from regular Saturday markets to the annual Shooting Star festival. Choose between a cat or a dog as a pet and accumulate toys and accessories for all your animals. My personal favourite is watching a duck and a rabbit play together on a seesaw.You’ll repair structures and buildings in town, such as the bridge or the Sleeping Dragon Inn. Donate supplies and funds, raise your renown level and town rank, and restore Mistria to its former glory. Along the way you’ll make friends with the townspeople: like Ryis the carpenter, who is shockingly quick at those repairs, or Hayden, the owner of Sweetwater Farm who has a haughty prize-winning chicken called Henrietta (and yes, you can befriend her, too).You can also fish, catch bugs and explore the mines; just be careful about selling anything immediately, because you might want to hold on to it to donate to the museum, or use it to craft cute furniture for your home. Your character evolves along with you: the more you do, the more you’ll be able to level up skills such as cooking, ironmongery, and archaeology.How is Fields of Mistriadifferent fromStardewValley?Fields of Mistria may sound like aclassic farming sim– but there’s a twist: you gain magical powers, thanks to the mysterious dragon Caldarus, who you can talk to by visiting a shrine on your farm. One spell lets you create rain, so you don’t have to painstakingly water all of your crops. Another lets you fully restore stamina, so you can get back to fishing for that golden eel. It seems the earthquake may have unearthed some unexpected parts of Mistria’s history.And while Stardew Valley – despite its lauded queer relationship options – has thus far only offered two choices forgender expression, in Mistria, character gender options also include “they/them”, “she/they,” “he/they,” and more.There are also some great accessibility features. In particular, you can make a day longer by slowing down time, giving yourself a truly leisurely pace to play. It’s an antidote to how frantic Stardew Valley can feel, especially during special events when you’re trying to pack as much into a day as you can.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre there romance-friendly characters in Fields of Mistria?View image in fullscreenEagerly awaited romance arcs … Fields of Mistria.Photograph: NPC StudioMistria is full of potential suitors, and you can woo any eligible villager regardless of gender. There’s Juniper, the sorceress who owns the local bathhouse, and who wouldn’t look out of place with the cast of Sailor Moon. Or maybe you’d like to romance March, the grumpy blacksmith who is a tough nut to crack – he’s atsundere, an anime archetype for someone who’s abrasive at first – until you know him better.Early accesscappedthe number of hearts you could unlock with each villager, and players have been eagerly awaiting the extended romance arcs in the full game. Without spoiling too much, let’s just say there’s also at least once romance option who isn’texactlyhuman.This lively cast of characters and love interests is ultimately what makes Fields of Mistria a standout in its genre. The town is always alive and bustling, encouraging you to spend time there – Friday nights at the Inn, where everyone gathers, being a highlight. Some of the villagers play Dungeons and Dragons, while others try out new desserts. You can ask socialite Elsie for gossip, or even join the kids in an adventuring club. There’s a real sense of place and kinship that makes playing Fields of Mistriafeel like a lovely escape.Explore more on these topicsGamesPCSimulation gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Catch of the day: a seafood safari on France’s culinary coast | France holidays | The Guardian
description: From Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafood
Author: Mary Novakovich
Headline: From Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafood
Content: A fish stall in Le Touquet.Photograph: Michael Juno/AlamyView image in fullscreenA fish stall in Le Touquet.Photograph: Michael Juno/AlamyFrance holidaysCatch of the day: a seafood safari on France’s culinary coastFrom Calais to Le Touquet, the Côte d’Opale is home to thriving fishing ports, grand old seaside resorts and restaurants serving the freshest seafoodMary NovakovichWed 5 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStellio Lestienne, chef atLa Matelotein Boulogne’s harbour, shows me his shopping list as we browse the city’s daily morning fish market. He wants to pick up some crab and sole, which are in season, but his usual lobster fisher is still out on his boat, so he’ll have to wait a bit for that. Although I’ve been a regular visitor to both Boulogne and the surrounding Hauts-de-France region for about 30 years, this is my first time in the fish market. Now I’m kicking myself for all that lost time.It’s not very big, nor is it remotely picturesque, stretching along a nondescript car park in the port. But it does have a fantastic selection of fish and seafood, both from fishers (pêcheurs artisansin light-blue stalls) and retailers (commerçantsin dark blue). And it’s considerably cheaper than other fish markets I’ve seen. “People come here from the UK with cool bags to do their shopping,” Stellio says, pointing to a man doing that very thing. I spot filletedroussettes(dogfish) going for €2 each. At another stall, a man deftly slices through a grotesque-looking monkfish, cutting out the prized cheeks.View image in fullscreenBoulogne harbour.Photograph: Anthony Hucks/AlamyBoulogne-sur-Mer is France’s largest fishing port and all of this bounty is just a short jaunt across the Channel. This makes the idea of a seafood safari along the Côte d’Opale – whose chalky cliffs, sand dunes and forests stretch south from Calais to Le Touquet and beyond – impossible for me to resist.I start in the fishing village of Audresselles, a pleasant 45-minute pootle along the coast road fromLeShuttle’s terminal.La Marie Galante, run by cheerful and talented sisters Béatrice and Godeleine Cuvellier, has a cosy interior and razor clams on the menu. Accustomed to seeing empty razor-clam shells on my favourite Norfolk beach but not on restaurant menus (too much of a faff to collect, a local fishmonger told me), I pounce on these shellfish smothered in garlic and parsley. This is followed by a typical plate offruits de mer– oysters, whelks, giant juicy prawns and half a crab. Around me echoes the sound of people studiously pounding their crab claws open, soon joined by my own. The sound of a happy restaurant.View image in fullscreenMary Novakovich tackles crab at La Marie Galante in Audresselles.Photograph: Adam BatterbeeOne of my favourite French towns awaits a little further along the coast – Wimereux, with its wonderfully whimsical 19th-century architecture and long expanse of beach. Its art deco grande dame,Hotel l’Atlantic, has had a major makeover since I last stayed. Chef Benjamin Delpierre, co-owner with his wife Aurélie, has also since handed back the restaurant’s Michelin star, throwing off the constraints that came with it. In a relaxed yet sophisticated atmosphere, I dip prawn croquettes into a curried beetroot puree before revelling in a fillet of roast cod with an addictive celery cream and rich chicken jus. All the while, I watch mesmerised as the sun dips across the Channel.Le Touquet, with its long sandy beaches, pine forests and golf courses loved by Channel-hopping Brits, is my next stop. But first I make a detour to its neighbour across the River Canche, Étaples-sur-Mer. This is another first for me: a visit toMaréis, an exhibition centre and aquarium telling the story of French sea fishing in the North Sea and Channel. And what an utterly fascinating story it turns out to be. What is caught in the sea and how it’s caught are vividly brought to life thanks to clever immersive and interactive exhibits (in French and English). Fish swim in an aquarium above my head, while another large tank holds enormous rays gliding through the water.double quotation markAround me echoes the sound of people studiously pounding their crab claws open. The sound of a happy restaurantThat evening in Le Touquet, the shouts of England fans from the Globe Trotter pub keep me abreast of the World Cup score while, across the lane atPérard, I dine on a whole grilled sea bream. I can’t remember the last time I could fillet a fish so effortlessly, such was the perfection of the grilling and freshness of the fish. On the way back to my hotel,Novotel Thalassa Le Touquet, I’m treated to the same sunset spectacle as in Wimereux, the sands and the sea glowing in the warm light.I spend an agreeable morning wandering through Le Touquet’s sprawling market, most of whose food stalls are under soaring wooden vaulted ceilings within the semicircular covered market. Not surprisingly, the fishmongers have their own section, where they’ve set up abar àhuitresso you can sit at high tables and orderfruits de merand a glass of wine. It’s tempting, but I go for a bowl of mussels covered in oozing maroilles cheese in nearbyLa Chope. The restaurant’s soundtrack of death metal isn’t exactly conducive to a relaxing lunch, but the food just about makes up for it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWimereux seafront and sea pool.Photograph: Yann Avril/AlamyI still have an evening in Boulogne to look forward to, but first a stroll around the Old Town near the imposing basilica. My B&B is here too, theStay Well Hôtel de Fiennes, an elegant 1732 townhouse with a courtyard made for unwinding. But the prospect of dinner at La Matelote drags me out of the comfy chairs and down to the port. Delicious flavours follow: langoustine with cauliflower cream; white asparagus with smoked salmon, caviar, basil cream and hummus; hake with pea puree and thyme-roasted carrots. And it’s all crowned by a quite stupendous lemon souffle. I’m not a dessert person, but this makes me want to applaud whoever made this divine creation.I have a final stop before the end of my little seafood safari – back to Audresselles, but this time to my regular haunt,Chez Mimi. Trying to be sensible after days of indulgence, I opt for a small plate of crustaceans instead of my usual calorific “crabe mimi” (stuffed crab with fries). My husband orders it instead, making me wish I were less sensible. In the village square, everything is being set up for that weekend’s annual crab festival, now in its 50th year and an event I enjoyed years ago. I might be missing the party, but I have my own seafood celebration to savour.The trip was provided byHauts-de-France tourismandPas-de-Calais tourism.Hotel l’Atlantichas doubles from €129room only,Novotel Le Touquetfrom €128 room only andThe Stay Well Hôtel de Fiennesfrom €160 B&BExplore more on these topicsFrance holidaysFood and drinkRestaurantsDay tripsShort breaksCalais holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn unwanted anchovy tin oil into salsa verde – recipe | Fish | The Guardian
description: This powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: This powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!
Content: Tom Hunt’s anchovy oil salsa verdePhotograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s anchovy oil salsa verdePhotograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFishHow to turn unwanted anchovy tin oil into salsa verde – recipeThis powerhouse ingredient injects umami and depth of flavour into a simple green sauce. Come on, chop-chop!Tom HuntWed 5 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe oil from a tin of anchovies is a powerhouse larder ingredient that you possibly never knew existed. It’s a flavour bomb that carries all the delicious flavour compounds of the fish themselves, especially if you want to add their wonderful flavour to a dish but want to save the anchovies to serve separately or as a garnish.This salsa verde is based on Giorgio Locatelli’s in his bookMade in Italy, and it’s made with a knife rather than a blender. Chopping by hand gives it a much better texture, especially when you’re also using the stalks, which a blender can turn fibrous. The boiled egg is optional but traditional, and helps emulsify the sauce. Locatelli uses just the yolk, but I’ve used the whole egg, not least to avoid the faff of finding a use for the spare white. This sauce is incredible with lamb or mutton and very good with grilled fish.Anchovy oil salsa verdeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appNever throw fat down the sink. In fact, never throw fat awayat all– it can be repurposed to use in cooking and is a wonderful ingredient in its own right that you never even knew you had. Anchovy oil specifically adds umami and a wonderful depth of flavour to a dish without overpowering it, and works brilliantly in salsa verde. (If need be, put the drained anchovies in a sterilised jar, top with extra-virgin olive oil – which can also be reused – seal and store in the fridge for up to two weeks.This is my first time adding boiled egg to the classic sauce, and I was really impressed with the results: it made a huge difference to the texture, and helped emulsify and fortify the sauce. It’s traditional to add just the hard-boiled egg yolk, but the whole egg, including the white, worked really well and disappeared into the salsa.100g flat-leaf parsley, leaves and stalks, or a mix of whatever soft herbs you have to hand1 small garlic clove, peeledSea salt and black pepper2 tbsp capers, drained and finely chopped1 hard-boiled egg(optional)2 tbsp caper brine, or white-wine vinegarOil from a standard tin of anchovies(roughly 15-30ml)30-50ml extra virgin olive oilFinely chop the parsley, stalks and all, then cross-chop with a rocking motion until evenly and very finely chopped. Pound the garlic and a pinch of sea salt in a mortar, to make a smooth paste, then add the capers and pound again to make a rough puree. Add the chopped herbs and an optional chopped hard-boiled egg, and pound to an smooth, emulsified paste.Stir in the caper brine and the anchovy oil, then work in enough extra-virgin olive oil to create a loose, spoonable sauce. Season to taste, then serve straight away or leave to rest for an hour. Store any excess in a clean jar in the fridge for up to two days, or freeze in an ice-cube tray to use later.Explore more on these topicsFishWaste notFoodFood wasteSauces and graviesHerbs and spicesItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Angela Hartnett’s Italian summer recipes: grilled peaches, green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in tomato sauce | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Two inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine
Author: Angela Hartnett
Headline: Two inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine
Content: Angela Hartnett’s grilled peaches mozzarella and green beansPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenAngela Hartnett’s grilled peaches mozzarella and green beansPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.Italian food and drinkAngela Hartnett’s Italian summer recipes: grilled peaches, green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in tomato sauceTwo inspiring summer dishes to enjoy in the sunshine: grilled peaches with green beans and mozzarella, and gnudi in a roast tomato sauceAngela HartnettWed 5 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtCicoria, peaches, green beans and tomatoes are among our favourites ingredients right now, inspiring dishes that celebrate freshness and flavour. The restaurant is perched at the top of the Royal Opera House in London, so our dining room is flooded with sunlight throughout the day, which is just as well because these vibrant, simple dishes are best enjoyed in the sunshine.Grilled peaches, mozzarella and green beans (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minCook15 minServes4Sea salt and black pepper200g fine green beans, trimmed250g buffalo mozzarella4 ripe peaches, halved and stonedExtra-virgin olive oil1 small shallot, peeled and finely sliced1 tbsp balsamic vinegar, or good white-wine vinegar1 small handfulbasil leavesToasted almonds or hazelnuts, to serve (optional)A little grated lemon zest, to serve (optional)Bring a pan of salted water to a boil, then blanch the beans for two to three minutes, until just tender. Drain, refresh in iced water, then drain again and set aside. Meanwhile, tear the mozzarella into large pieces, and leave it to come up to room temperature.Heat a griddle pan until it’s properly hot. Rub the flesh sides of the peach halves lightly with olive oil, then grill cut side down for two to three minutes, until charred and slightly softened, but still holding their shape.Put the beans and sliced shallot in a bowl, then dress them with olive oil, the vinegar, salt and black pepper. Taste and adjust the seasoning – it should be fresh and sharp.Arrange the grilled peaches, mozzarella and dressed beans on a platter, spoon over any dressing left in the bowl, then scatter over the basil leaves, toasted nuts and a little lemon zest, if using. Finish with a final drizzle of olive oil and a little sea salt, and serve slightly warm or at room temperature.Gnudi with roast tomato sauceWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenPrep10 minChill8 hr+Cook1 hr 10 minServes4For the roast tomato sauce500g ripe plum tomatoes2garlic cloves,peeled and lightly crushedA few thyme sprigsSea salt and black pepperExtra-virgin olive oil1 small splashred-wine vinegarFor the gnudi250g good-quality ricotta, well-strained50g finely grated parmesan,plus extra for servingFresh nutmeg250g semolinaWhite pepperTo finishBasil leavesGood olive oilTo make the tomato sauce, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the tomatoes in a roasting tray with the garlic and thyme, season well and drizzle generously with good olive oil. Roast for 35-40 minutes, until the tomatoes collapse and lightly caramelise. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs, then blend or crush the tomatoes to your preferred consistency. Add a dash of vinegar to sharpen the flavour, then check the seasoning and keep warm in a bowl.Meanwhile, to make the gnudi, beat the ricotta until smooth and light, then stir in the parmesan and grate in a little nutmeg to taste. Season generously, then chill for 30 minutes.Spread half the semolina on an oven tray and the rest on a clean work surface. Roll spoonfuls of the ricotta mixture into short, roughly 1½cm-thick sausages, then cut into smallpieces and shape gently into balls. Roll the gnudi lightly in the semolina on the work surface as you work, then arrange them on the semolina-covered tray.When all the gnocchi are on the tray, cover them generously with the remaining semolina, so they’re almost buried. Cill overnight, if possible, or for at least several hours.Bring a large pan of salted water to a gentle simmer, then, working in batches, drop in the gnudi and cook for three to four minutes, until they float to the surface. Lift out carefully with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.Spoon the warm tomato sauce on to plates, arrange the gnudi on top and finish with basil leaves, more parmesan and a final drizzle of olive oil.Angela Hartnett heads upCicoria at The Royal Opera House, LondonExplore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkSummer food and drinkFoodSaladAngela HartnettVegetablesCheeserecipesShareReuse this content
